baseline_protocol:
Age: 21 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three-day history of progressively worsening right scrotal pain with gradual right hemiscrotal swelling, now uncomfortable enough to impair walking; no relief with acetaminophen. No penile discharge, dysuria, hematuria, urinary frequency, fever, or trauma.
Analysis: The tempo of the illness is the key discriminator. The pain began gradually on waking and worsened over 3 days, which argues against testicular torsion; torsion characteristically produces abrupt, severe pain over minutes to hours. Supporting this, the cremasteric reflexes are present bilaterally, the patient is afebrile (37 C) and hemodynamically normal (pulse 80, BP 110/55), and Doppler ultrasonography shows normal echogenicity of the right testis with significantly increased vascularity compared with the left plus a small reactive hydrocele. Increased rather than absent or reduced flow effectively excludes torsion and instead indicates an inflammatory hyperemic process, i.e., epididymitis with reactive hydrocele. Tenderness localizes to both the right testis and epididymis, and there is no inguinal canal tenderness or fullness to suggest incarcerated hernia. The absence of trauma and of ecchymosis argues against testicular rupture or hematoma, and he specifically denies straining during the previous evening's basketball game. Etiologically, the strongest risk factor in this case is sexual behavior: he is sexually active with four partners and does not use condoms, which in a 21-year-old man makes sexually transmitted epididymitis (the STD panel is pending) the leading consideration despite the absence of urethral discharge and a normal urinalysis with a Gram stain negative for bacteria; these negative findings do not exclude an STI, as urethritis is frequently asymptomatic. Coliform/enteric bacterial epididymitis is less likely given the normal urinalysis and the absence of obstructive urinary symptoms or instrumentation. Non-infectious differential considerations that remain open but are less well supported include torsion of a testicular or epididymal appendage, orchitis (he reports a sore throat a few days ago, though the oropharynx is now normal and there is no parotitis and immunizations are up to date, making mumps orchitis unlikely), and testicular tumor, which is a diagnosis to keep in mind in this age group but is not supported by the ultrasound, which showed normal echogenicity without a mass. Fever, systemic toxicity, and abscess formation are absent, so this is not a complicated or septic presentation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Follow-up of the already-obtained pending results is what is actually needed: urine culture and the STD panel, specifically nucleic acid amplification testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Offer HIV and syphilis serology given the unprotected sexual activity with multiple partners. No repeat imaging is required unless symptoms fail to improve or worsen, in which case repeat scrotal Doppler ultrasonography to exclude abscess or an underlying mass.
Conclusion: Acute right epididymitis with a small reactive hydrocele in a sexually active 21-year-old man, most likely of sexually transmitted etiology given four partners and non-use of condoms. Testicular torsion is excluded by the subacute onset, preserved cremasteric reflexes, and Doppler demonstration of increased rather than absent testicular vascularity. The patient is nontoxic and hemodynamically stable, so this is an urgent outpatient rather than surgical emergency problem.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Begin empiric antibiotic therapy directed at Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae without waiting for the pending STD panel, since delaying treatment risks abscess formation and infertility. Provide symptomatic care with scrotal elevation and support, ice, rest, and a scheduled NSAID for anti-inflammatory effect, since acetaminophen alone has already failed to control his pain. Advise limiting strenuous activity, including basketball, until the pain and swelling resolve. Address the sexual-health considerations explicitly: counsel on consistent condom use, notify and arrange evaluation and empiric treatment of all four recent partners, and advise abstinence from sexual activity until he and his partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Screen for HIV and syphilis and complete the full STI panel. Arrange clinical follow-up in 48 to 72 hours to confirm improvement and again after culture and STD panel results return, so therapy can be narrowed or changed if an organism is identified or if urine culture grows an enteric pathogen. Give explicit return precautions: sudden severe pain, fever, worsening swelling, or systemic symptoms warrant immediate re-evaluation. Because a testicular mass can be masked by inflammation, arrange a repeat scrotal examination after the acute inflammation settles, and repeat ultrasonography if any abnormality persists.
Notes: Urine culture and the STD panel were still pending at the time of this protocol, so the etiologic diagnosis is presumptive and empiric therapy may need revision. A normal urinalysis and a Gram stain negative for bacteria do not exclude a sexually transmitted cause. Specific antibiotic agents, doses, and durations are not specified in the case.

Vignette:
A 62-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis managed with daily naproxen for the past 3 years presents with a 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, and occasional nausea. The pain is worse on an empty stomach and partially relieved by eating. She denies vomiting, hematemesis, melena, or unintentional weight loss. She does not smoke but drinks one glass of wine nightly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. A fecal occult blood test is negative. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 62 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Four-week history of gnawing epigastric pain that is worse on an empty stomach and partially relieved by eating, accompanied by early satiety and occasional nausea, in the setting of daily naproxen use for 3 years.
Analysis: The presentation is a classic NSAID-associated peptic ulcer syndrome. The strongest supporting facts are the 3 years of continuous daily naproxen, a well-established cause of gastroduodenal mucosal injury through prostaglandin inhibition, and the character and rhythm of the pain: gnawing, epigastric, worse when the stomach is empty and partially relieved by food, a pattern most typical of duodenal ulcer. Physical findings are concordant and reassuring: mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation only, no rebound or guarding to suggest perforation, normoactive bowel sounds arguing against gastric outlet obstruction, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Evidence against active bleeding is reasonably strong: she denies hematemesis and melena, the fecal occult blood test is negative, and the hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL is essentially normal for a woman. Helicobacter pylori infection is the other major etiology of peptic ulcer disease and can coexist with NSAID injury; her status is not stated and must be determined, because eradication changes both healing and recurrence risk. Differential considerations include functional dyspepsia, which can produce identical symptoms but would not explain the strong NSAID exposure; gastroesophageal reflux disease, less likely as she describes gnawing epigastric rather than retrosternal burning pain; gastric malignancy, which must be taken seriously because she is over 60 with new-onset dyspepsia and early satiety, both recognized indications for endoscopy irrespective of alarm features, although the absence of weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting, anemia, palpable mass, and occult blood makes it less likely; biliary colic, unlikely given the constant gnawing quality, relation to fasting, and lack of right upper quadrant pain or postprandial exacerbation; and pancreatic disease, not supported by the absence of back radiation or weight loss. Cardiac ischemia presenting as epigastric discomfort is a standard consideration in a 62-year-old but is not supported here, as the pain is clearly food- and fasting-related rather than exertional. Overall this is a subacute, uncomplicated problem: there is no evidence of perforation, obstruction, or significant bleeding, so it needs timely outpatient evaluation rather than emergency intervention.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) with biopsies, indicated by new-onset dyspepsia with early satiety at age 62, both to confirm and characterize ulceration and to exclude gastric malignancy. Helicobacter pylori testing, either by urea breath test or stool antigen (off acid suppression and antibiotics) or by gastric biopsy at the time of endoscopy. Complete blood count for follow-up of the hemoglobin. Basic laboratory assessment including renal function is appropriate before decisions about continuing or replacing chronic NSAID therapy.
Conclusion: A 62-year-old woman with chronic daily naproxen use and a 4-week history of fasting-relieved-by-food epigastric pain with early satiety, most consistent with NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease, probably duodenal. There is currently no evidence of a complication: no bleeding (negative fecal occult blood, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, no hematemesis or melena), no perforation (benign abdomen), and no obstruction. Her age and early satiety nevertheless mandate endoscopic evaluation to exclude gastric malignancy, and H. pylori status must be established.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Stop the naproxen. Discontinuing the offending NSAID is the single most important intervention and should not be deferred pending endoscopy. Substitute acetaminophen for her osteoarthritis pain, and add non-pharmacologic measures such as physical therapy, weight management if applicable, and topical therapy; if an NSAID ultimately proves unavoidable for her osteoarthritis, it should be resumed only at the lowest effective dose with continuous proton pump inhibitor co-therapy. Start a proton pump inhibitor at standard once-daily dosing for ulcer healing. Test for Helicobacter pylori and, if positive, treat with an appropriate eradication regimen followed by confirmation of cure with a urea breath test or stool antigen test at least 4 weeks after completing therapy. Refer for upper endoscopy on a routine outpatient basis given her age of 62 and early satiety, with biopsy of any gastric ulcer and follow-up endoscopy to document healing of a gastric ulcer. Regarding the additional considerations: advise reducing or eliminating the nightly glass of wine while the ulcer heals, since alcohol is a mucosal irritant, and reinforce that she does not smoke, which is favorable. Counsel her to avoid aspirin and other over-the-counter NSAIDs, which are often taken without being recognized as such. Recheck the hemoglobin after several weeks, since a single negative occult blood test does not exclude intermittent bleeding. Give explicit red-flag instructions to seek emergency care immediately for hematemesis, black tarry or bloody stools, severe or sudden worsening abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lightheadedness, or syncope. Arrange follow-up in 4 to 8 weeks to confirm symptom resolution.
Notes: Helicobacter pylori status is not specified in the case and must be determined, as it materially changes management. A negative fecal occult blood test and a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL do not exclude intermittent or low-grade ulcer bleeding. Endoscopy is indicated on the basis of her age and early satiety even though classic alarm features such as weight loss, dysphagia, and overt bleeding are absent.

Vignette: A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 34 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute left ankle injury sustained earlier today after an inversion twist stepping off a curb, with an audible crack, inability to bear weight, and lateral ankle swelling and ecchymosis.
Analysis: The mechanism, examination, and imaging are internally consistent and the diagnosis is established rather than presumptive. An inversion injury with an audible crack, inability to bear weight, and point bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the distal fibula and lateral malleolus fulfils the classic clinical criteria that mandate ankle radiography, and radiographs confirmed a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula classified as Weber B, that is, at the level of the syndesmosis. The two facts that dominate management are that the fracture is non-displaced and that there is no talar shift. Absence of talar shift and a nontender medial malleolus argue against a competent deltoid ligament injury and therefore against an unstable bimalleolar-equivalent pattern; a Weber B fracture with an intact medial side and a congruent mortise is generally a stable injury amenable to non-operative treatment, whereas medial tenderness, medial clear-space widening, or talar shift would indicate instability and a likely surgical indication. The neurovascular examination is intact with brisk capillary refill and preserved sensation, so there is no evidence of vascular compromise, nerve injury, or impending compartment syndrome, and the fracture is closed with no mention of skin compromise, tenting, or open wound, removing the usual reasons for emergent operative intervention. The anterior drawer test could not be assessed because of pain and guarding, so an associated lateral ligamentous injury cannot be excluded on this examination, but that does not alter immediate management. Differential and associated-injury considerations that remain relevant include syndesmotic (high ankle) injury, which can accompany a Weber B pattern; an occult proximal fibular Maisonneuve fracture, which is classically associated with a medial-sided injury and would be suggested by proximal fibular tenderness, although the medial malleolus is nontender here; occult talar dome osteochondral injury; and base-of-fifth-metatarsal or midfoot injury, which the described examination does not specifically address. A purely ligamentous lateral ankle sprain is effectively excluded by the radiographic fracture.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Palpation of the entire length of the fibula including the proximal shaft and knee to exclude a Maisonneuve fracture, with full-length tibia-fibula radiographs if proximal tenderness is found. Weight-bearing or gravity-stress ankle radiographs to confirm mortise stability and exclude latent talar shift once acute pain allows. Repeat ankle radiographs at approximately 1 to 2 weeks after immobilization to confirm that the fracture has not displaced. Advanced imaging such as CT or MRI is not required at present and should be reserved for suspected syndesmotic disruption, articular involvement, or persistent unexplained pain.
Conclusion: Closed, non-displaced Weber B distal fibular fracture of the left ankle from an inversion mechanism, with a congruent mortise (no talar shift), a nontender medial malleolus, and an intact neurovascular examination. This is a stable-appearing isolated lateral malleolar fracture appropriate for non-operative immobilization, protected weight-bearing, and orthopedic follow-up, with confirmation of stability on subsequent imaging.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Immobilize the ankle immediately in a well-padded posterior short-leg splint or a controlled ankle motion walking boot with the ankle in neutral dorsiflexion. Make the patient non-weight-bearing or protected weight-bearing with crutches according to pain, since he currently cannot bear weight. Apply rest, ice, compression, and elevation above heart level to control the significant swelling and ecchymosis, and provide analgesia. Refer to orthopedics for follow-up within approximately one week. Address the additional considerations explicitly. First, stability must be confirmed: because the anterior drawer test could not be performed and stress views were not obtained, arrange weight-bearing or stress radiographs and a repeat radiograph at 1 to 2 weeks; any medial clear-space widening or talar shift converts this into an unstable fracture requiring surgical fixation. Second, examine the proximal fibula and knee to exclude a Maisonneuve injury and image the full fibula if tenderness is present. Third, document and monitor the intact neurovascular status, and give explicit instructions to return immediately for increasing pain out of proportion, numbness, tingling, pallor, coldness, or a splint that becomes too tight, which could indicate compartment syndrome or neurovascular compromise. Fourth, advise elevation and swelling control before any definitive casting, as significant swelling makes early rigid casting hazardous. Expect roughly 6 weeks of immobilization with progression to weight-bearing as clinically and radiographically indicated, followed by ankle range-of-motion, strengthening, and proprioceptive rehabilitation to reduce the risk of chronic instability, particularly since an occult lateral ligament injury remains possible. Provide venous thromboembolism risk counseling given lower-limb immobilization and reduced weight-bearing.
Notes: Anterior drawer testing was not interpretable because of pain and guarding, so an associated lateral ligamentous injury cannot be excluded and should be reassessed once acute symptoms settle. Stability of this Weber B fracture is inferred from the absence of talar shift and a nontender medial malleolus on the initial films and requires confirmation on weight-bearing or stress imaging; demonstration of instability would change management to operative fixation.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man presents with difficulty falling and staying asleep over the past 5 nights. He recently took on a major project at work with a tight deadline and reports feeling anxious about it. He estimates sleeping only 4 to 5 hours per night and experiencing daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating. He denies depressed mood, loss of interest in activities, or suicidal ideation. baseline_protocol:
Age: 40 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five nights of difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep, sleeping only 4 to 5 hours per night, with daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating, occurring in the context of a new high-pressure work project with a tight deadline.
Analysis: This is short-term (acute, adjustment) insomnia with a clearly identifiable precipitant. The strongest supporting facts are the very short duration of 5 nights, the direct temporal link to a newly assumed major work project with a tight deadline, and the patient's own report of anxiety about that project. The disturbance affects both sleep initiation and maintenance and produces meaningful daytime consequences (fatigue, impaired concentration), which satisfies the requirement that insomnia cause daytime impairment rather than being simply short sleep. Duration is decisive for classification: chronic insomnia disorder requires symptoms of roughly 3 months, so at 5 nights this is by definition a short-term problem, which carries a good prognosis and generally resolves as the stressor resolves. A modifiable behavioral contributor is explicitly documented: he consumes coffee until mid-afternoon, and caffeine has a long enough half-life that mid-afternoon intake can impair sleep onset and continuity that night. Differential considerations are systematically addressed by the case. Major depressive disorder is unlikely because he explicitly denies depressed mood, anhedonia, and suicidal ideation. A primary anxiety disorder such as generalized anxiety disorder is a consideration since he reports feeling anxious, but the anxiety is situation-specific and tied to a single identifiable stressor rather than being pervasive, excessive, and long-standing. A primary sleep disorder is unlikely: he has no history of sleep disorders, and the case describes no snoring, witnessed apneas, restless legs symptoms, or circadian misalignment. Medical and substance causes are not supported: vital signs are normal, and the neurological and mental status examinations are unremarkable, which argues against thyrotoxicosis, a neurological process, or an underlying psychiatric disorder requiring separate treatment. Substance use other than caffeine is not specified. Importantly, there is no safety concern: he denies suicidal ideation and there is no evidence of psychosis, agitation, or functional collapse, so this is not an emergency; equally, the presence of genuine daytime impairment and a treatable behavioral contributor makes clinician-guided management appropriate rather than leaving it entirely to self-care.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Short-term (adjustment) insomnia in a 40-year-old man, precipitated by acute occupational stress and situational anxiety about a deadline, aggravated by mid-afternoon caffeine consumption, with resulting daytime fatigue and impaired concentration. There is no evidence of major depression, suicidality, a primary sleep disorder, or an underlying medical or neurological cause. The condition is expected to be self-limited once the stressor abates and is best managed with behavioral and sleep-hygiene measures rather than diagnostic testing.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Institute behavioral measures as first-line therapy, using the principles of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia: keep a fixed wake time every day regardless of how the night went, avoid staying in bed awake by getting up if unable to sleep within about 20 minutes and returning only when sleepy, avoid daytime napping which would reduce sleep drive, reserve the bed for sleep, and use a wind-down period without work or screens before bed. Address the stressor itself with practical stress management, including scheduled worry time earlier in the evening, writing down next-day task lists to offload rumination, and relaxation or breathing techniques at bedtime. Discuss workload and deadline management, since the insomnia will most reliably resolve when the precipitating stressor resolves. Regarding the additional considerations, warn against the common maladaptive coping strategies of using alcohol as a sleep aid or increasing caffeine to counter daytime fatigue, both of which worsen the cycle. Counsel on safety during the period of sleep deprivation, particularly caution with driving and other tasks requiring vigilance given his documented difficulty concentrating. Pharmacologic hypnotics are not first-line here and should be considered only briefly and at the lowest effective dose if behavioral measures fail and impairment is significant, with clear discussion of the risk of dependence and rebound. Complaint: Five-day history of a spreading rash around the mouth and nose that began as a small red spot near the left nostril and progressed to multiple crusted lesions, with similar sores among children at her daycare.

The infection is confined to the epidermis: there is no warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement, which argues against cellulitis, abscess, or a deeper soft-tissue infection. Age: 47 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Eight-week history of a persistent nonproductive cough occurring day and night and independent of activity, triggered by neighboring cigarette smoke, with new exertional wheezing and right parasternal chest pain provoked by stretching, coughing, and deep breathing.
Analysis: The cough has lasted 8 weeks, which places it in the chronic category and requires an explanation beyond a resolving post-infectious process. The pulmonary function testing is the decisive evidence: FEV1 is 60% of predicted with a normal FVC, indicating an obstructive rather than restrictive pattern, and after inhaled albuterol the FEV1 rises from 60% to 80% of predicted, a 20-percentage-point improvement, with PEF improving from 65% to 75%. This degree of bronchodilator responsiveness demonstrates reversible airflow obstruction and establishes reactive airway disease, and given that cough is the dominant symptom, cough-variant asthma is the best-supported diagnosis. Clinical findings corroborate this: bilateral wheezing on forced expiration, new exertional wheezing she has never had before, and a clear environmental trigger, namely a new downstairs neighbor who smokes outside her window at exactly the time the cough began, providing secondhand smoke as an ongoing airway irritant. She is a lifelong nonsmoker with no known pulmonary disease, so this is new-onset disease rather than an exacerbation of established illness. The main competing causes of chronic cough must be considered. Upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal drip) is possible since she feels congested at night, but the examination shows no nasal polyps, clear oropharynx, and no postnasal drip. Gastroesophageal reflux is a classic cause of chronic cough but she denies recent heartburn and has had no recent episodes. ACE-inhibitor-induced cough is an important consideration in a hypertensive patient, but her antihypertensives are losartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker, and verapamil, neither of which causes cough, so this is excluded by the medication list. Malignancy is a consideration in a 47-year-old with chronic cough and weight loss, but the 5- to 7-lb weight loss is explicitly intentional and achieved through activity tracking, she is a lifelong nonsmoker with no family history of lung cancer, and there is no hemoptysis, lymphadenopathy, or focal finding, making this unlikely though not formally excluded. Infection is unlikely: she is afebrile at 36.8 C, has no malaise, no sick contacts, no travel outside the East Coast for 20 years, and clear lungs without crackles. The right parasternal chest pain is separately and satisfactorily explained: it is sharp, lasts only a second or two, is reproduced by stretching, coughing, and deep breathing, never occurs with exertion, and there is direct tenderness on palpation at the junction of the sternum and the right third and fourth ribs. This reproducible point tenderness with a musculoskeletal, positional character is costochondritis, plausibly aggravated by 8 weeks of repetitive coughing, and the absence of exertional chest pain, normal cardiac examination, and normal jugular venous pressure argue against cardiac ischemia. Pulmonary embolism is not supported: she is not hypoxic at 95% on room air, is not tachycardic at 79 beats/min, is not dyspneic at rest, has no leg swelling or tenderness, and no immobilization. She is clinically stable and in no respiratory distress, so this is an outpatient problem despite the significantly reduced FEV1.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None additionally required to establish the working diagnosis, since spirometry with bronchodilator response has already been obtained and is diagnostic. Repeat spirometry after a treatment trial to document response and confirm the diagnosis. Peak flow meter for home monitoring. A chest radiograph is a reasonable adjunct to exclude an alternative structural or parenchymal cause of an 8-week cough if not already performed. Consider allergy evaluation only if symptoms persist despite adequate therapy and trigger avoidance.
Conclusion: New-onset cough-variant asthma (reactive airway disease) in a 47-year-old lifelong nonsmoker, confirmed by obstructive spirometry with marked bronchodilator reversibility (FEV1 60% to 80% of predicted), clinically manifest as an 8-week nonproductive cough with new exertional wheezing and driven by ongoing secondhand tobacco smoke exposure from a neighbor. A concurrent, independent musculoskeletal chest wall syndrome (costochondritis) explains the right parasternal pain, which is reproducible on palpation and by movement and respiration and is not cardiac in origin. She is stable, normoxic, and in no distress, and both problems can be managed in the outpatient setting.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Start inhaled controller therapy with an inhaled corticosteroid as the mainstay for cough-variant asthma, together with an inhaled short-acting bronchodilator for as-needed relief, since she has already demonstrated a substantial bronchodilator response. Verify and demonstrate correct inhaler technique. Address the trigger explicitly, as this is the most important environmental intervention: secondhand smoke from the downstairs neighbor smoking outside her window is documented to provoke her cough, so counsel on avoidance measures including keeping that window closed, using air filtration, and raising the issue with building management to relocate smoking away from her window; ongoing exposure will limit the response to any pharmacotherapy. Manage the costochondritis conservatively with reassurance, local heat, and analgesia, noting that effective asthma treatment reducing cough frequency should itself relieve the chest wall pain; explain clearly that this pain is chest-wall in origin and not cardiac, which addresses the natural concern raised by chest pain. Reassess with repeat spirometry after several weeks of therapy to confirm improvement in FEV1 and to validate the diagnosis, and provide a peak flow meter with an action plan since her baseline PEF was 65% of predicted. Regarding the additional considerations: review her extensive medication list, noting that neither losartan nor verapamil causes cough, so no antihypertensive change is required on that basis; her nighttime congestion should be reassessed and treated if upper airway cough syndrome contributes, since it may coexist with asthma; and although she denies recent heartburn, silent reflux should be reconsidered if the cough fails to respond adequately. Given her thyroidectomy and levothyroxine dependence, ensure thyroid status is adequately replaced, as this affects general symptom assessment. Advise annual influenza vaccination and appropriate pneumococcal vaccination for a patient with newly diagnosed airway disease. Provide return precautions for worsening dyspnea, dyspnea at rest, hemoptysis, fever, or falling peak flow. If the cough does not resolve with adequate inhaled corticosteroid therapy and removal of smoke exposure, broaden the evaluation, including chest imaging, before accepting the diagnosis.
Notes: The pulmonary function findings are reported as consistent with reactive airway disease, possibly cough-variant asthma; confirmation depends on documented symptomatic and spirometric response to therapy. Her FEV1 of 60% of predicted indicates moderate airflow obstruction despite her well appearance and normal oxygen saturation. Malignancy has not been formally excluded by imaging, though her lifelong nonsmoking status, intentional weight loss, and absence of hemoptysis make it unlikely.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 8 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two weeks of progressively worsening intense itching that is particularly severe at night and disrupts sleep, with a similar itching illness in her younger brother and father.
Analysis: The diagnosis is confirmed rather than presumptive. Microscopic examination of a mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping revealed mites, eggs, and fecal pellets, which is the definitive diagnostic finding for scabies caused by Sarcoptes scabiei. Every other element of the case aligns with this. The distribution is classic: interdigital web spaces of both hands, flexor surfaces of the wrists, axillary folds, and periumbilical area, all sites of predilection where the stratum corneum is thin. Short linear burrows 5 to 10 mm long in the finger web spaces are the pathognomonic primary lesion, representing the tunnel excavated by the female mite. The symptom pattern is characteristic: intense pruritus that is worse at night, which reflects both circadian mite activity and the delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens, and this nocturnal itch is disrupting her sleep. The 2-week worsening course fits the incubation of a primary infestation. The epidemiology is decisive: her younger brother and father have recently developed similar itching, consistent with the prolonged skin-to-skin household transmission by which scabies spreads. Sparing of the face and scalp is typical of classic scabies in an 8-year-old and older children and adults, in contrast to infants, in whom head, palm, and sole involvement is common. The excoriations and erythematous papules are secondary changes from scratching and from the hypersensitivity response. Differential considerations are readily excluded. An important teaching point in this case is the D-dimer of 395 ng/mL, which is within the normal range yet the CT is unequivocally positive. This illustrates that D-dimer is a rule-out test valid only in patients with low or intermediate pretest probability, and that a negative D-dimer cannot exclude pulmonary embolism when clinical suspicion is high; had the clinician stopped at the D-dimer, the diagnosis would have been missed. Risk factors and likely source are identifiable. She reports intermittent left leg swelling and discomfort over the past year, most recently about 10 days ago, which is consistent with intermittent deep venous thrombosis as the embolic source even though the lower extremities are currently free of swelling, erythema, or tenderness, a common finding once clot has embolized. She has no history of blood clots or a known clotting disorder and no injury or recent immobilization. Two further considerations bear directly on management. First, she has menorrhagia due to uterine fibroids with secondary iron-deficiency anemia, and her hemoglobin is 9.7 g/dL with minimal spotting after recent menses and a uterus palpable just below the umbilicus; this is a significant bleeding risk that must be weighed against anticoagulation and may itself require gynecologic intervention. Second, her mother was recently diagnosed with stage IV colon carcinoma, and occult malignancy is a well-recognized cause of unprovoked venous thromboembolism, making age-appropriate cancer screening relevant. The white blood cell count of 10,600/mcL and platelets of 330,000/mcL are unremarkable.

Serial troponin and BNP as risk-stratification markers. Lower extremity venous duplex ultrasonography to identify residual deep venous thrombosis given the year-long history of intermittent left leg swelling. Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry. Review of the ECG already obtained. Baseline coagulation studies, complete blood count, and renal and hepatic function before and during anticoagulation. Gynecologic evaluation with pelvic imaging of the known uterine fibroids given menorrhagia, anemia, and the need for anticoagulation. Age-appropriate malignancy screening, including colorectal cancer screening, in view of the unprovoked event and the recent maternal diagnosis of stage IV colon carcinoma.

Anticoagulation is urgently indicated and is complicated by a competing significant bleeding risk from fibroid-related menorrhagia with a hemoglobin of 9.7 g/dL. Notably, the D-dimer of 395 ng/mL was normal despite a confirmed embolism, underscoring that a normal D-dimer does not exclude pulmonary embolism when pretest probability is high.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Initiate therapeutic anticoagulation without delay, as this is the definitive treatment for acute pulmonary embolism, after an explicit assessment and documentation of bleeding risk in light of her menorrhagia and hemoglobin of 9.7 g/dL. Admit for continuous cardiac and oxygen saturation monitoring and serial reassessment for hemodynamic deterioration. Risk-stratify promptly with echocardiography and serial troponin: the mildly elevated troponin of 0.05 ng/mL and heart rate of 107 raise the possibility of submassive (intermediate-risk) pulmonary embolism, in which right ventricular dysfunction would warrant closer monitoring and consideration of escalation. Thrombolysis is not indicated at present because she is normotensive and normoxic, but the team should be prepared to escalate if hypotension, worsening hypoxemia, or right ventricular failure develops. Provide supplemental oxygen if saturation falls, and give analgesia; note that naproxen should be discontinued once anticoagulation begins because NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and it has provided no relief. Address the additional considerations explicitly. First, the bleeding and anemia problem: obtain urgent gynecologic consultation, since anticoagulation will likely worsen fibroid-related menorrhagia in a woman who already has iron-deficiency anemia; plan definitive management of the fibroids and menorrhagia, monitor hemoglobin closely, and provide iron repletion. Second, source and recurrence: obtain lower extremity venous duplex ultrasonography, since a year of intermittent left leg swelling suggests recurrent deep venous thrombosis, and plan a minimum of three months of anticoagulation with subsequent reassessment for extended therapy, since this event appears unprovoked and unprovoked events carry a high recurrence risk. Third, malignancy: perform age-appropriate cancer screening including colorectal screening, given that unprovoked venous thromboembolism can be the presenting manifestation of occult malignancy and her mother has stage IV colon carcinoma. Fourth, consider evaluation for an inherited or acquired thrombophilia, including antiphospholipid syndrome, given an apparently unprovoked event without immobilization or injury, recognizing that testing is best interpreted outside the acute period and off certain anticoagulants. Provide counselling on avoidance of estrogen-containing therapies, on prolonged travel and immobility precautions, and on the warning signs of recurrence and of bleeding. Arrange structured outpatient follow-up for anticoagulation management, hemoglobin monitoring, and reassessment of duration of therapy.

The ECG was obtained but its findings are not described in the case, so it must be reviewed before final risk assessment. The choice of anticoagulant, dose, and duration is not specified in the case and requires individualized selection given her anemia and menorrhagia. Right ventricular function has not yet been assessed, so classification as low-risk versus intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism remains provisional.

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Complaint: Two days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake, progressing to obtundation and inability to recognize his wife, in a man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and a recently treated urinary tract infection.
Analysis: This is septic shock arising from an obstructive urinary source, and it is a time-critical emergency. The critical mechanical insight is that this is obstructive uropathy: 800 mL of retained urine behind an obstructed outlet constitutes an undrained infected collection, and source control by bladder decompression is as important as antibiotics, because sepsis from an obstructed urinary tract will not resolve on antibiotics alone. Multi-organ dysfunction is documented across systems: neurologic (obtundation, confusion, failure to recognize his wife), cardiovascular (hypotension, heart rate 122, warm flushed skin reflecting the vasodilated distributive physiology of early septic shock), respiratory (respiratory rate 26, SpO2 93% on room air), renal (creatinine 3.2 mg/dL against a baseline of 1.2, a nearly threefold rise indicating acute kidney injury which may be both septic and post-obstructive in origin), and hematologic (platelets 82,000/mcL, a thrombocytopenia that raises concern for consumptive coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation). The inflammatory response is marked: WBC 24,800/mcL with 22% bands, a pronounced left shift indicating severe bacterial infection, and procalcitonin of 48 ng/mL, strongly supporting bacterial sepsis rather than a non-infectious mimic. Temperature is 39.4 C. Differential considerations are effectively subordinate. Delirium from other causes is excluded as a primary explanation because the fever, leukocytosis with bandemia, elevated procalcitonin, purulent urine, and shock all point to infection. Non-infectious causes of shock are unlikely: cardiogenic shock would typically present with cool, clammy skin rather than the warm flushed skin described, and hypovolemic shock alone would not explain the fever and inflammatory markers, although decreased oral intake over 2 days certainly contributes a hypovolemic component. Recent antibiotic exposure raises the practical concern of a resistant organism, which is directly relevant to empiric therapy choice. Complications that must be actively sought include emphysematous pyelonephritis, perinephric or prostatic abscess, and obstruction above the bladder, any of which would require additional drainage or intervention.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serial lactate measurement to assess response to resuscitation, since the initial value is 5.8 mmol/L. Hemodynamic monitoring with continuous blood pressure, ideally arterial line, cardiac monitoring, and continuous pulse oximetry, in an intensive care setting. Strict urine output monitoring via the newly placed Foley catheter. Repeat complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and coagulation studies including PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, and D-dimer to evaluate the thrombocytopenia for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Arterial blood gas to assess oxygenation and acid-base status. Imaging of the urinary tract, renal and bladder ultrasonography or CT of the abdomen and pelvis, to exclude upper tract obstruction, hydronephrosis, renal or perinephric abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis, and prostatic abscess. Echocardiography or bedside ultrasound to assess volume status and cardiac function to guide fluid and vasopressor therapy. Blood and urine cultures have already been obtained and require follow-up with susceptibility testing; review the organism and susceptibilities from the recent urinary tract infection if available.

Antibiotics and fluid resuscitation have been started and cultures obtained; source control has been partially achieved by Foley catheterization draining 800 mL of infected urine. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intensive care with vasopressor support and continued source control.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue and escalate resuscitation immediately. Complete adequate intravenous crystalloid fluid resuscitation guided by dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness, and if the mean arterial pressure remains below 65 despite fluid, start vasopressor therapy without delay to restore perfusion pressure. Admit to the intensive care unit for continuous hemodynamic monitoring. Maintain the broad-spectrum antibiotics already initiated, ensuring the regimen covers likely resistant Gram-negative organisms given the recent failed course of oral antibiotics, and de-escalate once blood and urine culture susceptibilities return. Emphasize source control as the decisive intervention alongside antibiotics: the Foley catheter must remain in place and patent to keep the obstructed bladder decompressed, and imaging must promptly exclude an obstruction or abscess above the bladder that would require percutaneous nephrostomy or drainage. Obtain urgent urology consultation for management of the bladder outlet obstruction and for any drainable collection. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Monitor closely for post-obstructive diuresis after draining 800 mL of retained urine, which can cause large fluid and electrolyte losses and worsen hypotension, and replace losses accordingly. Manage the acute kidney injury by maintaining perfusion pressure, avoiding nephrotoxic agents, adjusting all drug doses for renal function, and preparing for renal replacement therapy if oliguria, refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, or volume overload develop. Evaluate the thrombocytopenia with coagulation studies for disseminated intravascular coagulation and monitor for bleeding. Support oxygenation with supplemental oxygen for the SpO2 of 93% and the respiratory rate of 26, and anticipate the possible need for mechanical ventilation, which is also a consideration for airway protection given that he is obtunded. Reassess perfusion frequently with serial lactate and urine output. Give stress ulcer and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis as appropriate to the bleeding risk. Involve the family in early discussion of goals of care given the high mortality of septic shock at this severity in a 72-year-old. After recovery, arrange urologic follow-up to definitively address the benign prostatic hyperplasia and prevent recurrent obstruction and urosepsis.
Notes: Mortality is high at this severity of septic shock with SOFA 11, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, and multi-organ dysfunction. Antibiotic selection must account for possible resistance following the recent failed oral course, and all doses require adjustment for the acute kidney injury. Upper urinary tract obstruction and abscess have not yet been excluded by imaging and could mandate additional drainage procedures. Post-obstructive diuresis is anticipated after bladder decompression and may destabilize fluid and electrolyte balance.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 38 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset 90 minutes ago, while at work, of severe vertigo, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing, with dysarthria on arrival by ambulance.
Analysis: The neurological examination localizes the lesion precisely and the imaging confirms the mechanism. The constellation of left-sided Horner syndrome, ipsilateral (left) loss of pain and temperature sensation on the face with contralateral (right) loss of pain and temperature on the body, right-sided limb ataxia, absent left gag reflex, dysphagia, dysarthria, and vertigo is the classic lateral medullary syndrome. The crossed sensory pattern is the single most informative finding, since it can only arise from a brainstem lesion affecting the descending spinal trigeminal tract, which carries ipsilateral facial sensation, together with the ascending spinothalamic tract, which carries contralateral body sensation; no single hemispheric lesion can produce this. 1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a

cough with occasional production of white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies

respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.

Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of mild heart failure comes to the office because of a
1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a
flight of stairs without stopping. Now he must stop every few steps to rest because of dyspnea
but not chest discomfort. He also complains of lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea,
cough with occasional production of white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies
chest pain or discomfort, palpitations, syncope or near syncope. He has had no fever or upper
respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for
similar symptoms; both times he had an ECG and chest x-ray and was told he had "mild heart
failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient feels generally fatigued. No fever, night sweats, or chills.

Skin: No rash, bruising, or other skin lesions.

HEENT: Sensation of fullness in the mouth. No vision changes, sore throat, or nasal congestion.

Pulmonary: See HPI

Cardiovascular: See HPI

Gastrointestinal: Mild decrease in appetite. No abdominal pain or change in bowel habits. No
diarrhea. No dysphagia or odynophagia.

Genitourinary: Erectile dysfunction; no increased urinary frequency or urgency.

Musculoskeletal: Bilateral painless swelling of both lower extremities below the knee for several
weeks.

Neurologic: Occasional dizziness upon standing and an episode of syncope a few months ago.
No focal weakness, numbness, or tingling in his extremities.

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Coronary artery disease diagnosed 18 years ago as "small heart attack" that
was treated with percutaneous coronary angioplasty (PTCA). Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and
mitral regurgitation diagnosed 1 year ago, dyslipidemia, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and
monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).

Surgical history: PTCA of the right coronary artery 18 years ago.

Medications: Aspirin 81 mg once a day, atorvastatin 40 mg once a day, warfarin 5 mg once a
day, furosemide 40 mg once a day, nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingually as needed.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Father had hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Mother died of breast
cancer. No family history of premature coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death.

Social history: Patient is retired and lives with his wife. He has been able to do routine activities
of daily living and has not had recent prolonged immobilization. He does not exercise, and he
tries to follow a low-sodium diet. He consumes 1 to 2 alcoholic drinks per week. He denies illicit
drug or tobacco use. No recent travel outside the United States and no known sick exposures.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Thin male who appears fatigued and older than stated age; in no apparent
respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.8° C
Pulse: 77 beats/min, regular
BP: 92/64 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
Pulse oximetry: 96% on room air

Skin: Cool, dry, soft. No rashes, cyanosis, petechiae, or lesions.

HEENT: Sclera anicteric. Mild macroglossia without surface discoloration or masses.

Neck: Normal carotid upstrokes. Jugular venous distention 12 cm above sternal notch at 45°.

Pulmonary: Dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the base bilaterally.
Bibasilar crackles and faint end-expiratory wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. S1 soft, S2 normal, S3 at the apex. 2/6 holosystolic
murmur heard best at apex. PMI not displaced.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nondistended, nontender, bowel sounds in all quadrants; liver nontender,
span 15 cm.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: 2+ pitting lower extremity edema to the thighs bilaterally with no erythema,
venous distention, warmth, or tenderness. Full range of motion.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and show the following results:
Test (units)
Result
Serum brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level
1420 pg/mL
Serum troponin level
0.03 ng/mL

Chest x-ray: Perihilar opacities and small bilateral pleural effusions, no pericardial calcifications.

Transthoracic echocardiography: Normal left ventricular size and function with estimated LVEF
of 55%. Severe concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Normal right ventricular size and
function. Restrictive LV diastolic pattern with E/A>2, septal e’ of 7 cm/sec and lateral e’ of 9
cm/sec. Biatrial enlargement. Mild mitral regurgitation. Inspiratory decrease of 5% in mitral
diastolic flow velocity. No pericardial thickening.

ECG is also obtained and is shown below. This tracing is unchanged from prior ECG obtained 4
months ago.

Results of appropriate testing return and are shown:
Test (units)

CBC with differential
Normal

Fat pad biopsy: Amorphous extracellular pink deposits with hematoxylin and eosin stain and

baseline_protocol:
Age: 68 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: One-week history of worsening dyspnea on exertion (now must stop every few steps), bilateral lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea, cough with white phlegm, wheezing, and 3-kg weight gain, on a background of "mild heart failure" diagnosed recently and treated with escalating furosemide doses. Additional complaints include fatigue, sensation of fullness in the mouth, decreased appetite, erectile dysfunction, occasional dizziness on standing, and one syncopal episode a few months ago.

Analysis: The patient presents with a clearly decompensated heart failure syndrome: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, weight gain, jugular venous distention 12 cm at 45 degrees, S3, bibasilar crackles, dullness and decreased breath sounds at both bases, 2+ pitting edema to the thighs, hepatomegaly with a 15-cm span, BNP 1420 pg/mL, and a chest x-ray with perihilar opacities and small bilateral pleural effusions. Troponin is only minimally elevated at 0.03 ng/mL and there is no chest pain, so an acute coronary syndrome is not the driver of this decompensation despite the remote history of coronary artery disease treated with PTCA.

The key finding is that the echocardiogram shows a normal-sized left ventricle with preserved systolic function (LVEF 55%) yet severe concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, a restrictive diastolic filling pattern (E/A > 2) with strikingly reduced tissue Doppler velocities (septal e' 7 cm/sec, lateral e' 9 cm/sec) and biatrial enlargement. This combination of marked wall thickening with low myocardial tissue velocities and preserved ejection fraction is the signature of an infiltrative cardiomyopathy rather than hypertensive or hypertrophic disease; notably, the patient is not hypertensive but rather hypotensive (BP 92/64) despite severe hypertrophy, which is a classic discordance in infiltrative disease.

Constrictive pericarditis was appropriately considered as the main alternative cause of a restrictive filling pattern with elevated venous pressure, hepatomegaly and effusions, but it is effectively excluded here: there is no pericardial thickening on echocardiography, no pericardial calcification on chest x-ray, and respirophasic variation in mitral inflow is only 5%, well below the degree of ventricular interdependence expected in constriction. Severe left ventricular hypertrophy would also not be a feature of constriction.

The extracardiac features converge on the same diagnosis. The patient carries a diagnosis of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, has mild macroglossia with a sensation of fullness in the mouth, is thin and appears older than his stated age, has fatigue and decreased appetite, erectile dysfunction and orthostatic dizziness with a prior syncopal episode (suggesting autonomic involvement), and has failed to respond to repeated diuretic escalation. The diagnosis is confirmed histologically: the fat pad biopsy shows amorphous extracellular pink deposits on hematoxylin and eosin staining with apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining, which is diagnostic of amyloid deposition. Taken together with the cardiac imaging, this establishes cardiac amyloidosis presenting as restrictive cardiomyopathy with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Given the coexisting MGUS and macroglossia, immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis is the most likely type, but transthyretin amyloidosis remains a formal consideration in a 68-year-old man, and typing has not yet been performed in this case.

Anemia of another cause is not present (CBC with differential normal, ferritin 100 ng/mL), and there is no fever, night sweats, or upper respiratory symptoms to suggest infection as a precipitant. The mild mitral regurgitation and the 2/6 holosystolic apical murmur are consistent with the known valvular history and do not explain the degree of decompensation. Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is a further relevant comorbidity because atrial mechanical failure and biatrial enlargement in amyloid heart disease carry a high thromboembolic risk; the patient is currently in regular rhythm on warfarin.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light-chain assay to identify a clonal light chain; typing of the amyloid deposits (immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry on the biopsy material) to distinguish AL from transthyretin amyloidosis; bone marrow biopsy with plasma cell assessment if a monoclonal light chain is confirmed; bone scintigraphy with a bone-avid tracer and/or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for cardiac amyloid characterization; genetic testing for hereditary transthyretin variants if transthyretin type is established; repeat serum troponin and natriuretic peptide levels plus basic metabolic panel with renal function and electrolytes for staging and for monitoring diuretic therapy; 24-hour urine protein quantification to assess renal amyloid involvement; telemetry or ambulatory ECG monitoring given the prior syncope and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

Conclusion: Decompensated heart failure with preserved ejection fraction due to infiltrative restrictive cardiomyopathy from cardiac amyloidosis, confirmed by Congo red-positive fat pad biopsy with apple-green birefringence, in a patient with known MGUS, macroglossia, severe concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with low tissue Doppler velocities, biatrial enlargement, relative hypotension, autonomic symptoms, and diuretic-refractory volume overload. Constrictive pericarditis and ischemic decompensation have been excluded by the available data. The amyloid type has not yet been determined and this is the critical next step, since prognosis and treatment differ substantially between light-chain and transthyretin disease.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology
Recommendations: Continue careful decongestion with loop diuretics, but titrate cautiously and monitor closely, because in restrictive physiology with a small, stiff, preload-dependent ventricle and a systolic pressure of 92/64 mm Hg, overdiuresis will precipitate hypotension and syncope; track daily weights, orthostatic blood pressures, and renal function and electrolytes with every dose change. Reinforce continued sodium and fluid restriction, which the patient is already attempting. Recognize explicitly that standard heart failure therapy directed at reduced ejection fraction is not the treatment for this disease, and that agents which are poorly tolerated in infiltrative cardiomyopathy with borderline blood pressure and autonomic dysfunction should be used only with great caution or avoided. Continue anticoagulation with warfarin given paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and biatrial enlargement, both of which confer a high thromboembolic risk in amyloid heart disease; maintain therapeutic monitoring. Address the additional considerations directly: first, complete amyloid typing without delay through serum and urine immunofixation, serum free light chains, and immunohistochemical or mass-spectrometric typing of the biopsy tissue, since the coexisting MGUS raises concern for AL amyloidosis, which requires urgent hematology referral and plasma cell-directed therapy, whereas transthyretin amyloidosis is managed differently and warrants genetic testing to separate hereditary from wild-type disease. Second, refer promptly to a cardiologist experienced in amyloidosis and, in parallel, to hematology-oncology pending the typing results. Third, evaluate for extracardiac amyloid involvement, including renal involvement with quantified proteinuria, autonomic involvement explaining the orthostatic dizziness, prior syncope and erectile dysfunction, and gastrointestinal involvement suggested by the decreased appetite. Fourth, arrange rhythm monitoring and further evaluation of the prior syncopal episode, since conduction disease and arrhythmia are common in amyloid heart disease. Fifth, stop the pattern of repeated empiric furosemide escalation without further workup, which is what delayed the diagnosis over the past several months. Give the patient clear instructions to seek immediate care for rapid weight gain, worsening orthopnea, resting dyspnea, presyncope or syncope, palpitations, or lightheadedness, and arrange short-interval follow-up within days rather than weeks.

Notes: The amyloid subtype is not established by the data provided; the fat pad biopsy confirms amyloid but does not identify the precursor protein, and treatment decisions must await typing. Cardiac involvement is inferred from the characteristic echocardiographic phenotype together with tissue-confirmed systemic amyloidosis rather than from endomyocardial biopsy. The ECG tracing referenced in the case was not available for interpretation in this protocol, although it is described as unchanged from four months ago.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old obese man with a BMI of 34 presents with a 6-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite taking omeprazole 20 mg daily. He reports the heartburn is worse after large meals and when lying down, and he frequently wakes at night with a sour taste in his mouth and occasional coughing. He has tried elevating the head of his bed and avoiding late meals with only partial relief. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, or hematemesis. He drinks two to three beers on weekends and does not smoke. On examination, vital signs are normal. He is an obese man in no acute distress. Abdominal exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. His dentist has noted enamel erosion on posterior teeth.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 50 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Six-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation that has continued despite omeprazole 20 mg daily, worse after large meals and when recumbent, with nocturnal awakening, a sour taste in the mouth, and occasional cough; only partial relief from head-of-bed elevation and avoidance of late meals.

Analysis: The clinical picture is that of gastroesophageal reflux disease with typical symptoms. The two cardinal symptoms, heartburn and acid regurgitation, are present, and their behavior is characteristic: aggravation after large meals and in the recumbent position, both of which increase the gastroesophageal pressure gradient and promote reflux. Supporting evidence comes from several independent sources. The nocturnal awakening with a sour taste in the mouth represents recumbent regurgitation of gastric contents. The occasional cough is a recognized extraesophageal manifestation of reflux. The enamel erosion on the posterior teeth documented by his dentist is objective corroborating evidence of chronic exposure of the oral cavity to gastric acid and confirms that the reported regurgitation is real and long-standing rather than purely subjective. Obesity with a BMI of 34 is a well-established risk factor and a likely mechanistic contributor through increased intra-abdominal pressure, and his weekend alcohol intake of two to three beers may further reduce lower esophageal sphincter tone.

The most important issue in this case is that the symptoms are refractory to standard-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy after six months. Several explanations must be considered. The most common and most correctable is suboptimal dosing or timing: omeprazole 20 mg once daily is a standard rather than a maximal dose, and proton pump inhibitors require administration 30 to 60 minutes before a meal to be effective, a detail frequently missed by patients. Incomplete lifestyle modification is another contributor, and his obesity has not been addressed. Beyond these, genuinely refractory reflux may reflect a large hiatal hernia or mechanically incompetent lower esophageal sphincter, ongoing weakly acidic or nonacid reflux, or an alternative diagnosis.

The relevant differential considerations include erosive esophagitis and its complications, peptic stricture, and Barrett esophagus, all of which are consequences of prolonged reflux and are more likely in a middle-aged obese man with six months or more of symptoms; eosinophilic esophagitis, which can mimic proton pump inhibitor-refractory reflux; functional heartburn or reflux hypersensitivity, in which symptoms persist despite adequate acid suppression because the mucosa is hypersensitive rather than damaged; peptic ulcer disease, which is plausible given the mild epigastric tenderness on examination; and gastric or esophageal malignancy. Reassuringly, there are no alarm features in this case: he specifically denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, and hematemesis, and the examination shows normal vital signs, no lymphadenopathy, and no organomegaly, with only mild epigastric tenderness. The absence of alarm features makes malignancy and complicated ulcer disease considerably less likely, but does not exclude them, and it does not remove the indication for endoscopic evaluation of a patient whose symptoms have failed an adequate empiric trial. Cardiac chest pain is not suggested here, as the symptoms are clearly postprandial and positional with a sour taste and no exertional component.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) to evaluate for erosive esophagitis, hiatal hernia, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, peptic ulcer disease and malignancy, with esophageal biopsies including proximal and distal esophageal sampling to assess for eosinophilic esophagitis and biopsy of any suspicious mucosa; testing for Helicobacter pylori, which can be performed on gastric biopsies at the time of endoscopy given the epigastric tenderness. If endoscopy is normal and symptoms persist despite optimized acid suppression, ambulatory esophageal pH or pH-impedance monitoring to confirm pathologic acid exposure and to correlate symptoms with reflux episodes, and esophageal manometry to assess motility, which is also required before any consideration of antireflux surgery.

Conclusion: Chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, refractory to standard-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy, in a 50-year-old obese man with typical heartburn and regurgitation, nocturnal and postprandial symptom patterns, extraesophageal manifestations in the form of cough, and objective dental enamel erosion confirming chronic acid exposure. No alarm features are present and the examination is essentially benign apart from mild epigastric tenderness. Because symptoms have persisted for six months on therapy, empiric management alone is no longer adequate; optimization of medical therapy together with endoscopic evaluation is indicated to identify complications of reflux and to exclude alternative diagnoses.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: First, optimize the medical regimen before concluding that the disease is truly refractory. Verify that omeprazole is being taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal rather than with or after food or at bedtime, since incorrect timing is a common cause of apparent treatment failure. Escalate acid suppression to twice-daily dosing before breakfast and before the evening meal, and reassess response over a defined interval. Second, refer for upper endoscopy with biopsies, which is indicated on the basis of persistent symptoms despite an adequate trial of acid suppression, in order to identify erosive esophagitis, hiatal hernia, stricture, Barrett esophagus, peptic ulcer disease or eosinophilic esophagitis, and to test for Helicobacter pylori. Third, address obesity directly, since a BMI of 34 is both a driver of his reflux and the single modifiable factor most likely to produce durable improvement; recommend a structured weight-reduction program with dietary and physical activity counseling and appropriate follow-up. Fourth, reinforce and extend the lifestyle measures he has already partially adopted: continue elevation of the head of the bed and avoidance of meals within three hours of lying down, add reduction of meal size in place of large meals, and reduce or eliminate alcohol intake, since his weekend beer consumption lowers lower esophageal sphincter tone. Fifth, refer him back to his dentist for management and monitoring of the enamel erosion, and advise against brushing immediately after a regurgitation episode. Explicitly address the additional considerations: if endoscopy is normal and symptoms persist on optimized therapy, proceed to ambulatory pH-impedance testing off or on therapy as appropriate together with manometry, to distinguish persistent pathologic acid reflux from reflux hypersensitivity or functional heartburn, since these require different management, and to define candidacy for antireflux surgery, which becomes a reasonable option in a patient with objectively documented reflux, a mechanically incompetent sphincter or large hiatal hernia, and inadequate response to maximal medical therapy. Instruct the patient to report promptly if any alarm feature develops, specifically difficulty or pain with swallowing, unintentional weight loss, vomiting of blood, black stools, or anemia, as these would require expedited endoscopic evaluation.

Notes: The absence of alarm features lowers but does not eliminate the probability of a serious underlying lesion and does not substitute for endoscopy in a patient whose symptoms have failed adequate empiric therapy. No laboratory results, endoscopic findings, or imaging are available in this case, so all structural conclusions remain provisional pending evaluation.
