Vignette:
A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child checkup. The patient and his mother both state that the patient has been otherwise well except for occasional mild pain and stiffness in the upper back. Symptoms began gradually about a year ago and are present intermittently. The pain and stiffness do not bother him significantly or limit his activities, and they have never awakened him from sleep. He denies any trauma or overuse. He is not currently playing any organized sports although he is able to be normally active with friends and siblings.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient feels well except for occasional upper back pain and stiffness. No fever, chills, or night sweats. No weight loss or change in appetite. He is not yet shaving, and his voice has not yet changed.

Skin: Mild acne, no other rash or lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, hearing changes, neck stiffness, or pain in the throat.

Pulmonary: No shortness of breath or cough.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain or pressure.

Gastrointestinal: No diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Normal bowel movement once a day.

Genitourinary: No dysuria or increased urinary frequency.

Musculoskeletal: Positive for intermittent upper back stiffness and discomfort. No joint swelling or discomfort.

Neurologic: No numbness, tingling, or pain running down his arms or legs. No weakness or gait changes. No difficulty controlling bladder or bowels.

Psychiatric: No depression, psychosis, or hyperactivity.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Uncomplicated birth, no hospitalizations.

Surgical history: None

Medications: None

Allergies: Penicillin (rash)

Family history: His father had diabetes and hypertension and died when patient was very young. His maternal grandmother died of breast cancer at age 76 years. There is no history of skeletal dysplasia or muscular dystrophy in the family.

Social history: Patient was born at 37 weeks' gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery and had an uncomplicated postnatal course. He is in age-appropriate grade in school and doing well academically and behaviorally. On interview with the mother outside the room, the patient reports that he feels happy and supported at home with his mother and sisters. Patient reports that he has never tried alcohol, drugs, or cigarettes. He is not sexually active.

The patient's family is from Guinea Bissau but the patient was born and raised in the United States and has not traveled outside the country. No known history of tuberculosis exposure. He is up to date on all vaccinations, and he received an influenza vaccine this year. He eats a normal diet, including fruits and vegetables, and drinks milk daily.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: African-American male child in no apparent discomfort, normal build and appearance.

Height: 160 cm (92nd percentile), Weight: 40 kgs (47th percentile)

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 80 beats/min
BP: 105/66 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

Skin: No lesions or abnormal markings.

HEENT: Moist mucous membranes, normal dentition, no caries. Eye examination and vision normal bilaterally. Hearing grossly normal.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No chest deformity.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended.

Genitourinary: Normal male genitalia Tanner Stage 3, testes descended bilaterally.

Musculoskeletal: Back has mild paraspinous tenderness bilaterally in the thoracic region. When patient bends forward at the waist with his arms hanging and palms together, his shoulders are not level and his scapulae appear asymmetric. Palpation of the spinous processes show slight right thoracic and left lumbar curvature. There is no leg-length discrepancy, and iliac crests are symmetrical. Extremities have full range of motion, no visible or palpable deformities or tenderness of extremities or joints.

Neurologic: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Normal patellar relaxes 2+ bilaterally, 5/5 motor strength in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Normal gait. No clonus. No strictures or rigidity in the extremities.

Mental status: Appropriate affect and behavior.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and show the following results:

X-ray of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine:

No bony lesions noted. No signs of sacroiliitis. Scoliosis is present with right thoracic deviation and left lumbar deviation, Cobb angle 11°.

Focused musculoskeletal examination results:

Joint hypermobility: Absent
Ratio of upper body to lower body: 1.06
Ratio of wingspan to height: 0.98
baseline_protocol:
Age: 12 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Presented for a routine well-child checkup; reports occasional mild intermittent upper back pain and stiffness that began gradually about one year ago, does not limit activity, and has never awakened him from sleep, with no history of trauma or overuse. Examination incidentally revealed asymmetry of the shoulders and scapulae on forward bending.

Analysis: The findings establish adolescent idiopathic scoliosis of mild magnitude in a skeletally immature boy, with mild nonspecific mechanical back discomfort.

The structural diagnosis is objective. On forward bending with the arms hanging and palms together, which is the Adams forward bend test, his shoulders are not level and the scapulae are asymmetric, indicating a rotational rib and trunk deformity rather than a postural asymmetry. Palpation of the spinous processes confirms slight right thoracic and left lumbar curvature, and radiography of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine confirms scoliosis with right thoracic deviation and left lumbar deviation and a Cobb angle of 11 degrees. A right thoracic with compensatory left lumbar pattern is the most common curve pattern in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. There is no leg-length discrepancy and the iliac crests are symmetrical, which excludes a functional or compensatory curve secondary to pelvic obliquity and confirms that the curvature is structural.

The diagnosis is idiopathic by exclusion, and the case systematically excludes the alternatives. Neuromuscular scoliosis is excluded by a normal neurologic examination: he is alert and oriented, has 5 out of 5 motor strength in all four extremities, symmetric 2+ patellar reflexes, a normal gait, no clonus, no rigidity, and denies numbness, tingling, radiating limb pain, weakness, gait change, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. The absence of clonus and of abnormal reflexes is particularly important, since hyperreflexia or clonus would raise concern for an underlying intraspinal abnormality such as syringomyelia, tethered cord, or a spinal cord tumor. Congenital scoliosis and bony pathology are excluded by the radiographic report of no bony lesions. Infection and malignancy are excluded by the absence of fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, or change in appetite, by pain that has never awakened him from sleep, and by the absence of bony lesions on radiography; night pain and constitutional symptoms are the classic red flags for tumor and infection in pediatric back pain, and both are explicitly absent. Inflammatory spondyloarthropathy is excluded by the absence of sacroiliitis on radiographs, the absence of joint swelling, and the fact that his stiffness is intermittent and not associated with the inflammatory pattern of prolonged morning stiffness improving with activity.

A connective tissue disorder was specifically evaluated and is not supported. Joint hypermobility is absent, the ratio of upper body to lower body segment is 1.06 and the wingspan-to-height ratio is 0.98, both essentially normal and not showing the disproportionate long-limbed habitus of Marfan syndrome; there is no chest deformity, the cardiovascular examination shows a regular rate and rhythm with no murmur, and the eye examination and vision are normal bilaterally. The family history is explicitly negative for skeletal dysplasia and muscular dystrophy. Although his height is at the 92nd percentile with weight at the 47th percentile, the normal body proportions, absent hypermobility, and normal cardiac and ocular examinations argue against Marfan syndrome.

The most important prognostic consideration is skeletal immaturity and growth potential. He is 12 years old, at Tanner stage 3, is not yet shaving, and his voice has not yet changed, all of which indicate that he is in or approaching his adolescent growth spurt with substantial remaining skeletal growth. Curve progression in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis occurs predominantly during rapid growth, so despite a currently mild curve of 11 degrees, he carries a meaningful risk of progression and therefore requires scheduled surveillance rather than discharge. It is worth noting that scoliosis of this magnitude is generally not itself a cause of significant pain; his mild intermittent thoracic discomfort with mild bilateral paraspinous tenderness is most consistent with benign mechanical or muscular pain, and the reassuring history and examination make a sinister cause of back pain very unlikely.

A curve of 11 degrees is below the threshold at which the diagnosis of scoliosis is conventionally considered significant and well below the range at which bracing or surgery is considered. Management at this magnitude is observation with serial clinical and radiographic monitoring.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None immediately. Serial monitoring is required rather than further diagnostic workup: repeat clinical assessment with the Adams forward bend test and scoliometer measurement of trunk rotation at follow-up intervals of approximately every four to six months during the pubertal growth spurt, with repeat standing posteroanterior spine radiography and Cobb angle measurement if clinical examination suggests progression or at the intervals advised by the treating clinician; assessment of skeletal maturity to estimate remaining growth and refine progression risk. Advanced imaging of the neuraxis would be indicated only if neurologic signs, an atypical curve pattern, or significant progression were to emerge, and none of these is present now.

Conclusion: Mild adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with a right thoracic and left lumbar curve measuring 11 degrees by Cobb angle, discovered incidentally at a well-child visit in a 12-year-old boy at Tanner stage 3 with substantial remaining skeletal growth. Structural curvature is confirmed clinically and radiographically, and secondary causes have been excluded: the neurologic examination is entirely normal with no clonus or reflex asymmetry, there are no bony lesions or sacroiliitis, there is no leg-length discrepancy, there are no constitutional or night-time symptoms, and connective tissue disease is not supported by the normal body proportions, absent joint hypermobility, and normal cardiac and ocular examinations. The accompanying mild intermittent upper back pain and stiffness with bilateral paraspinous tenderness is benign and mechanical, does not limit function, and does not require investigation. No treatment is indicated for a curve of this magnitude; the essential management is structured observation through the growth spurt, because progression risk is highest during rapid growth.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Reassure the patient and his mother that this is a mild curvature that requires no bracing, no surgery, and no activity restriction at present, and that the normal neurologic examination and radiographs exclude serious underlying causes. Explain clearly, however, that observation is not the same as discharge, and that follow-up is essential because he is skeletally immature and curves can progress during the adolescent growth spurt.

Arrange scheduled monitoring, with clinical reassessment approximately every four to six months while he is growing rapidly, including serial height measurement, repeat Adams forward bend testing with scoliometer measurement of trunk rotation, and documentation of shoulder and scapular symmetry and waist asymmetry, with repeat radiography and Cobb angle measurement as clinically indicated rather than at every visit, in order to limit cumulative radiation exposure. Refer to orthopedics for scoliosis surveillance, or arrange orthopedic referral promptly if the curve progresses, since bracing becomes a consideration for progressive curves in a growing child and surgical consultation for larger curves.

For the back pain, advise simple measures: maintain normal activity, since it does not limit him and there is no reason for restriction; encourage general physical activity and core and back strengthening and stretching, which he can achieve through the normal activity he already enjoys with friends and siblings and, if he wishes, through return to organized sports, which are not contraindicated; attend to backpack weight and posture at school; and use simple over-the-counter analgesia only occasionally if needed. Note the documented penicillin allergy manifesting as rash for any future prescribing.

Address the additional considerations explicitly. First, the parents should be told which changes require earlier reassessment rather than waiting for the scheduled visit: any new or worsening back pain, particularly pain that wakes him from sleep or is severe or persistent; any numbness, tingling, weakness, or pain radiating into the arms or legs; any change in gait, balance, or coordination; any bowel or bladder dysfunction; or any visible worsening of shoulder, scapular, or waist asymmetry or the appearance of a rib hump. Second, counsel on the natural history: monitoring should continue until skeletal maturity, after which the risk of progression falls substantially for curves of this magnitude, and curves that remain small are not expected to cause cardiopulmonary compromise or long-term disability. Third, continue routine well-child care, including maintenance of his up-to-date immunizations, continued attention to his balanced diet with daily milk intake supporting bone health during this period of rapid growth, and continued monitoring of pubertal progression. Fourth, no laboratory testing, advanced imaging, or genetic evaluation is indicated at this time given the negative findings on focused musculoskeletal assessment.

Notes: A Cobb angle of 11 degrees is below the conventional 10-degree threshold only by a small margin and is at the mild end of the spectrum; measurement variability of a few degrees is expected between radiographs, so progression should be judged by a clearly increasing trend rather than by a single small change. Skeletal maturity grading, which most strongly determines progression risk, is not reported in the case and should be assessed. The reassurance regarding the back pain depends on the current absence of red flags and must be revisited if the symptom pattern changes.

Vignette: A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Vignette:
A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 19 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Twenty-four-hour history of high fever, diffuse sunburn-like rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea and progressive lightheadedness in a college student who left a menstrual tampon in place for approximately 3 days.
Analysis: The presentation fulfills the classic pattern of menstrual staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome. The strongest supporting facts are the retained tampon for about 3 days, temperature of 40.2C, hypotension with BP 72/40 and compensatory tachycardia of 136, and a diffuse blanching erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn that involves the trunk, extremities, palms and soles. Hyperemic mucous membranes indicate mucosal involvement. Multiorgan involvement is documented by at least three systems: gastrointestinal (vomiting and profuse watery diarrhea), renal (creatinine 2.8 mg/dL), hepatic (AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L), muscular (CK 1,240 U/L) and hematologic (platelets 88,000/mcL). Leukocytosis of 15,400/mcL supports a severe inflammatory response. The physiology is distributive shock from superantigen-mediated massive cytokine release, which explains the profound vasodilatory hypotension out of proportion to any localized infection; the pelvic exam confirmed a retained tampon with no abscess, so there is no drainable focus beyond removal of the tampon itself. Main differential considerations include streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (usually with a soft tissue focus and severe pain, absent here), septic shock from another source (no localizing findings and blood cultures pending; in staphylococcal TSS cultures are typically negative), meningococcemia (rash is petechial or purpuric rather than blanching and macular), Rocky Mountain spotted fever (would require tick exposure and typically a petechial rash progressing centripetally, not described), leptospirosis, severe drug reaction such as DRESS or Stevens-Johnson syndrome (no drug exposure or mucosal denudation described), scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, no shock or multiorgan failure), and Kawasaki disease (age and shock pattern do not fit). The combination of a removable vaginal foreign body, erythroderma involving palms and soles, hypotension and three-plus organ system dysfunction makes toxic shock syndrome the unifying diagnosis. Removal of the tampon and empiric clindamycin plus vancomycin are appropriate, since clindamycin suppresses toxin production while vancomycin covers possible methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac, blood pressure and pulse oximetry monitoring with large-bore intravenous access; serial complete blood count with platelets, comprehensive metabolic panel including creatinine and liver enzymes, and serial CK; coagulation studies with PT/INR, aPTT and fibrinogen to assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation; serum lactate and arterial or venous blood gas to gauge shock severity; vaginal and wound cultures plus the already drawn blood cultures; urinalysis and hourly urine output measurement via indwelling catheter; pregnancy test; chest radiograph to evaluate oxygenation and for pulmonary edema given SpO2 94%; central venous access and arterial line if vasopressors are required; bedside echocardiography or other cardiac output assessment if shock is refractory to fluids.
Conclusion: Menstrual staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome with distributive shock and multiorgan dysfunction (acute kidney injury, transaminitis, thrombocytopenia and rhabdomyolysis) in a 19-year-old woman with a retained tampon. The source has been removed and toxin-suppressing plus antistaphylococcal antibiotics have been started; she now requires aggressive hemodynamic resuscitation and intensive care monitoring because progression to refractory shock and organ failure is the principal threat to life.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Admit immediately to an intensive care unit. Begin aggressive isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, as these patients often require very large volumes because of capillary leak, and titrate to mean arterial pressure, mental status and hourly urine output; add norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor if hypotension persists despite adequate fluid loading. Continue clindamycin for antitoxin effect together with vancomycin for MRSA coverage, and de-escalate once culture and susceptibility data return; the retained tampon has been removed, and since no abscess was found, no further source control procedure is indicated at present, though re-examination should be performed if the patient fails to improve. Support the acute kidney injury with volume repletion, avoidance of nephrotoxic agents and appropriate dose adjustment of vancomycin with level monitoring; involve nephrology early and prepare for renal replacement therapy if oliguria, refractory hyperkalemia or acidosis develops. Treat the rhabdomyolysis indicated by CK 1,240 U/L with continued fluids and serial CK. Monitor platelets and coagulation for evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation and transfuse only for bleeding or profound thrombocytopenia. Provide supplemental oxygen and monitor closely for acute respiratory distress syndrome given the ongoing capillary leak. Regarding additional considerations: intravenous immunoglobulin may be considered for shock refractory to fluids, vasopressors and antibiotics, given the superantigen mechanism; counsel the patient before discharge that recurrence is possible and that she should avoid tampon use, or at minimum use the lowest absorbency needed and change tampons frequently; anticipate the characteristic desquamation of the palms and soles one to three weeks after onset and reassure her that this is expected; arrange follow-up to confirm normalization of renal and hepatic function.
Notes: Blood cultures are frequently negative in staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, so a negative result must not prompt discontinuation of therapy. The diagnosis remains clinical and treatment should not await microbiologic confirmation.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 32-year-old male singer presents with a hoarse voice that has persisted for 3 days following an intense concert performance. He reports mild sore throat and throat dryness but denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, or hemoptysis. He is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol regularly. He has no history of GERD or thyroid disease. On examination, he is afebrile. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His voice is notably hoarse and breathy. Respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing on auscultation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 32 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Hoarse, breathy voice for 3 days following an intense concert performance, with mild sore throat and throat dryness.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of acute laryngitis secondary to phonotrauma, that is vocal overuse during an intense concert performance. The strongest supporting facts are the clear temporal relationship between the demanding vocal performance and the onset of dysphonia, the short 3-day duration, and the associated mild sore throat and throat dryness. Examination is reassuring: he is afebrile, the oropharynx is only mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions, there is no cervical lymphadenopathy, and respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing. The voice is hoarse and breathy, which is consistent with incomplete glottic closure from vocal fold edema or inflammation. Critically, there are no airway red flags: he denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever and hemoptysis. Risk factors for more sinister causes are absent, as he is a non-smoker, does not drink alcohol regularly, and has no history of gastroesophageal reflux disease or thyroid disease. Differential considerations include viral upper respiratory infection with laryngitis, which is plausible given the mild sore throat and pharyngeal erythema; vocal fold hemorrhage or an acute phonotraumatic lesion such as a vocal fold polyp or nodule, which should be suspected if hoarseness fails to resolve; laryngopharyngeal reflux, though he has no reflux history; muscle tension dysphonia developing as a compensatory pattern; and, far less likely here, laryngeal neoplasm, which would be suggested by persistent hoarseness beyond several weeks in a smoker or drinker with weight loss or neck mass, none of which are present. Epiglottitis, deep neck space infection and airway obstruction are excluded by the absence of fever, dysphagia, drooling, stridor and distress. Acute laryngitis is self-limited and typically resolves within one to two weeks with voice rest.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute phonotraumatic laryngitis in a professional singer, three days after intense vocal use, presenting with hoarse breathy dysphonia and mild pharyngeal irritation in the absence of any airway compromise, systemic illness or malignancy risk factors. This is a benign, self-limited condition expected to resolve with relative voice rest and conservative measures; no immediate imaging or laboratory testing is warranted, and laryngoscopy is reserved for persistent or worsening symptoms.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Advise relative voice rest, meaning avoidance of singing, shouting, prolonged speaking and, importantly, whispering, which increases rather than decreases vocal fold strain; use a soft, easy conversational voice only when necessary. Maintain generous systemic hydration and use humidification of ambient air to counter the throat dryness he describes. Avoid throat clearing, which is traumatic to the vocal folds, and instead swallow or sip water. Since he is a non-smoker and not a regular drinker, no substance modification is required, but he should also avoid secondhand smoke and dry, dusty or smoky performance environments. Analgesia with simple over-the-counter agents and warm fluids or lozenges may ease the mild sore throat. Antibiotics are not indicated, as there is no fever, exudate or lymphadenopathy to suggest bacterial infection. Corticosteroids should not be used routinely for this benign self-limited condition. Regarding additional considerations, as a professional voice user he should not return to full singing until the voice has normalized, and he should be strongly advised against performing through hoarseness because continued phonotrauma risks vocal fold hemorrhage, polyp or nodule formation. He should seek in-person evaluation with flexible or videostroboscopic laryngoscopy by an otolaryngologist or laryngologist if hoarseness persists beyond about two weeks, worsens, or recurs with performances, and should seek urgent care immediately if he develops stridor, dyspnea, dysphagia, drooling, fever or hemoptysis. Referral for speech-language pathology and vocal technique training is advisable if episodes recur, to address vocal hygiene and prevent chronic phonotraumatic injury.
Notes: Persistent hoarseness beyond several weeks always warrants direct visualization of the larynx regardless of a benign initial presentation and low risk profile.

Age: 6 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Eight hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress unrelieved by albuterol every 20 minutes at home, in a child with moderate persistent asthma and two prior ICU admissions, following a recent upper respiratory infection.
Analysis: This is a near-fatal asthma exacerbation with impending respiratory failure. The strongest supporting facts are failure to respond to eight hours of frequent home albuterol, inability to speak more than single words, tripod posture with accessory muscle use, respiratory rate of 42 and heart rate of 152, and hypoxemia with SpO2 87% on room air. The most ominous findings are the markedly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with only minimal wheezing, which indicates severe air trapping and inadequate airflow rather than improvement, and the venous blood gas showing pH 7.28 with pCO2 55 mmHg. In an acute asthma attack the expected gas pattern is hyperventilation with hypocapnia; a normal or elevated pCO2 with acidemia signals that the child can no longer sustain the work of breathing and is progressing to respiratory failure. Peak flow is unobtainable because of fatigue, itself a marker of severity. Age: 53 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two months of intermittent palpitations described as irregular and racing heartbeats accompanied by fatigue, occurring once or twice weekly, lasting from 10 minutes to several hours and resolving spontaneously, with the most recent episode 3 days ago.
Analysis: The history is characteristic of a paroxysmal tachyarrhythmia, and the description of irregular as well as racing heartbeats makes paroxysmal atrial fibrillation the leading consideration. Supporting factors are her age of 53, a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes, which are both established risk factors for atrial fibrillation, episodes of variable duration from minutes to hours with spontaneous termination, a frequency of once or twice per week, and associated fatigue. Reassuring features that argue against an immediately dangerous arrhythmia are the complete absence of chest pain, dyspnea, lightheadedness and syncope, preserved exercise tolerance walking three miles several days per week without exertional symptoms, and the absence of any family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. baseline_protocol:
Age: 72 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five days of increased sputum production with a change in sputum color from white to yellow-green and mild worsening of baseline dyspnea, in a man with GOLD stage II COPD and a 40-pack-year smoking history.
Analysis: This is an acute exacerbation of COPD of mild to moderate severity. The strongest supporting facts are the presence of two of the three cardinal Anthonisen criteria, namely increased sputum volume and increased sputum purulence with the change from white to yellow-green, together with a mild increase in dyspnea over his baseline, which actually makes all three cardinal symptoms present in attenuated form. The clinical severity is low: he is afebrile at 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit, heart rate 82, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air against a stated baseline of 94 to 95 percent, a trivial decrement. He is speaking in full sentences comfortably and has no accessory muscle use, and the examination shows only mild bilateral expiratory wheezing. These features exclude impending respiratory failure and identify a patient who can be treated as an outpatient. Underlying risk is established by a 40-pack-year smoking history and known GOLD stage II disease, and he is already on maintenance tiotropium with albuterol as a rescue inhaler. Sputum purulence in this setting suggests a likely bacterial trigger, most commonly Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae or Moraxella catarrhalis, although viral infection is also a frequent precipitant. Differential considerations that must be weighed include community-acquired pneumonia, which is argued against by the absence of fever, absence of pleuritic chest pain and the absence of focal findings such as crackles, bronchial breathing or dullness; pulmonary embolism, less likely given no chest pain, no tachycardia, no hypoxemia beyond baseline and no risk factors described; decompensated heart failure, with no orthopnea, edema or crackles described; pneumothorax, excluded by symmetric findings and stable vitals; and lung malignancy, which remains a background concern given his heavy smoking history but is not suggested acutely as he denies hemoptysis and there is no weight loss reported. The absence of fever, hemoptysis, chest pain and significant increase in cough further supports an uncomplicated exacerbation rather than an alternative or superimposed diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pulse oximetry, already performed and to be repeated at follow-up; chest radiograph is reasonable to exclude pneumonia and to serve as a baseline given his heavy smoking history, though findings are not suggestive of consolidation; no routine sputum culture, blood gas, complete blood count, CT or D-dimer is needed for this uncomplicated outpatient exacerbation given normal vital signs and near-baseline saturation.
Conclusion: Uncomplicated acute exacerbation of GOLD stage II COPD, likely bacterial in origin given purulent sputum, presenting with increased sputum volume and purulence and mildly increased dyspnea, without fever, hypoxemia beyond baseline, tachypnea or signs of respiratory distress. This patient meets criteria for outpatient management with intensified bronchodilation, a short course of systemic corticosteroid and antibiotic therapy directed at the purulence, together with close follow-up and clear escalation criteria.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Manage as an outpatient. Intensify short-acting bronchodilator therapy by increasing the frequency of albuterol, using a spacer to optimize delivery, and continue maintenance tiotropium without interruption. Prescribe a short course of systemic corticosteroid, since a brief oral course improves lung function, oxygenation and recovery time in exacerbations, and keep the course short to limit adverse effects. Prescribe an oral antibiotic because he meets the purulence-based criterion with increased sputum volume, selecting an agent with activity against Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis according to local resistance patterns. Obtain a chest radiograph to exclude pneumonia and provide a baseline. Regarding additional considerations: monitor glucose while on corticosteroids and counsel on expected side effects. Reassess in 48 to 72 hours, either by telephone or in person, and instruct him to seek emergency care immediately if he develops worsening dyspnea at rest, inability to speak in full sentences, use of accessory muscles, confusion or drowsiness, fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or a fall in oxygen saturation clearly below his baseline. Reinforce smoking cessation as the single most effective intervention for altering the natural history of his disease, and offer pharmacologic and behavioral support. Verify that influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19 and RSV vaccinations are current, since exacerbations are commonly infection-triggered. Review inhaler technique and adherence, and once recovered, consider optimization of maintenance therapy given a documented exacerbation, referral to pulmonary rehabilitation, and assessment of whether long-term oxygen therapy criteria are met, which he does not currently meet at a baseline saturation of 94 to 95 percent. Given his 40-pack-year history, confirm that lung cancer screening with low-dose CT is up to date if he is within the eligible age and smoking-exposure window.
Notes: Antibiotics are justified here specifically by the presence of purulent sputum with increased volume; they should not be given reflexively for every exacerbation. A clinical worsening despite therapy should prompt reevaluation for pneumonia, pulmonary embolism or heart failure.

She bathes daily in hot water and uses regular bar soap. She denies any new medications, rash, jaundice, or unintentional weight loss. baseline_protocol:
Age: 72 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Generalized dry, itchy skin worsening over several weeks as winter has progressed, with the itching worst on the shins and forearms.
Analysis: The presentation is typical of xerosis cutis, that is winter dry skin, also termed asteatotic dermatitis in its more advanced form, in an older adult. The strongest supporting facts are the clear seasonal pattern with worsening as winter progressed, the distribution on the shins and forearms which are the classic sites of age-related xerosis, and two powerful modifiable aggravating behaviors: daily bathing in hot water and use of regular bar soap, both of which strip epidermal lipids and impair the skin barrier. Advanced age itself reduces sebum production, epidermal lipid content and stratum corneum water-binding capacity, predisposing to xerosis. The examination is consistent and reassuring: the skin on the extremities is diffusely dry with fine scaling and superficial cracking, and there are no excoriations, erythematous plaques or papules, meaning there is no primary inflammatory rash and no evidence of secondary infection or of a scratch-induced lichenified dermatitis. Skin turgor is appropriate for age, arguing against clinically significant dehydration. Important differential considerations for generalized pruritus in an older patient include systemic causes such as cholestatic liver disease, chronic kidney disease with uremic pruritus, thyroid dysfunction, iron deficiency and hematologic malignancy including lymphoma and polycythemia vera, as well as scabies, drug reaction, and pruritus as a paraneoplastic phenomenon. Several of these are actively argued against by the history and examination: she denies any new medications, has no rash, no jaundice and no unintentional weight loss, and there is no lymphadenopathy on examination. Scabies is unlikely given the absence of burrows, papules, excoriations and the non-classic distribution without web-space, wrist or waistline involvement, and no household contacts are described. The absence of a primary lesion, coupled with the seasonal course, the anatomic distribution and the identifiable bathing habits, makes xerosis the unifying and most parsimonious explanation. Systemic evaluation is therefore not the first step; a trial of barrier restoration is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Xerosis cutis with associated pruritus in a 72-year-old woman, driven by age-related barrier dysfunction, low winter humidity and aggravating hygiene practices of daily hot bathing with harsh bar soap. There is no primary rash, no jaundice, no lymphadenopathy and no weight loss to suggest a systemic cause, and no excoriation or secondary infection. The condition is benign and highly responsive to emollient therapy and behavioral modification, so self-directed conservative management with defined follow-up criteria is appropriate.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Correct the aggravating behaviors first, as these are the principal drivers. Advise shortening baths or showers to about five to ten minutes and using lukewarm rather than hot water, and reducing bathing frequency if tolerable. Replace the regular bar soap with a fragrance-free, non-soap, pH-balanced gentle cleanser applied only to the axillae, groin and feet rather than the whole body. After bathing, pat rather than rub the skin dry and apply a thick emollient within a few minutes while the skin is still damp to trap moisture; a bland ointment or cream containing petrolatum, ceramides or similar barrier lipids is preferable to a thin lotion, and it should be applied at least twice daily and generously to the shins and forearms where symptoms are worst. A urea- or lactic-acid-containing preparation may be added for the thickened, finely scaling areas. Use a humidifier in the bedroom during winter and avoid direct heat sources and rough or wool fabrics against the skin. Keep fingernails short to prevent skin breaks from scratching. Regarding additional considerations, if pruritus persists despite two to four weeks of consistent emollient therapy and behavior change, or if she develops jaundice, weight loss, night sweats, fever, lymphadenopathy or a new rash, then evaluation for systemic causes of pruritus is warranted, including complete blood count, liver function tests, renal function, thyroid-stimulating hormone and iron studies. A short course of a low- to mid-potency topical corticosteroid to inflamed or eczematous areas can be added if frank asteatotic eczema with erythema develops, though none is present now. Watch for signs of secondary bacterial infection through the superficial cracks, such as increasing redness, warmth, tenderness or crusting, and seek care if these appear. Sedating oral antihistamines are of limited value in xerosis and carry fall and confusion risk at her age, so they should be avoided.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. case_text:
Vignette:
A 20-year-old female college student who recently started a running program presents with bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins. The pain began about 1 week ago and occurs primarily during and shortly after running, then resolves with rest. She runs on paved surfaces in her current athletic shoes that are over a year old. She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 20 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: One week of bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins occurring during and shortly after running and resolving with rest, in a college student who recently started a running program.
Analysis: The findings are classic for medial tibial stress syndrome, commonly called shin splints. The strongest supporting facts are the recent initiation of a running program, which represents a sudden increase in training load on unconditioned bone and musculotendinous tissue; the bilateral and symmetric nature of the pain, which favors an overuse loading problem over a focal structural injury; the dull, aching quality; the activity-related pattern in which pain occurs during and shortly after running and resolves with rest; and, on examination, diffuse tenderness spread along roughly 5 cm of the medial border of each tibia. Two contributing extrinsic factors are explicitly present: running on hard paved surfaces and athletic shoes that are over a year old and therefore likely to have lost cushioning and support. The key differential considerations are tibial stress fracture, chronic exertional compartment syndrome, and less commonly popliteal artery entrapment, nerve entrapment or infection. Stress fracture is the most important alternative to exclude, and it is argued strongly against here by the absence of focal point tenderness over a discrete area of bone, the absence of night pain and rest pain, the short one-week symptom duration, the bilateral symmetric involvement, and the absence of swelling. She has no prior history of stress fractures. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome typically produces tightness, burning, or numbness building predictably with exercise and relieved over minutes to hours after stopping, often with neurologic symptoms, none of which are described, and her ankle range of motion and strength are normal with no edema or erythema. Deep vein thrombosis and cellulitis are excluded by the absence of swelling, erythema, warmth and by the bilateral exercise-linked pattern. The benign examination, with normal ankle range of motion and strength and no point tenderness, edema or erythema, permits confident clinical diagnosis without imaging at this stage.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Bilateral medial tibial stress syndrome caused by a rapid increase in running volume on hard paved surfaces in worn footwear, in a previously untrained 20-year-old runner. The diffuse rather than focal tibial tenderness, absence of rest and night pain, absence of swelling, and normal ankle examination make stress fracture unlikely and permit a clinical diagnosis without imaging. This is a benign, self-limited overuse injury that responds to relative rest, load modification and correction of the identified training and equipment errors.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Institute relative rest rather than complete inactivity: reduce or temporarily stop running and substitute low-impact cross-training such as swimming, cycling or elliptical work to preserve fitness while unloading the tibia. Use ice to the medial shins after activity and simple over-the-counter analgesia for symptom control. Replace her running shoes, which are over a year old and past their useful cushioning life, and have her fitted at a specialty store with attention to her foot type and gait; consider over-the-counter arch supports if she has pes planus or excessive pronation. Shift running from paved surfaces to softer terrain such as a track, trail or treadmill. Begin a program of calf, tibialis posterior and hip abductor strengthening along with gastrocnemius and soleus stretching, and address running mechanics by increasing cadence and avoiding overstriding. Return to running gradually and only once she is pain-free, restarting at a reduced volume and increasing weekly mileage by no more than about ten percent, with rest days interposed. Regarding additional considerations, she should seek in-person evaluation and imaging with plain radiographs and, if these are negative, MRI or bone scan if the pain becomes focal and point-tender over a small area of tibia, persists or worsens despite several weeks of appropriate rest and load reduction, occurs at rest or at night, or if she develops swelling. As a young female runner she should also be screened for relative energy deficiency in sport and the female athlete triad, including menstrual history, dietary adequacy and calcium and vitamin D intake, because these markedly increase stress fracture risk. Advise her that if exertional symptoms evolve into tightness, burning, numbness or foot drop that builds predictably with running and takes time to resolve after stopping, chronic exertional compartment syndrome should be evaluated with compartment pressure testing.
Notes: The distinction from tibial stress fracture rests largely on diffuse versus focal tenderness and the absence of rest and night pain; if the pain localizes to a single point, the diagnosis must be revisited before returning to running.

Vignette: A 17-year-old female is brought in by her parents after they discovered an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500 mg tablets, 50-count) in her room. She admits to intentionally ingesting approximately 25 grams 12 hours ago following a breakup. She initially felt fine but now reports nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is tearful but cooperative. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99%. Abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Scleral icterus is not yet present. Vignette:
A 17-year-old female is brought in by her parents after they discovered an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500 mg tablets, 50-count) in her room. She admits to intentionally ingesting approximately 25 grams 12 hours ago following a breakup. She initially felt fine but now reports nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is tearful but cooperative. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99%. Abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Scleral icterus is not yet present. Labs: acetaminophen level 180 mcg/mL (well above treatment line on Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 12 hours), AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L, INR 1.8, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, pH 7.34, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. N-acetylcysteine infusion is initiated immediately. Psychiatry and social work consultations are placed. Poison control is contacted.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 17 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Intentional ingestion of approximately 25 grams of extra-strength acetaminophen 12 hours ago following a breakup, now with nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
Analysis: This is a massive intentional acetaminophen overdose that has already progressed into stage II hepatotoxicity with established acute liver injury. The strongest supporting facts are the reported ingestion of about 25 grams, far above the hepatotoxic threshold, in a single acute overdose 12 hours before presentation; an acetaminophen concentration of 180 mcg/mL at 12 hours, described as well above the treatment line on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, which mandates antidotal therapy; and biochemical evidence that injury is already underway with AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL and, most concerning, an INR of 1.8 indicating impaired hepatic synthetic function. Clinically she has moved beyond the asymptomatic first stage: nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant tenderness correspond to the onset of hepatic injury, while scleral icterus is not yet present. Her hemodynamics are stable with heart rate 96, blood pressure 112/68, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent and temperature 37.2C, and renal function is preserved with creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, but a pH of 7.34 with lactate 2.8 mmol/L reflects early metabolic derangement and both are prognostic variables. The mechanism is saturation of sulfation and glucuronidation pathways with excess NAPQI generation and depletion of hepatic glutathione, producing centrilobular necrosis; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and is the definitive antidote, appropriately started immediately. Delay to 12 hours reduces but does not eliminate benefit, and N-acetylcysteine remains indicated even in late presentation and in established hepatotoxicity. Differential and co-ingestion considerations are important: a deliberate overdose may involve more than one substance, and combination acetaminophen products may contain opioids or antihistamines, so co-ingestants must be actively sought; other causes of acute transaminitis such as viral hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis and other hepatotoxins are far less likely given the documented drug level and clear history, but the possibility of a staggered rather than single ingestion should be clarified because it changes nomogram applicability. The psychiatric dimension is equally central: this was a deliberate self-harm act in an adolescent following an acute interpersonal stressor, and she requires formal suicide risk assessment and continuous supervision.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serial hepatic panel with AST, ALT, total and direct bilirubin, and serial INR and PT at least every 12 hours as the primary markers of trajectory; serial basic metabolic panel with creatinine, bicarbonate, electrolytes, glucose and phosphate, and serial lactate and arterial blood gas for pH; repeat acetaminophen concentration; salicylate concentration, ethanol level and urine toxicology screen to detect co-ingestants; urine pregnancy test; complete blood count and type and screen; viral hepatitis serologies if the course is atypical; continuous cardiac monitoring and frequent neurologic checks for encephalopathy; bedside glucose monitoring given the risk of hypoglycemia in liver failure; abdominal ultrasound with Doppler only if an alternative hepatic or biliary process is suspected; and formal psychiatric assessment with a structured suicide risk evaluation.
Conclusion: Acute acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity following a deliberate 25-gram ingestion 12 hours before presentation, with a supratherapeutic level above the treatment line, marked transaminase elevation, hyperbilirubinemia and coagulopathy with INR 1.8, in a hemodynamically stable but at-risk 17-year-old. N-acetylcysteine has been correctly initiated without delay, poison control has been contacted, and psychiatry and social work have been consulted. The critical issues now are uninterrupted antidotal therapy, close serial monitoring for progression to acute liver failure, early identification of criteria for transplant referral, and continuous psychiatric supervision for suicide risk.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Admit to a monitored inpatient setting, preferably an intensive care unit or step-down unit, given the coagulopathy and the risk of progression to fulminant hepatic failure. Continue the intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion without interruption and do not stop it at the end of the standard protocol duration; instead extend therapy until the acetaminophen level is undetectable, transaminases are clearly falling, the INR has normalized below approximately 1.5 and the patient is clinically improving. Activated charcoal is not useful at 12 hours after ingestion and should not be given. Provide antiemetics so that vomiting does not compromise treatment, maintain intravenous fluids and monitor and treat hypoglycemia aggressively, since it is a marker and complication of hepatic failure. Do not correct the INR with fresh frozen plasma or vitamin K in the absence of active bleeding or a planned invasive procedure, because the INR is the key prognostic marker of hepatic function and correcting it obscures the clinical picture. Avoid all additional hepatotoxic drugs and sedatives that could mask encephalopathy. Regarding the additional considerations explicitly raised in the case: continue collaboration with poison control for dosing and duration guidance; maintain the psychiatry and social work involvement with one-to-one continuous observation, removal of means, and a formal suicide risk assessment before any disposition decision, recognizing she is a minor so parental or guardian involvement and safety planning at home are required, including securing or removing medications; and contact a liver transplant center early. Apply the King's College criteria and refer for transplant evaluation if arterial pH falls below 7.3 after resuscitation, or if the combination of INR above 6.5, creatinine above 3.4 mg/dL and grade III or IV encephalopathy develops; rising lactate, worsening acidosis, hypoglycemia, rising INR beyond 72 hours or any alteration in mental status should prompt immediate escalation. Screen for co-ingestants with salicylate, ethanol and toxicology testing and obtain a pregnancy test. She must not be medically or psychiatrically cleared for discharge until hepatic parameters are clearly improving and psychiatric disposition is arranged.
Notes: N-acetylcysteine is indicated regardless of the delay and regardless of established hepatotoxicity, and the fixed-duration protocol must be extended while laboratory abnormalities persist. The reported ingested amount and timing in a self-harm presentation may be inaccurate, so management should be guided by the measured level and the laboratory trajectory rather than by history alone.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. baseline_protocol:
Age: 70 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Eighteen hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain with fever and rigors and progressive jaundice, in a man with prior choledocholithiasis treated by ERCP and sphincterotomy five years ago.
Analysis: This is acute ascending cholangitis with septic shock caused by choledocholithiasis and biliary obstruction. Charcot's triad is fully present with right upper quadrant pain, fever of 39.6C with rigors and prominent jaundice, and the picture extends to Reynolds' pentad through hypotension with a blood pressure of 88/52; altered mentation is not described, but hemodynamic instability alone marks this as suppurative cholangitis. The strongest supporting facts are the ultrasound demonstration of a dilated common bile duct at 14 mm containing a shadowing distal stone with mild intrahepatic ductal dilation, an obstructive laboratory pattern with total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL of which 6.8 mg/dL is direct, alkaline phosphatase 482 U/L, and only modest transaminase elevation with AST 188 and ALT 162, which is characteristic of obstruction rather than primary hepatocellular injury. Systemic infection and tissue hypoperfusion are documented by WBC 22,600/mcL with 15 percent bands, temperature 39.6C, heart rate 118, respiratory rate 22 and lactate 4.1 mmol/L, which together with the hypotension satisfy criteria for septic shock. A normal lipase argues against gallstone pancreatitis as the dominant process. The prior ERCP with sphincterotomy is directly relevant, since it identifies him as prone to recurrent stone disease and to bacterial colonization of the biliary tree through the incompetent sphincter. The positive Murphy sign and right upper quadrant tenderness raise the possibility of concomitant acute cholecystitis, but the ductal dilation, deep jaundice and rigors place the primary process in the common bile duct. Differential considerations include acute cholecystitis alone, which does not usually produce bilirubin of 8.4 mg/dL or rigors; gallstone pancreatitis, excluded by normal lipase; malignant biliary obstruction from pancreatic head or cholangiocarcinoma, which typically causes painless progressive jaundice without rigors and is not supported by the visualized stone; liver abscess; and acute viral hepatitis, which would show far higher transaminases with a different clinical tempo. Cholangitis with obstruction is a surgical and endoscopic emergency because antibiotics alone cannot control infection in an obstructed duct under pressure; biliary decompression is the definitive therapy and delay directly increases mortality.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures, already drawn, plus bile cultures obtained at the time of drainage; serial lactate, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel with liver tests and creatinine, and coagulation studies with PT/INR and platelets, which are also required before endoscopic sphincterotomy; type and screen; arterial or venous blood gas; continuous cardiac, blood pressure and oximetry monitoring with an indwelling urinary catheter for hourly urine output and consideration of arterial and central venous access for vasopressor therapy; ECG and chest radiograph as preoperative and pre-procedural assessment in a 70-year-old with sepsis; ERCP as both the diagnostic and therapeutic procedure of choice; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound only if ERCP is not feasible and the diagnosis is in doubt, which it is not here; percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography capability as a backup drainage route if ERCP fails.
Conclusion: Acute suppurative ascending cholangitis due to a distal common bile duct stone with a dilated 14 mm duct, complicated by septic shock with hypotension and lactate 4.1 mmol/L, in a 70-year-old with prior sphincterotomy and recurrent choledocholithiasis. This is a time-critical emergency in which resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics must be paired with urgent biliary decompression, preferably by ERCP with stone extraction and stent placement within hours, since antimicrobial therapy alone will not resolve an obstructed and infected biliary system.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Begin immediate sepsis resuscitation with aggressive intravenous crystalloid targeted to mean arterial pressure, urine output and lactate clearance, adding norepinephrine if hypotension persists after adequate fluid loading, and manage in an intensive care setting. Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately after the blood cultures already drawn, covering enteric gram-negative organisms, enterococci and anaerobes, with the choice reflecting local resistance patterns and his prior instrumentation, which raises the risk of resistant organisms; narrow therapy once blood and bile culture results return. Keep him nil by mouth and provide analgesia and antiemetics. Arrange urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy revision, stone extraction and biliary stent or nasobiliary drain placement as early as possible, ideally within a few hours, because emergent decompression is the definitive intervention in cholangitis with shock; involve gastroenterology and hepatobiliary surgery simultaneously so that alternatives are ready. Correct coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia if present before endoscopic sphincterotomy, and review and hold any anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. Regarding additional considerations: if ERCP fails or is not technically possible, proceed without delay to percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage, with open or laparoscopic common bile duct exploration reserved as a last resort in a septic elderly patient. The positive Murphy sign raises the possibility of concurrent acute cholecystitis, so reassess the gallbladder after decompression and plan definitive cholecystectomy during the same admission or shortly after recovery once sepsis has resolved, since stones recur and he has already had one prior episode; if he is not a surgical candidate, consider percutaneous cholecystostomy. Monitor closely for complications including acute kidney injury from hypoperfusion, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatic abscess and post-ERCP pancreatitis. Follow lactate serially as a marker of resuscitation adequacy, and escalate care immediately if mental status deteriorates, completing Reynolds' pentad.
Notes: Antibiotics and fluids are temporizing measures only; failure to achieve urgent biliary decompression in obstructive cholangitis with shock carries very high mortality, and the procedure should not be deferred for full hemodynamic normalization.

Age: 3 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Low-grade fever of 37.8C with small blisters on the hands and feet noticed this morning and a few small sores inside the mouth, with slightly increased fussiness but preserved eating and drinking.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of hand, foot and mouth disease, a self-limited viral exanthem most often caused by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71. The strongest supporting facts are the highly specific anatomic distribution of scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles and a few on the dorsal hands, together with two shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa, in the setting of a low-grade fever of 37.8C. The epidemiologic link is decisive: several children at her daycare have had similar symptoms, which fits the well-known pattern of outbreaks among young children in group childcare settings through fecal-oral and respiratory transmission. Age of 3 years is typical, as the disease predominantly affects children under 5. Most importantly, the clinical status is entirely reassuring: the child is alert, playful and well-hydrated, and she is eating and drinking well despite being slightly fussier than usual, which excludes the principal complication of this illness, namely dehydration from painful oral ulcers causing refusal to drink. Differential considerations include herpetic gingivostomatitis, which typically causes more extensive and painful gingival involvement with perioral vesicles and higher fever without palm and sole lesions; herpangina, which produces posterior oropharyngeal vesicles without the acral rash; varicella, which produces a generalized centripetal rash in successive crops of lesions at different stages rather than a palm-and-sole distribution; erythema multiforme, which shows target lesions; and hand dermatitis or scabies, which are neither febrile nor associated with oral ulcers or a daycare cluster. Bacterial infection is not supported, as there is no high fever, toxicity or lymphadenopathy. Complaint: Four-month history of gradually increasing lethargy and worsening memory, with her daughter concerned that she has stopped remembering whether she has taken her medications and may no longer be safe living alone.

Essentially every element of the clinical picture is explained by this single diagnosis. Constitutional and metabolic features include fatigue, persistent cold intolerance so severe that she wears a wool sweater and several layers in 89-degree weather, a measured temperature of 35.8C, and paradoxical 5 kg weight gain despite a poor appetite. Dermatologic and ENT features include dry skin, coarse and sparse hair with loss of the outer eyebrows, hoarseness, throat fullness and periorbital and facial puffiness, all classic for myxedema. Cardiovascular features include bradycardia at 56 beats per minute and peripheral edema, and it is notable that her previous palpitations have ceased over the last two months, which reflects slowing of her known atrial fibrillation as hypothyroidism deepened; her rhythm remains irregularly irregular. Gastrointestinal slowing produced constipation from daily to every three to four days requiring laxatives, with hard stool in the rectum and left iliac fossa discomfort, and occult blood is negative. Neuromuscular features include proximal lower limb weakness at 4+/5, generally decreased deep tendon reflexes with the characteristic prolonged relaxation phase, slow movements and slow speech. Hematologically there is normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, a recognized consequence of hypothyroidism. Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette, small fluid in the right interlobar fissure and bibasilar atelectasis, and there are fine bibasilar end-inspiratory crackles, raising the question of pericardial effusion, a classic myxedematous complication, alongside her known left ventricular failure history and furosemide use. Depressed mood, social withdrawal and staying in bed are also consistent with hypothyroid depression. The critical clinical reasoning point is the differential for the memory complaint: this must not be labeled as degenerative dementia. Head CT is normal, the onset was subacute over four months in a woman previously very active in community activities, and the entire syndrome is accompanied by systemic hypothyroid features, so this is a reversible metabolic encephalopathy rather than Alzheimer disease. Other differentials to consider are depression with pseudodementia, which is likely contributory, B12 deficiency, normal pressure hydrocephalus, excluded by a normal head CT, subdural hematoma, also excluded by CT, medication effects from bisoprolol contributing to bradycardia and fatigue, and anemia contributing to fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Her new exertional dyspnea after half a flight of stairs, bibasilar crackles and leg edema require distinguishing hypothyroid-related fluid retention and possible pericardial effusion from decompensated heart failure in a patient with prior fast atrial fibrillation complicated by acute left ventricular failure. Although she is hypothermic, bradycardic and profoundly hypothyroid, she is not comatose, her mental status shows slowing rather than obtundation, sodium is normal at 135 mEq/L, and respirations are 16 without evidence of hypoventilation, so this is severe hypothyroidism that has not progressed to myxedema coma, but she sits close to that threshold and warrants prompt, closely supervised treatment.

The apparent dementia is a reversible metabolic encephalopathy, not a neurodegenerative process, as supported by the normal head CT and the subacute onset alongside systemic hypothyroid features. She has not progressed to myxedema coma, but the disease is advanced and requires prompt, carefully titrated levothyroxine replacement, exclusion of adrenal insufficiency and pericardial effusion, and attention to home safety and medication adherence.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Initiate levothyroxine replacement promptly, but start at a low dose and titrate upward slowly rather than beginning at a full replacement dose, because she is 68 years old with known cardiac disease including atrial fibrillation and a prior admission with fast atrial fibrillation complicated by acute left ventricular failure; rapid restoration of euthyroidism in this setting risks precipitating tachyarrhythmia, angina or heart failure. Before the first dose, check morning cortisol and exclude adrenal insufficiency, and if there is any doubt, give glucocorticoid cover first. Recheck TSH and free T4 six to eight weeks after each dose change and titrate to a TSH in the normal range, taking levothyroxine on an empty stomach separated from other medications and from calcium or iron supplements. Obtain an echocardiogram to assess for pericardial effusion suggested by the enlarged heart on chest x-ray, and review the ECG for low voltage and for rate and rhythm. Monitor the INR closely and more frequently than usual, since correcting hypothyroidism increases the metabolism of clotting factors and typically reduces warfarin requirements, creating a real bleeding risk as she becomes euthyroid; her warfarin dose will likely need adjustment. Reassess bisoprolol as she becomes euthyroid, since her bradycardia at 56 beats per minute is partly drug-related and partly hypothyroid, and heart rate will rise with treatment. Reassess furosemide and blood pressure control as myxedematous fluid retention resolves. Regarding additional considerations: investigate and treat the normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL by checking iron studies, B12 and folate, recognizing that hypothyroidism itself is a cause and that anemia contributes to her fatigue and exertional dyspnea; treat the constipation with adequate hydration, fiber and an osmotic laxative and disimpact the hard rectal stool as needed, expecting improvement with thyroid replacement; address the safety concern raised by her daughter by arranging supervision of medication administration with a pill organizer or blister pack or family oversight, and by performing a home safety and functional assessment, since inability to remember whether medications have been taken is particularly hazardous while she is on warfarin; document her cognition formally now and repeat testing after three to six months of euthyroidism, deferring any diagnosis of dementia until thyroid function has been corrected and re-evaluating for degenerative causes only if deficits persist; her depressed mood should be monitored and reassessed after treatment, as hypothyroid depression frequently remits with replacement, and she denies suicidal thoughts; monitor for angina, palpitations, worsening dyspnea, orthopnea or edema during titration and slow the dose escalation if these appear; and counsel her that levothyroxine will be lifelong, that adherence is essential, and that she should seek urgent care for confusion, drowsiness, hypothermia, severe bradycardia or breathlessness, which would suggest progression toward myxedema coma.
Notes: Levothyroxine must not be started before adrenal insufficiency is excluded or empirically covered. Warfarin sensitivity increases as euthyroidism is restored, so INR monitoring must be intensified during titration.

She initially had fevers as high as 101 for 2 days, but those have now resolved. In the office, she has normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. She is otherwise healthy except for high cholesterol for which she is being treated with atorvastatin. She has no drug allergies.

"role_name": "Family Physician",
"role_description": (
    "Provides first-contact outpatient evaluation of adults with acute cough lasting less than three weeks. "
    "Separates uncomplicated acute bronchitis from community acquired pneumonia, influenza, pertussis, and acute sinusitis using vital signs, oxygen saturation, and careful chest auscultation rather than sputum color. "
    "Reviews comorbidity and medication for cardiac and drug induced causes, sets expectations for a cough that often persists several weeks, advises symptomatic care, and defines the red flags that should prompt return."

"role_description": (
    "Decides whether an antibiotic is genuinely indicated in an acute exacerbation of airway disease and selects the narrowest effective agent. "

    "Doses systemic corticosteroids, screens for interactions with existing inhaled and cardiovascular therapy, and counsels on adherence and on when to seek review."
)

)

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
