Vignette:
Mrs. L is a 61 year-old woman who presents with 4 days of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Her symptoms started 4 days ago with rhinorrhea and productive cough. She initially had fevers as high as 101 for 2 days, but those have now resolved. In the office, she has normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. She is otherwise healthy except for high cholesterol for which she is being treated with atorvastatin. She has no drug allergies.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 61 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Four days of cough productive of yellow sputum, which began with rhinorrhea and productive cough and was accompanied by fevers up to 101 degrees Fahrenheit for the first two days that have now resolved.
Analysis: This is acute bronchitis, almost certainly viral, following an upper respiratory infection. The strongest supporting facts are the short four-day course beginning with rhinorrhea, which locates the onset in the upper airway and is typical of a viral prodrome; the subsequent productive cough; and, decisively, normal vital signs and a completely normal physical examination in the office. The absence of tachycardia, tachypnea, fever at presentation and any abnormal lung findings such as crackles, bronchial breath sounds, dullness to percussion or egophony makes pneumonia very unlikely, since the negative predictive value of normal vital signs combined with a normal chest examination is high. The yellow color of the sputum is frequently misinterpreted: purulent-appearing sputum reflects the presence of inflammatory cells and desquamated epithelium and does not distinguish bacterial from viral infection, so it is not by itself an indication for antibiotics. The fever that lasted two days and then resolved spontaneously fits the natural history of a self-limited viral illness rather than an untreated bacterial pneumonia, which would typically be associated with persisting or worsening fever and systemic signs. Her background is low risk: she is otherwise healthy apart from hypercholesterolemia treated with atorvastatin, and she has no drug allergies. There is no immunosuppression, no chronic lung disease and no comorbidity described that would raise the threshold of concern. Differential considerations include community-acquired pneumonia, which is argued against by normal vitals and normal examination; influenza or other viral respiratory infection, which is entirely compatible and is likely the underlying cause; pertussis, which should be considered if cough becomes paroxysmal, is followed by post-tussive vomiting or whoop, or persists for many weeks; acute exacerbation of undiagnosed asthma or COPD, not supported by an absence of wheeze or dyspnea and no smoking history given; sinusitis, possible after the rhinorrhea but not indicated by any facial pain or purulent nasal discharge described; and heart failure or pulmonary embolism, which are not supported by any dyspnea, chest pain, edema or hemodynamic abnormality. Acute bronchitis is self-limited, with cough typically lasting two to three weeks and sometimes longer, and the central management task is symptomatic relief plus patient education to set expectations and avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Uncomplicated acute bronchitis, most likely viral, in an otherwise healthy 61-year-old woman four days into a self-limited respiratory illness that began with rhinorrhea and brief fever which has already resolved. Normal vital signs and a normal chest examination effectively exclude pneumonia, so no chest radiograph, sputum culture or laboratory testing is required, and antibiotics are not indicated despite yellow sputum. Symptomatic care with clear guidance on the expected duration of cough and on warning signs that should prompt reevaluation is the appropriate management.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Provide symptomatic treatment and explicit patient education. Explain that the illness is viral, that antibiotics will not shorten it or prevent complications, and that yellow or green sputum is not evidence of bacterial infection; this counseling is the key intervention because it addresses the most likely expectation driving the visit. Set the expectation that cough commonly persists for two to three weeks and may last longer, so that persistence alone does not prompt an unnecessary return or antibiotic prescription. Recommend adequate hydration, rest, honey or warm fluids for cough relief, humidified air, and over-the-counter analgesics or antipyretics as needed for discomfort; an over-the-counter cough suppressant may be used at night if cough disturbs sleep, recognizing that the evidence for benefit is modest. Continue atorvastatin. Regarding additional considerations, instruct her to return or seek urgent evaluation if she develops shortness of breath, pleuritic or persistent chest pain, recurrence or persistence of fever beyond a few days, rigors, hemoptysis, confusion, or if she feels progressively worse rather than gradually better, since these would prompt a chest radiograph and reassessment for pneumonia. If wheeze or exertional dyspnea emerges, evaluate for a bronchospastic component and consider a trial of an inhaled bronchodilator. If cough persists beyond about three weeks, or becomes paroxysmal with post-tussive vomiting, consider pertussis and other causes such as postnasal drip, gastroesophageal reflux and asthma, and reevaluate accordingly. Use this visit to confirm that age-appropriate preventive care is current, including annual influenza vaccination, COVID-19 vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination, which is indicated in her age group and would reduce the risk of future respiratory infection. Advise hand hygiene and cough etiquette to limit transmission.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 9 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Eight hours of episodic inconsolable crying with drawing the legs up to the abdomen, alternating with periods of lethargy; two episodes of vomiting and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material.
Analysis: The presentation is a textbook picture of ileocolic intussusception in an infant. The strongest supporting facts are the paroxysmal colicky crying with leg-drawing alternating with lethargy between attacks, vomiting, passage of dark red mucoid (currant jelly) stool confirmed on rectal examination, a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant with an empty right lower quadrant (Dance sign), and an abdominal ultrasound showing the target/doughnut sign in the right upper quadrant. The age of 9 months is the peak incidence window, and the preceding viral upper respiratory infection last week fits the typical antecedent lymphoid hyperplasia acting as a lead point. Vital signs show tachycardia (HR 168) with pallor and lethargy in the pain-free interval, indicating early hypovolemia and systemic compromise rather than a benign colic. Differential considerations that were weighed and are less consistent with the case include simple viral gastroenteritis (would not produce a palpable sausage-shaped mass, Dance sign, or a sonographic target sign), infantile colic (does not cause bloody stool, lethargy, or an abdominal mass), incarcerated hernia and malrotation with midgut volvulus (both can cause obstruction and vomiting, but the ultrasound findings here are diagnostic of intussusception), Meckel diverticulum bleeding (usually painless bleeding, though it can serve as a lead point), and Henoch-Schonlein purpura (no rash or joint findings are described). The ultrasound explicitly shows no perforation and no peritonitis, which is what makes non-operative air enema reduction the appropriate next step rather than immediate laparotomy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Abdominal ultrasound has already established the diagnosis; the needed next study is the fluoroscopy-guided air (pneumatic) enema, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is already arranged. Continuous vital sign monitoring with pulse oximetry, and intravenous access for fluid resuscitation, are required during the procedure. A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. baseline_protocol:
Age: 70 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three days of dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency with mild suprapubic discomfort and a low-grade fever of 100.4 F, on a background of benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with tamsulosin.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of a urinary tract infection in an older man, which by convention is treated as a complicated urinary tract infection because of male sex and the presence of an anatomic predisposing factor, benign prostatic hyperplasia. The strongest supporting facts are the classic irritative voiding triad of dysuria, frequency and urgency lasting three days, mild suprapubic tenderness on abdominal examination, and a urinalysis showing pyuria with positive nitrites, the latter indicating nitrate-reducing organisms such as Escherichia coli and other Enterobacterales. Localization within the urinary tract is important. The absence of flank pain, the absence of rigors, and the presence of only a low-grade temperature of 100.4 F with normal blood pressure of 138/82 and heart rate of 78 and no acute distress argue against acute pyelonephritis and against urosepsis. The digital rectal examination shows an enlarged but nontender prostate, which makes acute bacterial prostatitis unlikely, since that condition characteristically produces an exquisitely tender, boggy prostate along with high fever and systemic toxicity. The suprapubic tenderness together with the irritative symptoms localizes the infection to the bladder, supporting cystitis in a male with BPH. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include acute pyelonephritis (no flank or costovertebral angle tenderness, no rigors), acute bacterial prostatitis (prostate is nontender), urolithiasis (no colicky pain, no hematuria), bladder malignancy (no hematuria, and the acute febrile onset with pyuria and nitrites favors infection), and simple BPH progression with lower urinary tract symptoms alone (would not produce fever, pyuria or nitrites). Underlying BPH is clinically relevant because incomplete bladder emptying and post-void residual urine predispose to infection and to recurrence, and because bladder outlet obstruction can be aggravated by the infection.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing obtained before starting antibiotics, to confirm the pathogen and guide definitive therapy in this complicated infection. Post-void residual urine measurement by bladder ultrasound or bladder scan, given the known benign prostatic hyperplasia, to assess for incomplete emptying or urinary retention. Basic renal function testing including serum creatinine to guide antibiotic dosing in a 70-year-old. Blood cultures are not required at present in the absence of rigors, hemodynamic instability or signs of systemic infection. Cross-sectional or upper tract imaging is not needed unless the patient fails to improve on appropriate therapy.
Conclusion: A 70-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has a febrile lower urinary tract infection, that is, a complicated cystitis, supported by dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic tenderness, low-grade fever, pyuria and positive nitrites, with no clinical evidence of pyelonephritis, prostatitis or sepsis. He is hemodynamically stable and can be managed as an outpatient with a urine culture and an appropriately long course of oral antibiotics, with attention to his underlying outlet obstruction.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Send a urine culture with susceptibilities before the first antibiotic dose, then start empiric oral antibiotic therapy directed at Enterobacterales and chosen according to local resistance patterns and the patient's renal function; because this is a complicated urinary tract infection in a male with BPH, use an agent with adequate tissue penetration and treat for a longer course than the short regimens used for uncomplicated female cystitis, then narrow or adjust the antibiotic once culture and sensitivity results return. Advise adequate oral hydration and antipyretic or analgesic therapy for the dysuria and low-grade fever. Continue tamsulosin, which also helps bladder emptying. Measure post-void residual urine, since significant retention from his enlarged prostate would predispose to treatment failure and recurrence and might require catheter drainage or escalation of BPH therapy. Arrange clinical follow-up in 48 to 72 hours to confirm symptomatic improvement, and instruct the patient to seek immediate care if he develops flank pain, rigors, high fever, vomiting, confusion, inability to pass urine, or lightheadedness, as these would signal progression to pyelonephritis, urinary retention or sepsis and would change the disposition to emergent care. Regarding the additional considerations, the nontender prostate on rectal examination argues against acute bacterial prostatitis, but if symptoms persist or relapse after therapy, prostatic involvement or an unrecognized obstructive or structural abnormality should be reconsidered and urologic evaluation of the underlying BPH pursued, including assessment of whether his lower urinary tract symptoms and residual volume warrant a change in medical management. Avoid vigorous prostatic massage in the setting of suspected urinary infection. Because of his age, review his renal function and drug interactions when selecting the antibiotic dose.
Notes: This is by definition a complicated urinary tract infection because the patient is male and has benign prostatic hyperplasia, so a short-course regimen is inappropriate and a urine culture is mandatory. The distinction from acute bacterial prostatitis rests here on the nontender prostate and mild systemic findings; if the course deviates from expected, that diagnosis should be revisited. No allergy history, renal function values or prior culture data are specified in the case, and these would influence antibiotic selection.

She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. baseline_protocol:
Age: 66 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent, with no passage of flatus or stool for 36 hours.
Analysis: This is a complete mechanical small bowel obstruction, most likely adhesive, with imaging and laboratory features that raise serious concern for strangulation. The strongest supporting facts for mechanical obstruction are the cardinal tetrad of crampy abdominal pain, vomiting that has progressed to bilious and then feculent character, abdominal distension, and obstipation with no flatus or stool for 36 hours; the markedly distended tympanitic abdomen with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds; and the CT showing dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant and a small bowel feces sign. The etiology is almost certainly adhesive, given the two prior open abdominal operations, an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago, and the transition point in the right lower quadrant corresponds to the site of the previous appendectomy. Several findings elevate this from simple obstruction to a surgical emergency with suspected compromised bowel: the possible closed-loop configuration on CT, the involuntary guarding on examination, the low-grade fever of 37.8 C, the tachycardia of 110, the leukocytosis of 14,800, and above all the elevated lactate of 3.1 mmol/L, which together suggest bowel ischemia or impending strangulation. A closed-loop obstruction has a high risk of progressing rapidly to strangulation, necrosis and perforation and does not resolve with conservative management. The patient is also volume depleted with a prerenal pattern of renal impairment, BUN 42 with creatinine 1.6 giving a markedly elevated BUN to creatinine ratio, consistent with dehydration from the vomiting and third spacing, and her blood pressure of 108/68 with tachycardia indicates compensated hypovolemia. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include adynamic ileus (excluded by the discrete transition point and the tinkling hyperactive bowel sounds rather than a silent abdomen), large bowel obstruction from colonic malignancy or volvulus (the CT localizes dilatation to the small bowel with a small bowel transition point), incarcerated hernia (no hernia is described, but this is a classic cause and the CT identifies an intraluminal or adhesive transition point instead), Crohn stricture or malignancy at the transition point (possible but less likely given the adhesive surgical history), and gastroenteritis (does not cause obstipation, a transition point or a closed loop). The small bowel feces sign indicates a longer standing and more distal obstruction with stasis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: The CT abdomen has already established the diagnosis and the transition point, so no further diagnostic imaging is needed before intervention. Needed next are a type and screen or crossmatch and coagulation studies in preparation for operation, a complete metabolic panel with electrolytes to identify and correct the hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis expected from protracted vomiting, serial lactate measurement to track ischemia, and a repeat complete blood count. Continuous cardiac and hemodynamic monitoring with pulse oximetry, urinary catheter placement for accurate urine output measurement during resuscitation, and preoperative anesthetic assessment including an electrocardiogram in a 66-year-old undergoing urgent laparotomy. Blood cultures if fever progresses. Nasogastric tube placement is a therapeutic and monitoring measure rather than a diagnostic test.
Conclusion: A 66-year-old woman with two prior open abdominal operations has a complete mechanical small bowel obstruction, almost certainly adhesive, with a right lower quadrant transition point, small bowel feces sign and a possible closed loop on CT. Peritoneal signs with guarding, fever, leukocytosis, tachycardia and lactate of 3.1 mmol/L indicate suspected strangulation with bowel ischemia, superimposed on hypovolemia with prerenal acute kidney injury. This is a surgical emergency requiring resuscitation and urgent operative exploration rather than a trial of non-operative management.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Admit immediately and involve the general surgery team without delay. Keep the patient nil per os, place two large-bore intravenous catheters and begin aggressive isotonic crystalloid resuscitation targeted to heart rate, blood pressure and urine output, since she is dehydrated with a heart rate of 110, blood pressure of 108/68 and a BUN of 42 with creatinine 1.6 reflecting prerenal injury. Place a nasogastric tube on suction to decompress the stomach and control the feculent vomiting, which also reduces the substantial risk of aspiration. Insert a urinary catheter to monitor output. Correct electrolyte abnormalities, particularly potassium and chloride depletion from protracted vomiting, and repeat the lactate to see whether it clears with resuscitation. Give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering enteric gram-negative organisms and anaerobes in view of the fever, leukocytosis, guarding and suspected bowel compromise, and provide adequate analgesia and antiemetics. Regarding the additional considerations, the possible closed-loop configuration on CT combined with involuntary guarding, fever, leukocytosis and lactate of 3.1 mmol/L is the decisive point: a trial of non-operative management with nasogastric decompression, which would otherwise be reasonable for uncomplicated adhesive small bowel obstruction, is contraindicated here, and she should proceed to urgent operative exploration, laparotomy or laparoscopy, with adhesiolysis and assessment of bowel viability and resection of any non-viable segment. Do not delay operation for a water-soluble contrast challenge. Obtain informed consent including the possibility of bowel resection and stoma, arrange type and screen, and complete a rapid preoperative anesthetic evaluation while resuscitation proceeds. Postoperatively continue fluid and electrolyte management, monitor renal function for resolution of the prerenal injury, provide venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and use early mobilization and a structured feeding plan as bowel function returns.
Notes: Resuscitation should be started concurrently with, and must not delay, definitive operative management when strangulation is suspected. Lactate and leukocytosis are supportive but not fully sensitive for bowel ischemia, and normal values would not have excluded it; conversely, the elevated lactate may partly reflect hypovolemia, so it should be rechecked after fluid loading. No allergy history, medication list, comorbidities or prior obstruction episodes are specified in the case, and these would influence antibiotic choice and perioperative risk assessment.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 40 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Severe bilateral leg pain and numbness after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall for approximately 4 hours with both lower extremities pinned, with dark brown urine and markedly reduced urine output since extrication.
Analysis: This is crush syndrome, that is, traumatic rhabdomyolysis with systemic consequences, following a 4-hour crush injury to both lower extremities. The strongest supporting facts are the mechanism of prolonged compression, the massively elevated creatine kinase of 124,000 U/L and myoglobin of 48,000 ng/mL, and the dark brown urine, which reflects myoglobinuria rather than hematuria. Myoglobin released from necrotic muscle is directly nephrotoxic, causes intratubular cast formation and renal vasoconstriction, and together with the hypovolemia of third spacing into the injured limbs has already produced acute kidney injury, evidenced by creatinine 3.4 mg/dL and oliguria of only 50 mL over 2 hours. The classic biochemical signature of muscle necrosis is fully present: hyperkalemia at 6.8 mEq/L from release of intracellular potassium, hyperphosphatemia at 7.6 mg/dL, hypocalcemia at 6.2 mg/dL from calcium deposition in damaged muscle and binding by phosphate, hyperuricemia at 14.2 mg/dL, and high anion gap metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate 14 mEq/L and lactate 6.8 mmol/L. The most immediately life-threatening problem is the hyperkalemia with established electrocardiographic toxicity, since the ECG already shows peaked T waves, which can progress to widened QRS, a sine wave pattern and cardiac arrest; this is compounded by the hypocalcemia and the acidosis, both of which aggravate the cardiac effects of potassium. The second major threat is bilateral lower extremity compartment syndrome. The limbs are markedly swollen, tense and ecchymotic from thigh to ankle, sensation is diminished throughout both legs, the patient reports severe pain and numbness, and pedal pulses are weak bilaterally; distal pulses are typically preserved until late in compartment syndrome, so weak pulses in this context are an ominous rather than a reassuring finding. The tachycardia of 118 with blood pressure 96/62 and respiratory rate 24 reflects hypovolemia from massive third-space sequestration into the crushed muscle together with compensation for metabolic acidosis. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include primary arterial injury or vascular occlusion (possible but the diffuse bilateral tense swelling with the crush mechanism and biochemical profile points to compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis), hemorrhagic shock from other injuries (the hypotension is more consistent with third spacing, but occult trauma must be excluded by a full trauma survey), acute tubular necrosis from ischemia alone (contributory, but the myoglobin and CK values identify pigment nephropathy), and hematuria from urologic trauma (the urine is described as dark brown with markedly elevated myoglobin, indicating pigment rather than blood). The initiated management, aggressive normal saline at 1.5 L per hour with sodium bicarbonate, continuous cardiac monitoring and intravenous calcium gluconate for cardioprotection, is appropriate and addresses volume depletion, urinary alkalinization to reduce myoglobin cast precipitation, and membrane stabilization against hyperkalemia.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring with serial electrocardiograms to follow hyperkalemic changes. Frequent serial measurement of potassium, calcium, phosphate, bicarbonate, creatinine, urea and creatine kinase, with arterial or venous blood gas to follow the acidosis and serial lactate. Hourly urine output measurement via the indwelling Foley catheter and urine dipstick or urinalysis to document pigment (heme-positive dipstick with few red cells). Compartment pressure measurement of all compartments of both lower extremities with a needle manometry device, and calculation of the delta pressure against diastolic blood pressure, to confirm compartment syndrome. Full trauma assessment with primary and secondary survey and appropriate trauma imaging to exclude other crush-related injuries, including radiographs of the lower extremities for fracture, and evaluation for pelvic or intra-abdominal injury given the mechanism. Type and screen with coagulation studies including fibrinogen and platelet count to assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Central venous access and invasive hemodynamic or ultrasound-based volume assessment to guide the very large fluid volumes. Early nephrology consultation with preparation for renal replacement therapy, including vascular access for dialysis.
Conclusion: A 40-year-old man has crush syndrome after a 4-hour bilateral lower extremity crush injury, manifesting as severe rhabdomyolysis with CK 124,000 U/L and myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, life-threatening hyperkalemia of 6.8 mEq/L with peaked T waves on ECG, oliguric acute kidney injury with creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, high anion gap metabolic acidosis with lactate 6.8 mmol/L, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia and hypocalcemia, together with clinically evident bilateral lower extremity compartment syndrome. He is hypovolemic and at imminent risk of cardiac arrest and irreversible limb loss, and requires simultaneous emergency treatment of hyperkalemia, aggressive volume resuscitation, urgent surgical decompression and preparation for renal replacement therapy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Treat the hyperkalemia as an immediate threat to life. Continue the intravenous calcium gluconate already given for myocardial membrane stabilization and repeat it if the electrocardiographic changes persist or worsen, and add potassium-shifting therapy with intravenous insulin plus dextrose and nebulized high-dose beta-2 agonist, with sodium bicarbonate contributing both to shifting potassium and to correcting the acidosis of bicarbonate 14 mEq/L. Recognize that these measures are temporizing only, since the potassium load will continue to be released from necrotic muscle, so arrange emergency dialysis access and early nephrology involvement; with potassium 6.8 mEq/L, ECG changes, oliguria of 50 mL in 2 hours, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL and severe acidosis, renal replacement therapy is likely to be required and should be prepared for without waiting for further deterioration. Avoid all potassium-containing fluids, including lactated Ringer solution, and avoid nephrotoxic drugs and radiographic contrast where possible. Continue the aggressive normal saline resuscitation, but titrate to hourly urine output and monitor closely for volume overload and pulmonary edema, particularly because the patient is already oliguric and may not respond to fluid; large-volume resuscitation in an anuric patient risks fluid overload and mandates dialysis rather than continued escalation. Obtain urgent orthopedic or trauma surgical consultation for bilateral lower extremity fasciotomy: the tense swollen ecchymotic limbs, severe pain, diffusely diminished sensation and weak pedal pulses constitute clinical compartment syndrome, and measured compartment pressures should confirm it, but treatment must not be delayed for measurement if the clinical picture is unequivocal, since irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis occurs within hours. Regarding the additional considerations, monitor the hypocalcemia carefully but do not aggressively correct asymptomatic hypocalcemia beyond what is needed for cardioprotection, because calcium administered during the injury phase deposits in damaged muscle and rebound hypercalcemia is common in the recovery phase; give calcium primarily for cardiac protection against hyperkalemia and for symptomatic tetany or arrhythmia. Monitor the acid-base status while giving bicarbonate, since overcorrection can worsen hypocalcemia and precipitate calcium phosphate deposition given the phosphorus of 7.6 mg/dL. Provide adequate analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis and wound care, and consider antibiotic prophylaxis for open wounds or after fasciotomy. Complete a full trauma survey to exclude other injuries from the wall collapse, obtain limb radiographs for fracture, and check coagulation for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Admit to an intensive care unit with continuous cardiac monitoring, hourly urine output, and repeated laboratory testing every few hours during the acute phase, and follow creatine kinase serially to confirm it is trending down. Plan for prolonged multidisciplinary care involving critical care, nephrology, orthopedic surgery and rehabilitation.
Notes: Hyperkalemia in crush syndrome is recurrent and ongoing because necrotic muscle continues to release potassium, so temporizing measures must be repeated and definitive removal by dialysis anticipated. Distal pulses may remain palpable in compartment syndrome, so their presence never excludes the diagnosis, and here they are already weak. Fasciotomy in crush injury carries a risk of infection and of a surge in systemic potassium and myoglobin on reperfusion, so it should be performed with the patient monitored and resuscitated. The benefit of sodium bicarbonate and urinary alkalinization is debated and is secondary to adequate volume resuscitation. No allergy history, medication list or details of other injuries are specified in the case.

Vignette:
A 47-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life that began 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement. She describes it as a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds. She experienced one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Her past medical history includes migraines and she is a current smoker. On examination, she is photophobic, irritable, and has a stiff neck. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 178/96, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals intact cranial nerves, mild bilateral lower extremity weakness, and pronounced nuchal rigidity. Hunt and Hess grade III. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 47 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden onset of the worst headache of her life beginning 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, with one episode of vomiting, brief loss of consciousness, photophobia and neck stiffness.
Analysis: This is aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, and the diagnosis is already established rather than merely suspected. The strongest supporting facts are the thunderclap character of the headache, described as the worst of her life and reaching maximum intensity within seconds, its onset during Valsalva while straining at stool, which is a classic precipitant through an acute rise in transmural pressure across the aneurysm wall, the associated vomiting and brief loss of consciousness reflecting a transient surge in intracranial pressure, and the meningeal signs of photophobia, irritability and pronounced nuchal rigidity from blood irritating the meninges. Confirmation is definitive: non-contrast CT of the head shows diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns, and CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm as the culprit lesion. The blood pressure of 178/96 is markedly elevated and represents both a stress response and a major modifiable risk factor for rebleeding before the aneurysm is secured. She is classified as Hunt and Hess grade III, corresponding to drowsiness, confusion or mild focal deficit, which is consistent with her irritability and mild bilateral lower extremity weakness; that weakness is anatomically explained by the anterior communicating artery location, since this aneurysm sits adjacent to the medial frontal lobes supplied by the anterior cerebral arteries, whose territory includes the paracentral lobules controlling the legs. Her risk factors include current smoking, a well-established risk factor for aneurysm formation and rupture. The history of migraines is a relevant distractor, since a prior headache disorder can lead to anchoring and to under-investigation of a thunderclap headache; however, the abrupt maximal onset, the meningismus, the transient loss of consciousness and the imaging findings are entirely inconsistent with migraine. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include migraine (does not cause thunderclap onset with nuchal rigidity, loss of consciousness or CT-proven subarachnoid blood), bacterial meningitis (can cause headache, photophobia and neck stiffness, but the onset would not be instantaneous and the CT demonstrates hemorrhage; temperature is only 37.4 C), reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and cervical artery dissection (both cause thunderclap headache but are excluded by the demonstrated aneurysm and basal cistern hemorrhage), pituitary apoplexy and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (excluded by imaging), and hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage (the pattern is subarachnoid in the basal cisterns with an identified aneurysm). The overriding clinical priorities now are prevention of rebleeding, which carries very high mortality and is greatest in the first 24 hours, early securing of the aneurysm, and anticipation of hydrocephalus, delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm, seizures, hyponatremia and cardiac complications.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Digital subtraction cerebral angiography for definitive aneurysm characterization and treatment planning, and as the platform for endovascular coiling if that route is chosen. Continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring, ideally with an arterial line, in a neurocritical care setting, with frequent neurological observations and serial Glasgow Coma Scale scoring. Baseline complete blood count, coagulation studies, comprehensive metabolic panel with serum sodium, and type and screen in preparation for intervention. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram and cardiac troponin, since subarachnoid hemorrhage commonly causes neurogenic myocardial injury, arrhythmia and stress cardiomyopathy. Repeat non-contrast CT head if there is any neurological deterioration, to detect rebleeding or acute hydrocephalus. Transcranial Doppler ultrasonography from the following days onward, or CT angiography with perfusion imaging, to screen for and evaluate cerebral vasospasm. Serial serum sodium measurement to detect hyponatremia from cerebral salt wasting or syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone. Lumbar puncture is not required, since the CT is already diagnostic. External ventricular drain capability must be available if hydrocephalus develops.
Conclusion: A 47-year-old woman with a thunderclap headache precipitated by straining has aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, Hunt and Hess grade III, with diffuse basal cistern hemorrhage on CT and a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm on CT angiography, accompanied by meningismus, transient loss of consciousness, mild bilateral leg weakness and severe hypertension at 178/96. This is a time-critical neurosurgical emergency; she requires immediate neurocritical care admission, blood pressure control to prevent rebleeding, nimodipine for prevention of delayed cerebral ischemia, and urgent definitive securing of the aneurysm by clipping or coiling within the first 24 hours.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Admit immediately to a neurointensive care unit at a center with both neurosurgical and neurointerventional capability, and activate the neurosurgery and neurointerventional teams at once. Secure the airway if the level of consciousness declines, but she is currently alert enough at Hunt and Hess grade III that airway protection should be reassessed continuously rather than assumed. Control the blood pressure of 178/96 with a titratable intravenous antihypertensive agent to reduce the risk of rebleeding, avoiding abrupt or excessive lowering that would compromise cerebral perfusion pressure, and maintain the target continuously until the aneurysm is secured. Start oral nimodipine as soon as possible and continue it for the standard course, as it reduces poor outcome from delayed cerebral ischemia. Provide effective analgesia and antiemetics, since pain, vomiting and agitation all raise blood pressure and intracranial pressure, and treat her irritability with attention to avoiding oversedation that would obscure neurological monitoring. Institute strict measures to avoid Valsalva, including stool softeners and laxatives, which is directly relevant since her hemorrhage was precipitated by straining at stool; this must be addressed explicitly to prevent a repeat pressure surge. Maintain euvolemia with isotonic fluids, avoid hypotonic fluids, keep the head of the bed elevated, and enforce bed rest with a quiet environment. Arrange urgent definitive treatment of the 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm by endovascular coiling or microsurgical clipping, with the modality decided by the neurovascular team based on aneurysm morphology and patient factors; the aneurysm should be secured as early as feasible, ideally within 24 hours, because rebleeding risk is highest in that window. Regarding the additional considerations, anticipate and monitor for the major complications: acute hydrocephalus from blood obstructing cerebrospinal fluid pathways, which may require external ventricular drainage and should be suspected if consciousness declines; delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm, typically between days 4 and 14, monitored clinically and with transcranial Doppler; seizures, for which short-term prophylaxis may be considered in the pre-securing period; hyponatremia from cerebral salt wasting or inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, requiring serial sodium monitoring and avoidance of fluid restriction that would worsen cerebral perfusion; and neurogenic cardiac injury, warranting electrocardiogram and troponin. Screen for and correct any coagulopathy and reverse antithrombotic agents if any are found. Counsel on complete and permanent smoking cessation, since current smoking is her identified modifiable risk factor for both the original aneurysm and future ones. Once she recovers, arrange neurovascular follow-up imaging for aneurysm durability and for de novo aneurysm surveillance, and discuss screening implications for first-degree relatives. Document that the prior migraine history did not account for this event so that future thunderclap headaches are not misattributed.
Notes: The pre-existing migraine history is a diagnostic trap; a thunderclap headache must never be attributed to migraine, and here imaging has proven subarachnoid hemorrhage. Rebleeding before the aneurysm is secured is the greatest early threat, so time to definitive treatment is the critical determinant of outcome. Blood pressure lowering must be balanced against maintaining cerebral perfusion, particularly if intracranial pressure is raised. Nimodipine can cause hypotension and may require dose adjustment rather than discontinuation. No allergy history, current medications, pregnancy status or family history are specified in the case.

Vignette:
A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 5 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Difficulty and delay in passing hard stools with straining for several hours and sometimes missing a day, painful defecation with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper, beginning after weaning from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula.
Analysis: This is functional constipation with an anal fissure, precipitated by the dietary change from breast milk to cows' milk formula. The strongest supporting facts are the clear temporal relationship between the onset of symptoms and the recent weaning onto cows' milk formula, which produces firmer, bulkier and less frequent stools than breast milk; the character of the stool as hard and difficult to pass with prolonged straining; the painful passage with screaming; and, most tellingly, the small spots of fresh bright red blood seen on the outside of the stool or on the diaper, which is the signature of a superficial anal mucosal tear rather than of bleeding from higher in the gastrointestinal tract. The reluctance to drink the formula initially may also have contributed to relatively reduced fluid intake at the time of transition. The case supplies several explicit negatives that are decisive in excluding serious organic disease. There was no neonatal delay in defecation, which argues strongly against Hirschsprung disease, in which failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life is characteristic. There is no excessive vomiting and no abdominal distension, which further argues against Hirschsprung disease and against intestinal obstruction. The child is thriving and is now feeding normally, indicating normal growth and no failure to thrive, which argues against hypothyroidism, cystic fibrosis, celiac disease, metabolic disease and any significant malabsorptive or systemic cause. A self-perpetuating cycle is likely established: hard stool causes a painful fissure, pain leads to voluntary withholding and stool retention, retained stool becomes harder and larger, and the fissure is repeatedly re-torn, which explains the several hours of straining and the occasional missed day. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include Hirschsprung disease (excluded on history by normal neonatal passage of stool, absence of distension and vomiting, and normal growth), cows' milk protein allergy (worth considering given the recent introduction of cows' milk formula and the blood, but that condition typically presents with blood mixed in loose or mucousy stools, eczema, vomiting or poor feeding rather than hard constipated stools with fresh blood streaking, and the child is thriving and feeding normally), anal fissure secondary to another cause or perianal disease, intussusception (excluded by the absence of paroxysmal pain episodes, vomiting, lethargy or currant jelly stool, and by the chronic rather than acute course), hypothyroidism (no failure to thrive or other features described), and anorectal malformation or anal stenosis, which remains the main structural possibility and is the reason a careful perianal and anorectal examination is required.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: A careful physical examination is the principal requirement, including abdominal examination for palpable fecal loading or distension, inspection of the perianal region to visualize an anal fissure and to check anal position and patency, assessment of anal tone, and examination of the lumbosacral spine for a dimple, tuft of hair or other marker of occult spinal dysraphism, together with plotting of growth on a growth chart to confirm that the child is thriving. No laboratory tests or imaging are needed at this stage; the diagnosis is clinical. Specifically, abdominal radiography, contrast enema and rectal suction biopsy are not indicated, since there are no red flag features suggesting Hirschsprung disease. Thyroid function testing is not required in the absence of growth failure or other suggestive findings. Further investigation should be reserved for failure to respond to appropriate treatment or for the emergence of red flag features.
Conclusion: A thriving 5-month-old boy has functional constipation with hard painful stools and an associated anal fissure causing bright red rectal bleeding, temporally related to weaning from breast milk to cows' milk formula. The absence of neonatal delay in passing stool, of vomiting, of abdominal distension and of any growth failure makes Hirschsprung disease and other organic pathology unlikely. This is a benign, common and treatable problem requiring routine outpatient management with dietary and stool-softening measures and parental reassurance, not urgent intervention.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Explain to the mother that the problem began with the change from breast milk to cows' milk formula, that the bright red spots of blood come from a small tear at the anus caused by passing hard stool, and that this is common, benign and treatable, since parental anxiety about blood is itself a major driver of presentation. Confirm that the formula is being reconstituted exactly according to the manufacturer's instructions, as over-concentrated formula is a frequent and easily corrected cause of constipation in this age group. Ensure adequate total fluid intake. Break the pain and withholding cycle: soften the stool so that defecation is no longer painful, allowing the fissure to heal, using an age-appropriate stool softener or osmotic laxative prescribed at the appropriate infant dose under medical supervision, and continue it long enough for the fissure to heal and for the child to lose the fear of defecation rather than stopping at the first improvement. Provide local perianal care with barrier ointment and gentle cleaning, and warm baths for comfort. Once the infant reaches the appropriate age for complementary feeding, introduce fiber-containing weaning foods and fruits. Arrange follow-up in a few weeks to confirm resolution of the hard stools, healing of the fissure and cessation of the bleeding, and to reconfirm normal growth. Regarding the additional considerations, do not attribute the bleeding to anything more sinister without evidence, but do inspect the perianal area to visualize the fissure and to exclude anal stenosis, an anteriorly displaced anus or perianal sepsis, and examine the lower back for signs of spinal dysraphism. Keep cows' milk protein allergy in mind as an alternative explanation given the recent introduction of cows' milk formula, and if the constipation proves refractory to correct treatment or if the child develops eczema, vomiting, diarrhea, mucus in the stool or faltering growth, arrange a supervised trial of an extensively hydrolyzed formula and pediatric review. Instruct the parents to return promptly if the infant develops bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, larger volumes of blood, blood mixed within the stool, fever, lethargy, poor feeding or any faltering of weight gain, as these would prompt reassessment for organic disease including Hirschsprung disease.
Notes: Anal fissure explains only small amounts of bright red blood on the surface of the stool or on the diaper; larger volumes, blood mixed into the stool, or associated systemic symptoms require re-evaluation. Absence of neonatal delay in defecation makes Hirschsprung disease unlikely but does not absolutely exclude short-segment disease, so persistent symptoms despite adequate treatment warrant specialist referral. Laxative and softener choice and dosing in a 5-month-old must be made by a clinician appropriate to the infant's age and weight. No examination findings, growth measurements, medication history or family history are specified in the case.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 65 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute shortness of breath of 30 minutes' duration with an initial near-faint episode without loss of consciousness, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain worsening on deep inspiration, one week after total left hip replacement, with swelling and tenderness of the left calf.
Analysis: This is acute pulmonary embolism arising from a left lower limb deep vein thrombosis, and the patient is hemodynamically compromised. The strongest supporting facts fall into three groups. First, the risk profile is extreme: he underwent total left hip replacement one week ago, which is a major orthopedic operation carrying one of the highest thromboembolic risks in surgery, and this was compounded by three days of bed rest after discharge because of poorly controlled pain, producing prolonged immobility, and by his age of 65. Second, there is clinical evidence of the source thrombus, namely swelling of the left calf that is tender on examination, on the same side as the operated limb. Third, the presentation is that of acute embolism with right ventricular strain: sudden dyspnea of only 30 minutes' duration, pleuritic left-sided chest pain consistent with pulmonary infarction irritating the pleura, presyncope reflecting a transient fall in cardiac output, sinus tachycardia at 112, hypoxemia with oxygen saturation of 91 percent on room air, and, most importantly, hypotension with a blood pressure of 95/65. The low-grade fever of 38.0 C is consistent with pulmonary infarction and does not argue against embolism, although postoperative infection must be considered in parallel. The absence of any history of cardiopulmonary disease removes competing explanations for acute hypoxemic dyspnea and makes the postoperative thromboembolic mechanism still more likely. Taken together, this constitutes a very high clinical pretest probability, so much so that D-dimer testing would add nothing and a negative result would not be believed. The presence of hypotension is the critical prognostic discriminator: it raises the possibility of high-risk, that is, massive, pulmonary embolism with obstructive shock, which carries high short-term mortality and may warrant reperfusion therapy rather than anticoagulation alone. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include acute coronary syndrome (chest pain is pleuritic and positional with respiration rather than exertional and pressure-like, and there is no cardiac history, though electrocardiogram and troponin are still required), pneumonia (fever and pleuritic pain fit, but the abrupt 30-minute onset, the presyncope, the hypotension and the tender swollen calf point to embolism), pneumothorax (sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnea fit, and it must be excluded by imaging, but the risk profile and calf findings favor embolism), postoperative bleeding or hypovolemia causing hypotension (must be considered after recent major surgery, but does not explain the hypoxemia and pleuritic pain), aortic dissection (no tearing pain or pulse deficits described), fat embolism (a recognized complication of orthopedic surgery but typically within days of the operation and with neurologic and petechial features), and cellulitis of the calf or postoperative wound infection or hematoma as an alternative explanation of the calf findings and fever, which nonetheless would not account for hypoxemic dyspnea and presyncope.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT pulmonary angiography as the definitive confirmatory imaging study, performed urgently, provided the patient can be stabilized enough for transfer; if he is too unstable to leave the resuscitation area, bedside transthoracic echocardiography demonstrating right ventricular dilatation and dysfunction can be used to support presumptive diagnosis and to justify reperfusion. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram to look for sinus tachycardia, right heart strain and to exclude acute coronary syndrome. Continuous cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry and frequent noninvasive blood pressure measurement. Bedside echocardiography specifically to assess right ventricular size and function, which stratifies risk. Cardiac troponin and natriuretic peptide as markers of right ventricular injury and strain for risk stratification. Arterial blood gas to quantify hypoxemia and gas exchange. Chest radiograph to exclude pneumothorax, pneumonia and other causes of pleuritic pain and dyspnea. Compression ultrasonography of the left lower limb to confirm deep vein thrombosis, which is supportive and can be done at the bedside. Complete blood count, renal function, electrolytes and coagulation studies including baseline prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, and type and screen, all needed before anticoagulation or thrombolysis. D-dimer is not indicated because the clinical probability is high and a result either way would not change management.
Conclusion: A 65-year-old man one week after total left hip replacement, with three days of postoperative immobility and a tender swollen left calf, presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, presyncope, tachycardia at 112, hypoxemia at 91 percent on room air and hypotension at 95/65. This is acute pulmonary embolism from a left lower limb deep vein thrombosis with hemodynamic compromise suggesting high-risk embolism. He requires immediate resuscitation, urgent confirmatory imaging or bedside echocardiography, prompt therapeutic anticoagulation and consideration of reperfusion therapy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Manage him in a resuscitation area with continuous cardiac and oxygen saturation monitoring. Give supplemental oxygen titrated to correct the saturation of 91 percent, and obtain intravenous access. Treat the hypotension of 95/65 cautiously with a modest fluid challenge, because aggressive volume loading can worsen right ventricular overdistension in massive pulmonary embolism; if hypotension persists, start vasopressor support rather than continuing to give large fluid volumes. Begin therapeutic parenteral anticoagulation immediately on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for imaging results, since the pretest probability is very high and delay increases mortality; use a rapidly acting parenteral agent and check baseline blood counts, renal function and coagulation studies first. Obtain the electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, troponin and natriuretic peptide, and arrange urgent CT pulmonary angiography if he is stable enough for transfer, otherwise perform bedside echocardiography to look for right ventricular dysfunction. Confirm the source with compression ultrasonography of the left leg. Regarding the additional considerations, the decisive management question is risk stratification: if hypotension persists or he deteriorates into shock, this is high-risk pulmonary embolism and systemic thrombolysis should be considered urgently, with catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy as alternatives, and this decision must weigh the substantial bleeding risk conferred by major hip surgery only one week ago, which is a relative contraindication to systemic thrombolysis and may favor catheter-directed or surgical approaches; involve a pulmonary embolism response team, critical care and the operating orthopedic surgeon in that decision. If he stabilizes with anticoagulation alone but has right ventricular dysfunction or troponin elevation, he is intermediate-high risk and requires close monitoring in a high-dependency setting with readiness for rescue reperfusion. Address the fever of 38.0 C in parallel: it is consistent with pulmonary infarction, but obtain a full postoperative infection assessment including inspection of the hip wound and cultures if indicated, since surgical site infection would also require treatment and would influence anticoagulation and any operative decisions. Review why thromboprophylaxis after hip arthroplasty failed or was interrupted, and document the postoperative immobility from poorly controlled pain as the contributing factor. Plan for long-term anticoagulation of at least three months for this provoked event, with the agent and duration decided after the acute phase and in consultation with the orthopedic team regarding wound and surgical bleeding risk. Provide adequate analgesia for the pleuritic pain in a way that does not compromise respiration, and reassess the previously inadequate hip pain control so that immobility does not recur. Consider an inferior vena cava filter only if anticoagulation proves absolutely contraindicated because of bleeding.
Notes: D-dimer has no role here because the clinical probability is high; a negative result would not exclude embolism. Anticoagulation should not be delayed for confirmatory imaging in a hemodynamically compromised patient with a high pretest probability, provided bleeding risk has been considered. Major surgery within the preceding week is a relative contraindication to systemic thrombolysis and materially affects the choice of reperfusion strategy. Fluid loading must be limited because right ventricular overload can be worsened. Aggressive treatment decisions require weighing the postoperative bleeding risk, and this is a multidisciplinary decision. No medication history, thromboprophylaxis details, allergy history or renal function values are specified in the case, and these would influence anticoagulant selection and dosing.

Vignette: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2) presents with sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain that began 30 minutes ago. She has a history of chronic hypertension managed with labetalol and a prior placental abruption with her second pregnancy. She reports the baby's movements have decreased since the bleeding started. On examination, she is anxious, pale, and in significant distress. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 96%. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. - a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2) presents with sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain that began 30 minutes ago. She has a history of chronic hypertension managed with labetalol and a prior placental abruption with her second pregnancy. She reports the baby's movements have decreased since the bleeding started. On examination, she is anxious, pale, and in significant distress. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 96%. The uterus is firm, tender, and contracted (woody consistency) with no relaxation between contractions. Moderate dark red vaginal bleeding is present. Continuous fetal monitoring reveals a baseline fetal heart rate of 170 bpm with absent variability and repetitive late decelerations. Labs: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 108,000/mcL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL (low), PT 14.8 seconds, D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL. Transfusion is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is called.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 32 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain beginning 30 minutes ago at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2), with decreased fetal movement since the bleeding started.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of acute placental abruption with fetal compromise and developing consumptive coagulopathy. The strongest supporting facts are the triad of painful dark red vaginal bleeding, severe constant (non-intermittent) abdominal pain, and a firm, tender, woody uterus that does not relax between contractions. Risk factors are explicitly present: chronic hypertension on labetalol and a prior placental abruption in the second pregnancy, both of which markedly raise recurrence risk. Maternal hemodynamics show tachycardia at 124 with a relatively low BP of 96/62 in a patient known to be chronically hypertensive, indicating that the visible moderate bleeding underestimates true blood loss and that concealed retroplacental hemorrhage is likely. Hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL confirms significant anemia. The coagulation profile - platelets 108,000/mcL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL, PT 14.8 seconds, and D-dimer greater than 20,000 ng/mL - demonstrates disseminated intravascular coagulation, a well-recognized complication of abruption caused by release of placental thromboplastin. Fibrinogen is normally elevated in pregnancy, so a value of 142 mg/dL represents severe hypofibrinogenemia and correlates with abruption severity and ongoing hemorrhage. Fetal status is non-reassuring and pre-terminal: baseline tachycardia of 170 bpm, absent variability, and repetitive late decelerations indicate uteroplacental insufficiency with fetal hypoxia and acidemia. The main differential considerations for third-trimester bleeding are placenta previa, which is classically painless with a soft non-tender uterus and does not fit this woody, tender uterus; vasa previa, which produces fetal exsanguination with painless bleeding after membrane rupture; uterine rupture, which is a consideration with severe pain and fetal distress but is less likely given a G3P2 with no stated prior uterine surgery or scar and a uterus that is contracted rather than losing tone with loss of station; and bloody show of labor, which is excluded by the severity of pain, hemodynamic instability, coagulopathy, and fetal heart rate abnormalities. Preeclampsia with severe features and HELLP syndrome are relevant to the background of chronic hypertension and the low platelets, but the low fibrinogen with markedly elevated D-dimer points to DIC from abruption as the dominant process.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous electronic fetal heart rate and tocodynamometric monitoring (already in place); serial complete blood count with platelets; serial fibrinogen, PT/INR, aPTT and D-dimer to track DIC; type and crossmatch with activation of massive transfusion protocol; blood type and Rh status with quantitative fetal-maternal hemorrhage testing to guide anti-D immune globulin if Rh negative; basic metabolic panel, liver enzymes and urine protein assessment given chronic hypertension; arterial or venous blood gas with lactate; large-bore IV access and continuous maternal vital sign and pulse oximetry monitoring; operating room with immediate neonatal resuscitation equipment and neonatology attendance. Imaging with ultrasound is not required to make the diagnosis and must not delay delivery.
Conclusion: Severe acute placental abruption at 34 weeks gestation in a woman with chronic hypertension and a prior abruption, complicated by maternal hemorrhagic shock with anemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation with hypofibrinogenemia and thrombocytopenia, and a category III fetal heart rate tracing indicating fetal hypoxia. This is an immediately life-threatening obstetric emergency for both mother and fetus; transfusion has been started and emergent cesarean delivery has been correctly called as the definitive treatment.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Proceed without delay to the emergent cesarean delivery already activated - delivery is the definitive treatment for abruption with maternal instability and a category III tracing, and no test should postpone it. Maintain left lateral uterine displacement and high-flow supplemental oxygen while transferring to the operating room. Secure two large-bore IV lines and resuscitate with balanced blood product transfusion rather than crystalloid alone, activating the massive transfusion protocol given hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL and active bleeding. Correct the coagulopathy aggressively and in parallel with delivery: transfuse cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate targeting a fibrinogen above 200 mg/dL given the current value of 142 mg/dL, give fresh frozen plasma for the prolonged PT of 14.8 seconds, and transfuse platelets for the count of 108,000/mcL if it falls further or surgical bleeding is diffuse. Consider tranexamic acid as an adjunct for obstetric hemorrhage. Anticipate postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony and from ongoing DIC after delivery, and have uterotonics prepared, with intrauterine balloon tamponade, compression sutures, and uterine artery ligation available in a stepwise plan; hysterectomy should be considered if a Couvelaire uterus with uncontrollable bleeding is encountered. Continue labetalol-appropriate blood pressure management, but note that the current BP of 96/62 reflects hypovolemia rather than controlled hypertension, so avoid further antihypertensive dosing until volume is restored. Regarding the additional considerations: general anesthesia is generally preferred over neuraxial anesthesia here because of coagulopathy with platelets 108,000/mcL, hypofibrinogenemia, and hemodynamic instability, which raise the risk of spinal or epidural hematoma; antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity at 34 weeks and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection are not appropriate reasons to delay delivery in this unstable setting, and the neonatal team must be present at delivery to manage a likely hypoxic, anemic, preterm infant. Send the placenta for pathologic examination to confirm retroplacental hematoma. Monitor for acute kidney injury, Sheehan syndrome, and transfusion-related complications postpartum, and admit to a high-dependency or intensive care setting after surgery. Provide counseling before discharge on the substantially increased recurrence risk of abruption in future pregnancies, the importance of blood pressure control, and early prenatal care with close surveillance.
Notes: The moderate visible bleeding may substantially underestimate actual blood loss because a large portion of abruption hemorrhage can be concealed behind the placenta; maternal vital signs, hemoglobin trend, and fibrinogen are more reliable indicators of severity. Fibrinogen of 142 mg/dL is profoundly low for pregnancy and is the single most predictive marker of severe hemorrhage in this setting. Fetal outcome may already be compromised despite optimal management given absent variability and repetitive late decelerations.

Diagnosis10cm: Injury of conjunctiva and corneal abrasion without foreign body, left eye, initial encounter
Diagnosis10: Injury of conjunctiva and corneal abrasion without mention of foreign body
Vignette: A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.
Simplified (added symptoms): 30 y/o m, metal grinding without goggles, 6-hr L eye pain/tearing/photophobia/foreign body sensation, VA 20/30, fluorescein shows 3 mm corneal defect, Seidel negative, no foreign body

"role_description": (

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.
