Vignette:
A 29-year-old male software developer presents with eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsens throughout the workday. He spends 10 to 12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks. He reports that symptoms improve on weekends when he reduces screen time. He denies blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, or eye pain. He does not wear corrective lenses. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Extraocular movements are intact. Pupils are equal and reactive. Conjunctivae are mildly injected. The anterior segment and fundoscopic exams are normal bilaterally.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 29 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Eye fatigue, ocular dryness and a mild headache that worsen through the workday in a software developer who spends 10 to 12 hours daily at computer screens without taking breaks, with improvement on weekends when screen time is reduced.
Analysis: This is digital eye strain, also called computer vision syndrome, a benign asthenopic condition caused by prolonged near work at screens. The reasoning rests on a characteristic exposure-symptom relationship together with an entirely normal ophthalmic examination. The exposure is extreme and clearly documented: 10 to 12 hours daily of screen work with frequent failure to take breaks. The temporal pattern is the strongest single piece of evidence, since symptoms build progressively through the workday and improve on weekends when screen time falls, establishing a dose-response relationship with screen exposure and effectively excluding a fixed structural or progressive ocular disease. The symptom triad of eye fatigue, dryness and mild headache is the classic asthenopic cluster, arising from sustained accommodative and convergence effort at a fixed near working distance and from a markedly reduced blink rate and incomplete blinking during concentrated screen viewing, which increases tear film evaporation and produces the dryness and the mild conjunctival injection observed. The examination is reassuring and effectively rules out serious pathology: visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes, so there is no significant uncorrected refractive error or media or retinal disease affecting central vision; extraocular movements are intact and pupils are equal and reactive, so there is no cranial neuropathy, no pupillary abnormality and no evidence of a compressive or neurological lesion; and the anterior segment and fundoscopic examinations are normal bilaterally, excluding keratitis, uveitis, corneal pathology and retinal disease. The only positive sign is mild conjunctival injection, which is entirely consistent with ocular surface dryness. The explicit negatives further narrow the field and are decisive: he denies blurred vision, which argues against significant refractive error, accommodative failure and optic nerve disease; he denies floaters and flashes of light, which argues against posterior vitreous detachment and retinal tear or detachment; and he denies eye pain, which together with normal pupils, normal acuity and a normal anterior segment argues strongly against acute angle closure glaucoma, uveitis and scleritis. Differential considerations weighed against the case data therefore include uncorrected refractive error or presbyopia (acuity is 20/20 and he is 29, though a small latent refractive or accommodative or binocular vision anomaly can still contribute to asthenopia and is worth formal refraction), dry eye disease as a primary condition, which overlaps with and contributes to this picture, convergence insufficiency or a binocular vision disorder, which can produce identical near-work symptoms and is assessed by orthoptic testing if symptoms persist, acute angle closure glaucoma (excluded by absence of pain, halos, acuity loss and by normal reactive pupils), uveitis or keratitis (excluded by a normal anterior segment and absence of pain and photophobia), retinal detachment (excluded by absence of flashes, floaters and field loss and by a normal fundus), and a primary headache disorder such as tension-type headache or migraine, which can coexist and is plausibly aggravated by the same prolonged sedentary posture, although here the headache is mild and tracks screen exposure precisely.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical and the examination performed, comprising visual acuity, extraocular movements, pupillary responses, and anterior segment and fundoscopic examination, is already normal and sufficient. No laboratory tests, no imaging and no neurological investigation are indicated. If symptoms fail to improve after implementation of ergonomic and ocular surface measures, a formal cycloplegic refraction and an assessment of binocular vision and accommodative function, together with tear film assessment such as tear break-up time, would be the appropriate next steps, but these are not required at present.
Conclusion: A healthy 29-year-old software developer has digital eye strain with associated evaporative ocular surface dryness, caused by 10 to 12 hours of uninterrupted daily screen work. The diagnosis is supported by symptoms that worsen through the workday and remit at weekends with reduced screen exposure, by mild conjunctival injection as the sole objective finding, and by a completely normal ophthalmic examination with 20/20 acuity and no red flag symptoms. The condition is benign and reversible, requires no investigation, and is managed by behavioral, ergonomic and ocular surface measures that the patient can implement himself.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Reassure him explicitly that the examination is entirely normal, that there is no evidence of eye disease or of any threat to his vision, and that his symptoms are a functional consequence of prolonged screen work that will resolve with changed habits. Institute structured visual breaks, since he reports that he often forgets to take them and this is the central modifiable factor: adopt a regular rule of looking away from the screen at a distant object for a short period every twenty minutes or so, and take longer breaks away from the workstation periodically through the day, ideally with a scheduled reminder given that forgetting is his stated problem. Address the ocular surface dryness directly by making a conscious effort to blink fully and frequently while working, since blink rate falls sharply during screen concentration, and by using preservative-free artificial tears as needed for symptomatic relief; consider reducing air conditioning or fan airflow directed at the face and using humidification of the working environment. Optimize workstation ergonomics: position the monitor slightly below eye level and at approximately arm's length, which reduces both accommodative demand and the exposed ocular surface area, adjust screen brightness and contrast to match ambient lighting, reduce glare from windows and overhead lights with repositioning or an antiglare measure, and increase text size so that he is not straining to read. Attend to posture and to neck and shoulder position, which contribute to the headache. Where feasible, reduce total daily screen hours, since 10 to 12 hours is the underlying driver, and take short physical movement breaks. Regarding the additional considerations, although his acuity is 20/20 and he does not wear corrective lenses, a formal refraction with assessment of binocular vision, convergence and accommodation is worthwhile if symptoms persist despite good adherence to these measures, because a small uncorrected refractive error, an accommodative dysfunction or convergence insufficiency can produce exactly this symptom pattern with normal distance acuity, and dedicated computer-distance spectacle correction sometimes helps. Arrange routine, non-urgent optometric or ophthalmological review if there is no improvement after several weeks of consistent self-management. Instruct him to seek prompt ophthalmological assessment rather than continuing self-care if he develops any red flag features, specifically new blurred or reduced vision, eye pain, photophobia, halos around lights, new floaters, flashes of light, a curtain or shadow in the visual field, double vision, marked redness with discharge, or a headache that becomes severe, changes in character, wakes him from sleep or is accompanied by neurological symptoms, as these would indicate a different and potentially serious diagnosis. He does not require blue-light filtering lenses on the basis of the evidence in this case, and the emphasis should remain on breaks, blinking, lubrication and ergonomics.
Notes: Digital eye strain is a diagnosis of exclusion supported here by a normal examination and a clear exposure relationship, and it does not cause permanent visual damage. Normal 20/20 distance acuity does not exclude a small refractive or binocular vision anomaly contributing to near-work asthenopia, so persistent symptoms warrant formal refraction and orthoptic assessment. The mild headache is attributed to the same cause and postural factors, but a headache that changes character or acquires neurological features requires separate evaluation. No medication history, allergy history, systemic disease, prior eye history or contact lens use is specified in the case.

Diagnosis10: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation, unspecified
Vignette: A 56-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and cough for several days. Her symptoms began 3 days ago with rhinorrhea. She reports a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum, which has increased over the past 2 days. She has had similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years. She has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day for 40 years and continues to smoke. She denies hemoptysis, chills, or weight loss and has not received any relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.

Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case

- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and cough for several days. Her symptoms began 3 days ago with rhinorrhea. She reports a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum, which has increased over the past 2 days. She has had similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years. She has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day for 40 years and continues to smoke. She denies hemoptysis, chills, or weight loss and has not received any relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 56 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Shortness of breath and cough for several days, beginning 3 days ago with rhinorrhea, on a background of chronic morning cough productive of white sputum which has increased over the past 2 days, with similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years, in a current smoker of 1 to 2 packs per day for 40 years.
Analysis: The underlying diagnosis is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease of the chronic bronchitis phenotype, and the present illness is an acute exacerbation triggered by a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Two lines of reasoning support this. First, the history satisfies the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis: a chronic cough productive of sputum that has recurred in a similar fashion each winter for the past 4 years, that is, on most days for at least three months in each of two or more consecutive years. The morning predominance of the productive cough is characteristic of mucus accumulation overnight in a hypersecretory airway. Second, the exposure is overwhelming and causally decisive: 1 to 2 packs per day for 40 years amounts to a 40 to 80 pack-year smoking history in a patient who continues to smoke, which is the dominant risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is more than sufficient to explain fixed airflow limitation at age 56. The acute component is an exacerbation rather than a new disease, evidenced by the temporal sequence of a viral prodrome with rhinorrhea 3 days ago followed by an increase in the baseline cough and sputum over the past 2 days with new shortness of breath; viral upper respiratory infections are the commonest precipitant of exacerbations, and the seasonal winter recurrence pattern fits this mechanism. The sputum remains white rather than purulent, which argues against a bacterial exacerbation and against pneumonia and is relevant to the antibiotic decision. Several explicit negatives narrow the differential in important ways. She denies hemoptysis and weight loss, which is reassuring in a heavy long-term smoker in whom bronchogenic carcinoma is a genuine competing concern, though their absence does not exclude it. She denies chills, which together with the non-purulent sputum makes pneumonia and bacterial infection less likely. She has had no relief from over-the-counter cough preparations, which is expected, since these do not treat airflow obstruction and their failure supports the need for a proper diagnostic evaluation rather than further symptomatic self-treatment. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include asthma (the age at onset, the heavy smoking history, the chronic daily productive cough and the fixed seasonal recurrent pattern favor chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but reversibility testing distinguishes them), acute bronchitis in an otherwise healthy person (does not explain four winters of recurrent symptoms and a chronic morning productive cough), community-acquired pneumonia (no fever, chills or purulent sputum described, but examination and imaging are needed to exclude it), lung cancer (must remain an active consideration in a 40 to 80 pack-year smoker with chronic cough, and is a reason for chest imaging and for lung cancer screening eligibility assessment even though hemoptysis and weight loss are absent), bronchiectasis (chronic productive cough fits, but large-volume purulent sputum and recurrent infections are not described), congestive heart failure (a cause of dyspnea and cough in this age group that should be considered if findings suggest it), pulmonary embolism (no risk factors, pleuritic pain or abrupt onset described), and postnasal drip or gastroesophageal reflux as causes of chronic cough, which are less consistent with the exposure history and the seasonal exacerbation pattern. A crucial point is that chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has apparently never been formally diagnosed, since four years of winter episodes have been treated only with over-the-counter preparations; this visit is therefore both an opportunity to manage the exacerbation and, more importantly, to establish the underlying diagnosis with spirometry and to begin disease-modifying care, above all smoking cessation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete physical examination with pulse oximetry to measure oxygen saturation and assess the severity of the exacerbation, including auscultation for wheeze, prolonged expiration, reduced breath sounds and crackles. Chest radiography to exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, heart failure and a mass lesion, which is particularly warranted given the heavy smoking history and the new dyspnea. Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility testing to confirm the diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease by demonstrating a post-bronchodilator ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity below the diagnostic threshold, and to grade severity; this should be performed once she has recovered from the acute exacerbation, since spirometry during an exacerbation is not reliable for diagnosis. Assessment of eligibility for low-dose CT lung cancer screening based on her age and 40 to 80 pack-year smoking history. Arterial or venous blood gas only if oxygen saturation is low or if she appears severely unwell with suspected hypercapnia. Complete blood count if infection is suspected clinically. Sputum culture is not needed for a non-purulent exacerbation. Consideration of alpha-1 antitrypsin testing as part of a full evaluation of newly diagnosed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Electrocardiogram and cardiac assessment if the history or examination raises the possibility of coexisting heart disease.
Conclusion: A 56-year-old woman with a 40 to 80 pack-year smoking history and four years of recurrent winter episodes of chronic productive cough has previously undiagnosed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with a chronic bronchitis phenotype, now experiencing an acute exacerbation precipitated by a viral upper respiratory tract infection, with increased cough, increased white sputum and new dyspnea. There are no red flags for pneumonia or malignancy at present. She should be assessed clinically with pulse oximetry and a chest radiograph, treated for the exacerbation in the outpatient setting, and, critically, have the underlying diagnosis confirmed by spirometry after recovery while being given intensive smoking cessation support.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Examine her fully and measure oxygen saturation to gauge the severity of the exacerbation, and obtain a chest radiograph to exclude pneumonia, heart failure and a mass lesion in a heavy smoker with new dyspnea. Treat the exacerbation in the outpatient setting with inhaled short-acting bronchodilator therapy, ensuring correct inhaler technique is taught and checked. Consider a short course of systemic corticosteroids according to the severity of her symptoms and degree of functional limitation, as this shortens recovery and improves lung function in exacerbations. Regarding antibiotics, her sputum remains white rather than purulent and she has no fever or chills, so the exacerbation is most likely viral and antibiotics are not routinely indicated; reserve them for increased sputum purulence together with increased sputum volume or increased dyspnea, or for clinical or radiographic evidence of pneumonia. Advise adequate hydration and rest, and explain that over-the-counter cough preparations have not helped and will not help because they do not address airflow obstruction. Arrange follow-up within a short interval to confirm improvement, and schedule post-recovery spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility to establish the diagnosis formally and grade severity, since accurate diagnosis is the gateway to appropriate long-term inhaled maintenance therapy, which she currently is not receiving despite four years of symptoms. Regarding the additional considerations, smoking cessation is the single most important intervention and the only one that alters the natural history of the disease: deliver a clear personalized cessation message linking her 40-year smoking history to these recurrent winter illnesses, offer pharmacotherapy and behavioral support, and arrange structured follow-up on quitting rather than simply advising her to stop. Ensure she is up to date with influenza vaccination annually and with pneumococcal vaccination, since these reduce exacerbations and are directly relevant to her seasonal pattern. Assess her eligibility for low-dose CT lung cancer screening given her substantial pack-year history and current smoking, and discuss enrollment; this is important even though she has no hemoptysis or weight loss. Refer to pulmonary rehabilitation once the diagnosis is confirmed and if she has persisting exertional limitation. Provide a written action plan for recognizing and responding to future exacerbations. Instruct her to seek urgent care if she develops worsening breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fever with chills, purulent or blood-stained sputum, confusion or drowsiness, cyanosis, or inability to speak in full sentences, as these indicate a severe exacerbation, pneumonia or respiratory failure requiring emergency assessment. Review any cardiac symptoms and screen for the common comorbidities of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, anxiety and depression.
Notes: Spirometry is required to confirm chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and should be performed after recovery from the exacerbation, since values obtained during an exacerbation are unreliable for diagnosis. The absence of hemoptysis and weight loss does not exclude lung cancer in a smoker with this pack-year burden, and a persistent or changing cough, or an abnormal radiograph, requires further imaging. Antibiotics are not indicated for a non-purulent exacerbation and should be guided by sputum purulence and clinical severity. Vital signs, oxygen saturation, physical examination findings, current medications, allergy history and vaccination status are not specified in the case, and these would refine severity assessment and treatment; if oxygen saturation is significantly reduced or she is in respiratory distress, the disposition changes to emergent care.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with 3 days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat, and occasional sneezing. She works as a daycare teacher and reports several children in her class have had similar symptoms. She denies fever, cough, dyspnea, ear pain, or facial pressure. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The oropharynx shows mild erythema without exudates. Nasal mucosa is mildly edematous with clear discharge. Tympanic membranes are normal bilaterally. Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. She is well-appearing and in no distress.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 25 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat and occasional sneezing in a daycare teacher with known exposure to several children in her class who have had similar symptoms.
Analysis: This is an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection, the common cold. The reasoning is straightforward and rests on a typical symptom complex, a clear epidemiological exposure, an entirely benign examination and a comprehensive set of negative findings that exclude the conditions that would change management. The symptom triad of clear rhinorrhea, mild sore throat and sneezing over 3 days is the classic presentation of viral rhinosinusitis, and clear rather than purulent nasal discharge in the first days of illness is characteristic. The exposure history is strongly supportive and essentially settles the etiology: she works as a daycare teacher, an occupation with intense exposure to respiratory viruses, and several children in her class have had the same symptoms, establishing a clear source and a contact-transmission pattern. The examination is reassuring throughout and consistent only with mild viral inflammation: she is afebrile at 37.0 C, the oropharynx shows mild erythema without exudates, the nasal mucosa is mildly edematous with clear discharge, tympanic membranes are normal bilaterally, cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged, and she is well-appearing and in no distress. The explicit negatives are the analytic core of the case. Absence of fever, absence of tonsillar exudate and absence of cervical lymphadenopathy, combined with the presence of prominent cough-free coryzal symptoms such as rhinorrhea and sneezing, place her at the lowest end of the clinical scoring for group A streptococcal pharyngitis, since coryzal features argue against streptococcal infection and none of the streptococcal criteria are met; testing and antibiotics are therefore not indicated. Absence of facial pressure or pain, normal-appearing nasal findings and a duration of only 3 days exclude acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, which requires either symptoms persisting beyond about ten days without improvement, severe symptoms with high fever and purulent discharge, or the double-worsening pattern; none is present. Absence of ear pain with normal tympanic membranes excludes otitis media. Absence of cough and dyspnea, with no distress, excludes lower respiratory tract involvement including bronchitis and pneumonia. Differential considerations weighed against the case data include group A streptococcal pharyngitis (excluded on the grounds above), infectious mononucleosis (no fever, no exudative pharyngitis, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no fatigue described), influenza (typically abrupt onset with fever, myalgia and systemic prostration, which are absent here), allergic rhinitis (sneezing and clear rhinorrhea fit, but the acute 3-day onset with sore throat and the documented sick contacts point to infection; a seasonal or perennial pattern with itching and ocular symptoms is not described), acute bacterial rhinosinusitis and acute otitis media (both excluded above), and COVID-19 or other specific viral illnesses, which can present identically and which matter mainly for isolation and workplace considerations rather than for treatment of an otherwise mild illness. The natural history is important for counseling: symptoms typically peak within the first few days and resolve over approximately seven to ten days, and nasal discharge commonly becomes thicker or discolored in the middle of the illness without this indicating bacterial infection or requiring antibiotics.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical and the history and physical examination already performed are sufficient. Rapid antigen detection testing or throat culture for group A streptococcus is not indicated, because she is afebrile with no exudate and no cervical lymphadenopathy while having prominent coryzal symptoms, a combination that makes streptococcal pharyngitis very unlikely and for which testing is explicitly discouraged. No blood tests, no sinus or chest imaging and no viral studies are required for management of an uncomplicated cold in a well-appearing patient, although testing for specific respiratory viruses may be considered if required by local occupational or public health policy for a daycare worker.
Conclusion: A well-appearing, afebrile 25-year-old daycare teacher has an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection of 3 days' duration, acquired from documented sick contacts among the children in her class. The examination shows only mild oropharyngeal erythema and mild nasal mucosal edema with clear discharge, with normal tympanic membranes and no lymphadenopathy, and there is no evidence of streptococcal pharyngitis, sinusitis, otitis media or lower respiratory involvement. This is a self-limiting illness that requires no testing and no antibiotics, and is managed with symptomatic self-care, rest, hydration and hygiene measures, with clearly defined criteria for returning if the course deviates.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Reassure her that this is a self-limiting viral illness that will resolve on its own, typically over about seven to ten days, and explain explicitly that antibiotics have no role, will not shorten the illness, and carry a risk of adverse effects and of promoting resistance, since expectation of antibiotics is the commonest source of inappropriate prescribing in this presentation. Advise supportive symptomatic care: adequate rest, generous fluid intake, and over-the-counter symptomatic relief as needed, including simple analgesics or antipyretics for the sore throat, saline nasal irrigation or saline spray for nasal congestion and discharge, warm saline gargles and throat lozenges for throat discomfort, and humidified air; short-term topical decongestants may be used but should be limited to a few days to avoid rebound congestion. Regarding the additional considerations, her occupation as a daycare teacher is a central practical issue and should be addressed directly: counsel her on rigorous hand hygiene, covering coughs and sneezes, safe disposal of tissues and cleaning of shared surfaces and toys, since she is both a recipient and a potential source of transmission among young children and their families; advise her to stay home from work while she is most symptomatic and febrile if fever develops, and to follow her workplace's illness policy, which for childcare settings is often stricter than general advice. Recommend annual influenza vaccination and confirm that routine immunizations are up to date, given her high-exposure occupation. Explain the expected natural history, and specifically that nasal discharge often becomes thicker or yellow or green during the course of a cold and that this alone does not indicate a bacterial infection or need for antibiotics, because this misconception commonly drives return visits. Give clear return precautions and instruct her to seek medical review if symptoms persist beyond ten days without improvement, if she improves and then worsens again, which is the double-worsening pattern suggesting bacterial sinusitis, or if she develops high fever, severe or unilateral facial pain or swelling, ear pain or discharge, a severe sore throat with difficulty swallowing or drooling, tonsillar exudate with tender cervical nodes, shortness of breath, chest pain, productive cough, neck stiffness, severe headache, visual changes, or if she becomes generally unwell, as any of these would indicate a complication or a different diagnosis requiring assessment. No follow-up appointment is otherwise necessary.
Notes: The illness is only 3 days old, so persistence of symptoms for up to about ten days is expected and is not by itself an indication for antibiotics or reassessment. Testing for group A streptococcus is not appropriate here because the pretest probability is very low, and testing in such patients risks detecting carriage and leading to unnecessary antibiotic treatment. A viral upper respiratory infection can occasionally be complicated by secondary bacterial sinusitis or otitis media, which is why the return precautions are given. Pregnancy status, allergy history, current medications, comorbidities and vaccination status are not specified in the case, and pregnancy status in particular would influence the choice of over-the-counter symptomatic medications in a 25-year-old woman.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

Vignette:
A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 5 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Multiple itchy red bumps on the arms and legs appearing over the past 24 hours after an afternoon of playing outdoors in the backyard, with scratching but no systemic symptoms.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with uncomplicated insect bite reactions (papular urticaria / arthropod bite hypersensitivity). The strongest supporting facts are the temporal link to outdoor play in the backyard, onset within 24 hours, the distribution on exposed skin of the bilateral forearms and lower legs, the small number of lesions (approximately 8 to 10), their uniform small size of 3 to 5 mm, the erythematous papular morphology, and especially the small central puncta, which indicate a bite or puncture site. Pruritus without significant swelling beyond each individual lesion argues against a large local allergic reaction, and the absence of fever, joint pain, and recent travel argues against a systemic infectious or inflammatory cause. Importantly, the examination documents no cellulitis, no lymphangitis, and no regional lymphadenopathy, so secondary bacterial infection is not currently present. Main differential considerations grounded in the case include papular urticaria from arthropod bites (most likely), contact dermatitis from backyard plants, and early varicella or another vesicular exanthem; the latter is not supported because the lesions are papules with central puncta rather than vesicles on an erythematous base, and the child is afebrile. Systemic allergic reaction is excluded by the absence of any swelling beyond the local lesion and the absence of respiratory or systemic complaints. The main ongoing risk is excoriation from scratching leading to secondary bacterial infection such as impetigo.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 5-year-old boy with a benign, self-limited papular eruption of approximately 8 to 10 pruritic erythematous papules with central puncta on exposed forearms and lower legs, occurring after outdoor exposure, consistent with uncomplicated insect bite reactions. There is no evidence of secondary infection, systemic allergic reaction, or systemic illness, and no diagnostic testing is required at this time.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Manage symptomatically at home. Wash the affected areas gently with soap and water and keep the skin clean and dry. Apply cool compresses to the itchy papules for symptomatic relief. Use a topical anti-itch preparation and, if needed for troublesome itching that disturbs sleep, an oral antihistamine dosed for the child's age and weight. Keep the boy's fingernails cut short and discourage scratching to prevent excoriation, since scratching is already reported and is the main pathway to secondary bacterial infection. Prevent further bites by using age-appropriate insect repellent on exposed skin, dressing him in long sleeves and long trousers during outdoor play, and inspecting the backyard for insect nests, standing water, or other breeding sites. Regarding the additional considerations: no systemic allergic reaction is present because swelling is confined to each individual bump and there are no respiratory or systemic symptoms, so no emergency allergy treatment is indicated; no antibiotics are indicated because there is no cellulitis, lymphangitis, or lymphadenopathy; and no laboratory or imaging work-up is warranted for this localized, afebrile eruption. Expect gradual resolution over several days to two weeks. Seek medical evaluation if any lesion becomes enlarging, warm, painful, or develops spreading redness, pus, or honey-colored crusting; if red streaking or swollen lymph nodes appear; if fever develops; if lesions rapidly increase in number or spread; or if there is any facial or lip swelling, difficulty breathing, or generalized hives.
Notes: The causative arthropod is not identified in the case, and no specimen or exposure source is documented; the diagnosis rests on the clinical morphology and exposure history. The mother reports no fever, joint pain, or recent travel, so tick-borne or travel-related illness is not suggested by the available information, but the parent should monitor for any later development of expanding rash or fever.

Vignette: A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She reports nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had two previous urinary tract infections in the past year treated with antibiotics. She is sexually active and uses oral contraceptives. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She reports nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had two previous urinary tract infections in the past year treated with antibiotics. She is sexually active and uses oral contraceptives. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 24 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three days of dysuria and urinary frequency progressing over the past 24 hours to right flank pain, fever with rigors, nausea, and one episode of vomiting.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of acute pyelonephritis, an upper urinary tract infection, arising from an ascending lower urinary tract infection. The strongest supporting facts are the classic progression from three days of dysuria and frequency (lower tract irritative symptoms) to systemic illness with fever of 102.2 F and rigors within the last 24 hours, together with significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion, which localizes the infection to the right kidney. The urinalysis is confirmatory of urinary infection, showing large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria; positive nitrites specifically favor Enterobacteriaceae such as Escherichia coli. Systemic involvement is further supported by nausea with one episode of vomiting and by the vital signs showing tachycardia at 104 with a blood pressure of 108/66, a pattern of early hemodynamic stress although not yet frank hypotension; respiratory rate is 18 and the patient is flushed and mildly uncomfortable but not toxic. Two prior urinary tract infections within the past year mark her as having recurrent infection, which raises the possibility of a resistant organism and makes prior culture history relevant. The mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding is consistent with concurrent cystitis and argues against an acute surgical abdomen. Main differential considerations grounded in the case: uncomplicated cystitis alone is excluded by the fever, rigors, and costovertebral angle tenderness; pelvic inflammatory disease is unlikely given the absence of vaginal discharge, though she is sexually active; nephrolithiasis with obstruction is a consideration given unilateral flank pain, but she denies hematuria and the urinalysis pattern points to infection; ectopic pregnancy and other pregnancy-related causes are excluded by the negative point-of-care pregnancy test. The principal danger is progression to sepsis or, if there is coexisting obstruction, to an obstructed infected kidney, which is a urologic emergency.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine culture with antibiotic susceptibility testing obtained before starting antibiotics; blood cultures given fever with rigors; complete blood count; basic metabolic panel with serum creatinine and electrolytes to assess renal function and vomiting-related derangement; serum lactate to screen for sepsis; continuous or repeated vital sign monitoring including blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, and respiratory rate; renal and urinary tract imaging (renal ultrasound, or CT of the abdomen and pelvis) if she fails to improve within 48 to 72 hours of appropriate therapy or if obstruction or abscess is suspected.
Conclusion: A 24-year-old non-pregnant woman with recurrent urinary tract infections presents with acute right-sided pyelonephritis, evidenced by ascending lower urinary tract symptoms progressing to high fever with rigors, right costovertebral angle tenderness, and a urinalysis positive for leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria, and bacteriuria. She is febrile and tachycardic with a borderline blood pressure and is vomiting, so she requires prompt evaluation, cultures, and parenteral antibiotic therapy rather than outpatient oral treatment alone.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Evaluate her urgently in an acute care setting. Obtain urine culture and blood cultures before administering antibiotics, then start empiric intravenous antibiotic therapy directed at Gram-negative uropathogens without waiting for culture results; choose the empiric agent taking into account her two urinary tract infections in the past year and any prior organisms and resistance patterns, since recurrent treated infection raises the chance of a resistant strain. Give intravenous fluid resuscitation and rehydration because she has vomited, is febrile, is tachycardic at 104, and has a blood pressure of 108/66. Provide antiemetics for the nausea and vomiting and antipyretics and analgesia for fever and flank pain; the inability to tolerate oral intake is itself a reason she cannot be managed with oral antibiotics at home. Monitor vital signs closely for progression toward sepsis and check serum lactate and renal function. Narrow the antibiotic to the culture-directed agent once susceptibilities return, and complete a full course for pyelonephritis rather than a short cystitis course. Regarding the additional considerations: the pregnancy test is negative, so pregnancy-specific management and pregnancy-related diagnoses do not apply and there is no restriction on antibiotic choice for that reason; her oral contraceptive use should be noted when selecting antibiotics and she should continue contraception as prescribed; the absence of vaginal discharge makes a genital tract infection less likely, but as she is sexually active, testing for sexually transmitted infections may be considered if symptoms do not fully fit or if discharge later develops. If she does not defervesce or improve within 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, obtain renal imaging to exclude obstructing stone, perinephric or intrarenal abscess, or another complicating factor. Because she has had three urinary tract infections including this one within a year, arrange outpatient follow-up to discuss recurrence prevention, including hydration, post-coital voiding, and evaluation for any anatomic or behavioral contributors.
Notes: Blood pressure of 108/66 with a heart rate of 104 is not overtly hypotensive but warrants close monitoring for evolving sepsis. No imaging findings, prior culture organisms, allergy history, or renal function values are provided in the case, so antibiotic selection and dosing must be finalized against that missing information at the point of care.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. This is followed by the development of erythema and a maculopapular rash in this painful area, accompanied by headache and malaise. The rash progressed to develop clusters of clear vesicles for 3 to 5 days, evolving through stages of pustulation, ulceration, and crusting.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 77 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five days of burning and aching pain on the right side of the chest, followed by erythema and a maculopapular rash in the same painful area with headache and malaise, progressing over 3 to 5 days into clusters of clear vesicles that then pustulated, ulcerated, and crusted.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of herpes zoster (shingles) due to reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in a thoracic dorsal root ganglion. The strongest supporting facts are the prodrome of burning and aching neuropathic pain preceding the rash by 5 days, the strictly unilateral right-sided chest location corresponding to a thoracic dermatome, the appearance of erythema and a maculopapular eruption confined to that same painful area, and the classic evolution through clusters of clear vesicles over 3 to 5 days into pustulation, ulceration, and crusting. The accompanying headache and malaise are consistent with the systemic prodromal features of zoster. Age 77 is an important risk factor, since declining varicella-zoster virus specific cell-mediated immunity with advancing age both predisposes to reactivation and increases the risk of complications, particularly postherpetic neuralgia, which is the most common sequela in elderly patients. Main differential considerations grounded in the case: because the pain preceded the rash by several days and is on the chest, an initial cardiac or pleuritic cause of chest pain would be considered during the prodromal phase, but the subsequent appearance of a dermatomal vesicular eruption in exactly the painful area settles the diagnosis; herpes simplex virus infection can produce grouped vesicles but does not typically follow a unilateral dermatome across the chest in this manner; contact dermatitis and bullous impetigo do not present with a preceding several-day burning neuropathic prodrome or dermatomal distribution. The stage of the eruption is important for management: the lesions have already progressed to pustulation, ulceration, and crusting, meaning the presentation is beyond the earliest window in which antiviral therapy has the greatest benefit, though older patients with ongoing lesion evolution may still be considered for treatment.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 77-year-old man with unilateral right thoracic dermatomal herpes zoster, presenting with a 5-day neuropathic pain prodrome followed by a maculopapular then vesicular eruption in the same dermatome that has evolved through pustulation, ulceration, and crusting, with associated headache and malaise. The diagnosis is clinical, and management centers on pain control, prevention of secondary bacterial infection, and vigilance for postherpetic neuralgia, to which his advanced age places him at high risk.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Arrange prompt but non-emergent clinical evaluation. Consider antiviral therapy appropriate for herpes zoster, recognizing that he is an elderly patient at high risk of complications; the greatest benefit is with early initiation and his lesions have already reached the crusting stage, so the treating clinician should weigh whether new lesions are still forming. Provide analgesia adequate for neuropathic zoster pain, since the burning and aching pain has already been present for 5 days and is the dominant symptom; escalate analgesia in a stepwise fashion if simple measures are insufficient. Care for the rash with gentle cleansing, keeping the area clean and dry, and covering weeping or ulcerated lesions with a non-adherent dressing; advise against scratching or rupturing vesicles to reduce the risk of secondary bacterial infection and scarring at the ulcerated sites. Regarding the additional considerations: he remains potentially infectious to people who have never had varicella or been vaccinated until all lesions are fully crusted, so he should avoid close contact with pregnant women, infants, and immunocompromised individuals and should keep the rash covered until crusting is complete. Because the eruption is on the right chest and not on the face, there is no ocular involvement described and no ophthalmologic emergency, but any eye pain, redness, or rash near the eye or tip of the nose would require immediate ophthalmologic assessment. Counsel him explicitly about postherpetic neuralgia, the leading complication at his age, so that persistent pain after the rash resolves is reported and treated rather than tolerated. Arrange follow-up to confirm healing of the ulcerated areas and to reassess pain, and discuss herpes zoster vaccination for future prevention once the acute episode has resolved. Return promptly for spreading rash beyond the dermatome, rash on the opposite side, high fever, increasing redness, warmth or purulent discharge from the lesions suggesting bacterial superinfection, confusion, or new neurological symptoms such as weakness.
Notes: The case does not describe fever, immunosuppression, comorbid conditions, medications, or vaccination history, and no ocular or disseminated involvement is reported; management decisions, particularly antiviral choice and dosing, depend on renal function and comorbidity data that are not provided.

Age: 77 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five days of burning and aching pain on the right side of the chest, followed by erythema and a maculopapular rash in the same painful area with headache and malaise, progressing over 3 to 5 days into clusters of clear vesicles that then pustulated, ulcerated, and crusted.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of herpes zoster (shingles) due to reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in a thoracic dorsal root ganglion. The strongest supporting facts are the prodrome of burning and aching neuropathic pain preceding the rash by 5 days, the strictly unilateral right-sided chest location corresponding to a thoracic dermatome, the appearance of erythema and a maculopapular eruption confined to that same painful area, and the classic evolution through clusters of clear vesicles over 3 to 5 days into pustulation, ulceration, and crusting. The accompanying headache and malaise are consistent with the systemic prodromal features of zoster. Age 77 is an important risk factor, since declining varicella-zoster virus specific cell-mediated immunity with advancing age both predisposes to reactivation and increases the risk of complications, particularly postherpetic neuralgia, which is the most common sequela in elderly patients. Main differential considerations grounded in the case: because the pain preceded the rash by several days and is on the chest, an initial cardiac or pleuritic cause of chest pain would be considered during the prodromal phase, but the subsequent appearance of a dermatomal vesicular eruption in exactly the painful area settles the diagnosis; herpes simplex virus infection can produce grouped vesicles but does not typically follow a unilateral dermatome across the chest in this manner; contact dermatitis and bullous impetigo do not present with a preceding several-day burning neuropathic prodrome or dermatomal distribution. The stage of the eruption is important for management: the lesions have already progressed to pustulation, ulceration, and crusting, meaning the presentation is beyond the earliest window in which antiviral therapy has the greatest benefit, though older patients with ongoing lesion evolution may still be considered for treatment.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 77-year-old man with unilateral right thoracic dermatomal herpes zoster, presenting with a 5-day neuropathic pain prodrome followed by a maculopapular then vesicular eruption in the same dermatome that has evolved through pustulation, ulceration, and crusting, with associated headache and malaise. The diagnosis is clinical, and management centers on pain control, prevention of secondary bacterial infection, and vigilance for postherpetic neuralgia, to which his advanced age places him at high risk.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Arrange prompt but non-emergent clinical evaluation. Consider antiviral therapy appropriate for herpes zoster, recognizing that he is an elderly patient at high risk of complications; the greatest benefit is with early initiation and his lesions have already reached the crusting stage, so the treating clinician should weigh whether new lesions are still forming. Provide analgesia adequate for neuropathic zoster pain, since the burning and aching pain has already been present for 5 days and is the dominant symptom; escalate analgesia in a stepwise fashion if simple measures are insufficient. Care for the rash with gentle cleansing, keeping the area clean and dry, and covering weeping or ulcerated lesions with a non-adherent dressing; advise against scratching or rupturing vesicles to reduce the risk of secondary bacterial infection and scarring at the ulcerated sites. Regarding the additional considerations: he remains potentially infectious to people who have never had varicella or been vaccinated until all lesions are fully crusted, so he should avoid close contact with pregnant women, infants, and immunocompromised individuals and should keep the rash covered until crusting is complete. Because the eruption is on the right chest and not on the face, there is no ocular involvement described and no ophthalmologic emergency, but any eye pain, redness, or rash near the eye or tip of the nose would require immediate ophthalmologic assessment. Counsel him explicitly about postherpetic neuralgia, the leading complication at his age, so that persistent pain after the rash resolves is reported and treated rather than tolerated. Arrange follow-up to confirm healing of the ulcerated areas and to reassess pain, and discuss herpes zoster vaccination for future prevention once the acute episode has resolved. Return promptly for spreading rash beyond the dermatome, rash on the opposite side, high fever, increasing redness, warmth or purulent discharge from the lesions suggesting bacterial superinfection, confusion, or new neurological symptoms such as weakness.
Notes: The case does not describe fever, immunosuppression, comorbid conditions, medications, or vaccination history, and no ocular or disseminated involvement is reported; management decisions, particularly antiviral choice and dosing, depend on renal function and comorbidity data that are not provided.

Diagnosis10cm: Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, with status epilepticus

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided.
