Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of persistent dizziness described as a sensation of spinning. She reports the dizziness is constant rather than positional and is accompanied by an unsteady gait and difficulty walking in a straight line. She has had two episodes of nausea and vomiting. She denies hearing loss or tinnitus. Past medical history is notable for migraine headaches and hypertension. On examination, vital signs are stable. Neurological exam reveals vertical nystagmus that does not suppress with fixation, mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing on the right, and gait ataxia with veering to the right. baseline_protocol:
Age: 50 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Five days of constant, non-positional spinning dizziness with unsteady gait, difficulty walking in a straight line, and two episodes of nausea and vomiting, without hearing loss or tinnitus.
Analysis: The pattern is a central vestibular syndrome, and until proven otherwise this represents a posterior circulation (cerebellar or brainstem) ischemic event. The decisive findings are the character of the nystagmus and the presence of appendicular and gait ataxia. Vertical nystagmus is a central sign; peripheral vestibulopathy produces horizontal-torsional, unidirectional nystagmus. Failure of the nystagmus to suppress with visual fixation is likewise a central feature, since peripheral nystagmus characteristically diminishes with fixation. Mild dysmetria on right finger-to-nose testing indicates ipsilateral cerebellar hemispheric dysfunction, and gait ataxia with veering to the right localizes to the same side; severe gait instability out of proportion to the vertigo is a recognized marker of central disease. Supporting the central localization further, the dizziness is constant rather than positional and has persisted 5 days, the Dix-Hallpike maneuver is negative, and hearing is intact bilaterally with no tinnitus, arguing against labyrinthine involvement. Vascular risk is present in the form of hypertension, and age 50 is compatible with stroke. Mr. A is a 24 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, fever, and headache. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat and fever to 102.2. He has had no cough. His physical examination is normal, except for the presence of tonsillar exudates and some tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. baseline_protocol:
Age: 24 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two days of acute sore throat, fever to 102.2 F, and headache, without cough.
Analysis: The presentation is acute pharyngitis with a high clinical probability of group A streptococcal infection. The case explicitly states a Centor score of 4, and each of the four components is documented: fever by history to 102.2 F, tonsillar exudates on examination, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and absence of cough. Age 24 is in the range that neither adds nor subtracts a point in the age-modified scoring. The abrupt onset over 2 days with fever and headache and without any lower respiratory symptoms further favors a bacterial rather than viral etiology, since viral pharyngitis typically presents with coryza, cough, hoarseness, and conjunctival symptoms, none of which are described. The remainder of the physical examination is normal, which is reassuring: there is no trismus, no uvular deviation, no asymmetric tonsillar bulging, no muffled voice, no drooling, no stridor, and no neck swelling, so there is no evidence of peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal infection, or airway compromise. Differential considerations weighed: viral pharyngitis from adenovirus, influenza, or other respiratory viruses, less likely given the score of 4 and the absent cough but never fully excluded on clinical grounds alone; infectious mononucleosis from Epstein-Barr virus, which can produce exudative tonsillitis with fever in this exact age group and should be considered particularly if there is posterior cervical adenopathy, splenomegaly, marked fatigue, or if symptoms fail to resolve, though the examination here is otherwise normal with only anterior cervical nodes; peritonsillar abscess, excluded by the absence of trismus, asymmetry, and voice change; acute HIV seroconversion illness, worth remembering in a young adult with pharyngitis and fever; and gonococcal pharyngitis, not supported by the history given. He is otherwise healthy, on no medications except ibuprofen for fever, and has no drug allergies, so first-line antibiotic therapy is unrestricted. With a Centor score of 4, either empiric treatment or rapid antigen testing with treatment of a positive result is an accepted approach, as the case itself notes.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Rapid antigen detection test for group A Streptococcus from a throat swab, with throat culture as backup in the event of a negative rapid test, if a test-and-treat strategy is chosen; if empiric treatment is elected on the basis of a Centor score of 4, no additional testing is strictly required. Consider testing for infectious mononucleosis with a heterophile antibody test and complete blood count with differential if the streptococcal testing is negative or if symptoms persist or worsen despite appropriate antibiotic therapy.
Conclusion: Acute exudative pharyngitis in a healthy 24-year-old man with a Centor score of 4 (fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, no cough), indicating a high likelihood of group A streptococcal pharyngitis. There are no signs of suppurative complication or airway compromise. Management is outpatient antibiotic therapy, either empirically or after a positive rapid antigen test, combined with symptomatic care.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Treat for group A streptococcal pharyngitis, either empirically given the Centor score of 4 or after confirming with a rapid antigen test, using a first-line penicillin-class antibiotic, which is appropriate here because he reports no drug allergies; complete the full prescribed course even after symptoms improve, since the principal aims of treatment are to shorten symptoms, reduce transmission, and prevent acute rheumatic fever and suppurative complications. Continue symptomatic care with adequate analgesia and antipyretics, noting that he is already using ibuprofen, and add saltwater gargles, throat lozenges, cool fluids, soft foods, and rest; ensure adequate hydration, since pain can limit oral intake. Address the additional considerations explicitly: (1) he is no longer considered contagious after approximately 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy plus resolution of fever, and until then should avoid close contact, sharing utensils or drinks, and should not return to work or school; (2) replace his toothbrush after starting therapy; (3) reassess if there is no improvement within 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics, and specifically reconsider infectious mononucleosis, which is common in this age group and can mimic streptococcal pharyngitis; if mononucleosis is diagnosed, counsel on avoiding contact sports and heavy lifting for the risk of splenic rupture; (4) provide explicit red-flag return precautions for the development of drooling, trismus, muffled or "hot potato" voice, inability to swallow saliva or fluids, unilateral throat swelling with uvular deviation, neck stiffness or swelling, stridor, or difficulty breathing, all of which suggest peritonsillar or deep neck space abscess or airway compromise and require emergency evaluation; (5) advise return also for rash, dark urine, joint pain, or persistent high fever after completing therapy; (6) no follow-up test of cure is needed in an uncomplicated case in an otherwise healthy adult who responds to treatment.
Notes: A Centor score of 4 supports either empiric treatment or a test-and-treat approach; the choice should follow local practice and antibiotic stewardship considerations. Rapid antigen tests are specific but less sensitive, so a negative result in a patient with a score of 4 may warrant backup culture. Infectious mononucleosis remains the main alternative in this age group and should be reconsidered if there is no response to antibiotics.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 19 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five days of severe, progressively worsening sore throat despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin, now with odynophagia and inability to eat solid food for 2 days, muffled "hot potato" voice, trismus, and drooling.
Analysis: The findings are diagnostic of a left peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). The strongest supporting facts are the classic triad of trismus with mouth opening limited to approximately 2 cm, a muffled "hot potato" voice, and drooling from pain on swallowing, combined with the decisive intraoral finding of a bulging, erythematous soft palate on the left with the left tonsil displaced medially and inferiorly and the uvula deviated away from the lesion to the right. This unilateral asymmetry with contralateral uvular deviation is the hallmark that distinguishes a peritonsillar collection from diffuse tonsillitis. The course also fits: an initial pharyngitis that progressively worsened rather than improved despite 3 days of appropriate oral amoxicillin indicates a suppurative complication that has formed a walled-off collection requiring drainage, since antibiotics alone cannot sterilize an abscess cavity. Fever of 101.4 F and tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy confirm ongoing infection, while a heart rate of 98 and blood pressure of 124/78 indicate hemodynamic stability. Importantly, the airway is currently patent: he denies respiratory difficulty, lungs are clear, and there is no stridor, so this is an urgent but not yet an airway-crisis situation, although trismus and drooling mark it as an at-risk airway. Differential considerations weighed: severe uncomplicated streptococcal or viral tonsillitis, argued against by the marked unilateral asymmetry, uvular deviation, trismus, and failure of amoxicillin; peritonsillar cellulitis without a drainable collection, which can present similarly and is the main reason imaging or aspiration is used to distinguish, since cellulitis may respond to antibiotics alone; infectious mononucleosis, which can cause severe exudative tonsillitis and is common at 19 and can be complicated by peritonsillar abscess, and which is also relevant because amoxicillin frequently produces a rash in that setting; retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal abscess, which would more often present with neck stiffness, neck swelling, and midline posterior pharyngeal bulging rather than this discrete peritonsillar bulge, and which must be excluded if the presentation extends; epiglottitis, argued against by the absence of stridor and respiratory distress and by the visible oropharyngeal pathology; and Lemierre syndrome as a downstream complication if the infection extends to the internal jugular vein. Poor oral intake for 2 days makes dehydration likely.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urgent otolaryngology consultation for needle aspiration or incision and drainage, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck if the diagnosis or the extent of the collection is uncertain, if drainage is unsuccessful, if trismus prevents adequate examination and access, or if a deeper parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal extension is suspected; intraoral ultrasound is a useful alternative to localize the collection. Gram stain and aerobic and anaerobic culture with sensitivities of the aspirated pus. Complete blood count with differential, electrolytes, and renal function to assess the inflammatory response and the degree of dehydration after 2 days of inability to eat. Heterophile antibody testing for infectious mononucleosis given his age and the clinical picture. Continuous monitoring with pulse oximetry and equipment for emergency airway management available during the drainage procedure.
Conclusion: Left peritonsillar abscess in a 19-year-old man, arising as a suppurative complication of pharyngitis that progressed despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin, evidenced by trismus limiting mouth opening to 2 cm, muffled voice, drooling, a bulging erythematous left soft palate with medial and inferior displacement of the left tonsil, and uvular deviation to the right, with fever and tender ipsilateral cervical and submandibular adenopathy. The airway is currently patent without stridor or respiratory distress and he is hemodynamically stable, but the condition requires emergent drainage, parenteral antibiotics, rehydration, and airway vigilance.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Arrange emergent otolaryngology evaluation for drainage of the abscess by needle aspiration, incision and drainage, or, in selected cases, tonsillectomy; drainage is the definitive intervention because antibiotics alone will not resolve an established collection, as demonstrated by his failure on 3 days of amoxicillin. Send aspirated material for Gram stain and aerobic and anaerobic culture. Start intravenous antibiotics covering group A Streptococcus, oral anaerobes, and beta-lactamase-producing organisms, then narrow according to culture results and transition to oral therapy once he is improving and able to swallow. Address the additional considerations explicitly: (1) although he denies respiratory difficulty and has no stridor with clear lungs, the combination of trismus, drooling, and a muffled voice defines an at-risk airway, so he must be monitored continuously with immediate access to advanced airway equipment and personnel skilled in difficult airway management, especially during drainage, since trismus limiting opening to 2 cm complicates both examination and intubation; (2) correct dehydration with intravenous fluids, given 2 days without solid food and severe odynophagia, and monitor electrolytes and urine output; (3) provide adequate parenteral analgesia and antipyretics so that he can begin swallowing, and consider corticosteroids as an adjunct to reduce pharyngeal edema, trismus, and pain in consultation with the treating specialist; (4) keep him nil by mouth until after drainage and airway assessment, then advance to cool liquids and soft diet as tolerated; (5) reassess for extension beyond the peritonsillar space, and obtain contrast-enhanced neck CT if neck swelling, neck stiffness, worsening trismus, midline pharyngeal bulging, or failure to improve after drainage develops, and remain alert for parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spread, mediastinal extension, internal jugular septic thrombophlebitis (Lemierre syndrome), and airway obstruction; (6) test for infectious mononucleosis, which is a common predisposing condition at this age and would alter counseling, including avoidance of contact sports if splenomegaly is present, and which explains amoxicillin-associated rash if one appears; (7) admit for observation until fever, pain, trismus, and oral intake improve, and arrange otolaryngology follow-up with discussion of interval tonsillectomy if recurrence occurs or if he has a history of recurrent tonsillitis; (8) instruct him to return immediately for any breathing difficulty, stridor, inability to handle secretions, worsening neck swelling, or recurrent fever after discharge.
Notes: Peritonsillar cellulitis without a drainable collection can present identically; if aspiration returns no pus, treat with parenteral antibiotics and reassess, using imaging to guide further management. Trismus limiting mouth opening to 2 cm is both a diagnostic clue and a practical airway hazard that must be communicated to anyone managing the airway.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of mildly itchy, erythematous patches on both hands. He recently switched to a new laundry detergent approximately two weeks ago. He denies any history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or food allergies. On examination, there are bilateral, symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the dorsal hands with mild scaling. The skin is intact with no cracking, vesicles, or weeping. There is no involvement of the wrists or forearms. He works as an accountant and reports no occupational chemical exposures.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: One week of mildly itchy, erythematous, mildly scaling patches on the dorsal aspects of both hands, beginning about one week after switching to a new laundry detergent.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with a mild contact dermatitis of the hands attributable to the recently introduced laundry detergent. The strongest supporting facts are the clear temporal relationship, with the new detergent started approximately two weeks ago and the eruption appearing about one week later, a latency compatible with sensitization and delayed-type allergic contact dermatitis, and also compatible with cumulative irritant contact dermatitis from detergent residue. The morphology supports contact dermatitis: bilateral, symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with mild scaling. Symmetry and bilateral involvement point to an exogenous agent contacting both hands equally rather than an infectious or asymmetric process, and the well-demarcated borders are characteristic of contact-mediated inflammation confined to the area of exposure. The distribution on the dorsal hands, which have a thinner stratum corneum and are more susceptible than the palms, with no involvement of the wrists or forearms, further supports localized contact rather than a systemic or widespread eruption. The disease is mild and uncomplicated: the skin is explicitly intact with no cracking, no vesicles, and no weeping, so there is no fissuring to serve as a portal for infection, no acute vesicular phase, and no evidence of secondary bacterial infection. Main differential considerations grounded in the case: atopic hand dermatitis is unlikely because he denies any history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or food allergies, removing the atopic diathesis; occupational irritant hand dermatitis is unlikely because he works as an accountant and reports no occupational chemical exposures; tinea manuum typically presents with unilateral or asymmetric involvement with an active scaling border rather than symmetric well-demarcated dorsal plaques; psoriasis would generally show thicker, more sharply demarcated silvery plaques and would not have appeared abruptly in temporal lockstep with a detergent change; dyshidrotic eczema is excluded by the absence of vesicles. Distinguishing allergic from irritant contact dermatitis is not possible from the history alone and is not necessary to begin management, since the initial treatment for both is removal of the offending agent.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 30-year-old non-atopic man with no occupational exposures has mild, uncomplicated, bilateral symmetric contact dermatitis of the dorsal hands, temporally linked to a laundry detergent introduced two weeks ago. The skin barrier is intact with no cracking, vesicles, weeping, or signs of infection, and no diagnostic testing is required at this stage. Removing the suspected trigger and providing basic barrier care and topical anti-inflammatory treatment should resolve the eruption.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Stop using the new laundry detergent and revert to the previously tolerated product, since this is the only identified new exposure and its withdrawal is both the diagnostic test and the treatment. Rewash all clothing, towels, and bed linens that were laundered with the new detergent to remove residual product from fabrics, and run an extra rinse cycle; residue on shirt cuffs and towels is a common reason symptoms persist after switching back. Prefer a fragrance-free and dye-free detergent going forward, and avoid fabric softener and dryer sheets while the skin is recovering. Care for the skin barrier with frequent liberal application of a bland, fragrance-free emollient to both hands, especially after any hand washing, and use lukewarm rather than hot water with a gentle non-soap cleanser. Wear protective gloves for wet work and household cleaning to limit further irritant exposure. For the mild itch and erythema, a short course of a low-potency topical corticosteroid applied to the affected dorsal hands is reasonable, used for a limited period and not continued indefinitely. Regarding the additional considerations: no antibiotics or antifungals are indicated, because the skin is intact with no cracking, weeping, or vesicles and no features of bacterial or fungal infection; his lack of any atopic history means this is not an atopic flare requiring long-term eczema management; and his sedentary work as an accountant with no chemical exposures means no occupational modification or workplace investigation is required. Expect improvement within one to two weeks of avoiding the detergent. Seek medical evaluation if the rash does not improve after two to four weeks of strict avoidance and emollient use, if it spreads beyond the hands, or if the skin begins to crack, weep, blister, or develop pain, warmth, pus, or crusting suggesting secondary infection. If the dermatitis recurs or persists despite avoiding the detergent, referral to dermatology for patch testing would be appropriate to identify a specific allergen.
Notes: The case does not allow allergic contact dermatitis to be distinguished from irritant contact dermatitis, and confirmation of the detergent as the cause rests on the temporal association and on resolution after withdrawal. Patch testing is not needed now but would be the definitive test if the condition persists or recurs.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a 1-day history of nausea, three episodes of watery non-bloody diarrhea, and mild diffuse abdominal cramping. She reports her roommate had similar symptoms earlier in the week. She is able to tolerate oral fluids and has been sipping water and electrolyte drinks throughout the day. She denies fever, bloody stool, severe abdominal pain, or dizziness. On examination, vital signs are stable. The abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound. Mucous membranes are moist. Bowel sounds are hyperactive.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 28 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: One day of nausea, three episodes of watery non-bloody diarrhea, and mild diffuse abdominal cramping, with a roommate who had similar symptoms earlier in the week.
Analysis: The presentation is that of acute uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis. The strongest supporting facts are the short one-day duration, the watery non-bloody character of the diarrhea, the mild diffuse cramping typical of small bowel involvement, and above all the clear epidemiological link of a roommate with similar symptoms earlier in the week, which indicates person-to-person transmission of a contagious enteric pathogen and fits the incubation and household spread pattern of a viral agent such as norovirus. Equally important is what the case explicitly excludes. She denies fever, which argues against an invasive bacterial enterocolitis; she denies bloody stool, which argues against inflammatory or invasive pathogens and against inflammatory bowel disease; and she denies severe abdominal pain, which argues against an acute surgical abdomen. Her volume status is intact and this is the key determinant of disposition: she is tolerating oral fluids and has been sipping water and electrolyte drinks throughout the day, her vital signs are stable, her mucous membranes are moist, and she denies dizziness, so there is no orthostatic intolerance and no clinical dehydration. Only three stools have occurred, a low-volume loss. The abdominal examination is reassuring and inconsistent with peritonitis or a surgical cause: the abdomen is soft with only mild diffuse tenderness and specifically no guarding and no rebound, while hyperactive bowel sounds are the expected finding of increased intestinal motility in enteritis rather than a warning sign. Main differential considerations grounded in the case: bacterial enterocolitis is unlikely without fever or bloody stool; food poisoning from a preformed toxin is possible but the roommate's illness earlier in the week favors person-to-person spread over a shared single meal; appendicitis and other surgical causes are effectively excluded by diffuse rather than localized right lower quadrant pain, the absence of guarding or rebound, and the absence of fever; and inflammatory bowel disease is not supported by a one-day course with no blood in the stool. This illness is self-limited and expected to resolve within a few days, and the sole clinical priority is maintaining hydration.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 28-year-old woman with acute, mild, uncomplicated, likely viral gastroenteritis acquired from a symptomatic household contact. She is well hydrated and tolerating oral intake, has stable vital signs, moist mucous membranes, and a benign abdominal examination with no fever, no bloody stool, and no peritoneal signs. No laboratory testing, stool studies, imaging, or antibiotics are indicated, and she can be managed with supportive care at home with clear instructions on when to seek care.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Manage supportively at home. Continue and increase oral rehydration, which she is already doing successfully with water and electrolyte drinks; oral rehydration solution or a commercial electrolyte drink is preferable to plain water alone because the diarrhea causes electrolyte as well as water loss, and she should drink small amounts frequently rather than large volumes at once given the nausea. Resume eating as tolerated with bland, easily digestible foods once nausea allows, and there is no need for prolonged fasting or a restrictive diet. Temporarily limit alcohol, caffeine, and very fatty or highly spiced foods, and note that some people tolerate lactose poorly for a short period after gastroenteritis. Rest as needed. Regarding the additional considerations: antibiotics are not indicated and should be avoided, because the illness has the features of a viral gastroenteritis with no fever and no bloody stool, and antibiotics offer no benefit while risking adverse effects and Clostridioides difficile infection; stool cultures, ova and parasite testing, blood work, and abdominal imaging are likewise not indicated in a patient with a one-day mild illness, stable vital signs, moist mucous membranes, and a soft non-peritonitic abdomen. Antimotility agents may be used cautiously for symptom control in a non-bloody, afebrile diarrheal illness such as this one, but are not necessary given only three stools; they should be stopped if fever or bloody stool develops. Because her roommate had the same illness and these pathogens spread readily, emphasize infection control: thorough and frequent hand washing with soap and water, which is more effective than alcohol-based sanitizer against the likely viral agents; not sharing towels, utensils, or drinks; cleaning and disinfecting shared bathroom surfaces and door handles; and staying away from work involving food handling or care of others until at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve. Expect resolution over a few days. Seek medical evaluation if she develops high or persistent fever, blood or mucus in the stool, severe or localized abdominal pain, persistent vomiting preventing her from keeping fluids down, signs of dehydration such as dizziness on standing, marked reduction in urine output, dry mouth, or extreme weakness, or if the diarrhea continues beyond about one week without improvement.
Notes: The reassuring disposition rests on her preserved ability to tolerate oral fluids and her normal hydration status; if she becomes unable to drink or shows signs of volume depletion, the assessment changes and she requires in-person evaluation. Duration of the illness is only one day, so continued observation for evolution of symptoms is appropriate.

Vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presents with 5 days of progressive shortness of breath following a confirmed influenza A infection. Despite oseltamivir initiated 3 days ago, her respiratory status has continued to deteriorate. She has a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 38). On examination, she is in marked respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.9C, HR 118, RR 34, BP 106/62, SpO2 82% on high-flow nasal cannula at 60L/min and FiO2 100%. Lung auscultation reveals diffuse bilateral crackles. Chest X-ray demonstrates bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, but echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function with no evidence of volume overload. ABG: pH 7.22, pO2 58, pCO2 52, PaO2/FiO2 ratio 58. She is intubated for mechanical ventilation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 60 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Five days of progressive shortness of breath following confirmed influenza A infection, with continued deterioration despite oseltamivir started three days ago, now in marked respiratory distress with severe refractory hypoxemia requiring intubation.
Analysis: This is severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) caused by influenza A pneumonia. Every diagnostic criterion is met by the case. The onset is acute and within one week, with five days of progressive dyspnea following a confirmed influenza A infection, giving a clear precipitating insult. The imaging criterion is met by a chest X-ray showing bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities. The critical differentiating step is exclusion of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and this is definitively accomplished by the echocardiogram, which shows normal left ventricular function with no evidence of volume overload; the radiographic pattern that looks like pulmonary edema is therefore non-cardiogenic, reflecting inflammatory alveolar-capillary membrane injury with protein-rich fluid leak rather than elevated hydrostatic pressure. The oxygenation criterion establishes the severity: a PaO2 to FiO2 ratio of 58 is far below the threshold of 100 that defines severe ARDS, and this profound impairment is corroborated by an SpO2 of only 82 percent on high-flow nasal cannula delivering 60 litres per minute at 100 percent FiO2, meaning maximal non-invasive oxygen support has already failed. The arterial blood gas confirms life-threatening respiratory failure with combined hypoxemia and ventilatory failure: pO2 of 58 despite maximal oxygen, and pCO2 of 52 with a pH of 7.22, indicating acute respiratory acidosis from a patient who can no longer sustain the work of breathing at a respiratory rate of 34. The rising pCO2 in a tachypneic patient signals impending respiratory muscle fatigue and is itself an indication for intubation, which has correctly been performed. Diffuse bilateral crackles on auscultation are consistent with widespread alveolar filling. Her risk profile explains the severity: age 60, type 2 diabetes causing relative immune dysfunction even though well controlled, and obesity with a BMI of 38, which is an independent risk factor for severe influenza and for ARDS and which also reduces chest wall compliance and functional residual capacity, complicating ventilation. Temperature of 38.9 C and heart rate of 118 reflect the ongoing inflammatory and infectious state, and a blood pressure of 106/62 is maintained but at the lower end, warranting close monitoring for evolving shock. The failure to respond to oseltamivir started three days ago does not indicate antiviral failure in itself, since ARDS reflects established host inflammatory lung injury that continues after viral replication is suppressed, but it does raise the important question of a superimposed secondary bacterial pneumonia, a well-recognized and frequently lethal complication of influenza that must be actively considered given the fever and progressive deterioration. Main differential considerations grounded in the case: cardiogenic pulmonary edema is excluded by the echocardiogram; volume overload is excluded by the same study; secondary bacterial pneumonia superimposed on influenza remains an important and unresolved consideration; and pulmonary embolism could contribute to hypoxemia in a critically ill obese patient, though the bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities are better explained by ARDS.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Invasive mechanical ventilator with capability for high PEEP and lung-protective settings, and equipment for prone positioning; continuous cardiac, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry monitoring with capnography; serial arterial blood gases to guide ventilation and track the respiratory acidosis; arterial line for continuous blood pressure and repeated sampling; central venous access as needed for vasopressors; blood cultures, sputum or endotracheal aspirate Gram stain and culture, and respiratory pathogen testing including bacterial studies to evaluate for secondary bacterial pneumonia; complete blood count with differential; comprehensive metabolic panel with renal and hepatic function and electrolytes; serum lactate; coagulation studies; serial glucose monitoring given type 2 diabetes and critical illness; repeat chest radiography to follow the infiltrates and to confirm endotracheal tube position and exclude barotrauma; continuous cardiac output or dynamic fluid responsiveness assessment to guide conservative fluid management; repeat echocardiography if hemodynamics deteriorate or right heart strain is suspected; CT pulmonary angiography if pulmonary embolism is suspected clinically.
Conclusion: A 60-year-old woman with diabetes and obesity has developed severe influenza A associated ARDS, with a PaO2 to FiO2 ratio of 58, bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities, and a normal echocardiogram excluding a cardiogenic cause, complicated by acute respiratory acidosis with pH 7.22 and pCO2 52 after failure of maximal high-flow oxygen therapy. She has been appropriately intubated and now requires intensive care with lung-protective mechanical ventilation, prone positioning for her severe hypoxemia, continued antiviral therapy, evaluation and empiric coverage for secondary bacterial pneumonia, and consideration of extracorporeal support if refractory.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Admit immediately to intensive care. Institute lung-protective mechanical ventilation with low tidal volume ventilation based on predicted body weight, limiting plateau pressure and driving pressure, and titrate PEEP upward to recruit collapsed alveoli in this severe ARDS; permit hypercapnia within tolerable pH limits rather than injuring the lung with high tidal volumes, while addressing the current acidosis of pH 7.22. Note that her BMI of 38 reduces chest wall compliance and functional residual capacity, so higher PEEP is generally required and plateau pressure must be interpreted in the light of the elevated pleural pressure that obesity produces. Initiate prone positioning early, as her PaO2 to FiO2 ratio of 58 places her firmly in the severe category where prolonged prone sessions improve oxygenation and outcome; ensure adequate staffing and meticulous attention to pressure points and tube security given her body habitus. Provide deep sedation and analgesia to achieve ventilator synchrony, and use neuromuscular blockade if severe dyssynchrony or refractory hypoxemia persists. Apply a conservative fluid strategy, avoiding fluid overload that would worsen alveolar flooding, while maintaining adequate perfusion; the echocardiogram has already shown she is not volume overloaded and has normal left ventricular function, so hypotension if it develops should be treated with careful fluid assessment and vasopressors rather than large-volume resuscitation, and her blood pressure of 106/62 warrants monitoring for evolving shock. Continue oseltamivir; the lack of clinical response reflects established immune-mediated lung injury rather than a reason to stop antiviral therapy, and treatment should be completed. Regarding the additional considerations: start empiric antibiotics covering secondary bacterial pneumonia after obtaining blood cultures and respiratory specimens, because post-influenza bacterial superinfection is a leading cause of continued deterioration and her fever of 38.9 C with progressive decline over five days is compatible with it, and de-escalate promptly according to culture results. Manage her type 2 diabetes with an insulin protocol targeting controlled glucose in critical illness, recognizing that critical illness and any corticosteroid use will worsen glycemic control despite her disease being well controlled at baseline. Assess for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and involve or transfer to an ECMO-capable center early if hypoxemia or hypercapnic acidosis remains refractory despite lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning, and neuromuscular blockade, since a PaO2 to FiO2 ratio of 58 is within the range where ECMO referral is appropriate. Provide standard critical care supportive measures including venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, which is particularly important given her obesity and immobility, stress ulcer prophylaxis, head-of-bed elevation and a ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle, early enteral nutrition, and daily assessment of sedation and readiness to wean. Implement influenza infection control precautions for staff and visitors. Communicate with the patient's family about the severity of illness and prognosis and clarify goals of care.
Notes: The failure of oseltamivir to arrest deterioration is expected in established ARDS and should not be read as antiviral resistance or as a reason to discontinue it, but it does mandate an active search for secondary bacterial infection. Her obesity with a BMI of 38 requires that tidal volume be calculated from predicted rather than actual body weight and that plateau pressures be interpreted against the elevated pleural pressure of obesity. No allergy history, current medications, baseline functional status, or advance directives are provided in the case.

Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman who is 4 months postpartum presents with a 6-week history of pain along the radial (thumb) side of her right wrist. The pain began insidiously and has progressively worsened. She attributes it to the repetitive motions of lifting and holding her infant. The pain is sharp and radiates proximally into the forearm and distally into the thumb. She reports difficulty gripping objects, turning her wrist, and making a fist. She is right-hand dominant. On examination, there is tenderness and mild swelling over the radial styloid process and the first dorsal compartment. Finkelstein test is markedly positive, reproducing sharp pain along the radial wrist when the thumb is grasped in a fist and the wrist is ulnarly deviated. Grip strength is reduced due to pain. Thumb range of motion is preserved but painful at extremes. Neurovascular examination of the hand is intact. Wrist radiographs are normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 32 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Six weeks of progressively worsening sharp pain along the radial side of the right wrist in a woman 4 months postpartum, radiating proximally into the forearm and distally into the thumb, with difficulty gripping objects, turning the wrist, and making a fist.
Analysis: The diagnosis is de Quervain tenosynovitis of the right first dorsal compartment. The findings are essentially pathognomonic. A markedly positive Finkelstein test, reproducing sharp radial wrist pain when the thumb is grasped in a fist and the wrist ulnarly deviated, directly demonstrates that passive stretch of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons within the first dorsal compartment provokes the pain, which localizes the pathology precisely to that compartment. This is corroborated by tenderness and mild swelling over the radial styloid process and the first dorsal compartment, the anatomical site of the affected tendon sheath. The history fits the mechanism exactly: an insidious, progressively worsening overuse tendinopathy over six weeks in a 4-month postpartum woman who repeatedly lifts and holds her infant, a task performed with the wrist in radial deviation and the thumb abducted, which is the classic posture that loads these tendons and gives the condition its common association with new parenthood. Involvement of the right, dominant hand increases the loading and functional impact. The radiation of pain both proximally into the forearm and distally into the thumb follows the course of the involved tendons. Functional loss with reduced grip strength attributable to pain, preserved but painful thumb range of motion at extremes, and difficulty making a fist are all consistent with a painful tenosynovitis rather than a structural or neurological deficit. Important negatives narrow the differential decisively: neurovascular examination of the hand is intact, which excludes a compressive neuropathy such as carpal tunnel syndrome or superficial radial nerve entrapment as the primary problem and excludes vascular compromise; and wrist radiographs are normal, which excludes scaphoid fracture, radial styloid fracture, and significant first carpometacarpal osteoarthritis or other bony pathology. Main differential considerations grounded in the case therefore include intersection syndrome, which produces pain more proximally in the dorsal forearm rather than at the radial styloid, first carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis, made unlikely by normal radiographs and by the pain localizing to the first dorsal compartment with a positive Finkelstein test, scaphoid pathology, excluded by normal radiographs and the reproducible tendon-stretch pain, and a radial neuropathy, excluded by the intact neurovascular examination. The condition is benign, non-emergent, and highly responsive to conservative management, but grip weakness in the dominant hand of a mother caring for an infant carries real functional consequences.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A right-hand dominant woman 4 months postpartum has classic de Quervain tenosynovitis of the right first dorsal compartment, established clinically by a markedly positive Finkelstein test with focal tenderness and swelling over the radial styloid, arising from the repetitive infant lifting and holding that has loaded the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons for six weeks. Radiographs are normal and the neurovascular examination is intact, so no fracture, arthritis, or nerve lesion is present, and no further imaging or testing is needed. Management is conservative, with thumb spica immobilization, activity modification, anti-inflammatory measures, and consideration of corticosteroid injection if symptoms persist.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Begin conservative treatment. Immobilize with a thumb spica splint that includes the wrist and the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint while leaving the interphalangeal joint free, worn consistently and particularly during infant care activities and at night, to rest the inflamed first dorsal compartment tendons. Modify activity by altering how she lifts and carries her infant, which is the identified causative exposure: lift from under the infant's body using both forearms and hands as a scoop rather than gripping under the arms with abducted thumbs and radially deviated wrists, keep the wrist in neutral, use pillows or a supportive cushion for feeding so the wrist is not bearing weight, and use a carrier or sling to reduce carrying load on the hands. Apply ice over the radial styloid for symptomatic relief. Use oral or topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication for pain and inflammation if not contraindicated. Regarding the additional considerations: if she is breastfeeding, confirm this and select analgesics compatible with lactation, as this influences both oral medication choice and her willingness to accept treatment; this should be addressed explicitly at the visit since she is 4 months postpartum. Refer to hand therapy or occupational therapy for splint fitting, ergonomic instruction on infant handling, and a graded program of stretching and progressive strengthening once acute pain settles, in order to restore the grip strength that is currently reduced by pain. If symptoms do not improve after several weeks of splinting, activity modification, and anti-inflammatory treatment, corticosteroid injection into the first dorsal compartment is the next step and is highly effective for this condition; surgical release of the first dorsal compartment is reserved for cases refractory to splinting and injection. No further imaging is required, since radiographs are already normal and the diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound would only be considered if the diagnosis were in doubt or to guide an injection. Reassure her that this is a common, benign, and treatable postpartum condition with a good prognosis, and that symptoms often improve substantially as the infant grows and lifting demands change. Arrange follow-up in a few weeks to reassess pain, grip strength, and function. Seek earlier reassessment if she develops numbness or tingling in the hand, new weakness not explained by pain, spreading redness, warmth or fever suggesting infection, or if the pain becomes severe and unresponsive to the measures above.
Notes: Breastfeeding status is not stated in the case but is directly relevant to medication selection at 4 months postpartum and should be clarified before prescribing. The diagnosis is clinical and no additional testing is warranted; the normal radiographs and intact neurovascular examination already exclude the principal alternative diagnoses.

Analysis: This is life-threatening hyperkalemia with advanced cardiac toxicity, occurring in a dialysis-dependent patient with uremia and metabolic acidosis after two missed dialysis sessions. The mechanism is clear and multifactorial. He has chronic kidney disease stage 4 with a baseline GFR of 22 and is dependent on maintenance hemodialysis for potassium clearance; missing two consecutive sessions removed his only route of potassium elimination. He simultaneously continued a potassium-rich diet including bananas and orange juice, adding potassium input while output was zero. The metabolic acidosis, with bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L from accumulated uremic acids, shifts potassium extracellularly and further raises the serum level. The result is a potassium of 7.8 mEq/L. The severity is defined not by the number alone but by the ECG, which shows the most dangerous stage short of arrest: absent P waves indicating loss of atrial electrical activity, QRS widening to 180 ms reflecting profoundly slowed intraventricular conduction, peaked T waves, and, critically, an emerging sine wave pattern, which is the immediate precursor to ventricular fibrillation and asystole. The clinical examination corroborates severe hyperkalemia with a heart rate of 52 that is irregular, indicating bradyarrhythmia from conduction block, generalized weakness and muscle cramps from neuromuscular membrane depolarization, diminished deep tendon reflexes as an objective sign of hyperkalemic neuromuscular dysfunction, and palpitations from the arrhythmia. The missed dialysis has also produced the other expected consequences of uremia and volume accumulation: BUN of 112 mg/dL and creatinine of 11.4 mg/dL confirm marked uremic solute retention; phosphorus of 8.2 mg/dL reflects failure of phosphate clearance; and volume overload is evident from 2+ bilateral pitting edema, blood pressure of 172/96, mild shortness of breath, respiratory rate of 20, and SpO2 of 95 percent, indicating fluid accumulation with early pulmonary congestion. Main differential considerations grounded in the case: the bradycardia and irregular rhythm could raise the question of a primary cardiac conduction disorder, but the ECG pattern of absent P waves, wide QRS, peaked T waves, and sine wave morphology in the setting of a potassium of 7.8 mEq/L is diagnostic of hyperkalemia rather than intrinsic conduction disease; uremic encephalopathy or pericarditis are potential consequences of the missed dialysis but are not described; and volume overload with pulmonary edema is a coexisting and independent indication for urgent dialysis alongside the hyperkalemia. The single decisive point of management is that medical temporizing measures only shift or transiently antagonize potassium, whereas the only definitive treatment in an anuric dialysis-dependent patient is removal of potassium by emergency hemodialysis. Intravenous calcium gluconate has correctly been given first to stabilize the myocardium; it does not lower potassium and its effect lasts only a short time, so it buys time and must be followed immediately by shifting therapy and by dialysis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring with serial ECGs to track resolution of the QRS widening and sine wave pattern; defibrillator and full resuscitation equipment immediately available at the bedside; continuous blood pressure and pulse oximetry monitoring; secure intravenous access; serial serum potassium measurements during and after treatment to detect rebound; venous or arterial blood gas to assess the metabolic acidosis; complete blood count; serum calcium, magnesium, and repeat phosphorus; assessment of the hemodialysis access for patency and usability; chest radiograph to evaluate the pulmonary congestion suggested by his dyspnea and edema; urgent nephrology and dialysis unit availability.
Conclusion: A 62-year-old dialysis-dependent man presents with severe hyperkalemia at 7.8 mEq/L and ECG evidence of imminent cardiac arrest, showing absent P waves, a QRS of 180 ms, peaked T waves, and an emerging sine wave pattern, precipitated by two missed hemodialysis sessions combined with continued potassium-rich dietary intake and compounded by metabolic acidosis with a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L. He additionally has uremia with a BUN of 112 mg/dL, hyperphosphatemia at 8.2 mg/dL, and volume overload with hypertension, peripheral edema, and mild dyspnea. Intravenous calcium gluconate has been appropriately given for membrane stabilization, and he requires immediate potassium-shifting therapy followed by emergency hemodialysis, which is the only definitive treatment.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Nephrology
Recommendations: Treat as an immediate cardiac emergency with continuous monitoring and resuscitation equipment at the bedside. Having given intravenous calcium gluconate for myocardial membrane stabilization, repeat the calcium dose if the ECG abnormalities persist or recur, recognizing that calcium does not lower serum potassium and its protective effect is short-lived. Immediately begin potassium-shifting therapy with intravenous insulin together with dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia, monitoring glucose closely afterwards; add high-dose nebulized beta-2 agonist as an additional shifting agent; and give intravenous sodium bicarbonate, which is particularly rational here given the metabolic acidosis with a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L, while understanding it is an adjunct rather than a primary therapy. Arrange emergency hemodialysis without delay and consider it the definitive intervention; contact nephrology and the dialysis unit immediately and confirm that his dialysis access is patent and usable, because in an anuric dialysis-dependent patient all shifting measures are temporary and potassium will rebound within hours as it redistributes back out of cells. Do not rely on loop diuretics, which are ineffective in this setting. A gastrointestinal potassium binder may be given as an adjunct to remove potassium from the body but must never delay dialysis. Withhold all potassium administration, review and stop any medication that raises potassium or impairs its excretion, and place him on a strict potassium-restricted diet with nothing by mouth until stabilized. Monitor serum potassium serially during and after treatment and repeat the ECG to confirm narrowing of the QRS and resolution of the sine wave pattern. Regarding the additional considerations: dialysis will simultaneously treat the other consequences of the missed sessions, namely the uremia with BUN 112 mg/dL and creatinine 11.4 mg/dL, the metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, the hyperphosphatemia at 8.2 mg/dL, and the volume overload manifest as 2+ pitting edema, blood pressure 172/96, and mild dyspnea, so ultrafiltration should be prescribed to remove the accumulated fluid; his hypertension is largely volume-dependent and should improve with fluid removal rather than being treated aggressively with additional antihypertensives in isolation. Address hyperphosphatemia with phosphate binders and dietary phosphate restriction once he is eating again. Most importantly, address the root cause before discharge: the crisis was caused entirely by missed dialysis due to transportation problems, so engage social work and the dialysis unit case manager to arrange reliable medical transport and a plan for missed-session outreach, since without this the event will recur and may be fatal. Provide renal dietitian counselling on potassium restriction, specifically addressing the bananas and orange juice he continued to consume, and educate him and his family on the warning symptoms of hyperkalemia such as weakness, cramps, and palpitations, and on the imperative to attend every dialysis session or seek emergency care immediately if a session is missed. Ensure he is admitted or observed until potassium and the ECG have normalized after dialysis, given the risk of post-dialysis rebound.
Notes: Calcium gluconate stabilizes the myocardium but does not lower serum potassium, and its effect is transient, so definitive potassium removal by dialysis must not be delayed. Insulin-based shifting therapy requires close glucose monitoring for delayed hypoglycemia, which is more likely in renal failure. Potassium rebound after shifting therapy is expected in an anuric patient, mandating continued monitoring after initial treatment. Allergy history, current medication list, urine output, and dry weight are not provided in the case.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with her mother for evaluation of bumps on her forehead and chin that have been present for the past 3 months. She reports they are not painful but she finds them cosmetically bothersome. She has been washing her face with regular soap twice daily. She denies any cystic lesions, scarring, or use of new cosmetics. Menarche was 1 year ago and her cycles are regular. She takes no medications. On examination, there are scattered open and closed comedones on the forehead and chin numbering approximately 15 to 20. A few small inflammatory papules, each less than 5 mm, are noted on the chin. There are no nodules, cysts, or scarring.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 15 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three months of non-painful but cosmetically bothersome bumps on the forehead and chin.
Analysis: This is mild comedonal acne vulgaris with a minor inflammatory component, typical of adolescence. The strongest supporting facts are the morphology and distribution: scattered open and closed comedones numbering approximately 15 to 20 on the forehead and chin, which is the T-zone where sebaceous gland density is greatest, together with a few small inflammatory papules on the chin, each less than 5 mm. Comedones are the defining primary lesion of acne and reflect follicular hyperkeratinization with sebum plugging, and their predominance over inflammatory lesions places this at the mild comedonal end of the spectrum. The timing is consistent with physiological androgen-driven sebum production following puberty, with menarche one year ago. Severity grading is important because it determines therapy, and the case explicitly documents the features that establish this as mild disease: there are no nodules, no cysts, and critically no scarring, and the patient herself denies cystic lesions and scarring. Absence of scarring means there is no urgency to prevent permanent disfigurement, though early effective treatment remains the best way to keep it that way. Main differential considerations grounded in the case have been addressed. An underlying hyperandrogenic disorder such as polycystic ovary syndrome is not supported: her menarche was one year ago and her cycles are regular, and no hirsutism, virilization, or menstrual irregularity is reported, so endocrine investigation is not indicated. Drug-induced acne is excluded because she takes no medications. Cosmetic-induced acne, or acne cosmetica, is excluded because she denies use of new cosmetics. Perioral dermatitis would present with grouped papules and pustules around the mouth without true comedones, and the presence of open and closed comedones distinguishes acne from it. Rosacea is not applicable at this age and is not associated with comedones. One modifiable contributing factor is identified in the history: she is washing her face with regular soap twice daily, which is likely too harsh and can strip the skin barrier and cause irritation, and this becomes clinically relevant because topical acne therapies themselves cause dryness and irritation. The psychosocial dimension deserves weight even in mild disease; she finds the lesions cosmetically bothersome, and facial acne in an adolescent commonly affects self-esteem, so effective treatment is warranted rather than dismissal.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 15-year-old girl with mild comedonal acne vulgaris of the forehead and chin, comprising approximately 15 to 20 open and closed comedones plus a few small inflammatory papules, with no nodules, cysts, or scarring, and no evidence of an underlying endocrine, drug-related, or cosmetic cause. baseline_protocol:
Age: 52 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Several weeks of polydipsia with large water intake, polyuria with nocturia disrupting sleep, blurry vision, increased fatigue, and 10-pound unintentional weight loss over 2 months, noticed by his wife.
Analysis: The presentation is a classic hyperglycemic symptom complex - polydipsia, polyuria/nocturia, blurred vision, fatigue and unintentional weight loss - developing over weeks in a 52-year-old obese man (BMI 36). The laboratory data are diagnostic rather than merely suggestive: fasting plasma glucose 210 mg/dL is well above the 126 mg/dL diagnostic threshold, and HbA1c 9.2% is well above 6.5%, with two concordant abnormal tests plus classic symptoms confirming diabetes mellitus. The phenotype strongly favors type 2 diabetes: central obesity, acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck and axillae as a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance, sedentary desk work with no regular exercise, first-degree family history of type 2 diabetes in both parents, and coexisting hypertension (144/92 on lisinopril) and hyperlipidemia consistent with a metabolic syndrome cluster. The HbA1c of 9.2% indicates the hyperglycemia has been present for months, not days.
The main differential consideration is type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, but the absence of ketonuria on urinalysis, the older age, the marked obesity and the insulin-resistance stigmata argue against autoimmune beta-cell failure; the weight loss here is best explained by osmotic diuresis and glycosuric caloric loss rather than absolute insulin deficiency. Acute hyperglycemic emergencies are also considered and excluded on the available data: there is no ketonuria, no reported Kussmaul respiration, no altered mental status, and hemodynamics are stable (heart rate 78, blood pressure 144/92), so neither diabetic ketoacidosis nor hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is supported. Secondary causes of hyperglycemia such as steroid exposure, pancreatic disease or endocrinopathy are not suggested by anything in the case. The blurry vision at this stage is most consistent with osmotic lens swelling from hyperglycemia rather than established retinopathy, though retinopathy cannot be excluded without fundoscopic assessment. Importantly, the complication screen is partly reassuring: the foot examination shows intact monofilament sensation and palpable pedal pulses, so there is no clinical evidence of peripheral neuropathy or peripheral arterial disease at diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Repeat/confirmatory fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c; basic metabolic panel with serum creatinine and estimated GFR and electrolytes; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio for diabetic kidney disease screening; fasting lipid panel given known hyperlipidemia; liver function tests; dilated retinal (fundoscopic) examination by ophthalmology to evaluate the blurry vision and screen for retinopathy; serum ketones or repeat urine ketone testing if symptoms worsen; home glucose meter with test strips for self-monitoring; sphygmomanometer for ongoing blood pressure monitoring; monofilament and pedal pulse examination at follow-up as a baseline-repeat foot screen. Consider C-peptide and GAD-65/islet autoantibodies only if the clinical course later suggests autoimmune diabetes rather than type 2 diabetes.
Conclusion: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus with marked symptomatic hyperglycemia (fasting glucose 210 mg/dL, HbA1c 9.2%) in an obese 52-year-old man with insulin resistance evidenced by acanthosis nigricans, a strong family history, and coexisting hypertension and hyperlipidemia. There is no evidence of an acute hyperglycemic emergency - no ketonuria, no hemodynamic instability - and no clinical diabetic foot complications at presentation. This requires prompt but non-emergent initiation of glucose-lowering therapy, structured lifestyle intervention, and complete baseline complication screening with cardiovascular risk factor management.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Initiate metformin as first-line pharmacotherapy with dose titration as tolerated, after confirming renal function is adequate; because HbA1c is 9.2% and the patient is symptomatic, plan for early combination therapy or short-term insulin if glycemic targets are not approached, and reassess HbA1c in approximately 3 months. Provide structured diabetes education covering the disease, medication use, hypoglycemia recognition, and sick-day rules, and teach home glucose self-monitoring with a meter, recording fasting and postprandial values. Refer to a dietitian for a calorie-reduced, carbohydrate-aware eating plan targeting meaningful weight loss given the BMI of 36, and prescribe a graded increase in physical activity to counter the sedentary desk job, aiming for regular aerobic exercise plus resistance training. Address the additional cardiovascular considerations explicitly: blood pressure is above target at 144/92, so intensify antihypertensive therapy - the existing lisinopril is an appropriate agent given diabetes and provides renal protection, and the dose should be up-titrated or a second agent added with home blood pressure monitoring; treat the known hyperlipidemia with statin therapy for cardiovascular risk reduction guided by a fasting lipid panel. Arrange a dilated eye examination to evaluate the blurry vision and establish retinopathy screening, and counsel that the visual blurring often improves as glucose normalizes. Document the baseline normal foot examination and schedule annual comprehensive foot screening with daily self-inspection and appropriate footwear. Obtain a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and monitor renal function periodically, particularly with metformin and ACE inhibitor therapy. Advise the patient to seek urgent care immediately if he develops vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion, as these suggest ketoacidosis or severe hyperosmolar hyperglycemia. Because both parents have type 2 diabetes, discuss the familial risk and screening for at-risk relatives. Arrange follow-up within a few weeks to assess symptom response, medication tolerance and early glycemic trend.
Notes: Vaccination status, smoking and alcohol history, current lipid values, renal function and full medication list are not specified in the case, and these should be established before finalizing pharmacotherapy - in particular renal function must be confirmed before metformin is started. Islet autoantibody and C-peptide testing were not performed; while the clinical picture is strongly typical of type 2 diabetes, atypical progression or unexpected ketosis should prompt reconsideration of autoimmune diabetes.

A 52-year-old woman with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 3-month history of progressively worsening stiffness and pain in her left shoulder. The pain is deep and aching, worse at night, and has made it increasingly difficult to reach behind her back, comb her hair, and fasten her bra. She denies any preceding trauma or injury. Her diabetes is managed with metformin and her last HbA1c was 7.8%. On examination, there is globally restricted active and passive range of motion of the left shoulder. External rotation is limited to 20 degrees (compared to 70 degrees on the right). Abduction is limited to 80 degrees, and internal rotation is severely restricted. There is no tenderness over specific rotator cuff tendons. Strength testing is limited by pain and stiffness. Shoulder radiographs show no fracture or dislocation and mild osteopenia.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 52 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three months of progressively worsening stiffness and deep aching pain in the left shoulder, worse at night, with growing difficulty reaching behind her back, combing her hair, and fastening her bra; no preceding trauma or injury.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) of the left shoulder. The single most decisive finding is the global restriction of both active AND passive range of motion, with external rotation reduced to 20 degrees against 70 degrees on the contralateral side, abduction limited to 80 degrees, and severe restriction of internal rotation. Loss of passive motion in the same pattern as active motion localizes the problem to the joint capsule itself rather than to the muscle-tendon unit, and the disproportionate loss of external rotation is the characteristic signature of capsular contracture. The functional complaints map directly onto this pattern: reaching behind the back and fastening a bra require internal rotation and extension, combing the hair requires abduction and external rotation.
The strongest supporting contextual fact is her 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus with HbA1c 7.8%, since diabetes is the best-established risk factor for adhesive capsulitis and is associated with more severe, more protracted and more often bilateral disease. The insidious onset over 3 months without any preceding trauma, and the deep aching pain that is worse at night, fit the painful (freezing) phase of the condition.
Differential considerations are addressed by the examination and imaging. Rotator cuff tendinopathy or a cuff tear would characteristically produce weakness and pain with preserved or near-preserved passive range of motion and focal tendon tenderness; here there is no tenderness over specific rotator cuff tendons and passive motion is equally lost, arguing against a primary cuff problem, although strength testing is uninterpretable because it is limited by pain and stiffness. Glenohumeral osteoarthritis can also cause global motion loss but would be expected to show joint space narrowing, osteophytes or subchondral sclerosis, whereas the radiographs show no such changes. Fracture and dislocation are excluded by the radiographs. Septic or acute inflammatory arthritis is not supported: the course is chronic and progressive over months with no reported fever, erythema or acute swelling. The mild osteopenia noted on radiographs is a nonspecific finding that can accompany relative disuse of the limb, and is not by itself explanatory. Referred cervical radicular pain is unlikely given the purely mechanical, motion-restricted local findings without neurological complaints.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Goniometer for serial documentation of active and passive range of motion in all planes for both shoulders; repeat HbA1c and fasting glucose to guide optimization of diabetic control; thyroid function testing, as thyroid dysfunction is an additional recognized association that would be worth excluding in refractory or bilateral disease. Shoulder radiographs have already been obtained and are adequate; no repeat plain films are needed. MRI or ultrasound of the shoulder is not required for the initial diagnosis, which is clinical, and should be reserved for cases that fail to respond to conservative treatment or in which a concurrent rotator cuff tear is suspected once pain-free strength testing becomes possible.
Conclusion: Left-sided adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) in the painful/freezing phase, arising in a 52-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and suboptimal glycemic control (HbA1c 7.8%). The diagnosis rests on globally restricted active and passive glenohumeral motion with a disproportionate loss of external rotation, absence of focal rotator cuff tenderness, and radiographs excluding fracture, dislocation and structural arthropathy. This is a benign but functionally disabling and typically protracted condition requiring scheduled outpatient orthopedic or musculoskeletal management, not emergency care.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Explain the natural history clearly: adhesive capsulitis is self-limiting but slow, commonly evolving through painful, stiff and thawing phases over many months to a couple of years, and recovery is often slower and less complete in patients with diabetes - setting these expectations improves adherence. Begin a supervised physical therapy programme centred on gentle, pain-limited passive and active-assisted stretching with emphasis on external rotation and internal rotation, progressing as pain allows, combined with a daily home exercise programme; aggressive forced stretching during the painful phase should be avoided as it can worsen symptoms. Provide analgesia for the night pain that is disturbing her sleep, using simple analgesics or a short course of anti-inflammatory medication as tolerated, and advise sleeping positions that support the arm. Consider an intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection, which is most effective in the painful early phase to reduce pain and permit therapy participation; because she is diabetic, warn her explicitly that a steroid injection can cause a transient rise in blood glucose over several days and arrange closer home glucose monitoring around the injection. Address the additional consideration of glycemic control directly: her HbA1c of 7.8% on metformin alone is above target, and optimizing diabetic control should be pursued in parallel both for general diabetic health and because poor control is linked to more severe and prolonged capsulitis - review therapy and consider intensification. Advise continued functional use of the arm within comfort rather than immobilization in a sling, since disuse aggravates stiffness and may contribute to the observed osteopenia. Screen the opposite shoulder at follow-up, since diabetes-associated adhesive capsulitis is often bilateral, and review other diabetic complications while she is engaged in care. Reassess range of motion with a goniometer at intervals of roughly 6 to 12 weeks; if there is no meaningful improvement after several months of well-conducted conservative therapy, refer for orthopedic consideration of hydrodilatation, manipulation under anaesthesia, or arthroscopic capsular release. Instruct her to return sooner if she develops fever, rapid swelling, new true weakness once pain settles, or new neurological symptoms in the arm.
Notes: Strength testing could not be reliably assessed because it was limited by pain and stiffness, so a coexisting rotator cuff tear cannot be fully excluded at this stage and should be reassessed once pain and motion improve. Thyroid status, symptom status of the right shoulder, occupation, hand dominance, and other diabetic complications are not specified in the case and should be established at follow-up.

He has had recurrent sinus infections averaging four to five times per year and has previously undergone polypectomy two years ago. He reports postnasal drip and a productive cough worse at night. He denies fever, visual changes, or severe headache.
