baseline_protocol:
Age: 40 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Ten days of worsening facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion and anosmia, with postnasal drip and a productive cough worse at night, on a background of chronic rhinosinusitis with bilateral nasal polyps and recurrent sinus infections four to five times per year.
Analysis: This is an acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis. Several features support the diagnosis. First, the symptom duration and trajectory: 10 days of symptoms that are worsening rather than improving fits the pattern used to separate bacterial sinusitis from a self-limited viral upper respiratory infection, which typically peaks and begins resolving within the first week. Second, the cardinal sinusitis symptom cluster is complete - facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, nasal obstruction and loss of smell. Third, the examination provides direct objective confirmation: mucopurulent drainage visualized in the middle meatus, the drainage pathway of the maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses, together with bilaterally edematous and erythematous mucosa, visible polypoid tissue, and tenderness over the maxillary and frontal sinuses.
The underlying substrate is chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, evidenced by the known diagnosis, the visible polypoid tissue on examination, the anosmia, which is characteristic of polypoid disease obstructing the olfactory cleft, the recurrence rate of four to five infections per year, and prior polypectomy two years ago with clear recurrence of polyps since. The cobblestoning of the posterior pharyngeal wall and the postnasal drip with a nocturnal productive cough are downstream consequences of chronic mucus drainage rather than a separate lower respiratory illness.
The most important differential consideration is a complicated sinus infection with orbital or intracranial extension, and this is actively argued against by the history and examination: he denies fever, visual changes and severe headache, and there is no reported periorbital swelling, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, altered mental status or meningism. Invasive fungal sinusitis is a consideration in severe or refractory disease but there is nothing in the case indicating immunosuppression, diabetes, necrotic or black mucosa, or systemic toxicity. A purely viral rhinosinusitis is less likely given the 10-day worsening course with frank purulence. Allergic rhinitis alone would not explain the purulent middle meatal drainage or sinus tenderness, though an allergic or type 2 inflammatory drive is a plausible contributor to the recurrent polyposis. A unilateral mass lesion or neoplasm is not suggested, as the disease is bilateral and symmetric. Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease and asthma are recognized associations with recurrent nasal polyposis but neither aspirin sensitivity nor asthma is mentioned in this case, so they cannot be assumed and remain to be established by history.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Nasal endoscopy for direct assessment of the extent of polyposis, the middle meatus and the sinus drainage pathways, and for endoscopically guided culture of the middle meatal purulent drainage with sensitivities, which is particularly valuable given his recurrent infections and prior surgery and repeated antibiotic exposure. Non-contrast CT of the paranasal sinuses to define the extent of chronic disease, assess post-surgical anatomy after the previous polypectomy, and provide a surgical roadmap if further intervention is considered. Complete blood count with differential to assess peripheral eosinophilia. Allergy evaluation with skin prick testing or specific IgE to identify treatable atopic triggers of the polypoid disease. Consider immunoglobulin levels and evaluation for immunodeficiency given four to five infections per year. Consider spirometry or pulmonary evaluation to detect coexisting asthma, given the productive nocturnal cough. Sweat chloride testing or cystic fibrosis screening and ciliary function assessment would only be indicated if the pattern of disease suggests these, which is not established here. Urgent contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the orbits and brain is not indicated now but would become necessary if orbital or intracranial warning features appear.
Conclusion: Acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic rhinosinusitis with bilateral nasal polyposis in a 40-year-old man with recurrent disease and prior polypectomy, presenting with 10 days of worsening facial pressure, purulent middle meatal drainage, congestion and anosmia. There are no clinical features of orbital or intracranial complication - no fever, no visual change, no severe headache - so this does not require emergency intervention, but it does require prompt outpatient otolaryngology-directed treatment of the acute infection together with a structured plan for the underlying polypoid chronic rhinosinusitis, which is clearly recurrent and inadequately controlled.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Treat the acute bacterial exacerbation with an appropriate course of oral antibiotics, ideally guided by endoscopically directed middle meatal culture given his repeated prior antibiotic exposure and recurrent infections, and select an agent with adequate coverage for the resistant organisms that colonize previously operated and chronically inflamed sinuses. Start or intensify intranasal corticosteroid therapy, which is the cornerstone of medical management for chronic rhinosinusitis with polyps and directly targets the polypoid obstruction and anosmia; a short course of oral corticosteroids may be considered to reduce polyp bulk and restore sinus drainage and smell, with the usual precautions. Add high-volume saline nasal irrigation, which also serves as a vehicle for topical steroid delivery and improves mucociliary clearance and postnasal drip. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Because he averages four to five sinus infections per year and polyps have recurred within two years of polypectomy, refer him to otolaryngology for reassessment for revision endoscopic sinus surgery rather than repeated cycles of antibiotics alone, and obtain sinus CT to plan this. Investigate the drivers of recurrence: obtain allergy testing and treat any identified atopy, check for peripheral eosinophilia, and evaluate for coexisting asthma given the nocturnal productive cough, since lower airway disease frequently accompanies polypoid sinus disease and would change management. Take a careful history of aspirin and NSAID reactions, since aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease is a recognized cause of recurrent polyposis and would require avoidance and specialist input; this has not been documented in this case and must be asked about. Consider screening for immunodeficiency given the infection frequency. In refractory, recurrent polyposis that fails surgery and topical therapy, biologic therapy targeting type 2 inflammation is an option to discuss with the specialist. Counsel him to seek emergency assessment immediately if he develops fever, periorbital swelling or redness, eye pain, double or reduced vision, proptosis, severe or new headache, neck stiffness, or confusion, as these indicate orbital or intracranial spread. Arrange otolaryngology follow-up after completion of the antibiotic course to confirm resolution of the acute infection and to establish long-term maintenance therapy, and emphasize that the anosmia may improve only partially and may recur with polyp regrowth.
Notes: Aspirin/NSAID sensitivity, asthma status, allergy history, smoking status, immune status and current medications are not specified in the case and must be clarified, as several of these would materially alter long-term management. Antibiotic choice should ideally follow culture results rather than empiric selection given repeated prior treatment courses.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 35-year-old male teacher presents with 2 days of nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, mild sore throat, and a low-grade temperature of 37.6°C. He reports several students in his classroom have been out sick recently. He notes mild fatigue but denies cough, dyspnea, myalgias, or ear pain. On examination, the nasal turbinates are mildly swollen with clear discharge. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without tonsillar enlargement or exudates. Tympanic membranes are clear. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. He is well-hydrated and in no acute distress.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 35 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two days of nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, mild sore throat, low-grade temperature of 37.6 C, and mild fatigue.
Analysis: The presentation is a short, 2-day course of upper respiratory symptoms dominated by nasal congestion, sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea, with only a mild sore throat and low-grade temperature. The strongest supporting facts for an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection are the recent sick contacts among his students, the mildly swollen nasal turbinates with clear rather than purulent discharge, a mildly erythematous oropharynx without tonsillar enlargement or exudate, clear tympanic membranes, and lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. He is well-hydrated and in no acute distress, which argues against any systemic or lower respiratory complication. Differential considerations grounded in this case include streptococcal pharyngitis, which is unlikely given the absence of tonsillar exudate or enlargement, the presence of prominent sneezing and nasal congestion, and only mild throat discomfort; allergic rhinitis, which could explain sneezing and clear discharge but does not account for fever or the abrupt onset following documented sick contacts; acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, which is not supported at only 2 days of symptoms without facial pain, purulent discharge, or a worsening biphasic course; influenza, which is less likely given the absence of myalgias, high fever, and severe abrupt systemic illness; and lower respiratory tract infection, which is argued against by the absence of cough or dyspnea and by normal lung auscultation. Acute otitis media is excluded by clear tympanic membranes and absent ear pain.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Uncomplicated acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) in an otherwise well 35-year-old man with a plausible classroom exposure source. Symptoms are mild, confined to the upper airway, of short duration, and unaccompanied by red-flag findings; the illness is expected to be self-limited over roughly seven to ten days.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Manage symptomatically at home. Maintain adequate oral fluid intake and rest; he is already well-hydrated and should remain so. Use saline nasal irrigation or saline spray for congestion, and if congestion is bothersome a topical decongestant may be used for no more than three consecutive days to avoid rebound congestion. Acetaminophen or an NSAID may be used for the sore throat and low-grade fever; warm fluids, lozenges, or salt-water gargles may ease throat discomfort. Antibiotics are not indicated for this viral illness. Regarding the occupational exposure that likely produced this illness, advise hand hygiene, covering coughs and sneezes, and limiting close contact while symptomatic to reduce transmission to students and colleagues; he may continue or resume teaching as he feels able given he is in no acute distress. Advise re-evaluation if symptoms persist beyond ten days without improvement, if they improve and then worsen again, if fever rises or persists, or if he develops purulent nasal discharge with facial pain, ear pain, productive cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, difficulty swallowing, or signs of dehydration.
Notes: No antibiotic therapy is warranted at this stage. If sneezing, nasal itching, and clear rhinorrhea persist after the febrile phase resolves, allergic rhinitis should be reconsidered as a contributing factor.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old man presents with 3 days of progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling, worsening trismus, odynophagia, and a muffled "hot potato" voice. Five days ago, he had a lower left second molar extracted at a dental clinic. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is sitting upright and drooling, appearing anxious and in respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.8C, HR 114, RR 24, BP 138/82, SpO2 91% on room air. There is firm, woody, bilateral submandibular swelling with erythema and warmth. The floor of the mouth is elevated and indurated, displacing the tongue posteriorly and superiorly. Age: 35 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three days of progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling with worsening trismus, odynophagia, muffled "hot potato" voice, drooling, and respiratory distress, five days after a lower left second molar extraction.
Analysis: This is an advanced presentation of Ludwig angina, a rapidly progressive bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces arising from an odontogenic source. The strongest supporting facts are the temporal relationship to a lower left second molar extraction five days ago, the firm, woody, bilateral submandibular swelling with erythema and warmth, and the elevated, indurated floor of the mouth displacing the tongue posteriorly and superiorly. Airway compromise is already established and progressing: he is sitting upright and drooling, has trismus preventing full mouth opening, a muffled hot-potato voice, inspiratory stridor, respiratory rate 24, and hypoxemia with SpO2 91 percent on room air. Fever of 38.8 C and heart rate 114 confirm a systemic inflammatory response. The contrast-enhanced neck CT objectively confirms a multiloculated fluid collection in the bilateral submandibular and sublingual spaces with significant airway narrowing at the oropharynx, indicating that the process has progressed beyond simple cellulitis to a drainable abscess. Differential considerations include peritonsillar abscess, which would typically be unilateral with uvular deviation rather than bilateral floor-of-mouth induration; parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal space abscess, which must be considered because these deep neck spaces communicate and inferior extension to the mediastinum is the feared complication; submandibular sialadenitis or salivary calculus, which would not produce bilateral woody induration, stridor, and this degree of systemic toxicity; and epiglottitis, which can cause stridor, drooling, and a muffled voice but does not explain the bilateral submandibular woody swelling or the CT findings. The combination of stridor, drooling, inability to open the mouth, and posterior tongue displacement identifies an imminently threatened airway that is also anatomically difficult to secure.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Difficult-airway equipment at the bedside, including a flexible fiberoptic bronchoscope or videolaryngoscope and a surgical airway (cricothyrotomy and tracheostomy) set, with continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring. Blood cultures, and Gram stain with aerobic and anaerobic culture of purulent material obtained at surgical drainage. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and lactate. Imaging extended through the chest to evaluate for mediastinal extension. Type and screen. No further neck imaging is needed before intervention, as the contrast CT neck is already diagnostic.
Conclusion: Ludwig angina with a bilateral submandibular and sublingual multiloculated abscess of odontogenic origin following mandibular second molar extraction, complicated by acute upper airway obstruction with stridor, drooling, trismus, and hypoxemia. This is a life-threatening surgical emergency in which loss of the airway, rather than the infection itself, is the immediate threat to life; definitive airway control, operative drainage, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics are required without delay.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Treat this as an immediate airway emergency. Do not leave the patient unattended and do not force him supine; allow him to remain sitting upright, which is his position of airway patency. Give supplemental oxygen to correct the SpO2 of 91 percent. Mobilize otolaryngology and anesthesia immediately for definitive airway control: given trismus, posterior tongue displacement, and floor-of-mouth induration, direct laryngoscopy and rapid-sequence intubation carry a high risk of failure, so awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation is preferred, with a surgeon scrubbed and prepared for immediate tracheostomy or cricothyrotomy as backup. Avoid neuromuscular blockade until an airway plan with a surgical backup is in place. Draw blood cultures and start empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering oral streptococci, oral anaerobes, and staphylococci immediately, without waiting for the operating room. Proceed to the operating room for incision and drainage of the multiloculated submandibular and sublingual collections demonstrated on CT, with debridement or extraction addressing the odontogenic source and placement of drains; needle aspiration alone is inadequate for a multiloculated collection. Begin intravenous fluid resuscitation for fever and tachycardia and admit to intensive care postoperatively with the airway secured. Addressing the additional considerations: image through the chest to exclude descending necrotizing mediastinitis, monitor for internal jugular thrombophlebitis and carotid sheath involvement, arrange oral and maxillofacial follow-up for definitive dental management, and perform serial airway assessment so that extubation occurs only after the induration and airway edema have resolved and a cuff leak is demonstrated.
Notes: Extubation must not be attempted until floor-of-mouth induration and airway edema have resolved. Repeated blind intubation attempts risk converting partial obstruction into complete obstruction and should be avoided.

Vignette:
A 16-year-old female volleyball player presents with mild right ankle pain after landing awkwardly on another player's foot during practice 2 hours ago. She was able to walk off the court on her own. She denies hearing a pop or experiencing giving way of the ankle. She has no prior history of ankle injuries. baseline_protocol:
Age: 16 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Mild right ankle pain and mild lateral swelling after landing awkwardly on another player's foot during volleyball practice 2 hours ago.
Analysis: This is a mild lateral ankle sprain, grade I, involving the anterior talofibular ligament. The mechanism, landing on another player's foot, is the classic inversion injury of the lateral ligament complex, and the anterior talofibular ligament is the most commonly and first injured structure. The strongest supporting facts for a low-grade, stable injury are that she walked off the court under her own power, can bear weight with minimal discomfort, denies hearing a pop or any sensation of the ankle giving way, and has only mild swelling and mild tenderness confined to the anterior talofibular ligament with no ecchymosis. Ligamentous stability is intact: both the anterior drawer test and the talar tilt test are negative, arguing against a complete anterior talofibular or calcaneofibular ligament rupture. Fracture is very unlikely on clinical grounds: bony landmarks are non-tender, meaning there is no tenderness over the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, the navicular, or the base of the fifth metatarsal, and she is able to bear weight, so the Ottawa ankle rules are not satisfied and radiographs are not indicated. Differential considerations include a distal fibular or lateral malleolar avulsion fracture, excluded clinically by absent bony tenderness and preserved weight-bearing; a Salter-Harris type I distal fibular physeal injury, which merits thought given her skeletal immaturity at 16 but is not supported here because there is no tenderness over the distal fibular physis and the bony landmarks are non-tender; a high ankle (syndesmotic) sprain, which would be suggested by tenderness proximal to the joint over the syndesmosis and pain on external rotation rather than isolated anterior talofibular ligament tenderness; a fifth metatarsal base fracture, excluded by the absence of bony tenderness; and peroneal tendon injury, which would produce posterolateral retromalleolar tenderness rather than the anterior talofibular ligament tenderness described.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute grade I lateral ankle sprain of the right anterior talofibular ligament in a 16-year-old volleyball player, sustained by an inversion mechanism. The examination shows a stable ankle with preserved weight-bearing, no bony tenderness, and negative stress testing, so imaging is not required and functional management is appropriate. Recovery is expected within one to three weeks.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Manage functionally. In the first 48 to 72 hours apply ice for about 15 to 20 minutes several times daily with a barrier against the skin, use a compressive elastic wrap or a lace-up or semi-rigid ankle brace, and elevate the ankle above heart level when resting; relative rest with weight-bearing as tolerated is preferred over immobilization, and she may continue to walk since she tolerates weight-bearing with minimal discomfort. Acetaminophen or a short course of an oral or topical NSAID may be used for pain. Begin early range-of-motion exercises such as ankle alphabet and dorsiflexion-plantarflexion within a day or two, progressing to peroneal and calf strengthening with resistance bands and then to proprioceptive and balance training, such as single-leg stance work, before return to sport. Given that she is a volleyball player, return to jumping, cutting, and landing drills should be graded and permitted only when she has full pain-free range of motion, symmetric strength, and can hop and land without pain or instability; an ankle brace or taping during play for the remainder of the season is advised, as proprioceptive deficits after a first sprain are the main risk factor for recurrent sprain and chronic ankle instability. Advise re-evaluation with radiographs if she develops inability to bear weight, new focal bony tenderness over the malleoli, navicular, or fifth metatarsal base, or if pain and swelling fail to improve over one to two weeks.
Notes: In a skeletally immature 16-year-old, a distal fibular physeal injury can mimic a lateral sprain; it is not supported here by the non-tender bony landmarks, but persistent localized tenderness over the distal fibula at follow-up should prompt radiographs.

Vignette:
A 34-year-old woman with no known underlying lung disease 12-day history of cough. She initially had nasal congestion and a mild sore throat, but now her symptoms are all related to a productive cough without paroxysms. She denies any sick contacts. On physical examination she is not in respiratory distress and is afebrile with normal vital signs. No signs of URI are noted. Scattered wheezes are present diffusely on lung auscultation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 34 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Twelve-day history of cough, initially preceded by nasal congestion and mild sore throat, now a productive cough without paroxysms.
Analysis: This is acute bronchitis, most likely postviral, in a woman with no known underlying lung disease. The strongest supporting facts are the illness pattern, which began as an upper respiratory infection with nasal congestion and mild sore throat and then evolved into an isolated cough that has now persisted for 12 days, with the upper respiratory findings resolved so that no signs of upper respiratory infection remain on examination. The cough is productive, which is common in acute bronchitis and does not by itself imply bacterial infection, as sputum color and purulence reflect inflammatory cells rather than a bacterial cause. Scattered diffuse wheezes on auscultation are consistent with the bronchial inflammation and transient airway hyperresponsiveness that characterize acute bronchitis. The findings that argue strongly against pneumonia are that she is afebrile with normal vital signs, is not in respiratory distress, and has no focal findings such as crackles, dullness, or bronchial breath sounds; the wheezing is diffuse rather than localized. Differential considerations include community-acquired pneumonia, made unlikely by the absence of fever, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, and focal auscultatory findings, so chest radiography is not required; pertussis, which is specifically addressed and made unlikely by the explicit absence of paroxysms, whoop, and post-tussive emesis, and by the absence of known sick contacts; new-onset asthma or cough-variant asthma, which is worth considering because of the diffuse wheezes and should be revisited if wheeze and cough persist beyond the expected course; postinfectious upper airway cough syndrome from postnasal drainage, which is less supported now that the upper respiratory findings have resolved; and gastroesophageal reflux or ACE inhibitor cough, for which the case provides no supporting history. The 12-day duration is within the normal course of acute bronchitis, in which cough commonly lasts two to three weeks.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Acute bronchitis following a viral upper respiratory infection in an afebrile, hemodynamically normal 34-year-old woman with no underlying lung disease. The absence of fever, abnormal vital signs, respiratory distress, and focal lung findings makes pneumonia unlikely and obviates chest imaging, and the absence of paroxysmal cough makes pertussis unlikely. The illness is expected to be self-limited, with cough potentially persisting for two to three weeks in total.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Manage symptomatically and do not prescribe antibiotics, which have no meaningful benefit in acute bronchitis in an otherwise healthy adult without pneumonia. Reassure her explicitly that a cough lasting two to three weeks is the expected natural course, since unmet expectations about duration are the usual driver of repeat visits and unnecessary antibiotic use. Advise adequate hydration, rest, and humidified air; honey or warm fluids may soothe the cough, and an over-the-counter antitussive or expectorant may be used for symptomatic relief if the cough disturbs sleep. Because she has diffuse wheezes, a trial of an inhaled short-acting bronchodilator is reasonable and may reduce cough and the sensation of chest tightness; it should be discontinued if it produces no benefit. Advise avoidance of tobacco smoke and other airway irritants. Addressing the additional considerations: she should return promptly if she develops fever, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, or worsening rather than improving symptoms, since these would prompt reassessment for pneumonia with chest radiography and pulse oximetry; and if the cough or wheezing persists beyond roughly three to four weeks, or recurs with exertion, nocturnally, or with allergen exposure, she should be evaluated with spirometry for underlying or new-onset asthma. Ensure her routine immunizations, including influenza vaccination, are up to date.
Notes: Sputum production and its appearance do not indicate a bacterial infection and are not an indication for antibiotics in this setting.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 24-year-old man presents with a painful small bump in his beard area that appeared 2 days after shaving. He shaves with a multi-blade razor and shaves against the grain. He denies fever, spreading redness, or drainage. He has no history of recurrent skin infections. On examination, there is a single erythematous, firm papule approximately 4 mm in diameter on the right submandibular area. Mild swelling is present around the lesion. A curled hair is visible beneath the surface of the skin. There is no fluctuance, induration, or streaking erythema.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 24 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A painful small bump in the beard area that appeared two days after shaving.
Analysis: This is a localized superficial folliculitis, with features of pseudofolliculitis barbae from shaving trauma and ingrown hair. The strongest supporting facts are the direct temporal relationship to shaving two days earlier, the shaving technique described, which uses a multi-blade razor and shaving against the grain, and the visible curled hair beneath the skin surface within the lesion, which is the hallmark of an ingrown hair re-entering the skin and provoking a foreign-body inflammatory follicular reaction. The lesion is a single erythematous, firm papule of about 4 mm on the right submandibular area with only mild surrounding swelling. The features that establish this as a minor, uncomplicated process are the absence of fluctuance, meaning no abscess has formed and there is nothing to drain; the absence of induration and of streaking erythema, meaning no cellulitis or lymphangitis; the absence of drainage and of spreading redness; and the absence of fever, meaning no systemic involvement. He has no history of recurrent skin infections, which argues against staphylococcal carriage or recurrent furunculosis. Differential considerations include bacterial folliculitis, typically staphylococcal, which can look identical and may coexist, but there is no pustule, drainage, or surrounding cellulitis described; a furuncle or early abscess, excluded by the absence of fluctuance; epidermal inclusion cyst, which would not appear acutely two days after shaving and would not contain a visible ingrown hair; herpetic sycosis or tinea barbae, neither of which is supported since there are no grouped vesicles, no scaling annular plaques, and only a single lesion; and acne vulgaris, which would present with multiple comedones and papules over a longer course rather than a single lesion tied to a shaving event.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Single uncomplicated ingrown-hair folliculitis (pseudofolliculitis barbae) of the right submandibular beard area, caused by shaving trauma with a multi-blade razor against the grain. There is no abscess, cellulitis, or systemic involvement, so no incision, culture, or systemic antibiotic is required, and the lesion should resolve with conservative measures and shaving modification.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Stop shaving the affected area until the lesion resolves, which is the single most effective immediate measure. Apply warm compresses to the papule several times daily to encourage the trapped hair to release and to speed resolution. Keep the area clean with gentle washing; a topical antiseptic or an over-the-counter topical antibacterial may be applied, but oral antibiotics are not indicated because there is no fluctuance, spreading erythema, streaking, or fever. Do not squeeze, pick at, or attempt to dig out the lesion, as this risks introducing bacterial infection and scarring; if the tip of the curled hair is freely visible above the surface it may be gently lifted out with a sterile needle or fine tweezers without cutting into the skin, but the lesion should not be incised. Addressing the underlying cause and preventing recurrence, advise changing shaving technique: shave in the direction of hair growth rather than against the grain, use a single-blade or electric razor instead of a multi-blade razor since closer shaves promote ingrown hairs, soften the beard with warm water and a lubricating shaving gel before shaving, use a fresh sharp blade with minimal passes and no stretching of the skin, rinse with cool water afterward, and consider reducing shaving frequency or growing the beard slightly longer. Gentle exfoliation between shaves may reduce recurrence. He should seek reassessment if the lesion becomes fluctuant, enlarges, develops drainage, if redness spreads or streaks appear, or if he develops fever, as these would indicate abscess formation or cellulitis requiring drainage or antibiotics.
Notes: Recurrent or multiple lesions in the beard area would warrant reconsideration of bacterial folliculitis with staphylococcal carriage, tinea barbae, or herpetic sycosis, none of which is supported by this single-lesion presentation.

At her last visit 3 months ago, her HbA1C was 7.6%, where it had been for several visits. You recommended beginning treatment with insulin, which she refused because of her fear of needles. You then increased her dose of glimepiride from 4 mg to 8 mg once a day and advised her to more strictly follow her diet and exercise regimen, which she claims to be doing. Since the last visit, her home fingerstick glucose levels have ranged from 119 mg/dL to 263 mg/dL (6.6 to 14.6 mmol/L) and her weight on her home scale is unchanged at about 98 kg. She describes increased thirst and urination but denies blurry vision, nonhealing ulcers, or lethargy.

Per office protocol, a fingerstick glucose test on arrival today shows glucose level of 221mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L) and hemoglobin A1C 8.1%; urine dipstick is normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Increased thirst and is drinking more water. Appetite is normal and her weight at home has been unchanged for several months. She denies lethargy, fever, chills, or night sweats.

Skin: No rash, pruritus, or lesions

Pulmonary: No cough, shortness of breath, wheezing

Cardiovascular: No chest pain, pressure, or discomfort; no orthopnea, dyspnea on exertion, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and obesity

Surgical history: Cholecystectomy 5 years prior

Medications: Metformin 1000 mg twice a day, atorvastatin 80 mg once a day, glimepiride 8 mg once a day with breakfast, lisinopril 40 mg once a day, all of which she claims to be taking faithfully.

Allergies: Penicillin, which causes rash

Family history: Father died from myocardial infarction at age 89 years, mother age 88 years has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

Social history: Patient works as a social worker, has never smoked cigarettes, denies any illicit drug use, drinks 1 to 2 glasses of wine with dinner every night. baseline_protocol:
Age: 56 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Scheduled follow-up for type 2 diabetes with chronically elevated blood glucose; reports increased thirst and urination, with home glucose readings ranging 119 to 263 mg/dL despite maximal glimepiride and lifestyle measures.
Analysis: This patient has type 2 diabetes with progressive loss of glycemic control on maximal sulfonylurea therapy. The strongest supporting facts are that her HbA1c has risen from 7.6 percent, where it had been stable for several visits, to 8.1 percent over three months despite the glimepiride dose being doubled from 4 mg to 8 mg daily and despite reported adherence to diet and exercise; her home fingerstick glucose values span 119 to 263 mg/dL, and today's office fingerstick is 221 mg/dL. This is secondary sulfonylurea failure, reflecting continued decline of beta-cell function, and demonstrates that further intensification of glimepiride is not a viable strategy since she is already at the maximum dose and the last dose increase produced worsening rather than improvement. Her symptoms of increased thirst and increased urination are osmotic symptoms consistent with sustained hyperglycemia and confirm that the elevation is symptomatic rather than merely a laboratory finding. Importantly, she denies blurry vision, nonhealing ulcers, and lethargy, and the urine dipstick is normal, which argues against ketosis, significant infection, and overt proteinuria, and there is no evidence of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. Her weight is unchanged at approximately 98 kg, indicating obesity that is untreated by her current regimen; glimepiride is weight-neutral to weight-promoting and offers no benefit here. The central barrier to the previously recommended treatment is her explicit refusal of insulin because of fear of needles, which must be addressed directly rather than circumvented. Differential considerations include nonadherence or inaccurate dietary reporting, which cannot be excluded but is at least partly addressed by her stable weight and consistent home monitoring; a secondary cause of hyperglycemia such as an intercurrent infection or a hyperglycemia-inducing medication such as corticosteroids, neither of which is described in the case; and latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, which would be atypical in this long-standing patient with obesity but is a consideration in sulfonylurea failure. The normal urine dipstick and the absence of ketosis symptoms make acute decompensation unlikely, so this is a management intensification problem rather than an emergency.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Basic metabolic panel with creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate, and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, to screen for diabetic kidney disease and to guide the safety and choice of the next agent. Fasting lipid panel and blood pressure measurement for cardiovascular risk assessment. Dilated retinal examination and comprehensive foot examination with monofilament testing if not current. Continued home fingerstick glucose monitoring, with consideration of continuous glucose monitoring. Repeat HbA1c in approximately three months to assess the response to the new regimen. The fingerstick glucose, HbA1c, and urine dipstick performed today are already available and need not be repeated now.
Conclusion: Uncontrolled type 2 diabetes with secondary failure of maximal-dose sulfonylurea therapy, evidenced by an HbA1c rising from 7.6 to 8.1 percent, home glucose values up to 263 mg/dL, an office glucose of 221 mg/dL, and symptomatic polydipsia and polyuria, in an obese 56-year-old woman who has declined insulin because of needle fear. There is no evidence of acute metabolic decompensation. Treatment intensification with a non-insulin agent that also addresses her weight is indicated, alongside targeted work on her needle phobia so that insulin remains available if needed later.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Intensify therapy now rather than making another glimepiride adjustment, since she is at the maximum dose and the last increase failed. Add a second agent with a mechanism complementary to the sulfonylurea, prioritizing options that also promote weight loss and carry low hypoglycemia risk given her weight of 98 kg; discuss metformin if she is not already taking it and renal function permits, and discuss the injectable and oral incretin-based and SGLT2 inhibitor options with her explicitly, framing the choice around her stated preferences. Whenever an agent is added, plan to reduce or eventually withdraw the glimepiride to limit hypoglycemia and weight gain, and counsel her on recognizing and treating hypoglycemia, including while driving. Addressing her needle fear directly: acknowledge it as a legitimate barrier rather than dismissing it, demonstrate the actual pen needle and injection device so she can see and handle the very fine, short needle, offer a supervised in-office trial injection with saline or a first dose, and consider referral for behavioral or graded exposure therapy for needle phobia. Point out that she already performs fingersticks, which is evidence she can tolerate a lancing device, and note that a once-weekly injectable pen requires far fewer needle events than basal insulin, which may make it more acceptable to her. If a non-insulin regimen fails to bring her to target, insulin should be revisited, and the work on needle phobia now makes that transition feasible later. Reinforce medical nutrition therapy with referral to a dietitian and structured physical activity, and set an explicit weight-loss goal, since even modest weight reduction will improve her glycemic control. Address her osmotic symptoms by explaining they should resolve as glucose falls, and ensure adequate fluid intake in the interim. Addressing the additional considerations: complete the microvascular screening described above, assess and treat blood pressure and lipids for cardiovascular risk reduction, ensure vaccinations are current, and schedule follow-up in about three months with a repeat HbA1c, with earlier contact if home glucose values rise further or symptoms worsen.
Notes: Doubling glimepiride to 8 mg without benefit indicates secondary sulfonylurea failure; continuing at this dose while adding another agent increases hypoglycemia risk, so dose reduction should be planned. Her refusal of insulin is a modifiable barrier, not a permanent contraindication.

Vignette:
A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 78/48, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs. Pelvic exam demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and a tender left adnexal mass. Quantitative beta-hCG is 4,200 mIU/mL. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch. Hemoglobin returns at 7.8 g/dL. O-negative blood is ordered and the OR is alerted for emergent laparotomy.

Age: 28 years
Sex: Female

Analysis: This is a ruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum and hemorrhagic shock. The strongest supporting facts are the abrupt onset of severe unilateral pelvic pain with lightheadedness in a woman with 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a confirmed pregnancy, in the setting of two major risk factors, prior pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate. She is in decompensated shock with heart rate 132, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 24, and is pale, diaphoretic, and acutely ill. The abdominal examination shows diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs, and the pelvic examination shows cervical motion tenderness with a tender left adnexal mass. The imaging is diagnostic: bedside transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an empty uterus with a beta-hCG of 4,200 mIU/mL, which is above the discriminatory threshold at which an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible, together with a complex left adnexal mass showing a ring-of-fire sign indicating peritrophoblastic vascular flow, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and extending to Morison's pouch, which indicates a substantial volume of intraperitoneal blood. The hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL confirms significant acute blood loss. Differential considerations include ovarian torsion, which can cause acute unilateral pelvic pain and an adnexal mass but does not produce free fluid in Morison's pouch, this degree of hemorrhagic shock, or a hemoglobin of 7.8; a ruptured hemorrhagic ovarian corpus luteum cyst, which can cause hemoperitoneum but does not explain the empty uterus with a beta-hCG above the discriminatory zone and a ring-of-fire adnexal mass; a threatened or incomplete miscarriage, excluded by the empty uterus with hemoperitoneum and shock; a heterotopic pregnancy, effectively excluded by the empty uterus; and pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess, which her history makes plausible but which would not cause acute hemoperitoneum with hemorrhagic shock over 45 minutes. Prior methotrexate treatment of an ipsilateral tubal ectopic pregnancy substantially raises the risk of recurrence in the same tube, as seen here.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Type and crossmatch with immediate release of uncrossmatched O-negative blood, which has already been ordered, and activation of massive transfusion protocol capability. Complete blood count with serial hemoglobin, coagulation studies including INR and fibrinogen, comprehensive metabolic panel, lactate, and blood type with Rh status. Continuous cardiac, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry monitoring with large-bore intravenous access. Definitive diagnosis is already established by bedside transvaginal ultrasound and beta-hCG, so no further imaging should delay surgery.
Conclusion: Ruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy at approximately 7 weeks with hemoperitoneum extending to Morison's pouch and hemorrhagic shock, in a woman with prior pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior ipsilateral methotrexate-treated ectopic pregnancy. This is a surgical emergency; medical management with methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated in a ruptured, hemodynamically unstable ectopic pregnancy. Emergent laparotomy as planned is the correct management.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Proceed immediately to the operating room for emergent laparotomy; do not delay surgery for further imaging, for laboratory results, or to await full hemodynamic resuscitation, since the bleeding source can only be controlled operatively. Continue resuscitation in parallel with transport: two large-bore intravenous lines or intraosseous access, transfusion beginning with the ordered O-negative blood while crossmatched product is prepared, and a balanced transfusion strategy with plasma and platelets rather than large volumes of crystalloid, given a hemoglobin of 7.8 with ongoing hemorrhage. Give supplemental oxygen and keep her warm to prevent the coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia of the lethal triad. Notify anesthesia, the blood bank, and the surgical team simultaneously. At operation, expect a ruptured left tube; salpingectomy is generally preferred over salpingostomy in a ruptured tube with hemorrhage and in a tube already damaged by a prior ipsilateral ectopic pregnancy, with evacuation of hemoperitoneum and inspection of the contralateral adnexa. Send the specimen for pathology to confirm trophoblastic tissue. Addressing the additional considerations: determine her Rh status and administer anti-D immune globulin if she is Rh-negative; monitor postoperative serial beta-hCG to zero if any tubal tissue is conserved; monitor for postoperative anemia, acute kidney injury, and transfusion-related complications; and provide counseling once she is stable regarding the significantly increased risk of recurrent ectopic pregnancy, the implications of unilateral salpingectomy for future fertility with consideration of early ultrasound in any future pregnancy as soon as a positive test occurs, and screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infection given her history of pelvic inflammatory disease. Offer contraception counseling and psychological support for pregnancy loss before discharge.
Notes: Methotrexate has no role here; rupture with hemodynamic instability is an absolute contraindication. Ultrasound and laboratory results are already sufficient for diagnosis, and no additional investigation should delay operative hemorrhage control.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 42 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Mild low back ache developing after several hours of gardening the previous day, which involved bending and lifting bags of soil.
Analysis: This is acute nonspecific mechanical low back pain, most consistent with a lumbar paraspinal muscular strain from unaccustomed bending and lifting. The strongest supporting facts are the clear mechanical precipitant, several hours of bending and lifting bags of soil the day before, the mild severity, the strictly axial location in the lower back without radiation to the legs, and the examination finding of bilateral paraspinal muscle tenderness in the lumbar region with only mildly reduced flexion. There is no evidence of nerve root involvement: he denies numbness, tingling, and weakness, the straight leg raise is negative bilaterally, and the neurological examination of the lower extremities is normal. A 35-year-old man who jogs regularly presents with a 1-week history of an itchy rash in his groin folds. He reports the itch worsens after running and sweating. He denies any genital lesions, urinary symptoms, or prior similar episodes. On examination, there are bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases extending to the proximal inner thighs. The scrotum is spared. baseline_protocol:
Age: 35 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: One-week history of an itchy rash in the groin folds, with itching that worsens after running and sweating.
Analysis: This is tinea cruris, a dermatophyte infection of the groin. The strongest supporting facts are the morphology and distribution: bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases extending onto the proximal inner thighs. A sharply demarcated, scaly, raised advancing border is the characteristic feature of a dermatophyte infection. Sparing of the scrotum is the single most discriminating finding in this case, because tinea cruris characteristically spares the scrotum whereas candidal intertrigo typically involves it. The predisposing context fits well: he jogs regularly, and the itch worsens after running and sweating, reflecting the warm, moist, occluded environment in which dermatophytes thrive. The duration of one week and the absence of genital lesions, urinary symptoms, and prior similar episodes further characterize this as a new, localized cutaneous problem without systemic or genitourinary involvement, and there is no inguinal lymphadenopathy to suggest secondary bacterial infection. Differential considerations include candidal intertrigo, argued against by the sparing of the scrotum and by the explicit absence of satellite lesions, which are typical of candidiasis; erythrasma, a corynebacterial infection that produces well-demarcated brown-red patches in the groin but with fine wrinkled scale rather than a raised active border, and which would show coral-red fluorescence under Wood lamp; inverse psoriasis, which typically produces sharply demarcated but smooth, shiny, non-scaly red plaques in the folds without a raised scaly border and often with lesions elsewhere; seborrheic dermatitis and contact or irritant dermatitis, which usually lack a well-demarcated raised border; and simple intertrigo from friction and moisture, which would not show the discrete scaly advancing edge. The absence of central clearing does not argue against tinea cruris, which frequently lacks the classic central clearing seen in tinea corporis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Tinea cruris, a bilateral dermatophyte infection of the inguinal creases and proximal inner thighs in a regular jogger, with the diagnosis supported clinically by well-demarcated plaques with raised scaly borders and characteristic sparing of the scrotum. The presentation is uncomplicated, localized, and without secondary bacterial infection, and it should respond to topical antifungal therapy combined with moisture-control measures.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Treat with a topical antifungal applied to the affected inguinal creases and inner thighs, extending application a few centimeters beyond the visible border onto normal-appearing skin, once or twice daily as directed, and continue for one to two weeks beyond the point at which the rash appears to have cleared, since stopping at the time of visible clearance is the usual cause of relapse; expect a total treatment course of roughly two to four weeks. A topical allylamine or azole antifungal is appropriate. Avoid topical corticosteroids or combination steroid-antifungal preparations, which can blunt the appearance of the rash, permit the infection to extend, and produce tinea incognito and striae in this thin, occluded skin. For symptomatic itch, keeping the area cool and dry is more helpful than a steroid. Addressing the moisture and friction factors that drive this condition in a runner: shower promptly after running and dry the groin folds thoroughly, patting rather than rubbing, and dry the groin before the feet to avoid transferring fungus; wear loose-fitting, moisture-wicking or cotton underwear and change out of damp athletic clothing immediately; use a drying or antifungal powder in the creases for maintenance; and avoid sharing towels and launder towels, underwear, and athletic clothing regularly in hot water. Examine and treat the feet and toenails for tinea pedis or onychomycosis, since autoinoculation from the feet is the most common source of recurrent tinea cruris, and advise him to put socks on before underwear to prevent transfer. He should return if the rash fails to improve after two to four weeks of adherent topical therapy, spreads extensively, becomes painful, weeping, or pustular, or develops surrounding tenderness and lymphadenopathy suggesting secondary bacterial infection, any of which might prompt confirmatory KOH microscopy or fungal culture and consideration of oral antifungal therapy.
Notes: If the eruption fails to respond to appropriate topical antifungal therapy, reconsider erythrasma, inverse psoriasis, or candidal involvement, and confirm the diagnosis with KOH microscopy, fungal culture, or Wood lamp examination before escalating treatment.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. She was unable to bear full weight and has been using crutches since. She denies any prior knee injuries. On examination, there is a moderate effusion of the left knee. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 22 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Left knee injury sustained two days ago while pivoting during a soccer game, with an audible pop, immediate swelling, inability to continue playing, and inability to bear full weight.
Analysis: This presentation is characteristic of an acute anterior cruciate ligament rupture of the left knee. The strongest supporting facts are the mechanism and the history: a non-contact pivoting and change-of-direction movement, the classic mechanism for anterior cruciate ligament injury; a sudden audible and felt pop; immediate swelling within the first hours, which indicates hemarthrosis and is strongly associated with an intra-articular structural injury, most often anterior cruciate ligament rupture; and immediate inability to continue playing with subsequent inability to bear full weight, requiring crutches. The examination confirms this: a positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint is the most sensitive clinical test for anterior cruciate ligament rupture, and increased anterior tibial translation on the anterior drawer test compared with the uninjured right knee corroborates anterior instability. A moderate effusion is present, consistent with hemarthrosis, and range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. Differential and associated considerations include meniscal tear, which is a very common concomitant injury with anterior cruciate ligament rupture and cannot be excluded here since the McMurray test is equivocal and is unreliable in an acutely swollen, guarded knee; collateral ligament injury, made unlikely by the explicitly stable collateral ligaments; patellar dislocation with spontaneous relocation, which can also produce a pop and immediate hemarthrosis but would not explain the positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint and increased anterior translation; osteochondral fracture or tibial spine avulsion, which can accompany this mechanism and produce hemarthrosis and must be excluded by imaging; and posterior cruciate ligament injury, which is not supported by the anterior translation findings and typically follows a different mechanism. She is neurovascularly intact distally, which excludes an associated vascular or nerve injury and argues against a knee dislocation. The injury is significant and requires specialist evaluation and imaging, but there is no emergency: there is no neurovascular compromise, no open injury, and no deformity.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Plain radiographs of the left knee, including anteroposterior and lateral views, to exclude fracture, tibial eminence avulsion, and a Segond fracture, which is a lateral capsular avulsion highly associated with anterior cruciate ligament rupture. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee to confirm the anterior cruciate ligament tear and to assess for associated meniscal tears, collateral and posterolateral corner injury, chondral damage, and bone bruising, which the equivocal McMurray test cannot resolve clinically. Referral for orthopedic sports medicine examination, with repeat ligamentous examination once the effusion and guarding have decreased.
Conclusion: Acute anterior cruciate ligament rupture of the left knee in a 22-year-old competitive soccer player, sustained by a non-contact pivoting mechanism, supported by an audible pop, immediate hemarthrosis, functional disability, a positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint, and increased anterior tibial translation, with stable collateral ligaments and an intact distal neurovascular examination. Associated meniscal injury cannot be excluded clinically and requires magnetic resonance imaging. Prompt but non-emergent orthopedic evaluation with imaging and a decision on reconstruction is indicated.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Manage acutely with protection, relative rest, ice, compression, and elevation of the left knee to reduce the effusion and pain, with a hinged knee brace or immobilizer for comfort and stability, and continue crutches with weight-bearing as tolerated until she can bear weight comfortably. Provide analgesia with acetaminophen or an NSAID as tolerated. Arrange radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee and refer to orthopedic sports medicine promptly, ideally within days rather than weeks, because she is a young athlete for whom operative reconstruction is likely to be recommended in order to return to pivoting sport and to protect the menisci and articular cartilage from further injury. Begin early physical therapy, with initial goals of restoring full extension, reducing swelling, and reactivating the quadriceps, since achieving a quiet knee with full range of motion before surgery improves postoperative outcomes and lowers the risk of arthrofibrosis. Counsel her that continuing to play or pivot on an anterior cruciate ligament deficient knee risks giving-way episodes with secondary meniscal and chondral damage, and that she should not return to sport until cleared. Addressing the additional considerations: the equivocal McMurray test means a meniscal tear must be actively excluded on magnetic resonance imaging, and any locking, a true block to extension, or joint-line pain should be reported promptly, since a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear would accelerate the surgical timeline; the collateral ligaments are stable and the limb is neurovascularly intact, so no urgent vascular assessment is needed; and after definitive treatment she will require a structured, criteria-based rehabilitation and return-to-sport program with neuromuscular and landing retraining, both to return safely and to reduce the substantial risk of re-injury or contralateral anterior cruciate ligament injury.
Notes: Ligamentous examination performed in an acutely swollen, guarded knee can underestimate injury; the equivocal McMurray test in particular does not exclude a meniscal tear, and reassessment after the effusion subsides, together with magnetic resonance imaging, is required.

Vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 6 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Patches of scaly hair loss on the scalp enlarging over the past three weeks, with mild itching and no pain, noticed by his mother.
Analysis: This is tinea capitis caused by an endothrix-pattern dermatophyte, most consistent with a Trichophyton species. The diagnosis is established mycologically: the KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores within and surrounding the hair shaft, which is definitive evidence of dermatophyte invasion of the hair. The clinical picture corroborates it fully. There are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter, enlarging over three weeks. Within the patches the hair shafts are broken off at the scalp surface, producing the black-dot appearance that is typical of endothrix infection, in which fungal invasion weakens the shaft so that it fractures at the level of the skin. The surrounding scalp shows fine gray-white scale, and there is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, a characteristic accompanying feature of tinea capitis that helps distinguish it from noninfectious causes of alopecia. The epidemiological context supports it as well, since he attends elementary school where several classmates have had similar issues, and tinea capitis is highly contagious among school-aged children. The negative Wood lamp examination is entirely consistent and does not argue against the diagnosis, because endothrix Trichophyton species do not fluoresce, whereas ectothrix Microsporum species do; the absence of fluorescence therefore helps identify the causative genus rather than excluding infection. Differential considerations include alopecia areata, which produces well-defined round patches but with smooth, non-scaly skin, exclamation point hairs rather than black dots, and no lymphadenopathy; seborrheic dermatitis or scalp psoriasis, which cause scale but not discrete patches of alopecia with broken hairs; trichotillomania, which produces irregular patches with hairs broken at varying lengths and no scale or adenopathy; and a kerion, the inflammatory boggy suppurative form of tinea capitis, which is not present here since there is no boggy swelling, pustulation, or pain, but which can develop if the infection is untreated. Because the hair follicle is invaded, this infection is located within the hair shaft where topical agents cannot adequately penetrate.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Fungal culture of plucked hairs and scalp scale to identify the causative species and guide the choice and duration of oral antifungal therapy. Baseline laboratory testing as indicated by the specific oral antifungal selected, in accordance with its monitoring requirements. Examination of household members and close contacts for scalp scaling, alopecia, or asymptomatic carriage. No further diagnostic testing is otherwise needed, as the KOH preparation is already diagnostic.
Conclusion: Tinea capitis of the parietal and occipital scalp in a 6-year-old boy, with an endothrix pattern confirmed on KOH microscopy and a black-dot clinical presentation, non-fluorescent on Wood lamp consistent with a Trichophyton species, accompanied by regional posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a plausible school-based source of transmission. Systemic oral antifungal therapy is required; topical therapy alone is inadequate because the organism resides within the hair shaft.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Start systemic oral antifungal therapy, which is mandatory for tinea capitis, with an agent and duration appropriate for the identified organism, typically several weeks of treatment continued until clinical and mycological cure rather than stopping when the scalp looks better; weight-based dosing and adherence should be reviewed explicitly with the mother, since premature discontinuation is the leading cause of treatment failure. Take the medication as directed with respect to food, as absorption of some oral antifungals is affected by dietary fat. Add an adjunctive antifungal shampoo, such as a selenium sulfide or ketoconazole preparation, used two or three times weekly by the patient and considered for household contacts; this does not cure the infection but reduces spore shedding and transmission to others. Do not use topical antifungal cream as monotherapy, and avoid topical corticosteroids. Addressing the contagion and public health considerations raised by the school exposure: examine household members and close contacts for scalp scale, alopecia, or asymptomatic carriage and treat those affected; advise against sharing combs, brushes, hats, pillows, towels, and hair clippers, and clean or replace those already used; and notify the school so that other affected children can be identified, noting that with treatment initiated and adjunctive shampoo he can generally continue attending school and does not require prolonged exclusion. Address the child's and family's concerns about the appearance of the patches by explaining that hair regrowth is expected once the infection is eradicated, provided scarring does not occur. Arrange follow-up in several weeks to confirm clinical response and consider repeat mycological testing before stopping therapy, and advise earlier review if the area becomes painful, boggy, swollen, or pustular, which would signal development of a kerion requiring prompt reassessment because of the risk of permanent scarring alopecia.
Notes: A negative Wood lamp examination does not exclude tinea capitis, since endothrix Trichophyton infections do not fluoresce; the diagnosis here rests on the positive KOH microscopy. Oral therapy is essential, as topical agents cannot penetrate the hair shaft.

Vignette: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the ER after being stung by a bee at a picnic. He is crying hysterically. After 15 minutes of calming him down, exam reveals a swollen tender upper lip but no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash, and no other complaints.

[1]
points: 9
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Identifies localized bee sting reaction WITHOUT anaphylaxis based on isolated upper lip swelling, no tongue/airway involvement, no stridor/drooling, no rash, and no systemic symptoms.

[2]
points: 9
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Correctly determines that epinephrine is NOT indicated in the absence of anaphylaxis criteria (no respiratory compromise, no hypotension, no systemic urticaria, no GI symptoms).

[3]
points: 8
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Recommends conservative care: remove stinger if visible (scrape away rather than pinch), cold compress, oral antihistamine (e.g., diphenhydramine or cetirizine), and weight-based acetaminophen/ibuprofen for pain.

[4]
points: 8
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Recommends an observation period (typically 1-2 hours) in the ED to monitor for delayed allergic progression before discharge.

[5]
points: 8
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Provides clear anaphylaxis red flags to caregivers: tongue/throat swelling, difficulty breathing, wheeze, hives, vomiting, lightheadedness, or any rapid worsening - call 911 immediately and administer epinephrine if prescribed.

[6]
points: 6
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Differentiates a normal local reaction from a large local reaction (>10 cm, evolves over 24-48h) and from anaphylaxis; explains expected swelling course (peaks 24-48h, resolves over 5-7 days).

[7]
points: 6
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Asks about prior sting reactions, family history, atopic conditions, and number of stings to risk-stratify and guide follow-up.

[8]
points: 5
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Discusses follow-up with primary care/allergist if reactions worsen with future stings or for systemic reactions; venom immunotherapy is not indicated for isolated local reactions.

[9]
points: 5
tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
Provides age-appropriate, calm reassurance to the child and caregiver while validating their concern about the lip swelling.

[10]
points: 4
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Counsels on bee sting prevention: avoid bright clothing/scents at picnics, keep food covered outdoors, wear shoes outside, and remain calm if a bee approaches.

[11]
points: -10
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Penalize administering epinephrine, prescribing an epinephrine auto-injector, or recommending hospital admission without anaphylaxis indications.

[12]
points: -6
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Penalize failing to provide anaphylaxis red-flag warnings or instructions on when to call 911 after discharge.

[13]
points: -5
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Penalize prescribing systemic corticosteroids or antibiotics for an uncomplicated localized sting reaction.

[14]
points: -3
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Penalize overdiagnosing this as anaphylaxis based on isolated lip swelling without other systemic features.
