Vignette:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the ER after being stung by a bee at a picnic. He is crying hysterically. After 15 minutes of calming him down, exam reveals a swollen tender upper lip but no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash, and no other complaints.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 9 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Bee sting sustained at a picnic, with a swollen and tender upper lip and marked distress; brought to the emergency room by caregivers.
Analysis: This is a localized reaction to a hymenoptera (bee) sting involving the upper lip. The reasoning turns almost entirely on distinguishing a local reaction from systemic anaphylaxis, and the case provides an unusually clean set of negatives that make that distinction. After 15 minutes of settling, the examination shows swelling and tenderness confined to the upper lip, the site of the sting, with no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash, and no other complaints. The absence of stridor and drooling argues against upper airway involvement; the absence of tongue swelling means the swelling has not extended to a structure that threatens the airway; the absence of any rash means there is no urticaria or generalized flushing; and the absence of any other complaint means no respiratory distress, no vomiting or abdominal pain, no dizziness or syncope. Anaphylaxis requires involvement of more than one organ system or hypotension after an allergen exposure, and none of that is present. The reaction is therefore a single-system, single-site cutaneous and soft tissue response.
An important point of clinical judgement is that the initial presentation was dominated by hysterical crying. Distress of that magnitude can mimic or mask respiratory compromise, and it is only after 15 minutes of calming that a reliable examination was possible - the reassuring findings come from that settled examination, which is what makes them interpretable. The 15-minute interval also has diagnostic value in itself: anaphylaxis after an insect sting characteristically begins within minutes, so a child who remains free of systemic features at this point is considerably less likely to progress, although progression is not formally excluded by a single time point.
The main differential considerations are systemic anaphylaxis, which is argued against as above; angioedema from another cause, which is unlikely given the clear temporal and anatomical link to the sting site; and local infection or cellulitis at the sting site, which would not develop this rapidly and is a consideration only over subsequent days. The anatomical location does deserve specific weight: swelling of the lip and face lies close to the airway, so although the airway is currently entirely uninvolved, the site warrants a period of observation rather than immediate discharge.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No laboratory or imaging studies are needed. Clinical monitoring is what is required: serial airway assessment with inspection of the lips, tongue, and oropharynx, auscultation of the chest for wheeze, pulse oximetry, and measurement of blood pressure and heart rate during a period of observation. Examination of the sting site for a retained stinger, which should be removed if present. Later allergy referral with specific IgE or skin testing to hymenoptera venom would be considered only if a systemic reaction occurs now or has occurred previously, which is not documented in this case.
Conclusion: Localized reaction to a bee sting of the upper lip in a healthy-appearing 9-year-old boy, with a swollen tender lip as the sole finding and no clinical evidence of anaphylaxis - specifically no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash and no other symptoms on a settled examination performed 15 minutes after presentation. The presentation is benign and requires symptomatic treatment plus a period of observation for evolving airway involvement given the perioral location, rather than emergency resuscitation.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Inspect the sting site and remove any retained stinger promptly by scraping or gentle extraction, then clean the area. Apply a cold compress to the upper lip to limit swelling and provide comfort, and give weight-appropriate simple analgesia for the tenderness. An oral antihistamine may be given for the local swelling and itching. Observe the child in the emergency department for a period of continued monitoring before discharge, with repeated checks of the lips, tongue and oropharynx, breathing, and vital signs, precisely because the sting is perioral and any extension of swelling toward the tongue or airway would change management immediately; epinephrine, airway equipment and resuscitation capability should remain available during that observation even though no systemic reaction is present. Explicitly address the additional consideration that this is a first-documented reaction with no systemic component: routine epinephrine autoinjector prescription is not mandated by a purely local reaction, but the family should be counselled that future stings can behave differently, and if the history reveals prior systemic reactions or if any systemic feature appears now, an autoinjector prescription and allergy referral become appropriate. Give the caregivers clear written return instructions: seek emergency care immediately for tongue or throat swelling, drooling, a change or hoarseness in the voice, noisy breathing or stridor, difficulty breathing, widespread rash or hives, vomiting, faintness, pallor or collapse. Advise them also to watch the site over the next several days for increasing redness, warmth, spreading induration or fever, which would suggest secondary infection and warrant reassessment. Provide sting-prevention advice for outdoor eating, including avoiding open sweet drinks and food outdoors, wearing footwear, and not swatting at bees. Arrange routine follow-up with the child's primary care provider if symptoms persist beyond a few days.
Notes: Prior sting history, known allergies, past medical history, medications and immunization status are not specified in the case; a history of previous systemic reaction would substantially change the risk assessment and should be obtained. The initial hysterical crying limited the first examination, so the documented reassuring findings rest on the later settled assessment and should be repeated during observation.

Age: 32 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Ten months of recurrent lower abdominal cramping relieved by defecation, with bowel habits alternating between several days of diarrhea and week-long periods of constipation, worsening during work-related stress.
Analysis: This presentation fulfils the clinical picture of irritable bowel syndrome with a mixed bowel habit pattern. The core positive features are highly characteristic: chronic recurrent lower abdominal pain of at least 10 months' duration, pain that is relieved by defecation, and pain associated with a change in both stool frequency and form, alternating between diarrhea lasting several days and constipation lasting a week. The reproducible aggravation by work-related stress is consistent with the brain-gut interaction that underlies the disorder, and her anxious appearance on examination supports a stress-related component while she remains in no acute distress.
Equally important is the completeness of the negative work-up, because irritable bowel syndrome is a positive diagnosis supported by the absence of alarm features. The case explicitly excludes rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, fever and weight loss, all of which would point toward organic disease. She is 32, below the age at which new-onset bowel change mandates structural investigation, and family history is negative for both inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer. Vital signs are normal. The abdominal examination shows only mild left lower quadrant tenderness with a palpable sigmoid colon on deep palpation, a common and benign finding in functional bowel disorder reflecting a loaded or spastic sigmoid, with no masses, no organomegaly and no guarding, and a normal rectal examination.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 55 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of severe, constant, throbbing perianal pain rated 8 out of 10 beginning yesterday while straining at stool, markedly worse with sitting and defecation, with a palpable lump at the anal verge.
Analysis: The diagnosis is a thrombosed external hemorrhoid, and the case supports it on both mechanism and morphology. The onset is the classic one: abrupt, severe pain arising at the precise moment of straining during defecation, which is the event that raises venous pressure in the external hemorrhoidal plexus and precipitates thrombosis. The pain character is equally typical - constant and throbbing rather than intermittent, severe at 8 out of 10, and aggravated by sitting and by defecation, because the external hemorrhoidal territory below the dentate line is somatically innervated and therefore genuinely painful, unlike internal hemorrhoids which are typically painless.
The examination is essentially diagnostic. A tense, bluish-purple, spherical, tender nodule approximately 2 cm in diameter located at the anal verge describes a clotted vein under pressure: the tension reflects the contained thrombus, the bluish-purple color reflects deoxygenated clotted blood visible through thin perianal skin, and the anal verge location places it in the external hemorrhoidal plexus.
The risk factor profile is coherent and explains both the acute event and the chronic background. He works as a long-haul truck driver with prolonged sitting for 10 to 12 hours daily, which promotes perianal venous stasis; he has a low-fiber diet with poor fluid intake, which produces hard stool and habitual straining; and he has a long history of intermittent hemorrhoidal symptoms with minor bleeding and itching managed only with over-the-counter preparations, indicating pre-existing hemorrhoidal disease that has now thrombosed.
The important differentials are actively excluded by the findings. A perianal or perirectal abscess is the most consequential alternative and is argued against by the absence of fever, the absence of purulent drainage, and the absence of erythema; the lesion is discretely spherical and bluish-purple rather than fluctuant, hot and red with cellulitic spread, and there is only mild surrounding edema. This distinction matters because an abscess would require urgent incision and drainage and antibiotic consideration. An anal fissure would cause sharp tearing pain with defecation and a visible posterior midline tear rather than a discrete bluish nodule. A prolapsed, strangulated internal hemorrhoid would present as circumferential or segmental prolapsing mucosa rather than a single subcutaneous nodule at the verge. Anal neoplasm is very unlikely given the abrupt onset over one day and the typical thrombotic appearance, and the case explicitly notes no change in bowel habits. A pilonidal abscess is anatomically distinct, sitting in the natal cleft rather than at the anal verge. The digital rectal examination was deferred because of pain, which is clinically reasonable, but it leaves the anal canal and lower rectum unassessed.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required to establish this diagnosis, which is made by inspection. Adequate lighting and positioning for perianal inspection is the essential equipment. A digital rectal examination and anoscopy should be completed once pain is controlled or after treatment, to assess internal hemorrhoidal disease and to exclude a coexisting anal canal or low rectal lesion. Given his age of 55, consideration of colorectal cancer screening with colonoscopy is appropriate as a separate, elective matter, particularly in light of a history of rectal bleeding attributed to hemorrhoids. Laboratory testing and imaging are not indicated in the absence of systemic signs; if fever, spreading erythema or fluctuance were to develop, evaluation for abscess including imaging would then be warranted.
Conclusion: Acute thrombosed external hemorrhoid at the anal verge, approximately 2 cm, in a 55-year-old long-haul truck driver with chronic hemorrhoidal disease, precipitated by straining during defecation and driven by prolonged daily sitting, a low-fiber diet and poor fluid intake. There is no evidence of perianal infection or abscess - no fever, no purulent drainage, no erythema - and no systemic compromise. Because the thrombosis occurred only yesterday, he falls within the window in which surgical excision of the thrombosed hemorrhoid gives the fastest and most durable pain relief; this warrants prompt but non-emergency surgical evaluation, and conservative management is a reasonable alternative if he prefers it or if pain begins to subside.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Offer excision of the thrombosed external hemorrhoid under local anaesthesia, discussing that presentation within the first 48 to 72 hours of onset is the period in which excision produces the most rapid resolution of severe pain and the lowest rate of recurrence, and that excision of the clot and overlying skin is preferred to simple incision because incision alone allows residual clot and re-thrombosis. Explain the alternative of conservative management, which is appropriate if he declines intervention or if the pain is already improving, since thrombosed external hemorrhoids resolve spontaneously over one to two weeks. Whichever route is chosen, provide symptomatic care: adequate oral analgesia, warm sitz baths several times daily and after bowel movements, topical anaesthetic or hemorrhoidal preparations, cold compresses in the first day for edema, and stool softeners to prevent painful straining on the next bowel movement. Vignette:
A 22-year-old student presents with a 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching. Symptoms are year-round but worse during the spring season. On further questioning it is revealed that he has significant eye itching, redness, and tearing as well as palate and throat itching during the spring season. baseline_protocol:
Age: 22 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five years of progressively worsening nasal congestion, sneezing and nasal itching, present year-round but markedly worse in spring, accompanied during spring by itchy, red, watering eyes and itching of the palate and throat.
Analysis: The presentation is allergic rhinitis of a persistent (perennial) pattern with a clear seasonal exacerbation, accompanied by allergic conjunctivitis. Several elements of the history make the allergic mechanism convincing rather than merely possible. The symptom triad of sneezing, nasal itching and congestion is the signature of IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the nasal mucosa; itching in particular is the discriminating symptom, since infectious and vasomotor rhinitis characteristically cause congestion and rhinorrhea without prominent itch. The involvement of the conjunctivae with itching, redness and tearing extends the same mechanism to a second mucosal surface and is strongly associated with aeroallergen sensitization rather than with infection. Itching of the palate and throat during the same season reflects allergen contact with oropharyngeal mucosa and is another characteristically allergic symptom.
The temporal pattern is informative and points to two coexisting sensitization patterns. Symptoms that are present all year suggest sensitization to perennial indoor allergens, while the definite spring worsening with prominent ocular and oropharyngeal itch suggests additional sensitization to a seasonal outdoor pollen. This dual pattern is common and matters practically, because it means seasonal avoidance alone will not control his baseline symptoms.
The atopic background strengthens the diagnosis further. His mother reports eczema in infancy, which places him on the atopic march - the recognized progression from infantile atopic dermatitis to later allergic rhinitis and, in some patients, asthma. A five-year course that is worsening rather than resolving, in a young adult, is entirely consistent with established allergic rhinitis.
Differential considerations are as follows. Non-allergic or vasomotor rhinitis is unlikely because it does not typically produce nasal or ocular itch, and does not usually show a reproducible seasonal pattern. Recurrent infectious rhinosinusitis is unlikely given the absence of any reported fever, purulent discharge, facial pain or pressure. Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps could cause chronic congestion but the case reports no anosmia, no facial pressure and no purulence, and the itch and seasonality do not fit. Rhinitis medicamentosa from over-use of topical decongestants is a possibility in any patient with chronic congestion but no such medication use is described. A structural cause such as septal deviation or adenoidal hypertrophy could contribute to fixed congestion but would not explain sneezing, itching, or the ocular and palatal symptoms. Notably, no physical examination findings and no test results are provided in this case, so the diagnosis rests entirely on a characteristic history; examination and confirmatory allergy testing are still required. Two additional considerations deserve attention: asthma, which frequently coexists with allergic rhinitis in atopic patients and is not addressed in this case, and pollen-food allergy syndrome, which should be considered given the seasonal palate and throat itching, although the case does not state that these symptoms are food-related.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Anterior rhinoscopy and, where available, nasal endoscopy to document mucosal appearance and to exclude polyps and structural obstruction. Allergy testing with skin prick testing to a panel of relevant perennial indoor and seasonal outdoor aeroallergens, or serum allergen-specific IgE if skin testing is unsuitable, to identify the specific triggers driving both the perennial and the spring components. Complete blood count with differential to assess eosinophilia if clinically useful. Spirometry with bronchodilator response to screen for coexisting asthma, given the atopic background and the recognized united airway association. Ophthalmologic assessment is not required unless ocular symptoms are severe or fail to respond. Sinus CT is not indicated in the absence of features suggesting chronic rhinosinusitis.
Conclusion: Persistent allergic rhinitis with a spring seasonal exacerbation and associated allergic conjunctivitis in a 22-year-old atopic man with a history of infantile eczema, symptomatic and progressively worsening over five years. The combination of sneezing, nasal itch, congestion, ocular itch, redness and tearing, and palatal and throat itch, with both a year-round baseline and a clear seasonal peak, indicates sensitization to both perennial and seasonal aeroallergens. This is a chronic, quality-of-life-limiting but non-dangerous condition requiring scheduled outpatient evaluation with allergy testing and stepwise pharmacological management, with screening for coexisting asthma.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Confirm and characterize the sensitization with skin prick testing or specific IgE against both perennial indoor allergens and spring pollens, since targeted identification of triggers is what converts general advice into effective avoidance. Institute allergen avoidance measures tailored to the results: for perennial indoor allergens this typically means measures addressing bedding, soft furnishings, humidity, and pet exposure; for the spring component, advise keeping windows closed and using air conditioning during high pollen periods, showering and changing clothes after prolonged outdoor exposure, wearing wrap-around sunglasses to reduce ocular pollen contact, and limiting outdoor activity on high-pollen, dry, windy days. Start an intranasal corticosteroid as first-line maintenance therapy, since it is the most effective single agent for congestion as well as sneezing and itch; instruct him carefully on correct spray technique aiming away from the septum, and emphasize that benefit accrues over days to weeks with regular daily use rather than as-needed use. Add a non-sedating oral or intranasal antihistamine for the itch and sneezing, and begin it before and throughout the spring season rather than waiting for symptoms to peak. Treat the eye symptoms specifically with a topical antihistamine or mast cell stabilizer eye drop, as intranasal therapy alone often under-treats allergic conjunctivitis. Saline nasal irrigation is a useful adjunct to clear allergen and mucus. Reserve short courses of topical decongestants for severe congestion only, with an explicit warning about rebound rhinitis medicamentosa if used beyond a few days. Address the additional considerations explicitly: screen for asthma with directed questioning about cough, wheeze, chest tightness and exercise limitation and with spirometry, because allergic rhinitis and asthma frequently coexist in atopic patients and undiagnosed asthma is a real risk given his infantile eczema and atopic march; and take a careful dietary history regarding the seasonal palate and throat itching to determine whether raw fruits or vegetables provoke it, since pollen-food allergy syndrome would require specific counselling and, if any systemic or airway symptoms have occurred with food, allergy specialist review. If symptoms remain inadequately controlled on optimized pharmacotherapy, or if he wishes to modify the disease rather than suppress symptoms, refer for consideration of allergen immunotherapy, which is the only treatment that alters the underlying allergic disease and is well suited to a young patient with a five-year progressive course. Counsel him that the condition is chronic and that adherence to daily maintenance therapy, particularly in the weeks before spring, is what determines control. Arrange follow-up in about 4 to 6 weeks to assess response and adjust therapy.
Notes: No physical examination findings and no laboratory or allergy test results are provided in the case, so the working diagnosis rests on history alone and must be confirmed by examination and testing. Current medications, asthma symptoms, environmental and pet exposures, smoking status, and any food-related symptoms are not specified and should be established at the first visit.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman presents in January with 2-day history of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness. She was in her usual state of health before an abrupt onset of these symptoms. A few viral illnesses have affected her during the current winter, but not to this severity. She reports sick contacts at work and did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this season.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of fever, cough, headache and generalized weakness, of abrupt onset in a previously well woman presenting in January, with sick contacts at work and no seasonal influenza vaccination this season.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of an acute influenza-like illness, and influenza is the leading diagnosis. The reasoning rests on four converging strands. First, the symptom complex itself: the combination of fever, cough, headache and generalized weakness is the classic influenza syndrome, with prominent systemic features - headache and marked malaise - accompanying the respiratory symptom rather than following it. Second, and diagnostically important, the onset was abrupt in a woman who was in her usual state of health immediately beforehand; influenza is characteristically sudden in onset, whereas most other common respiratory viruses produce a more gradual prodrome beginning with sore throat or nasal symptoms. Third, the epidemiology fits precisely: the presentation is in January, within the typical influenza season, and she reports sick contacts at work, establishing plausible exposure. Fourth, she did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this season, which removes the principal protection against both infection and severe disease and materially raises the pre-test probability.
A further supporting observation is her own comparison: she has had a few viral illnesses this winter but none of this severity, which points to a more intense systemic illness than her usual seasonal upper respiratory infections and is consistent with influenza rather than a common cold.
The main differential considerations are other respiratory viral infections, including COVID-19 and RSV, which can be clinically indistinguishable from influenza at the bedside and would be separated only by testing; a common cold from rhinovirus or coronavirus, which is argued against by the abrupt onset, the fever and the severity relative to her previous winter illnesses; and bacterial pneumonia, which must be considered whenever fever and cough occur together, but which typically produces focal chest findings, pleuritic pain, purulent sputum or dyspnea - none of which is reported here. Streptococcal pharyngitis is unlikely given the presence of cough and the absence of any reported sore throat or exudate. Acute bacterial sinusitis is not supported at two days of illness with no facial pain or purulent nasal discharge. Meningitis warrants explicit thought because of the headache and fever, but the headache here occurs within a typical influenza syndrome, and no neck stiffness, photophobia, rash or altered mental status is reported.
A significant limitation must be stated: the case provides no vital signs, no physical examination findings and no test results. Without a respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, heart rate, blood pressure and chest auscultation, the severity of this illness cannot be fully graded, and complications such as pneumonia cannot be excluded on the information given. She is 30 years old with no stated comorbidity, pregnancy status or immunosuppression, which on the available information places her outside the recognized high-risk groups, but this too rests on absence of information rather than on documented negatives.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Full vital signs including temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and pulse oximetry, plus a complete physical examination with chest auscultation and examination of the pharynx, ears and neck - these are the essential and currently missing data. Rapid molecular or antigen testing for influenza A and B, ideally on a multiplex respiratory panel that also covers SARS-CoV-2 and RSV, since the results would guide antiviral therapy, isolation and return-to-work advice. Chest radiography only if examination reveals focal findings, hypoxemia, tachypnea, dyspnea, or if symptoms fail to improve or worsen, to evaluate for pneumonia. Basic blood tests are not routinely required in an otherwise healthy adult with an uncomplicated influenza-like illness and should be reserved for those with severe illness or suspected complications. Pregnancy testing should be considered in a woman of childbearing age, since pregnancy would place her in a high-risk group and change management.
Conclusion: Acute influenza-like illness, most consistent with seasonal influenza, in a previously healthy 30-year-old unvaccinated woman presenting on day 2 of an abruptly-onset febrile respiratory illness during January with documented workplace sick contacts. There is no information in the case indicating complication, hypoxemia, or high-risk comorbidity, so on the available data this is an uncomplicated illness suitable for outpatient assessment, confirmatory testing, symptomatic care, and consideration of antiviral therapy given that she is within the effective treatment window. Vital signs and examination are required to confirm this severity assessment.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Obtain vital signs and a complete examination first, since the severity grading in this protocol rests on their absence of abnormality rather than on documented normality. Perform rapid testing for influenza, with combined testing for SARS-CoV-2 and RSV where available, because the illnesses are clinically indistinguishable and the results direct antiviral choice and isolation. Address the antiviral consideration explicitly: she is on day 2 of symptoms and therefore still inside the window in which neuraminidase inhibitor therapy is most effective, and antiviral treatment should be offered without waiting for test results if influenza is strongly suspected clinically, since early initiation shortens illness duration and reduces complications; treatment is particularly warranted if she is found to be pregnant, immunosuppressed, or to have a chronic medical condition, or if she deteriorates. Provide supportive care: rest, generous fluid intake to counter fever-related losses, antipyretics and analgesia for the fever and headache, and cough relief as needed. Advise her to stay home from work until she has been afebrile for at least 24 hours without antipyretics, and to practise hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette and mask use around others, both to protect colleagues and because she reports an ongoing chain of transmission at work. Give explicit return precautions: she should seek urgent reassessment for difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, chest pain, persistent or high fever beyond several days or fever that resolves and then recurs, coughing up purulent or bloody sputum, confusion or drowsiness, severe or worsening headache with neck stiffness or rash, dizziness or inability to keep fluids down, since these suggest pneumonia, secondary bacterial infection or another complication. Do not prescribe antibiotics for this presentation, as it is a viral syndrome and antibiotics are indicated only if a bacterial complication is demonstrated. Address the vaccination gap directly: she did not receive this season's influenza vaccine, and she should be counselled and offered vaccination once she recovers, and encouraged to receive it annually before each season, with the same message extended to household and workplace contacts. Consider post-exposure prophylaxis discussion only for high-risk close contacts. Arrange follow-up if she is not improving within about 3 to 5 days, as most uncomplicated influenza begins to settle within that period, though cough and fatigue may persist longer.
Notes: No vital signs, physical examination findings, or test results are provided in the case, so severity cannot be definitively graded and complications such as pneumonia cannot be excluded on the given information. Pregnancy status, comorbidities, immunosuppression, allergies and current medications are not specified and must be established, as any of these would place her in a high-risk category and strengthen the indication for antiviral therapy.

A 38-year-old male computer programmer presents with perianal discomfort and a small palpable lump that he noticed 3 days ago. He reports mild itching in the area, particularly after prolonged sitting. He denies rectal bleeding, pain during bowel movements, fever, or changes in bowel habits. He spends 8 to 10 hours daily seated at his desk. He has no family history of colorectal cancer. On examination, a small non-tender, soft, external perianal skin tag approximately 5 mm is noted at the 6 o'clock position. There is no thrombosis, bleeding, prolapse, or surrounding erythema.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 38 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Perianal discomfort with a small palpable lump noticed 3 days ago, and mild itching in the area that is worse after prolonged sitting.
Analysis: The findings describe a benign external perianal skin tag. The examination is the decisive element and it is entirely reassuring in every respect that matters. The lesion is small at approximately 5 mm, soft, non-tender, external, and located at the 6 o'clock position, and the examination explicitly documents no thrombosis, no bleeding, no prolapse and no surrounding erythema. A perianal skin tag is redundant fibrovascular skin at the anal verge, typically the residue of a previously resolved thrombosed external hemorrhoid or of chronic local irritation, and it is a cosmetic and hygienic issue rather than a disease process.
The history is equally reassuring and reinforces the benign interpretation. He denies rectal bleeding, pain during bowel movements, fever, and any change in bowel habits - four of the features that would otherwise prompt concern about anorectal or colorectal pathology. He has no family history of colorectal cancer, and at 38 he is below the usual age threshold for screening. The mild itching, worse specifically after prolonged sitting, and his occupational pattern of 8 to 10 hours seated daily as a computer programmer, together explain a mechanism of local moisture, warmth and friction producing pruritus ani and drawing his attention to a tag that has probably been present longer than the 3 days since he noticed it. Notably, he noticed the lump 3 days ago, which is not the same as the lump having formed 3 days ago.
The differential considerations are each addressed by specific findings. A thrombosed external hemorrhoid is excluded: it would be acutely and severely painful, tense and bluish-purple, whereas this lesion is soft and non-tender and thrombosis is explicitly absent. Prolapsed internal hemorrhoids are excluded by the absence of prolapse and of bleeding. A perianal abscess is excluded by the absence of fever, tenderness, fluctuance and erythema. An anal fissure is argued against by the absence of pain on defecation and of bleeding. A sentinel tag associated with a chronic fissure would classically sit at the posterior midline, which is the 6 o'clock position, so this association deserves a moment's thought, but the complete absence of defecation-related pain and of bleeding makes an underlying active fissure unlikely. Anal condyloma from human papillomavirus would typically be verrucous or papillomatous and often multiple rather than a single soft smooth tag. Anal neoplasm is very unlikely in a soft, small, non-tender, non-ulcerated, non-bleeding lesion in a 38-year-old with no bowel change and no bleeding, but any lesion that grows, ulcerates, bleeds or indurates would require biopsy. Perianal Crohn disease can produce characteristic large fleshy skin tags, but there is nothing here to suggest it - no diarrhea, no bowel habit change, no fistula, no ulceration and no systemic features. A digital rectal examination and anoscopy have not been described in the case, so the anal canal itself remains formally unassessed.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required. The diagnosis is made by inspection and the clinical picture is unambiguous. Adequate lighting and positioning for perianal inspection suffices; a digital rectal examination and, if any internal symptoms emerge, anoscopy can be performed to confirm the absence of internal hemorrhoidal disease or a fissure. Laboratory testing, imaging, biopsy and colonoscopy are not indicated in the absence of bleeding, bowel change, weight loss, family history or age-based screening criteria.
Conclusion: Benign external perianal skin tag, approximately 5 mm at the 6 o'clock position, in a healthy 38-year-old man, with associated mild pruritus ani attributable to prolonged daily sitting and local moisture and friction. There are no alarm features whatsoever - no bleeding, no defecation pain, no fever, no bowel habit change, no thrombosis, prolapse or erythema, and no family history of colorectal cancer. This is a benign condition of cosmetic and hygienic significance only, requiring reassurance and simple local self-care measures rather than medical or surgical intervention.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Provide firm and explicit reassurance that this is a benign skin tag, not a tumour, not an infection, and not a hemorrhoid requiring treatment, and explain that such tags are common, often the residue of a previous local irritation or resolved thrombosis, and do not require removal for medical reasons. Focus treatment on the pruritus, which is the only symptom actually bothering him. Advise gentle perianal hygiene: clean with water rather than vigorous wiping with dry paper, use unscented wipes or a rinse after bowel movements, and dry the area thoroughly by patting rather than rubbing, since retained moisture is the main driver of itching. Advise against soaps, perfumed products, and prolonged use of topical steroid or over-the-counter hemorrhoid preparations, which frequently worsen pruritus ani; a short course of a barrier or zinc-based ointment is a reasonable simple measure. Recommend loose, breathable cotton underwear. Address the occupational factor explicitly, since he sits 8 to 10 hours daily and his itching is worse after prolonged sitting: advise scheduled breaks to stand and walk at least hourly, use of a supportive or breathable cushion, and avoidance of continuous uninterrupted sitting - this is the single most modifiable contributor in his case. Encourage adequate dietary fiber and fluid intake and avoidance of straining or prolonged sitting on the toilet, which prevents the hemorrhoidal and fissure problems that lead to further tags. Explain that surgical excision of a skin tag is elective and is generally reserved for tags that cause persistent hygiene difficulty or significant symptoms despite these measures, and that excision in the perianal region carries a risk of a painful and slow-healing wound, so it should not be undertaken casually. Because it sits at the posterior midline, review at follow-up for any pain or bleeding on defecation that would suggest an underlying chronic anal fissure. Ask him to seek medical review if the lesion grows, becomes hard, ulcerates, bleeds, or becomes painful, or if he develops rectal bleeding, a change in bowel habit, unintentional weight loss, fever, or perianal discharge, as any of these would require reassessment. Ensure he enters routine age-appropriate colorectal cancer screening at the recommended age.
Notes: A digital rectal examination and anoscopy are not described in the case, so the anal canal has not been formally assessed; this is acceptable given the absence of internal symptoms but should be completed if bleeding, pain on defecation or bowel change develops. The lesion was noticed 3 days ago but its true duration is not specified. Sexual history, HPV risk factors, and any history of prior anorectal problems are not specified in the case.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 58-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class C) presents after two episodes of large-volume hematemesis over the past hour, each estimated at 500 mL of bright red blood with clots. He also reports black tarry stools for the past 2 days. He has known esophageal varices documented on prior endoscopy and has been non-compliant with propranolol therapy. On examination, he is pale, confused, and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 36.2C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 78/42, SpO2 94%. Abdominal exam reveals ascites, splenomegaly, and caput medusae. Rectal exam shows melena. Labs: hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL (baseline 10.4), platelets 62,000/mcL, INR 2.4, BUN 58 mg/dL. Two large-bore IVs are placed and massive transfusion protocol is activated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 58 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two episodes of large-volume hematemesis within the past hour, each approximately 500 mL of bright red blood with clots, preceded by 2 days of black tarry stools, with pallor, confusion and distress.
Analysis: This is acute variceal hemorrhage with hemorrhagic shock in a patient with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis, and it is an immediately life-threatening emergency. The source is almost certain: he has known esophageal varices documented on prior endoscopy and has been non-compliant with propranolol, so the single most effective prophylaxis against variceal bleeding has not been in place. The physical findings confirm the portal hypertension that drives the varices - ascites, splenomegaly and caput medusae are all direct manifestations of portal hypertension with portosystemic collateral formation.
The magnitude and acuity of blood loss are severe. Two 500 mL episodes of bright red hematemesis with clots within one hour indicates ongoing active arterial or high-flow venous bleeding, and the 2 days of melena show the bleeding began before the acute episodes. The hemoglobin has fallen from a baseline of 10.4 to 6.2 g/dL, and because equilibration lags acute loss, the true deficit is likely greater than that figure suggests. The elevated BUN of 58 mg/dL with disproportionate elevation relative to an upper gastrointestinal source reflects absorbed blood protein load together with reduced renal perfusion, and reinforces that the bleeding is upper gastrointestinal and substantial.
The hemodynamics establish decompensated hemorrhagic shock: blood pressure 78/42 is frankly hypotensive, heart rate 128 shows maximal compensatory tachycardia, respiratory rate 24 reflects compensation for metabolic acidosis and reduced oxygen delivery, and the pallor is consistent with profound anemia. Critically, he is confused. In this patient confusion has two plausible and non-exclusive explanations that both demand attention: cerebral hypoperfusion from shock, and hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by the large protein load of blood in the gut in a Child-Pugh C cirrhotic. Either way, the confusion signals a patient at high risk of aspirating blood and unable to protect his own airway, which is a central management concern.
His hemostatic reserve is severely impaired and compounds the bleeding: INR 2.4 reflects failure of hepatic synthesis of clotting factors, and platelets of 62,000/mcL reflect hypersplenism from the splenomegaly and reduced thrombopoietin. Child-Pugh class C denotes the most advanced stage of cirrhosis and carries the highest mortality in variceal hemorrhage.
Differential considerations for upper gastrointestinal bleeding in a cirrhotic include peptic ulcer disease, gastric or duodenal erosions, portal hypertensive gastropathy, gastric varices, and a Mallory-Weiss tear. These cannot be excluded without endoscopy, and endoscopy is required both diagnostically and therapeutically; nonetheless the prior documented esophageal varices, the untreated portal hypertension, the propranolol non-compliance, and the volume and character of bleeding make variceal hemorrhage overwhelmingly the most likely source, and initial management must be directed at it without waiting for confirmation. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis must also be considered given the ascites, as bacterial infection commonly precipitates variceal bleeding and independently worsens outcome. Temperature of 36.2C does not exclude infection in a cirrhotic patient, who may not mount fever.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, which is simultaneously the diagnostic and definitive therapeutic step, performed as soon as the patient is sufficiently resuscitated and with the airway secured. Continuous cardiac monitoring, non-invasive or arterial blood pressure monitoring, and pulse oximetry. Serial complete blood counts, coagulation studies including INR and fibrinogen, type and crossmatch with ongoing blood product availability, comprehensive metabolic panel with renal function and electrolytes, liver function tests, lactate and arterial or venous blood gas to gauge shock severity, and blood cultures. Diagnostic paracentesis of the ascites with cell count, differential and culture to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Ammonia level may be considered in evaluating encephalopathy but should not delay treatment. Airway equipment for endotracheal intubation, large-bore intravenous access already established, consideration of central venous access, urinary catheter for output monitoring, and immediate availability of balloon tamponade equipment as a rescue device. Abdominal imaging with Doppler ultrasound of the portal system is useful once stabilized, and CT angiography or interventional radiology assessment would be relevant if a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is contemplated.
Conclusion: Massive acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, almost certainly from known esophageal varices, causing decompensated hemorrhagic shock in a 58-year-old man with Child-Pugh class C alcoholic cirrhosis who had discontinued propranolol prophylaxis. He has hypotension at 78/42 with tachycardia of 128, hemoglobin fallen from 10.4 to 6.2 g/dL, coagulopathy with INR 2.4 and thrombocytopenia of 62,000/mcL, and confusion that places his airway at immediate risk from aspiration of blood and may additionally represent hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by the intestinal blood load. Two large-bore intravenous lines are in place and massive transfusion protocol has been activated. This is a maximal-acuity emergency with high mortality requiring simultaneous airway protection, aggressive resuscitation, vasoactive and antibiotic pharmacotherapy, and urgent therapeutic endoscopy in an intensive care setting.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Manage this as a simultaneous rather than sequential resuscitation. Secure the airway first: given confusion, ongoing large-volume hematemesis and a high aspiration risk, proceed with early endotracheal intubation for airway protection and to permit safe endoscopy, and give supplemental oxygen while preparing. Continue aggressive resuscitation through the two large-bore intravenous lines with the activated massive transfusion protocol, transfusing packed red cells with a restrictive target appropriate to variceal bleeding rather than over-transfusing, because excessive volume and red cell loading raise portal pressure and can worsen variceal bleeding; correct the coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia with plasma, fibrinogen replacement and platelets guided by the INR of 2.4, the platelet count of 62,000/mcL and ongoing bleeding, and avoid over-resuscitation with crystalloid for the same reason. Start a vasoactive splanchnic vasoconstrictor infusion such as octreotide or terlipressin immediately and before endoscopy, to reduce portal venous pressure and bleeding. Give prophylactic intravenous antibiotics, typically a third-generation cephalosporin, to every cirrhotic patient with gastrointestinal bleeding, since this reduces infection, rebleeding and mortality and is a specific, evidence-based and frequently omitted step. Consider intravenous proton pump inhibitor until endoscopy defines the source, since a peptic source has not yet been excluded. Arrange urgent therapeutic upper endoscopy as soon as feasible after stabilization, with endoscopic band ligation as the treatment of choice for esophageal varices, and injection or glue therapy if gastric varices are found. If bleeding cannot be controlled endoscopically, use balloon tamponade or an esophageal covered stent as a temporizing bridge, and escalate urgently to transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, which should be discussed early in a Child-Pugh C patient with high-risk bleeding rather than only after failure. Admit to intensive care with continuous monitoring, urine output measurement, and serial hemoglobin, lactate and coagulation studies. Address the additional considerations explicitly: perform diagnostic paracentesis of the ascites and send cultures to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis as a precipitant; treat presumed hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose once the airway is protected, as the intestinal blood load is a potent precipitant in Child-Pugh C disease, and identify and correct other precipitants including infection, electrolyte disturbance and renal impairment; monitor for alcohol withdrawal, which may emerge during admission, and give thiamine. After hemostasis is achieved, prevent rebleeding, which is high-risk in the first days: restart and maintain non-selective beta-blocker therapy once hemodynamically stable, combined with a programme of scheduled repeat band ligation until varices are eradicated, and address directly the non-compliance with propranolol that contributed to this event through education, simplified regimens and structured follow-up. Arrange addiction support and alcohol cessation treatment, which is the single most important determinant of long-term survival in alcoholic cirrhosis, and refer for liver transplant evaluation, which is appropriate to consider in Child-Pugh class C disease with variceal hemorrhage provided abstinence and other criteria can be met. Monitor renal function closely for hepatorenal syndrome and acute kidney injury, both of which are common after variceal bleeding and hypotension.
Notes: The prognosis is guarded: Child-Pugh class C cirrhosis with active variceal hemorrhage and hemodynamic shock carries high in-hospital mortality, and this should be communicated to the patient's family with early goals-of-care discussion. The confusion has at least two possible causes - hypoperfusion from shock and hepatic encephalopathy - and both must be addressed. Allergies, current medications, prior variceal bleeding episodes, alcohol use timeline and last drink, and code status are not specified in the case and should be obtained from family or records as resuscitation proceeds.

Vignette:
A man who appears to be in his 50s is brought to the emergency department. The history is
given by emergency medical technicians (EMTs), who state they were called to a store for a 50-
yr-old man who possibly had a stroke. At the store, they found him lying on the ground

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. baseline_protocol:
Age: Approximately 50 years (man who appears to be in his 50s; EMTs were called for a 50-year-old man)
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden collapse from a sitting position at a store with generalized shaking of arms and legs, drooling, and loss of consciousness, followed by postictal confusion; on arrival he is incoherent, later becomes transiently lethargic and hemodynamically unstable, and after recovery complains only of mild headache.
Analysis: The witnessed event is far more consistent with a generalized convulsive seizure than with the stroke initially suspected by the callers. The strongest supporting facts are the abrupt fall from a sitting position without preceding illness, sustained shaking of all four limbs, drooling, a puncture wound on the undersurface of the tongue (a classic lateral/inferior tongue bite from a convulsion), urinary incontinence evidenced by urine on the trousers, and a prolonged postictal state with disorientation to everything but his name and incoherent answers. The absence of scalp trauma, absence of meningismus, symmetric pupils, symmetric face and gag reflex, symmetric 2+ reflexes with downgoing plantars, and equal limb movement to command argue against a large hemispheric stroke, brainstem event, or meningitis as the primary cause of the presentation. Vital signs at triage showed only hypertension (165/90), which is common postictally. Laboratory data do not point to an alternative metabolic explanation: hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, hematocrit 45.4%, WBC 9700/mcL, and a normal serum chemistry profile exclude anemia, an obvious infection, and electrolyte or glucose derangements as recorded. The ECG shows sinus rhythm without arrhythmia or ischemia, arguing against a primary cardiac arrhythmic syncope. The transient episode of bradycardia to 30/min with hypotension to 74/52, respirations of 10/min and deep lethargy while pupils remained equal and reactive and the airway remained protected represents a self-limited period of profound autonomic and cerebral depression in the postictal period; it resolved spontaneously with return to sinus rhythm in the 80s and full alertness, and no arrhythmia was documented on ECG. The decisive localizing finding is on re-examination: after full recovery of consciousness, gait, balance and gross motor function, subtle dysdiadochokinesia persists in the LEFT upper extremity. A residual left-sided deficit localizes the lesion to the RIGHT cerebral hemisphere and indicates that this was a symptomatic (structurally provoked) seizure rather than an idiopathic first seizure. Among the four proposed CT interpretations, an acute intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the right parietal area best reconciles the case: it is the only option that is both immediately visible on non-contrast CT within this timeframe and capable of producing abrupt loss of consciousness with a generalized convulsion, a right-hemispheric focal deficit, and a persisting mild headache. An acute ischemic stroke in the right parietal area is unlikely to be radiographically apparent this early and only rarely presents with a convulsion at onset; a dilated right lateral ventricle would be an incidental or chronic finding that does not explain an acute convulsion with a new focal deficit; and mild cerebral edema is a nonspecific descriptor that does not account for a lateralized left-sided cerebellar-type deficit. Additional differential considerations that must be kept open include an underlying mass lesion or vascular malformation presenting with hemorrhage, post-traumatic injury from the fall itself, and a toxic or withdrawal-related seizure, although the social history records only social drinking with no recreational drug use.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Non-contrast head CT (already obtained; formal radiologic interpretation required). Continuous cardiac telemetry and pulse oximetry with serial vital signs given the documented transient bradycardia and hypotension. Repeat/serial neurologic examination. Bedside capillary glucose. Continuous or urgent EEG to characterize the seizure and exclude ongoing nonconvulsive seizure activity given the fluctuating level of consciousness. Brain MRI with and without contrast, and vascular imaging (CT or MR angiography/venography), to define the underlying structural cause of a right parietal lesion. Toxicology screen and serum ethanol level. Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT, platelet count) given the aspirin use, the fish oil use, the punctate red spots on the right lower leg, and a suspected intracranial hemorrhage. Twelve-lead ECG has been done; repeat if bradycardia or hypotension recurs.
Conclusion: A previously well man in his 50s sustained an unprovoked, witnessed generalized convulsive seizure with tongue laceration, incontinence, and a prolonged postictal state, complicated by a transient self-limited episode of bradycardia, hypotension and depressed consciousness. He has since returned to baseline alertness with mild headache but retains a subtle left upper extremity dysdiadochokinesia, localizing to the right cerebral hemisphere. Taken together with the head CT options offered, the correct interpretation of the scan is an intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the right parietal area, making this a symptomatic first seizure caused by an acute structural right parietal lesion rather than an idiopathic seizure or the ischemic stroke originally suspected.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Admit to a monitored neurologic or intensive care setting with continuous cardiac and neurologic monitoring; this patient has already demonstrated an episode of bradycardia to 30/min with a systolic pressure of 74 mm Hg and hypoventilation, so airway equipment must remain immediately available even though he currently protects his airway. Obtain immediate formal neuroradiologic reading of the head CT and urgent neurosurgical consultation for the right parietal intraparenchymal hemorrhage, including assessment of hematoma size, mass effect, and the need for operative intervention. Institute strict blood pressure control targets and avoid both hypertensive surges (he presented at 165/90) and hypotension, given the second recorded pressure of 74/52. Withhold aspirin and the over-the-counter fish oil immediately because of their antiplatelet and antithrombotic effects in the setting of intracranial bleeding, and check coagulation parameters and platelet count; reverse any identified coagulopathy. Start an antiseizure medication for a symptomatic seizure due to a structural cortical lesion, and monitor for recurrence with EEG. Address the additional considerations explicitly: examine and document the punctate red spots on the right lower leg and the blood at the corner of the mouth in relation to a possible bleeding diathesis and the tongue puncture wound respectively; perform an oral and tongue wound assessment for hemostasis and secondary infection; screen for traumatic injury sustained during the fall despite the absence of scalp trauma, deformity or bruising on the initial survey; continue to withhold oral intake until swallowing and mental status are formally reassessed; and counsel the patient and his family, once he is fully alert, regarding driving restrictions and avoidance of swimming, heights, and operating machinery until cleared, which is directly relevant to his work as an attorney and his ability to return to independent activity. Manage his known mild intermittent asthma by keeping the albuterol inhaler available, and document no known drug allergies before initiating new therapy. Arrange definitive MRI and vascular imaging to identify an underlying tumor or vascular malformation once he is stabilized, with neurology follow-up for long-term seizure management.
Notes: The head CT image itself is not reproducible in this protocol; the interpretation given is the one best supported by the clinical facts in the case among the four offered options, and it must be confirmed against the actual images by a radiologist. The transient bradycardia and hypotension are described in the case but no rhythm strip from that episode is provided, so an arrhythmic contribution cannot be entirely excluded despite a normal ECG in sinus rhythm. The duration of the convulsion could not be quantified by the store employees, so status epilepticus cannot be excluded retrospectively.

A 16-year-old male competitive swimmer presents with a 4-day history of progressive right ear pain and itching. He has been swimming daily for the past 3 weeks during summer training. The pain worsens when he chews food and when he lies on his right side. He reports a sensation of fullness in the ear and mild hearing reduction. He denies fever, ear discharge, or recent upper respiratory symptoms. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is marked tenderness on manipulation of the right tragus and with traction on the right auricle. Otoscopic examination reveals a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris. The tympanic membrane is barely visible but appears intact. baseline_protocol:
Age: 16 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Four-day history of progressive right ear pain and itching with a sensation of fullness and mild hearing reduction in a competitive swimmer who has been swimming daily for the past three weeks.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of acute diffuse otitis externa (swimmer's ear) of the right ear. The strongest supporting facts are the exposure history of daily swimming for three weeks, which causes repeated maceration and loss of the protective cerumen barrier of the external auditory canal; the prodrome of itching preceding pain, which is characteristic of canal skin inflammation; and above all the physical findings of marked tenderness on manipulation of the tragus and on traction of the auricle, which is the hallmark sign distinguishing external canal disease from middle ear disease. Otoscopy confirms the diagnosis directly: a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris. Pain that worsens with chewing supports canal involvement, because temporomandibular joint movement transmits to the anterior canal wall, and pain when lying on the affected side reflects direct pressure on the inflamed auricle and canal. The reported fullness and mild hearing reduction are explained by canal narrowing and debris producing a conductive obstruction rather than by a middle ear effusion. The main differential considerations are addressed by the examination. Acute otitis media is unlikely because the tympanic membrane, although barely visible, appears intact and there is no fever, no preceding upper respiratory infection, and no discharge; furthermore, tragal tenderness is not a feature of uncomplicated otitis media. Otomycosis is a consideration given the scant white debris and prominent itching, but there is no description of the typical fluffy hyphal or black spore appearance, and the macerated erythematous canal with an aquatic exposure favors bacterial otitis externa, most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus. Furuncle of the canal is excluded because the process is diffuse rather than a localized pustule. Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa is effectively excluded by this patient's youth, the absence of any stated immunocompromise or diabetes, the absence of granulation tissue, and the explicitly documented absence of mastoid tenderness and facial nerve dysfunction. Contact or eczematous dermatitis of the canal and referred otalgia from temporomandibular joint dysfunction are lower on the list because of the objective inflammatory otoscopic findings. The absence of periauricular lymphadenopathy, fever, mastoid tenderness, and facial nerve involvement indicates the infection remains confined to the canal without local or deep extension, so this is an uncomplicated case.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Otoscope for serial examination of the canal and tympanic membrane (already performed). If the canal is too edematous to permit visualization of the tympanic membrane or to allow topical drops to reach the affected skin, an ear wick and gentle aural toilet under direct vision or microscopic otoscopy are required. No laboratory studies, cultures, or imaging are needed for this uncomplicated presentation; reserve canal culture for failure to respond to initial therapy and reserve imaging only if signs of deep extension develop.
Conclusion: This is an uncomplicated acute diffuse bacterial otitis externa of the right ear in an adolescent competitive swimmer, established by the combination of water exposure, itching progressing to pain, exquisite tragal and auricular traction tenderness, and an edematous, erythematous, macerated external auditory canal with debris and an intact tympanic membrane. There is no evidence of middle ear infection, perichondritis, mastoiditis, facial nerve involvement, or necrotizing otitis externa. The condition is expected to resolve with topical therapy, canal cleaning if needed, adequate analgesia, and temporary avoidance of water exposure, and it does not require emergency intervention but does require timely clinical management and follow-up.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Begin topical otic therapy directed at the canal, which is the mainstay of treatment; systemic antibiotics are not indicated in this uncomplicated case without fever, lymphadenopathy, or evidence of spread beyond the canal. Because the canal is narrowed and edematous and the tympanic membrane is only barely visible, perform gentle aural toilet to remove the white debris under direct visualization so that drops can reach the inflamed skin, and place a wick if the canal is too swollen for drops to penetrate; the wick should be reassessed and typically removed or replaced within a few days as the edema subsides. Instruct on proper instillation technique with the head tilted and the affected ear upward for several minutes after each dose. Provide scheduled analgesia, as pain in otitis externa can be substantial and this patient's pain is aggravated by chewing and by lying on the right side. Address the water exposure directly: he must stop swimming and keep the ear dry until pain and canal edema resolve, which for a competitive swimmer in daily summer training is the single most important behavioral intervention; discuss the timeline for return to training with his coach and family. Advise against inserting cotton swabs, fingers, or any objects into the canal, and against use of earplugs or in-ear headphones during the acute phase, since these worsen maceration and trauma. For prevention after recovery, recommend thorough drying of the ears after swimming, using a towel and tilting the head to allow water egress, and consider well-fitted swim caps or properly fitted earplugs once the skin has healed, with acidifying or drying preventive drops after swimming if recurrent episodes occur. Explicitly counsel on return precautions: seek re-evaluation urgently if fever develops, if pain escalates despite therapy, if swelling or redness extends onto the auricle or over the mastoid, if the ear begins to protrude, if hearing loss worsens or persists after the canal edema resolves, if facial weakness develops, or if there is no improvement within roughly 48 to 72 hours of appropriate topical therapy. Arrange follow-up to confirm resolution and, importantly, to visualize the tympanic membrane fully once the canal edema has settled, because it could not be adequately inspected at this visit; documentation of an intact membrane also determines whether ototopical agents that are potentially ototoxic should be avoided.
Notes: The tympanic membrane was only barely visible at this examination, so perforation cannot be completely excluded; until the membrane is confirmed intact, preference should be given to a non-ototoxic topical preparation, and this must be verified at follow-up. If the canal debris proves to be fungal on re-inspection or if there is no response to antibacterial drops, otomycosis should be reconsidered and treated accordingly.

Vignette:
A 35-year-old female office worker presents with a dull, bilateral headache described as a band-like pressure around her head. The headache started in the late afternoon after a long day of meetings and computer work. She rates the pain as 4 out of 10. She denies nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, or visual changes. There is no aura. She reports similar headaches occurring a few times per month for the past year. On examination, vital signs are normal. There is mild tenderness of the bilateral temporal and occipital muscles on palpation. Neurological examination is entirely normal. Fundoscopic exam is unremarkable.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 35 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Dull, bilateral, band-like pressure headache rated 4 out of 10 that began in the late afternoon after a long day of meetings and computer work, similar to episodes recurring a few times per month for the past year.
Analysis: The presentation is a textbook episodic tension-type headache. The strongest supporting facts are the bilateral distribution, the dull non-pulsating band-like pressure quality, the mild to moderate intensity of 4 out of 10, the onset in the late afternoon following prolonged sedentary computer work and meetings, the recurrence a few times per month for a year without progression, and the explicit absence of nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, aura, and visual changes. The pericranial tenderness of the bilateral temporal and occipital muscles on palpation is a recognized and supportive finding in tension-type headache and points to a musculoskeletal and postural contribution from sustained forward head and neck posture at a workstation. Migraine is the principal alternative diagnosis and is argued against by the bilateral rather than unilateral location, the pressing rather than pulsating quality, the mild intensity, the absence of aura, and the complete absence of the associated features of nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia that define migraine. Cluster headache is excluded by the bilateral non-severe pain, the lack of a strictly unilateral orbital or temporal location, the absence of any autonomic features, and the daytime pattern tied to work rather than a circadian attack pattern. Secondary and dangerous causes of headache are effectively excluded by the history and examination: there is no thunderclap onset, no fever or neck stiffness to suggest meningitis, no positional or Valsalva-related worsening, no new or progressive pattern, and no immunosuppression or trauma described. Critically, the vital signs are normal, the neurological examination is entirely normal, and fundoscopy is unremarkable, arguing against raised intracranial pressure, papilledema, an intracranial mass, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension. At age 35 with a one-year stable pattern there are no red flags such as new headache after age 50, systemic symptoms, or a change in headache character. Giant cell arteritis is not tenable at this age despite the temporal tenderness, since the tenderness is muscular and bilateral rather than over indurated pulseless temporal arteries and there are no systemic or visual symptoms. Medication overuse headache should be kept in mind as a driver of chronification but is not established here because no analgesic frequency is documented in the case. Cervicogenic headache and refractive or ocular strain related to prolonged screen work remain reasonable contributing considerations given the occupational context and occipital muscle tenderness.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The history is characteristic, the pattern has been stable for a year without progression, the neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal, and there are no red flag features; neuroimaging and laboratory testing are not indicated and would not change management.
Conclusion: This is episodic tension-type headache in a 35-year-old office worker, precipitated by prolonged computer work and sustained poor workstation posture, and supported by bilateral pericranial muscle tenderness with an otherwise entirely normal neurological and fundoscopic examination. There is no clinical evidence of migraine, cluster headache, or any secondary or structural cause of headache. Management should focus on simple symptomatic relief of acute episodes together with ergonomic, postural, and lifestyle modification to reduce attack frequency, with headache diary tracking and re-evaluation only if the pattern changes.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Reassure the patient explicitly that her examination, including the neurological and fundoscopic assessment, is normal and that this headache pattern is benign; this reassurance is itself therapeutic and reduces anxiety-driven amplification. For acute episodes at this intensity, simple over-the-counter analgesia taken early in the attack is appropriate and usually sufficient. Address the occupational trigger directly, since the headaches consistently begin in the late afternoon after long days of meetings and computer work: arrange an ergonomic review of her workstation with attention to monitor height at eye level, chair and lumbar support, keyboard and mouse position to keep the shoulders relaxed, and adequate lighting to reduce screen glare. Institute scheduled micro-breaks away from the screen with neck, shoulder, and upper back stretching every 30 to 60 minutes, and encourage regular aerobic exercise, consistent sleep timing, regular meals, and adequate hydration during long meeting days. Given the demonstrable bilateral temporal and occipital muscle tenderness, targeted physical measures such as neck and shoulder stretching, postural retraining, heat application, and physiotherapy for the pericranial musculature are reasonable adjuncts, and relaxation training, breathing exercises, or biofeedback may be useful for a headache pattern so clearly linked to prolonged work stress. Ask her to keep a headache diary recording frequency, timing, duration, severity, triggers, and analgesic use, which will both identify modifiable precipitants and detect early progression toward a chronic pattern. Counsel clearly about medication overuse: limit acute analgesic use to no more than a few days per week, since frequent use can convert episodic headache into a chronic daily headache. Consider a formal preventive discussion if attacks increase in frequency, duration, or severity, or if they begin to interfere with work or daily function. Because prolonged screen work is central here, an eye examination to exclude uncorrected refractive error or ocular strain is a sensible additional consideration. Advise her to seek prompt medical assessment if any of the following develop: a sudden severe thunderclap headache, headache that is worst on waking or worsened by coughing, straining, or lying flat, fever with neck stiffness, any new neurological symptoms such as weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, visual loss or double vision, seizure, confusion, a headache following head injury, or a clear change in the established character, frequency, or severity of her headaches.
Notes: The frequency of analgesic use is not specified in the case, so medication overuse headache cannot be assessed at this visit and should be reviewed at follow-up. The diagnosis rests on the stability of the pattern; any change in character, escalation in frequency, or emergence of neurological signs would mandate reassessment and consideration of neuroimaging.
