A 38-year-old female office worker presents with a 6-week history of pain over the outer aspect of her right elbow. She works at a computer for 8 to 10 hours daily and recently increased her keyboard and mouse usage during a major project. The pain worsens with gripping activities such as opening jars, turning doorknobs, and shaking hands. She denies trauma, swelling, or locking of the elbow. On examination, there is point tenderness over the lateral epicondyle of the right elbow. Pain is reproduced with resisted wrist extension and resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley test). Grip strength is reduced on the right compared to the left. Range of motion of the elbow is full and painless. There is no joint instability or effusion. Neurovascular examination is normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 38 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Six-week history of pain over the outer (lateral) aspect of the right elbow, worsened by gripping activities such as opening jars, turning doorknobs and shaking hands, in the setting of recently increased keyboard and mouse use during a major project.

Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of lateral epicondylitis, more accurately termed lateral epicondylalgia or common extensor tendinopathy of the right elbow, an overuse tendinopathy of the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin. The strongest supporting facts are the tight correspondence between the anatomical site, the provocative tests and the mechanism. There is point tenderness precisely over the lateral epicondyle, the origin of the common extensor tendon. Pain is reproduced by resisted wrist extension, which selectively loads that tendon, and by resisted middle finger extension, a positive Maudsley test, which is relatively specific for extensor carpi radialis brevis involvement. Grip strength is reduced on the affected right side, a typical and objective finding in this condition because gripping requires wrist extensor co-contraction and therefore loads the painful tendon, which also explains why jar opening, doorknob turning and handshaking are the reported aggravators. The occupational history supplies the causative overload: 8 to 10 hours of daily computer work with a recent increase in keyboard and mouse usage, a classic repetitive low-load wrist extension exposure, and the 6-week duration matches the subacute course of a degenerative overuse tendinopathy rather than an acute injury.
The examination systematically excludes the main alternatives. Absence of trauma, swelling, locking, effusion and instability, together with full and painless elbow range of motion, argues strongly against intra-articular pathology such as radiocapitellar osteoarthritis, osteochondritis dissecans, a loose body or a plica, and against ligamentous injury including lateral collateral ligament insufficiency or posterolateral rotatory instability, which would produce instability findings. A normal neurovascular examination makes radial tunnel syndrome or posterior interosseous nerve compression less likely; that entity is the most important mimic, since it also causes lateral elbow pain and pain on resisted middle finger extension, but it typically produces tenderness more distally over the mobile wad about 4 to 5 cm distal to the epicondyle, night pain, and sometimes extensor weakness, none of which is described here. Cervical radiculopathy referring to the lateral elbow, particularly C6, is unlikely given the strictly local tenderness, absence of neck symptoms, and normal neurological examination. Inflammatory arthropathy or septic arthritis is excluded by the absence of effusion, systemic symptoms and a normal painless arc of motion. Medial epicondylitis is anatomically excluded by the lateral location.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical and is adequately established by the history, focal lateral epicondylar tenderness, positive resisted wrist extension and positive Maudsley test with a normal neurovascular and joint examination. Imaging is not indicated at this stage. Reserve elbow radiographs for a history of trauma, mechanical symptoms such as locking, or suspicion of intra-articular or bony pathology; ultrasound or MRI of the elbow only if symptoms fail to respond to an adequate course of conservative treatment, if a common extensor tendon tear is suspected, or if the diagnosis becomes uncertain; and electrodiagnostic studies only if radial tunnel syndrome or cervical radiculopathy is suspected on reassessment. A hand-held dynamometer may be used to document grip strength objectively and to track recovery.

Conclusion: Right lateral epicondylitis (common extensor tendinopathy) of 6 weeks' duration, caused by occupational repetitive overload from prolonged keyboard and mouse use, with the typical findings of focal lateral epicondylar tenderness, pain on resisted wrist and middle finger extension, and reduced grip strength, and with no evidence of joint, ligamentous or neurovascular pathology. This is a benign but often protracted self-limiting condition that is managed conservatively; no urgent intervention is required.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics

Recommendations: Manage conservatively with an emphasis on load modification and progressive tendon loading, since the great majority of cases resolve without surgery. Modify the provoking activity rather than immobilizing the arm: adjust the workstation ergonomics directly targeting the identified cause, with a neutral wrist position while typing, a supported forearm, a keyboard and mouse at elbow height, a vertical or larger ergonomic mouse to reduce forearm pronation and sustained wrist extension, reduced use of a sustained pinch grip, and scheduled micro-breaks with stretching every 30 to 60 minutes across the 8 to 10 hour workday. Temporarily limit forceful gripping tasks such as jar opening and use two hands or gripping aids, and enlarge tool and utensil handles to reduce grip force. Begin a structured exercise program, which is the intervention with the best evidence: gentle wrist extensor and flexor stretching, followed by progressive eccentric and isometric loading of the wrist extensors, performed daily and advanced gradually as tolerated, together with scapular and shoulder girdle strengthening; refer to physical therapy or occupational therapy to supervise progression and to address grip strength, which is currently reduced. Adjunctive measures include ice or cold application after aggravating activity, a counterforce forearm brace worn just distal to the epicondyle during provoking tasks or a wrist extension splint at night, and short-term topical or oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptom control if not contraindicated, recognizing these help pain but do not alter the underlying tendinopathy. Address expectations explicitly: improvement is typically measured in months, and adherence to the loading program matters more than passive treatments. Arrange follow-up in about 6 weeks to reassess pain, grip strength and function. If there is no meaningful improvement after 6 to 12 months of well-executed conservative treatment, escalate to specialist orthopedic review for consideration of further options; corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but is associated with worse long-term outcomes and higher recurrence and should therefore be used sparingly if at all, with surgery reserved for genuinely refractory cases. Reassess the diagnosis and consider radial tunnel syndrome, cervical radiculopathy or intra-articular pathology if night pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, swelling, locking or instability develops, or if tenderness localizes distally rather than at the epicondyle.

Notes: Despite the traditional name, this is a degenerative tendinopathy rather than an inflammatory tendinitis, which is why load management and progressive tendon loading, not anti-inflammatory treatment or rest alone, form the core of therapy. Complete immobilization should be avoided as it promotes deconditioning and stiffness. Repeated corticosteroid injections carry a risk of tendon degeneration and higher recurrence rates. The case does not specify hand dominance, prior treatments, comorbidities or medications, so those remain Not specified and should be clarified when planning treatment and any occupational accommodations.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with a 6-month history of progressive fatigue, weight gain of 15 pounds despite no change in diet, constipation, cold intolerance, and dry skin. She reports her hair has become thin and brittle and she has noticed puffiness around her eyes in the morning. Her menstrual periods have become heavier and more irregular. She has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. Family history is positive for thyroid disease in her mother and sister. Vital signs show heart rate 56, blood pressure 136/88, temperature 97.2°F. On examination, she appears sluggish. Skin is cool, dry, and pale. There is periorbital edema and non-pitting edema of the lower extremities. The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged without nodules. Deep tendon reflexes show delayed relaxation phase. TSH is markedly elevated at 48 mIU/L and free T4 is low at 0.4 ng/dL. Anti-TPO antibodies are positive.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 45 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Six-month history of progressive fatigue, 15-pound weight gain despite an unchanged diet, constipation, cold intolerance, dry skin, thin and brittle hair, morning periorbital puffiness, and heavier, more irregular menstrual periods.

Analysis: The case represents overt primary hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto (chronic autoimmune lymphocytic) thyroiditis. The biochemical pattern is decisive: a markedly elevated TSH of 48 mIU/L together with a low free T4 of 0.4 ng/dL establishes primary thyroid failure, because the pituitary is responding appropriately with high TSH drive to inadequate thyroid hormone output; this excludes central (secondary or tertiary) hypothyroidism, in which TSH would be low or inappropriately normal alongside a low free T4. The etiology is established by positive anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies in combination with a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland without nodules, the classic goitrous form of Hashimoto thyroiditis, and it is further supported by the family history of thyroid disease in her mother and sister, reflecting the strong familial and female predominance of autoimmune thyroid disease.
The clinical findings coherently map onto hypothyroid physiology and reinforce the diagnosis. Reduced metabolic rate explains the fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain without dietary change, low-normal temperature of 97.2 F, and the sluggish appearance. Bradycardia at 56 beats per minute reflects reduced beta-adrenergic responsiveness and decreased cardiac chronotropy, while the diastolic-predominant blood pressure of 136/88 fits the increased systemic vascular resistance seen in hypothyroidism. Slowed gastrointestinal motility accounts for constipation. Dermatological changes, namely cool, dry, pale skin and thin brittle hair, are typical. Periorbital edema and non-pitting lower extremity edema represent myxedema, that is, dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, which is distinctive and separates this from pitting edema of cardiac, renal or hepatic origin. The delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes is a highly characteristic neuromuscular sign of hypothyroidism. Menorrhagia with irregular cycles is a recognized hypothyroid effect on the menstrual cycle, mediated by anovulation and by hemostatic changes, and is a clinically important detail because it raises the possibility of secondary iron deficiency anemia.
Differential considerations were relevant before the laboratory results but are now largely settled. Depression, chronic fatigue, anemia and obesity could each explain fatigue and weight gain but none explains the delayed reflex relaxation, myxedematous edema, goiter and the biochemical profile. Nephrotic syndrome, congestive heart failure and hepatic disease could cause edema, but the edema here is non-pitting and myxedematous and the picture is unified by thyroid failure. Other causes of primary hypothyroidism are unlikely: there is no history of thyroid surgery, radioiodine treatment, external neck irradiation, or of amiodarone, lithium, interferon or checkpoint inhibitor exposure, and she takes no medications; a painless or subacute thyroiditis in a hypothyroid phase would not typically present with 6 months of steady progression, a firm diffuse goiter and strongly positive anti-TPO antibodies. Iodine deficiency is a theoretical alternative cause of goiter but does not fit the positive autoimmunity. Importantly, although the disease is severe biochemically, there is no evidence of myxedema coma: mental status is described only as sluggish rather than obtunded, and there is no hypothermia, hypotension, hypoventilation or precipitating illness described, so this is severe but not decompensated hypothyroidism.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count and iron studies including ferritin, given the heavy and irregular menstrual bleeding, to identify iron deficiency anemia, which is common in this setting and can also worsen fatigue and impair the response to levothyroxine. Fasting lipid panel, since hypothyroidism commonly causes hypercholesterolemia that often improves with treatment. Basic metabolic panel with sodium and creatinine to detect hyponatremia and the reversible reduction in glomerular filtration seen in hypothyroidism, and creatine kinase if myopathic symptoms are present. Electrocardiogram to document the bradycardia and assess for conduction abnormality, QT prolongation and low voltage, particularly relevant before initiating full replacement. Follow-up serum TSH and free T4 repeated 6 to 8 weeks after starting levothyroxine and after each dose adjustment; this is the essential test for titration. Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies and thyroid ultrasound are not routinely required, since anti-TPO positivity and a diffuse goiter without nodules already establish the diagnosis; reserve thyroid ultrasound for a nodule, asymmetry, compressive symptoms or rapid gland enlargement. Screening for associated autoimmune disease, in particular a fasting glucose or HbA1c and consideration of celiac serology and vitamin B12, and morning cortisol only if adrenal insufficiency is clinically suspected. Pregnancy testing before initiating treatment in a woman of reproductive age with menstrual irregularity, since pregnancy substantially changes the dosing target.

Conclusion: Overt primary hypothyroidism of autoimmune origin, that is, goitrous Hashimoto thyroiditis, in a 45-year-old woman, confirmed by a markedly elevated TSH of 48 mIU/L with a low free T4 of 0.4 ng/dL and positive anti-TPO antibodies, and clinically corroborated by myxedematous periorbital and lower extremity edema, bradycardia, delayed deep tendon reflex relaxation, cold dry skin, constipation, weight gain and menorrhagia. The disease is biochemically severe but clinically compensated, with no features of myxedema coma. It requires prompt but non-emergent initiation of thyroid hormone replacement with structured biochemical follow-up, and lifelong therapy.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Recommendations: Initiate levothyroxine replacement as the definitive treatment; it should be started promptly on an outpatient basis rather than urgently, since she is clinically stable. Because she is 45 with no known cardiac disease but has a resting heart rate of 56 and long-standing severe hypothyroidism, a prudent approach is to start at a modest dose and titrate upward rather than beginning at full weight-based replacement, so that cardiac work is not increased abruptly; obtain a baseline electrocardiogram and advise her to report chest pain or palpitations. Counsel her carefully on administration, as absorption determines success: take levothyroxine on an empty stomach with water, ideally 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime several hours after the last meal, and separate it by at least 4 hours from calcium supplements, iron supplements, multivitamins containing iron or calcium, proton pump inhibitors and antacids. This point is directly relevant here, because if iron replacement is started for menorrhagia-related iron deficiency, the two must be timed apart. Recheck TSH and free T4 in 6 to 8 weeks and adjust the dose in small increments, repeating testing 6 to 8 weeks after every change, until TSH is within the reference range; thereafter monitor annually or sooner if symptoms change. Explain that symptomatic improvement is gradual over weeks to months and that fatigue, weight and hair changes lag behind biochemical correction, so she should not expect immediate resolution and should not self-adjust the dose. Address the heavy and irregular menses specifically: evaluate for and treat iron deficiency anemia, and advise that menstrual regularity commonly improves once euthyroidism is restored; if bleeding remains heavy or irregular after adequate replacement, arrange gynecological evaluation for an independent structural or endometrial cause, which is important at age 45. Recheck the lipid panel after euthyroidism is achieved before deciding on any lipid-lowering therapy, as hypercholesterolemia frequently resolves with treatment. Discuss reproductive implications and instruct her to inform her physician immediately if she becomes pregnant or plans pregnancy, since levothyroxine requirements rise substantially in pregnancy and untreated maternal hypothyroidism carries fetal risk. Given the strong family history in her mother and sister, advise that first-degree relatives with suggestive symptoms be tested. Counsel that treatment is lifelong and that adherence and consistent brand or formulation are important. Watch for and avoid overtreatment, which risks atrial fibrillation and accelerated bone loss in a woman approaching the perimenopausal years. Arrange screening for associated autoimmune conditions as indicated, and instruct her to seek urgent care if she develops confusion, marked lethargy, hypothermia or severe bradycardia, which would suggest decompensation toward myxedema coma.

Notes: The markedly elevated TSH reflects severity but should not by itself prompt aggressive loading doses; titration guided by repeat testing at 6 to 8 week intervals is the correct approach, because TSH takes that long to re-equilibrate. If unrecognized adrenal insufficiency coexisted, thyroid hormone replacement could precipitate adrenal crisis; this should be considered if she has features suggesting it, though none are described in the case. The case does not specify her weight, cardiac history, alcohol or smoking status, symptoms of compression from the goiter, or pregnancy status, so these remain Not specified and must be clarified before final dosing decisions.

Vignette:
A 48-year-old woman with a history of migraine headaches presents to the emergency room with altered mental status over the last several hours. She was found by her husband, earlier in the day, to be acutely disoriented and increasingly somnolent. On physical examination, she has scleral icterus, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, and asterixis. Preliminary laboratory studies are notable for a serum ALT of 6498 units/L, total bilirubin of 5.6 mg/dL, and INR of 6.8. Her husband reports that she has consistently been taking pain medications and started taking additional 500 mg acetaminophen pills several days ago for lower back pain. Further history reveals a medication list with multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 48 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Altered mental status over several hours, with acute disorientation and progressive somnolence noted by her husband earlier in the day, in a woman who has been taking multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations and added extra 500 mg acetaminophen tablets over the past several days for lower back pain.

Analysis: This is acute liver failure due to unintentional (therapeutic misadventure) acetaminophen (paracetamol) hepatotoxicity, complicated by hepatic encephalopathy. The three defining elements of acute liver failure are all present: acute hepatocellular injury, coagulopathy with an INR of 6.8, and encephalopathy manifested by acute disorientation, increasing somnolence and asterixis, in a patient with no stated pre-existing liver disease.
The strongest supporting facts are the magnitude and pattern of the transaminase elevation together with the exposure history. An ALT of 6498 units/L is in the range of massive hepatocellular necrosis, and such extreme elevations, generally above 3000 to 5000 units/L, occur in only a narrow set of conditions: acetaminophen toxicity, ischemic hepatitis (shock liver), acute viral hepatitis, and less commonly autoimmune hepatitis or Budd-Chiari syndrome. Of these, the history points decisively to acetaminophen: the husband reports she has consistently been taking pain medications and started additional 500 mg acetaminophen tablets several days ago for lower back pain, and her medication list contains multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations. This is the classic mechanism of staggered supratherapeutic ingestion, in which the patient does not take a single overdose but exceeds the daily maximum by combining a dedicated acetaminophen product with combination analgesics, often opioid-acetaminophen or migraine preparations, without realizing it. Her migraine history is directly relevant, because many migraine and combination analgesic products contain acetaminophen and this is the likely hidden source of the additional dose burden. Repeated supratherapeutic dosing over several days depletes hepatic glutathione, allowing the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine to accumulate and produce centrilobular necrosis.
The remaining findings fit this synthesis. Scleral icterus and a total bilirubin of 5.6 mg/dL indicate that hepatic dysfunction has progressed beyond simple transaminitis. Mild right upper quadrant tenderness reflects hepatic capsular stretch from an acutely injured, swollen liver. The INR of 6.8 is critical: it reflects failure of hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, particularly factor VII with its short half-life, and it is both a diagnostic criterion and one of the most important prognostic variables. Asterixis with disorientation and somnolence establishes hepatic encephalopathy, most consistent with grade II progressing toward grade III, which converts this from severe acute liver injury into acute liver failure and markedly worsens prognosis.
Differential considerations must be weighed but fit less well. Ischemic hepatitis produces comparable ALT elevations but requires a hypotensive or hypoxic insult, and none is described. Acute viral hepatitis A, B, or E can cause fulminant hepatitis, but the bilirubin is relatively modest for the enormous ALT, whereas acetaminophen classically produces a very high ALT with a disproportionately lower bilirubin early on, and there is no reported exposure or prodrome. Autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease (which typically shows a low alkaline phosphatase to bilirubin ratio and hemolysis in younger patients), Budd-Chiari syndrome and other idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury remain in the differential and should be screened for, but the medication history makes acetaminophen overwhelmingly the most likely cause. Non-hepatic causes of altered mental status such as intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, sepsis, or metabolic derangement including hypoglycemia must be considered in parallel, particularly since hypoglycemia is a direct complication of liver failure and can itself cause somnolence, and because the coagulopathy raises the risk of spontaneous intracranial bleeding. A key clinical trap is that in staggered or delayed presentations the serum acetaminophen concentration may be low or undetectable even though severe toxicity is established; a negative level must never be used to withhold treatment.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Immediate point-of-care and serum glucose with continuous monitoring, since hypoglycemia is common in acute liver failure and is an immediately reversible cause of altered mental status. Serum acetaminophen concentration (recognizing it may be low in staggered ingestion), and a toxicology screen including salicylate and ethanol levels. Complete hepatic panel with AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, total and direct bilirubin, albumin, and repeat measurement at least every 12 hours to track trajectory. Coagulation studies with INR, PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and factor V level, repeated serially as the key prognostic marker. Complete blood count with platelets. Comprehensive metabolic panel with creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, phosphate and magnesium to detect acute kidney injury, which frequently accompanies acetaminophen toxicity and is a prognostic criterion. Arterial blood gas with arterial pH and serum lactate and arterial ammonia, all of which carry prognostic weight in acute liver failure. Type and screen. Viral hepatitis serologies (hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and core IgM, hepatitis C, and hepatitis E where relevant) plus HSV and consideration of autoimmune markers, ceruloplasmin and a pregnancy test, to exclude alternative and coexisting causes. Blood, urine and, if indicated, other cultures, since infection is common and may precipitate deterioration. Right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound with Doppler assessment of hepatic and portal vasculature to evaluate liver architecture and exclude Budd-Chiari syndrome and biliary obstruction. Non-contrast head CT to exclude intracranial hemorrhage and cerebral edema, particularly given the coagulopathy and altered mental status. Continuous cardiac, respiratory and neurological monitoring with frequent neurological checks and an intensive care setting; airway equipment ready for intubation as encephalopathy deepens.

Conclusion: Acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy in a 48-year-old woman, resulting from staggered supratherapeutic ingestion of multiple acetaminophen-containing preparations combined with additional 500 mg acetaminophen tablets over several days. The diagnosis is supported by an ALT of 6498 units/L, total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL, INR 6.8, scleral icterus, right upper quadrant tenderness, and asterixis with disorientation and somnolence. This is a life-threatening, rapidly progressive condition that requires immediate N-acetylcysteine therapy, intensive care admission, and urgent discussion with a liver transplant center, because the combination of severe coagulopathy and encephalopathy places her in a high-mortality group in whom transplantation may be the only definitive treatment.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency

Recommendations: Start intravenous N-acetylcysteine immediately and do not delay it for the acetaminophen level or any other test result; in a staggered supratherapeutic ingestion with established hepatotoxicity, treatment is indicated on clinical grounds alone, and a low or undetectable acetaminophen concentration must not be used to withhold or stop it. Continue N-acetylcysteine as a prolonged infusion beyond the standard course, until the INR is falling, the transaminases are clearly improving, encephalopathy has resolved, or the patient undergoes transplantation, since N-acetylcysteine also improves outcomes in established acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure. Admit to an intensive care unit and contact a liver transplant center urgently for early transfer and listing evaluation, as an INR of 6.8 with encephalopathy signals a poor prognosis; apply the King's College criteria for acetaminophen-induced liver failure, which weigh arterial pH, INR, creatinine and grade of encephalopathy, and obtain the arterial pH, creatinine and lactate needed to apply them. Protect the airway: with disorientation and progressive somnolence, reassess neurological status frequently and intubate for airway protection if encephalopathy advances to grade III or IV or if she cannot protect her airway. Manage cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure proactively in advanced encephalopathy by elevating the head of the bed to 30 degrees, avoiding stimulation, controlling agitation cautiously, avoiding hypotonic fluids, and treating surges with hypertonic saline or mannitol; avoid or minimize sedatives and any hepatically metabolized agents that would confound neurological assessment. Monitor and treat hypoglycemia aggressively with dextrose-containing intravenous fluids and frequent glucose checks, and correct electrolyte and acid-base disturbances including hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Regarding the coagulopathy, do not routinely correct the INR with fresh frozen plasma, because the INR is the principal prognostic marker used for transplant decision-making and correcting it obscures the trajectory; reserve plasma or factor replacement for active bleeding or before an invasive procedure. Give intravenous vitamin K, since a coexisting deficiency may contribute, and provide stress ulcer prophylaxis. Have a low threshold for empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial cover with surveillance cultures, as infection is frequent and can precipitate multiorgan failure. Monitor renal function and urine output closely and avoid nephrotoxic agents, given the risk of acetaminophen-associated acute kidney injury; involve nephrology if renal replacement therapy or ammonia clearance becomes necessary. Address the underlying cause explicitly and definitively: perform a complete reconciliation of every medication she takes, identify all acetaminophen-containing products including migraine and combination analgesic preparations, and stop all of them immediately; this is essential both to halt ongoing exposure and to prevent recurrence. Consult the poison control center or medical toxicology for dosing and duration guidance. Consult hepatology or gastroenterology, and involve the intensive care and transplant teams together. Clarify intent by history from the husband and, when she is able, from the patient, and arrange psychiatric or psychosocial assessment if there is any suggestion the ingestion was not accidental; the case describes it as unintentional, but this must be verified. Once recovered, provide structured counselling on the maximum daily acetaminophen dose, on reading labels of all over-the-counter and combination products, on the hidden acetaminophen content of migraine and opioid combination medications, and on safer alternatives for her back pain and migraine, and arrange follow-up for the underlying lower back pain so that she is not driven back to the same pattern of use.

Notes: A serum acetaminophen level may be low or undetectable in this staggered, delayed presentation and cannot exclude toxicity; the Rumack-Matthew nomogram does not apply to repeated supratherapeutic ingestion and must not be used here. Correction of the INR with plasma removes the most useful prognostic indicator and should be avoided unless bleeding or an invasive procedure requires it. A falling ALT can be misleading and may reflect either recovery or exhaustion of viable hepatocytes, so trends in INR, bilirubin, lactate, pH and mental status are more reliable indicators of trajectory. The case does not specify vital signs, exact acetaminophen dose or duration, alcohol use, nutritional status, chronic liver disease, or the identity of the other medications, so those remain Not specified and must be established urgently, as chronic alcohol use and malnutrition lower the toxic threshold.

Vignette:
Consider a 35-year-old man who developed low back pain after shoveling snow 3 weeks ago. He presents to the office for an evaluation. On examination there is a new left foot drop. In study 82% physicians recommend MRI (sciatica/sprain)
baseline_protocol:
Age: 35 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Low back pain that began after shoveling snow 3 weeks ago, now presenting for office evaluation with a new left foot drop found on examination.

Analysis: The central issue in this case is not the back pain itself but the new focal motor deficit. A new left foot drop, that is, weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, in a patient with mechanical low back pain of 3 weeks' duration following a lifting and axial-loading activity (shoveling snow) is a recognized red flag that changes the entire management pathway. The most likely mechanism is compressive lumbar radiculopathy, typically an L4-L5 disc herniation compressing the L5 nerve root, since the L5 root supplies tibialis anterior and the extensor hallucis longus and is the classic source of foot drop of radicular origin; an L5-S1 herniation with a far-lateral or extruded fragment affecting the L5 root, or a high L4-L5 lesion affecting L4, can produce the same picture. The mechanism of injury supports this: shoveling snow combines repetitive flexion, rotation and axial load, which is a well-recognized precipitant of acute disc herniation in a man of this age, and the age of 35 is precisely the demographic peak for symptomatic lumbar disc herniation. The three-week interval with an emergent, newly documented motor deficit implies either progression of a herniation or a deficit that developed after the initial injury, and progressive motor loss carries a real risk of permanent weakness if decompression is delayed.
The critical clinical point embedded in the vignette is that in the referenced study 82 percent of physicians recommended MRI while framing the problem as sciatica or a lumbar sprain. That framing understates the urgency. Uncomplicated sciatica and lumbar strain, even with pain radiating down the leg, are appropriately managed conservatively for 4 to 6 weeks without imaging, and imaging in that setting frequently reveals incidental degenerative findings that lead to unnecessary intervention. However, that conservative rule explicitly does not apply when there is a significant or progressive neurological deficit. A new foot drop is exactly such a deficit. Therefore MRI here is not the low-value test it would be in ordinary sciatica; it is indicated, and it is indicated urgently rather than routinely. The reasoning error to avoid is the opposite of over-imaging: it is treating a true motor deficit as if it were ordinary sciatica and allowing an observation period during which an already-established weakness becomes fixed.
The main differential considerations are as follows. Lumbar disc herniation with L5 radiculopathy is by far the most likely, given the mechanism, timing, back pain and dermatomal-myotomal deficit. Cauda equina syndrome must be actively excluded, since it is the one diagnosis that would require immediate surgical decompression within hours; the case does not describe saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence or bilateral leg symptoms, so those elements are Not specified and must be sought directly on examination and history. Common peroneal (fibular) neuropathy at the fibular head is the principal peripheral mimic of foot drop and can result from compression, prolonged squatting or crossing the legs, or weight loss; it is distinguished by preserved hip abduction and inversion strength, sensory loss confined to the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg without back-related radiation, absence of a positive straight-leg raise, and tenderness or a Tinel sign at the fibular neck. A sciatic neuropathy proximal to the knee is less common. Other structural causes of back pain with neurological deficit that must be considered because the vignette gives limited history include spinal epidural abscess, vertebral osteomyelitis, spinal epidural hematoma, and malignancy with epidural extension; these would be suggested by fever, night pain, unexplained weight loss, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, anticoagulation or a cancer history, none of which is stated in the case. A central nervous system cause of foot drop, such as a stroke or an intracranial or cord lesion, would be accompanied by upper motor neuron signs rather than the flaccid radicular pattern expected here.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine without contrast, which is the imaging study of choice and is genuinely indicated here because of the objective motor deficit; add gadolinium contrast if infection, malignancy or prior surgery is a consideration. CT myelography or lumbar CT only if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. A complete and documented neurological examination is itself the essential immediate assessment: graded manual motor testing of ankle dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus, ankle plantarflexion, eversion and inversion, knee extension and hip abduction to localize the level and to separate an L5 radiculopathy from a peroneal neuropathy; dermatomal sensory testing; deep tendon reflexes at the knee and ankle; straight-leg raise and crossed straight-leg raise; and gait assessment including heel and toe walking. Mandatory assessment for cauda equina syndrome with perianal and saddle sensory testing, anal sphincter tone, and post-void residual bladder volume measurement by bladder ultrasound. Basic laboratory studies including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein if there is any suspicion of infection or malignancy. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies are not needed acutely and would not change immediate management, but may be useful later to confirm localization, distinguish a peroneal neuropathy, or assess reinnervation if the deficit persists; note that they are typically uninformative for the first 3 to 4 weeks after onset.

Conclusion: Acute low back pain following a lifting and axial-loading injury 3 weeks ago, now complicated by a new left foot drop, most consistent with a compressive lumbar radiculopathy affecting the L5 nerve root, most likely from an L4-L5 disc herniation. The new objective motor deficit is a red flag that removes this case from the routine sciatica pathway, mandates urgent MRI of the lumbar spine rather than a period of watchful waiting, and requires immediate exclusion of cauda equina syndrome. Prompt imaging and surgical evaluation are warranted because delay risks permanent weakness.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations: Treat the new foot drop as a neurosurgical red flag rather than as ordinary sciatica. First, at this visit, complete and document a detailed neurological examination and specifically screen for cauda equina syndrome by asking about urinary retention or overflow incontinence, fecal incontinence and saddle numbness, and by testing perianal sensation, anal sphincter tone and post-void residual volume; if any of these are abnormal or if there is bilateral leg weakness, refer immediately to the emergency department for emergency MRI and same-day surgical decompression, since cauda equina syndrome is a time-critical surgical emergency. Second, arrange urgent, not routine, MRI of the lumbar spine, ideally the same day or within 24 to 48 hours, and do not wait for the conventional 4 to 6 week conservative trial that would apply to sciatica without a deficit; this directly addresses the point raised in the vignette, in that MRI is the right recommendation here but its urgency, not merely its ordering, is what matters. Third, obtain urgent spine surgery consultation, either neurosurgery or orthopedic spine, in parallel with imaging rather than after it, because progressive or severe motor deficit from nerve root compression is one of the accepted indications for early surgical decompression, and outcomes for motor recovery are better when decompression is not delayed. Document the exact motor grade of ankle dorsiflexion at baseline so that progression or improvement can be objectively tracked, and re-examine within a short interval; instruct the patient to seek emergency care immediately if the weakness worsens, if numbness spreads, if the opposite leg becomes involved, or if any bladder or bowel dysfunction develops. Explicitly evaluate the alternative diagnosis of a common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head by testing hip abduction, foot inversion and eversion and by examining for tenderness or a Tinel sign at the fibular neck, since that would change management entirely; and take a targeted history for infection, malignancy, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, fever, night pain and weight loss, since these would prompt inflammatory markers and contrast-enhanced imaging for epidural abscess, hematoma or tumor. While awaiting imaging and consultation, provide symptomatic care with analgesia, advise against bed rest and encourage maintenance of normal activity within pain limits, and provide an ankle-foot orthosis for the foot drop to improve gait safety and prevent tripping and falls. Refer to physical therapy for gait training and to prevent contracture, though therapy must not substitute for or delay imaging and surgical assessment. Counsel the patient honestly that recovery of a motor deficit depends substantially on the duration and severity of compression, and arrange close structured follow-up, with electromyography and nerve conduction studies later if the deficit persists or the localization remains uncertain.

Notes: The case provides no information about bowel or bladder function, saddle sensation, sensory distribution, reflexes, straight-leg raise, the severity or grade of the weakness, red-flag features for infection or malignancy, or the patient's comorbidities and medications, so all of these remain Not specified and must be established at the bedside before management is finalized. The observation that 82 percent of physicians recommended MRI while labelling the problem sciatica or sprain describes practice patterns, not this patient's diagnosis, and should not be used as a substitute for clinical reasoning; the label chosen matters, because it determines whether the MRI is ordered routinely or urgently. In the absence of a neurological deficit, imaging in the first 4 to 6 weeks of low back pain is generally not indicated, but the new foot drop is precisely the exception to that rule.

A 48-year-old male factory worker presents with a long-standing history of chronic low back pain that has worsened over the past 3 weeks with new radiating pain down the left posterior thigh and calf to the lateral foot. He describes the pain as sharp and shooting, rated 7 out of 10, aggravated by prolonged sitting and forward bending. He has been lifting heavy machinery parts for over 20 years. He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, or fever. On examination, he has a positive straight leg raise on the left at 40 degrees. Decreased ankle reflex on the left is noted. baseline_protocol:
Age: 48 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Long-standing chronic low back pain that has worsened over the past 3 weeks, with new sharp shooting pain rated 7 out of 10 radiating down the left posterior thigh and calf to the lateral foot, aggravated by prolonged sitting and forward bending.

Analysis: This is a left lumbosacral radiculopathy, most consistent with S1 nerve root compression, almost certainly from a lumbar disc herniation at the L5-S1 level. The evidence is strongly concordant across history, symptom distribution and examination. The pain distribution is dermatomal and follows the S1 dermatome precisely: posterior thigh, posterior calf and the lateral aspect of the foot. The sensory deficit matches, with diminished light touch over the lateral left foot, and the reflex finding is the most specific localizing sign, since the ankle jerk (Achilles reflex) is mediated by S1 and is decreased on the left. A positive straight leg raise at 40 degrees indicates mechanical tension on an irritated lower lumbosacral nerve root and is a sensitive sign of disc herniation; reproduction of radicular pain at a low angle increases the likelihood of true root compression. The character of the pain, sharp and shooting rather than dull and axial, is neuropathic and radicular rather than referred musculoskeletal pain. The positional aggravation is classic for discogenic radicular pain: prolonged sitting and forward bending both raise intradiscal pressure and increase posterior disc bulge, worsening root compression. The occupational history of over 20 years lifting heavy machinery parts is a powerful risk factor for degenerative disc disease and disc herniation, and the pattern of chronic axial back pain with acute-on-chronic worsening and new radicular symptoms is typical of an acute herniation superimposed on pre-existing degenerative change.
One finding requires careful interpretation. Motor strength is 4 out of 5 in left ankle dorsiflexion. Dorsiflexion is principally an L5 function, whereas the sensory and reflex findings localize to S1. This mild discordance can be explained in several ways: a large paracentral or extruded L5-S1 disc can compress both the traversing S1 root and, if it migrates superiorly or is far lateral, affect the L5 root; an L4-L5 herniation may coexist with an L5-S1 lesion in a patient with 20 years of heavy manual work and multilevel degenerative disease; or the mild weakness may reflect antalgic effort limitation from severe pain rather than true motor loss. What matters clinically is that the weakness is mild (4 out of 5), not a foot drop, and is not described as progressive, which places this in the category of radiculopathy with a minor, non-progressive motor deficit rather than a surgical emergency.
The reassuring features are explicit and important. He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction and saddle anesthesia, which argues strongly against cauda equina syndrome, the one condition in this presentation that would demand emergency decompression. He denies fever, which together with the absence of any stated immunosuppression, intravenous drug use, recent instrumentation or constitutional symptoms makes spinal epidural abscess and vertebral osteomyelitis unlikely. There is no stated history of malignancy, unexplained weight loss, night pain or age over 50 at first onset, so metastatic disease is a lower-probability consideration, though it cannot be excluded on the given information alone.
The main differential considerations are lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication, which is plausible in a 48-year-old with degenerative disease but fits less well because stenosis typically produces pain worsened by extension and walking and relieved by sitting and forward flexion, the opposite of this patient's pattern; piriformis syndrome or extraspinal sciatic nerve entrapment, which can produce buttock and posterior leg pain but would not typically abolish the ankle reflex; sacroiliac joint dysfunction or facet-mediated referred pain, which does not produce a dermatomal sensory deficit or reflex loss; peripheral neuropathy, which would be distally symmetric rather than unilateral and dermatomal; and vascular claudication, which would present with exertional calf pain relieved by rest with diminished pulses rather than positional shooting pain with neurological signs.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No emergency imaging is required at this moment given the absence of red flags, and initial management may proceed clinically. MRI of the lumbar spine without contrast is the appropriate study and is indicated because of the objective neurological deficits (diminished ankle reflex, sensory loss, and 4 out of 5 dorsiflexion weakness) and because it will be needed to guide any interventional or surgical treatment; it should be arranged on a non-urgent but timely basis, and it becomes urgent if the deficit progresses. CT of the lumbar spine or CT myelography only if MRI is contraindicated. Plain lumbar radiographs are of limited value for radiculopathy and are needed only if instability, fracture or spondylolisthesis is suspected. Serial documented neurological examination with graded manual motor testing of ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, eversion and extensor hallucis longus, dermatomal sensory mapping, knee and ankle reflexes, straight leg raise and crossed straight leg raise, and gait assessment including heel and toe walking, so that progression can be detected objectively. Assessment for cauda equina syndrome, including perianal and saddle sensation, anal sphincter tone and post-void residual bladder volume, should be documented at baseline even though symptoms are currently denied. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies are not required now but may help later if the localization remains ambiguous given the L5-versus-S1 discordance, if symptoms persist, or if peripheral neuropathy or an extraspinal entrapment is suspected; they are typically uninformative in the first 3 to 4 weeks. Inflammatory markers and a complete blood count only if infection or malignancy becomes a concern.

Conclusion: Acute-on-chronic left lumbosacral radiculopathy, most consistent with S1 root compression from an L5-S1 disc herniation, with a possible additional L5 component suggested by mild ankle dorsiflexion weakness, arising on a background of 20 years of occupational heavy lifting and chronic degenerative low back pain. The diagnosis is supported by S1-dermatomal shooting pain, positive straight leg raise at 40 degrees, diminished left ankle reflex and lateral foot sensory loss. Cauda equina syndrome, infection and malignancy are not supported by the available findings. This is appropriately managed with structured conservative treatment, close neurological surveillance and timely MRI, with escalation to interventional or surgical care if the deficit progresses or symptoms fail to resolve.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics

Recommendations: Begin structured conservative management, since the majority of lumbar disc herniations with radiculopathy improve substantially within 6 to 12 weeks without surgery. Provide multimodal analgesia: scheduled nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs if not contraindicated, with consideration of a neuropathic agent such as gabapentin or pregabalin for the sharp shooting radicular component, and short-term muscle relaxants for spasm; avoid long-term opioids, and if used at all, restrict them to a brief course for severe pain given the risks in a chronic pain context. Advise against bed rest and encourage continued activity within tolerance, since prolonged rest worsens outcomes. Address the specific aggravating factors identified in this case directly: because pain is worsened by prolonged sitting and forward bending, counsel on avoiding sustained sitting, taking frequent standing breaks, using lumbar support and maintaining a neutral spine, and on avoiding flexed-spine lifting. Refer to physical therapy for a program including nerve root mobilization or neural gliding, core and lumbar stabilization, hip and hamstring flexibility work, and education in safe lifting mechanics. Address the occupational contribution explicitly, since 20 years of lifting heavy machinery parts is both the likely cause and the main obstacle to recovery: arrange temporary work restrictions with a defined lifting limit and avoidance of repetitive bending and twisting, involve occupational health for a workplace ergonomic assessment, consider modified or light duty during the acute phase, and plan a graded return to full duties with permanent ergonomic modifications and mechanical lifting aids where possible. Arrange MRI of the lumbar spine on a timely basis to define the level and morphology of the herniation, given the objective deficits and the need to plan any escalation of care. Document the current motor grade of 4 out of 5 in ankle dorsiflexion as a precise baseline and re-examine in 1 to 2 weeks, then at defined intervals, so that any deterioration is detected early. Give explicit return precautions: the patient must seek emergency care immediately for new or worsening leg weakness, foot drop, numbness in the saddle or perineal region, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence, bilateral leg symptoms, fever or severe unremitting night pain, since these would indicate cauda equina syndrome, progressive neurological compromise or infection. If radicular pain remains severe and disabling after approximately 4 to 6 weeks of adequate conservative treatment, consider a fluoroscopically guided transforaminal epidural corticosteroid injection at the affected level for symptomatic relief. Refer for spine surgical consultation, either orthopedic spine or neurosurgery, if there is progressive or significant motor weakness, if disabling radicular pain persists beyond 6 to 12 weeks of appropriate conservative care with concordant MRI findings, or at any point if red flags emerge; microdiscectomy in that setting reliably accelerates relief of radicular pain. Address the chronic pain dimension as well, with attention to sleep, mood, activity pacing, weight and conditioning, since a long-standing pain history predicts a more difficult course.

Notes: The mild ankle dorsiflexion weakness at 4 out of 5 does not localize to the same root as the sensory and reflex findings and therefore warrants careful serial re-examination and MRI correlation; the key clinical distinction is that it is mild and non-progressive, so it does not by itself mandate emergency intervention, but any progression toward a true foot drop converts this into an urgent surgical problem. The absence of bowel and bladder symptoms and saddle anesthesia was explicitly documented and should be re-documented at each visit rather than assumed to persist. MRI findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture, since degenerative changes and asymptomatic disc bulges are extremely common at this age and in this occupation, and only findings that correlate with the S1 and possible L5 distribution should drive intervention. The case does not specify vital signs, comorbidities, medications, prior treatments, imaging history, smoking status or the exact functional limitation, so these remain Not specified and should be clarified.

The main differential considerations are lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication, which is plausible in a 48-year-old with degenerative disease but fits less well because stenosis typically produces pain worsened by extension and walking and relieved by sitting and forward flexion, the opposite of this patient's pattern; piriformis syndrome or extraspinal sciatic nerve entrapment, which can produce buttock and posterior leg pain but would not typically abolish the ankle reflex; sacroiliac joint dysfunction or facet-mediated referred pain, which does not produce a dermatomal sensory deficit or reflex loss; peripheral neuropathy, which would be distally symmetric rather than unilateral and dermatomal; and vascular claudication, which would present with exertional calf pain relieved by rest with diminished pulses rather than positional shooting pain with neurological signs.

Plain lumbar radiographs are of limited value for radiculopathy and are needed only if instability, fracture or spondylolisthesis is suspected. The diagnosis is supported by S1-dermatomal shooting pain, positive straight leg raise at 40 degrees, diminished left ankle reflex and lateral foot sensory loss. Cauda equina syndrome, infection and malignancy are not supported by the available findings. This is appropriately managed with structured conservative treatment, close neurological surveillance and timely MRI, with escalation to interventional or surgical care if the deficit progresses or symptoms fail to resolve.

Advise against bed rest and encourage continued activity within tolerance, since prolonged rest worsens outcomes. Address the specific aggravating factors identified in this case directly: because pain is worsened by prolonged sitting and forward bending, counsel on avoiding sustained sitting, taking frequent standing breaks, using lumbar support and maintaining a neutral spine, and on avoiding flexed-spine lifting. Refer to physical therapy for a program including nerve root mobilization or neural gliding, core and lumbar stabilization, hip and hamstring flexibility work, and education in safe lifting mechanics. Address the occupational contribution explicitly, since 20 years of lifting heavy machinery parts is both the likely cause and the main obstacle to recovery: arrange temporary work restrictions with a defined lifting limit and avoidance of repetitive bending and twisting, involve occupational health for a workplace ergonomic assessment, consider modified or light duty during the acute phase, and plan a graded return to full duties with permanent ergonomic modifications and mechanical lifting aids where possible. Arrange MRI of the lumbar spine on a timely basis to define the level and morphology of the herniation, given the objective deficits and the need to plan any escalation of care. Document the current motor grade of 4 out of 5 in ankle dorsiflexion as a precise baseline and re-examine in 1 to 2 weeks, then at defined intervals, so that any deterioration is detected early. Give explicit return precautions: the patient must seek emergency care immediately for new or worsening leg weakness, foot drop, numbness in the saddle or perineal region, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence, bilateral leg symptoms, fever or severe unremitting night pain, since these would indicate cauda equina syndrome, progressive neurological compromise or infection. If radicular pain remains severe and disabling after approximately 4 to 6 weeks of adequate conservative treatment, consider a fluoroscopically guided transforaminal epidural corticosteroid injection at the affected level for symptomatic relief. The absence of bowel and bladder symptoms and saddle anesthesia was explicitly documented and should be re-documented at each visit rather than assumed to persist. MRI findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture, since degenerative changes and asymptomatic disc bulges are extremely common at this age and in this occupation, and only findings that correlate with the S1 and possible L5 distribution should drive intervention. A 14-year-old boy who swims competitively is brought in by his parent for evaluation of a bump on the bottom of his right foot that has been growing over the past 2 months. It is generally painless but occasionally mildly uncomfortable with direct pressure during walking. He denies any pain at rest or other similar lesions. On examination, there is a single well-circumscribed, rough, raised lesion approximately 8 mm on the plantar surface of the right foot at the base of the third metatarsal. baseline_protocol:
Age: 14 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A bump on the bottom of the right foot, growing over the past 2 months, generally painless but occasionally mildly uncomfortable with direct pressure during walking.

Analysis: The lesion is a plantar wart (verruca plantaris), caused by cutaneous human papillomavirus infection of the epidermis. The diagnosis rests on a set of findings that together are essentially pathognomonic. First, pinpoint black dots are visible within the lesion; these are thrombosed capillaries within the dermal papillae, the classic and most specific clinical sign of a verruca, and they are the single most discriminating feature in this case. Second, the skin lines are interrupted around the lesion. Normal dermatoglyphics, that is, the skin furrows of the sole, are displaced and interrupted by a wart because the viral proliferation disrupts the epidermal architecture, whereas in a callus or corn the skin lines run continuously across the surface of the thickened skin. This single distinction is the most reliable way to separate a verruca from a callus at the bedside. Third, the lesion is a well-circumscribed, rough, raised, hyperkeratotic papule approximately 8 mm in size, which is the expected morphology.
The history reinforces the diagnosis and identifies the likely source of exposure. He swims competitively, which means repeated barefoot walking on wet communal surfaces such as pool decks, locker rooms and shower floors; these are the classic environments for transmission of cutaneous HPV, because maceration of the plantar skin from prolonged moisture facilitates viral inoculation through microabrasions. Adolescence is the peak age of incidence for plantar warts. The slow growth over 2 months is consistent with the indolent natural history of a viral wart rather than an aggressive process. The symptom pattern is also typical: plantar warts are generally painless or minimally symptomatic but become uncomfortable with direct vertical pressure during weight bearing, precisely as described, because the lesion is pressed inward by the body's weight at a load-bearing site at the base of the third metatarsal.
The findings that argue against alternatives are equally important. There is no surrounding erythema, no rest pain and no systemic feature, which makes an infectious or inflammatory process such as an abscess, a foreign body granuloma or cellulitis unlikely. A callus or corn is the main mimic; it is excluded by the interrupted skin lines and the black dots, and additionally by the fact that a callus is typically painful with lateral pinching rather than direct pressure, whereas a wart is characteristically tender with direct downward pressure and with pinching. A foreign body reaction, such as a retained splinter or glass, could produce a growing plantar nodule but would usually be accompanied by a puncture history, more constant pain and often inflammation. A plantar epidermal inclusion cyst would be smooth and dome-shaped rather than rough and hyperkeratotic, without black dots. Molluscum contagiosum would show umbilicated dome-shaped papules and is uncommon on the thick plantar skin. Benign neoplasms such as a fibroma, or the plantar fibromatosis of Ledderhose disease, would present as a firm subcutaneous nodule along the fascia with intact overlying skin lines. Malignancy, in particular verrucous carcinoma or amelanotic acral melanoma, is an important consideration for any solitary, persistent, growing plantar lesion, but is very unlikely in a 14-year-old with a lesion showing entirely typical verrucous features; it would become a real concern only if the lesion behaved atypically, ulcerated, bled spontaneously, pigmented irregularly, or failed to respond to appropriate treatment.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. This is a clinical diagnosis established by the characteristic morphology, the pinpoint black dots representing thrombosed capillaries, and the interruption of skin lines. Dermoscopy may be used as a simple bedside adjunct to confirm the thrombosed capillaries and the absence of a pigment network if any doubt exists. Paring of the overlying hyperkeratosis with a scalpel blade is both diagnostic and therapeutic, as it reveals the punctate bleeding points of a wart while a callus pares down to homogeneous translucent keratin without bleeding. No laboratory testing, no HPV typing, and no imaging are required. A skin biopsy is not indicated at present and should be reserved for a lesion that is atypical in appearance, ulcerated, spontaneously bleeding, pigmented, rapidly enlarging, or that fails to resolve despite appropriate and adequate treatment, in order to exclude verrucous carcinoma or amelanotic melanoma.

Conclusion: A solitary plantar wart (verruca plantaris) of approximately 8 mm on the plantar surface of the right foot at the base of the third metatarsal in a 14-year-old competitive swimmer, acquired most probably through barefoot exposure to communal wet surfaces. The diagnosis is confirmed clinically by pinpoint thrombosed capillaries and interrupted skin lines, with no evidence of secondary infection or of any alternative or worrisome pathology. This is a benign, self-limiting viral condition that requires no urgent intervention; treatment is elective and is directed at symptom relief, reduction of transmission and cosmetic or functional concerns.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Recommendations: Reassure the patient and parent that this is a benign viral wart, not a tumour or a serious infection, and that many plantar warts in children and adolescents resolve spontaneously over months to two years as cell-mediated immunity clears the virus; observation alone is a legitimate option for a lesion that is only mildly symptomatic. However, because this lesion is enlarging, is at a weight-bearing site and causes discomfort with pressure during walking, active treatment is reasonable and appropriate. Begin with first-line topical therapy: salicylic acid, generally 17 to 40 percent for plantar skin, applied daily after soaking the foot in warm water for about 10 minutes and gently paring the hyperkeratotic surface with a pumice stone or emery board dedicated to that use only, then occluded with tape; the family should be told that this requires consistent daily application over 8 to 12 weeks or longer and that adherence, not the specific product, determines success. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, applied at 2 to 3 week intervals, may be used alone or in combination with salicylic acid and is more effective in combination; counsel that it is painful, that plantar skin is thick and needs paring before treatment, that blistering is expected, and that several sessions are usually required. Reserve second-line options such as topical immunotherapy, intralesional treatment, cantharidin or laser for lesions that fail an adequate first-line trial. Avoid aggressive surgical excision and destructive electrosurgery in this weight-bearing location, since scarring on the plantar surface can produce persistent, disabling pain that is worse than the wart itself, and recurrence remains common. Provide symptomatic relief in the interim with a donut-shaped felt pad or a cushioned insole to offload the lesion at the base of the third metatarsal so that walking is comfortable. Address the additional considerations that arise from his competitive swimming directly, since they matter for both cure and prevention of spread: advise wearing waterproof sandals or shower shoes on pool decks, in locker rooms and in showers; drying the feet thoroughly, especially between the toes; not sharing towels, socks or footwear; covering the lesion with a waterproof adhesive dressing or wearing a swim sock during shared-facility use to reduce shedding and transmission to teammates and family; and not picking, scratching or shaving the lesion, since autoinoculation is how satellite and mosaic warts develop and he currently has only a single lesion, which is a favourable feature to preserve. He does not need to stop swimming or competing, and the condition is not a reason for exclusion from sport. Arrange follow-up in about 8 to 12 weeks to assess response, and advise earlier review if the lesion becomes painful at rest, develops surrounding redness, swelling, warmth or discharge suggesting secondary bacterial infection, bleeds spontaneously, changes colour or pigmentation, ulcerates, or grows rapidly. Instruct on inspecting the rest of the feet and hands periodically for new lesions.

Notes: Treatment of plantar warts is often prolonged and recurrence is common regardless of modality, so realistic expectations should be set with the family at the outset to avoid frustration and repeated escalation. Salicylic acid and cryotherapy should be applied only to the wart, as surrounding normal skin can be damaged. The case describes no immunosuppression, diabetes or peripheral vascular disease; if any such condition were present, self-treatment with keratolytics and paring would be unsafe and specialist podiatric or dermatological care would be required, so this should be confirmed. A solitary plantar lesion that persists despite correct and sustained treatment warrants biopsy to exclude verrucous carcinoma, although this is rare at his age. The case does not specify past medical history, medications, immunization status, prior treatments or family history, so those remain Not specified.

Third, the lesion is a well-circumscribed, rough, raised, hyperkeratotic papule approximately 8 mm in size, which is the expected morphology.
The history reinforces the diagnosis and identifies the likely source of exposure. He swims competitively, which means repeated barefoot walking on wet communal surfaces such as pool decks, locker rooms and shower floors; these are the classic environments for transmission of cutaneous HPV, because maceration of the plantar skin from prolonged moisture facilitates viral inoculation through microabrasions. Adolescence is the peak age of incidence for plantar warts. The slow growth over 2 months is consistent with the indolent natural history of a viral wart rather than an aggressive process. The symptom pattern is also typical: plantar warts are generally painless or minimally symptomatic but become uncomfortable with direct vertical pressure during weight bearing, precisely as described, because the lesion is pressed inward by the body's weight at a load-bearing site at the base of the third metatarsal.
The findings that argue against alternatives are equally important. There is no surrounding erythema, no rest pain and no systemic feature, which makes an infectious or inflammatory process such as an abscess, a foreign body granuloma or cellulitis unlikely. A callus or corn is the main mimic; it is excluded by the interrupted skin lines and the black dots, and additionally by the fact that a callus is typically painful with lateral pinching rather than direct pressure, whereas a wart is characteristically tender with direct downward pressure and with pinching. A foreign body reaction, such as a retained splinter or glass, could produce a growing plantar nodule but would usually be accompanied by a puncture history, more constant pain and often inflammation. A plantar epidermal inclusion cyst would be smooth and dome-shaped rather than rough and hyperkeratotic, without black dots. Molluscum contagiosum would show umbilicated dome-shaped papules and is uncommon on the thick plantar skin. Benign neoplasms such as a fibroma, or the plantar fibromatosis of Ledderhose disease, would present as a firm subcutaneous nodule along the fascia with intact overlying skin lines. Malignancy, in particular verrucous carcinoma or amelanotic acral melanoma, is an important consideration for any solitary, persistent, growing plantar lesion, but is very unlikely in a 14-year-old with a lesion showing entirely typical verrucous features; it would become a real concern only if the lesion behaved atypically, ulcerated, bled spontaneously, pigmented irregularly, or failed to respond to appropriate treatment.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. This is a clinical diagnosis established by the characteristic morphology, the pinpoint black dots representing thrombosed capillaries, and the interruption of skin lines. Dermoscopy may be used as a simple bedside adjunct to confirm the thrombosed capillaries and the absence of a pigment network if any doubt exists. Paring of the overlying hyperkeratosis with a scalpel blade is both diagnostic and therapeutic, as it reveals the punctate bleeding points of a wart while a callus pares down to homogeneous translucent keratin without bleeding. No laboratory testing, no HPV typing, and no imaging are required. A skin biopsy is not indicated at present and should be reserved for a lesion that is atypical in appearance, ulcerated, spontaneously bleeding, pigmented, rapidly enlarging, or that fails to resolve despite appropriate and adequate treatment, in order to exclude verrucous carcinoma or amelanotic melanoma.

Conclusion: A solitary plantar wart (verruca plantaris) of approximately 8 mm on the plantar surface of the right foot at the base of the third metatarsal in a 14-year-old competitive swimmer, acquired most probably through barefoot exposure to communal wet surfaces. The diagnosis is confirmed clinically by pinpoint thrombosed capillaries and interrupted skin lines, with no evidence of secondary infection or of any alternative or worrisome pathology. This is a benign, self-limiting viral condition that requires no urgent intervention; treatment is elective and is directed at symptom relief, reduction of transmission and cosmetic or functional concerns.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Recommendations: Reassure the patient and parent that this is a benign viral wart, not a tumour or a serious infection, and that many plantar warts in children and adolescents resolve spontaneously over months to two years as cell-mediated immunity clears the virus; observation alone is a legitimate option for a lesion that is only mildly symptomatic. However, because this lesion is enlarging, is at a weight-bearing site and causes discomfort with pressure during walking, active treatment is reasonable and appropriate. Begin with first-line topical therapy: salicylic acid, generally 17 to 40 percent for plantar skin, applied daily after soaking the foot in warm water for about 10 minutes and gently paring the hyperkeratotic surface with a pumice stone or emery board dedicated to that use only, then occluded with tape; the family should be told that this requires consistent daily application over 8 to 12 weeks or longer and that adherence, not the specific product, determines success. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, applied at 2 to 3 week intervals, may be used alone or in combination with salicylic acid and is more effective in combination; counsel that it is painful, that plantar skin is thick and needs paring before treatment, that blistering is expected, and that several sessions are usually required. Reserve second-line options such as topical immunotherapy, intralesional treatment, cantharidin or laser for lesions that fail an adequate first-line trial. Avoid aggressive surgical excision and destructive electrosurgery in this weight-bearing location, since scarring on the plantar surface can produce persistent, disabling pain that is worse than the wart itself, and recurrence remains common. Provide symptomatic relief in the interim with a donut-shaped felt pad or a cushioned insole to offload the lesion at the base of the third metatarsal so that walking is comfortable. Address the additional considerations that arise from his competitive swimming directly, since they matter for both cure and prevention of spread: advise wearing waterproof sandals or shower shoes on pool decks, in locker rooms and in showers; drying the feet thoroughly, especially between the toes; not sharing towels, socks or footwear; covering the lesion with a waterproof adhesive dressing or wearing a swim sock during shared-facility use to reduce shedding and transmission to teammates and family; and not picking, scratching or shaving the lesion, since autoinoculation is how satellite and mosaic warts develop and he currently has only a single lesion, which is a favourable feature to preserve. He does not need to stop swimming or competing, and the condition is not a reason for exclusion from sport. Arrange follow-up in about 8 to 12 weeks to assess response, and advise earlier review if the lesion becomes painful at rest, develops surrounding redness, swelling, warmth or discharge suggesting secondary bacterial infection, bleeds spontaneously, changes colour or pigmentation, ulcerates, or grows rapidly. Instruct on inspecting the rest of the feet and hands periodically for new lesions.

Notes: Treatment of plantar warts is often prolonged and recurrence is common regardless of modality, so realistic expectations should be set with the family at the outset to avoid frustration and repeated escalation. Salicylic acid and cryotherapy should be applied only to the wart, as surrounding normal skin can be damaged. The case describes no immunosuppression, diabetes or peripheral vascular disease; if any such condition were present, self-treatment with keratolytics and paring would be unsafe and specialist podiatric or dermatological care would be required, so this should be confirmed. A solitary plantar lesion that persists despite correct and sustained treatment warrants biopsy to exclude verrucous carcinoma, although this is rare at his age. The case does not specify past medical history, medications, immunization status, prior treatments or family history, so those remain Not specified.
