Vignette:
A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after a skiing accident in which he sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture of the right leg, which was splinted in the field by ski patrol. He reports that his pain has been escalating dramatically despite receiving IV morphine 10 mg total, which is atypical for the degree of injury. He describes the pain as deep and burning, significantly worse with any passive movement of his right toes. On examination, the right lower leg appears tense and swollen within the splint. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 142/88, SpO2 99%. After splint removal, the anterior compartment of the right leg is firm and exquisitely tender. Pain is markedly worsened with passive extension of the right toes. Sensation is diminished in the first web space (deep peroneal nerve distribution). Dorsalis pedis pulse is still palpable but diminished compared to the left. Compartment pressure measurement reveals 48 mmHg in the anterior compartment (diastolic BP 88, delta pressure 40 mmHg). Orthopedic surgery is consulted for emergent four-compartment fasciotomy.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Escalating, disproportionate deep burning pain in the right lower leg 6 hours after a skiing accident causing a closed right tibial shaft fracture, unrelieved by 10 mg of intravenous morphine, markedly worsened by passive movement of the toes, with a tense swollen leg within the field splint.

Analysis: This is acute compartment syndrome of the anterior compartment of the right leg complicating a closed tibial shaft fracture, and it is a surgical emergency in which time to fasciotomy determines limb outcome.

The diagnosis rests first on the clinical picture, which is close to textbook. Pain out of proportion to the injury is the earliest and most reliable sign, and it is present in its most convincing form here: the pain is escalating dramatically, the patient and the clinician both judge it atypical for the degree of injury, and it has failed to respond to a total of 10 mg of intravenous morphine. The character of the pain is deep and burning, consistent with ischaemic muscle rather than fracture pain. Pain on passive stretch is the classic provocative sign, and passive extension of the toes, which stretches the anterior compartment musculature (tibialis anterior and the long toe extensors), markedly worsens it. On direct examination after splint removal, the anterior compartment is firm, tense and exquisitely tender, and the leg is swollen. Sensation is diminished in the first web space, the autonomous zone of the deep peroneal nerve, which traverses the anterior compartment; sensory change in the nerve running through the affected compartment is an early and specific sign of compartment ischaemia and indicates that neural compromise has already begun. The tachycardia at 108 beats/min and the blood pressure of 142/88 mm Hg are consistent with severe uncontrolled pain and sympathetic activation.

The mechanism fits: tibial shaft fracture is the single most common cause of acute compartment syndrome; bleeding and oedema within the non-compliant osteofascial anterior compartment raise the intracompartmental pressure, which is then compounded by the circumferential field splint. Six hours have elapsed since injury, which places the limb near the beginning of the window in which irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis develops.

The compartment pressure of 48 mmHg is markedly elevated and corroborates the clinical diagnosis. It should be noted that the case reports the delta pressure (diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure) as 40 mmHg, whereas the conventional threshold prompting fasciotomy is a delta pressure below 30 mmHg. This numerical discrepancy does not change the management: an absolute pressure of 48 mmHg together with an unequivocal and progressing clinical syndrome mandates fasciotomy. Acute compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis, and pressure measurement is an adjunct; a reassuring or borderline number must never override convincing clinical findings, particularly when a sensory deficit is already established.

An important pitfall addressed by the case is the pulse. The dorsalis pedis pulse remains palpable, though diminished compared with the left. Preserved distal pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome, because compartment pressures that are lethal to muscle and nerve are still well below systolic arterial pressure. Pulselessness and pallor are late findings that appear after irreversible damage; waiting for them is the classic cause of limb loss.

Differential considerations weighed and rejected. Simple fracture pain is excluded by the failure of 10 mg of morphine, by the escalation over six hours and by the pain on passive stretch with a tense compartment. Splint that is too tight causing pressure symptoms was a genuine contributor, but the syndrome persisted and was confirmed after splint removal. Arterial injury or vascular occlusion is less likely with a palpable, albeit diminished, dorsalis pedis pulse and no other ischaemic signs, though vascular status should be documented. Deep venous thrombosis would not produce this acuity, pain on passive stretch and deep peroneal sensory loss six hours after injury. Peroneal nerve injury from the fracture itself could explain the first web space numbness in isolation but does not explain the tense compartment or the stretch pain. Fat embolism and infection are not supported by the temperature of 37.0 C, oxygen saturation of 99 percent and the local findings.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Intracompartmental pressure monitoring device with serial or continuous measurement of all four leg compartments (anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior), not the anterior alone; plain radiographs of the tibia and fibula in two planes including the knee and ankle to characterise the fracture for fixation planning; preoperative laboratory studies including complete blood count, coagulation profile, type and screen, electrolytes, renal function and serum creatine kinase; urinalysis for myoglobin to assess for rhabdomyolysis; ECG if hyperkalaemia is suspected; operating theatre and orthopaedic surgical team for emergent four-compartment fasciotomy. Advanced imaging such as CT or MRI is not required and must not delay operative decompression.

Conclusion: A 30-year-old man with a closed right tibial shaft fracture has developed acute compartment syndrome of the anterior compartment six hours after injury. The diagnosis is established clinically by pain out of proportion and refractory to opioid analgesia, a tense and exquisitely tender anterior compartment, severe pain on passive extension of the toes, and diminished sensation in the deep peroneal nerve distribution over the first web space, and is corroborated by an intracompartmental pressure of 48 mmHg. The dorsalis pedis pulse remains palpable, which is expected and does not exclude the diagnosis. Emergent four-compartment fasciotomy is indicated, and orthopaedic surgery has appropriately been consulted for this. Delay risks irreversible muscle necrosis, Volkmann ischaemic contracture, permanent deep peroneal nerve injury with foot drop, rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury, and limb loss.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Proceed to emergent four-compartment fasciotomy of the right leg without delay; the elapsed six hours means the ischaemic window is already closing and no further investigation should be allowed to postpone decompression. Keep all circumferential dressings and the splint fully released; the splint has already been removed and must not be reapplied circumferentially. Position the limb at the level of the heart, neither elevated nor dependent — elevation lowers the arterial perfusion gradient and worsens compartment ischaemia, while dependency increases oedema. Do not apply ice or cold packs to the compartment. Maintain normotension and adequate intravascular volume, since hypotension reduces the perfusion pressure across the compartment and accelerates injury. Provide effective analgesia intravenously, but avoid regional or peripheral nerve blocks and avoid heavy sedation before decompression, because these mask the very pain that is the monitoring parameter. Nil by mouth and standard preoperative preparation, with anaesthesia notified urgently. Address the additional considerations explicitly: (1) release all four compartments through appropriate incisions rather than the anterior compartment alone, since deep posterior compartment involvement is easily missed and its neglect is a common cause of failed decompression; assess muscle viability intraoperatively; (2) leave the fasciotomy wounds open with a plan for staged return to theatre for inspection, debridement of any non-viable muscle and delayed closure or skin grafting; (3) plan definitive stabilisation of the tibial shaft fracture in coordination with the fasciotomy; (4) monitor for rhabdomyolysis with serial creatine kinase, renal function, potassium and urine myoglobin, and maintain adequate fluid resuscitation and urine output, watching for hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury, particularly after reperfusion; (5) monitor for reperfusion injury and recurrent compartment hypertension after decompression, with continued serial examinations; (6) document a detailed neurovascular examination now and repeatedly thereafter, specifically recording deep peroneal sensation, toe dorsiflexion strength and distal pulses, and counsel the patient that first web space numbness and possible motor weakness may persist even after successful fasciotomy; (7) provide tetanus prophylaxis as indicated and thromboprophylaxis once bleeding risk permits, in discussion with the surgical team; (8) arrange physiotherapy and rehabilitation for ankle and toe dorsiflexion, with orthotic support if foot drop develops.
Notes: The reported delta pressure of 40 mmHg is above the conventional 30 mmHg fasciotomy threshold and is inconsistent with the unequivocal clinical syndrome; the clinical findings and the absolute pressure of 48 mmHg govern the decision, and fasciotomy must not be withheld on the basis of the calculated delta value. A palpable distal pulse never excludes acute compartment syndrome. The neurological deficit already present indicates the process is advanced and time-critical.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old white man presents to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of sudden onset of left-sided flank pain radiating down toward his groin. The patient is writhing in pain, which is unrelieved by position. He also complains of nausea and vomiting.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 45 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: One-hour history of sudden-onset left-sided flank pain radiating toward the groin, with the patient writhing in pain that is not relieved by any position, accompanied by nausea and vomiting.

Analysis: Every feature given points to acute ureteral colic from an obstructing left ureteral calculus, and the specific descriptors in the case are the ones that discriminate this diagnosis from its alternatives.

The onset is sudden and the pain reached severity within an hour, which is characteristic of acute obstruction of the ureter by a stone rather than of a gradually evolving inflammatory process. The location and radiation are classic: flank pain radiating down toward the groin follows the course of the ureter and reflects the shared innervation of the ureter with the T11 to L1 dermatomes, so a stone at the ureteropelvic junction or proximal ureter produces flank pain, and as it descends the pain refers to the groin and genitalia.

The most discriminating feature described is the behaviour. The patient is writhing in pain and cannot find a position of relief. This restless, non-positional pain is characteristic of colic from a hollow viscus in spasm; by contrast, patients with peritoneal irritation from an intra-abdominal inflammatory process lie still because movement worsens the pain. This single observation strongly favours renal or ureteral colic over an intraperitoneal cause.

Nausea and vomiting are expected accompaniments, arising from the shared autonomic and coeliac plexus innervation of the renal capsule and the gastrointestinal tract, and are not evidence of a primary gastrointestinal disorder in this context. The demographic profile — a man in his fifth decade — is the typical one for a first stone presentation.

Differential considerations that must be weighed. The most dangerous alternative in a man of this age with acute flank pain is a leaking or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, which classically mimics renal colic and must be considered before the diagnosis of stone is accepted; the case provides no vital signs, no abdominal examination and no pulse findings, so this cannot be excluded on the information given and must be actively addressed. Other considerations include pyelonephritis, which would be expected to produce fever and costovertebral angle tenderness, neither documented here; renal infarction or renal vein thrombosis; a ureteral obstruction from a blood clot or from an extrinsic mass; testicular torsion, which can refer pain to the flank and requires genital examination; a perforated or inflammatory intra-abdominal process such as diverticulitis or a perforated viscus, made less likely by the writhing, non-positional character of the pain; incarcerated hernia; musculoskeletal or radicular pain, which does not fit the acute onset with vomiting; and, less commonly at this age, herpes zoster before the rash appears.

The case as presented contains no vital signs, no physical examination findings, no laboratory data and no imaging, so the diagnosis at this point is a clinical impression based on the history alone and requires objective confirmation. Two determinations govern management and neither can be made from the history: whether there is superimposed infection in an obstructed system, which is a urological emergency, and whether renal function or the anatomy of the stone demands intervention rather than conservative passage.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Full vital signs including temperature, heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation; complete abdominal, flank and genital examination with assessment of peripheral pulses; non-contrast helical CT of the abdomen and pelvis (CT KUB), which is the definitive study to confirm a calculus, localise it, measure its size and assess the degree of hydronephrosis; renal and bladder ultrasound as the preferred first-line imaging alternative where radiation avoidance is desired or as a bedside adjunct, including bedside ultrasound of the aorta to exclude an abdominal aortic aneurysm; urinalysis with microscopy for haematuria, pyuria, nitrites and crystals, with urine culture; complete blood count; serum creatinine and electrolytes; C-reactive protein if infection is suspected; blood cultures if febrile; ECG and cardiac assessment only if the presentation suggests an alternative vascular cause.

Conclusion: A 45-year-old man presents with acute, severe, colicky left flank pain of one hour's duration radiating to the groin, with restless writhing that is unrelieved by position and associated nausea and vomiting. This constellation is highly characteristic of acute ureteral colic due to an obstructing left ureteral calculus. The diagnosis nonetheless requires objective confirmation by urinalysis and imaging, and the dangerous mimics — in particular a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm in a man of this age, and infection proximal to an obstructing stone — must be actively excluded before the presentation is treated as uncomplicated colic. The immediate clinical priorities are effective analgesia, antiemesis, confirmation of the diagnosis and identification of any complicating feature that would require urgent urological decompression.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Treat the pain promptly and adequately; severe renal colic is one of the most intense pains in clinical medicine and analgesia should not be withheld pending imaging. A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug given parenterally is the preferred first-line agent because it reduces ureteral wall oedema and intraluminal pressure as well as providing analgesia, with opioids added if the response is inadequate or if NSAIDs are contraindicated; check renal function and contraindications before use. Give a parenteral antiemetic for the nausea and vomiting, and provide intravenous fluids to correct any deficit from vomiting, without forced diuresis. Obtain the vital signs and a full examination immediately, then confirm the diagnosis with urinalysis and CT KUB or ultrasound. Address the additional considerations explicitly: (1) exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm before accepting a diagnosis of first-episode renal colic in a 45-year-old man — check blood pressure in both arms, palpate the abdomen for a pulsatile mass, assess femoral and distal pulses, and use bedside aortic ultrasound or the CT to evaluate the aorta; this mimic is lethal if missed; (2) look actively for infection above an obstruction — fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension, pyuria or a positive nitrite test in a patient with a confirmed obstructing stone constitutes obstructive pyelonephritis, a urological emergency requiring immediate antibiotics and urgent decompression by ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, not conservative management; (3) check the serum creatinine and consider urgent urology involvement if the patient has a solitary or transplanted kidney, bilateral obstruction, acute kidney injury, or pain refractory to adequate analgesia; (4) examine the testes to exclude torsion, since referred flank and groin pain can be the presenting complaint; (5) if imaging confirms a small distal stone with no infection, normal renal function and controlled pain, manage conservatively with oral analgesia, adequate oral hydration, urine straining to capture the stone for analysis, and consideration of medical expulsive therapy with an alpha blocker, with planned urology follow-up and repeat imaging to confirm passage; larger or proximal stones and those that fail to pass are managed with ureteroscopy or shock wave lithotripsy; (6) give clear return precautions — fever, rigors, uncontrolled pain, persistent vomiting preventing oral intake, or reduced urine output require immediate return; (7) after the acute episode, send any retrieved stone for composition analysis and arrange metabolic evaluation and preventive advice, including increased fluid intake to maintain high urine output and dietary modification appropriate to the stone type.
Notes: The case supplies no vital signs, no physical examination findings and no laboratory or imaging results, so this protocol rests on the history alone; the diagnosis is provisional until confirmed. Fever or haemodynamic instability with an obstructing stone changes the management entirely and demands emergent decompression. Absence of haematuria does not exclude a stone, as a proportion of patients with confirmed calculi have no red cells in the urine.

difficulty in getting up in the morning despite getting 8 hours of sleep. He was recently

baseline_protocol:
Age: 54 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Ten-kilogram weight gain over three months without dietary change, proximal bilateral leg weakness on rising from sitting and climbing stairs, lethargy and difficulty getting up despite eight hours of sleep, poorly controlled newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, low mood unresponsive to citalopram, worsening short-term memory, and new-onset diplopia with a left eye abnormality found on examination.

Analysis: The case establishes Cushing syndrome and then asks which cause is responsible. The evidence points to pituitary ACTH secretion, that is Cushing's disease.

Cushing syndrome itself is confirmed by an unambiguous clinical phenotype together with biochemistry. The discriminating physical signs, those that carry real specificity, are all present: wide purple striae on the lower abdomen and around the axillae, generally thin skin with easy bruising on the legs and forearms, and proximal myopathy with quadriceps weakness of 4+/5 bilaterally in a man whose strength is otherwise 5/5. The truncal adiposity with relatively thin limbs, moon face and posterior cervical fat pad complete the picture. Supporting features are the ten-kilogram weight gain over three months, new hypertension at 188/92 mm Hg in a man with no history of hypertension, new type 2 diabetes with a glucose of 306 mg/dL that is poorly controlled on metformin, hypokalaemia of 2.9 mEq/L with a bicarbonate of 28 mEq/L reflecting a mineralocorticoid effect of cortisol excess, acne on the upper back and thorax, thin sparse hair with temporal balding, depression with mood swings, and cognitive complaints. The biochemical confirmation is a midnight serum cortisol of 43.5 mcg/dL (1200 nmol/L), which demonstrates complete loss of the normal circadian nadir, and repeated cortisol measurements ranging from 36.6 to 52.6 mcg/dL.

The cause is then determined by the ACTH. The ACTH is 188 pg/mL against a normal range of 10 to 60 pg/mL, with repeated values of 122 to 167 pg/mL. An ACTH that is frankly elevated in the face of grossly elevated cortisol proves that the syndrome is ACTH-dependent. This immediately excludes two of the four options. A cortisol-secreting adrenal tumour would suppress ACTH to undetectable levels, and exogenous corticosteroid use would likewise suppress both ACTH and endogenous cortisol; moreover the patient's medication list contains no corticosteroid, only citalopram, mesalazine, ranitidine, ursodeoxycholic acid and metformin, so iatrogenic Cushing syndrome is excluded on both biochemical and historical grounds.

The remaining choice is between a pituitary source and ectopic ACTH secretion, and several independent lines of evidence resolve it in favour of the pituitary.

The decisive evidence is the pituitary MRI, which was performed and is presented as part of the diagnostic workup, together with the neuro-ophthalmological findings that localise a lesion to the cavernous sinus region. The left eye is deviated down and laterally with mild ptosis, and the left pupil is 1 mm larger than the right and reacts weakly to light, with diplopia. This is a complete left oculomotor (third cranial) nerve palsy with pupillary involvement. The third cranial nerve runs through the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus immediately adjacent to the pituitary fossa, and a pituitary macroadenoma with lateral extension into the cavernous sinus is a direct and sufficient explanation. An ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour has no mechanism to produce an isolated third nerve palsy.

The second line of evidence is the pattern of anterior pituitary failure caused by a sellar mass. The TSH is 0.04 mIU/L with a free T4 of 0.65 ng/dL (8.4 pmol/L): a low free T4 with an inappropriately low rather than elevated TSH is central hypothyroidism, indicating loss of thyrotroph function. Simultaneously, the LH is 0.4 mU/mL and the FSH is 0.9 mU/mL, both well below their reference ranges, with a testosterone of 78 ng/dL against a normal of 300 to 1200 ng/dL: this is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, indicating loss of gonadotroph function. Although cortisol excess itself suppresses the gonadal and thyroid axes to some degree, the combination of two failed axes with a mass effect on the third cranial nerve is the signature of a pituitary macroadenoma compressing and displacing normal pituitary tissue. The prolactin of 5.6 ng/mL is normal, which argues against a prolactinoma and is consistent with a corticotroph adenoma.

The third line is the negative search for an ectopic source: the chest radiograph is reported as unremarkable, and the classic thoracic sources of ectopic ACTH, small cell lung carcinoma and bronchial carcinoid, are not evident. In addition, the clinical picture here is that of a slowly evolving classical Cushing phenotype with striae, central obesity and moon facies developing over months, whereas ectopic ACTH secretion from an aggressive tumour typically produces a more fulminant syndrome dominated by profound hypokalaemia, severe myopathy, hyperpigmentation and weight loss, with less time for the classical cushingoid habitus to develop. Ectopic secretion also characteristically produces higher ACTH concentrations than the 122 to 188 pg/mL seen here.

Therefore the most likely cause of Cushing syndrome in this patient is pituitary ACTH secretion, that is Cushing's disease, arising from a corticotroph macroadenoma with cavernous sinus extension.

Several findings in the case require separate attention and should not be attributed reflexively to the cortisol excess. The bilateral pitting leg oedema, the bibasal end-inspiratory crackles, the mild exertional dyspnoea and the exertional left-sided chest pain relieved by rest, occurring in a man with new severe hypertension and new diabetes, raise the possibility of cardiac decompensation and of ischaemic heart disease, both recognised consequences of chronic glucocorticoid excess. The glucose of 306 mg/dL with negative capillary ketones is significant hyperglycaemia without ketoacidosis. The potassium of 2.9 mEq/L is a clinically important hypokalaemia. His background of ulcerative colitis for 30 years and primary biliary cirrhosis is relevant to treatment choices but does not explain the presentation, and his liver function tests are normal.

tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

dizziness for the past 2 months. He says his symptoms began just after surgery to repair a
diaphragmatic hernia caused by a stab wound to the chest 6 months ago. He first went to the
emergency department 3 weeks after surgery because of sharp right-sided chest pain. At that

because he was found to have low blood pressure along with his chest pain. No evidence of

acetaminophen. Today he says that, since the operation, he has had gradually worsening

baseline_protocol:
Age: 29 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two months of progressive weight loss of 12 kg, lethargy, generalized weakness and postural dizziness, with morning nausea and occasional vomiting and generalized mild abdominal pain, beginning shortly after repair of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia; he has also noticed new darkening of his nipples and knuckles.

Analysis: This is primary adrenal insufficiency in adrenal crisis, caused by bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in the aftermath of penetrating chest trauma and subsequent diaphragmatic hernia repair.

The clinical syndrome is that of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency developing over two months: profound lethargy, generalized weakness that prevents him working as a builder, anorexia with 12 kg of weight loss, morning nausea with vomiting, non-specific generalized abdominal pain unrelated to meals, position or activity, postural dizziness with palpitations on standing, and low mood. Each of these is non-specific in isolation, and it is their combination with the objective findings that makes the diagnosis.

The single most discriminating clinical sign is the hyperpigmentation. He describes recent darkening of the nipples and the knuckles of his hands, and examination confirms a tanned appearance with darkened knuckles and nipples. Pigmentation of the palmar creases, knuckles, buccal mucosa, scars and areolae reflects the melanocyte-stimulating action of markedly elevated ACTH and its precursor peptides. Its presence establishes that the defect is at the adrenal gland, not the pituitary, because a pituitary cause would produce low rather than high ACTH and hence pallor rather than pigmentation.

The biochemistry is diagnostic and internally consistent. The 9 AM cortisol is 1.8 mcg/dL (49 nmol/L) against a normal of 6.5 to 22.5 mcg/dL; a morning cortisol this low is essentially diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency. The short Synacthen test shows a flat response, with a baseline of 1.4 mcg/dL rising only to 1.9 mcg/dL at 30 minutes against an expected response above 15.5 to 18 mcg/dL, confirming that the adrenal cortex cannot respond to exogenous ACTH. The 9 AM ACTH is 880 pg/mL against a normal of 10 to 60 pg/mL, roughly fifteen-fold elevated, which localises the lesion to the adrenal gland itself and excludes secondary or tertiary insufficiency. The upright plasma renin activity is 600 ng/mL/hour against a normal of 2.9 to 10.8, an extreme elevation confirming aldosterone deficiency with consequent sodium wasting and volume depletion. This mineralocorticoid failure is the reason primary adrenal insufficiency, unlike secondary, produces the salt-losing picture seen here.

The electrolyte and metabolic pattern follows directly. The sodium is 130 mEq/L and the potassium is 6.2 mEq/L: hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia is the classic combination of aldosterone deficiency and is the pattern that should prompt consideration of Addison disease in any patient. The pH is 7.32 with a bicarbonate of 18 mEq/L, a mild metabolic acidosis consistent with mineralocorticoid deficiency and hypovolaemia, with a normal lactate of 1.4 mmol/L indicating that tissue hypoperfusion is not yet severe. The urea nitrogen of 42 mg/dL with a creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL shows acute kidney injury with a disproportionately raised urea, the signature of profound volume depletion in a 29-year-old man. The glucose of 75.6 mg/dL is at the low end of normal, consistent with cortisol deficiency impairing gluconeogenesis, and represents a hypoglycaemia risk. The white cell count of 11,800 cells/mcL and the temperature of 37.8 C are consistent with the stress state of crisis rather than proven infection.

The haemodynamics confirm crisis: a pulse of 112 beats/min with cold peripheries and delayed capillary refill, a jugular venous pressure not visible at 45 degrees, and hypotension. The recorded blood pressure of 75/92 mm Hg is internally impossible as written and is evidently a transcription error, but the systolic value of 75 mm Hg together with the tachycardia, cold peripheries, flat neck veins and postural symptoms establishes shock from hypovolaemia.

The cause is established by the CT of the adrenal glands, reported as bilateral subacute adrenal haemorrhage. This ties the entire presentation to the history. The patient sustained a stab wound to the left chest six months ago and underwent repair of a resulting diaphragmatic hernia two months ago; his symptoms began immediately after that surgery. Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in the setting of major trauma and surgery destroyed sufficient adrenal cortex to produce insufficiency, and the two-month tempo matches a subacute rather than fulminant destruction.

The case also documents a missed opportunity that is instructive. Three weeks after surgery he attended the emergency department with sharp right-sided chest pain and was noted to be hypotensive; a CT of the chest was performed to exclude pulmonary embolism and was negative, and he was discharged on an antiemetic and acetaminophen. The hypotension was the early manifestation of evolving adrenal insufficiency and was not investigated; the cyclizine he was prescribed then treated the symptom of nausea while the underlying disorder progressed for a further two months.

Alternative causes of primary adrenal insufficiency were systematically excluded by the investigations. Autoimmune adrenalitis, the commonest cause in developed countries, is excluded by negative anti-adrenal cortex antibodies; the family history of maternal primary hypothyroidism raised this possibility, but his own thyroid function is normal with a TSH of 0.9 mU/L and a free T4 of 1.6 ng/dL. Tuberculous adrenalitis is not supported: the PPD is negative and the chest radiograph is normal. Haemochromatosis is excluded by a normal ferritin. Metastatic infiltration is not suggested by the imaging, which shows haemorrhage. Myasthenia gravis was considered in the differential of generalized weakness and is not supported, with normal acetylcholine esterase levels and a normal neurological examination including normal power, tone, reflexes and cranial nerves. Adrenoleukodystrophy would be accompanied by neurological findings that are absent. Testicular function is preserved with a testosterone of 320 ng/dL, LH of 4.4 and FSH within range, and prolactin is normal at 12.3 ng/mL, all arguing against a broader pituitary process. Other differentials for the presenting syndrome — occult malignancy, chronic infection, depression as a primary cause of the weight loss and lethargy, and a gastrointestinal cause of the vomiting and abdominal pain — are all excluded by the definitive hormonal results.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring with an immediate ECG to assess for the changes of hyperkalaemia at a potassium of 6.2 mEq/L; frequent blood pressure, heart rate and urine output monitoring; bedside capillary glucose measurement with serial testing given the hypoglycaemia risk; serial serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine and venous blood gases to follow the response to resuscitation; a paired aldosterone level with the plasma renin activity to document mineralocorticoid deficiency; a random cortisol drawn before the first hydrocortisone dose if not already available; septic screen with blood and urine cultures given the temperature of 37.8 C and leucocytosis, to identify any precipitant; repeat or review of the adrenal CT to characterise the haemorrhage and follow its evolution; coagulation screen and, if the haemorrhage is otherwise unexplained, testing for antiphospholipid syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; renal ultrasound if the acute kidney injury does not resolve with volume repletion; 17-hydroxyprogesterone and very long chain fatty acids only if the aetiology remained in doubt, which it does not here.

Conclusion: A 29-year-old man presents two months after repair of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia with weight loss of 12 kg, lethargy, weakness, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, postural dizziness and new hyperpigmentation of the nipples and knuckles, and is found to be in shock with tachycardia at 112 beats/min, hypotension, cold peripheries and flat neck veins. Investigations establish primary adrenal insufficiency in adrenal crisis: 9 AM cortisol 1.8 mcg/dL with a flat short Synacthen response (1.4 to 1.9 mcg/dL), ACTH markedly elevated at 880 pg/mL, upright plasma renin activity extremely elevated at 600 ng/mL/hour, sodium 130 mEq/L, potassium 6.2 mEq/L, urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL with creatinine 2.5 mg/dL, pH 7.32 with bicarbonate 18 mEq/L and glucose at the low normal limit. CT of the adrenal glands demonstrates bilateral subacute adrenal haemorrhage, which is the cause, arising in the setting of penetrating chest trauma and subsequent surgery; autoimmune, tuberculous, infiltrative and pituitary causes are excluded by negative adrenal antibodies, a negative PPD with a normal chest radiograph, a normal ferritin, and the elevated ACTH. This is an immediately life-threatening endocrine emergency requiring parenteral glucocorticoid and fluid resuscitation without delay.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Treat immediately; do not wait for further confirmatory testing, since he is already in adrenal crisis with shock, hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury. Establish intravenous access, draw a cortisol and ACTH sample if not already taken, and give parenteral hydrocortisone at once as a stress dose, followed by continued regular parenteral hydrocortisone or a continuous infusion until he is stable and tolerating oral intake. Resuscitate aggressively with intravenous isotonic saline to correct the profound volume depletion, guided by blood pressure, heart rate, peripheral perfusion and urine output; this alone will begin to correct the hyponatraemia, the hyperkalaemia and the prerenal acute kidney injury. Monitor the capillary glucose frequently and give intravenous dextrose if hypoglycaemia develops, since cortisol deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis. Obtain an urgent ECG and cardiac monitoring for the potassium of 6.2 mEq/L and treat the hyperkalaemia if there are ECG changes, recognising that volume repletion and glucocorticoid replacement will correct it as the underlying cause is addressed. Admit to a monitored bed with critical care involvement and refer urgently to endocrinology. Address the additional considerations explicitly: (1) correct the hyponatraemia of 130 mEq/L gradually and monitor the sodium closely during hydrocortisone and saline therapy, since cortisol replacement removes the stimulus to antidiuretic hormone release and can cause a rapid rise in sodium with the risk of osmotic demyelination; (2) once stabilised, transition to oral maintenance glucocorticoid in divided doses mimicking the diurnal rhythm and add mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone, which is necessary in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency and is indicated here by the renin activity of 600 ng/mL/hour, the hyponatraemia and the hyperkalaemia; titrate the fludrocortisone against blood pressure, postural symptoms, sodium, potassium and renin, and allow liberal salt intake; (3) provide comprehensive patient education before discharge — sick-day rules with doubling or tripling of the glucocorticoid dose during febrile illness, injury or surgical procedures, the need for parenteral hydrocortisone if vomiting prevents oral absorption, and prompt presentation for illness; (4) supply an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit and train the patient and his wife in its use, and provide a steroid emergency card and a medical alert bracelet; (5) evaluate the temperature of 37.8 C and the white cell count of 11,800 cells/mcL with blood and urine cultures and treat any identified infection, since infection is both a common precipitant of crisis and a consequence of untreated cortisol deficiency; (6) review the acute kidney injury after resuscitation and confirm the creatinine returns toward normal; (7) stop cyclizine once the underlying cause is treated, since the nausea will resolve with hormone replacement and the antiemetic was masking the diagnosis; (8) reassess the low mood after replacement is established, as it is likely a manifestation of untreated adrenal insufficiency and should improve; (9) determine whether the adrenal haemorrhage was purely traumatic or whether there is an underlying coagulopathy or thrombophilia that requires investigation; (10) advise on smoking cessation given his one pack per day for ten years; (11) arrange lifelong endocrine follow-up with periodic assessment of replacement adequacy, and counsel that a small proportion of patients recover partial adrenal function after haemorrhage, so adrenal reserve may be reassessed later by the specialist team, but replacement must not be stopped on the patient's own initiative.
Notes: The recorded blood pressure of 75/92 mm Hg is internally inconsistent and is interpreted as a transcription error; the clinical picture of tachycardia, cold peripheries, delayed capillary refill, flat neck veins and postural symptoms confirms hypotension and shock. Treatment with parenteral hydrocortisone must not be delayed for any test result. This presentation was missed three weeks after surgery when unexplained hypotension was attributed to suspected pulmonary embolism; unexplained hypotension with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia should always prompt consideration of adrenal insufficiency. Sodium correction must be gradual once glucocorticoid replacement begins.

The 9 AM ACTH is 880 pg/mL against a normal of 10 to 60 pg/mL, roughly fifteen-fold elevated, which localises the lesion to the adrenal gland itself and excludes secondary or tertiary insufficiency. The upright plasma renin activity is 600 ng/mL/hour against a normal of 2.9 to 10.8, an extreme elevation confirming aldosterone deficiency with consequent sodium wasting and volume depletion. This mineralocorticoid failure is the reason primary adrenal insufficiency, unlike secondary, produces the salt-losing picture seen here.

The electrolyte and metabolic pattern follows directly. The sodium is 130 mEq/L and the potassium is 6.2 mEq/L: hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia is the classic combination of aldosterone deficiency and is the pattern that should prompt consideration of Addison disease in any patient. The pH is 7.32 with a bicarbonate of 18 mEq/L, a mild metabolic acidosis consistent with mineralocorticoid deficiency and hypovolaemia, with a normal lactate of 1.4 mmol/L indicating that tissue hypoperfusion is not yet severe. The urea nitrogen of 42 mg/dL with a creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL shows acute kidney injury with a disproportionately raised urea, the signature of profound volume depletion in a 29-year-old man. The glucose of 75.6 mg/dL is at the low end of normal, consistent with cortisol deficiency impairing gluconeogenesis, and represents a hypoglycaemia risk. The white cell count of 11,800 cells/mcL and the temperature of 37.8 C are consistent with the stress state of crisis rather than proven infection.

The haemodynamics confirm crisis: a pulse of 112 beats/min with cold peripheries and delayed capillary refill, a jugular venous pressure not visible at 45 degrees, and hypotension. The recorded blood pressure of 75/92 mm Hg is internally impossible as written and is evidently a transcription error, but the systolic value of 75 mm Hg together with the tachycardia, cold peripheries, flat neck veins and postural symptoms establishes shock from hypovolaemia.

The cause is established by the CT of the adrenal glands, reported as bilateral subacute adrenal haemorrhage. This ties the entire presentation to the history. The patient sustained a stab wound to the left chest six months ago and underwent repair of a resulting diaphragmatic hernia two months ago; his symptoms began immediately after that surgery. Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in the setting of major trauma and surgery destroyed sufficient adrenal cortex to produce insufficiency, and the two-month tempo matches a subacute rather than fulminant destruction.

The case also documents a missed opportunity that is instructive. Three weeks after surgery he attended the emergency department with sharp right-sided chest pain and was noted to be hypotensive; a CT of the chest was performed to exclude pulmonary embolism and was negative, and he was discharged on an antiemetic and acetaminophen. The hypotension was the early manifestation of evolving adrenal insufficiency and was not investigated; the cyclizine he was prescribed then treated the symptom of nausea while the underlying disorder progressed for a further two months.

Alternative causes of primary adrenal insufficiency were systematically excluded by the investigations. Autoimmune adrenalitis, the commonest cause in developed countries, is excluded by negative anti-adrenal cortex antibodies; the family history of maternal primary hypothyroidism raised this possibility, but his own thyroid function is normal with a TSH of 0.9 mU/L and a free T4 of 1.6 ng/dL. Tuberculous adrenalitis is not supported: the PPD is negative and the chest radiograph is normal. Haemochromatosis is excluded by a normal ferritin. Metastatic infiltration is not suggested by the imaging, which shows haemorrhage. Myasthenia gravis was considered in the differential of generalized weakness and is not supported, with normal acetylcholine esterase levels and a normal neurological examination including normal power, tone, reflexes and cranial nerves. Adrenoleukodystrophy would be accompanied by neurological findings that are absent. Testicular function is preserved with a testosterone of 320 ng/dL, LH of 4.4 and FSH within range, and prolactin is normal at 12.3 ng/mL, all arguing against a broader pituitary process. Other differentials for the presenting syndrome — occult malignancy, chronic infection, depression as a primary cause of the weight loss and lethargy, and a gastrointestinal cause of the vomiting and abdominal pain — are all excluded by the definitive hormonal results.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring with an immediate ECG to assess for the changes of hyperkalaemia at a potassium of 6.2 mEq/L; frequent blood pressure, heart rate and urine output monitoring; bedside capillary glucose measurement with serial testing given the hypoglycaemia risk; serial serum electrolytes, urea, creatinine and venous blood gases to follow the response to resuscitation; a paired aldosterone level with the plasma renin activity to document mineralocorticoid deficiency; a random cortisol drawn before the first hydrocortisone dose if not already available; septic screen with blood and urine cultures given the temperature of 37.8 C and leucocytosis, to identify any precipitant; repeat or review of the adrenal CT to characterise the haemorrhage and follow its evolution; coagulation screen and, if the haemorrhage is otherwise unexplained, testing for antiphospholipid syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; renal ultrasound if the acute kidney injury does not resolve with volume repletion; 17-hydroxyprogesterone and very long chain fatty acids only if the aetiology remained in doubt, which it does not here.

Conclusion: A 29-year-old man presents two months after repair of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia with weight loss of 12 kg, lethargy, weakness, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, postural dizziness and new hyperpigmentation of the nipples and knuckles, and is found to be in shock with tachycardia at 112 beats/min, hypotension, cold peripheries and flat neck veins. Investigations establish primary adrenal insufficiency in adrenal crisis: 9 AM cortisol 1.8 mcg/dL with a flat short Synacthen response (1.4 to 1.9 mcg/dL), ACTH markedly elevated at 880 pg/mL, upright plasma renin activity extremely elevated at 600 ng/mL/hour, sodium 130 mEq/L, potassium 6.2 mEq/L, urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL with creatinine 2.5 mg/dL, pH 7.32 with bicarbonate 18 mEq/L and glucose at the low normal limit. CT of the adrenal glands demonstrates bilateral subacute adrenal haemorrhage, which is the cause, arising in the setting of penetrating chest trauma and subsequent surgery; autoimmune, tuberculous, infiltrative and pituitary causes are excluded by negative adrenal antibodies, a negative PPD with a normal chest radiograph, a normal ferritin, and the elevated ACTH. This is an immediately life-threatening endocrine emergency requiring parenteral glucocorticoid and fluid resuscitation without delay.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Treat immediately; do not wait for further confirmatory testing, since he is already in adrenal crisis with shock, hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury. Establish intravenous access, draw a cortisol and ACTH sample if not already taken, and give parenteral hydrocortisone at once as a stress dose, followed by continued regular parenteral hydrocortisone or a continuous infusion until he is stable and tolerating oral intake. Resuscitate aggressively with intravenous isotonic saline to correct the profound volume depletion, guided by blood pressure, heart rate, peripheral perfusion and urine output; this alone will begin to correct the hyponatraemia, the hyperkalaemia and the prerenal acute kidney injury. Monitor the capillary glucose frequently and give intravenous dextrose if hypoglycaemia develops, since cortisol deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis. Obtain an urgent ECG and cardiac monitoring for the potassium of 6.2 mEq/L and treat the hyperkalaemia if there are ECG changes, recognising that volume repletion and glucocorticoid replacement will correct it as the underlying cause is addressed. Admit to a monitored bed with critical care involvement and refer urgently to endocrinology. Address the additional considerations explicitly: (1) correct the hyponatraemia of 130 mEq/L gradually and monitor the sodium closely during hydrocortisone and saline therapy, since cortisol replacement removes the stimulus to antidiuretic hormone release and can cause a rapid rise in sodium with the risk of osmotic demyelination; (2) once stabilised, transition to oral maintenance glucocorticoid in divided doses mimicking the diurnal rhythm and add mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone, which is necessary in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency and is indicated here by the renin activity of 600 ng/mL/hour, the hyponatraemia and the hyperkalaemia; titrate the fludrocortisone against blood pressure, postural symptoms, sodium, potassium and renin, and allow liberal salt intake; (3) provide comprehensive patient education before discharge — sick-day rules with doubling or tripling of the glucocorticoid dose during febrile illness, injury or surgical procedures, the need for parenteral hydrocortisone if vomiting prevents oral absorption, and prompt presentation for illness; (4) supply an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit and train the patient and his wife in its use, and provide a steroid emergency card and a medical alert bracelet; (5) evaluate the temperature of 37.8 C and the white cell count of 11,800 cells/mcL with blood and urine cultures and treat any identified infection, since infection is both a common precipitant of crisis and a consequence of untreated cortisol deficiency; (6) review the acute kidney injury after resuscitation and confirm the creatinine returns toward normal; (7) stop cyclizine once the underlying cause is treated, since the nausea will resolve with hormone replacement and the antiemetic was masking the diagnosis; (8) reassess the low mood after replacement is established, as it is likely a manifestation of untreated adrenal insufficiency and should improve; (9) determine whether the adrenal haemorrhage was purely traumatic or whether there is an underlying coagulopathy or thrombophilia that requires investigation; (10) advise on smoking cessation given his one pack per day for ten years; (11) arrange lifelong endocrine follow-up with periodic assessment of replacement adequacy, and counsel that a small proportion of patients recover partial adrenal function after haemorrhage, so adrenal reserve may be reassessed later by the specialist team, but replacement must not be stopped on the patient's own initiative.
Notes: The recorded blood pressure of 75/92 mm Hg is internally inconsistent and is interpreted as a transcription error; the clinical picture of tachycardia, cold peripheries, delayed capillary refill, flat neck veins and postural symptoms confirms hypotension and shock. Treatment with parenteral hydrocortisone must not be delayed for any test result. This presentation was missed three weeks after surgery when unexplained hypotension was attributed to suspected pulmonary embolism; unexplained hypotension with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia should always prompt consideration of adrenal insufficiency. Sodium correction must be gradual once glucocorticoid replacement begins.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for the past 12 years presents with a 4-month history of progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue, and difficulty with balance. She reports her tongue has been sore intermittently. She has noticed increased forgetfulness and mild cognitive slowing. She takes no supplements. On examination, vital signs are normal. She appears pale with a smooth, beefy red tongue (glossitis). Neurological examination reveals diminished vibration and proprioception in both feet and ankles, absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Gait is wide-based and mildly ataxic. baseline_protocol:
Age: 68 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Four-month history of progressive tingling and numbness in both feet, fatigue and difficulty with balance, with intermittent sore tongue, increased forgetfulness and mild cognitive slowing, in a woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for 12 years without taking any supplements.

Analysis: This is severe vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency causing megaloblastic anaemia, glossitis, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and cognitive impairment, on a background of 12 years of unsupplemented strict veganism.

The dietary history is the key aetiological fact. Vitamin B12 is available almost exclusively from animal-derived foods; a strict vegan diet with no supplementation is a well-recognised cause of dietary deficiency. Hepatic stores are large, which is why deficiency takes years to become symptomatic, and a 12-year exposure is entirely consistent with the emergence of symptoms now.

The biochemical diagnosis is unequivocal and confirmed at three levels. The serum B12 is 85 pg/mL against a normal range of 200 to 900, a critically low value. More importantly, the functional metabolites confirm true tissue deficiency rather than a spuriously low assay: both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are elevated. This pattern is decisive. B12 is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and for methionine synthase; deficiency blocks both reactions, so methylmalonic acid and homocysteine accumulate together. This combination distinguishes B12 deficiency from folate deficiency, in which homocysteine rises but methylmalonic acid remains normal, and it is the single most useful discriminator between the two, since both produce an identical megaloblastic blood picture.

The haematological findings are classical for megaloblastic anaemia. The haemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL, a marked macrocytosis. The peripheral smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; hypersegmentation is a specific marker of megaloblastic maturation and reflects impaired DNA synthesis with continued cytoplasmic maturation. Her pallor is the clinical correlate.

The mucosal manifestation is the smooth, beefy red tongue with atrophic glossitis, corresponding to her intermittent sore tongue, and results from impaired turnover of the rapidly dividing epithelium.

The neurological findings are the most important part of the presentation, because they determine urgency and prognosis. The examination localises the lesion to the dorsal columns: diminished vibration sense and proprioception in both feet and ankles, a positive Romberg sign indicating that balance is dependent on visual compensation for lost proprioceptive input, and a wide-based mildly ataxic gait that is sensory rather than cerebellar in origin. The absent ankle reflexes indicate an accompanying peripheral neuropathy affecting the longest nerves first, consistent with the length-dependent distal tingling and numbness. This combination of dorsal column and peripheral nerve involvement is subacute combined degeneration of the cord, caused by defective myelin synthesis. The upper extremity examination is normal, which is consistent with a length-dependent process that has not yet ascended. The forgetfulness and cognitive slowing represent the central nervous system manifestation of the same deficiency and are potentially reversible.

Differential considerations that were weighed. Folate deficiency produces an identical macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia with glossitis but does not cause subacute combined degeneration and does not raise methylmalonic acid; it is therefore excluded by the elevated methylmalonic acid, though folate should still be measured. Pernicious anaemia due to autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor is the commonest cause of B12 deficiency in this age group and produces an identical clinical and biochemical picture; the dietary history makes nutritional deficiency the likely mechanism here, but the two are not mutually exclusive and pernicious anaemia must be actively excluded in a 68-year-old, because it changes lifelong management. Other causes of malabsorption warrant consideration, including atrophic gastritis, previous gastric or ileal surgery, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth and metformin or proton pump inhibitor use, none of which is described. Alternative explanations for the neurological picture include diabetic or other peripheral neuropathy, alcohol-related neuropathy, hypothyroidism, copper deficiency which can produce an identical myelopathy, tabes dorsalis, and cervical spondylotic myelopathy; the concurrent megaloblastic anaemia, glossitis and the metabolite profile make B12 deficiency the unifying diagnosis, but the cognitive changes should not be attributed to a primary dementia before treatment and reassessment. Other causes of macrocytosis such as alcohol excess, hypothyroidism, liver disease and myelodysplastic syndrome do not explain the low B12 with raised metabolites.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum and red cell folate, and serum iron studies with ferritin, since concurrent deficiencies are common in long-term veganism and iron deficiency can mask macrocytosis; intrinsic factor antibodies and anti-parietal cell antibodies to exclude pernicious anaemia; serum gastrin and consideration of upper endoscopy with biopsy if autoimmune atrophic gastritis is suspected; thyroid function tests; reticulocyte count before and after starting treatment to document the haematological response; serum potassium at baseline and monitored during the first days of treatment; renal and liver function; serum copper and ceruloplasmin if the myelopathy does not respond to B12 replacement; vitamin D, calcium and iodine status given the long-term unsupplemented vegan diet; MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine if the myelopathy is atypical, progresses, or fails to improve, to look for dorsal column signal change and exclude a compressive lesion; formal cognitive assessment now as a baseline for later comparison; ECG only if anaemia-related cardiac symptoms emerge.

Conclusion: A 68-year-old woman on an unsupplemented strict vegan diet for 12 years has severe vitamin B12 deficiency with a serum B12 of 85 pg/mL and elevation of both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirming functional deficiency. Age: 42 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Eight hours of severe, constant epigastric pain rated 9 out of 10, radiating straight through to the back, beginning after a fatty meal, with persistent nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting, in a woman with known cholelithiasis who declined elective cholecystectomy six months ago.

Analysis: This is acute gallstone pancreatitis of moderate to severe grade, with evidence of concurrent biliary obstruction and early systemic compromise.

The diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is established beyond doubt. Two of the three standard diagnostic criteria are met independently and the third confirms them. First, the pain is characteristic: severe, constant, epigastric, boring straight through to the back, and the patient lies very still with her knees drawn up, the classic posture adopted because the retroperitoneal position of the pancreas makes the pain worse on lying flat and eased by flexion. Second, the lipase is 2,840 U/L against a normal below 60, roughly forty-seven times the upper limit, far exceeding the threefold elevation required for diagnosis; lipase is more specific and remains elevated longer than amylase. Third, the CT of the abdomen demonstrates a diffusely oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid collections, which is confirmatory imaging.

The aetiology is gallstones, and this is established by convergent evidence. She has documented cholelithiasis diagnosed six months ago and declined elective cholecystectomy, leaving her at continued risk of exactly this complication. The pain began after a fatty meal, the classic precipitant for gallbladder contraction and stone migration. Most importantly, the liver chemistry shows an obstructive and hepatocellular pattern with an AST of 210 U/L, ALT of 185 U/L and a total bilirubin of 3.2 mg/dL. An ALT elevation of this degree in acute pancreatitis has a high positive predictive value for a biliary aetiology, and the raised bilirubin indicates that a stone is obstructing, or has recently obstructed, the common bile duct. Alcohol, the other common cause, is not mentioned; hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia (her calcium is low, not high), drugs, trauma and post-ERCP causes are not supported by anything in the case.

The severity assessment is the decisive clinical judgement here, and multiple independent markers indicate that this is not mild pancreatitis. The BISAP score is 3, which places her in a higher mortality category and identifies her as at risk of severe disease. She has a systemic inflammatory response with a temperature of 38.2 C, a heart rate of 116 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min and a white cell count of 16,200/mcL. criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
