Vignette:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with 4 days of profuse watery diarrhea (10-12 episodes daily) and vomiting (6-8 episodes daily). They report he has been increasingly listless and has had no wet diapers in the past 10 hours. He recently started daycare and several children there have been ill with gastroenteritis. On examination, the infant is limp and lethargic with a weak, barely audible cry. Vital signs: T 38.2C, HR 182, RR 32, BP 68/38 (hypotensive for age), capillary refill 5 seconds. The anterior fontanelle is markedly sunken. Eyes appear deeply sunken with absent tears. Mucous membranes are parched. Skin tenting persists for more than 3 seconds when pinched. Weight is 9.8 kg (previous weight at well-child visit 2 weeks ago was 11.2 kg, representing a 12.5% weight loss). Labs: sodium 158 mEq/L, potassium 2.8 mEq/L, BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (elevated for age), bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, glucose 62 mg/dL. IV normal saline bolus 20 mL/kg is initiated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 18 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Four days of profuse watery diarrhoea (10 to 12 episodes daily) and vomiting (6 to 8 episodes daily) with progressive listlessness and no wet nappies for the past 10 hours, following recent entry into a daycare where several children have had gastroenteritis.

Analysis: This child has severe hypernatraemic dehydration with hypovolaemic shock, complicating acute infectious gastroenteritis, and he is in immediate danger of death.

The degree of fluid loss is quantified objectively rather than estimated. His weight is 9.8 kg against a documented 11.2 kg at a well-child visit two weeks ago, a loss of 1.4 kg or 12.5 percent of body weight over four days. In a child of this age, acute weight loss of this magnitude is essentially all fluid, and a deficit above 10 percent defines severe dehydration. This measured weight change is the single most reliable index of the deficit available and is far superior to clinical estimation.

The examination confirms severe dehydration at every point. The anterior fontanelle is markedly sunken, the eyes are deeply sunken with absent tears, the mucous membranes are parched, and skin tenting persists for more than three seconds, which indicates markedly reduced skin turgor. There have been no wet nappies for ten hours, indicating anuria or profound oliguria.

More importantly, he is not merely dehydrated but in decompensated hypovolaemic shock. The heart rate of 182 beats/min is markedly tachycardic even for an 18-month-old, the capillary refill is prolonged at five seconds indicating grossly impaired peripheral perfusion, and the blood pressure of 68/38 mm Hg is hypotensive for age. Hypotension is a late and ominous sign in paediatric shock, because children maintain blood pressure through intense vasoconstriction and tachycardia until compensation fails; its appearance means that decompensation has already occurred. The neurological state confirms this: he is limp and lethargic with a weak, barely audible cry, indicating impaired cerebral perfusion and an obtunded conscious level.

The biochemistry defines the type of dehydration and the specific dangers. The sodium of 158 mEq/L establishes hypernatraemic dehydration, meaning free water has been lost in excess of sodium, which occurs when profuse watery diarrhoea is combined with vomiting that prevents adequate water replacement. This is clinically crucial for two reasons. First, in hypernatraemic dehydration the extracellular osmolality is high and water shifts out of cells into the extracellular compartment, which partially preserves intravascular volume and masks the true severity of the deficit; the fact that he is nonetheless shocked means the deficit is enormous. Second, the brain generates idiogenic osmoles to protect cell volume during hypernatraemia, so if the serum sodium is lowered too quickly, water rushes into brain cells and causes cerebral oedema, seizures and death. The rate of sodium correction is therefore the central management issue after shock is reversed.

The potassium of 2.8 mEq/L is significant hypokalaemia from gastrointestinal losses in both stool and vomitus, compounded by any secondary hyperaldosteronism. It carries a risk of arrhythmia, ileus and muscle weakness, and it will fall further when acidosis is corrected and potassium shifts back into cells.

The bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L indicates a metabolic acidosis, arising both from bicarbonate loss in diarrhoeal stool and from lactic acidosis due to tissue hypoperfusion in shock; the respiratory rate of 32 breaths/min represents partial respiratory compensation.

The urea nitrogen of 42 mg/dL with a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, which is elevated for an 18-month-old, indicates acute kidney injury. The pattern with a disproportionately raised urea is consistent with a prerenal cause from volume depletion, though the duration and severity raise concern for established acute tubular injury.

The glucose of 62 mg/dL is low and reflects depleted glycogen stores with poor intake over four days; young children have limited reserves and are prone to hypoglycaemia during acute illness, which can itself contribute to lethargy.

The aetiology is almost certainly viral gastroenteritis. The epidemiology is decisive: he recently started daycare and several children there have been ill with gastroenteritis, establishing a clear exposure with person-to-person spread. The clinical pattern of profuse watery, non-bloody diarrhoea with prominent vomiting and low-grade fever at 38.2 C in a child of this age is characteristic of rotavirus or norovirus.

Differential considerations weighed. Bacterial enteritis is possible but less likely with watery non-bloody stool, no mention of blood or mucus, and only a low-grade fever. Diabetic ketoacidosis is excluded by the glucose of 62 mg/dL. Other causes of shock in a toddler include sepsis, which must remain a consideration given the fever and obtundation and should be treated if there is any doubt, and surgical causes such as intussusception, which classically presents with intermittent severe pain, drawing up of the legs and bloody stools, none described here. Diabetes insipidus, salt poisoning or an inappropriately prepared hypertonic feed can cause hypernatraemia and should be considered if the history did not so clearly explain the losses. Non-accidental injury or neglect is not suggested here, since the parents brought him for care and the illness has an obvious infectious explanation.

The initial management already begun is correct: an intravenous bolus of normal saline at 20 mL/kg is the appropriate first action, since restoring circulating volume takes absolute priority over concerns about the rate of sodium correction while the child is shocked.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac, respiratory and oxygen saturation monitoring with frequent blood pressure measurement and strict input and output charting, with urinary catheterisation to measure urine output accurately; frequent bedside capillary glucose measurement; serial serum sodium measurement at least every two to four hours during rehydration, which is the essential monitoring test governing the rate of fluid administration; serial electrolytes including potassium, chloride, calcium and magnesium, with urea and creatinine; blood gas with lactate to assess perfusion and the acidosis; complete blood count; serum osmolality and paired urine osmolality, urine sodium and urine specific gravity to characterise the renal response; ECG to assess for changes of hypokalaemia; stool studies including viral antigen or PCR testing and bacterial culture if the stool is bloody or the course atypical; blood culture and full septic screen if sepsis is considered; daily weights on the same scale as the objective measure of rehydration progress; head imaging only if seizures or a deteriorating conscious level occur during correction, to assess for cerebral oedema.

Conclusion: An 18-month-old boy with four days of profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting, acquired from a daycare outbreak of gastroenteritis, presents in decompensated hypovolaemic shock with severe hypernatraemic dehydration. The deficit is objectively quantified as 12.5 percent of body weight (11.2 kg falling to 9.8 kg). Shock is established by a heart rate of 182 beats/min, capillary refill of five seconds, hypotension at 68/38 mm Hg and an obtunded, limp child with a weak cry, and the dehydration is confirmed by a markedly sunken fontanelle, deeply sunken eyes without tears, parched mucous membranes and skin tenting beyond three seconds, with no urine output for ten hours. Biochemistry shows hypernatraemia at 158 mEq/L, hypokalaemia at 2.8 mEq/L, metabolic acidosis with a bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L, acute kidney injury with a urea nitrogen of 42 mg/dL and a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL that is elevated for age, and hypoglycaemia at 62 mg/dL. The initiated 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus is appropriate. This is a life-threatening emergency in which the priorities are restoration of circulating volume first, then deliberately slow correction of the hypernatraemia to avoid cerebral oedema, alongside correction of hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Manage in a resuscitation area with immediate escalation to paediatric intensive care; this child is in decompensated shock and requires senior paediatric involvement now. Continue isotonic fluid resuscitation with 20 mL/kg boluses of normal saline, repeated and reassessed after each bolus against heart rate, capillary refill, blood pressure, conscious level and urine output, until perfusion is restored; do not withhold or slow boluses out of concern for the sodium while shock persists, because uncorrected shock kills faster than the hypernatraemia and isotonic saline at a sodium of 154 mEq/L is close to his serum sodium and will not drop it abruptly. Secure reliable vascular access immediately and use intraosseous access without hesitation if intravenous access is difficult. Treat the hypoglycaemia of 62 mg/dL with an appropriate weight-based dextrose bolus and then include dextrose in maintenance fluids, monitoring the glucose frequently. Address the additional considerations explicitly: (1) once shock is reversed, correct the hypernatraemia slowly — the serum sodium should fall by no more than about 0.5 mEq/L per hour, or approximately 10 to 12 mEq/L in 24 hours, with the total deficit replaced over 48 hours or longer; measure the sodium every two to four hours and slow the infusion or increase the sodium content of the fluid if it is falling faster than the target, because rapid correction causes cerebral oedema, seizures and death; (2) replace potassium once urine output is established and renal function confirmed — the potassium of 2.8 mEq/L will fall further as the acidosis corrects and potassium re-enters cells, so add potassium to maintenance fluids with cardiac monitoring, and check magnesium and calcium since hypomagnesaemia perpetuates hypokalaemia; (3) do not give bicarbonate for the acidosis; the bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L reflects stool losses and hypoperfusion and will correct as perfusion and renal function are restored, and bicarbonate administration risks worsening hypokalaemia and paradoxical intracellular acidosis; (4) monitor for seizures and any deterioration in conscious level during rehydration, and if these occur, stop or slow the correction, reassess the sodium urgently and treat as cerebral oedema; (5) follow the renal function serially — the acute kidney injury should improve with volume repletion, and failure to improve suggests established tubular injury requiring nephrology input; (6) do not use antidiarrhoeal or antimotility agents in a child of this age, and do not give routine antibiotics for a presentation consistent with viral gastroenteritis; antiemetics may be considered by the paediatric team to facilitate later oral rehydration, but sepsis must be excluded before ascribing everything to viral illness given the fever and obtundation, and empirical antibiotics should be given if sepsis is suspected; (7) reintroduce oral or nasogastric rehydration and normal age-appropriate feeding as early as tolerated once vomiting settles and the child is haemodynamically stable, since early feeding shortens illness duration; oral rehydration solution is preferred to plain water, and continued milk feeds should not be withheld; (8) weigh the child daily on the same scale, aiming to return toward the documented pre-illness weight of 11.2 kg as the objective marker of successful rehydration; (9) counsel the parents on infection control — strict hand hygiene, exclusion from daycare until 48 hours after symptoms resolve, and notification of the daycare given the ongoing outbreak — and review the child's rotavirus immunisation status; (10) give explicit discharge advice on the signs of recurrent dehydration, particularly reduced wet nappies, lethargy, absent tears and refusal of fluids, with instructions to return immediately, and arrange early clinical follow-up to confirm continued weight gain and recovery of renal function.
Notes: Restoration of circulating volume takes absolute priority over the rate of sodium correction while the child is in shock; the caution about slow correction applies to the rehydration phase that follows, not to the emergency boluses. Correcting a sodium of 158 mEq/L too rapidly can cause fatal cerebral oedema, so serial sodium measurement during rehydration is mandatory. Potassium must not be given until urine output is established. Hypotension in a child is a late sign of shock and indicates that compensatory mechanisms have already failed.

Vignette: A 40-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 2-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain. He describes the pain as a dull, gnawing ache. The pain sometimes wakes him at night, is relieved by food and drinking milk, and is helped partially by ranitidine. He had a similar but milder episode about 5 years ago, which was treated with omeprazole. Physical examination reveals a fit, apparently healthy man in no distress. The only abnormal finding is mild epigastric tenderness on palpation of the abdomen.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 2-month history of intermittent upper abdominal pain. He describes the pain as a dull, gnawing ache. The pain sometimes wakes him at night, is relieved by food and drinking milk, and is helped partially by ranitidine. He had a similar but milder episode about 5 years ago, which was treated with omeprazole. Physical examination reveals a fit, apparently healthy man in no distress. The only abnormal finding is mild epigastric tenderness on palpation of the abdomen.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 40 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two-month history of intermittent upper abdominal (epigastric) pain, described as a dull, gnawing ache, sometimes waking him at night, relieved by food and milk, and partially relieved by ranitidine.
Analysis: The symptom pattern is highly characteristic of acid-peptic disease, specifically duodenal ulcer. The strongest supporting facts are: (1) dull, gnawing epigastric pain that is chronic and intermittent over two months; (2) nocturnal pain awakening the patient, which reflects unopposed nocturnal acid secretion; (3) relief with food and milk, the classic buffering pattern of duodenal ulcer rather than gastric ulcer, where food more typically provokes pain; (4) partial response to ranitidine, an H2-receptor antagonist, confirming an acid-related mechanism; (5) a similar milder episode five years ago that responded to omeprazole, indicating a relapsing acid-peptic disorder rather than a new process; and (6) isolated mild epigastric tenderness as the only abnormal physical finding, with an otherwise fit, healthy, non-distressed appearance. Main differential considerations grounded in this presentation include duodenal ulcer (most likely), gastric ulcer, functional (non-ulcer) dyspepsia, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Because relapsing peptic ulcer disease in a patient of this age is most often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID exposure, aetiological assessment is required; NSAID use is not specified in this case. The absence of alarm features in the case is reassuring: no reported weight loss, vomiting, dysphagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, anaemia, palpable mass, or systemic illness, and no signs of perforation such as peritonism, guarding, or rigidity, and no distress. This argues against complicated ulcer disease or malignancy at present, though the recurrent nature and duration warrant definitive diagnosis and eradication of any underlying infection rather than continued empirical symptomatic suppression.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Helicobacter pylori testing (urea breath test or stool antigen test, performed after an adequate interval off acid-suppressing therapy to avoid false negatives); full blood count to exclude anaemia from occult blood loss; upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (oesophagogastroduodenoscopy) with biopsy if symptoms persist or recur after treatment, if alarm features develop, or to confirm ulcer healing and exclude malignancy; endoscopy equipment with biopsy forceps and rapid urease testing capability for that purpose.
Conclusion: A fit 40-year-old man with a two-month history of chronic, relapsing, food- and antacid-responsive, nocturnal epigastric pain and isolated mild epigastric tenderness, on a background of a similar episode five years ago responsive to omeprazole. The clinical picture is that of uncomplicated acid-peptic disease, most consistent with duodenal ulcer, without alarm features or evidence of complication. Management should move from empirical symptom suppression to establishing the aetiology, principally Helicobacter pylori status, and treating it definitively.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Arrange outpatient testing for Helicobacter pylori by urea breath test or stool antigen assay, ensuring the patient has stopped H2-blocker and proton pump inhibitor therapy for the appropriate washout interval beforehand so the result is valid. If positive, treat with a standard eradication regimen combining a proton pump inhibitor with appropriate antibiotics, then confirm eradication by repeat non-invasive testing after completing therapy. Start or continue a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole for symptom control, given the documented prior response, in preference to ranitidine, which has produced only partial relief in this episode. Take a careful medication history for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and aspirin, including over-the-counter preparations, and stop them if identified; avoid NSAIDs going forward given relapsing ulcer disease. Advise on lifestyle contributors: avoid smoking and alcohol, limit foods that reproduce his symptoms, and avoid large late-evening meals given the nocturnal pain. Explain that milk gives only transient relief and produces rebound acid secretion, so it should not be used as ongoing therapy. Arrange follow-up in four to eight weeks to assess symptom response. Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy if symptoms fail to settle on adequate acid suppression, recur after eradication, or if any alarm feature develops. Regarding additional considerations, counsel the patient explicitly to seek urgent medical attention for sudden severe or generalized abdominal pain, vomiting of blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stools, persistent vomiting, difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss, or faintness, as these would indicate ulcer complications such as bleeding, perforation, or gastric outlet obstruction and would convert this into an emergency presentation.
Notes: The prior five-year-old episode and the current relapse indicate recurrent rather than first-presentation disease, which strengthens the case for definitive aetiological diagnosis and eradication rather than repeated empirical courses of acid suppression. Acid-suppressing drugs already taken may cause false-negative Helicobacter pylori testing, so timing of the test relative to therapy is important. NSAID use, smoking, alcohol intake, family history, and alarm symptoms are not specified in the case and must be elicited directly.

Vignette:
An 18-year-old man presents with dry, cracked lips that have persisted for the past 2 weeks. He reports the condition worsened with the onset of cold, dry winter weather. He admits to habitual lip-licking throughout the day. He denies any angular fissures, oral lesions, recent new lip products, or medications such as isotretinoin. He has no history of atopic dermatitis. On examination, the vermilion border of both lips is dry with fine vertical fissures and mild peeling. There is no bleeding, crusting, or angular cheilitis. The perioral skin is mildly dry but not erythematous. The oral mucosa is normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 18 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Dry, cracked lips for two weeks, worsened by the onset of cold, dry winter weather, in a patient with a habit of licking his lips throughout the day.
Analysis: The presentation is that of a simple irritant contact cheilitis, specifically lip-licker's cheilitis compounded by environmental xerosis. The strongest supporting facts are the habitual repeated lip-licking, which strips the thin vermilion of its lipid barrier and causes evaporative water loss and irritation from salivary enzymes; the clear temporal association with the onset of cold, dry winter air, a well-recognised aggravator of transepidermal water loss at the lips; the short two-week duration; and the entirely benign examination showing only dryness of the vermilion border of both lips with fine vertical fissures and mild peeling, with mildly dry but non-erythematous perioral skin. Several important alternative causes are explicitly excluded by the history and examination. Angular cheilitis, which would suggest candidal or bacterial infection or nutritional deficiency such as iron or B-vitamin deficiency, is absent both by history and on examination. Allergic contact cheilitis is unlikely as he denies any recent new lip products. Drug-induced cheilitis, notably from isotretinoin, is excluded by history. Atopic cheilitis is unlikely given no history of atopic dermatitis. There are no oral lesions and the oral mucosa is normal, arguing against a mucocutaneous disorder such as lichen planus or an infectious stomatitis. There is no bleeding or crusting, which argues against impetiginisation or herpes labialis. There is no induration, ulceration, persistent scaling plaque, or leukoplakia to suggest actinic cheilitis or malignancy, which would in any case be very unlikely at 18 years. The condition is symmetrical, superficial, self-limited in character, and directly attributable to a modifiable behaviour and modifiable environmental exposure.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: An 18-year-old man with a two-week history of bilateral dry, fissured, mildly peeling lips arising in cold, dry weather in the setting of habitual lip-licking. The findings are those of a benign, self-limited irritant contact cheilitis (lip-licker's cheilitis) with environmental xerosis. There are no features of infection, nutritional deficiency, allergic contact reaction, drug effect, or systemic or premalignant disease. The condition is expected to resolve with barrier restoration and cessation of the lip-licking habit, without any need for laboratory or imaging investigation.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Explain to the patient that lip-licking is the principal driver, because evaporating saliva removes moisture and its digestive enzymes irritate the vermilion, creating a cycle in which the lips feel dry, are licked, and become drier still. Advise deliberate cessation of the habit, using an emollient applied whenever the urge to lick occurs as a substitute behaviour. Apply a bland occlusive lip barrier such as white petrolatum or a petrolatum-based ointment frequently through the day, after eating and drinking, and particularly at bedtime, to restore the lipid barrier and allow the fissures to heal. Prefer plain occlusive ointments over flavoured, scented, or medicated lip balms containing agents such as menthol, camphor, phenol, salicylic acid, or fragrance, since these can perpetuate irritation and provoke further licking. Protect the lips from cold, dry, and windy conditions by covering the mouth with a scarf outdoors, and consider humidifying indoor air and maintaining adequate oral fluid intake during winter. Do not peel or bite off the loose scale, as this deepens the fissures and risks bleeding and secondary infection. Expect improvement within one to two weeks of consistent barrier care and habit cessation. Addressing the additional considerations: because there is no angular cheilitis, no oral lesion, no new product exposure, no isotretinoin or other implicated medication, and no atopic history, no laboratory testing, patch testing, swab for candida, or nutritional screening is indicated at this time. Seek medical review if the lips fail to improve after two to four weeks of proper care, or if new features develop, specifically fissuring or maceration at the mouth corners, yellow crusting, pustules, painful grouped vesicles, bleeding, swelling of the lips, a persistent single non-healing ulcer or thickened white patch, or if oral mucosal lesions, systemic symptoms, or a new medication or lip product coincide with worsening. At that point, targeted evaluation for candidal or bacterial infection, allergic contact cheilitis with patch testing, or nutritional deficiency would become appropriate.
Notes: This assessment is based only on the presentation described; management is behavioural and barrier-based, and no prescription therapy is indicated at present. Persistence beyond a few weeks despite adequate barrier care and habit cessation would warrant reassessment for an alternative cause.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 8 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute febrile illness with fever, chills, malaise, arthralgias, and headache, accompanied by a maculopapular rash most prominent on the wrists and ankles, presenting to the emergency department in Oklahoma over the Fourth of July weekend.
Analysis: The combination of an acute febrile systemic illness with headache, chills, malaise, and arthralgias together with a maculopapular rash that is most prominent acrally on the wrists and ankles is the classic presentation of Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a tick-borne rickettsiosis caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. Several features in this case converge strongly on that diagnosis. First, the rash distribution is the single most discriminating finding: an eruption that begins and is most marked on the distal extremities, at the wrists and ankles, is highly characteristic of rickettsial disease and is unusual for most other childhood exanthems, which typically spread centrifugally from the trunk or face. Second, the geography is highly supportive, as Oklahoma lies within the south-central region of the United States that carries among the highest incidence of Rocky Mountain spotted fever in the country. Third, the timing is supportive: early July falls squarely within the peak spring-to-summer season of tick activity and human outdoor exposure, and the holiday weekend implies outdoor recreational activity in an endemic area. Fourth, the age group is typical, with children in this age range disproportionately affected and at higher risk of severe outcomes. Fifth, the constitutional prodrome of fever, headache, myalgias and arthralgias preceding or accompanying a rash that appears a few days after fever onset fits the recognised natural history. The main differential considerations from the presenting features include other tick-borne illnesses endemic to the same region, particularly ehrlichiosis, which can produce a similar febrile illness with headache and, less often, a rash; meningococcaemia, which can present with fever, headache, malaise and a rash that may be maculopapular early before becoming petechial or purpuric, and which is also life-threatening; other viral exanthems and enteroviral infections, which are common in summer in children; drug eruption; and less likely, secondary syphilis or measles, neither of which fits this acute presentation and age in the way rickettsial disease does. The critical clinical point is that Rocky Mountain spotted fever is rapidly progressive and potentially fatal, causing a systemic small-vessel vasculitis that can lead to vascular leak, shock, meningoencephalitis, pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, and multi-organ failure, with mortality concentrated in patients whose treatment is delayed. Diagnosis in the acute phase is clinical and epidemiological, because serology is often negative in the first week of illness and confirmatory testing is retrospective. Therefore therapy must not be withheld pending laboratory confirmation. It should also be noted that the rash may be absent or atypical early in the course, so its presence here supports but is not required for the diagnosis, and its acral prominence at this stage should be regarded as a warning sign rather than a reassurance.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Full blood count with differential and platelet count, looking for thrombocytopenia, leukopenia or a normal white cell count with a left shift, and anaemia; serum electrolytes with particular attention to hyponatraemia; renal function tests including urea and creatinine; liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin; coagulation studies; C-reactive protein; blood cultures to evaluate for bacteraemia and meningococcal disease; serology for Rickettsia rickettsii by indirect immunofluorescence antibody assay on acute serum with a paired convalescent sample two to four weeks later; polymerase chain reaction testing on whole blood, and skin biopsy of a rash lesion for immunohistochemistry or PCR if available, for early confirmation; serology or PCR for Ehrlichia given the overlapping regional epidemiology; lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid analysis if meningismus, altered mental status, or other neurological signs are present or develop; continuous vital sign and haemodynamic monitoring; pulse oximetry; and chest radiography if respiratory signs develop.
Conclusion: An 8-year-old boy in an endemic region of Oklahoma presents in peak tick season with an acute febrile illness comprising fever, chills, malaise, headache and arthralgias, together with a maculopapular rash maximal on the wrists and ankles. The condition is a potentially fatal rickettsial vasculitis in which outcome depends critically on how early treatment is started, and in which laboratory confirmation is typically unavailable during the window when treatment matters most. Vignette:
A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of bloating, excessive gas, and loose stools that occur approximately 30 minutes after consuming dairy products. She first noticed the pattern about 6 months ago. She denies symptoms when avoiding dairy. She has no abdominal pain between episodes, no blood in stool, no weight loss, and no fever. She has no family history of inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease. On examination, the abdomen is soft, mildly distended with tympany to percussion, and non-tender. Bowel sounds are active. No masses or organomegaly are noted.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 22 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Six-month history of recurrent bloating, excessive flatulence, and loose stools beginning about 30 minutes after consuming dairy products, with complete resolution of symptoms when dairy is avoided.
Analysis: The history is essentially diagnostic of lactose intolerance due to lactase deficiency. The strongest supporting facts are the tight and reproducible temporal relationship between dairy ingestion and symptom onset within roughly 30 minutes, the specific symptom triad of bloating, excessive gas and loose stools that reflects osmotic retention of unabsorbed lactose in the small bowel followed by colonic bacterial fermentation producing hydrogen, carbon dioxide and methane along with short-chain fatty acids, and above all the complete absence of symptoms when she avoids dairy, which constitutes an informal but persuasive dietary elimination trial. The examination findings corroborate a gas-related, non-inflammatory process: the abdomen is soft, mildly distended with tympany to percussion consistent with intraluminal gas, non-tender, with active bowel sounds and no masses or organomegaly. Equally important is the systematic absence of alarm features. There is no abdominal pain between episodes, no blood in the stool, no weight loss, and no fever, and there is no family history of inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease. This negative profile makes the principal serious alternatives unlikely. Inflammatory bowel disease would be expected to produce persistent rather than strictly food-triggered symptoms, often with rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, systemic features, or abdominal tenderness, none of which are present. Coeliac disease is not food-specific to dairy, is triggered by gluten rather than lactose, and typically causes more chronic symptoms with possible weight loss or nutritional deficiency; the absence of family history and of any of these features makes it unlikely, though secondary lactase deficiency can occur as a consequence of coeliac disease or other mucosal injury. Irritable bowel syndrome remains a differential consideration since bloating and loose stools are common in it, but the strict dependence on dairy exposure and the freedom from pain between episodes and from pain as a dominant feature argue against it as the primary explanation. Infectious gastroenteritis is excluded by the six-month recurrent course, the absence of fever, and the reproducible dietary trigger. A true IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy is not supported, as that typically produces urticaria, angioedema, respiratory or anaphylactic features rather than isolated fermentative gastrointestinal symptoms, and none of those are described. Her age is entirely consistent with primary adult-type hypolactasia, in which lactase expression declines after childhood, and the onset six months ago fits the usual gradual emergence of symptoms in late adolescence or early adulthood. This is a benign, functional, non-progressive condition whose management is dietary rather than pharmacological or investigative.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 22-year-old woman with a six-month history of dairy-triggered bloating, flatulence and loose stools occurring within about 30 minutes of ingestion, resolving fully with dairy avoidance, with a benign abdominal examination showing only mild tympanitic distension and no tenderness, masses or organomegaly, and with no alarm features and no relevant family history. The clinical picture is that of lactose intolerance from lactase deficiency. The diagnosis can be made confidently on history alone, supported by the effective elimination and reproducible rechallenge already occurring in daily life, and no further investigation is required at this stage. Management is dietary self-management with education, with reassessment reserved for symptoms that fail to follow the dairy-dependent pattern.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Explain the mechanism to the patient, namely that reduced intestinal lactase leaves lactose undigested, drawing water into the bowel and being fermented by colonic bacteria to produce gas, which accounts for the bloating, flatulence and loose stools that follow dairy within about half an hour. Confirm the diagnosis pragmatically by continuing structured dietary management: maintain avoidance or restriction of lactose-containing dairy for two to four weeks and note the resolution of symptoms, then reintroduce a measured dairy portion to observe recurrence, keeping a simple food and symptom diary to document the relationship and to identify her personal threshold. Emphasise that most people with lactose intolerance tolerate small amounts of lactose, especially when taken with other foods and spread through the day, so complete elimination is usually unnecessary. Advise practical substitutions: lactose-free milk, plant-based milk alternatives, hard aged cheeses such as cheddar and parmesan, and live-culture yogurt, all of which are typically well tolerated because of low residual lactose or bacterial lactase activity. Over-the-counter lactase enzyme supplements taken with the first bite of a dairy-containing meal are a reasonable option when she wishes to eat dairy at social occasions or when eating out. Advise her to read labels for hidden lactose in processed foods, baked goods, sauces, protein powders, and some medications. Address the additional considerations directly. Because she is a young woman restricting dairy, ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake to protect long-term bone health, through lactose-free or fortified dairy alternatives, fortified plant milks, canned fish with bones, tofu set with calcium, leafy greens, nuts and seeds, with supplementation if dietary intake is insufficient. Because no alarm features are present, no blood tests, stool studies, breath testing, imaging, or endoscopy are indicated now; a hydrogen breath test or a coeliac serology screen would only become appropriate if the diagnosis becomes uncertain. Advise her to return for medical evaluation if the symptom pattern changes, specifically if symptoms persist despite strict dairy avoidance, if she develops abdominal pain between episodes, rectal bleeding, black stools, unintentional weight loss, fever, nocturnal diarrhoea waking her from sleep, persistent vomiting, or signs of anaemia or nutritional deficiency, since these would prompt evaluation for coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or another secondary cause of lactase deficiency. Also advise her to seek prompt assessment if she ever develops rash, lip or facial swelling, wheeze or breathing difficulty after dairy, as that would suggest milk protein allergy rather than lactose intolerance and requires a different approach.
Notes: Lactase deficiency may be secondary to underlying mucosal disease such as coeliac disease or a post-infectious enteropathy, so a diagnosis of primary lactose intolerance should be revisited if symptoms do not remit fully with dairy restriction or if alarm features emerge. Long-term dairy restriction carries a risk of inadequate calcium and vitamin D intake that should be actively managed.

Analysis: The history is essentially diagnostic of lactose intolerance due to lactase deficiency. The strongest supporting facts are the tight and reproducible temporal relationship between dairy ingestion and symptom onset within roughly 30 minutes, the specific symptom triad of bloating, excessive gas and loose stools that reflects osmotic retention of unabsorbed lactose in the small bowel followed by colonic bacterial fermentation producing hydrogen, carbon dioxide and methane along with short-chain fatty acids, and above all the complete absence of symptoms when she avoids dairy, which constitutes an informal but persuasive dietary elimination trial. The examination findings corroborate a gas-related, non-inflammatory process: the abdomen is soft, mildly distended with tympany to percussion consistent with intraluminal gas, non-tender, with active bowel sounds and no masses or organomegaly. Equally important is the systematic absence of alarm features. There is no abdominal pain between episodes, no blood in the stool, no weight loss, and no fever, and there is no family history of inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease. This negative profile makes the principal serious alternatives unlikely. Inflammatory bowel disease would be expected to produce persistent rather than strictly food-triggered symptoms, often with rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, systemic features, or abdominal tenderness, none of which are present. Coeliac disease is not food-specific to dairy, is triggered by gluten rather than lactose, and typically causes more chronic symptoms with possible weight loss or nutritional deficiency; the absence of family history and of any of these features makes it unlikely, though secondary lactase deficiency can occur as a consequence of coeliac disease or other mucosal injury. Irritable bowel syndrome remains a differential consideration since bloating and loose stools are common in it, but the strict dependence on dairy exposure and the freedom from pain between episodes and from pain as a dominant feature argue against it as the primary explanation. Infectious gastroenteritis is excluded by the six-month recurrent course, the absence of fever, and the reproducible dietary trigger. A true IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy is not supported, as that typically produces urticaria, angioedema, respiratory or anaphylactic features rather than isolated fermentative gastrointestinal symptoms, and none of those are described. Her age is entirely consistent with primary adult-type hypolactasia, in which lactase expression declines after childhood, and the onset six months ago fits the usual gradual emergence of symptoms in late adolescence or early adulthood. This is a benign, functional, non-progressive condition whose management is dietary rather than pharmacological or investigative.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 22-year-old woman with a six-month history of dairy-triggered bloating, flatulence and loose stools occurring within about 30 minutes of ingestion, resolving fully with dairy avoidance, with a benign abdominal examination showing only mild tympanitic distension and no tenderness, masses or organomegaly, and with no alarm features and no relevant family history. The clinical picture is that of lactose intolerance from lactase deficiency. The diagnosis can be made confidently on history alone, supported by the effective elimination and reproducible rechallenge already occurring in daily life, and no further investigation is required at this stage. Management is dietary self-management with education, with reassessment reserved for symptoms that fail to follow the dairy-dependent pattern.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Explain the mechanism to the patient, namely that reduced intestinal lactase leaves lactose undigested, drawing water into the bowel and being fermented by colonic bacteria to produce gas, which accounts for the bloating, flatulence and loose stools that follow dairy within about half an hour. Confirm the diagnosis pragmatically by continuing structured dietary management: maintain avoidance or restriction of lactose-containing dairy for two to four weeks and note the resolution of symptoms, then reintroduce a measured dairy portion to observe recurrence, keeping a simple food and symptom diary to document the relationship and to identify her personal threshold. Emphasise that most people with lactose intolerance tolerate small amounts of lactose, especially when taken with other foods and spread through the day, so complete elimination is usually unnecessary. Advise practical substitutions: lactose-free milk, plant-based milk alternatives, hard aged cheeses such as cheddar and parmesan, and live-culture yogurt, all of which are typically well tolerated because of low residual lactose or bacterial lactase activity. Over-the-counter lactase enzyme supplements taken with the first bite of a dairy-containing meal are a reasonable option when she wishes to eat dairy at social occasions or when eating out. Advise her to read labels for hidden lactose in processed foods, baked goods, sauces, protein powders, and some medications. Address the additional considerations directly. Because she is a young woman restricting dairy, ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake to protect long-term bone health, through lactose-free or fortified dairy alternatives, fortified plant milks, canned fish with bones, tofu set with calcium, leafy greens, nuts and seeds, with supplementation if dietary intake is insufficient. Because no alarm features are present, no blood tests, stool studies, breath testing, imaging, or endoscopy are indicated now; a hydrogen breath test or a coeliac serology screen would only become appropriate if the diagnosis becomes uncertain. Advise her to return for medical evaluation if the symptom pattern changes, specifically if symptoms persist despite strict dairy avoidance, if she develops abdominal pain between episodes, rectal bleeding, black stools, unintentional weight loss, fever, nocturnal diarrhoea waking her from sleep, persistent vomiting, or signs of anaemia or nutritional deficiency, since these would prompt evaluation for coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or another secondary cause of lactase deficiency. Also advise her to seek prompt assessment if she ever develops rash, lip or facial swelling, wheeze or breathing difficulty after dairy, as that would suggest milk protein allergy rather than lactose intolerance and requires a different approach.
Notes: Lactase deficiency may be secondary to underlying mucosal disease such as coeliac disease or a post-infectious enteropathy, so a diagnosis of primary lactose intolerance should be revisited if symptoms do not remit fully with dairy restriction or if alarm features emerge. Long-term dairy restriction carries a risk of inadequate calcium and vitamin D intake that should be actively managed.

Age: 18 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden-onset left scrotal pain of several hours' duration with associated nausea, beginning abruptly during snow shoveling, transiently resolving, then returning with progressive scrotal swelling.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for acute testicular torsion of the left testis. The strongest supporting facts are abrupt onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain during physical exertion, accompanying nausea without gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, transient spontaneous resolution followed by recurrence consistent with torsion-detorsion preceding fixed torsion, a swollen and exquisitely tender left hemiscrotum in which the testis cannot be palpated because of pain, an absent left cremasteric reflex, and a horizontal lie of the contralateral right testis indicating an underlying bell-clapper deformity that predisposes bilaterally. Definitive confirmation is provided by Doppler ultrasonography showing a heterogeneous left testis with no demonstrable arterial or venous flow, while the right testis has normal echotexture and flow. The heterogeneous parenchymal echotexture suggests ischemic change and raises concern for compromised viability. Main differential considerations are epididymo-orchitis, torsion of a testicular appendage, incarcerated inguinal hernia, and traumatic hematoma. Epididymo-orchitis is strongly argued against by the abrupt exertional onset, absent fever with temperature 37 C, absent dysuria or urethral discharge, a normal urinalysis with negative leukocyte esterase, nitrites and bacteria, an absent cremasteric reflex, and above all by the absence of Doppler flow, since infection produces increased rather than absent perfusion. Torsion of an appendage typically produces focal upper-pole tenderness with preserved flow and a preserved cremasteric reflex. Hernia is excluded by the absence of tenderness or fullness over the inguinal canals and a soft, nontender abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Trauma is not reported. The history of multiple sexual partners with inconsistent condom use raises background risk for sexually transmitted epididymitis, but the imaging and clinical picture establish torsion, and this history must not delay operative management.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None additional for diagnosis; scrotal color Doppler ultrasonography and urinalysis have already established the diagnosis. What is needed next is immediate urologic surgical availability with standard preoperative preparation.
Conclusion: Acute left testicular torsion in an 18-year-old man, confirmed by absent arterial and venous Doppler flow within a heterogeneous left testis, with a contralateral horizontal testicular lie indicating bell-clapper anatomy. This is a time-critical surgical emergency in which the probability of testicular salvage falls sharply with each additional hour of ischemia.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Obtain immediate urologic surgical consultation for emergent scrotal exploration with detorsion and orchiopexy, and do not delay surgery for further imaging or laboratory testing. Keep the patient nil per os, establish intravenous access, and give parenteral analgesia and an antiemetic for the pain and nausea. Manual detorsion may be attempted at the bedside only as a temporizing measure if operative intervention will be delayed, never as a substitute for exploration. At operation, assess viability of the left testis; a nonviable testis requires orchiectomy, and the heterogeneous echotexture on ultrasound means the patient should be counseled preoperatively about this possibility. Contralateral right orchiopexy must be performed at the same operation because the horizontal lie of the right testis indicates the same predisposing deformity and risk of subsequent torsion. Postoperatively advise scrotal support, activity restriction, and wound care, and arrange urologic follow-up to assess testicular viability and to discuss fertility and, if orchiectomy is performed, prosthesis options. Addressing the additional considerations: given his sexual activity with multiple partners and inconsistent condom use, offer screening for sexually transmitted infections and safer-sex counseling, but only after definitive surgical management, since the normal urinalysis and absent Doppler flow exclude infection as the cause of this episode. Note his seasonal allergies and daily cetirizine for the anesthesia team; no known drug allergies are reported.
Notes: Time from symptom onset is the principal determinant of salvage, and the intermittent pain pattern indicates that total ischemic duration may exceed the current episode. Absent Doppler flow is confirmatory, but preserved flow would not exclude torsion in a compelling clinical presentation.

The strongest supporting facts are abrupt onset of severe unilateral scrotal pain during physical exertion, accompanying nausea without gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, transient spontaneous resolution followed by recurrence consistent with torsion-detorsion preceding fixed torsion, a swollen and exquisitely tender left hemiscrotum in which the testis cannot be palpated because of pain, an absent left cremasteric reflex, and a horizontal lie of the contralateral right testis indicating an underlying bell-clapper deformity that predisposes bilaterally. Definitive confirmation is provided by Doppler ultrasonography showing a heterogeneous left testis with no demonstrable arterial or venous flow, while the right testis has normal echotexture and flow. The heterogeneous parenchymal echotexture suggests ischemic change and raises concern for compromised viability. Main differential considerations are epididymo-orchitis, torsion of a testicular appendage, incarcerated inguinal hernia, and traumatic hematoma. Epididymo-orchitis is strongly argued against by the abrupt exertional onset, absent fever with temperature 37 C, absent dysuria or urethral discharge, a normal urinalysis with negative leukocyte esterase, nitrites and bacteria, an absent cremasteric reflex, and above all by the absence of Doppler flow, since infection produces increased rather than absent perfusion. Torsion of an appendage typically produces focal upper-pole tenderness with preserved flow and a preserved cremasteric reflex. Hernia is excluded by the absence of tenderness or fullness over the inguinal canals and a soft, nontender abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Trauma is not reported. The history of multiple sexual partners with inconsistent condom use raises background risk for sexually transmitted epididymitis, but the imaging and clinical picture establish torsion, and this history must not delay operative management.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None additional for diagnosis; scrotal color Doppler ultrasonography and urinalysis have already established the diagnosis. What is needed next is immediate urologic surgical availability with standard preoperative preparation.
Conclusion: Acute left testicular torsion in an 18-year-old man, confirmed by absent arterial and venous Doppler flow within a heterogeneous left testis, with a contralateral horizontal testicular lie indicating bell-clapper anatomy. This is a time-critical surgical emergency in which the probability of testicular salvage falls sharply with each additional hour of ischemia.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Obtain immediate urologic surgical consultation for emergent scrotal exploration with detorsion and orchiopexy, and do not delay surgery for further imaging or laboratory testing. Keep the patient nil per os, establish intravenous access, and give parenteral analgesia and an antiemetic for the pain and nausea. Manual detorsion may be attempted at the bedside only as a temporizing measure if operative intervention will be delayed, never as a substitute for exploration. At operation, assess viability of the left testis; a nonviable testis requires orchiectomy, and the heterogeneous echotexture on ultrasound means the patient should be counseled preoperatively about this possibility. Contralateral right orchiopexy must be performed at the same operation because the horizontal lie of the right testis indicates the same predisposing deformity and risk of subsequent torsion. Postoperatively advise scrotal support, activity restriction, and wound care, and arrange urologic follow-up to assess testicular viability and to discuss fertility and, if orchiectomy is performed, prosthesis options. Addressing the additional considerations: given his sexual activity with multiple partners and inconsistent condom use, offer screening for sexually transmitted infections and safer-sex counseling, but only after definitive surgical management, since the normal urinalysis and absent Doppler flow exclude infection as the cause of this episode. Note his seasonal allergies and daily cetirizine for the anesthesia team; no known drug allergies are reported.
Notes: Time from symptom onset is the principal determinant of salvage, and the intermittent pain pattern indicates that total ischemic duration may exceed the current episode. Absent Doppler flow is confirmatory, but preserved flow would not exclude torsion in a compelling clinical presentation.

Vignette:
A 17-year-old male student presents with recurrent mouth ulceration since his early schooldays. He has no respiratory, anogenital, gastrointestinal, eye, or skin lesions. His mother had a similar history as a teenager. The social history includes no tobacco use and virtually no alcohol consumption. He has no history of recent drug or medication ingestion. Extraoral exam reveals no significant abnormalities and specifically no pyrexia
baseline_protocol:
Age: 17 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Recurrent mouth ulceration since early schooldays, with no lesions at any other mucocutaneous site.
Analysis: The picture is that of recurrent aphthous stomatitis. The strongest supporting facts are the long-standing recurrent nature of the oral ulceration dating from early schooldays, strict confinement of lesions to the oral mucosa, an unremarkable extraoral examination, and the explicit absence of pyrexia. The positive family history in his mother, who had a similar history as a teenager, is characteristic, since a familial tendency is common in this condition. The main differential considerations are systemic diseases that present with recurrent oral ulceration. Behcet disease is argued against by the stated absence of anogenital, ocular, and skin lesions. Inflammatory bowel disease is argued against by the absence of gastrointestinal symptoms. Vesiculobullous disease and erythema multiforme are argued against by the absence of skin, ocular, and anogenital involvement. Drug-induced oral ulceration is excluded by the stated absence of recent drug or medication ingestion. Tobacco-related and alcohol-related mucosal disease and oral malignancy are unlikely given no tobacco use, virtually no alcohol consumption, his young age, and a chronic recurrent rather than a persistent solitary lesion. An acute infectious stomatitis such as primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is inconsistent with a recurrent pattern spanning many years and with the absence of fever. The case does not specify the number, size, duration, or precise site of individual ulcers or whether they scar, so the clinical subtype cannot be determined, and no laboratory data are provided.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Full blood count with differential and haematinic assays including serum ferritin, vitamin B12, and folate to exclude a deficiency-related cause of recurrent aphthous ulceration; coeliac serology given the recognised association with recurrent oral ulceration. No imaging is required, and biopsy is not indicated unless an individual ulcer fails to heal or the pattern changes.
Conclusion: A healthy 17-year-old male with a many-year history of recurrent oral ulceration confined to the mouth, no extraoral or systemic features, no pyrexia, no drug exposure, and a positive maternal family history. The findings are consistent with recurrent aphthous stomatitis, a benign but relapsing condition managed symptomatically after exclusion of haematinic deficiency and underlying systemic disease.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Arrange routine outpatient evaluation, as this is not urgent. Perform the screening blood work above to identify a correctable iron, B12, or folate deficiency or coeliac disease, since deficiency states are a recognised and treatable contributor. Provide symptomatic care during episodes with an antiseptic or anti-inflammatory mouthwash, a topical corticosteroid preparation applied to individual ulcers at the earliest prodromal stage, and a topical anaesthetic before meals if eating is painful. Advise gentle oral hygiene with a soft toothbrush, avoidance of oral trauma, and avoidance of any foods the patient identifies as precipitants. Ask him to keep a simple diary of ulcer frequency, number, size, and healing time, which will define the clinical pattern that the case does not currently specify and will guide any escalation of therapy. Addressing the additional considerations: reassure him and his mother that the familial pattern is typical and benign; reinforce continued abstinence from tobacco and minimal alcohol intake; and instruct him to return promptly if he develops genital or ocular lesions, skin rash, eye pain or redness, diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, weight loss, or fever, since these would prompt reassessment for Behcet disease or inflammatory bowel disease. A single ulcer persisting beyond three weeks, becoming indurated, or enlarging warrants urgent specialist referral and biopsy.
Notes: The case does not specify ulcer number, size, duration, or healing pattern, so the aphthous subtype cannot be classified from the information provided. No laboratory results are given; the tests recommended are screening investigations, since recurrent aphthous stomatitis remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.

Vignette:
A 42-year-old man with a history of Crohn disease managed with azathioprine presents with a 3-day history of burning pain along the left side of his chest followed by the eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. The rash follows a band-like distribution along the T5 dermatome and does not cross the midline. He reports associated malaise and low-grade fever. Vital signs are stable with temperature 99.8°F. On examination, there are clustered vesicles in various stages, some with clear fluid and others beginning to crust. There is notable allodynia in the affected dermatome. No ocular or facial involvement is present.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 42 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three-day history of burning pain along the left side of the chest followed by eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a band-like distribution, with malaise and low-grade fever.
Analysis: The findings are diagnostic of herpes zoster involving the left T5 dermatome. The strongest supporting facts are the prodrome of burning neuropathic pain preceding the rash by three days, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, a strictly band-like unilateral dermatomal distribution that does not cross the midline, lesions in various stages with some clear and others crusting, and marked allodynia confined to the affected dermatome. Constitutional malaise and low-grade fever at 99.8 F are consistent. The critical modifying factor is that he is immunosuppressed by azathioprine taken for Crohn disease, which increases the risk of severe, prolonged, or disseminated zoster, visceral involvement, and postherpetic neuralgia, and this raises the urgency of the case above that of uncomplicated zoster in an immunocompetent host. Differential considerations include herpes simplex virus infection, which can be zosteriform but rarely respects a dermatome so precisely and typically recurs at the same site; contact dermatitis, which would not follow a dermatome, would itch rather than burn, and would not be preceded by neuropathic prodromal pain; bullous impetigo or cellulitis, which lack a dermatomal pattern and the preceding neuralgic prodrome; and, before the rash appeared, cardiac or pleuritic chest pain, now excluded by the characteristic eruption. Notably absent are ocular and facial involvement, so herpes zoster ophthalmicus is excluded, and there is no evidence of disseminated disease described.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for diagnosis, which is clinical in this classic dermatomal presentation. If confirmation is needed because of his immunosuppression, polymerase chain reaction testing of vesicle fluid for varicella zoster virus is the appropriate confirmatory test.
Conclusion: Acute herpes zoster of the left T5 dermatome in a 42-year-old immunosuppressed man on azathioprine for Crohn disease, presenting within the therapeutic window for antiviral therapy and carrying an elevated risk of complications and postherpetic neuralgia because of his immunocompromised state.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Start systemic antiviral therapy without delay, since he remains within the effective window with lesions still forming and some only beginning to crust; because he is immunosuppressed on azathioprine, use full-dose oral antiviral therapy with close observation, and admit for intravenous antiviral therapy if new lesions appear outside the T5 dermatome, if cranial or ocular involvement develops, or if systemic toxicity emerges. Provide analgesia proportionate to the neuropathic pain and allodynia, adding a neuropathic agent if simple analgesics are inadequate. Advise keeping the lesions covered with a clean dry dressing; while lesions are unhealed and not fully crusted he is infectious by direct contact and should avoid contact with pregnant women, neonates, and other immunocompromised individuals until all lesions have crusted. Addressing the additional considerations, discuss with his gastroenterologist whether azathioprine should be temporarily held or dose-adjusted during the acute infection, balanced against the risk of a Crohn disease flare; this decision should not delay antiviral therapy. Arrange follow-up within a few days to confirm the rash is not disseminating and to assess pain control, and counsel him that persisting pain after the rash resolves represents postherpetic neuralgia and merits specific treatment. Instruct him to seek immediate care for new vesicles at distant sites, eye pain or redness, visual change, facial involvement, headache, altered mental status, or breathlessness. Once the acute episode has resolved, discuss recombinant zoster vaccination with his treating team given his ongoing immunosuppression.
Notes: The diagnosis is clinical and the case provides no virological confirmation. Immunosuppression is the dominant risk factor here and warrants a lower threshold for escalation to inpatient intravenous therapy; the absence of ocular or facial involvement is reassuring but does not exclude later dissemination.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset severe generalized abdominal pain associated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. On exam she appears ill and has a temperature of 104°F (40°C). Her abdomen is tense with generalized tenderness and guarding. No bowel sounds are present.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 12 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden-onset severe generalized abdominal pain with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, accompanied by high fever.
Analysis: The child presents with an acute surgical abdomen with peritonitis. The strongest supporting facts are the sudden onset of severe generalized abdominal pain, an ill general appearance, a temperature of 104 F (40 C) indicating a marked systemic inflammatory response, and a tense abdomen with generalized tenderness and guarding, which are signs of peritoneal irritation. The complete absence of bowel sounds indicates paralytic ileus, which in the context of generalized guarding points to established peritonitis rather than a simple gastroenteritis. The combination of generalized rather than localized peritoneal signs suggests free intraperitoneal contamination, most typically from a perforated viscus; in a 12-year-old the leading cause is perforated appendicitis, and the diarrhea and vomiting are consistent with peritoneal irritation and ileus rather than being reassuring for an enteric infection. Main differential considerations include perforated appendicitis with generalized peritonitis, primary bacterial peritonitis, perforation of another hollow viscus, intussusception or another obstructive lesion with ischemia and perforation, severe bacterial enterocolitis, mesenteric adenitis, and, in a girl of this age, gynecologic causes such as ovarian torsion or tubo-ovarian pathology. Gastroenteritis alone is strongly argued against by the tense abdomen with guarding and the absent bowel sounds, which are not features of uncomplicated enteritis. Diabetic ketoacidosis and other medical mimics cannot be excluded from the information given but do not explain guarding with a silent abdomen. The case provides no vital signs other than temperature, no laboratory data, and no imaging, so the degree of hemodynamic compromise cannot be assessed from the text.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count with differential, C-reactive protein, serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine, glucose, lactate, liver function tests, and blood cultures; urinalysis and a pregnancy test given her age and sex; abdominal ultrasonography as the first-line imaging study in a child, with contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis if ultrasound is nondiagnostic and the child is stable enough; upright or lateral decubitus abdominal radiography to look for free intraperitoneal air; continuous vital sign and pulse oximetry monitoring.
Conclusion: A 12-year-old girl with a clinically evident acute abdomen and generalized peritonitis with high fever and an ileus, most consistent with a perforated intra-abdominal process such as perforated appendicitis. This is a life-threatening surgical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent surgical evaluation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Manage as an emergency. Keep the child nil per os, establish large-bore intravenous access, and begin isotonic crystalloid fluid resuscitation for the losses from vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and third-spacing into the inflamed peritoneum. Obtain immediate pediatric surgical consultation; the generalized guarding with a silent abdomen mandates surgical assessment before, and in parallel with, completion of imaging. Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics with coverage of enteric gram-negative organisms and anaerobes after drawing blood cultures. Provide intravenous analgesia and an antiemetic; adequate analgesia does not obscure the surgical assessment and should not be withheld. Place a nasogastric tube if vomiting persists or ileus is significant, monitor urine output, and correct electrolyte abnormalities identified on laboratory testing. Send the laboratory and imaging studies listed above without allowing them to delay resuscitation or surgical review. Addressing the additional considerations: perform a pregnancy test and include gynecologic causes such as ovarian torsion in the differential, since she is a 12-year-old girl; verify glucose to exclude diabetic ketoacidosis as a medical mimic of an acute abdomen; and reassess frequently for progression to septic shock, escalating care and involving pediatric intensive care if perfusion deteriorates. Definitive management will most likely be operative exploration with source control, with the approach determined by intraoperative and imaging findings.
Notes: Only temperature is provided among vital signs and no laboratory or imaging data are available, so shock cannot be excluded and hemodynamic status must be assessed immediately at the bedside. Diarrhea in this setting should not be misread as evidence of simple gastroenteritis, since peritonitis with ileus is the dominant finding.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a painful, swollen right eye for the past day. He reports minor pain on palpation of the eyelid and denies any history of trauma, crusting, or change in vision. baseline_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: One day of a painful, swollen right eye with focal tenderness and erythema of the lower eyelid near the lid margin.
Analysis: The findings are those of an external hordeolum, an acute localized infection of a lid margin gland. The strongest supporting facts are the acute one-day onset, localized tenderness to palpation and erythema confined to the midline of the lower eyelid near the lid margin, and the explicit statement that the remainder of the examination, including the globe, is normal. Pain on palpation with a discrete tender focus at the lid margin distinguishes an acute hordeolum from a painless chalazion, which is a chronic non-tender granulomatous lipogranuloma. Preseptal cellulitis is argued against by the localized rather than diffuse lid involvement and the absence of systemic features described. Orbital cellulitis is excluded by the normal globe examination with no reported proptosis, no restriction or pain on eye movement, and no visual change. Allergic or contact dermatitis of the lid is argued against by the absence of any allergy history, the denial of new soaps, lotions, or creams, and the focal tender erythema rather than diffuse itchy edema. Blepharitis is argued against by the denial of crusting and by the focal rather than diffuse lid margin involvement. Dacryocystitis is unlikely because the lesion is on the midline of the lower lid at the margin rather than over the medial canthal lacrimal sac. Trauma is denied. Vision is explicitly unchanged, which is reassuring and supports a benign, superficial, self-limited process.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None; the diagnosis is clinical. Slit-lamp examination with visual acuity testing may be used at initial assessment to confirm the globe is uninvolved, but no laboratory studies or imaging are needed.
Conclusion: An acute, uncomplicated external hordeolum (stye) of the right lower eyelid in an otherwise healthy 30-year-old man, with a normal globe, preserved vision, and no evidence of preseptal or orbital cellulitis. The condition is benign and typically resolves with conservative measures.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Apply warm compresses to the affected lid for approximately ten to fifteen minutes, four times daily, which promotes drainage of the obstructed gland and is the mainstay of treatment. Perform gentle lid hygiene, cleansing the lid margin with a mild cleanser or dilute baby shampoo on a clean cloth. Massage the lid gently toward the lid margin after warm compresses to encourage drainage. Do not squeeze, incise, or attempt to express the lesion, as this can spread infection into the surrounding lid tissue. Avoid eye makeup and contact lens wear until the lesion has resolved, and do not share towels or facecloths. Simple oral analgesia may be used for discomfort. Topical or systemic antibiotics are not routinely required for an uncomplicated hordeolum and are not indicated on the findings described. Addressing the additional considerations: the denial of trauma, of vision change, of crusting, and of new topical product exposure supports the benign diagnosis and means no further workup is needed at this time; because there is no allergy or prior eye disease history, no chronic condition needs management. Advise the patient to seek prompt medical review if the swelling spreads across the lid or into the surrounding face, if fever develops, if the eye becomes red or painful in itself, if vision blurs or double vision occurs, if eye movements become painful or restricted, or if the lesion has not improved within one to two weeks, since a persistent painless nodule would suggest a chalazion requiring ophthalmologic evaluation for possible incision and curettage.
Notes: None
