Vignette:
A 78-year-old man is brought in after a syncopal episode at home witnessed by his wife. She reports he has been increasingly fatigued and lightheaded for the past week. His past medical history includes aortic stenosis, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. On examination, he is alert but pale and mildly confused. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 32, RR 18, BP 82/50, SpO2 93%. Cannon A waves are visible in the jugular venous pulse. Heart sounds reveal a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border and variable intensity of S1. ECG demonstrates complete atrioventricular dissociation with a ventricular escape rate of 32 bpm, wide QRS complexes, and independent P waves at a rate of 82 bpm.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 78 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Witnessed syncopal episode at home, preceded by a week of increasing fatigue and lightheadedness.
Analysis: This is symptomatic complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block with hemodynamic compromise. The strongest supporting facts are the electrocardiogram showing complete atrioventricular dissociation with independent P waves at 82 per minute and a ventricular escape rate of 32 per minute with wide QRS complexes, corroborated at the bedside by a pulse of 32 per minute, cannon A waves in the jugular venous pulse produced by atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve, and variable intensity of S1 from the changing atrioventricular relationship. The block is hemodynamically significant: blood pressure is 82/50, he is pale and mildly confused, indicating inadequate cerebral and systemic perfusion, and the syncopal episode represents a Stokes-Adams attack. The wide QRS escape rhythm localizes the escape focus below the atrioventricular node, in the His-Purkinje system, which is an unstable and unreliable pacemaker with a real risk of asystole or degeneration into ventricular arrhythmia. His aortic stenosis compounds the situation in two ways: it is associated with calcific infiltration of the conduction system as a cause of block, and a fixed obstructive valve lesion limits the ability to compensate for bradycardia by increasing stroke volume, worsening the hypotension. The systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border is consistent with his known aortic stenosis, and aortic stenosis is itself an independent cause of exertional syncope, but the documented complete heart block with a rate of 32 fully explains the presentation. Differential considerations for the syncope include aortic stenosis alone, orthostatic hypotension, drug-induced bradycardia from atrioventricular nodal blocking agents, hyperkalemia or other metabolic derangement, and acute myocardial ischemia causing conduction block; the specific medications are not given in the case, and no laboratory or troponin data are provided.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator and transcutaneous pacing capability immediately at the bedside; serum electrolytes with potassium, magnesium and calcium, renal function, and glucose; serum troponin to assess for acute myocardial infarction as a cause of the block; thyroid function; medication reconciliation for atrioventricular nodal blocking drugs and digoxin level if applicable; transthoracic echocardiography to quantify the severity of his known aortic stenosis and assess ventricular function; and, given his diabetes and the confusion, a capillary glucose measurement.
Conclusion: A 78-year-old man with symptomatic complete atrioventricular block and a wide-complex ventricular escape rhythm at 32 per minute, producing syncope, hypotension at 82/50, pallor, and confusion, on a background of aortic stenosis, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. This is an unstable bradyarrhythmia with an unreliable infranodal escape focus, and it requires emergent pacing and admission.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology
Recommendations: Treat as an unstable bradycardia. Place the patient on continuous cardiac monitoring with pads applied and transcutaneous pacing immediately available, secure intravenous access, and give supplemental oxygen titrated to his saturation of 93 percent. Because he is symptomatic and hypotensive, initiate transcutaneous pacing without delay, with sedation and analgesia for pacing discomfort; atropine is unlikely to be effective in an infranodal wide-complex escape rhythm and must not delay pacing, and a chronotropic infusion may be used as a temporizing bridge if pacing capture is delayed. Obtain immediate cardiology consultation for temporary transvenous pacing and for permanent pacemaker implantation, which is the definitive therapy for symptomatic complete heart block with a wide-complex escape. Admit to a coronary care or intensive care setting. Address the additional considerations explicitly: review and withhold every atrioventricular nodal blocking or bradycardia-inducing medication; check and correct potassium, magnesium, and calcium, since hyperkalemia is a reversible cause of block particularly relevant with diabetes and possible renal impairment; send troponin and evaluate for acute ischemia as a precipitant; check glucose given his diabetes and confusion; and perform echocardiography to define the severity of his aortic stenosis, which will influence both hemodynamic management and any subsequent valve intervention. Use fluids cautiously in the setting of aortic stenosis and avoid agents that drop systemic vascular resistance. Reassess mental status frequently, as improvement in confusion with restoration of an adequate rate confirms that the bradyarrhythmia is the cause. Screen for injury sustained during the syncopal fall.
Notes: The confusion is most plausibly hypoperfusion-related but glucose and electrolytes must be checked to exclude reversible metabolic contributors. Medications are not specified in the case, so a drug-induced or drug-aggravated component cannot be excluded and reconciliation is essential. A wide-complex escape rhythm at 32 per minute is unreliable and may fail abruptly, so pacing capability must remain at the bedside at all times.

Vignette: A 28-year-old man presents to his physician with a 5-day history of fever, chills, and rigors, not improving with acetaminophen (paracetamol), along with diarrhea. He had been traveling in Central America for 3 months, returning 8 weeks ago. He had been bitten by mosquitoes on multiple occasions, and although he initially took malaria prophylaxis, he discontinued it due to mild nausea. He does not know the specifics of his prophylactic therapy. On examination he has a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C), and is mildly tachycardic with a BP of 126/82 mmHg. The remainder of the examination is normal.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 28-year-old man presents to his physician with a 5-day history of fever, chills, and rigors, not improving with acetaminophen (paracetamol), along with diarrhea. He had been traveling in Central America for 3 months, returning 8 weeks ago. He had been bitten by mosquitoes on multiple occasions, and although he initially took malaria prophylaxis, he discontinued it due to mild nausea. He does not know the specifics of his prophylactic therapy. On examination he has a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C), and is mildly tachycardic with a BP of 126/82 mmHg. The remainder of the examination is normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 28 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five-day history of fever, chills, and rigors unresponsive to acetaminophen, with diarrhea, in a traveler who returned from Central America eight weeks ago.
Analysis: This is a febrile illness in a returned traveler, and malaria must be assumed until excluded. The strongest supporting facts are three months of travel in Central America, multiple mosquito bites, and incomplete malaria chemoprophylaxis that was discontinued because of nausea, with the patient unable to name the agent used. Fever with chills and rigors is the cardinal presentation of malaria, and the eight-week interval since return is fully compatible with relapsing infection due to a hepatic hypnozoite stage, which is the predominant pattern in Central America and would not be prevented by prophylaxis that was stopped early and that in any case does not eradicate liver-stage parasites. The failure to respond to acetaminophen is consistent with an ongoing infective cause rather than a self-limited viral illness. Diarrhea is a recognised nonspecific accompaniment of malaria and can mislead toward a purely enteric diagnosis. On examination he has a documented temperature of 100.4 F (38 C), mild tachycardia, and a normal blood pressure of 126/82, with an otherwise normal examination; there are no reported features of severe malaria such as altered consciousness, jaundice, respiratory distress, or hypotension. Main differential considerations in this exposure setting include dengue and other arboviral infections such as chikungunya and Zika, enteric fever, leptospirosis, amebiasis and other travel-associated enteric infections, acute HIV infection, viral hepatitis, and a nontravel-related cause such as influenza or another common community infection. The eight-week latency argues against dengue and chikungunya, whose incubation periods are short, and is more supportive of malaria relapse or enteric fever. No laboratory data are provided in the case.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urgent thick and thin peripheral blood smears for malaria parasites with species identification and parasite density, repeated at least three times over 24 to 48 hours if initially negative, together with a rapid malaria antigen detection test; complete blood count with differential and platelet count; comprehensive metabolic panel with renal and liver function; glucose; blood cultures; stool studies including culture and microscopy for ova and parasites given the diarrhea; urinalysis; and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity before any primaquine-class therapy for radical cure. Serologic or molecular testing for dengue and screening for HIV should be included in the travel fever workup.
Conclusion: A 28-year-old returned traveler from Central America with a five-day febrile illness with rigors and diarrhea, incomplete malaria prophylaxis, and no current features of severe disease. Malaria, particularly a relapsing hepatic-stage species, is the leading diagnosis and requires urgent same-day parasitological testing, with enteric fever and other travel-related infections as the principal alternatives.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Treat this as an urgent same-day evaluation rather than a routine appointment: send thick and thin blood films and a rapid diagnostic test immediately, since fever in a returned traveler from a malaria-endemic region is a medical urgency even when the patient looks well. If smears are negative but suspicion remains, repeat them at 12 to 24 hour intervals on at least three occasions before excluding malaria. Consult infectious diseases for species-directed antimalarial therapy once the parasite is identified; if a relapsing species is confirmed, radical cure directed at hepatic hypnozoites will be needed in addition to blood-stage treatment, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status must be documented before that therapy is given. Provide supportive care with oral rehydration for the diarrhea and antipyretics, and monitor hydration and urine output. Address the additional considerations explicitly: the discontinued and unidentified prophylaxis means no assumption of protection can be made, and prior partial prophylaxis may lower parasitaemia and produce an initially negative smear, so a single negative test is not sufficient; the diarrhea should be investigated with stool studies but must not divert attention from malaria; send blood cultures to cover enteric fever, and include dengue and HIV testing in the workup. Arrange close follow-up within 24 hours and counsel the patient to return immediately or attend an emergency department if he develops confusion, drowsiness, seizures, jaundice, breathlessness, persistent vomiting preventing oral intake, reduced urine output, bleeding, or lightheadedness on standing, as these indicate severe malaria requiring parenteral therapy and inpatient care. Counsel on completing full-course chemoprophylaxis and on strategies for tolerating it, and on bite-avoidance measures for future travel.
Notes: The specific prophylactic agent is unknown, which limits inference about which species remain possible and about drug-resistance considerations. No laboratory results are provided in the case, so severity classification rests only on the normal examination and stable vital signs; malaria can deteriorate rapidly and a well appearance at presentation does not exclude progression.

Vignette:
A 56-year-old man presents to urgent care with acute onset of excruciating pain in his right great toe that woke him from sleep at 3 AM. The pain developed rapidly over several hours and is now the worst pain he has ever experienced, rated 10 out of 10. He reports the toe is so sensitive that even the weight of a bedsheet is unbearable. He had a steak dinner with several beers the evening before onset. His past medical history includes hypertension managed with hydrochlorothiazide and hyperlipidemia. He is overweight with a BMI of 30. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is intensely erythematous, swollen, warm, and exquisitely tender to even light palpation. Active and passive range of motion is severely limited by pain. Vital signs show temperature 99.4°F, heart rate 88. Serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers show ESR 42 and CRP 6.2.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 56 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute, excruciating nocturnal-onset pain, swelling, and redness of the right great toe, rated 10 out of 10, with extreme sensitivity to light touch.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of acute gouty arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, that is, podagra. The strongest supporting facts are the abrupt onset waking him from sleep at 3 AM with rapid escalation over hours to maximal pain, involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, intense erythema, swelling, warmth, and exquisite tenderness such that even the weight of a bedsheet is intolerable, and severe restriction of both active and passive movement by pain. The monoarticular pattern with this degree of allodynia in the great toe is highly specific. Multiple risk factors are present and reinforce the diagnosis: a purine-rich meal of steak with several beers on the preceding evening as a proximate trigger, hydrochlorothiazide therapy for hypertension, which reduces renal urate excretion, obesity with a body mass index of 30, and hyperlipidemia as part of the associated metabolic profile. Serum uric acid is elevated at 9.8 mg/dL, and inflammatory markers are raised with an ESR of 42 and CRP of 6.2, consistent with an acute crystal-induced inflammatory arthritis. The temperature of 99.4 F is only marginally raised and the heart rate of 88 is normal, arguing against systemic sepsis. The critical differential consideration is septic arthritis, which can present identically with a hot, red, exquisitely tender monoarthritis and elevated inflammatory markers; it cannot be excluded on clinical grounds alone, and an elevated serum uric acid does not confirm gout nor exclude infection. Other differentials are calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout), which more typically affects larger joints such as the knee and wrist; cellulitis of the toe, which would not restrict passive joint motion to this degree and would show a less sharply joint-centred distribution; traumatic or stress injury, which is not reported; and acute reactive or psoriatic arthritis, for which there are no supporting features in the case.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Arthrocentesis of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint with synovial fluid analysis under compensated polarized light microscopy for negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals, together with synovial fluid cell count with differential, Gram stain, and culture, which is the definitive test and the only way to exclude septic arthritis; complete blood count with differential; serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate and liver function tests to guide safe selection of anti-inflammatory therapy. Plain radiography of the foot only if trauma or an alternative bony diagnosis is suspected. Blood cultures if joint infection remains a concern.
Conclusion: Acute gout with podagra of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint in a 56-year-old obese hypertensive man on a thiazide diuretic, precipitated by a purine-rich meal and alcohol, with serum urate of 9.8 mg/dL and raised inflammatory markers. Septic arthritis remains the key alternative and should be excluded by joint aspiration, but the clinical picture and risk profile strongly favour crystal arthropathy.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Begin anti-inflammatory therapy promptly, since treatment started early in the attack is far more effective. Choose one of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine, or a corticosteroid, selecting on the basis of comorbidity and renal function; given his hypertension, an intra-articular or short course of systemic corticosteroid or colchicine may be preferable to a nonsteroidal agent, and renal function should be checked before dosing. Aspirate the joint to confirm urate crystals and to exclude infection before or at the same time as initiating steroid therapy. Advise rest and elevation of the foot, avoidance of pressure on the toe including a bed cradle to keep bedding off it, ice application, and adequate hydration. Address the additional considerations explicitly: review the hydrochlorothiazide with his prescriber and consider substituting an antihypertensive that does not raise serum urate, since the diuretic is a modifiable contributor; counsel on reduction of alcohol, particularly beer, and of red meat and other high-purine foods, and on weight reduction given the body mass index of 30, as these are directly implicated in this attack; and address his hyperlipidemia and overall cardiometabolic risk, as gout is associated with cardiovascular disease. Do not start urate-lowering therapy during the acute attack unless it is part of a planned strategy with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis, but arrange outpatient follow-up in two to four weeks to discuss long-term urate-lowering treatment with a target serum urate below the saturation threshold, given a level of 9.8 mg/dL and a symptomatic first attack; if urate-lowering therapy is started, continue anti-inflammatory prophylaxis during initiation to prevent mobilization flares. Instruct him to seek urgent care if fever rises, if he develops rigors or systemic illness, if the redness spreads up the foot, or if the pain fails to improve within a few days of treatment, as these would raise concern for infection.
Notes: An elevated serum uric acid supports but does not prove gout, and urate can be normal or low during an acute attack; conversely hyperuricemia does not exclude septic arthritis. Synovial fluid analysis is the definitive test and should not be omitted because the clinical picture appears classic. Renal function is not reported in the case and must be established before choosing anti-inflammatory therapy.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 68 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Found confused and diaphoretic on the floor at home, obtunded with tremors, after two days of poor oral intake from a vomiting and diarrheal illness while continuing all diabetes medications.
Analysis: This is severe, recurrent, drug-induced hypoglycemia with neuroglycopenia. The strongest supporting facts are a finger-stick glucose of 28 mg/dL with an obtunded mental state, and the immediate improvement in consciousness within minutes of 25 g of intravenous dextrose 50 percent, which confirms hypoglycemia as the cause of the encephalopathy and completes Whipple triad. The mechanism is clear from the history: he takes glipizide, a long-acting sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin secretion independently of intake, and he continued all medications through two days of vomiting and diarrhea with poor oral intake, so insulin secretion continued without carbohydrate substrate. The examination shows the expected mixed autonomic and neuroglycopenic picture, with drenching diaphoresis, tachycardia at 108, tremors, and hypertension at 162/94 reflecting catecholamine discharge, alongside obtundation from cerebral glucose deprivation. Bilateral extensor plantar responses and generalized hyperreflexia with no focal deficits are recognised reversible manifestations of neuroglycopenia rather than evidence of a structural lesion, and the absence of focal signs argues against stroke, though a fall was possible and head injury cannot be excluded from the text. Mild hypothermia at 35.8 C is consistent with prolonged hypoglycemia and with lying on the floor for an unknown period. Critically, glucose fell again to 42 mg/dL after the initial dextrose bolus, requiring a continuous dextrose 10 percent infusion; this recurrence is the hallmark of sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia and demonstrates that the driving insulin secretagogue effect persists far beyond the duration of a single dextrose bolus. The gastrointestinal illness also risks volume depletion and acute kidney injury, which would further impair clearance of glipizide and of metformin, prolonging hypoglycemia and raising the separate concern of metformin-associated lactic acidosis. Differential considerations for altered mental status such as stroke, intracranial hemorrhage from a fall, sepsis, or a metabolic encephalopathy are largely addressed by the documented hypoglycemia and its reversal with dextrose, but persistent or recurrent confusion despite normalised glucose would require reassessment.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Frequent bedside capillary glucose monitoring, at least hourly initially, with continuous cardiac and neurologic observation; laboratory serum glucose to confirm the point-of-care values; complete blood count; comprehensive metabolic panel with electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and bicarbonate to assess volume depletion and renal function; venous or arterial blood gas with lactate given continued metformin exposure with possible acute kidney injury; magnesium and phosphate; electrocardiogram; and non-contrast head computed tomography if confusion persists after glucose correction or if there is any sign of head injury from the fall.
Conclusion: Severe, prolonged, and recurrent sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia in a 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on glipizide and metformin, precipitated by two days of vomiting, diarrhea, and poor oral intake with continued medication use. Glucose responded transiently to intravenous dextrose but relapsed to 42 mg/dL, requiring continuous dextrose infusion, indicating ongoing risk and the need for admission with prolonged monitoring.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Admit for continuous dextrose infusion and prolonged glucose monitoring; do not discharge after apparent correction, because glipizide is long-acting and hypoglycemia predictably recurs, as it already has in this patient. A 34-year-old male with a history of HIV (CD4 count 45 cells/mcL, not on antiretroviral therapy) presents with a 2-week history of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and low-grade fevers. He reports significant fatigue and an unintentional 10-pound weight loss over the past month. On examination, he appears cachectic and is in mild respiratory distress. Vital signs: T 38.4C, HR 112, RR 28, BP 108/68, SpO2 88% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals bilateral diffuse crackles. baseline_protocol:
Age: 34 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two-week history of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and low-grade fevers, with significant fatigue and unintentional 10-pound weight loss over the past month, in a patient with advanced untreated HIV.
Analysis: The case describes a profoundly immunosuppressed patient with HIV, a CD4 count of 45 cells/mcL, and no antiretroviral therapy. At this degree of immunosuppression the risk of opportunistic infection is high. The subacute, two-week course of progressive dyspnea with a dry (non-productive) cough and low-grade fever is the classic tempo and symptom triad for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia rather than a bacterial pneumonia, which typically evolves over days with productive cough and focal consolidation. The strongest supporting facts are: CD4 count of 45 cells/mcL (well below the 200 cells/mcL threshold at which Pneumocystis risk rises sharply and above which prophylaxis is usually not required), the subacute dry cough with progressive exertional dyspnea, fever of 38.4 C, and hypoxemia with SpO2 88% on room air that is disproportionate to the relatively unremarkable focal findings on auscultation apart from bilateral diffuse crackles. The chest X-ray pattern of bilateral, diffuse interstitial infiltrates with ground-glass opacity matches the expected radiographic appearance, and the markedly elevated LDH of 580 U/L is a well-recognized supportive, though non-specific, marker in this disease. The clinician has already sent induced sputum for silver stain, which is the appropriate stain for detecting Pneumocystis cysts and confirms the working diagnosis under consideration. The physiologic picture is one of a patient who is decompensating: tachycardia at 112, tachypnea at 28, borderline blood pressure of 108/68, cachexia, and mild respiratory distress. Room-air saturation of 88 percent constitutes significant hypoxemic respiratory failure and is the single most urgent abnormality in this case. Main differential considerations grounded in the case include other causes of a diffuse interstitial or ground-glass process in advanced HIV: disseminated or pulmonary tuberculosis, which can present with weight loss, fever, and cough in this population; disseminated fungal infection; cytomegalovirus pneumonitis; atypical or viral pneumonia; and, given the constitutional weight loss, a neoplastic process. However, the combination of CD4 45, subacute dry cough, ground-glass bilateral interstitial infiltrates, elevated LDH, and marked hypoxemia makes Pneumocystis pneumonia by far the leading diagnosis. The 10-pound weight loss and cachexia also indicate advanced untreated HIV disease with a wasting component and raise the possibility of a concurrent second opportunistic process.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pulse oximetry and continuous vital sign monitoring; arterial blood gas to quantify the degree of hypoxemia and calculate the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, which also guides the decision on adjunctive corticosteroids; result of the already-submitted induced sputum silver stain for Pneumocystis jirovecii, with bronchoalveolar lavage by bronchoscopy if the induced sputum is non-diagnostic; chest imaging as already obtained, with chest CT if the diagnosis remains unclear; sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and mycobacterial culture to evaluate for tuberculosis; blood cultures; complete blood count with differential; comprehensive metabolic panel including renal and hepatic function; serum LDH as already obtained for trending; repeat CD4 count and HIV viral load to stage disease and guide antiretroviral therapy; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level before any consideration of alternative sulfa-sparing agents such as primaquine or dapsone; supplemental oxygen delivery equipment.
Conclusion: A 34-year-old man with advanced, untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 45 cells/mcL presents with subacute progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fever, weight loss, and hypoxemic respiratory failure with SpO2 88% on room air. Bilateral diffuse crackles, bilateral interstitial ground-glass infiltrates on chest X-ray, and a markedly elevated LDH of 580 U/L together constitute a presentation highly characteristic of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, with confirmation pending on the induced sputum silver stain. This is severe disease by oxygenation criteria and requires immediate hospital-based care, oxygen support, and empiric therapy without waiting for the confirmatory stain. The underlying advanced HIV with wasting requires parallel management.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Admit the patient urgently for inpatient management of hypoxemic respiratory failure; the room-air saturation of 88 percent mandates immediate supplemental oxygen titrated to an acceptable saturation and close monitoring for further deterioration, with escalation to higher-level respiratory support if the work of breathing or oxygenation worsens. Start empiric therapy directed at Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia immediately rather than waiting for the silver stain result, since organisms persist for days after treatment starts and the diagnostic yield is not compromised by early treatment. Because the patient is hypoxemic on room air at 88 percent, he meets the severity threshold for adjunctive corticosteroid therapy given alongside the antimicrobial agent; obtain the arterial blood gas to document the alveolar-arterial gradient, but do not delay steroid initiation in a patient this hypoxemic, as steroids given early reduce the risk of the treatment-associated deterioration that occurs as organisms lyse. Monitor closely for adverse effects of therapy including cytopenias, renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, hepatotoxicity, and rash, with regular complete blood counts and metabolic panels. Concurrently evaluate for co-existing opportunistic infection given the CD4 of 45 and the weight loss: send acid-fast bacilli studies and place the patient in airborne isolation until tuberculosis is excluded, and obtain blood cultures. Address the additional consideration of the untreated HIV itself: engage HIV specialty care so that antiretroviral therapy can be initiated during or shortly after the acute treatment course, since early initiation improves outcomes at this CD4 level, while remaining alert to immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Once the acute illness is controlled, ensure secondary prophylaxis against Pneumocystis is maintained until immune reconstitution occurs, and evaluate the need for prophylaxis against other opportunistic pathogens appropriate to a CD4 count of 45. Address the cachexia and 10-pound weight loss with nutritional assessment and support. Arrange adherence counselling and close outpatient follow-up to prevent recurrence of the treatment gap that led to this presentation.
Notes: The diagnosis is not yet microbiologically confirmed; the induced sputum silver stain is pending, and a negative induced sputum does not exclude the diagnosis and should prompt bronchoalveolar lavage. Specific drug names and doses are not stated in the case and are therefore not specified here. Tuberculosis cannot be excluded on the information provided and must be actively evaluated with appropriate isolation precautions given the epidemiologic risk in advanced untreated HIV.

Vignette:
A 7-month-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she has been unusually fussy for the past 3 days. They have noticed increased drooling and that she constantly chews on her fingers and toys. She is eating slightly less than usual but still taking adequate formula. She has no fever, no diarrhea, and no rash. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The infant is mildly irritable but consolable. The lower gingiva is mildly swollen and erythematous over the area of the central incisors, and a tooth bud is palpable beneath the surface. The remainder of the exam is normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 7 months
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three days of unusual fussiness with increased drooling and constant chewing on fingers and toys, with slightly reduced oral intake but adequate formula consumption, and no fever, diarrhea, or rash.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of normal primary tooth eruption, commonly called teething, in an infant of exactly the age at which the mandibular central incisors typically erupt. The strongest supporting facts are the localized examination findings: the lower gingiva is mildly swollen and erythematous specifically over the area of the central incisors, and a tooth bud is palpable beneath the gingival surface. This anatomically localized finding directly explains the symptom cluster the parents describe. Increased drooling and constant chewing on fingers and toys are classic behaviors associated with eruption, representing increased salivation and the infant's instinctive counter-pressure on the sore gum. The mild irritability that is consolable, together with only a slight reduction in intake while still taking adequate formula, indicates a benign self-limited process rather than systemic illness. Equally important are the negatives that argue against alternative diagnoses. The temperature is 37.0 C, which is normal, so there is no fever to suggest an infectious cause; teething itself does not produce true fever, and attributing fever to teething is a known clinical pitfall that can delay recognition of genuine infection. There is no diarrhea and no rash, which argues against a viral syndrome such as a hand-foot-and-mouth type illness or a roseola-like exanthem. The remainder of the examination is normal, which makes occult infection such as otitis media, urinary tract infection, or pharyngitis unlikely, and there is no described oral ulceration to suggest herpetic gingivostomatitis, which would characteristically produce painful vesicles or ulcers, high fever, and marked refusal to feed. Fussiness in an infant always warrants consideration of non-oral causes such as occult trauma, corneal abrasion, hair tourniquet, incarcerated hernia, or infection, but the case states the remainder of the examination is normal and provides a positive, localized explanation for the symptoms. The three-day duration with preserved feeding and consolability is reassuring and consistent with a benign course.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A well-appearing, afebrile 7-month-old girl with three days of fussiness, drooling, and chewing behavior has localized gingival swelling and erythema over the lower central incisors with a palpable underlying tooth bud, consistent with normal primary tooth eruption. She is consolable, feeding adequately, and has an otherwise normal examination with no fever, diarrhea, or rash. This is a benign, self-limited physiologic process requiring symptomatic comfort measures and parental reassurance rather than diagnostic testing or medical intervention.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Reassure the parents that the findings represent normal tooth eruption and that the symptoms are expected to be self-limited as the incisors emerge. Advise simple comfort measures: allow the infant to chew on a clean, firm chilled (not frozen) teething ring or a cool clean washcloth, and gently rub the swollen gum with a clean finger, both of which provide counter-pressure that relieves discomfort. Manage the increased drooling by keeping the chin and neck area clean and dry to prevent a drool rash, patting rather than rubbing the skin, and applying a bland barrier ointment if the skin becomes irritated. Continue normal formula feeding on demand; the slight reduction in intake is acceptable as long as feeding remains adequate and wet diapers remain normal. Ensure any teething object is one solid piece, appropriately sized so it cannot be swallowed, and inspected regularly for damage. Address the additional considerations explicitly: do not use topical numbing gels or teething tablets, and avoid amber or any other teething necklaces and bracelets, which pose strangulation and choking hazards. Do not attribute any future fever to teething; teething does not cause fever, and a documented temperature elevation, particularly at this age, should prompt evaluation for a separate cause. Counsel the parents on return precautions: seek medical assessment if the infant develops fever, becomes inconsolable, refuses feeds or has a significant drop in intake with fewer wet diapers, develops vomiting, diarrhea, a rash, oral ulcers or vesicles, or appears lethargic or unwell, since these findings would indicate a process other than teething. Begin oral hygiene appropriate to this stage by wiping the erupting teeth and gums with a clean soft cloth or an infant toothbrush, avoid bottles in bed and prolonged bottle use to prevent early childhood caries, and plan an initial dental visit around the time of first tooth eruption or by the first birthday. Routine well-child follow-up is otherwise sufficient.
Notes: Teething does not cause fever; any subsequent fever in an infant of this age requires independent evaluation and must not be attributed to tooth eruption. Topical anesthetic gels and homeopathic teething tablets carry recognized risks and are not recommended.

Vignette: A 48-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of recurrent episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours per episode, occurring approximately twice monthly. Each episode is preceded by a sensation of fullness in her right ear and accompanied by roaring tinnitus and reduced hearing on the right side. She denies headache, visual changes, or focal neurological symptoms. Audiometry demonstrates low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear with normal hearing on the left. On examination between episodes, vital signs are normal. The Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,

Vignette:
A 48-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of recurrent episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours per episode, occurring approximately twice monthly. Each episode is preceded by a sensation of fullness in her right ear and accompanied by roaring tinnitus and reduced hearing on the right side. Between episodes she notes persistent mild tinnitus and a sense that her right ear hearing has gradually deteriorated. She experiences nausea and sometimes vomiting during attacks. She denies headache, visual changes, or focal neurological symptoms. Audiometry demonstrates low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear with normal hearing on the left. On examination between episodes, vital signs are normal. The Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Neurological exam is nonfocal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 48 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Six-month history of recurrent episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours, occurring about twice monthly, preceded by right ear fullness and accompanied by roaring tinnitus, reduced right-sided hearing, nausea and sometimes vomiting, with persistent mild tinnitus and progressive right-sided hearing deterioration between attacks.
Analysis: The presentation fits the classic symptom complex of Meniere disease affecting the right ear. The strongest supporting facts are the four cardinal features occurring together and lateralized consistently to one side: episodic spinning vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, all referable to the right ear. The duration of each attack is highly discriminating. Episodes lasting 2 to 4 hours fall squarely within the characteristic range of twenty minutes to twelve hours. This duration excludes benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, in which vertigo lasts seconds to at most a minute and is triggered by specific head position changes rather than preceded by aural fullness, and it excludes vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis, which produce a single prolonged episode of continuous vertigo lasting days rather than recurrent discrete attacks over six months. The premonitory sensation of right ear fullness before each attack is a characteristic aura of endolymphatic hydrops and is a strong positive feature. The roaring quality of the tinnitus is the classically described low-pitched tinnitus of this condition, as opposed to the high-pitched tinnitus typical of noise-induced or presbycusic hearing loss. The audiometric finding is confirmatory and highly specific in context: low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear with a normal left ear. Low-frequency predominant sensorineural loss is the hallmark early audiometric pattern of this disease and differs from the high-frequency loss of noise exposure or age, and from the retrocochlear pattern of a vestibular schwannoma. The bedside tuning fork tests corroborate the audiogram and localize the lesion correctly: Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally, indicating no conductive component in either ear, and Weber lateralizes to the left, the better-hearing ear, which is the expected pattern for a right sensorineural loss. Together these confirm a right cochlear sensorineural deficit rather than a middle ear or conductive problem. The clinically important element of progression is the interval history: persistent mild tinnitus between attacks and a gradual, subjective deterioration of right ear hearing over the six months indicate that the hearing loss is no longer fully reversible and that permanent cochlear injury is accruing, which raises the priority of definitive management. Differential considerations addressed by the case: vestibular migraine can produce recurrent vertigo of similar duration, but the patient explicitly denies headache and visual changes, and vestibular migraine does not typically cause a progressive unilateral low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry. Vestibular schwannoma must be considered in any unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus, though it usually produces progressive high-frequency loss and continuous imbalance rather than discrete vertiginous attacks, and the nonfocal neurological examination is reassuring but not exclusionary. Transient ischemic attack or posterior circulation events are unlikely given the six-month stereotyped recurrent pattern, the absence of focal neurological symptoms, and the nonfocal neurological examination. Autoimmune inner ear disease and syphilitic labyrinthitis can mimic this picture but typically progress more rapidly or involve both ears.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals and posterior fossa to exclude vestibular schwannoma or other retrocochlear pathology, which is indicated because of the asymmetric unilateral sensorineural hearing loss; serial audiometry with tympanometry to document and monitor the fluctuating and progressive right-sided threshold changes over time; vestibular function testing such as videonystagmography or caloric testing and video head impulse testing to quantify the right vestibular deficit and support the diagnosis; blood tests to exclude treatable mimics of asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss, including syphilis serology and screening for autoimmune disease; the audiometry and tuning fork examination already performed require no repetition for diagnosis but should be repeated longitudinally.
Conclusion: A 48-year-old woman has a six-month history of stereotyped, recurrent attacks of spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours, each preceded by right aural fullness and accompanied by roaring tinnitus and reduced right hearing, with nausea and vomiting. Audiometry confirms right-sided low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with a normal left ear, and tuning fork testing localizes a right sensorineural deficit with no conductive component. Neurological examination is nonfocal and there is no headache or visual disturbance. The findings are diagnostic of Meniere disease of the right ear, now showing interictal tinnitus and progressive hearing deterioration indicating early permanent cochlear injury. This requires prompt but non-emergency specialist otolaryngology evaluation, MRI to exclude retrocochlear pathology, and initiation of staged medical management.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Refer to otolaryngology, ideally to a neurotology or otology service, for confirmation and staged management of right-sided Meniere disease; the referral should be arranged promptly rather than urgently, since the progressive interictal hearing deterioration means delay carries a risk of permanent loss, but there is no acute threat. Obtain gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a vestibular schwannoma, which is a mandatory step given the asymmetric unilateral sensorineural hearing loss even though the neurological examination is nonfocal. Begin first-line conservative management with dietary sodium restriction and reduction or elimination of caffeine, alcohol, and nicotine, all of which are recognized triggers of hydrops-related attacks, and encourage regular sleep, adequate hydration, and stress reduction, since attacks are frequently precipitated by fatigue and stress. Institute a symptom and trigger diary recording attack frequency, duration, and preceding aural fullness, which is valuable both for confirming the diagnostic pattern and for judging response to treatment given her baseline of roughly two attacks monthly. Provide the patient with an acute attack plan: at the onset of the premonitory right ear fullness she should stop driving or any hazardous activity, sit or lie down in a safe position, and use vestibular suppressant and antiemetic medication as prescribed by her clinician for the acute episode only, since prolonged vestibular suppressant use impedes central compensation; the nausea and vomiting during attacks make an antiemetic particularly relevant for her. Discuss maintenance therapy with the specialist, which may include a diuretic and betahistine where available, with escalation to intratympanic therapy or other interventional options if attacks remain frequent despite conservative measures. Address the additional considerations explicitly: counsel her about safety, including the risk of sudden attacks while driving, operating machinery, working at heights, or swimming, and advise avoiding these activities during a symptomatic period; local driving regulations regarding recurrent vertigo should be reviewed. Arrange serial audiometry to track the right ear thresholds, and refer for vestibular rehabilitation to promote central compensation for the interictal imbalance rather than relying on chronic suppressants. Discuss hearing rehabilitation, including amplification for the right ear, as hearing loss progresses, and advise hearing protection for the currently normal left ear, since bilateral involvement can develop and preservation of the better ear is critical. Reassess promptly if the pattern changes, particularly if she develops headache, visual disturbance, focal neurological signs, sudden severe hearing loss, or drop attacks.
Notes: The clinical diagnosis of Meniere disease remains one of exclusion until MRI has ruled out retrocochlear pathology, which is required here because of the asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss. The persistent interictal tinnitus and progressive hearing deterioration indicate that permanent cochlear damage is already occurring, which increases the urgency of specialist review despite the non-emergent classification. Any sudden marked hearing loss or the emergence of focal neurological signs would represent a change in status requiring urgent reassessment.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. case_text:
Vignette:
Mr. E is a 26 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, headache, and non-productive cough. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat. He has been afebrile. His physical examination is normal, except for some pharyngeal erythema. He is otherwise in good health, and is on no medications except for acetaminophen for his sore throat and fever. He has no drug allergies.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 26 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two-day history of acute-onset sore throat with headache and non-productive cough, afebrile, in an otherwise healthy man taking only acetaminophen.
Analysis: This is a short-duration, self-limited upper respiratory illness, most consistent with a viral upper respiratory tract infection or viral pharyngitis. The reasoning rests on a small number of highly discriminating findings. First, the presence of a non-productive cough is the single most useful negative predictor of streptococcal pharyngitis; cough is characteristically absent in group A streptococcal infection and its presence points strongly toward a viral etiology. Second, the patient has been afebrile, which removes another of the classic features that would raise suspicion for bacterial pharyngitis. Third, the physical examination is normal except for pharyngeal erythema; specifically, no tonsillar exudate and no cervical lymphadenopathy are described, and both of these would be expected features of streptococcal disease. Taken together, the patient has essentially none of the classic clinical criteria that would justify testing or empiric antibiotic treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis, and his pretest probability of that diagnosis is very low. Fourth, the constellation of sore throat plus headache plus cough occurring together over 48 hours is the typical pattern of a viral syndrome, in which the pharyngeal symptom simply began first. The two-day duration is early and entirely consistent with the natural history of a viral illness, which typically resolves over roughly a week to ten days. He is a healthy young adult with no comorbidities, no medications other than acetaminophen, and no drug allergies, so there is no immunosuppression or other host factor that would alter the risk assessment. Differential considerations worth naming include streptococcal pharyngitis, which is rendered unlikely by the cough, absence of fever, and lack of exudate or adenopathy; infectious mononucleosis, which is plausible in this age group but is not supported here since the examination shows no tonsillar exudate, no lymphadenopathy, no splenomegaly, and no reported profound fatigue, and the illness is only two days old rather than following the more indolent prodrome typical of that disease; and serious causes of sore throat such as peritonsillar abscess, epiglottitis, or deep neck space infection, all of which are excluded by the normal examination and the absence of any reported drooling, trismus, voice change, stridor, respiratory distress, severe unilateral pain, or neck swelling. There is nothing in the vignette suggesting an atypical bacterial pneumonia or lower respiratory involvement, since the lung examination is described as normal and the cough is non-productive without dyspnea. A minor internal inconsistency in the history should be noted: the patient is described as afebrile yet is taking acetaminophen for sore throat and fever, which may reflect subjective feverishness or antipyretic masking rather than documented fever, and does not change the overall low-risk assessment given the otherwise normal examination.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A healthy 26-year-old man presents on day two of an acute viral upper respiratory illness manifesting as sore throat, headache, and non-productive cough, with an unremarkable examination apart from pharyngeal erythema and no fever. The presence of cough and the absence of fever, tonsillar exudate, and cervical adenopathy make group A streptococcal pharyngitis very unlikely, so neither rapid antigen testing nor throat culture nor antibiotic therapy is indicated. This is a self-limited condition that should be managed with symptomatic care, adequate fluids and rest, and clearly defined return precautions, with expected resolution over about a week.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Manage this illness symptomatically at home; no antibiotics are indicated, and this should be explained explicitly to the patient so that the absence of a prescription is understood as appropriate care rather than a withheld treatment. Continue acetaminophen at standard over-the-counter dosing for sore throat pain and headache, without exceeding the maximum daily dose and counting any acetaminophen contained in combination cold preparations toward that total, since inadvertent duplication is the commonest cause of overdose. Encourage generous oral fluid intake, adequate rest, and warm fluids; saline gargles, throat lozenges or hard candy, and honey in warm liquid provide additional relief of throat discomfort and cough. A humidifier or steam inhalation may ease the dry cough and nasal symptoms. Advise hand hygiene and covering coughs to limit transmission to household and workplace contacts, and suggest staying home while symptomatic. Set expectations for the natural course: symptoms should peak within the first few days and resolve over roughly seven to ten days, with cough sometimes lingering longer, and the illness should show gradual improvement rather than progression. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Do not perform rapid streptococcal antigen testing or throat culture in this presentation, since the presence of cough with absent fever, exudate, and adenopathy places him in the lowest-risk category where testing is not recommended and a positive result would more likely reflect carriage than acute infection. Counsel the patient on specific return precautions: seek reassessment if fever develops or symptoms persist beyond about ten days without improvement, or worsen after an initial improvement; and seek urgent or emergency evaluation for difficulty swallowing or inability to swallow saliva, drooling, difficulty opening the mouth, muffled or hot-potato voice, noisy breathing or stridor, shortness of breath, severe or strictly one-sided throat pain, neck swelling or stiffness, a rash, or dehydration. Advise return also if he develops marked fatigue, prolonged fever, or tender neck glands, which would prompt reconsideration of infectious mononucleosis. No follow-up appointment is otherwise required if he improves as expected.
Notes: The case records the patient as afebrile while also stating he takes acetaminophen for fever; temperature should be objectively rechecked when he is not on an antipyretic, as documented fever would change the assessment. Antibiotics carry risk without benefit in this presentation and are not warranted. This assessment is based only on the information provided; any change or progression in symptoms requires reassessment.

Vignette: Mr. Y is a 64 year old Chinese male who presents with chest pain for 24 hours. One day prior to presentation, the patient began to experience 8/10, non-radiating substernal chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. The pain intially improved with Tylenol, however over the following 24 hours, his symptoms worsened. The patient went to his primary physician, where an EKG was performed which showed ST elevation in leads V2-V6.

points: 10
tags: ['axis:urgency']

Recognizes anterolateral STEMI (ST elevation V2-V6) as a time-critical emergency requiring immediate activation of cath lab for primary PCI (door-to-balloon time less than 90 minutes).

[2]
points: 9
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Interprets ECG findings correctly: ST elevation in V2-V6 indicates extensive anterior wall MI (likely LAD occlusion), with significant risk of LV dysfunction and complications.

points: 9
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Recommends immediate initial treatment: aspirin 162-325 mg chewed, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation (heparin), nitrates if not hypotensive, and morphine for pain if needed.

[4]
points: 8
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:

tags: ['axis:completeness']

points: 6
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:

[7]
points: 6
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Monitors for and addresses complications: arrhythmias (VF/VT), cardiogenic shock, mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture), and heart failure.

points: 5
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Discusses post-PCI care: guideline-directed medical therapy (dual antiplatelet, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, high-intensity statin), cardiac rehab, and risk factor modification.

[9]
points: 4
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Asks about prior cardiac history, medications, allergies (especially contrast/aspirin), bleeding risk, and recent surgeries before anticoagulation.

points: -10
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Penalize failing to recognize STEMI urgency or delaying reperfusion in favor of conservative/outpatient management.

[11]
points: -8
tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Penalize misinterpreting the ECG (e.g., diagnosing pericarditis without distinguishing features, or non-STEMI).

[12]
points: -6
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
Penalize omitting dual antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation in initial management.

[13]
points: -4
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Penalize dwelling on differential diagnoses (such as MSK pain or GERD) at the expense of timely reperfusion.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Vignette:
Mr. Y is a 64 year old Chinese male who presents with chest pain for 24 hours. One day prior to presentation, the patient began to experience 8/10, non-radiating substernal chest pressure associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. The pain intially improved with Tylenol, however over the following 24 hours, his symptoms worsened. The patient went to his primary physician, where an EKG was performed which showed ST elevation in leads V2-V6.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 64 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Twenty-four hours of severe 8/10 non-radiating substernal chest pressure with diaphoresis and shortness of breath, initially transiently improved with Tylenol but progressively worsening, with an EKG showing ST elevation in leads V2 through V6.
Analysis: This is an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction involving the anterior and anterolateral wall. The single most decisive finding is the electrocardiogram: ST elevation across leads V2 through V6 represents a contiguous anterior precordial lead territory and indicates transmural ischemic injury in the distribution of the left anterior descending coronary artery, extending laterally. Anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction of this extent, involving five contiguous precordial leads, implies a large volume of jeopardized myocardium and carries the highest risk of pump failure, cardiogenic shock, malignant ventricular arrhythmia, and mechanical complications among infarct territories. The clinical history corroborates the electrocardiographic diagnosis in every respect. The pain is substernal and described as pressure rather than sharp or pleuritic, it is severe at 8 out of 10, and it is accompanied by diaphoresis and shortness of breath, which are autonomic and hemodynamic accompaniments that substantially raise the likelihood of an acute coronary syndrome over non-cardiac causes. The patient is a 64-year-old man, an age and sex demographic with high baseline coronary risk. The transient improvement with Tylenol is a clinically important false-reassurance feature and must not be interpreted as evidence against a cardiac cause; response or non-response to analgesics has no diagnostic value in chest pain, and this apparent early relief likely contributed to the delay in seeking care. The critical management issue in this case is time. Symptoms began 24 hours before presentation and have been progressively worsening rather than resolving. Ongoing symptoms with persistent ST elevation at 24 hours indicate that ischemia is still active and that viable myocardium remains at risk, which is what determines whether reperfusion is still beneficial. This is a late presentation, and the extended ischemic time both narrows the benefit of reperfusion and markedly increases the risk of complications including left ventricular systolic dysfunction, heart failure, left ventricular thrombus formation, arrhythmia, and, in the days that follow, mechanical complications such as ventricular septal rupture, free wall rupture, and papillary muscle rupture. Differential considerations for ST elevation with chest pain include acute pericarditis, which typically produces diffuse rather than territorial ST elevation with PR depression and pleuritic positional pain, not the pressure-like pain with diaphoresis seen here; aortic dissection, which classically produces abrupt severe tearing pain and must be considered before antithrombotic therapy since dissection can involve a coronary ostium and produce ST elevation, though the case describes non-radiating pressure without the migratory or tearing quality; pulmonary embolism, which can cause dyspnea and chest pain but would not typically produce contiguous anterior ST elevation; Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, which can mimic anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction and is distinguished only at angiography; and myopericarditis. None of these alternatives displaces the primary diagnosis, and the territorial ST elevation in a contiguous anterior distribution with typical ischemic symptoms in a 64-year-old man is an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction until proven otherwise at angiography.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Immediate continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator immediately available; repeat and serial 12-lead electrocardiograms, with right-sided and posterior leads to assess for right ventricular and posterior extension; serial cardiac troponin measurement; urgent coronary angiography with a view to primary percutaneous coronary intervention, which is both the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic study; transthoracic echocardiography to assess left ventricular systolic function, regional wall motion, and to screen for mechanical complications and left ventricular thrombus given the large anterior territory and late presentation; complete blood count, basic metabolic panel with electrolytes including potassium and magnesium, renal function before contrast administration, coagulation studies, lipid panel, and glycated hemoglobin and glucose; portable chest radiograph; pulse oximetry and full vital signs including bilateral blood pressures; intravenous access.
Conclusion: A 64-year-old man presents 24 hours after the onset of severe substernal chest pressure with diaphoresis and dyspnea, with symptoms that have progressively worsened and an electrocardiogram demonstrating ST elevation in leads V2 through V6. This constitutes an acute anterior and anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction with ongoing symptoms at a late time point, involving a large area of myocardium supplied by the left anterior descending artery. This is a time-critical, life-threatening emergency requiring immediate transfer by emergency medical services to a facility capable of primary percutaneous coronary intervention, with continuous cardiac monitoring and immediate initiation of guideline-directed acute therapy. Because symptoms are ongoing and ST elevation persists, urgent invasive reperfusion remains indicated despite the delayed presentation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology
Recommendations: Treat this as an immediate emergency. The patient must not be sent home, told to follow up, or transported by private vehicle. Activate emergency medical services and the receiving hospital's ST-elevation myocardial infarction pathway from the primary care office, transmitting the electrocardiogram ahead so the catheterization laboratory can be activated before arrival, and transfer directly to a percutaneous coronary intervention capable center. Establish continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring with a defibrillator at the bedside from this moment onward, since the highest risk of ventricular fibrillation is in the early hours of a large anterior infarction; ensure personnel capable of immediate defibrillation and advanced cardiac life support accompany the patient throughout transfer. Obtain intravenous access and full vital signs including bilateral blood pressures and oxygen saturation. Initiate acute therapy per institutional protocol: give aspirin to be chewed immediately unless contraindicated, add a second antiplatelet agent and anticoagulation as directed by the receiving interventional team, treat ischemic pain, and give supplemental oxygen only if the patient is hypoxemic rather than routinely. Withhold nitrates if there is hypotension, suspicion of right ventricular infarction, or recent phosphodiesterase inhibitor use, and confirm the blood pressure before administering them. Pursue primary percutaneous coronary intervention as the reperfusion strategy of choice; this remains indicated here because symptoms are ongoing and ST elevation persists at 24 hours, and mechanical reperfusion is preferred over fibrinolysis at this late time point, where fibrinolytic efficacy is substantially reduced and bleeding risk is not. Address the additional considerations explicitly. First, the delayed presentation of 24 hours is the dominant modifier of prognosis and complication risk: anticipate and monitor for left ventricular systolic dysfunction and heart failure, cardiogenic shock, ventricular arrhythmia, pericarditis, left ventricular thrombus, and mechanical complications, and obtain early echocardiography to establish left ventricular function and screen for thrombus in this large anterior territory. Second, the transient relief with Tylenol must be explicitly recognized as clinically meaningless for excluding cardiac ischemia; document this so that it is not used to downgrade suspicion. Third, before administering antithrombotic therapy, briefly consider aortic dissection given that it can produce ST elevation and would be worsened by anticoagulation, checking for pulse or blood pressure asymmetry and any tearing or radiating pain quality, though the presentation described is typical of infarction and this consideration must not delay reperfusion. After revascularization, admit to a coronary care unit for monitoring, and begin secondary prevention with dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, beta blockade, and renin-angiotensin system blockade as tolerated and as indicated by left ventricular function, with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism if left ventricular function is reduced. Arrange cardiac rehabilitation, risk factor assessment and modification including lipids, glucose, blood pressure and smoking status, and structured cardiology follow-up with reassessment of left ventricular function to determine any need for device therapy. Counsel the patient and family, with interpretation support if needed, on the importance of calling emergency services immediately for recurrent chest pain rather than waiting or self-treating, since the delay in this episode materially worsened his risk.
Notes: The time from symptom onset is 24 hours, which places this outside the optimal reperfusion window; reperfusion is still indicated here because symptoms are ongoing and ST elevation persists, and primary percutaneous coronary intervention rather than fibrinolysis is the appropriate strategy at this time point. Vital signs, hemodynamic status, cardiac examination, past medical history, risk factors, allergies, and current medications are not specified in the case and must be obtained; the presence of hypotension, signs of shock, or right ventricular involvement would change acute management, particularly the use of nitrates. Specific drug doses are not stated in the case and are therefore not specified here.
