A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of constant right-sided
scrotal pain. The pain began several hours prior to presentation and awoke him from sleep. He
is an otherwise healthy boy who states he has never experienced pain like this before. He
denies a history of genital trauma or any sexual activity, and he has not noticed any swelling or
lumps in his groin. He has not had any fevers, chills, urinary frequency, dysuria, hematuria, or
urethral discharge.

Review of Systems:
General: Denies subjective fevers or chills.

Skin: Denies itching and rashes or other lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: Noncontributory

Cardiovascular: Denies palpitations, chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: Denies abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, or vomiting.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, frequency, or urgency.

Musculoskeletal: Denies joint pain.

Neurologic: Denies numbness or paresthesias in any extremities.

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Eczema

Surgical history: Neonatal circumcision

Medications: Daily pediatric multivitamin

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Grandfather with hypertension.

Social history: He is currently in 4th grade; immunizations are up-to-date; not exposed to
tobacco smoke at home; no known sick contacts; has not traveled to any foreign countries.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: In mild distress due to pain.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.7° C
Pulse: 87 beats/min
BP: 123/68 mm Hg

Respirations: 16/min
Height: 137 cm
Weight: 32 kg

Skin: Warm and dry to the touch, no rashes.

HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic.

Pulmonary: Breath sounds present and equal bilaterally. No stridor, no rales, no wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Regular heart rate and rhythm, no murmurs, radial pulses are present and
equal bilaterally.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen is flat, no visible lesions, bowel sounds normal. On palpation,
abdomen is soft, nontender, no guarding, no masses.

Genitourinary: Circumcised phallus, no urethral discharge or lesions, no scrotal swelling or
erythema. Testes normal size, no masses.

Musculoskeletal: No costovertebral angle tenderness.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event.

Test Results:
Appropriate testing is ordered and results are shown:

Urinalysis: Normal

Doppler ultrasonography of the scrotum: 8 x 5 mm microcystic lesion adjacent to the right epididymal head. There is no significant flow within or surrounding the lesion. The testes appear normal bilaterally with appropriate arterial and venous flow.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 10 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Constant right-sided scrotal pain of several hours duration that awoke him from sleep, without trauma, fever, urinary symptoms, or urethral discharge, and with no prior similar episode.
Analysis: The presentation is acute scrotum in a prepubertal boy, and the reasoning proceeds in two stages: first excluding testicular torsion, and then identifying the actual cause. Testicular torsion is the diagnosis that must be excluded first in any boy with acute scrotal pain because it is time-critical for testicular salvage, and this case has several features that would raise that concern, namely constant unilateral pain of abrupt onset severe enough to wake him from sleep in a boy of exactly the peak age range. However, torsion is confidently excluded here by the imaging: Doppler ultrasonography demonstrates bilaterally normal testes with appropriate arterial and venous flow. Preserved intratesticular arterial and venous flow with normal testicular size and echotexture is inconsistent with testicular torsion. The examination further argues against it, since there is no scrotal swelling, no erythema, normal testicular size, and no mass, whereas torsion typically produces a swollen, high-riding, transversely oriented, exquisitely tender testis with an absent cremasteric reflex, along with nausea and vomiting, which he explicitly denies. The positive finding that explains the pain is the ultrasound demonstration of an 8 by 5 mm microcystic lesion adjacent to the right epididymal head with no significant flow within or surrounding it. This location and this appearance are characteristic of a torsed testicular appendage, that is, torsion of the appendix testis or appendix epididymis. These vestigial embryologic remnants sit at the upper pole of the testis and at the epididymal head, they are pedunculated and therefore prone to twisting, and torsion of an appendage is in fact the single most common cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal boys, more common than testicular torsion in this age group. The absence of flow within and around the lesion indicates that the appendage is infarcted, which is precisely the expected finding, and it is this ischemic appendage rather than the testis that is generating the pain. Critically, the avascularity is confined to the small paratesticular lesion while the testis itself retains normal perfusion, which is the key discriminator from testicular torsion. The differential considerations are otherwise systematically excluded by the data given. Epididymitis and orchitis are unlikely because he is afebrile at 36.7 C, the urinalysis is normal, there is no dysuria, frequency, hematuria, or urethral discharge, there is no scrotal erythema or swelling, and he denies sexual activity; furthermore epididymitis would typically show increased rather than absent Doppler flow. Incarcerated inguinal hernia is excluded by the absence of any groin swelling or lump and a soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Trauma and hematoma are excluded by the explicit denial of genital trauma and an atraumatic examination. Testicular tumor is excluded by normal testes of normal size with no masses. Referred pain from a ureteric stone or from appendicitis is unlikely given the normal urinalysis, absence of costovertebral angle tenderness, and a benign abdominal examination. Henoch-Schonlein purpura, which can involve the scrotum, is excluded by the absence of rash, joint pain, and abdominal pain. He is systemically well with normal vital signs and is in only mild distress, which is consistent with a benign, self-limited process.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with acute constant right-sided scrotal pain that woke him from sleep. He is afebrile and systemically well, with a normal urinalysis and a genitourinary examination showing no swelling, erythema, or mass. Doppler ultrasonography demonstrates normal bilateral testicular arterial and venous flow, which excludes testicular torsion, and identifies an 8 by 5 mm avascular microcystic lesion adjacent to the right epididymal head. The findings are diagnostic of torsion of a testicular appendage, the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal boys. This is a benign, self-limited condition that does not threaten the testis and does not require surgery or antibiotics. Management is conservative with analgesia, scrotal support, and activity limitation, with symptoms typically resolving over one to two weeks, and with clear instructions to return if pain changes in character or worsens.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Manage conservatively; no operative intervention, no antibiotics, and no further imaging are indicated given that testicular torsion has been definitively excluded by documented normal bilateral testicular perfusion and that the urinalysis is normal with no signs of infection. Provide scheduled rather than as-needed analgesia in the first days using a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent at weight-appropriate pediatric dosing for this 32 kg boy, with acetaminophen as an adjunct, since the pain is inflammatory in origin and responds well to anti-inflammatory therapy. Advise supportive measures: scrotal elevation and supportive underwear or a scrotal support, intermittent cold application to the scrotum in the first 24 to 48 hours, and relative rest with avoidance of sports, bicycle riding, straddle activities, and vigorous physical education for approximately one to two weeks or until the pain resolves. Explain the natural history explicitly to the boy and his parents so they can manage expectations: the torsed appendage infarcts and then involutes, pain typically improves substantially within several days and resolves over about one to two weeks, and a small firm nodule or the classic bluish discoloration at the upper pole may persist for a period without significance. Reassure them directly that the testis itself is healthy and normally perfused, that this condition does not affect future fertility, and that it carries no increased risk of testicular torsion. Address the additional considerations. Give explicit return precautions: the family should seek immediate emergency reassessment if the pain suddenly worsens or becomes severe, if the scrotum becomes markedly swollen, red, or hard, if the testis becomes high-riding or the pain changes in character, or if nausea, vomiting, or fever develops, since these would raise concern for testicular torsion or infection and would require repeat evaluation and Doppler ultrasound; emphasize that a subsequent episode of acute scrotal pain must never be assumed to be a recurrence of this benign condition. Arrange outpatient follow-up with the pediatrician or a pediatric urologist in one to two weeks to confirm resolution, with earlier review if pain has not begun improving within several days or if it persists beyond the expected course, at which point re-evaluation and consideration of surgical exploration or excision of the appendage would be appropriate. His eczema, daily multivitamin, absence of drug allergies, and up-to-date immunizations require no change. Document a return-to-activity plan for school and physical education. Provide age-appropriate reassurance to the child himself, as unexplained genital pain is frightening at this age.
Notes: The diagnosis rests on ultrasound demonstrating preserved bilateral testicular perfusion; testicular torsion remains a clinical diagnosis and can occasionally coexist with or follow other findings, so any change in symptoms mandates immediate reassessment rather than reassurance based on this study. Doppler ultrasound is operator dependent and a single normal study does not permanently exclude torsion at a later time. Specific analgesic agents and doses are not stated in the case and should be selected by weight according to standard pediatric dosing.

Vignette:
A 15-year-old girl presents with a superficial scrape on her left knee after falling off her skateboard approximately 1 hour ago. She was wearing shorts and fell onto pavement. She cleaned the wound with water at home. She denies hitting her head, loss of consciousness, or any other injuries. Her tetanus immunization is up to date. On examination, there is a 6 by 4 cm superficial abrasion on the anterior left knee with minor oozing of serous fluid. There is no active arterial bleeding, no embedded foreign material visible, and no involvement of deeper tissue. The surrounding skin is intact. Range of motion of the knee is full and painless.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 15 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Superficial abrasion of the anterior left knee sustained approximately one hour ago in a fall from a skateboard onto pavement, already rinsed with water at home, with no other injuries.
Analysis: This is an uncomplicated superficial abrasion from a low-energy fall, and every element of the history and examination supports a benign, self-limited soft tissue injury requiring only basic wound care. The strongest supporting facts are the wound characteristics themselves. The lesion is explicitly described as a superficial abrasion measuring 6 by 4 cm with only minor oozing of serous fluid. Serous rather than sanguineous or pulsatile drainage indicates that the injury is confined to the epidermis and superficial dermis, above the level of the dermal vascular plexus and well above deeper structures. There is no active arterial bleeding, so there is no vascular injury requiring control or repair. There is no involvement of deeper tissue, which excludes injury to the joint capsule, extensor mechanism, tendon, bone, or neurovascular structures, and it also means the wound is not a laceration and requires no suturing, adhesive closure, or other primary closure; abrasions heal by secondary intention and should not be closed. The surrounding skin is intact, indicating no undermining, flap, or avulsion component. No embedded foreign material is visible, which is the key check after a fall onto pavement, since retained grit is the principal cause of both infection and permanent traumatic tattooing in this injury type. The functional assessment is equally reassuring: range of motion of the knee is full and painless, which effectively excludes a significant intra-articular injury, fracture, ligamentous disruption, or extensor mechanism injury, and makes radiography unnecessary. The mechanism is low energy, a fall from a skateboard onto pavement while wearing shorts, which fully explains a friction injury to the exposed anterior knee and does not suggest high-energy trauma. Two specific risk questions are directly answered in the negative by the history. First, head injury is excluded, as she denies hitting her head and denies loss of consciousness, so no neurological observation or imaging pathway is triggered. Second, tetanus is addressed, as her immunization is up to date, so no tetanus toxoid or immunoglobulin is required despite this being a contaminated outdoor wound. She also denies any other injuries, so there is no indication to pursue occult trauma elsewhere. The main relevant differential and complication considerations are therefore narrow: retained foreign material in the abrasion bed, which must be actively excluded by careful inspection during thorough irrigation rather than relying on the initial visual survey, since the home rinse with plain water is unlikely to have been adequate for a pavement injury; wound infection, which is the principal delayed risk and which develops over the following days rather than at one hour; and an occult underlying injury, which is made very unlikely by the full painless range of motion. The one-hour interval since injury is well within the window for effective cleansing and carries no adverse implication.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A healthy 15-year-old girl has a 6 by 4 cm superficial abrasion of the anterior left knee sustained one hour ago in a low-energy skateboard fall onto pavement. The wound is superficial with only serous oozing, no arterial bleeding, no visible embedded debris, no deep tissue involvement, and intact surrounding skin. Knee range of motion is full and painless, there is no head injury or loss of consciousness, no other injuries, and tetanus immunization is current. This is an uncomplicated abrasion requiring no imaging, no wound closure, no tetanus prophylaxis, and no systemic antibiotics. It can be managed with thorough cleansing and irrigation, moist wound care with a non-adherent dressing, simple analgesia, and observation for signs of infection, with expected healing over one to two weeks.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Clean the wound properly, since the home rinse with plain water was likely insufficient for a pavement injury. Wash hands, then irrigate the abrasion copiously with clean running tap water or normal saline under moderate pressure, and gently but thoroughly cleanse the entire abraded surface with mild soap and water or a soft gauze to remove any grit, dirt, or asphalt particles from the wound bed. Inspect the base of the abrasion carefully under good light during and after irrigation, because retained pavement debris is the main preventable cause of both infection and permanent traumatic tattooing; if any embedded material cannot be removed with irrigation and gentle scrubbing, or if the area is too painful to clean adequately, she should be seen by a clinician for cleansing with local anesthesia. Do not use hydrogen peroxide, alcohol, or iodine directly in the wound bed, as these damage healing tissue. Do not close the wound with sutures, glue, or closure strips; abrasions heal by secondary intention. After cleaning, pat the area dry, apply a thin layer of a bland ointment such as petroleum jelly to keep the wound bed moist, and cover with a non-adherent dressing. Moist covered healing produces faster re-epithelialization and less scarring than allowing a scab to form. Change the dressing daily and whenever it becomes wet or soiled, re-cleansing gently at each change, and if the dressing sticks, soak it off with water rather than pulling it free. Provide simple analgesia with acetaminophen or an over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug as needed at age-appropriate dosing. No systemic or topical antibiotics are indicated for this clean superficial abrasion. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Tetanus prophylaxis is not required, as her immunization status is confirmed up to date; document this. No radiographs of the knee are needed given full painless range of motion and no deep tissue involvement. No head injury assessment or observation protocol is triggered, as she denies both head strike and loss of consciousness, but advise the family to seek care if any headache, vomiting, confusion, or drowsiness were to develop, as head injury history is by self-report. Give clear infection return precautions: seek medical assessment for spreading redness, warmth, or swelling around the wound, increasing rather than decreasing pain after the first day or two, purulent or foul drainage, red streaking from the wound, fever, or failure to show progressive healing over about two weeks. Advise activity modification for comfort: she may bear weight and move the knee freely since motion is painless, but should avoid kneeling and avoid re-abrading the area, keep the wound covered and out of dirt during sports, and keep the dressing dry, using showers rather than baths, pools, hot tubs, lakes, or the ocean until the surface has fully re-epithelialized. Once healed, advise sun protection with sunscreen or clothing over the new skin for several months, since the immature epithelium hyperpigments readily. Finally, take the opportunity to counsel on injury prevention, specifically the use of knee pads, elbow pads, wrist guards, and a helmet while skateboarding, since a helmet is what would prevent the head injury she happened to avoid on this occasion. Routine follow-up is not required if healing progresses normally.
Notes: The absence of embedded foreign material was assessed visually before formal irrigation; the wound bed must be re-inspected after thorough cleansing, as pavement debris is frequently obscured until the surface is cleaned. The denial of head injury, loss of consciousness, and other injuries is by patient report only.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man with hypertension and degenerative joint disease presents to the emergency department with a three-day history of a productive cough and fever. He has a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F), a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 90 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 92 percent while breathing room air. Physical examination reveals only crackles and egophony in the right lower lung field. The white-cell count is 14,000 per cubic millimeter, and the results of routine chemical tests are normal. A chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 65 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three-day history of productive cough and fever, with tachypnea and hypoxemia, in a man with hypertension and degenerative joint disease.
Analysis: This is community-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe. The diagnosis rests on the convergence of a compatible clinical syndrome, focal examination findings, a supportive laboratory profile, and confirmatory imaging. The history of a three-day productive cough with fever establishes an acute lower respiratory tract infection. The examination is focal rather than diffuse and localizes precisely: crackles and egophony are confined to the right lower lung field. Egophony is a particularly valuable finding because it indicates consolidated lung transmitting sound through an airless, fluid-filled alveolar space, and it is far more specific for lobar consolidation than crackles alone, which can arise from heart failure, atelectasis, or fibrosis. The chest radiograph confirms the anatomical correlate with a right lower lobe infiltrate in exactly the territory of the abnormal auscultation, closing the loop between symptom, sign, and image. The white-cell count of 14,000 per cubic millimeter demonstrates a leukocytosis consistent with a bacterial process, and the temperature of 38.3 C confirms objective fever. The absence of any other examination abnormality argues against a multifocal or systemic alternative process. Severity assessment is the decisive clinical task here, because the diagnosis of pneumonia is straightforward whereas the site-of-care decision determines outcome and resource use. Applying the standard severity variables to this patient: he is 65 years old, which itself meets the age criterion; there is no confusion described, so mental status is intact; the respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, which is elevated but below the threshold of 30; the blood pressure at 144/92 mm Hg is not low and in fact reflects his known hypertension, so there is no hypotension criterion; and the routine chemical tests are normal, which means renal function and urea are not deranged. He therefore scores on age alone, placing him at low to moderate risk by CURB-65 criteria. The countervailing finding, and the most important single abnormality in this case, is the oxygen saturation of 92 percent on room air. This sits at the accepted threshold below which hypoxemia is considered clinically significant, and, combined with a respiratory rate of 22 and an age of 65 with comorbid hypertension, it indicates that gas exchange is already compromised and that he has limited physiological reserve should the consolidation progress. Hypoxemia is an independent indication for hospital-based assessment irrespective of a favorable severity score, and severity scores are decision aids that do not override clinical judgment or objective oxygenation. His heart rate of 90 is normal and he is not in shock. Relevant differential considerations include aspiration pneumonia, which is anatomically plausible given right lower lobe involvement since the right mainstem bronchus is more vertical, although no aspiration risk factor is described; pulmonary embolism with infarction, which can produce fever, hypoxemia, and a peripheral infiltrate, but is less consistent with a productive cough, three-day febrile prodrome, leukocytosis, and egophonic consolidation; heart failure, argued against by the focal rather than bilateral findings, the fever, and the leukocytosis; tuberculosis or malignancy with post-obstructive pneumonia, which are not supported by this acute presentation but become relevant if the infiltrate fails to resolve; and empyema or parapneumonic effusion, which should be sought if there is clinical deterioration. His degenerative joint disease is relevant chiefly to mobility and to analgesic choice rather than to the pulmonary diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous pulse oximetry and serial vital signs; blood cultures drawn before the first antibiotic dose; sputum Gram stain and culture given the productive cough; urinary antigen testing for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila; respiratory viral testing including influenza and SARS-CoV-2; arterial or venous blood gas if oxygenation deteriorates or work of breathing increases; complete blood count with differential and comprehensive metabolic panel as already obtained, with repeat monitoring including renal function and electrolytes; serum lactate to screen for occult tissue hypoperfusion and sepsis; the chest radiograph as already performed, with repeat or cross-sectional imaging only if there is clinical deterioration or failure to improve; supplemental oxygen delivery equipment; intravenous access.
Conclusion: A 65-year-old hypertensive man presents on day three of a productive cough and fever with a temperature of 38.3 C, respiratory rate of 22, leukocytosis of 14,000, and focal right lower lung crackles with egophony, confirmed by a right lower lobe infiltrate on chest radiograph. This is community-acquired pneumonia. Formal severity scoring places him at low to moderate risk on age alone, since he has no confusion, no tachypnea above 30, no hypotension, and normal chemistry. However, an oxygen saturation of 92 percent on room air constitutes clinically significant hypoxemia and, together with his age, comorbidity, and elevated respiratory rate, warrants supervised hospital-based assessment, supplemental oxygen as required, and prompt initiation of empiric antimicrobial therapy after cultures are obtained, with close reassessment to determine whether he can be safely stepped down to outpatient care.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Manage this as community-acquired pneumonia with hypoxemia requiring immediate treatment in a supervised setting. Obtain blood cultures and sputum for Gram stain and culture before administering antibiotics, then initiate empiric antimicrobial therapy without delay, since time to first antibiotic dose is a key determinant of outcome; do not allow the pursuit of microbiological confirmation to postpone treatment. Select the empiric regimen according to local guidelines and antibiogram, covering typical and atypical community-acquired pathogens and taking into account that he is 65 with comorbid hypertension, a group in whom broader coverage than for a healthy young adult is standard. Administer supplemental oxygen titrated to maintain a saturation above 92 percent, and place him on continuous pulse oximetry with serial vital signs, given that a room-air saturation of exactly 92 percent leaves no margin for deterioration. Provide adequate hydration, antipyretics, and analgesia. Address the additional considerations explicitly. First, on site of care: although his CURB-65 score of 1 based on age alone would ordinarily support outpatient management, the hypoxemia at 92 percent on room air overrides that score, and severity indices must never be applied mechanically in the presence of significant hypoxemia; admit for observation and oxygen unless a repeat assessment shows he maintains saturation comfortably off oxygen and can be reliably followed. Second, his degenerative joint disease is directly relevant to disposition, since impaired mobility and functional dependence affect the ability to manage at home and to return for review; assess his functional status, social support, and reliability of follow-up before considering discharge. Third, choose analgesia and antipyretics with awareness of his hypertension, avoiding sustained nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory use where it could raise blood pressure or impair renal function, and monitor renal function and electrolytes, especially if he takes antihypertensive agents. Reassess clinically at 48 to 72 hours; expect defervescence and improving oxygenation, and if he fails to improve, reconsider the differential, specifically resistant or atypical organisms, a parapneumonic effusion or empyema, an obstructing endobronchial lesion, or an alternative diagnosis such as pulmonary embolism, and pursue further imaging. Plan de-escalation of intravenous to oral antibiotics once he is afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and able to take oral medication, and complete a standard treatment duration rather than an extended course. On discharge, arrange follow-up with his primary physician within about a week, give explicit return precautions for worsening breathlessness, recurrent fever, confusion, chest pain, or inability to maintain oral intake, and advise that cough and fatigue may persist for several weeks after cure. Ensure a follow-up chest radiograph is arranged if symptoms fail to resolve or if there are risk factors for underlying malignancy, in order to document radiographic resolution. Before discharge, review and update pneumococcal and influenza vaccination status, offer smoking cessation support if applicable, and optimize management of his hypertension.
Notes: Smoking history, alcohol use, aspiration risk factors, immunosuppression, recent hospitalization or antibiotic exposure, current medications, allergies, and vaccination status are not specified in the case and are needed to finalize antibiotic selection and risk stratification. Specific antibiotic agents and doses are not stated in the case and are therefore not specified here; selection should follow local resistance patterns and guidelines. The oxygen saturation of 92 percent is borderline and should be rechecked and trended, including with ambulation if discharge is contemplated.

Vignette:
A 33-year-old man presents with a several-month history of persistent flaky, scaly patches on his scalp and eyebrows. He reports mild itching that is worse after showering. He has tried regular shampoo without improvement. He denies hair loss, spreading to other body areas, or any joint symptoms. He has no history of psoriasis or HIV. On examination, there are yellowish, greasy scales on the scalp, particularly along the hairline and in the eyebrow region. Mild erythema underlies the scales. There are no excoriations or signs of secondary infection.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 33 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Several-month history of persistent flaky, scaly patches on the scalp and eyebrows with mild itching worse after showering, unresponsive to regular shampoo.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of seborrheic dermatitis. The diagnosis is clinical and is established by the morphology and the distribution together. The morphology is the most discriminating feature: the scales are described as yellowish and greasy with mild underlying erythema. Greasy yellow scale is the hallmark of seborrheic dermatitis and contrasts sharply with the dry, silvery-white, thick, adherent scale of scalp psoriasis and with the fine dry white flaking of simple dandruff or xerosis. The distribution is equally characteristic and is the second pillar of the diagnosis: involvement of the scalp, particularly along the hairline, together with the eyebrows, corresponds precisely to the sebaceous-gland-rich seborrheic areas of the head where Malassezia yeast proliferates and drives the inflammatory response. The chronicity of several months fits the persistent, relapsing and remitting natural history of the condition rather than an acute dermatosis. The symptom detail that itching is worse after showering is consistent with the drying and irritant effect of washing on already inflamed skin. The failure of regular shampoo to help is expected and diagnostically useful, because ordinary cosmetic shampoo has no antifungal or anti-inflammatory activity and therefore does not address the underlying Malassezia-driven inflammation; this history establishes that first-line self-treatment has genuinely been attempted and failed, which is what escalates management to medicated therapy. The negatives in the case systematically exclude the principal differential diagnoses. Scalp psoriasis is the closest mimic, and it is argued against by the greasy yellowish rather than silvery scale, by the absence of well-demarcated thickened plaques, by the absence of any spread to other body sites such as the extensor elbows and knees or the nails, by the absence of joint symptoms which would suggest psoriatic arthritis, and by the explicit absence of any personal history of psoriasis. Tinea capitis is unlikely given the absence of hair loss, alopecic patches, broken hairs, boggy swelling, or lymphadenopathy, and it is uncommon in a 33-year-old adult. Contact or atopic dermatitis is not supported by the greasy scale morphology, the strictly seborrheic distribution, and the absence of excoriations. Discoid lupus and lichen planopilaris are excluded by the absence of scarring and hair loss. Secondary bacterial infection is excluded by the absence of any signs of infection or excoriation. One important systemic association deserves explicit mention because severe, extensive, or treatment-refractory seborrheic dermatitis can be a cutaneous marker of HIV infection or of parkinsonism and other neurological disease; the case states he has no history of HIV, and the disease here is mild and localized to two typical sites without extensive or explosive involvement, so no such underlying condition is suggested by the findings. There are no red flags: no hair loss, no spread, no joint involvement, no systemic symptoms, and no signs of infection. This is a benign, chronic, cosmetically and symptomatically bothersome but medically minor condition.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 33-year-old man has a several-month history of yellowish, greasy scales with mild underlying erythema on the scalp hairline and eyebrows, with mild pruritus worse after showering, unimproved by ordinary shampoo. The morphology and the seborrheic distribution are diagnostic of seborrheic dermatitis. There is no hair loss, no extension to other sites, no joint symptoms, no signs of secondary infection, and no history of psoriasis or HIV, so no laboratory testing, biopsy, or fungal culture is required. This is a benign chronic relapsing condition that responds well to over-the-counter medicated antifungal shampoos used correctly, with a gentle low-potency approach for the eyebrow skin, and requires only reassessment if it fails to improve or worsens.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Begin treatment with an over-the-counter medicated antifungal shampoo, since ordinary shampoo has already failed and is not expected to work. Suitable active ingredients include ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, ciclopirox, zinc pyrithione, or a coal tar preparation; use it two to three times per week initially. Application technique matters more than product choice and is the commonest reason for treatment failure: the shampoo must be massaged into the scalp skin itself, not merely the hair, and left in contact for approximately five minutes before rinsing, since the active agent needs dwell time on the affected skin. Rotating between two shampoos with different active ingredients can improve response and reduce tolerance. Expect improvement over roughly two to four weeks. For the eyebrow involvement, the same antifungal shampoo can be applied carefully as a brief wash to the eyebrow area during showering with meticulous care to avoid the eyes, or a ketoconazole cream may be used on that skin; because eyebrow and facial skin is thin, use only gentle, low-potency preparations there and avoid strong or prolonged topical corticosteroid application to the face, which causes skin atrophy, telangiectasia, and perioral dermatitis. A short course of a low-potency topical corticosteroid or a topical calcineurin inhibitor may be used for a few days to settle marked inflammation and itching, but should not be used continuously as maintenance. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Counsel the patient clearly that seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic relapsing condition rather than a curable one; the goal is control, and flares are common with stress, cold or dry weather, fatigue, and illness, so intermittent maintenance treatment once or twice weekly after clearance is usually needed to prevent recurrence, and stopping treatment entirely upon improvement predictably leads to relapse. Reassure him that this condition is not contagious, is not caused by poor hygiene, and does not cause permanent hair loss. For the itching that is worse after showering, advise using lukewarm rather than hot water, limiting shower duration, avoiding harsh or fragranced hair products and alcohol-based styling products, patting rather than rubbing the scalp dry, and applying a bland non-comedogenic moisturizer to the eyebrow region after washing. Advise him not to pick or scratch the scales, since this risks excoriation and secondary infection, neither of which is present now. Set clear reassessment criteria: he should see a clinician if there is no meaningful improvement after four to six weeks of correctly applied medicated shampoo, if the rash spreads beyond the scalp and eyebrows, if hair loss develops, if joint symptoms appear, or if the skin becomes weeping, crusted, painful, or shows other signs of infection, since these would prompt reconsideration of psoriasis, tinea, or another diagnosis and might warrant dermatology referral, potassium hydroxide preparation or fungal culture, or biopsy. Note also that unusually severe, extensive, or treatment-resistant seborrheic dermatitis can be associated with underlying immunosuppression or neurological disease and would justify further evaluation, although nothing in his current presentation suggests this. No follow-up appointment is otherwise required if he responds as expected.
Notes: The diagnosis is clinical and rests on the greasy yellow scale in a seborrheic distribution; no testing is needed unless the condition fails to respond to appropriate therapy, at which point psoriasis and tinea should be reconsidered. Avoid potent or prolonged topical corticosteroids on the eyebrow and facial skin. Duration of symptom control depends on ongoing intermittent maintenance therapy.

Vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother after 6 days of persistent high fever unresponsive to acetaminophen and ibuprofen. Over the past several days, she has noticed redness in both eyes without discharge, a rash on his trunk, swelling of his hands and feet, cracked bleeding lips, and a red bumpy tongue. Vignette:
A 30-year-old man who describes himself as an avid gamer presents with a dull ache in his right wrist that has been gradually worsening over the past 2 weeks. The pain is worse during and after prolonged gaming sessions and improves with rest. He denies any specific injury, swelling, numbness, or locking of the wrist. He is right-hand dominant. On examination, the right wrist has full range of motion. There is mild tenderness along the dorsal extensor tendons without visible swelling or erythema. Finkelstein test is negative. Grip strength is mildly reduced compared to the left. Neurovascular exam is intact.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Dull ache in the right wrist gradually worsening over 2 weeks, worse during and after prolonged gaming sessions and improving with rest, with no injury, swelling, numbness, or locking.
Analysis: The presentation is that of an activity-related overuse injury of the dominant right wrist in an avid gamer. The strongest supporting facts are the gradual 2-week onset without trauma, the clear activity-dependent pattern (pain provoked by prolonged repetitive gaming and relieved by rest), tenderness localized along the dorsal extensor tendons, and the absence of swelling, erythema, locking, or neurovascular deficit. Full range of motion and a mildly reduced grip strength are consistent with pain inhibition rather than structural damage. This pattern fits repetitive strain of the dorsal wrist extensor tendons (extensor tendinopathy/tenosynovitis) from sustained non-neutral wrist positioning and repetitive keyboard/controller use. Main differential considerations addressed by the case findings: de Quervain tenosynovitis is made unlikely by the negative Finkelstein test and the dorsal rather than radial styloid tenderness; carpal tunnel syndrome or another compressive neuropathy is unlikely given denial of numbness and an intact neurovascular examination; intra-articular pathology such as a triangular fibrocartilage complex tear or ganglion cyst is less likely with full painless range of motion, no locking, and no visible swelling; inflammatory or septic arthritis is not supported, as there is no erythema, swelling, warmth, or systemic complaint; occult fracture is not supported given the explicit denial of injury.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical; no imaging or laboratory testing is indicated at this point given the absence of trauma, swelling, deformity, neurovascular deficit, or systemic features.
Conclusion: A 30-year-old right-hand-dominant man with a 2-week history of activity-related, rest-relieved dorsal right wrist pain, dorsal extensor tendon tenderness, negative Finkelstein test, full range of motion, and intact neurovascular status has an overuse dorsal wrist extensor tendinopathy/repetitive strain injury related to prolonged gaming. There are no findings suggesting fracture, infection, inflammatory arthritis, nerve compression, or internal derangement, so conservative activity modification is the appropriate initial approach.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Reduce or temporarily interrupt prolonged gaming sessions and any other repetitive wrist loading until symptoms settle; resume gradually as pain allows. Take frequent breaks during play (short pauses every 20 to 30 minutes) with gentle wrist and finger range-of-motion and stretching of the extensor group. Apply local cold after sessions that provoke symptoms and use relative rest as the primary treatment, since the pain already improves with rest. Optimize ergonomics: keep the wrist in a neutral rather than extended position, use wrist and forearm support, and adjust chair, desk, and controller or keyboard height; the tight-fitting hand posture of prolonged play should be avoided. A removable wrist splint, particularly at night or during activity, may reduce symptoms. Simple analgesia may be used for comfort. Once pain has settled, begin progressive grip and wrist extensor strengthening to address the mildly reduced grip strength and to prevent recurrence. Seek non-emergent medical review if pain persists or worsens beyond a few weeks of activity modification, or urgent review if new swelling, erythema, warmth, fever, numbness, tingling, locking, marked weakness, or deformity develops.
Notes: Grip strength is only mildly reduced and is most consistent with pain-related inhibition; persistent or progressive weakness, or the appearance of numbness, would require reassessment for nerve involvement or intra-articular pathology. The case does not specify duration of daily gaming, occupation, or prior wrist problems.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 48 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Nasal-sounding voice with a sensation of air escaping through the nose while speaking, first noted a week after balloon sinus surgery one year ago and more apparent over the last 3 months, worse later in the day, with occasional nasal regurgitation of liquids.
Analysis: The core abnormality is hypernasal speech due to velopharyngeal incompetence, supported by the sensation of nasal air escape during speech and nasal regurgitation of liquids but not solids. The single most important feature is fatigability: the voice is better in the morning and worse later in the day. This diurnal, fatigable pattern of bulbar weakness, together with minimal left ptosis elicited only on sustained upward gaze, points to a disorder of neuromuscular transmission rather than a structural or purely otolaryngologic problem. The testing confirms this: repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz shows a decremental response in two separate territories (median nerve recording from abductor pollicis brevis and accessory nerve recording from trapezius), with the decrement improving after 10 seconds of exercise (postactivation facilitation) and worsening after 60 seconds (postactivation exhaustion). The serum acetylcholine receptor antibody titer is elevated at 0.28 nmol/L against a normal reference of less than 0.02 nmol/L, and the creatine kinase is normal at 50 U/L, which argues against a myopathic process. Together these findings establish an autoimmune postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, myasthenia gravis, presenting predominantly with bulbar (palatal) involvement and minimal ocular signs. Differential considerations: a structural complication of the balloon rhinoplasty causing velopharyngeal insufficiency was a reasonable initial hypothesis given the temporal link to surgery, but it does not explain diurnal fatigability, the ptosis, or the electrophysiologic and serologic abnormalities, and the nasal passages and pharynx are normal on examination. A brainstem or cranial nerve lesion is unlikely with cranial nerves 2 to 12 otherwise grossly intact and with normal sensation, reflexes, coordination, and gait. Myopathy is excluded by normal strength (5/5 in all four extremities), normal tone and bulk, and a normal creatine kinase. A presynaptic disorder such as Lambert-Eaton syndrome typically shows a marked incremental response after exercise and depressed reflexes, whereas here reflexes are normal, the pattern is decrement with only transient facilitation, and the acetylcholine receptor antibody is positive. A purely functional or phonatory voice disorder does not explain the objective electrophysiologic decrement or the antibody result.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT or MRI of the chest to evaluate for thymoma or thymic hyperplasia. Thyroid function testing and screening for associated autoimmune disease. Baseline pulmonary function testing with forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force to assess respiratory reserve. Formal speech and swallowing assessment to quantify velopharyngeal incompetence and aspiration risk.
Conclusion: A 48-year-old woman with fatigable hypernasal speech, nasal regurgitation of liquids, and subtle fatigable left ptosis has myasthenia gravis with predominantly bulbar involvement, confirmed by a decremental response on 3-Hz repetitive nerve stimulation with postactivation facilitation and exhaustion in two nerve territories and by an elevated acetylcholine receptor antibody titer with a normal creatine kinase. The onset shortly after balloon sinus surgery is temporally coincidental rather than causal, since the nasal passages and pharynx are structurally normal. She currently has no limb weakness, no dysphagia for solids, and no respiratory symptoms, so she needs prompt specialist management rather than emergency intervention, with explicit counseling about the risk of bulbar and respiratory deterioration.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Refer promptly to neurology for confirmation and initiation of treatment of myasthenia gravis. Obtain chest imaging to look for thymoma, since its presence would change management and may indicate thymectomy. Begin symptomatic treatment with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as pyridostigmine, and discuss immunomodulatory therapy (corticosteroids with or without a steroid-sparing agent) with the specialist, given progression of bulbar symptoms over the last 3 months. Measure and periodically repeat forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force to detect respiratory involvement early. Advise on swallowing safety given nasal regurgitation of liquids: upright posture while eating and drinking, small sips, and avoiding meals when fatigued; arrange speech and swallowing therapy for the velopharyngeal incompetence. Counsel her explicitly about myasthenic crisis, so that worsening dysphagia, new dyspnea, a weak cough, or inability to clear secretions prompts immediate emergency evaluation. Review all medications for agents that impair neuromuscular transmission, notably aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta blockers, and magnesium; her documented erythromycin allergy is separately relevant because macrolides should be avoided. Continue her asthma regimen of twice-daily beclomethasone and as-needed albuterol, and note that systemic corticosteroids, if started, can transiently worsen myasthenic weakness and require close monitoring at initiation. Address her stated concern about her voice by explaining the diagnosis and that the sinus surgery is not the cause. Evaluate the occasional left occipital shooting pains separately if they persist or change, as they are not explained by this diagnosis. Arrange follow-up to reassess bulbar function, ptosis, and limb strength.
Notes: The left occipital shooting pains since sinus surgery are not accounted for by the neuromuscular diagnosis and warrant separate consideration if persistent. Thymoma status is not specified in the case and must be determined before definitive management planning. Bedside testing showed no deltoid fatigue despite an electrophysiologic decrement, so clinical strength testing alone can underestimate disease severity.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 58 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of increasing pain, redness, and swelling of the right foot with low-grade fever and mild chills, four days after stepping on a nail while walking barefoot in her yard.
Analysis: This is an acute soft tissue infection of the foot arising from a plantar puncture wound in a patient with two major risk factors for a complicated course: a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and clinically evident peripheral arterial disease with diminished pulses bilaterally. The strongest supporting facts are the clear inoculating event four days ago, cleaned but never medically evaluated, the progression over the last 2 days, the local findings of a plantar puncture wound with 6 cm of surrounding erythema, warmth, edema, and tenderness, and the systemic signs of temperature 100.6 F with chills. This constitutes a diabetic foot infection with spreading cellulitis of at least moderate severity. Reassuring findings are the absence of crepitus and fluctuance and the stable hemodynamics with heart rate 84 and blood pressure 142/88, which argue against necrotizing soft tissue infection and against septic shock at this moment. The differential and complication considerations that must be actively excluded rather than assumed absent are: deep plantar space abscess, which may lack palpable fluctuance through the thick sole; retained foreign body such as a nail fragment or debris driven inward; osteomyelitis or septic arthritis, since plantar puncture wounds can penetrate to bone or joint and this infection is already four days old in a diabetic foot; necrotizing fasciitis, which must be reconsidered urgently if pain becomes disproportionate or bullae, skin discoloration, crepitus, or systemic toxicity appear; and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, classically associated with puncture wounds, in addition to the more common staphylococcal and streptococcal pathogens. The diminished peripheral pulses raise the further concern of limb ischemia impairing healing and antibiotic delivery. Tetanus is a genuine risk because the last booster was more than 10 years ago and the wound is a contaminated puncture. A purely non-infectious inflammatory reaction to the puncture is not tenable given fever, chills, and spreading erythema.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Plain radiographs of the right foot for radiopaque retained foreign body, soft tissue gas, and bony changes of osteomyelitis. MRI of the foot if osteomyelitis, deep abscess, or an occult radiolucent foreign body remains a concern after plain films. Bedside wound exploration with probe-to-bone testing. baseline_protocol:
Age: 28 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of increasing pain, redness, and swelling of the right breast with fever, chills, and malaise in a woman 3 weeks postpartum who is exclusively breastfeeding, preceded by nipple soreness and cracking and difficulty with the baby latching on that side.
Analysis: The presentation is classic acute lactational (puerperal) mastitis of the right breast. The strongest supporting facts are the timing at 3 weeks postpartum during exclusive breastfeeding, a wedge-shaped area of erythema, warmth, and induration in the upper outer quadrant that follows the distribution of a lobe or duct system, exquisite tenderness, systemic features with temperature 101.2 F, chills, and feeling generally unwell, and mild ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. The mechanism is evident in the history: a cracked nipple provides a portal of entry for skin flora, and poor latch on that side causes incomplete drainage with milk stasis, the two principal predisposing factors. The most likely pathogen in this setting is Staphylococcus aureus, with streptococci also possible. The critical differential considerations are: breast abscess, which is not currently supported since there is no fluctuance or palpable mass, but which must be reconsidered if symptoms fail to improve within 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics and continued drainage; simple milk stasis or a plugged duct, which is unlikely here because of the fever, chills, and systemic malaise; engorgement, which is typically bilateral and diffuse rather than a localized wedge; and inflammatory breast carcinoma, which is rare, does not usually present acutely with fever in a lactating woman, but should be considered if the erythema and induration do not resolve with treatment. She denies a palpable mass and abnormal nipple discharge, and the mild axillary nodes are consistent with reactive change from the infection. There are no features of sepsis described, with heart rate 94 and blood pressure 118/72.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Breast ultrasound if there is no clinical improvement within 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics, or if fluctuance or a mass develops, to exclude abscess. Milk culture with sensitivities if the infection is severe, recurrent, hospital-acquired, or fails first-line therapy.
Conclusion: A 28-year-old woman 3 weeks postpartum has acute right-sided lactational mastitis, caused by milk stasis from poor latch combined with bacterial entry through a nipple fissure, presenting with a wedge-shaped area of erythema and induration in the upper outer quadrant, fever of 101.2 F, chills, malaise, and reactive axillary nodes. There is currently no fluctuance or mass to suggest abscess. She requires prompt outpatient antibiotic therapy, effective continued breast drainage, analgesia, and lactation support, with reassessment in 48 to 72 hours to detect abscess formation or treatment failure.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Start empiric oral antibiotics effective against Staphylococcus aureus, such as a penicillinase-resistant penicillin or a first-generation cephalosporin, with coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus if local prevalence or risk factors warrant it; choose an agent compatible with breastfeeding and complete the prescribed course. Emphasize that breastfeeding should continue and should not be interrupted, since effective and frequent emptying of the affected breast is central to treatment; if feeding on the right is too painful or the infant will not latch, express or pump that breast to keep it drained. Address the mechanical cause directly: arrange lactation consultant review for latch correction on the right side, since difficulty latching is driving the milk stasis, and treat the nipple fissure with proper latch technique, nipple care, and attention to positioning. Provide analgesia and anti-inflammatory treatment compatible with lactation, warm compresses or a warm shower before feeds to aid milk let-down and cold compresses after feeds for pain and swelling, adequate hydration, and rest. Instruct her to begin feeds on the affected side when tolerated and to vary infant positioning to drain all quadrants, particularly the upper outer quadrant. Schedule reassessment in 48 to 72 hours; if fever or the area of induration persists or worsens, or if fluctuance or a discrete mass develops, obtain breast ultrasound to look for abscess, which would require aspiration or drainage in addition to antibiotics. Advise immediate return for worsening systemic symptoms such as rigors, hypotension, confusion, or rapidly expanding erythema, which could indicate progression to sepsis. Explain that erythema and induration that fail to resolve after adequate treatment require further evaluation to exclude inflammatory carcinoma. Also assess the infant, since latch difficulty may reflect an infant factor such as ankyloglossia or oral thrush, and consider candidal infection of the nipple if burning pain persists after the bacterial infection resolves.
Notes: Absence of fluctuance does not exclude an early or deep abscess; failure to improve within 48 to 72 hours is the key trigger for imaging. Antibiotic choice must account for lactation safety, and no drug allergies are specified in the case. The infant's feeding assessment and any maternal allergy history are not specified.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 22 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of worsening nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, and progressive lethargy in a woman with type 1 diabetes who ran out of insulin 3 days ago because she could not afford a refill.
Analysis: This is diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by absolute insulin deficiency after insulin was stopped 3 days ago for financial reasons. Every diagnostic element is present and severe. Hyperglycemia is documented at 486 mg/dL. Ketosis is documented by beta-hydroxybutyrate of 8.2 mmol/L and the fruity acetone odor of the breath. High anion gap metabolic acidosis is documented by pH 7.08, bicarbonate 4 mEq/L, and anion gap 32, with appropriate respiratory compensation shown by pCO2 of 14 mmHg and deep labored Kussmaul respirations at a rate of 32. By the usual severity criteria, a pH below 7.10 with bicarbonate below 10 and altered mental status places this in the severe category. Volume depletion from osmotic diuresis and vomiting is marked, evidenced by dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, tachycardia at 128, borderline hypotension at 92/54, and a prerenal pattern with BUN 38 and creatinine 1.9. The sodium of 128 mEq/L is a dilutional pseudohyponatremia that corrects to 134, consistent with hyperglycemia rather than true sodium loss. The potassium of 5.6 mEq/L is misleading and clinically critical: it reflects extracellular shift from acidosis and insulin deficiency on a background of profound total body potassium depletion, and it will fall rapidly once insulin and fluids are given, which is why the case notes it is expected to drop with treatment. The diffuse abdominal pain without peritoneal signs and the vomiting are typical manifestations of ketoacidosis itself. Drowsiness reflects acidosis and hyperosmolality and indicates a threatened airway if it progresses. Differential considerations: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is excluded by the profound acidosis and high ketones with only moderate glucose elevation; a primary intra-abdominal surgical emergency is less likely given the absence of peritoneal signs and a mechanism that fully explains the pain, though a precipitant such as infection must still be sought; alcoholic or starvation ketoacidosis is not supported because glucose is markedly elevated and insulin omission is documented; lactic acidosis or toxic ingestion could contribute to an elevated anion gap but the beta-hydroxybutyrate of 8.2 accounts for the gap. The acute kidney injury is most consistent with volume depletion. The most important precipitant here is non-adherence driven by cost, and the presentation carries the risks of hypokalemia during treatment, cerebral edema, arrhythmia, and hemodynamic collapse.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring and an ECG for hyperkalemia-related changes and arrhythmia. Hourly capillary glucose and serial venous blood gas, basic metabolic panel with electrolytes, anion gap, and beta-hydroxybutyrate every 2 to 4 hours during treatment. Serum magnesium and phosphate. Complete blood count. Assessment for a precipitating infection with urinalysis, and chest radiograph and cultures if clinically indicated. Serum osmolality. Pregnancy test. Strict intake and output monitoring.
Conclusion: A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has severe diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by 3 days of insulin omission due to inability to afford a refill, with pH 7.08, bicarbonate 4 mEq/L, anion gap 32, beta-hydroxybutyrate 8.2 mmol/L, glucose 486 mg/dL, Kussmaul respirations, marked dehydration, borderline hypotension, altered mental status, and prerenal acute kidney injury. This is a life-threatening metabolic emergency requiring immediate resuscitation with intravenous fluids, insulin infusion, and meticulous potassium management, followed by a solution to the underlying access and cost barrier to prevent recurrence.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Manage immediately in an emergency or critical care setting with continuous cardiac and neurologic monitoring. Begin aggressive isotonic intravenous crystalloid resuscitation for the marked volume depletion and hypotension, then adjust the rate and fluid composition according to hemodynamics, corrected sodium, and urine output. Start a continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion, and do not delay it beyond confirming that potassium is above the threshold for safe insulin administration; the presenting potassium of 5.6 mEq/L permits insulin now, but recheck it within an hour. Anticipate a rapid fall in potassium once insulin and fluids begin and add potassium to the intravenous fluids as soon as the level falls into the normal range, with frequent recheck, since total body potassium is severely depleted despite the elevated serum value. When glucose falls to approximately 200 mg/dL, add dextrose-containing fluid and continue the insulin infusion until the anion gap and ketosis have resolved, since correcting glucose alone does not correct ketoacidosis. Do not give routine bicarbonate; reserve it for extreme acidemia per local protocol, and avoid it if the pH improves with fluid and insulin. Monitor for cerebral edema, especially with any deterioration in mental status, and avoid overly rapid correction of glucose and osmolality. Protect the airway if the level of consciousness declines further. Search for and treat any additional precipitant such as infection, even though insulin omission is the documented cause. Correct magnesium and phosphate if significantly deranged. Overlap subcutaneous basal insulin with the infusion before discontinuing it, so that rebound ketosis is avoided, and only transition once the patient is eating and the gap has closed. Reassess renal function as volume is restored, since the creatinine of 1.9 is expected to improve. Before discharge, address the root cause directly: arrange social work and case management support, patient assistance or subsidized insulin programs, insurance enrollment, and a reliable prescription plan so that she never again runs out of insulin; provide diabetes education on sick day rules, never stopping basal insulin, home ketone testing, and early contact when supplies run low; and arrange prompt endocrinology and primary care follow-up. Screen for depression and other barriers to adherence.
Notes: The serum potassium of 5.6 mEq/L represents extracellular shift with severe total body depletion and will fall quickly with therapy, making frequent monitoring and timely potassium replacement the highest-risk element of treatment. The sodium of 128 mEq/L is factitious and corrects to 134, so it should not prompt treatment for hyponatremia. Insulin omission is documented, but an additional precipitant such as infection has not been excluded by the information given. Drug allergies and pregnancy status are not specified.

Vignette:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back between his shoulder blades that began 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy boxes. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and takes amlodipine intermittently. On examination, he is writhing in pain and appears ashen. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 108, RR 24, BP 210/118 in the right arm and 162/90 in the left arm. A diastolic murmur is auscultated along the left sternal border. Pulses are diminished in the left upper extremity. Chest X-ray shows widened mediastinum. CT angiography of the chest reveals a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 58 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back between the shoulder blades, beginning 45 minutes ago while lifting heavy boxes.
Analysis: The presentation is a classic acute aortic syndrome. The pain is abrupt in onset, maximal at onset, severe, tearing in quality, and radiates interscapularly, which is the characteristic pain pattern of aortic dissection rather than the crescendo pressure-like pain of myocardial ischemia. Several objective findings converge on the same diagnosis. There is a 48 mmHg systolic inter-arm blood pressure differential (210/118 right arm versus 162/90 left arm) with diminished pulses in the left upper extremity, indicating that the dissection flap compromises flow into the left subclavian territory arising from the arch. A diastolic murmur along the left sternal border indicates acute aortic regurgitation from disruption of the aortic root and valve commissural support, a well-recognized complication of ascending aortic involvement. The chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum, and CT angiography is confirmatory, demonstrating a Stanford type A dissection originating in the ascending aorta with an intimal flap extending into the aortic arch. Poorly controlled hypertension with only intermittent amlodipine use is the dominant risk factor, and the severe hypertension at presentation together with the exertional trigger of heavy lifting supplied the acute shear stress. He is tachycardic at 108, tachypneic at 24, writhing in pain and ashen, indicating significant sympathetic activation and possible early hemodynamic compromise. Differential considerations that were reasonably entertained and are now displaced by the imaging include acute coronary syndrome (which can coexist if the dissection flap involves a coronary ostium, and which must not be treated with thrombolysis in this setting), pulmonary embolism, esophageal rupture, tension pneumothorax, and acute pericarditis. The inter-arm pressure differential, diastolic murmur, widened mediastinum, and CT findings make type A aortic dissection the established diagnosis. The principal immediate threats are aortic rupture, cardiac tamponade, acute severe aortic regurgitation with heart failure, coronary ostial occlusion, and malperfusion of arch vessels including cerebral branches.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Diagnosis is already established by CT angiography, so no further confirmatory imaging is required. Needed next are immediate cardiac surgical evaluation, transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography to assess the severity of aortic regurgitation, pericardial effusion or tamponade, and root involvement; continuous cardiac monitoring with arterial line for beat-to-beat blood pressure measurement in both arms; 12-lead ECG to detect coronary ostial involvement; type and crossmatch with availability of blood products; complete blood count, coagulation studies, basic metabolic panel with creatinine, lactate, and troponin as preoperative and malperfusion assessment.
Conclusion: Confirmed acute Stanford type A aortic dissection of the ascending aorta extending into the aortic arch, complicated by acute aortic regurgitation and left upper extremity malperfusion, occurring in a hypertensive man with severe uncontrolled blood pressure. This is a surgical emergency with high hour-by-hour mortality without operative repair.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology
Recommendations: Activate emergency cardiothoracic surgical consultation immediately for urgent open repair of the ascending aorta; type A dissection is a surgical emergency and mortality rises with every hour of delay. Transfer to a center with cardiac surgical capability without delay if not already at one. Begin anti-impulse therapy at once, targeting heart rate below 60 and systolic blood pressure of roughly 100 to 120 mmHg using an intravenous beta blocker first to reduce aortic wall shear stress, with a vasodilator added only after adequate rate control has been achieved so that reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt are avoided. Control pain aggressively with intravenous opioids, which also lowers sympathetic drive and assists blood pressure control. Place large-bore intravenous access, obtain an arterial line, and measure blood pressure in both arms, titrating therapy to the higher reading since the left arm reading underestimates central pressure due to subclavian involvement. Maintain nil by mouth and prepare for immediate operative repair. Do not administer thrombolytics or full anticoagulation even if the ECG suggests ischemia, since ischemia here would reflect coronary ostial involvement by the dissection flap and lysis would be catastrophic. Serially assess for tamponade, new neurologic deficit, abdominal or limb malperfusion, and widening pulse pressure or hypotension signaling rupture. Regarding the additional considerations: the inter-arm pressure differential and diminished left arm pulses reflect arch branch involvement and mandate bilateral pressure monitoring and neurovascular checks; the new diastolic murmur reflects acute aortic regurgitation and should be characterized by echocardiography since it may require valve repair or replacement at the time of aortic repair; the history of poorly controlled hypertension with intermittent amlodipine use requires long-term, strictly adherent antihypertensive therapy after recovery, with lifelong surveillance imaging of the aorta and avoidance of heavy lifting and isometric straining.
Notes: Blood pressure targets must be guided by the higher arm reading and by evidence of end-organ perfusion; excessive lowering risks cerebral, coronary, renal, and spinal cord malperfusion. Beta blockade must precede vasodilator therapy. Aortic regurgitation severity may worsen abruptly, and hypotension in this patient should be presumed to indicate rupture, tamponade, or severe acute regurgitation until proven otherwise.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Vignette:
A 45-yr-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 6-h history of acute-onset
left-sided lower abdominal pain. He describes the pain as starting over his left flank and
radiating down toward his groin. The pain comes and goes but is intense when present. He has
had some mild nausea without vomiting. The pain does not change with eating. The pain is less
when he walks around than when he sits or lies down flat. He has not had any bloody stools,
black stools, or change in bowel habits. He denies having diarrhea and constipation. He has
noticed his urine looks "dark" but denies pain during urination and urinary frequency. He says
that he swims several times a week for exercise, and this pain started immediately after
swimming. He also notes that several days ago, his son ran into his left side while playing
football. He took some acetaminophen, which minimally relieved his discomfort. He now
presents for evaluation at the emergency department because the pain has not subsided. He
says he has never experienced pain like this.

Review of Systems:

weight loss, and fatigue.

Skin: Denies rashes, itching, and any lesions.

Cardiovascular: Denies palpitations and chest pain. No lower-extremity edema.

Gastrointestinal: Reports nausea when pain is at its most intense but no vomiting. No
constipation or diarrhea. Last bowel movement yesterday; no hematochezia or melena. No
appetite; he has not eaten since the pain began.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, urinary frequency or urgency, or increased volume of
urine. States urine appears "dark."

Musculoskeletal: Occasional low back pain with strenuous activity

Past Medical History:
Diabetes mellitus since his 20s that is well-controlled with oral drugs, diet, and exercise.
Hypertension and hyperlipidemia both well-controlled on drugs. Obstructive sleep apnea for
which he uses a CPAP machine. Recent deep venous thrombosis that developed after a long
international flight and that is currently being treated with an oral anticoagulant. Denies history

Surgical history: Wisdom tooth extraction as a teenager; no abdominal surgical procedures.

Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg daily, rivaroxaban

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother and father have hypertension; sibling has history of kidney stones.

Social history: He denies current and previous tobacco use. He works at a desk job and swims
