Analysis: This is carpal tunnel syndrome, that is compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel at the wrist, and the case is unusually complete in its supporting evidence. The sensory distribution is the most specific feature: symptoms involve the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the radial half of the ring finger, which is exactly the cutaneous territory of the median nerve in the hand, and the splitting of the ring finger along its midline is characteristic of a median rather than a proximal or root-level lesion. Nocturnal predominance with waking from sleep is the classic temporal pattern, explained by the tendency to sleep with the wrist flexed or extended, which raises carpal tunnel pressure, and by the redistribution of interstitial fluid to the hands when recumbent. The flick sign, in which shaking the hand transiently relieves the symptoms, is highly suggestive of carpal tunnel syndrome and is reported here explicitly. The provocative tests are both positive and mutually corroborating: Tinel sign at the wrist reproduces paresthesias radiating into the fingers, indicating mechanical irritability of the median nerve at the level of the flexor retinaculum, and Phalen test reproduces symptoms within 20 seconds, a rapid reproduction that suggests significant compression. Objective sensory loss is documented as decreased two-point discrimination in the median distribution, and two-point discrimination is a late-deteriorating modality, so its impairment indicates that the compression has progressed beyond purely intermittent physiological conduction block. The most important findings, however, are the motor ones. Early thenar eminence atrophy compared with the contralateral side, together with reduced grip and pinch strength and functional loss manifested as dropping objects, indicates axonal loss affecting the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve supplying abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis. Thenar atrophy signifies severe carpal tunnel syndrome and carries prognostic weight, because motor axon loss recovers slowly and often incompletely, and its presence changes the management calculus in favour of decompression rather than indefinite conservative therapy. Risk factors are identifiable and dual. Occupationally, she performs eight hours daily of keyboard data entry with minimal ergonomic support, involving sustained repetitive wrist and finger activity in a poorly supported posture. Medically, she has hypothyroidism, which is a recognised systemic cause of carpal tunnel syndrome through deposition of mucopolysaccharide and myxoedematous soft tissue within the tunnel, and although her thyroid disease is described as well controlled, thyroid status is worth confirming since undertreatment could be contributing. Female sex and the fourth decade also fit the classic epidemiology. Differential considerations must be addressed. Cervical radiculopathy, particularly at C6 or C7, can produce hand paresthesias, but would typically involve neck pain, symptoms provoked by neck movement or Spurling manoeuvre, a dermatomal rather than median-specific pattern that does not split the ring finger, and reflex changes; none of these are described. Proximal median nerve entrapment such as pronator teres syndrome would additionally affect sensation over the thenar eminence, since the palmar cutaneous branch arises above the carpal tunnel, and would spare the nocturnal pattern; the present distribution is confined to the digits. Ulnar neuropathy is excluded by the sparing of the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger. Thoracic outlet syndrome typically causes lower trunk symptoms in an ulnar distribution with positional provocation of the whole limb. A generalised peripheral polyneuropathy from diabetes or another cause would be bilateral, symmetric, and length-dependent starting in the feet, whereas this is strictly unilateral and confined to one nerve territory. De Quervain tenosynovitis and basal thumb arthritis produce pain without sensory loss or nocturnal paresthesias. Given the median-specific sensory territory, the nocturnal pattern with flick sign, two positive provocative tests, objective sensory impairment, and thenar atrophy with measurable weakness, the diagnosis is secure and the severity is advanced.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Electrodiagnostic studies comprising nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography of the right upper limb, to confirm median neuropathy at the wrist, grade its severity objectively by documenting distal motor and sensory latencies and the presence of denervation in abductor pollicis brevis, exclude a coexisting cervical radiculopathy or polyneuropathy, and provide a preoperative baseline; this is the key study given documented thenar atrophy and planned surgical referral. Thyroid function tests with TSH and free T4 to confirm that the hypothyroidism is genuinely well controlled, since inadequate replacement is a reversible contributor. Screening laboratory studies for other systemic contributors where clinically indicated, specifically fasting glucose or glycated haemoglobin for diabetes mellitus. Formal quantitative measurement of grip and pinch strength with a dynamometer and pinch gauge for baseline and follow-up, and standardised sensory testing. High-resolution ultrasound of the median nerve at the wrist may be used where available as an adjunct to demonstrate nerve swelling and to exclude a space-occupying lesion such as a ganglion, an anomalous muscle, or tenosynovitis. Cervical spine imaging is not required unless clinical features of radiculopathy emerge. A pregnancy history is not applicable here as no such information is provided.
Conclusion: Severe right-sided carpal tunnel syndrome with median nerve compression at the wrist, evidenced by four months of progressive median-distribution sensory symptoms with nocturnal predominance and a positive flick sign, positive Tinel and rapidly positive Phalen tests, objective loss of two-point discrimination, and, critically, early thenar atrophy with reduced grip and pinch strength indicating established motor axonal loss. Contributing factors are prolonged daily keyboard work without ergonomic support and a background of hypothyroidism. The presence of atrophy and functional motor deficit places this beyond mild disease and makes prompt electrodiagnostic confirmation and surgical referral appropriate, since delay risks permanent thenar muscle loss.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Refer for electrodiagnostic testing promptly to confirm the diagnosis, grade severity, and exclude alternative or coexisting lesions, and refer in parallel to a hand or orthopaedic surgeon, because early thenar atrophy with objective weakness and sensory loss after four months of progressive symptoms constitutes an indication for carpal tunnel release rather than for prolonged conservative management alone. Counsel her that surgical decompression is highly effective for relieving pain and paresthesias, but that recovery of thenar bulk and strength is slower and may be incomplete once atrophy has begun, which is precisely why further delay should be avoided. In the interim, begin conservative measures immediately since they cost nothing and may provide symptomatic relief while she awaits definitive care. Prescribe a neutral-position wrist splint to be worn nightly, and during provocative daytime activities if tolerated, as night splinting directly targets the nocturnal wrist flexion that drives her symptoms and is the single most useful conservative measure. Consider a short course of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for symptomatic burning pain, recognising that it does not alter the underlying compression. A local corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel may provide temporary relief and has some diagnostic value, but should be viewed as a temporising measure here and not as a substitute for decompression given the motor findings; repeated injections are not advisable. Refer to occupational or hand therapy for nerve and tendon gliding exercises, activity modification, and instruction. Addressing the additional considerations explicitly: undertake a formal workplace ergonomic assessment, since eight hours of daily keyboarding with minimal ergonomic support is a direct and modifiable contributor. Practical measures include positioning the keyboard so the wrists remain in neutral rather than extended, using a keyboard with a negative or flat tilt, providing forearm rather than wrist support, setting chair and desk height so elbows rest at approximately ninety degrees, using a vertical or ergonomic mouse, keeping the wrist off hard edges, and instituting scheduled microbreaks with stretching every twenty to thirty minutes. Consider voice-recognition software or task rotation to reduce total keystroke exposure, and discuss temporary modified duties with her employer, as well as the possibility that this represents a reportable occupational condition depending on jurisdiction. Verify thyroid status with TSH and free T4 and optimise levothyroxine replacement if it is suboptimal, as correcting hypothyroidism can improve carpal tunnel symptoms; screen for diabetes and other systemic contributors. Advise her to report immediately any worsening weakness, further loss of thenar bulk, complete numbness, or inability to oppose the thumb, as these indicate progressive axonal loss and warrant expedited surgery. Arrange follow-up within four to six weeks to reassess symptoms, grip and pinch strength, and thenar bulk, and to review electrodiagnostic and thyroid results, with surgical planning proceeding on that basis. After any surgical release, arrange structured hand therapy, and counsel that nocturnal symptoms typically improve within days to weeks while strength and sensory recovery take months.
Notes: Early thenar atrophy is the pivotal finding in this case; it denotes severe disease with axonal loss, distinguishes this from mild intermittent carpal tunnel syndrome, and is the reason that indefinite conservative therapy is inappropriate. Recovery of motor function after decompression may be partial once atrophy is established, so the patient should be counselled honestly about expectations. Normal electrodiagnostic studies do not entirely exclude carpal tunnel syndrome, and in the presence of these clinical findings a negative study should prompt re-evaluation rather than dismissal of the diagnosis. Corticosteroid injection provides only temporary benefit and should not delay definitive treatment in the presence of motor deficit. Coexisting cervical radiculopathy, the so-called double crush phenomenon, should be reconsidered if symptoms fail to resolve after adequate decompression.

Vignette:
A 12-year-old boy is brought by his parents for a persistent cough that has lasted 3 weeks and is progressively worsening. The illness began with 1 week of runny nose and mild cough that was initially thought to be a cold. The cough then intensified into severe paroxysms of rapid, consecutive coughs followed by a whooping inspiratory sound. He has had several episodes of post-tussive vomiting. He occasionally turns red in the face during coughing fits. Between episodes he appears relatively well. His vaccination records show he received DTaP at 2, 4, and 6 months but missed his preschool and adolescent boosters. Vital signs are normal between episodes. Lungs are clear to auscultation. baseline_protocol:
Age: 12 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three weeks of persistent and progressively worsening cough that began with a week of runny nose and mild cough, then intensified into severe paroxysms of rapid consecutive coughs followed by a whooping inspiratory sound, with several episodes of post-tussive vomiting and facial reddening during fits, and relative wellness between episodes.
Analysis: This is pertussis, and the case provides confirmation at clinical, laboratory, and microbiological levels. The clinical course follows the textbook biphasic pattern of the disease. The first week of rhinorrhoea and mild cough corresponds to the catarrhal stage, which is indistinguishable from a common cold and is the period of maximal contagiousness. The subsequent two weeks correspond to the paroxysmal stage, defined by staccato bursts of rapid consecutive coughs during a single expiration, followed by a forced inspiration against a partially closed glottis that produces the characteristic whoop, which is explicitly described here. Post-tussive vomiting is a further hallmark and is reported. Facial reddening during fits reflects the marked rise in intrathoracic and venous pressure generated by the paroxysms. The observation that he appears relatively well between episodes is itself diagnostically important, because it is highly characteristic of pertussis and distinguishes it from pneumonia or other lower respiratory infections, in which the patient is unwell continuously; consistently, the vital signs are normal between episodes and the lungs are clear to auscultation, since Bordetella pertussis produces a toxin-mediated tracheobronchial illness rather than parenchymal consolidation. The laboratory findings corroborate the diagnosis with a white blood cell count of 18,000 and 70 percent lymphocytes. This absolute lymphocytosis, giving a lymphocyte count of roughly 12,600, is a distinctive feature of pertussis and results from pertussis toxin blocking lymphocyte egress from the circulation into lymphoid tissue; a lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis in a patient with a paroxysmal cough is essentially diagnostic in the right context. Definitive confirmation is provided by the positive nasopharyngeal swab polymerase chain reaction for Bordetella pertussis. The susceptibility is fully explained by the immunisation history. He received DTaP at 2, 4, and 6 months but missed both the preschool booster and the adolescent Tdap booster. Acellular pertussis vaccine immunity wanes substantially within five to ten years of the primary series, so a 12-year-old whose last dose was in infancy has minimal residual protection; this is the direct reason he is presenting now, and adolescents with waned immunity are a recognised reservoir for transmission. Differential considerations warrant explicit weighing but are effectively excluded. Post-viral or post-infectious cough is common but does not produce a true whoop, paroxysms of this severity, post-tussive vomiting, or lymphocytosis. Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydophila pneumoniae can cause a protracted cough but generally produce abnormal auscultation or radiographic findings and do not produce this paroxysmal pattern or lymphocytosis. Adenovirus and respiratory syncytial virus can cause pertussis-like illness, and Bordetella parapertussis causes a milder version of the same syndrome, but the polymerase chain reaction result settles the aetiology. Cough-variant asthma would typically involve wheeze, nocturnal and exertional triggers, and would not cause leukocytosis with lymphocytosis. Foreign body aspiration would usually produce focal findings and a sudden onset. Tuberculosis would be accompanied by constitutional symptoms and abnormal imaging. A critical point about staging and treatment is that he is now in the third week of illness. Antimicrobial therapy in pertussis eradicates the organism from the nasopharynx and thereby halts transmission, but it does not appreciably shorten the cough once the paroxysmal stage is established, because the symptoms at that point are driven by toxin-mediated airway epithelial injury rather than by ongoing bacterial burden. Treatment is nonetheless clearly indicated because he remains within the window in which antibiotics reduce infectiousness, and because interrupting transmission to vulnerable contacts, particularly unimmunised or partially immunised infants under one year of age in whom pertussis causes apnoea, pneumonia, encephalopathy, and death, is the paramount public health objective. He himself is at low risk of severe complications given his age, normal vital signs, clear chest, and well appearance between paroxysms, but he should be monitored for the recognised complications of the paroxysms themselves, including subconjunctival haemorrhage, epistaxis, rib fracture, pneumothorax, hernia, syncope, and secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: The diagnosis is already confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction supported by the characteristic lymphocytosis, so no further diagnostic testing is needed to establish the aetiology. What is needed next is assessment and monitoring rather than further diagnosis: pulse oximetry during and after paroxysms to document that oxygenation is maintained, since the case reports facial reddening but no cyanosis or apnoea. A chest radiograph should be obtained only if focal findings, tachypnoea, hypoxaemia, persistent fever, or clinical deterioration develop, to evaluate for secondary bacterial pneumonia or pneumothorax, both of which are recognised complications; it is not indicated at present given a clear chest and normal vital signs. Review of the full immunisation record to plan catch-up vaccination, and identification and immunisation and vaccination status review of all household and close contacts, especially any infant under twelve months, any pregnant woman in the third trimester, and any immunocompromised person. Repeat complete blood count is not routinely required, though extreme leukocytosis is a marker of severity in infants. No serology is needed once polymerase chain reaction is positive.
Conclusion: Laboratory-confirmed pertussis in an under-immunised 12-year-old boy, currently in the paroxysmal stage at three weeks of illness, with the classic whooping paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting, a characteristic absolute lymphocytosis of 70 percent with a white cell count of 18,000, and a positive nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction for Bordetella pertussis. He is clinically stable with normal vital signs, clear lungs, and preserved wellbeing between paroxysms, so outpatient management is appropriate. The illness is a direct consequence of missed preschool and adolescent booster doses with waning vaccine-derived immunity. The central management priorities are macrolide therapy to eliminate carriage and stop transmission, supportive care with realistic expectations about the prolonged cough, chemoprophylaxis and protection of close contacts particularly infants, exclusion from school until non-infectious, and completion of catch-up immunisation.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Start a macrolide antibiotic promptly. Azithromycin is the preferred agent in children for its short course and tolerability, given for five days at age-appropriate weight-based dosing; clarithromycin for seven days or erythromycin for fourteen days are acceptable alternatives, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the alternative for patients with macrolide intolerance or allergy, provided there is no contraindication. Explain clearly to the family that at three weeks into the illness the antibiotic is given chiefly to eliminate the organism from the nasopharynx and stop him infecting others, and that it will not substantially shorten his cough, which is toxin-mediated and may continue for many weeks; pertussis is known as the hundred-day cough for this reason, and paroxysms often persist for six to ten weeks and may recur transiently with subsequent respiratory infections. Set this expectation explicitly to prevent repeated presentations and inappropriate additional antibiotics. Provide supportive care: adequate hydration, small frequent meals to reduce post-tussive vomiting, rest, and avoidance of known cough triggers such as tobacco smoke, cold air, exertion, and irritants. Advise that cough suppressants, antihistamines, corticosteroids, and bronchodilators have not been shown to be effective in pertussis and should not be used. Vignette:
A 76-year-old man comes to the office because of shortness of breath. He is presently being
managed for end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. Today, the patient states that over the
past 6 months he has noted increasing difficulty breathing when he exerts himself. He is
relatively sedentary but does climb a flight of stairs to his bedroom at night; he says he used to
be able to do this without any problem, but now he reports he needs to stop halfway up the
stairs to rest. Occasionally he has mild substernal chest pressure along with the shortness of
breath. The chest pressure does not radiate and is not accompanied by nausea or diaphoresis.
He has noted increased swelling in his legs. He denies any shortness of breath at rest,
orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. He denies any episodes of palpitations,
lightheadedness, or syncope. He denies any cough, fever, chills, or night sweats.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient generally feels fatigued. No recent weight changes.

Skin: No rashes or skin lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, nasal congestion or discharge, or sore throat.

Pulmonary: See HPI

Cardiovascular: See HPI

Gastrointestinal: Good appetite. No abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or change in bowel
patterns.

Genitourinary: Has not produced urine for several years since beginning dialysis. Has not
missed any dialysis treatments.

Musculoskeletal: No redness or pain in extremities. He has noticed increased swelling of his
feet and ankles in recent months.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, end-stage renal disease
on hemodialysis.

Surgical history: Left knee replacement at age 65 years.

Medications: Lisinopril 10 mg orally daily, atorvastatin 40 mg orally daily, insulin glargine 50 U
subcutaneously daily, calcium carbonate 500 mg orally twice a day with meals, darbepoietin 40
mcg IV weekly.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Father had hypertension and stroke. Mother had type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Social history: Patient is married and is a retired teacher. He has never smoked and does not
use alcohol or illicit drugs.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Thin, elderly male in no apparent distress.

Vital signs:

Temperature: 37.2° C
Pulse: 72 beats/min
Blood Pressure: 155/86 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

Skin: No rashes or cyanosis

upstrokes.

Pulmonary: Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheezes, rhonchi, or rales. No
dullness to percussion.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, normal S1, diminished S2, crescendo/decrescendo
systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids. No rubs or
gallops.

quadrants. Rectal exam: Nontender, stool heme negative.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Age: 76 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Six-month history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, now limiting him to half a flight of stairs, with occasional mild non-radiating substernal chest pressure on exertion, increasing bilateral leg swelling, and general fatigue, in a man with end-stage renal disease on maintenance haemodialysis.
Analysis: The unifying diagnosis is severe calcific aortic stenosis that has become symptomatic. The strongest supporting evidence is the echocardiogram, which shows severe calcific aortic stenosis with a mean gradient of 45 mm Hg and an aortic valve area of 0.85 cm2, together with moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, the expected adaptive response to chronic pressure overload. The physical examination independently corroborates severity: a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border and radiating to the carotids is the classic murmur of aortic stenosis, while the diminished S2 and the delayed carotid upstrokes, that is pulsus parvus et tardus, are specific bedside markers of haemodynamically severe obstruction. The history supplies the critical clinical element, namely the transition from asymptomatic to symptomatic disease. He now has exertional dyspnoea where previously he climbed the stairs without difficulty, and he has exertional substernal chest pressure. These are two of the three cardinal symptoms of aortic stenosis, angina and dyspnoea, the third being syncope, which he denies. The onset of symptoms in severe aortic stenosis marks a decisive change in prognosis, since survival without valve intervention is measured in a small number of years and the risk of sudden death rises substantially. The exertional chest pressure is best explained by the supply-demand mismatch of hypertrophied myocardium with elevated wall stress and impaired subendocardial perfusion rather than by an acute coronary syndrome: it does not radiate, is unaccompanied by nausea or diaphoresis, occurs only on exertion, and has been present intermittently over months, and the troponin of 0.05 ng/mL is minimally elevated in a pattern typical of chronic renal failure and left ventricular hypertrophy rather than of acute infarction. Concomitant coronary artery disease nevertheless remains a serious consideration given his age, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and dialysis dependence, and must be defined before any valve procedure. The alternative explanations for his dyspnoea are addressed by the data. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is excluded by an ejection fraction of 60 per cent with normal left and right ventricular size and function and no regional wall motion abnormalities. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction due to diastolic dysfunction is argued against by the explicitly normal diastolic function on echocardiography and by the absence of orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. The BNP of 465 pg/mL and the elevated jugular venous pressure of 5 cm above the clavicle, together with 1+ pitting oedema to mid-shin and mild costophrenic angle blunting on chest radiograph, indicate volume overload, which in an anuric dialysis patient reflects interdialytic fluid accumulation and dry weight that is set too high, compounded by the increased filling pressures imposed by the stenotic valve; BNP is also chronically elevated in end-stage renal disease and must be interpreted with that caveat. Pulmonary disease is unlikely, as the lungs are clear with no wheeze, rhonchi or rales, the parenchyma is clear on chest radiograph, and he has never smoked and denies cough, fever, chills or night sweats. Anaemia with a haemoglobin of 9 g/dL is a genuine contributor to exertional dyspnoea and fatigue, is expected from erythropoietin deficiency in end-stage renal disease, and is already being treated with darbepoetin; it aggravates but does not explain the murmur, the delayed carotid upstrokes, or the valve findings. Arrhythmia is unlikely given the regular rate and rhythm and the absence of palpitations, lightheadedness or syncope. Infection and malignancy are not supported by the normal white cell count, absence of fever or weight loss, and preserved appetite. Two management-relevant points arise from the medication list and comorbidity. First, lisinopril and other afterload-reducing agents require caution in severe aortic stenosis with a relatively fixed obstruction, since excessive preload or afterload reduction can precipitate hypotension, although his blood pressure remains elevated at 155/86 mm Hg. Second, dialysis dependence with disordered calcium and phosphate metabolism accelerates valvular calcification and materially raises the perioperative risk profile, making multidisciplinary planning essential.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram interpretation, which is referenced in the case and should be reviewed for left ventricular hypertrophy with strain, conduction disease, ischaemic changes, and rhythm; serial troponin measurements to establish whether the value of 0.05 ng/mL is a stable chronic elevation or shows an acute rising or falling pattern; coronary angiography to define coronary anatomy before valve intervention, given his age, diabetes, and cardiovascular risk profile; computed tomography angiography of the aorta, iliofemoral vessels and aortic root with valve calcium scoring for procedural planning and access assessment if transcatheter aortic valve replacement is contemplated; carotid duplex ultrasonography if a bruit or cerebrovascular disease is suspected preoperatively; iron studies, ferritin and transferrin saturation together with reticulocyte count to evaluate the anaemia and optimise erythropoiesis-stimulating agent therapy; serum calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and albumin to assess mineral and bone disorder contributing to valvular calcification; pre-dialysis and post-dialysis weights with a formal reassessment of dry weight; pulmonary function testing and frailty assessment as part of preoperative risk stratification; dental evaluation before valve replacement; and repeat transthoracic echocardiography for surveillance and post-intervention assessment. Transoesophageal echocardiography if valve morphology requires further definition.
Conclusion: A 76-year-old haemodialysis-dependent man with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and type 2 diabetes presents with six months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and exertional angina, physical findings of a radiating crescendo-decrescendo right upper sternal border systolic murmur, diminished S2 and delayed carotid upstrokes, and echocardiographic confirmation of severe calcific aortic stenosis with a mean gradient of 45 mm Hg, an aortic valve area of 0.85 cm2, preserved ejection fraction of 60 per cent and moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. This is symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, a class indication for aortic valve replacement, with a superimposed and separately treatable component of volume overload related to dialysis and an aggravating anaemia of chronic kidney disease. He is currently stable, in no distress, with clear lungs and normal vital signs apart from hypertension, so he does not require emergency intervention, but he does require prompt and definitive specialist evaluation for valve replacement, since medical therapy alone does not alter the natural history and delay carries a real risk of heart failure and sudden death.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology
Recommendations: Refer urgently to cardiology and to a structural heart or multidisciplinary heart valve team for evaluation for aortic valve replacement, since symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is a definite indication for intervention and no medical therapy alters its natural history. The team should weigh surgical aortic valve replacement against transcatheter aortic valve replacement, taking into account his age of 76 years, dialysis dependence, diabetes, anaemia, frailty and surgical risk, and should choose prosthesis type with dialysis-related durability and anticoagulation considerations in mind. Obtain coronary angiography as part of preprocedural assessment to identify concomitant coronary disease amenable to revascularisation at the time of valve intervention. Review the electrocardiogram and obtain serial troponins to confirm that the mildly elevated troponin reflects chronic renal disease and hypertrophy rather than an acute coronary syndrome, and escalate immediately if the pattern is dynamic or if rest or crescendo chest pain develops. Coordinate closely with nephrology to optimise volume status by reassessing and lowering the dry weight and adjusting ultrafiltration to relieve the raised jugular venous pressure, peripheral oedema and costophrenic blunting, while avoiding overly aggressive fluid removal, since patients with severe aortic stenosis and a hypertrophied, preload-dependent ventricle tolerate hypovolaemia and hypotension poorly and may become haemodynamically unstable during dialysis. Anticipate and plan for haemodynamic instability during dialysis sessions, including gentler ultrafiltration rates, careful sodium and temperature management, and close intradialytic blood pressure monitoring. Review lisinopril with the cardiologist, monitoring closely for hypotension given the fixed obstruction, while recognising that his blood pressure remains elevated and that blood pressure control remains appropriate; adjust antihypertensive therapy cautiously and avoid abrupt or excessive preload and afterload reduction, and avoid nitrates and other vasodilators outside specialist supervision. Continue atorvastatin for cardiovascular risk reduction, recognising that statins do not retard progression of calcific aortic stenosis. Optimise anaemia management with darbepoetin, guided by iron studies, targeting a haemoglobin that improves exertional symptoms without exceeding recommended limits, since correcting anaemia will improve his fatigue and exertional tolerance and reduce cardiac workload. Address mineral and bone disorder with attention to calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone, and review calcium carbonate dosing with nephrology, given the contribution of disordered mineral metabolism to progressive valvular calcification. Continue insulin glargine with attention to glycaemic control and monitoring, particularly around any procedure. Ensure dental assessment and clearance before valve replacement and provide endocarditis prevention counselling, which is especially pertinent given his indwelling dialysis access and the good thrill in his right forearm graft that must be preserved and protected from venepuncture and blood pressure cuffs. Counsel the patient explicitly to avoid strenuous or competitive exertion until the valve is treated and to seek immediate emergency care for syncope or near-syncope, chest pain at rest or of increasing frequency or severity, dyspnoea at rest, new orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, palpitations, or rapid weight gain, as these mark decompensation and greatly increase risk. Arrange early cardiology follow-up and, if intervention is deferred for any reason, close clinical and echocardiographic surveillance.
Notes: BNP and troponin are both chronically elevated in end-stage renal disease and in left ventricular hypertrophy, so the BNP of 465 pg/mL and troponin of 0.05 ng/mL must be interpreted against the patient's own baseline and trend rather than as isolated values. Symptom onset, not gradient alone, is the pivotal prognostic event in severe aortic stenosis, and this patient has crossed that threshold. Dialysis-dependent patients face higher perioperative and prosthesis-related risk and accelerated bioprosthetic valve calcification, which must inform the choice of intervention and prosthesis. baseline_protocol:
Age: 62 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two days of progressively worsening pain in the right lower leg between knee and ankle, with an area of redness on the calf, and, in the hours before arrival, generalized malaise, diffuse aching, subjective fever and loss of appetite, without any recalled injury to the leg.
Analysis: The clinical picture is that of acute bacterial cellulitis of the right lower leg with a systemic inflammatory response. The strongest supporting facts are the local findings and the systemic findings taken together. Locally there is a 15 by 10 cm area of erythema on the lateral aspect of the right calf that is warm, indurated and mildly tender, the classic tetrad of rubor, calor, tumor and dolor confined to a single limb, with an acute two-day onset and progressive worsening. Systemically he has a documented temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius, tachycardia of 118 to 120 beats per minute, diffuse flushing and diaphoresis, generalized myalgia, and anorexia, and the laboratory studies show a leukocytosis of 14,500 per cubic millimetre with 86 per cent neutrophils and 8 per cent bands, a left shift that indicates a significant bacterial infection. The bicarbonate of 21 mmol/L suggests a mild metabolic acidosis consistent with the systemic stress response and hypoperfusion, and the blood urea nitrogen of 28 mg/dL with a creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL indicates prerenal azotaemia from reduced intake, fever and insensible losses. Two elements of the history explain his particular susceptibility. First, he underwent coronary artery bypass grafting seven years ago with harvesting of the right saphenous vein, leaving a healed scar running from ankle to mid-thigh on that same leg; saphenous venectomy produces chronic lymphatic and venous disruption of the harvested limb, which is why that leg is habitually mildly swollen at the end of the day, and such limbs carry a markedly elevated lifelong risk of recurrent cellulitis, which characteristically occurs without an identifiable portal of entry. This directly accounts for the localisation of infection to the right leg and for the absence of any visible wound, skin break, abrasion, or tinea pedis on examination. Second, he has type 2 diabetes of five years' duration managed by diet alone, is not monitoring glucose at home, does not know his most recent HbA1c, and presents with a glucose of 220 mg/dL, indicating that his diabetes is poorly controlled and impairing host defence, while the acute infection is itself worsening the hyperglycaemia. Ketones are negative and the anion gap is essentially normal, so diabetic ketoacidosis is excluded. The most important competing diagnosis is deep venous thrombosis, which shares unilateral leg pain, swelling and erythema and is plausible here given a right calf diameter 2 cm greater than the left and 1+ pitting shin oedema. This is excluded by a normal venous Doppler ultrasound of the right lower leg, and is further argued against by the absence of calf tenderness on compression, absence of distended veins, no recent immobilisation or injury, no history of clots or clotting disorder, no malignancy, and the presence of a discrete cutaneous erythematous plaque with fever and neutrophilic left shift that DVT would not explain. The asymmetry in calf diameter and the shin oedema are better attributed to the chronic post-harvest venous and lymphatic insufficiency described in the history plus acute inflammatory oedema. The second critical differential is necrotising fasciitis, a surgical emergency that must be actively considered in any diabetic patient with a hot, painful, erythematous limb and systemic toxicity. Reassuring against it are the absence of bullae, crepitus and fluctuance, only mild tenderness rather than pain out of proportion to findings, no skin necrosis or dusky discolouration, no anaesthesia over the area, a normal plain radiograph without soft tissue gas, a normal blood pressure of 128/74 mm Hg, and a patient who is alert, fully oriented and in no apparent distress. However, the presence of bandaemia, tachycardia and fever means he must be observed closely for any rapid progression, since early necrotising infection can mimic cellulitis. Other considerations are less likely: abscess is argued against by the absence of fluctuance, though it can develop; septic arthritis and osteomyelitis are unsupported, as the pain is between knee and ankle without joint involvement and the radiograph is normal; stasis dermatitis is chronic, usually bilateral, and does not cause fever or leucocytosis; gout and other crystal arthropathy do not fit the distribution or the absence of joint findings; and deep vein or superficial thrombophlebitis is excluded by the imaging and examination. Two findings deserve separate attention. The jugular venous distension of 12 cm above the sternal notch at 45 degrees is markedly abnormal and is not explained by cellulitis; in a man with established coronary artery disease and prior bypass grafting it raises concern for elevated right-sided filling pressures or a cardiac contribution, although the lungs are clear without crackles, there are no gallops or murmurs, he denies dyspnoea, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and the electrocardiogram shows only sinus tachycardia unchanged from five years ago. The tachycardia at 118 to 120 beats per minute is most plausibly explained by fever, infection and volume depletion, but in a patient with coronary artery disease it also increases myocardial oxygen demand and requires monitoring. Overall this represents a systemically unwell diabetic patient with an acute limb infection, meeting criteria for a systemic inflammatory response, in whom infection can progress rapidly and in whom outpatient oral therapy would be inappropriate.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures, at least two sets drawn before antibiotics are administered; serum lactate to assess for tissue hypoperfusion and sepsis severity; C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate as inflammatory markers for baseline and serial monitoring; HbA1c to define the degree of chronic glycaemic control, which the patient does not know; bedside and serial capillary glucose monitoring; repeat complete blood count with differential and repeat basic metabolic panel including renal function to track response; continuous cardiac monitoring and serial vital signs including pulse oximetry; marking of the erythematous border with an indelible skin marker at presentation to allow objective serial assessment of spread; measured limb circumference recorded serially; bedside soft tissue ultrasound of the calf if abscess or fluid collection is suspected; contrast-enhanced computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging of the right lower leg urgently if any feature suggesting necrotising soft tissue infection or deep abscess emerges; surgical consultation with consideration of operative exploration if necrotising infection is suspected, since imaging must never delay surgery; wound or aspirate culture only if a drainable collection, bulla or portal of entry becomes apparent; and echocardiography to evaluate the unexplained jugular venous distension and assess cardiac filling pressures and valvular status in a man with known coronary artery disease.
Conclusion: A 62-year-old diabetic man with coronary artery disease and prior right saphenous vein harvesting for coronary artery bypass grafting presents with two days of progressive right lower leg pain and a 15 by 10 cm warm, indurated, tender erythematous plaque on the lateral calf, together with fever of 38.5 degrees Celsius, tachycardia of 118 beats per minute, malaise, myalgias, anorexia, diaphoresis, a neutrophilic leucocytosis of 14,500 with 8 per cent bands, hyperglycaemia of 220 mg/dL and prerenal azotaemia. Deep venous thrombosis is excluded by normal venous Doppler ultrasonography, and there is currently no bulla, crepitus or fluctuance to indicate necrotising infection, with a normal radiograph. The diagnosis is acute bacterial cellulitis of the right lower leg arising in a limb rendered susceptible by post-venectomy lymphatic and venous insufficiency, in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes, now complicated by a systemic inflammatory response. He requires immediate parenteral antibiotic therapy, intravenous fluid resuscitation, glycaemic control and inpatient observation, with close serial reassessment for progression to necrotising infection and evaluation of the unexplained elevated jugular venous pressure.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Manage him as an inpatient rather than as an outpatient, because he is febrile, tachycardic, systemically unwell with bandaemia, diabetic with poor glycaemic control, and has rapidly progressive symptoms over two days, all of which are recognised indications for parenteral therapy and observation. Draw two sets of blood cultures immediately and then start empirical intravenous antibiotics without delay, directed at the beta-haemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus that cause the great majority of lower limb cellulitis, and cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus empirically given his systemic toxicity, adjusting therapy once culture and sensitivity data return and de-escalating to oral therapy once he is afebrile and clearly improving, for a total course guided by clinical response. Provide intravenous fluid resuscitation to correct the volume depletion indicated by the blood urea nitrogen of 28 mg/dL with creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL, the tachycardia and the diaphoresis, but titrate fluid carefully and monitor closely given the jugular venous distension of 12 cm and his cardiac history, reassessing perfusion, oxygenation and lung fields frequently rather than administering large fixed volumes. Mark the leading edge of the erythema with an indelible marker and reassess at least every few hours, since expansion of the marked border despite appropriate antibiotics is the key early signal of treatment failure or of a necrotising process. Elevate the affected limb to reduce oedema and hasten resolution, and provide analgesia and antipyretics. Institute a formal plan for glycaemic control with capillary glucose monitoring and short-acting insulin as required, recognising that diet-controlled diabetes is inadequate during acute infection and that hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and delays healing; check an HbA1c, since the patient does not know his last result, and arrange outpatient diabetes follow-up to reassess whether pharmacological therapy is now needed. Obtain immediate surgical consultation and consider urgent operative exploration if pain becomes disproportionate to the findings, or if bullae, crepitus, skin necrosis, dusky discolouration, cutaneous anaesthesia, rapid spread, hypotension or clinical deterioration appear, as these indicate necrotising fasciitis, which requires surgical debridement rather than antibiotics alone. Addressing the additional considerations, investigate the jugular venous distension of 12 cm, which is not explained by the infection, with echocardiography and cardiology input, and continue cardiac monitoring given that sustained tachycardia at 118 to 120 beats per minute increases myocardial oxygen demand in a man with prior bypass grafting; note that his electrocardiogram shows only sinus tachycardia unchanged from five years ago and he denies chest pain and dyspnoea. Review his medications: hydrochlorothiazide may aggravate volume depletion and prerenal azotaemia and should be held during acute illness, and enalapril at 40 mg daily should be reviewed in the setting of a rising creatinine and possible hypotension, while aspirin and pravastatin can generally continue. On discharge planning, address the strong risk of recurrence in a leg with post-venectomy lymphatic disruption by advising daily skin inspection of both legs, prompt treatment of any minor break, meticulous foot and skin care with emollients to prevent fissuring, treatment of tinea pedis or interdigital maceration should it appear even though none is present now, weight reduction given lifelong overweight, and consideration of graduated compression once the acute infection has resolved to control the chronic end-of-day swelling; discuss suppressive antibiotic prophylaxis with an infectious disease specialist if he develops recurrent episodes. Advise him not to return to squash and basketball or to work until the infection has resolved, and to seek immediate reassessment for spreading redness, worsening pain, fever despite antibiotics, blistering, blackening of the skin, confusion or faintness. Arrange follow-up within 48 to 72 hours of discharge with reassessment of the marked erythema, renal function and glucose.
Notes: Necrotising soft tissue infection can present initially as ordinary cellulitis, so the current absence of bullae, crepitus, fluctuance and radiographic gas does not exclude it, and serial reassessment with a low threshold for surgical exploration is mandatory in this diabetic, systemically unwell patient. A normal venous Doppler study reduces but does not entirely eliminate the possibility of thrombosis, and repeat imaging should be considered if the leg findings evolve atypically or fail to respond to antibiotics. The elevated jugular venous pressure is an unexplained finding that is not attributable to cellulitis and requires independent cardiac evaluation. Blood cultures are frequently negative in cellulitis, so negative results should not prompt discontinuation of therapy in a patient who is improving clinically.

This directly accounts for the localisation of infection to the right leg and for the absence of any visible wound, skin break, abrasion, or tinea pedis on examination. Second, he has type 2 diabetes of five years' duration managed by diet alone, is not monitoring glucose at home, does not know his most recent HbA1c, and presents with a glucose of 220 mg/dL, indicating that his diabetes is poorly controlled and impairing host defence, while the acute infection is itself worsening the hyperglycaemia. Ketones are negative and the anion gap is essentially normal, so diabetic ketoacidosis is excluded. The most important competing diagnosis is deep venous thrombosis, which shares unilateral leg pain, swelling and erythema and is plausible here given a right calf diameter 2 cm greater than the left and 1+ pitting shin oedema. This is excluded by a normal venous Doppler ultrasound of the right lower leg, and is further argued against by the absence of calf tenderness on compression, absence of distended veins, no recent immobilisation or injury, no history of clots or clotting disorder, no malignancy, and the presence of a discrete cutaneous erythematous plaque with fever and neutrophilic left shift that DVT would not explain. The asymmetry in calf diameter and the shin oedema are better attributed to the chronic post-harvest venous and lymphatic insufficiency described in the history plus acute inflammatory oedema. The second critical differential is necrotising fasciitis, a surgical emergency that must be actively considered in any diabetic patient with a hot, painful, erythematous limb and systemic toxicity. Reassuring against it are the absence of bullae, crepitus and fluctuance, only mild tenderness rather than pain out of proportion to findings, no skin necrosis or dusky discolouration, no anaesthesia over the area, a normal plain radiograph without soft tissue gas, a normal blood pressure of 128/74 mm Hg, and a patient who is alert, fully oriented and in no apparent distress. However, the presence of bandaemia, tachycardia and fever means he must be observed closely for any rapid progression, since early necrotising infection can mimic cellulitis. Other considerations are less likely: abscess is argued against by the absence of fluctuance, though it can develop; septic arthritis and osteomyelitis are unsupported, as the pain is between knee and ankle without joint involvement and the radiograph is normal; stasis dermatitis is chronic, usually bilateral, and does not cause fever or leucocytosis; gout and other crystal arthropathy do not fit the distribution or the absence of joint findings; and deep vein or superficial thrombophlebitis is excluded by the imaging and examination. Two findings deserve separate attention. The jugular venous distension of 12 cm above the sternal notch at 45 degrees is markedly abnormal and is not explained by cellulitis; in a man with established coronary artery disease and prior bypass grafting it raises concern for elevated right-sided filling pressures or a cardiac contribution, although the lungs are clear without crackles, there are no gallops or murmurs, he denies dyspnoea, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and the electrocardiogram shows only sinus tachycardia unchanged from five years ago. The tachycardia at 118 to 120 beats per minute is most plausibly explained by fever, infection and volume depletion, but in a patient with coronary artery disease it also increases myocardial oxygen demand and requires monitoring. Overall this represents a systemically unwell diabetic patient with an acute limb infection, meeting criteria for a systemic inflammatory response, in whom infection can progress rapidly and in whom outpatient oral therapy would be inappropriate.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures, at least two sets drawn before antibiotics are administered; serum lactate to assess for tissue hypoperfusion and sepsis severity; C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate as inflammatory markers for baseline and serial monitoring; HbA1c to define the degree of chronic glycaemic control, which the patient does not know; bedside and serial capillary glucose monitoring; repeat complete blood count with differential and repeat basic metabolic panel including renal function to track response; continuous cardiac monitoring and serial vital signs including pulse oximetry; marking of the erythematous border with an indelible skin marker at presentation to allow objective serial assessment of spread; measured limb circumference recorded serially; bedside soft tissue ultrasound of the calf if abscess or fluid collection is suspected; contrast-enhanced computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging of the right lower leg urgently if any feature suggesting necrotising soft tissue infection or deep abscess emerges; surgical consultation with consideration of operative exploration if necrotising infection is suspected, since imaging must never delay surgery; wound or aspirate culture only if a drainable collection, bulla or portal of entry becomes apparent; and echocardiography to evaluate the unexplained jugular venous distension and assess cardiac filling pressures and valvular status in a man with known coronary artery disease.
Conclusion: A 62-year-old diabetic man with coronary artery disease and prior right saphenous vein harvesting for coronary artery bypass grafting presents with two days of progressive right lower leg pain and a 15 by 10 cm warm, indurated, tender erythematous plaque on the lateral calf, together with fever of 38.5 degrees Celsius, tachycardia of 118 beats per minute, malaise, myalgias, anorexia, diaphoresis, a neutrophilic leucocytosis of 14,500 with 8 per cent bands, hyperglycaemia of 220 mg/dL and prerenal azotaemia. Deep venous thrombosis is excluded by normal venous Doppler ultrasonography, and there is currently no bulla, crepitus or fluctuance to indicate necrotising infection, with a normal radiograph. The diagnosis is acute bacterial cellulitis of the right lower leg arising in a limb rendered susceptible by post-venectomy lymphatic and venous insufficiency, in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes, now complicated by a systemic inflammatory response. He requires immediate parenteral antibiotic therapy, intravenous fluid resuscitation, glycaemic control and inpatient observation, with close serial reassessment for progression to necrotising infection and evaluation of the unexplained elevated jugular venous pressure.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Manage him as an inpatient rather than as an outpatient, because he is febrile, tachycardic, systemically unwell with bandaemia, diabetic with poor glycaemic control, and has rapidly progressive symptoms over two days, all of which are recognised indications for parenteral therapy and observation. Draw two sets of blood cultures immediately and then start empirical intravenous antibiotics without delay, directed at the beta-haemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus that cause the great majority of lower limb cellulitis, and cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus empirically given his systemic toxicity, adjusting therapy once culture and sensitivity data return and de-escalating to oral therapy once he is afebrile and clearly improving, for a total course guided by clinical response. Provide intravenous fluid resuscitation to correct the volume depletion indicated by the blood urea nitrogen of 28 mg/dL with creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL, the tachycardia and the diaphoresis, but titrate fluid carefully and monitor closely given the jugular venous distension of 12 cm and his cardiac history, reassessing perfusion, oxygenation and lung fields frequently rather than administering large fixed volumes. Mark the leading edge of the erythema with an indelible marker and reassess at least every few hours, since expansion of the marked border despite appropriate antibiotics is the key early signal of treatment failure or of a necrotising process. Elevate the affected limb to reduce oedema and hasten resolution, and provide analgesia and antipyretics. Institute a formal plan for glycaemic control with capillary glucose monitoring and short-acting insulin as required, recognising that diet-controlled diabetes is inadequate during acute infection and that hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and delays healing; check an HbA1c, since the patient does not know his last result, and arrange outpatient diabetes follow-up to reassess whether pharmacological therapy is now needed. Obtain immediate surgical consultation and consider urgent operative exploration if pain becomes disproportionate to the findings, or if bullae, crepitus, skin necrosis, dusky discolouration, cutaneous anaesthesia, rapid spread, hypotension or clinical deterioration appear, as these indicate necrotising fasciitis, which requires surgical debridement rather than antibiotics alone. Addressing the additional considerations, investigate the jugular venous distension of 12 cm, which is not explained by the infection, with echocardiography and cardiology input, and continue cardiac monitoring given that sustained tachycardia at 118 to 120 beats per minute increases myocardial oxygen demand in a man with prior bypass grafting; note that his electrocardiogram shows only sinus tachycardia unchanged from five years ago and he denies chest pain and dyspnoea. Review his medications: hydrochlorothiazide may aggravate volume depletion and prerenal azotaemia and should be held during acute illness, and enalapril at 40 mg daily should be reviewed in the setting of a rising creatinine and possible hypotension, while aspirin and pravastatin can generally continue. On discharge planning, address the strong risk of recurrence in a leg with post-venectomy lymphatic disruption by advising daily skin inspection of both legs, prompt treatment of any minor break, meticulous foot and skin care with emollients to prevent fissuring, treatment of tinea pedis or interdigital maceration should it appear even though none is present now, weight reduction given lifelong overweight, and consideration of graduated compression once the acute infection has resolved to control the chronic end-of-day swelling; discuss suppressive antibiotic prophylaxis with an infectious disease specialist if he develops recurrent episodes. Advise him not to return to squash and basketball or to work until the infection has resolved, and to seek immediate reassessment for spreading redness, worsening pain, fever despite antibiotics, blistering, blackening of the skin, confusion or faintness. Arrange follow-up within 48 to 72 hours of discharge with reassessment of the marked erythema, renal function and glucose.
Notes: Necrotising soft tissue infection can present initially as ordinary cellulitis, so the current absence of bullae, crepitus, fluctuance and radiographic gas does not exclude it, and serial reassessment with a low threshold for surgical exploration is mandatory in this diabetic, systemically unwell patient. A normal venous Doppler study reduces but does not entirely eliminate the possibility of thrombosis, and repeat imaging should be considered if the leg findings evolve atypically or fail to respond to antibiotics. The elevated jugular venous pressure is an unexplained finding that is not attributable to cellulitis and requires independent cardiac evaluation. Blood cultures are frequently negative in cellulitis, so negative results should not prompt discontinuation of therapy in a patient who is improving clinically.

Vignette:
A 14-year-old boy with no significant past medical history presents 3 days after developing a red, irritated right eye that spread to the left eye today. He has watery discharge from both eyes and they are stuck shut in the morning. He reports recent upper respiratory symptoms and that several children at his day camp recently had pink eye. He denies significant pain or light sensitivity and does not wear contact lenses. On examination, his pupils are equal and reactive and he has a right-sided, tender preauricular lymph node. Penlight examination does not reveal any corneal opacity
baseline_protocol:
Age: 14 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three days of a red, irritated right eye that spread to the left eye today, with watery discharge from both eyes and lids stuck shut in the morning, following recent upper respiratory symptoms and exposure to other children with pink eye at day camp.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of acute viral conjunctivitis, most commonly adenoviral. Several features converge on this diagnosis. The discharge is watery rather than thick and purulent, which is the hallmark distinction from bacterial conjunctivitis, where a mucopurulent discharge that continuously reaccumulates through the day is typical; the morning crusting that sticks the lids together is common to both and does not discriminate. The illness began unilaterally in the right eye and spread to the fellow eye three days later, a sequential pattern typical of viral spread by autoinoculation. There is a clear antecedent and epidemiological context: recent upper respiratory symptoms in the patient himself, which is strongly associated with adenoviral infection and can produce a pharyngoconjunctival pattern, and a documented cluster of pink eye among children at his day camp, reflecting the high contagiousness and the propensity of adenovirus for institutional outbreaks. The most specific single physical finding is the tender right preauricular lymph node, ipsilateral to the eye first and most affected. Preauricular lymphadenopathy is characteristically absent in simple bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis and is a well-recognised marker of adenoviral conjunctivitis, so its presence here substantially raises the likelihood of a viral aetiology. The examination is otherwise reassuring in ways that exclude the sight-threatening alternatives. Pupils are equal and reactive, which argues against acute angle-closure glaucoma and against anterior uveitis with a miotic or irregular pupil. Penlight examination shows no corneal opacity, arguing against keratitis, corneal ulcer and corneal infiltrate. He denies significant pain and denies photophobia, and this combination of a red eye that is irritated rather than painful, with no light sensitivity, no visual complaint and clear cornea, places the process on the ocular surface rather than within the eye. He does not wear contact lenses, which removes the principal risk factor for microbial and specifically Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba keratitis in this age group and is an important negative in an adolescent with a red eye. Alternative diagnoses are considered and are less consistent with the findings. Bacterial conjunctivitis is possible but is argued against by watery rather than purulent discharge and by the tender preauricular node. Allergic conjunctivitis typically causes prominent bilateral itching, is often seasonal or exposure-related, and does not produce preauricular lymphadenopathy, fever or an antecedent upper respiratory illness, and no itching or atopic history is described. Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis usually is unilateral, often with vesicular lid lesions and dendritic corneal changes, and would be expected to cause pain and photophobia; none of these are present, though corneal staining has not been performed. Anterior uveitis and acute angle-closure glaucoma are excluded by normal reactive pupils, absent pain and absent photophobia. Foreign body and trauma are not suggested by the history. Gonococcal conjunctivitis, which is hyperacute with copious purulent discharge and carries a risk of corneal perforation, does not fit this three-day watery course. The condition, while highly contagious and often prolonged and uncomfortable, is self-limited, does not threaten sight in the absence of corneal involvement, and does not respond to antibiotics.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A previously healthy 14-year-old boy presents with a three-day history of sequentially bilateral conjunctival injection and irritation with watery discharge and morning crusting, in the setting of a recent upper respiratory illness and a day-camp outbreak of conjunctivitis, with a tender ipsilateral right preauricular lymph node, equal reactive pupils, no significant pain or photophobia, no contact lens use, and no corneal opacity on penlight examination. This is acute viral conjunctivitis, most likely adenoviral. It is a self-limited condition requiring supportive care, strict hygiene and infection-control measures rather than antibiotics, with no indication for laboratory testing or imaging. Formal ophthalmological reassessment is required only if red-flag features develop.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Explain that this is a viral infection of the conjunctiva which will resolve on its own, typically over one to three weeks, and that antibiotic eye drops are not indicated because they neither shorten the illness nor prevent complications and may cause irritation or allergy. Provide symptomatic relief with preservative-free artificial tears used liberally through the day to relieve grittiness and irritation, and cool compresses applied to the closed lids for comfort and to soften the morning crusting; the lashes can be gently cleaned with a clean warm damp cloth, using a separate cloth for each eye. Advise against topical vasoconstrictor or decongestant redness-relieving drops, which give only transient benefit and cause rebound hyperaemia, and against any topical corticosteroid unless prescribed after a formal slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist, since steroids can markedly worsen an undiagnosed herpetic keratitis. Advise against eye patching and against rubbing the eyes. Emphasise infection control, since adenoviral conjunctivitis is highly contagious for one to two weeks and can survive on surfaces: frequent and thorough handwashing, especially after touching the eyes or face, no sharing of towels, washcloths, pillowcases, eye drops, or eye cosmetics, changing pillowcases and towels frequently, and cleaning shared surfaces. Regarding the additional considerations, he should stay away from day camp and from close-contact and shared-equipment activities such as swimming pools while the eyes remain red with active discharge, given the documented outbreak among other campers, and should return when symptoms have substantially settled or as directed by camp and local public health guidance; the camp should be informed so that other affected children can be identified. Although he does not wear contact lenses, he should not begin wearing any until the eyes have been white and symptom-free for a period, and any lenses or cases in the household should not be shared. He should also be told that the second eye becoming involved and the illness appearing to worsen over the first several days before improving is the expected course and does not by itself indicate treatment failure. Advise prompt reassessment by an ophthalmologist, including slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining and formal visual acuity testing, if he develops any of the following red flags: decreased or blurred vision, significant or worsening eye pain, true photophobia, thick purulent or copious discharge, corneal cloudiness or a white spot on the cornea, marked eyelid swelling, an irregular or poorly reactive pupil, vesicular lesions on the eyelid or face, symptoms persisting beyond two to three weeks or worsening after the first week, or systemic features such as high fever. He should also be reviewed if he becomes unable to open the eyes because of severe discomfort or if a household member develops a severe or painful red eye.
Notes: Only a penlight examination was performed; visual acuity and slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining are not documented in the case and would be needed to definitively exclude corneal epithelial involvement, subepithelial infiltrates, or herpetic dendritic keratitis if any red-flag feature emerges. Adenoviral conjunctivitis can be followed by subepithelial corneal infiltrates causing blurred vision after the acute phase, which warrants ophthalmological review if it occurs. Topical corticosteroids must not be used without specialist examination. Visual acuity, presence of itching, and vaccination and atopic history are not specified in the case.

Complaint: Three days of a red, irritated right eye that spread to the left eye today, with watery discharge from both eyes and lids stuck shut in the morning, following recent upper respiratory symptoms and exposure to other children with pink eye at day camp.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of acute viral conjunctivitis, most commonly adenoviral. Several features converge on this diagnosis. The discharge is watery rather than thick and purulent, which is the hallmark distinction from bacterial conjunctivitis, where a mucopurulent discharge that continuously reaccumulates through the day is typical; the morning crusting that sticks the lids together is common to both and does not discriminate. The illness began unilaterally in the right eye and spread to the fellow eye three days later, a sequential pattern typical of viral spread by autoinoculation. There is a clear antecedent and epidemiological context: recent upper respiratory symptoms in the patient himself, which is strongly associated with adenoviral infection and can produce a pharyngoconjunctival pattern, and a documented cluster of pink eye among children at his day camp, reflecting the high contagiousness and the propensity of adenovirus for institutional outbreaks. The most specific single physical finding is the tender right preauricular lymph node, ipsilateral to the eye first and most affected. Preauricular lymphadenopathy is characteristically absent in simple bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis and is a well-recognised marker of adenoviral conjunctivitis, so its presence here substantially raises the likelihood of a viral aetiology. The examination is otherwise reassuring in ways that exclude the sight-threatening alternatives. Pupils are equal and reactive, which argues against acute angle-closure glaucoma and against anterior uveitis with a miotic or irregular pupil. Penlight examination shows no corneal opacity, arguing against keratitis, corneal ulcer and corneal infiltrate. He denies significant pain and denies photophobia, and this combination of a red eye that is irritated rather than painful, with no light sensitivity, no visual complaint and clear cornea, places the process on the ocular surface rather than within the eye. He does not wear contact lenses, which removes the principal risk factor for microbial and specifically Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba keratitis in this age group and is an important negative in an adolescent with a red eye. Alternative diagnoses are considered and are less consistent with the findings. Bacterial conjunctivitis is possible but is argued against by watery rather than purulent discharge and by the tender preauricular node. Allergic conjunctivitis typically causes prominent bilateral itching, is often seasonal or exposure-related, and does not produce preauricular lymphadenopathy, fever or an antecedent upper respiratory illness, and no itching or atopic history is described. Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis usually is unilateral, often with vesicular lid lesions and dendritic corneal changes, and would be expected to cause pain and photophobia; none of these are present, though corneal staining has not been performed. Anterior uveitis and acute angle-closure glaucoma are excluded by normal reactive pupils, absent pain and absent photophobia. Foreign body and trauma are not suggested by the history. Gonococcal conjunctivitis, which is hyperacute with copious purulent discharge and carries a risk of corneal perforation, does not fit this three-day watery course. The condition, while highly contagious and often prolonged and uncomfortable, is self-limited, does not threaten sight in the absence of corneal involvement, and does not respond to antibiotics.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A previously healthy 14-year-old boy presents with a three-day history of sequentially bilateral conjunctival injection and irritation with watery discharge and morning crusting, in the setting of a recent upper respiratory illness and a day-camp outbreak of conjunctivitis, with a tender ipsilateral right preauricular lymph node, equal reactive pupils, no significant pain or photophobia, no contact lens use, and no corneal opacity on penlight examination. This is acute viral conjunctivitis, most likely adenoviral. It is a self-limited condition requiring supportive care, strict hygiene and infection-control measures rather than antibiotics, with no indication for laboratory testing or imaging. Formal ophthalmological reassessment is required only if red-flag features develop.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: Explain that this is a viral infection of the conjunctiva which will resolve on its own, typically over one to three weeks, and that antibiotic eye drops are not indicated because they neither shorten the illness nor prevent complications and may cause irritation or allergy. Provide symptomatic relief with preservative-free artificial tears used liberally through the day to relieve grittiness and irritation, and cool compresses applied to the closed lids for comfort and to soften the morning crusting; the lashes can be gently cleaned with a clean warm damp cloth, using a separate cloth for each eye. Advise against topical vasoconstrictor or decongestant redness-relieving drops, which give only transient benefit and cause rebound hyperaemia, and against any topical corticosteroid unless prescribed after a formal slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist, since steroids can markedly worsen an undiagnosed herpetic keratitis. Advise against eye patching and against rubbing the eyes. Emphasise infection control, since adenoviral conjunctivitis is highly contagious for one to two weeks and can survive on surfaces: frequent and thorough handwashing, especially after touching the eyes or face, no sharing of towels, washcloths, pillowcases, eye drops, or eye cosmetics, changing pillowcases and towels frequently, and cleaning shared surfaces. Regarding the additional considerations, he should stay away from day camp and from close-contact and shared-equipment activities such as swimming pools while the eyes remain red with active discharge, given the documented outbreak among other campers, and should return when symptoms have substantially settled or as directed by camp and local public health guidance; the camp should be informed so that other affected children can be identified. Although he does not wear contact lenses, he should not begin wearing any until the eyes have been white and symptom-free for a period, and any lenses or cases in the household should not be shared. He should also be told that the second eye becoming involved and the illness appearing to worsen over the first several days before improving is the expected course and does not by itself indicate treatment failure. Advise prompt reassessment by an ophthalmologist, including slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining and formal visual acuity testing, if he develops any of the following red flags: decreased or blurred vision, significant or worsening eye pain, true photophobia, thick purulent or copious discharge, corneal cloudiness or a white spot on the cornea, marked eyelid swelling, an irregular or poorly reactive pupil, vesicular lesions on the eyelid or face, symptoms persisting beyond two to three weeks or worsening after the first week, or systemic features such as high fever. He should also be reviewed if he becomes unable to open the eyes because of severe discomfort or if a household member develops a severe or painful red eye.
Notes: Only a penlight examination was performed; visual acuity and slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining are not documented in the case and would be needed to definitively exclude corneal epithelial involvement, subepithelial infiltrates, or herpetic dendritic keratitis if any red-flag feature emerges. Adenoviral conjunctivitis can be followed by subepithelial corneal infiltrates causing blurred vision after the acute phase, which warrants ophthalmological review if it occurs. Topical corticosteroids must not be used without specialist examination. Visual acuity, presence of itching, and vaccination and atopic history are not specified in the case.
