A 30-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of runny nose and sore throat. He feels hot and sweaty, has a mild headache, is coughing up clear sputum and complains of muscle aches. He would like antibiotics as he was prescribed them last year when he had a similar condition. On examination, he is afebrile, has a normal pulse, a slightly inflamed pharynx and nontender cervical lymphadenopathy. There is no neck stiffness and his chest is clear. baseline_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two days of runny nose and sore throat with feeling hot and sweaty, mild headache, cough productive of clear sputum, and muscle aches, together with a request for antibiotics because he received them for a similar illness last year.
Analysis: This is an uncomplicated acute viral upper respiratory tract infection, the common cold. The strongest supporting facts are the very short duration of two days, the constellation of coryza, sore throat, mild headache, myalgia and a cough producing clear rather than purulent sputum, and above all a reassuring examination: he is afebrile with a normal pulse, the pharynx is only slightly inflamed, cervical lymph nodes are nontender, there is no neck stiffness, and the chest is clear. This combination of multiple simultaneous upper respiratory symptoms with a normal general examination is typical of a viral syndrome and argues against a bacterial process. The main differential considerations are streptococcal pharyngitis, which is made unlikely by the presence of cough and coryza, the absence of fever, the absence of tonsillar exudate and the nontender rather than tender anterior cervical nodes, giving a very low Centor score for which neither testing nor antibiotics is warranted; influenza, which usually begins abruptly with high fever and prominent systemic symptoms rather than the mild, gradual picture described here; acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, which requires persistence beyond about ten days, worsening after initial improvement, or severe symptoms with high fever, none of which are present at two days; acute bronchitis or pneumonia, effectively excluded by a clear chest, absence of fever, normal pulse and clear sputum; infectious mononucleosis, which typically causes marked tonsillar enlargement with tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and prolonged fatigue; and meningitis, excluded by the absence of neck stiffness, fever or altered consciousness. His smoking of ten cigarettes per day is clinically relevant because it irritates the airways, prolongs cough after a viral infection, and is a modifiable risk factor for recurrent respiratory infection and for chronic respiratory disease. The central management issue in this case is his expectation of antibiotics based on a previous prescription for a similar illness, which is a request that is not supported by the clinical findings; antibiotics would confer no benefit against a viral illness, would expose him to adverse effects, allergic reactions and Clostridioides difficile infection, would promote antimicrobial resistance, and would reinforce the belief that antibiotics are needed for future colds. His report that over-the-counter cough preparations have not helped is consistent with their limited evidence base and does not indicate that antibiotics are the alternative.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical in a well, afebrile patient with a normal examination and a clear chest; no throat swab, rapid streptococcal test, blood tests, sputum culture or chest radiography is indicated at this stage.
Conclusion: A 30-year-old smoker has an uncomplicated acute viral upper respiratory tract infection of two days' duration, with a normal examination apart from mild pharyngeal inflammation and nontender cervical lymphadenopathy, and no clinical evidence of streptococcal pharyngitis, sinusitis or lower respiratory tract infection. Antibiotics are not indicated. Management consists of explanation, symptomatic self-care, smoking cessation advice, and clear safety-netting for the small minority of patients whose illness evolves into a bacterial complication.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Explain clearly and respectfully why antibiotics are not appropriate, addressing his request directly rather than dismissing it: the illness is viral, his examination is normal and he has no fever, and antibiotics would not shorten the illness or prevent complications, while carrying risks of diarrhea, rash, allergic reaction and antimicrobial resistance. Vignette:
A 19-year-old man presents with diffuse redness and small bumps on his neck that appeared shortly after shaving this morning. He reports a mild burning sensation. He used a new razor and shaved without moisturizing first. He denies any prior skin conditions or allergies. On examination, there is diffuse erythema with multiple small non-follicular papules along the anterior and lateral neck. There is no pustulation, vesiculation, or excoriation. baseline_protocol:
Age: 19 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Diffuse redness and small bumps on the neck with a mild burning sensation, appearing shortly after shaving this morning with a new razor and without moisturizing beforehand.
Analysis: The findings are those of an acute irritant reaction of the skin caused by shaving, that is, razor burn or irritant contact dermatitis of the shaved area. The strongest supporting facts are the immediate temporal relationship between shaving and the eruption, the identifiable mechanical provocation of a new razor used on dry, unmoisturized skin, and the confinement of the changes to the shaved anterior and lateral neck with an otherwise entirely normal skin examination. The morphology is decisive: the papules are described as small and non-follicular, with diffuse erythema, mild burning and slight local warmth, and there is no pustulation, no vesiculation and no excoriation. Non-follicular papules without pustules argue against an infectious folliculitis, which would be centered on hair follicles and typically show follicular pustules; the absence of vesicles argues against an acute allergic contact dermatitis, which also usually requires prior sensitization and develops over 24 to 72 hours rather than within minutes to hours, and he reports no prior skin conditions or allergies. Pseudofolliculitis barbae, caused by ingrown hairs after shaving, is an important consideration in a young man who shaves the neck, but that condition produces firm follicular papules and sometimes pustules developing over days with visible ingrown hairs and typically a history of recurrence, whereas this eruption is diffuse, non-follicular and appeared within hours of a single shave. Cellulitis is excluded by the absence of a spreading tender indurated plaque, absence of fever, absence of lymphadenopathy and absence of any deeper tissue involvement; the slight warmth described is consistent with superficial irritation rather than infection. Other considerations such as acne keloidalis nuchae, tinea barbae, herpetic infection and urticaria are not supported by the described morphology, distribution or time course. The examination is entirely reassuring, with no regional lymphadenopathy, no systemic features and no evidence of infection, so this is a benign, self-limited process expected to resolve over one to a few days with simple measures and modification of shaving technique.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical and is established by the history and the appearance of the lesions; no cultures, swabs, fungal studies, patch testing or blood work is indicated at this time.
Conclusion: A 19-year-old man has acute irritant shaving dermatitis, or razor burn, of the anterior and lateral neck, produced by shaving with a new razor on dry skin without a lubricating preparation. The eruption is superficial, non-follicular, non-infected and self-limited, with no signs of folliculitis, allergic contact dermatitis or cellulitis. Management is supportive skin care with correction of shaving technique, and no medical intervention beyond self-care is required.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Advise him to stop shaving the affected area until the redness and papules have fully settled, which usually takes a few days, and to avoid rubbing, scratching or applying alcohol-based aftershave or other astringent products that will aggravate the irritation. For symptomatic relief of the burning and erythema, recommend gentle cleansing with lukewarm water and a mild, fragrance-free cleanser, cool compresses, and a bland fragrance-free emollient or moisturizer applied to restore the skin barrier; a short course of a low-potency topical corticosteroid may be used if the irritation is troublesome, and topical antibiotics are not indicated because there is no evidence of infection. Address the additional considerations explicitly by correcting the causative technique, since the mechanism is identified in the history: wet the skin and soften the hair with warm water before shaving, always use a shaving cream, gel or other lubricant rather than shaving dry, shave in the direction of hair growth with light pressure and few passes, rinse the blade frequently, replace blades before they become dull, avoid stretching the skin taut, and consider an electric razor or a single-blade razor if irritation recurs; apply a moisturizer after shaving. Note that the new razor is the likely mechanical trigger and that he does not need to avoid shaving permanently, only to modify how he does it. Reassure him that no testing or antibiotics are needed. Instruct him to seek medical review if the rash does not improve within several days or worsens, or if he develops pustules, spreading or increasing redness, significant pain, swelling, blistering, weeping or crusting, fever, or tender swollen lymph nodes, as these would suggest secondary bacterial infection or cellulitis rather than simple razor burn, and to seek care sooner if the redness spreads rapidly.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 22-year-old woman presents with tender, reddened skin on her shoulders and upper back after spending approximately 5 hours at the beach the previous day without reapplying sunscreen. She reports mild burning pain that worsens with contact from clothing. She denies blistering, nausea, dizziness, or fever. On examination, there is diffuse erythema across the bilateral shoulders, upper back, and posterior neck with well-demarcated borders corresponding to her swimsuit lines. The skin is warm to touch. There is no blistering, peeling, or edema. She is well-appearing and afebrile.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 22 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Tender, reddened skin over the shoulders and upper back with mild burning pain worsened by contact with clothing, following approximately five hours at the beach the previous day without reapplying sunscreen.
Analysis: This is a first-degree, superficial sunburn, that is, an acute ultraviolet radiation injury limited to the epidermis. The reasoning is straightforward and the history and examination corroborate each other precisely. The exposure is documented and sufficient: roughly five hours of beach sun exposure the previous day with sunscreen that was not reapplied. The timing fits the natural history of sunburn, in which erythema begins within hours and peaks around 12 to 24 hours after exposure. The distribution is decisive for a photic rather than an infectious or allergic cause: the erythema is confined to sun-exposed areas of the bilateral shoulders, upper back and posterior neck, and its borders are well demarcated and correspond exactly to her swimsuit lines, so covered skin was spared. The findings are limited to diffuse erythema with warmth and tenderness, with mild burning pain aggravated by clothing contact. Crucially, there is no blistering, no peeling and no edema, which places the injury in the superficial first-degree category rather than a partial-thickness second-degree burn, and she is well-appearing and afebrile with no nausea, dizziness or fever, so there is no evidence of the systemic sunburn reaction sometimes called sun poisoning, nor of dehydration or heat illness. The main differential considerations are a second-degree sunburn with blistering, excluded by the explicit absence of blisters and edema; phototoxic or photoallergic drug eruption, which would follow the same sun-exposed distribution and should be considered, although no medication or topical product exposure is stated in the case; polymorphous light eruption, which typically produces pruritic papules or plaques rather than uniform confluent erythema and usually appears in spring on newly exposed skin; contact dermatitis from sunscreen or another topical agent, which would be pruritic, would not respect the swimsuit line so exactly, and would typically follow the pattern of application rather than of sun exposure; cellulitis, which is excluded by the bilateral symmetric distribution, the sharp demarcation at clothing lines, the absence of fever and the absence of a spreading indurated focus; and heat-related illness, excluded by her well appearance, normal temperature and absence of dizziness or nausea. Nothing in the case indicates a photosensitizing condition or medication, and none should be assumed. The expected course is spontaneous resolution over several days, often with subsequent peeling, and management is entirely supportive.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis is clinical, established by the exposure history and the characteristic distribution and appearance; no laboratory studies, imaging, cultures or photo-testing are indicated.
Conclusion: A 22-year-old well-appearing, afebrile woman has an acute first-degree sunburn of the shoulders, upper back and posterior neck following prolonged unprotected sun exposure, with erythema sharply demarcated at her swimsuit lines, warmth and mild burning tenderness, and without blistering, edema or systemic symptoms. This is a superficial, self-limited injury requiring only symptomatic care, skin protection during healing, and counseling on future sun protection.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Manage supportively at home. Advise cool compresses or cool showers or baths for symptomatic relief, avoiding harsh soaps and vigorous scrubbing of the affected skin, and applying a bland fragrance-free moisturizer or an aloe vera preparation while the skin is still damp to reduce dryness and discomfort. Recommend a simple oral analgesic or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent for the burning pain, which may also reduce inflammation if started early, and encourage generous oral fluid intake since even superficial burns increase insensible fluid loss. Advise loose, soft clothing over the affected area, since she reports that contact with clothing worsens the pain. Tell her not to apply topical anesthetic sprays containing benzocaine or lidocaine, petroleum-based occlusive ointments, butter or other home remedies to the burn, and not to break any blisters should they appear. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Advise strict avoidance of further sun exposure to the affected areas until the skin has fully healed, since damaged skin burns far more readily. Counsel on future prevention: use a broad-spectrum sunscreen of adequate sun protection factor applied generously about 15 to 30 minutes before exposure and reapplied at least every two hours and after swimming or sweating, which directly addresses the failure to reapply that caused this burn; seek shade during peak midday hours; and use protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses. Explain that peeling over the coming days is expected and normal and should not be picked, and that she should moisturize during that phase. Explain that each sunburn adds to lifetime risk of skin cancer and photoaging, and encourage periodic attention to any changing skin lesions. Instruct her to seek medical assessment if blisters develop, especially if extensive, or if she develops fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, faintness, severe headache, confusion, marked swelling, or increasing pain, spreading redness, pus or other signs of secondary infection of the burned skin.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.

Vignette:
A 28-yr-old man comes to the outpatient clinic for evaluation of a lump in his right testis. About 1
month ago, while taking a shower, he noted a hard area in his right testis that felt "like a
marble." He had never noticed this before and decided to wait and see if anything would
change. When the mass did not go away, he scheduled this appointment. Today, he states the
lump is not painful or tender to the touch and has not changed in size. He has had annual
physical exams and was never told that a lump was present. Four years ago, he had a scrotal
ultrasound following a brief episode of scrotal discomfort after competing in a bicycle race; the
result of the ultrasound was normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Overall feels well. Denies any weight loss, fevers, or chills.

Skin: Denies rashes, itching, or other lesions.

HEENT: Noncontributory

Pulmonary: No cough or shortness of breath.

Cardiovascular: No palpitations or chest pain.

Gastrointestinal: Good appetite, bowel movements are normal. Denies nausea or vomiting.
Denies abdominal or flank pain.

Genitourinary: No dysuria, hematuria, frequency, or urgency. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No back or joint pain, no leg swelling.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: No reported medical history. Denies history of urinary tract infections, difficulty
with urination, immunosuppressive disorders, or sexually transmitted infections.

Surgical history: Rotator cuff repair 4 yr ago; left inguinal hernia repair as a child.

Medications: Occasional NSAIDs.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Mother and father healthy. No history of genitourinary malignancies in any
known relatives.

Social history: He denies current or previous tobacco use. He exercises almost every day with a
combination of weight training and cardio. He works primarily at a desk job with somewhat
frequent travel. All relevant immunizations are up to date. He denies exposure to any sick
contacts. He has had unprotected sex only with his wife for the past 3 yr.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Thin male who appears fatigued and older than stated age; in no apparent
respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 60 beats/min
BP: 112/65 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
Height: 6'
Weight: 180 lb
BMI: 24.4

Skin: Warm and dry to the touch.

HEENT: Nasopharynx appears normal; no neck masses or lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Breath sounds present and equal bilaterally. No stridor, rales, or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Heart rate is regular; radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are present and equal
bilaterally; no pedal edema.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen is not distended; there are no ecchymoses. Normal bowel sounds
are present. Abdomen is soft and nontender to light and deep palpation; no masses are present.

Genitourinary: Circumcised phallus, no visible lesions, bilateral descended testes. Left testis
smooth and nontender. Left epididymis is normal in texture and nontender. Right testis has firm
mass in the midsection that is nontender on palpation. Right epididymis is normal in texture and
nontender. There are no palpable inguinal lymph nodes. No urethral discharge.

Musculoskeletal: No costovertebral angle tenderness.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 28 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A painless hard lump in the right testis, first noticed about one month ago while showering, described as feeling "like a marble," which has not resolved or changed in size.
Analysis: The presentation is that of a painless intratesticular solid mass in a young adult man, which must be treated as testicular malignancy until proven otherwise. The strongest supporting facts are the physical findings: the right testis contains a firm mass in its midsection that is nontender on palpation, while the right epididymis is normal in texture and nontender and the entire left testis and epididymis are normal. This localization is the key discriminator, because a mass arising within the testis itself, as opposed to a paratesticular or epididymal lesion, carries a high probability of germ cell tumor, whereas most extratesticular scrotal masses are benign. The history reinforces this: the lump is painless, persistent for a month without change, and new, since he has had annual physical examinations at which no lump was noted, and a scrotal ultrasound performed four years ago after transient post-cycling discomfort was normal, establishing that this is an interval development rather than a long-standing finding. His age of 28 falls squarely within the peak incidence for testicular germ cell tumors, which are the most common solid malignancy in men between about 15 and 35 years. Regarding the imaging question posed in the case, the clinical findings of a firm, palpable, persistent intratesticular mass correspond to a solid testicular mass on scrotal ultrasonography; a hydrocele would be a fluid collection surrounding the testis and would transilluminate rather than feel like a discrete firm marble, an inguinal hernia would be an extratesticular inguinoscrotal lesion with bowel contents and would not be confined to the midsection of the testis with a normal epididymis, a purely cystic testicular mass would not be palpable as a hard firm nodule, and a normal study is incompatible with the unequivocal abnormal finding on examination. The main differential considerations and how they are addressed are as follows. Epididymal cyst, spermatocele and epididymitis are excluded by the normal, nontender epididymis on both sides. Varicocele is excluded because the mass is a discrete firm intratesticular nodule rather than a compressible venous plexus. Hydrocele is excluded by the firm consistency and discrete character. Testicular torsion is excluded by the painless, chronic, unchanging course over a month with a viable non-tender testis. Orchitis and other infectious causes are argued against by the absence of pain, fever, dysuria, urethral discharge, urinary symptoms, sexually transmitted infection history, and by a temperature of 37 degrees Celsius with a normal general examination. Trauma-related hematoma is not supported by any history of injury. Benign testicular lesions such as epidermoid cyst or Leydig cell tumor are possible but far less likely and cannot be distinguished clinically. Reassuringly for staging, there are no palpable inguinal lymph nodes, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no abdominal mass or tenderness, no back or flank pain, no leg swelling, no respiratory symptoms, and no weight loss, fever or chills, so there is no clinical evidence of metastatic disease at this point, though the case notes a general appearance of fatigue and of looking older than his stated age, which warrants attention. His prior left inguinal hernia repair as a child is relevant background because inguinal surgery can alter lymphatic drainage patterns, and it is on the contralateral side. His delay of one month before seeking care is a common pattern in this disease and should be addressed with education rather than reproach.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Scrotal ultrasonography with high-frequency transducer and Doppler, which is the primary imaging modality and, per the case, has already been performed; the appropriate interpretation consistent with the examination is a solid testicular mass. Serum tumor markers before any intervention, comprising alpha-fetoprotein, beta human chorionic gonadotropin and lactate dehydrogenase, drawn preoperatively because they are required for diagnosis, staging, risk stratification and post-treatment monitoring. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to evaluate the retroperitoneal lymph nodes, which are the primary landing site, and chest imaging by radiography or computed tomography to assess for pulmonary metastases. Baseline complete blood count, renal function and liver function tests in preparation for surgery and possible chemotherapy. Semen analysis and sperm cryopreservation counseling before any definitive treatment. Percutaneous or transscrotal biopsy of the mass is contraindicated and must not be performed, as it risks tumor seeding and alters lymphatic drainage; the diagnosis is established by radical inguinal orchiectomy.
Conclusion: A 28-year-old man has a painless, firm, persistent intratesticular mass of the right testis, new since a normal scrotal ultrasound four years ago, with a normal epididymis bilaterally and no clinical evidence of infection, torsion or metastatic disease. The scrotal ultrasonography is correctly interpreted as showing a solid testicular mass. In a man of this age this constitutes presumed testicular germ cell tumor until proven otherwise, and requires prompt urologic referral, preoperative serum tumor markers, staging imaging, and radical inguinal orchiectomy for diagnosis and treatment. Any watchful waiting or antibiotic trial would be inappropriate.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Refer him urgently to urology for definitive management; this is not an emergency department presentation, but it should not be deferred, as prognosis in germ cell tumors depends strongly on the stage at treatment. Draw serum alpha-fetoprotein, beta human chorionic gonadotropin and lactate dehydrogenase before surgery, since post-orchiectomy values cannot substitute for baseline levels in staging and risk assessment. Obtain computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis and chest imaging for staging. Plan radical inguinal orchiectomy as both the diagnostic and the initial therapeutic procedure, and explicitly avoid a transscrotal approach or any scrotal or percutaneous biopsy. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Discuss fertility before treatment and offer sperm banking, since orchiectomy, and any subsequent chemotherapy or radiotherapy, may impair fertility; this matters to a 28-year-old married man and should be raised proactively rather than after treatment begins. Discuss testicular prosthesis placement as an option at the time of orchiectomy, and counsel that the remaining normal left testis usually maintains adequate testosterone production, with hormonal assessment if symptoms of deficiency arise. Explain the favorable prognosis of testicular cancer when treated, to support engagement with prompt care, and address the anxiety that a cancer diagnosis at this age produces, involving his wife in discussions as he wishes. Educate him that a painless testicular lump should never be observed at home and that he should seek assessment promptly for any new scrotal finding in the future, teaching testicular self-examination of the remaining testis, which will require long-term surveillance because of the increased risk of a contralateral tumor. Evaluate the reported fatigue and appearance of looking older than his stated age further during workup rather than dismissing it. Arrange multidisciplinary follow-up after orchiectomy for pathology-directed management, which may include surveillance, chemotherapy, radiotherapy or retroperitoneal lymph node dissection depending on histology and stage, with a defined schedule of marker measurement and imaging. Instruct him to seek prompt care in the interim for new back or abdominal pain, shortness of breath, cough or hemoptysis, a supraclavicular lump, leg swelling, or acute scrotal pain.
Notes: The ultrasound image referred to in the case is not available for direct visual review, so its interpretation is derived from the described clinical findings; the correct interpretation consistent with those findings is a solid testicular mass. Normal serum tumor markers do not exclude a germ cell tumor, since a substantial proportion of tumors, particularly pure seminomas, are marker negative, so a normal result must not reverse the plan for orchiectomy.

Vignette:
A 7-year-old girl presents with abrupt onset of fever, nausea, vomiting, and sore throat. The child denies cough, rhinorrhea, or nasal congestion. On physical exam, oral temperature is 101°F (38.5°C) and there is an exudative pharyngitis, with enlarged cervical lymph nodes. A rapid antigen test is positive for group A Streptococcus (GAS).
baseline_protocol:
Age: 7 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Abrupt onset of fever, nausea, vomiting and sore throat.
Analysis: This is acute group A streptococcal pharyngitis, and the diagnosis is confirmed rather than merely suspected. The strongest supporting fact is the positive rapid antigen test for group A Streptococcus obtained in a child whose clinical presentation fits the disease closely, which makes the result highly specific and clinically meaningful; rapid antigen testing has high specificity, so a positive result in a symptomatic child is sufficient to diagnose and treat without confirmatory culture. The clinical features align with the classic picture and satisfy several of the standard clinical criteria: abrupt onset rather than gradual, fever with an oral temperature of 101 degrees Fahrenheit, exudative pharyngitis, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Equally important are the negative findings, since the child explicitly denies cough, rhinorrhea and nasal congestion; the absence of these coryzal features argues strongly against a viral upper respiratory cause, because viral pharyngitis characteristically occurs with cough and nasal symptoms. The associated nausea and vomiting and the abdominal complaints often seen with streptococcal infection are common in school-aged children and further support the diagnosis. The age of 7 years is within the peak incidence range of 5 to 15 years. The main differential considerations are viral pharyngitis from adenovirus, rhinovirus, influenza or coronavirus, which is made unlikely by the exudative appearance combined with the complete absence of cough and nasal symptoms; infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein-Barr virus, which can produce exudative tonsillitis with lymphadenopathy but typically causes prominent posterior cervical adenopathy, marked fatigue, splenomegaly and a more protracted course, and is less common at this age, and which remains a consideration only if the child fails to improve on appropriate therapy; herpangina or hand-foot-and-mouth disease from enterovirus, which produce vesicles and ulcers rather than tonsillar exudate; peritonsillar abscess, which would present with severe unilateral pain, trismus, uvular deviation and a muffled voice, none of which are described; retropharyngeal abscess or epiglottitis, which would produce drooling, stridor, respiratory distress, neck stiffness or a toxic appearance, none of which are present; and diphtheria, which is essentially excluded in an immunized population and produces an adherent grey pseudomembrane. There is no evidence of airway compromise, dehydration requiring parenteral fluid, systemic toxicity, or the diffuse sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue of scarlet fever, so this is uncomplicated pharyngitis appropriate for outpatient oral therapy. The important reason to treat is not primarily symptom relief, since the illness is largely self-limited, but the prevention of acute rheumatic fever, which antibiotic therapy started within nine days of symptom onset reliably prevents, along with reduction of suppurative complications and of the period of contagiousness. The vomiting is clinically relevant to management because it may affect tolerance of oral medication and hydration.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None additional. The rapid antigen test is positive and, given its high specificity, a confirmatory throat culture is not required when the test is positive; back-up culture is reserved for children with a negative rapid test. No blood tests, imaging or antistreptolysin O titers are indicated in this uncomplicated presentation. Reassess clinically, and consider testing for infectious mononucleosis or evaluation for a suppurative complication only if she fails to improve within 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy or develops new concerning features.
Conclusion: A 7-year-old girl has acute group A streptococcal pharyngitis, confirmed by a positive rapid antigen test in the setting of abrupt-onset fever, exudative pharyngitis, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, nausea and vomiting, and the absence of cough or nasal symptoms. There are no signs of airway compromise, deep neck infection, dehydration or systemic toxicity. She requires prompt outpatient oral antibiotic therapy to prevent acute rheumatic fever and to reduce symptoms and transmission, together with supportive care and clear return precautions.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Begin oral antibiotic therapy with penicillin or amoxicillin as first-line treatment, which remains fully effective since group A Streptococcus has not developed penicillin resistance, and prescribe a weight-appropriate pediatric dose for the full standard ten-day course. Confirm any history of penicillin allergy before prescribing, since none is stated in the case, and use an appropriate alternative such as a first-generation cephalosporin, or a macrolide or clindamycin for immediate-type hypersensitivity, if allergy is present. Emphasize to the caregivers that the entire course must be completed even though the child will feel better within one to two days, because the prevention of acute rheumatic fever depends on eradication of the organism and not merely on symptom resolution. Provide supportive care with weight-based acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever and throat pain, encouragement of fluids, and soft or cool foods; note that adequate analgesia also helps maintain oral intake. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Because she has nausea and vomiting, confirm that she can tolerate and retain the oral antibiotic and adequate fluids, monitor hydration by urine output and general activity, and arrange for a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G as an alternative if oral therapy cannot be kept down or adherence is uncertain. Advise that she remain out of school until she has received at least 24 hours of antibiotic therapy and is afebrile, since she is contagious before that; reinforce hand hygiene and advise replacing her toothbrush and not sharing utensils or drinking vessels. Testing or treating asymptomatic household contacts is not routinely required, but symptomatic household members should be evaluated. Explain that routine post-treatment test of cure is not needed in an uncomplicated case. Instruct caregivers to seek prompt medical review if she develops difficulty breathing, noisy breathing or drooling, an inability to swallow or open the mouth, a muffled or hot potato voice, severe or one-sided throat swelling, neck stiffness or swelling, persistent high fever beyond 48 to 72 hours of treatment, inability to keep fluids down or signs of dehydration such as reduced urination or lethargy, a new rash, or later dark or reduced urine or joint swelling, which would raise concern for a suppurative complication, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis or rheumatic fever.
Notes: A positive rapid antigen test in a symptomatic child is sufficient for diagnosis and does not require confirmatory culture; only negative tests warrant back-up culture in children. Antibiotic dosing must be weight-based, and the child's weight and allergy history are not specified in the case.

Diagnosis10cm: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goiter with thyrotoxic crisis or storm
Vignette: A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Burch-Wartofsky score is 65 (highly suggestive of thyroid storm). Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone, and iodine solution are initiated.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 32-year-old woman with a history of Graves disease (non-compliant with methimazole for 2 months) presents with 2 days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating, and diarrhea. She had a dental extraction 3 days ago. On examination, she is markedly agitated, tremulous, and unable to remain still. Vital signs: T 40.0C (104F), HR 162 (atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response), RR 28, BP 168/60 (widened pulse pressure), SpO2 97%. She has a fine tremor, bilateral proptosis, lid lag, diffuse goiter with an audible bruit, and brisk reflexes throughout. Skin is warm and moist. She becomes increasingly confused during the examination. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 7.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8), free T3 22 pg/mL (normal 2.3-4.2). Burch-Wartofsky score is 65 (highly suggestive of thyroid storm). Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone, and iodine solution are initiated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 32 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of palpitations, agitation, profuse sweating and diarrhea in a woman with Graves disease who has not taken methimazole for two months, with progressive confusion developing during the examination.
Analysis: This is thyroid storm, the decompensated and life-threatening extreme of thyrotoxicosis, occurring in a patient with known Graves disease. The reasoning rests on the combination of an established underlying disease, an identifiable precipitant, a multisystem decompensated presentation, and confirmatory biochemistry. The underlying disease is documented Graves disease, and the examination shows its characteristic features: bilateral proptosis and lid lag from thyroid eye disease, and a diffuse goiter with an audible bruit reflecting the hypervascularity of a hyperstimulated gland. Two precipitants are present and mutually reinforcing: discontinuation of methimazole for two months, which allowed uncontrolled hormone synthesis, and a dental extraction three days ago, since surgical or procedural stress and possible infection are classic triggers. Decompensation is evident across the systems used to define storm. Thermoregulatory failure is present with a temperature of 40.0 degrees Celsius, well beyond the mild heat intolerance of uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis. Cardiovascular decompensation is present with a heart rate of 162 in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and a blood pressure of 168/60 showing a widened pulse pressure from the hyperdynamic circulation and reduced systemic vascular resistance. Central nervous system dysfunction is present and progressing, with marked agitation, inability to remain still, and confusion evolving during the examination, which is the single most ominous feature and the one that most clearly separates storm from severe uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis. Gastrointestinal-hepatic involvement is present with diarrhea. Adrenergic features of fine tremor, brisk reflexes, warm moist skin and profuse sweating, with a respiratory rate of 28, complete the picture. The biochemistry confirms severe thyrotoxicosis of primary thyroid origin, with TSH suppressed below 0.01 mIU/L and markedly elevated free T4 at 7.8 ng/dL and free T3 at 22 pg/mL, values far above the reference ranges; importantly, the absolute hormone levels do not define storm, which is a clinical diagnosis, and the Burch-Wartofsky score of 65 formally places her well above the threshold of 45 that is highly suggestive of thyroid storm. The main differential considerations are sepsis, which shares fever, tachycardia, confusion and a widened pulse pressure and must be actively considered given the recent dental extraction as a potential source of infection, and which can also precipitate storm, so the two are not mutually exclusive; neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome, which produce hyperthermia with altered mental status but characteristically with rigidity or clonus and a relevant drug history not described here; sympathomimetic or anticholinergic toxicity, including cocaine or amphetamine use, which lacks proptosis, goiter and the biochemical profile; pheochromocytoma, which causes paroxysmal hypertension and adrenergic surges but not a diffuse goiter with bruit or suppressed TSH with elevated free hormones; heat stroke; and alcohol or drug withdrawal. None of these explain the combination of a diffuse goiter with bruit, proptosis, suppressed TSH with grossly elevated free T4 and free T3, and a documented history of Graves disease with treatment interruption. The treatment already initiated is appropriate and follows the correct pathophysiologic sequence: propranolol to blunt adrenergic effects and impair peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, propylthiouracil to block new hormone synthesis and also inhibit peripheral conversion, which is why it is preferred over methimazole in storm, hydrocortisone to reduce peripheral conversion and to treat the relative adrenal insufficiency of the hypermetabolic state, and iodine solution to block release of preformed hormone from the gland. The critical sequencing point is that iodine must be given at least one hour after the thionamide, otherwise the iodine substrate can be used for further hormone synthesis and worsen the storm. Mortality remains substantial even with treatment, so this requires intensive care management.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring with electrocardiography to characterize and follow the atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, continuous pulse oximetry, core temperature monitoring, and frequent or invasive blood pressure measurement, in an intensive care setting. Complete blood count with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel with electrolytes including calcium, magnesium and phosphate, glucose, renal function and liver function tests, since hepatic dysfunction and jaundice contribute to the Burch-Wartofsky score and propylthiouracil carries hepatotoxic risk. Baseline white cell count before and during thionamide therapy because of the risk of agranulocytosis. Blood cultures and a focused search for infection with examination of the dental extraction site, given the recent procedure and the fever, since occult sepsis is both a differential diagnosis and a possible precipitant. Chest radiograph and urinalysis with culture as part of the infection screen. Blood gas with lactate to assess perfusion, and coagulation studies. Serum cortisol drawn before or at the time corticosteroid is given if feasible. TSH receptor antibodies to confirm the Graves etiology if not previously documented. Serial free T4 and free T3, recognizing that these guide trend rather than define resolution. Echocardiography and brain natriuretic peptide if heart failure is suspected, since high-output failure and pulmonary edema are recognized complications. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin to exclude pregnancy in a woman of childbearing age, since this affects drug selection. Neuroimaging or lumbar puncture only if the altered mental status does not fit the storm picture or fails to improve with therapy.
Conclusion: A 32-year-old woman with Graves disease who stopped methimazole two months ago and underwent dental extraction three days ago presents in thyroid storm, with hyperpyrexia at 40.0 degrees Celsius, atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 162, widened pulse pressure, profuse sweating, diarrhea, tremor, brisk reflexes, agitation and progressive confusion, on a background of proptosis, lid lag and a diffuse goiter with bruit, with TSH below 0.01 mIU/L, free T4 of 7.8 ng/dL and free T3 of 22 pg/mL and a Burch-Wartofsky score of 65. Multimodal therapy with propranolol, propylthiouracil, hydrocortisone and iodine solution has been correctly initiated. This is an immediately life-threatening endocrine emergency requiring intensive care admission, aggressive supportive management, identification and treatment of the precipitant, and definitive therapy planning once she is stabilized.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Admit to an intensive care unit for continuous monitoring and support. Continue the four-component regimen already begun, ensuring correct sequencing so that the iodine solution is given at least one hour after propylthiouracil, and continue propranolol titrated to heart rate while monitoring closely for evidence of heart failure, since high-output cardiac failure can be unmasked by beta blockade and an intravenous short-acting agent such as esmolol may be preferable if hemodynamic titration is needed. Continue propylthiouracil at storm dosing and hydrocortisone at stress dosing. Manage the hyperpyrexia aggressively with acetaminophen and external cooling measures, and avoid salicylates entirely, because they displace thyroid hormone from binding proteins and raise free hormone levels. Provide vigorous intravenous fluid and electrolyte resuscitation with attention to glucose, since the hypermetabolic state, fever, sweating and diarrhea produce large losses, while monitoring for volume overload in the presence of atrial fibrillation and possible cardiac decompensation. Manage the atrial fibrillation primarily by treating the thyrotoxicosis and controlling rate, and address anticoagulation according to bleeding risk and the recent dental procedure. Address the additional considerations explicitly. Actively search for and treat the precipitant: examine the dental extraction site for infection, obtain blood cultures, and start empiric antibiotics if there is any suspicion of sepsis, recognizing that infection may be both trigger and coexisting diagnosis and that fever alone in storm does not exclude it. Explore the reasons for non-compliance with methimazole, whether cost, adverse effects, misunderstanding or access, and address them in the discharge plan, since recurrence risk depends on it. Monitor for propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity with liver function tests and for agranulocytosis, and instruct her to report fever, sore throat, jaundice or dark urine. Provide nutritional support and thiamine and vitamin supplementation given the catabolic state, along with thromboprophylaxis. Plan the transition once the storm resolves: taper hydrocortisone and iodine, convert from propylthiouracil to methimazole for maintenance because of the better long-term safety profile, and arrange endocrinology follow-up to plan definitive treatment with radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy, noting that her active thyroid eye disease influences the choice and that radioactive iodine may worsen ophthalmopathy. Arrange ophthalmology assessment for the proptosis and lid lag and advise lubricating drops and eye protection. Counsel on contraception and on the importance of pre-conception thyroid control, and educate her and her family that any future surgery, dental procedure, infection or pregnancy requires that her thyroid status be controlled and her medication continued, with clear instructions to seek immediate care for recurrent palpitations, fever or agitation.
Notes: Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis; the degree of free T4 and free T3 elevation does not distinguish it from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis, and treatment must never await laboratory results. Salicylates are contraindicated for fever. Iodine must follow, never precede, the thionamide. Mortality remains significant despite optimal therapy, so a search for and treatment of the precipitating cause is as important as antithyroid therapy itself.

Vignette:
A 70-year-old man with a history of chronic HTN and atrial fibrillation is witnessed by a family member to have nausea, vomiting, and right-sided weakness, as well as difficulty speaking and comprehending language. The symptoms started with only mild slurred speech before progressing over several minutes to severe aphasia and right arm paralysis. The patient is taking warfarin.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 70 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Witnessed acute onset of nausea, vomiting, right-sided weakness, and difficulty both speaking and comprehending language, beginning as mild slurred speech and progressing over several minutes to severe aphasia and right arm paralysis, in a man with chronic hypertension and atrial fibrillation who is anticoagulated with warfarin.
Analysis: This is an acute focal neurological deficit of sudden onset referable to the left cerebral hemisphere, and it must be treated as an acute stroke until proven otherwise. The strongest supporting facts are: (1) a witnessed, abrupt onset with a definable time of symptom onset, which is the single most important variable for treatment eligibility; (2) a deficit combination of right hemiparesis with right arm paralysis together with impairment of both expression and comprehension of language, which localizes to the dominant, in the great majority of right-handed patients the left, hemisphere and involves both anterior and posterior language territories, a pattern typical of a large left middle cerebral artery syndrome or a proximal left MCA or internal carotid terminus occlusion; (3) atrial fibrillation, the archetypal source of cardioembolic stroke and a strong predictor of large-vessel occlusion, in a 70-year-old with chronic hypertension, the dominant modifiable vascular risk factor for both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke; and (4) treatment with warfarin, which is the pivotal management variable in this case because it simultaneously raises the probability of intracerebral hemorrhage and, depending on the INR, may contraindicate intravenous thrombolysis. The two principal differential considerations are acute ischemic stroke from cardioembolism, favored by the atrial fibrillation and the abrupt large-territory syndrome, and warfarin-associated intracerebral hemorrhage, favored by the anticoagulation, the chronic hypertension, and the accompanying nausea and vomiting with stepwise progression over several minutes, features that can reflect raised intracranial pressure and expanding hematoma volume. These two possibilities are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside and have diametrically opposed treatments, so emergent non-contrast neuroimaging is mandatory before any antithrombotic or thrombolytic decision. Additional differentials that must be briefly considered and excluded are hypoglycemia, which is a readily reversible stroke mimic, seizure with a postictal Todd paralysis, hypertensive encephalopathy, and a space-occupying lesion, although the abrupt witnessed onset in a patient with atrial fibrillation makes a vascular cause overwhelmingly the most likely. Vomiting in this setting also creates an immediate aspiration risk in a patient who cannot reliably protect the airway or follow commands because of severe aphasia.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Immediate non-contrast CT of the head to distinguish ischemic stroke from intracerebral hemorrhage, followed without delay by CT angiography of the head and neck to identify a large-vessel occlusion amenable to mechanical thrombectomy, with CT perfusion or MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging where available to assess core and penumbra if the onset window is uncertain or extended. Urgent point-of-care capillary blood glucose before any other test to exclude hypoglycemia. Stat coagulation studies with prothrombin time and INR, which are decisive in this warfarin-treated patient, together with activated partial thromboplastin time, complete blood count with platelet count, comprehensive metabolic panel with renal function and electrolytes, and type and screen. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac telemetry to document the atrial fibrillation and detect ischemia or arrhythmia, plus cardiac troponin. Continuous non-invasive blood pressure monitoring, pulse oximetry, and temperature. Formal stroke severity scoring with the NIH Stroke Scale, and a bedside dysphagia screen before any oral intake. Subsequent etiological workup with transthoracic echocardiography and carotid imaging once the patient is stabilized.
Conclusion: A 70-year-old man with chronic hypertension and atrial fibrillation on warfarin presents with a witnessed, rapidly progressive left hemispheric syndrome comprising severe global aphasia, right arm paralysis, right-sided weakness, and nausea with vomiting. The presentation is a hyperacute stroke, most probably a cardioembolic left middle cerebral artery territory infarction given the atrial fibrillation, but warfarin-associated intracerebral hemorrhage is a serious and clinically indistinguishable alternative that the accompanying vomiting and the anticoagulation make impossible to exclude on clinical grounds. Emergent non-contrast head CT and an immediate INR determine the entire subsequent pathway. This is a time-critical neurological emergency in which every minute of delay costs salvageable brain tissue.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Activate the emergency medical system and transport immediately to the nearest hospital with acute stroke capability, ideally a comprehensive stroke center with endovascular thrombectomy and neurosurgical support, and pre-notify the stroke team en route so that imaging is ready on arrival. Record and communicate the exact last known well time, since the deficit was witnessed and this timing governs eligibility for reperfusion therapy. On arrival, follow a code stroke pathway: check capillary glucose first and correct hypoglycemia if present, obtain non-contrast head CT and a stat INR as the immediate priorities, and proceed to CT angiography of the head and neck in the same imaging session. If the CT excludes hemorrhage and the INR is at or below 1.7 within the thrombolytic window, intravenous thrombolysis may be considered by the stroke team; if the INR is supratherapeutic or above that threshold, thrombolysis is contraindicated and mechanical thrombectomy becomes the reperfusion strategy of choice, which is particularly relevant here because the severity of the syndrome, with global aphasia and arm plegia in a patient with atrial fibrillation, strongly suggests a proximal large-vessel occlusion that responds poorly to lysis alone. If the CT shows intracerebral hemorrhage, reverse the warfarin immediately with four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate together with intravenous vitamin K, avoid delay while awaiting the INR result if hemorrhage is confirmed, obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation, and lower blood pressure according to hemorrhage protocol. Addressing the additional considerations explicitly: the vomiting mandates airway protection with the patient positioned to reduce aspiration risk, suction available, supplemental oxygen titrated to maintain normal saturation, antiemetics as needed, and strict nil by mouth status including withholding all oral medication until a formal swallow screen is passed, which is essential because severe aphasia prevents reliable participation in a bedside assessment; the warfarin therapy must be flagged to every treating clinician as the central determinant of both thrombolysis eligibility and hemorrhage reversal, and the last dose timing and INR history should be sought from the family member who witnessed the event; the atrial fibrillation requires rate and rhythm monitoring and, after imaging clarifies the diagnosis, a deliberate decision on the timing of resumption or modification of long-term anticoagulation for secondary prevention, balancing recurrent embolic risk against hemorrhagic transformation or rebleeding; and the chronic hypertension requires blood pressure management according to the diagnosis reached, with permissive hypertension in untreated ischemic stroke, tighter targets before and after thrombolysis, and active lowering in hemorrhage. Provide general neuroprotective supportive care with normoglycemia, normothermia with treatment of fever, avoidance of hypotension, head of bed positioning as indicated, and serial neurological observations to detect deterioration or malignant cerebral edema, which is a recognized risk with a large dominant hemisphere MCA infarct in this age group. Admit to a stroke unit or neurological intensive care, involve the family early for collateral history and goals of care discussion given the severity of the deficit, and begin early multidisciplinary rehabilitation planning with speech and language therapy for the aphasia and physiotherapy and occupational therapy for the right-sided weakness, alongside deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis appropriate to the confirmed diagnosis.
Notes: Ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke cannot be distinguished clinically in this patient, and no antithrombotic, thrombolytic, or antiplatelet agent may be given before non-contrast head CT and an INR result are available. Handedness, baseline functional status, exact time of last known well, current vital signs, blood pressure and glucose values, warfarin dose and recent INR history, and other medications and comorbidities are not specified in the case, yet several of these directly determine treatment eligibility and must be established immediately on presentation.

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with a 4-day history of an itchy red rash on both wrists. She recently purchased a new costume jewelry bracelet and has been wearing it daily. She denies any blistering, weeping, or spreading of the rash beyond the areas of contact. She has no history of eczema or other skin conditions. On examination, there are well-demarcated erythematous patches on both wrists corresponding to where the bracelet sits. There is mild scaling but no vesiculation, excoriation, or secondary infection. The remainder of the skin exam is normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 25 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Itchy red rash on both wrists for 4 days, appearing in the areas where a newly purchased costume jewelry bracelet is worn daily.
Analysis: The presentation is characteristic of allergic contact dermatitis. The strongest supporting facts are the temporal relationship between the onset of the rash and the recent daily use of a new costume jewelry bracelet, and the strictly localized distribution: well-demarcated erythematous patches on both wrists corresponding exactly to where the bracelet sits. Costume jewelry is a common source of nickel exposure, and nickel is the leading cause of allergic contact dermatitis on the wrists. The pruritus and mild scaling are consistent with a subacute eczematous reaction. The rash does not spread beyond the contact areas, which argues against a systemic or generalized dermatosis. Differential considerations include irritant contact dermatitis (possible, but the marked itching and sharply demarcated erythema favor an allergic mechanism), atopic dermatitis (unlikely: she has no history of eczema and the distribution is confined to contact sites rather than flexural areas), tinea corporis (unlikely: bilateral symmetric distribution matching an object, no annular lesions with central clearing described), and secondary bacterial infection or cellulitis (excluded by the absence of weeping, vesiculation, excoriation, or signs of secondary infection). There are no blisters, no weeping, and no spread, indicating a mild, uncomplicated reaction.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 25-year-old healthy woman with mild, uncomplicated contact dermatitis of both wrists, most consistent with an allergic reaction to her new costume jewelry bracelet (nickel being the most likely allergen). The condition is localized, non-infected, and clinically mild, and the causative exposure has been clearly identified by history.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Stop wearing the costume jewelry bracelet immediately and avoid re-exposure; this is the single most important step, as the rash should resolve within one to three weeks once contact ceases. Wash the wrists with mild soap and water to remove residual allergen. Apply a bland emollient regularly to restore the skin barrier, and an over-the-counter low-potency topical corticosteroid to the affected wrists once or twice daily for a short course to relieve itching and inflammation. Cool compresses and an oral antihistamine at night may help with pruritus. Avoid scratching to prevent excoriation and secondary infection. For the future, avoid inexpensive costume jewelry and choose items labeled nickel-free, such as surgical stainless steel, titanium, or high-karat gold; a barrier coating on jewelry backs can also be used. Seek medical review if the rash does not begin to improve within one to two weeks after removing the bracelet, if it spreads beyond the contact areas, if blistering or weeping develops, or if signs of infection appear (increasing pain, warmth, pus, fever). If the reaction recurs or the responsible allergen remains unclear, referral for patch testing can confirm nickel or another specific contact allergen.
Notes: No formal allergy testing has been performed, so the specific allergen is inferred from the exposure history rather than confirmed. The diagnosis rests on avoidance and clinical response; failure to improve after stopping the bracelet would require reassessment.
