The strongest supporting facts are the prodrome of tingling and burning that preceded the eruption by about a day, the morphology of grouped fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base, the location at the vermilion border of the lip, and the stereotyped recurrence roughly twice a year over 5 years. Psychological stress at work is a well-recognized trigger for reactivation of latent virus in the trigeminal ganglion. The absence of fever, sore throat, and intraoral ulcers argues against primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, which typically presents with systemic symptoms and widespread intraoral involvement in a first episode. Differential considerations include impetigo (usually honey-colored crusts, not a grouped vesicular cluster with a neuralgic prodrome, and not stereotypically recurrent at the same site), angular cheilitis (fissuring at the oral commissures rather than vesicles at the vermilion border), aphthous stomatitis (intraoral ulcers, which are explicitly absent), herpes zoster of the trigeminal nerve (would follow a dermatomal distribution with more extensive involvement, and does not recur biannually), and contact or perioral dermatitis (not vesicular in clusters with a prodrome). The examination documents no facial nerve involvement, no lymphadenopathy, and no intraoral lesions, indicating a localized, uncomplicated recurrence.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 28-year-old immunocompetent woman with a mild, uncomplicated recurrent herpes labialis outbreak on the left lower lip, presenting within the first 24 hours of vesicle formation after a classic prodrome, with a probable stress-related trigger. The diagnosis is clinical and the episode is self-limited, typically healing within 7 to 10 days.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Because she presented very early in the episode and had a recognizable prodrome, antiviral therapy is most beneficial now: a topical antiviral applied to the lesion, or short-course oral antiviral therapy, started as soon as possible will modestly shorten the outbreak. Given a documented pattern of recurrence with a reliable prodrome, she can be given a supply of oral antiviral medication to keep on hand and self-start at the first tingling in future episodes. For symptom relief, use cool compresses, a bland lip balm or petrolatum to prevent cracking, and an over-the-counter oral analgesic as needed. Do not pick, squeeze, or unroof the vesicles. Wash hands after touching the lip and avoid touching the eyes, since autoinoculation can cause herpetic keratitis. The lesions are contagious until fully crusted and healed: avoid kissing, oral sex, and sharing cups, utensils, lip balm, razors, or towels during this period, and take particular care to avoid contact with newborns, pregnant women, and immunocompromised people. Address the identified trigger by working on work-related stress management and adequate sleep; sun exposure is another common trigger, so a lip balm with sun protection is reasonable for prevention. If outbreaks become substantially more frequent, daily suppressive antiviral therapy can be discussed. Seek medical attention if the lesions spread widely, do not heal within about two weeks, become secondarily infected (increasing pain, swelling, pus, fever), or if any eye pain, redness, or visual change develops.
Notes: The diagnosis is made clinically; no laboratory confirmation is required in a typical recurrent episode. Antiviral treatment shortens but does not cure the infection, and the virus remains latent with the possibility of future recurrences.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of worsening lower back pain radiating bilaterally to both legs, progressive bilateral leg weakness, and difficulty urinating since yesterday. He has a history of lumbar disc disease with two prior episodes of sciatica managed conservatively. On examination, he walks with a wide-based unsteady gait. Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological exam reveals decreased strength (3/5) in bilateral ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, diminished patellar and absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally, and decreased perianal sensation with reduced anal sphincter tone on rectal exam. Post-void residual bladder scan shows 650 mL of retained urine. MRI of the lumbar spine reveals a large L4-L5 central disc herniation with severe compression of the cauda equina nerve roots.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 50 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Three days of worsening low back pain radiating to both legs, with progressive bilateral leg weakness and difficulty urinating since yesterday.
Analysis: This is cauda equina syndrome due to a large central lumbar disc herniation, and it is a surgical emergency. The case contains the full classic constellation: bilateral radicular pain, bilateral lower extremity weakness (3/5 ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion), diminished patellar and absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally (a lower motor neuron, polyradicular pattern), saddle anesthesia with decreased perianal sensation, reduced anal sphincter tone on rectal examination, and urinary retention with a post-void residual of 650 mL. The wide-based unsteady gait reflects the bilateral motor and sensory deficits. The diagnosis is confirmed objectively by MRI of the lumbar spine showing a large L4-L5 central disc herniation with severe compression of the cauda equina nerve roots, which anatomically explains every finding. His history of lumbar disc disease with two prior conservatively managed episodes of sciatica establishes the substrate, but the current episode differs fundamentally: prior episodes were unilateral radicular pain without red flags, whereas this one has bilateral deficits and sphincter dysfunction. Differential considerations that must be excluded and are effectively excluded here include conus medullaris syndrome (would give more upper motor neuron signs and earlier symmetric sphincter involvement; MRI localizes the lesion to L4-L5 with cauda equina root compression), spinal epidural abscess (vital signs are normal with no fever, and MRI shows disc herniation, not a collection), spinal epidural hematoma (no anticoagulation or procedure history given, MRI shows disc herniation), metastatic epidural spinal cord compression (no cancer history given and imaging shows disc pathology), and simple recurrent sciatica (excluded by bilateral deficits, saddle anesthesia, sphincter dysfunction, and retention). The transition from urinary difficulty to overt retention within a day indicates a rapidly evolving, incomplete-to-retention stage of the syndrome, in which the time to decompression is the strongest determinant of recovery of bladder, bowel, and sexual function.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the lumbar spine has already been obtained and is diagnostic; no further imaging is required to establish the diagnosis. Immediate urgent neurosurgical or spine surgical consultation is required. Urgent urinary catheterization to decompress the bladder and document residual volume. Preoperative laboratory workup and anesthesia assessment for emergent surgery: complete blood count, basic metabolic panel including renal function, coagulation studies, and blood type and screen. Serial neurological examinations including motor strength, perianal sensation, and sphincter tone to track progression.
Conclusion: A 50-year-old man with acute cauda equina syndrome caused by a large central L4-L5 disc herniation severely compressing the cauda equina nerve roots, presenting with bilateral leg weakness, hyporeflexia and areflexia, saddle anesthesia, reduced anal sphincter tone, and urinary retention of 650 mL. This is a time-critical neurosurgical emergency requiring immediate surgical decompression; delay risks permanent paralysis and irreversible bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Treat as an immediate surgical emergency. Activate urgent neurosurgical or orthopedic spine surgery consultation without delay and arrange emergent surgical decompression (urgent discectomy and decompression of the L4-L5 level); the evidence supports operating as soon as feasible, since outcome for bladder and bowel recovery correlates with the interval from onset of retention to decompression. Place a urinary catheter now to relieve the 650 mL of retained urine and prevent bladder overdistension injury, and monitor urine output. Keep the patient nil by mouth in anticipation of emergent surgery, establish intravenous access, and complete preoperative labs, type and screen, and anesthesia evaluation in parallel rather than sequentially so that surgical readiness is not the rate-limiting step. Provide adequate analgesia and consider corticosteroids only if directed by the surgical team; steroids do not substitute for decompression. Perform and document serial neurological examinations, including perianal sensation and sphincter tone, to detect further deterioration while awaiting the operating room. Explicitly counsel the patient and family that this is different from his previous episodes of sciatica: conservative management, which was appropriate for the two prior unilateral episodes, is now contraindicated, and the presence of saddle anesthesia, sphincter dysfunction, and urinary retention mandates emergency surgery. Document the neurological deficit and informed consent, including the realistic possibility that some deficits, particularly bladder and sexual function, may not fully recover even after timely surgery. Postoperatively, arrange continued bladder function assessment with post-void residual measurements and a trial of voiding, deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis, early physiotherapy and rehabilitation for the motor deficits, and urology follow-up if bladder dysfunction persists.
Notes: Do not delay surgical decompression for any nonessential investigation; the diagnostic MRI is already available. Post-void residual volume markedly above 500 mL with saddle anesthesia and reduced sphincter tone is a definitive red flag, and further conservative management would be inappropriate. Prognosis depends critically on the time from onset of retention to decompression.

Vignette:
A 25-year-old woman presents with bilateral thigh soreness that began yesterday, approximately 36 hours after her first gym session involving squats and lunges. She has not exercised regularly before. The soreness is worse with movement, particularly going downstairs. She denies any acute injury, popping sensation, bruising, or swelling. She has no history of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis. On examination, both quadriceps and hamstrings are mildly tender to palpation bilaterally. There is no edema, ecchymosis, warmth, or joint effusion. baseline_protocol:
Age: 25 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Bilateral thigh soreness beginning yesterday, about 36 hours after her first gym session of squats and lunges, worse with movement and particularly going downstairs.
Analysis: This is delayed-onset muscle soreness following unaccustomed eccentric exercise. The strongest supporting facts are the timing and the mechanism: the soreness began approximately 24 to 36 hours after her very first gym session in a previously sedentary person, which matches the characteristic delayed onset of this condition, and the exercises performed (squats and lunges) load the quadriceps and hamstrings eccentrically, precisely the muscle groups that are tender. Pain that is worse going downstairs is classic, because descending stairs is an eccentric quadriceps task. The distribution is bilateral, symmetric, and diffuse over muscle bellies rather than focal or joint-centered, which points to muscle rather than structural injury. Differential considerations include acute muscle strain or tear (excluded by the absence of an acute injury event, no popping sensation, no bruising, no focal defect, and by the bilateral symmetric distribution), rhabdomyolysis (an important consideration after unaccustomed intense exercise, but there is no report of dark or cola-colored urine, severe disproportionate pain, marked swelling, or reduced urine output, and she has no history of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis; range of motion is full and she ambulates normally, so the clinical picture does not support it), compartment syndrome (excluded by the absence of tense swelling, severe or escalating pain, neurovascular compromise, and by the full painless-at-rest range of motion), deep vein thrombosis (unlikely: bilateral symmetric muscle-belly soreness explained by exercise, no unilateral edema, warmth, or erythema), and joint pathology such as an effusion or arthritis (excluded by full range of motion and absence of effusion, warmth, or joint-line findings). The examination is entirely reassuring: no edema, ecchymosis, warmth, or joint effusion, full range of motion, and normal gait. The condition is benign and self-limited, typically peaking at 24 to 72 hours and resolving within 5 to 7 days.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A 25-year-old previously untrained woman with typical, uncomplicated delayed-onset muscle soreness of the quadriceps and hamstrings after her first session of squats and lunges. There are no clinical features of muscle tear, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome, or thrombosis, and no investigations are indicated. The condition is benign, self-limited, and expected to resolve within about a week, with a protective adaptation reducing severity after subsequent sessions.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Reassure her that this is a normal and expected response to unaccustomed eccentric exercise, not an injury, and that it should settle within 5 to 7 days. Maintain gentle activity rather than complete rest: light walking, cycling, or easy mobility work promotes blood flow and comfort, whereas total inactivity tends to prolong stiffness. Avoid repeating a heavy squat and lunge session on the same muscle groups until the soreness has largely resolved. Use simple measures for comfort, including gentle stretching within a pain-free range, warm baths or a heat pack, light massage or foam rolling, and an over-the-counter analgesic such as paracetamol or a short course of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug if needed. Maintain good hydration and adequate protein intake. To prevent recurrence of this severity, progress training gradually: begin with lighter loads and fewer repetitions, increase volume by only a modest amount each week, and include a warm-up before and a cool-down after sessions; the soreness will be markedly less after the next few sessions because of the repeated-bout adaptation. Regarding the specific concerns raised in her history, she should seek prompt medical assessment if any of the following develop, as they would suggest rhabdomyolysis or another complication rather than simple soreness: dark, brown, or cola-colored urine, a marked reduction in urine output, pain that is severe and out of proportion or worsening rather than improving after 72 hours, marked swelling or tightness of the thighs, numbness or tingling, fever, or soreness that has not resolved after about 7 to 10 days. Given the absence of any of these features and her lack of a myopathy or rhabdomyolysis history, no blood testing such as creatine kinase is required at this time.
Notes: No red flags are present at this visit; the safety advice above defines the threshold for re-evaluation. This assessment is based on the initial presentation, and persistent or worsening symptoms beyond the expected time course would warrant reassessment.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. - a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,

Vignette:
A 26-year-old female marathon runner presents with a 3-week history of gradually worsening pain over the dorsum of her right foot, specifically in the region of the third metatarsal. The pain initially occurred only during long runs but now is present with walking and at rest. She significantly increased her training mileage six weeks ago in preparation for an upcoming marathon. She has a history of irregular menstrual periods and follows a restrictive diet. On examination, there is focal tenderness and mild soft-tissue swelling over the mid-shaft of the third metatarsal. Pain is elicited with the tuning fork test and with axial loading of the third toe. She has a BMI of 19. Foot radiographs obtained at another facility one week ago were normal.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 26 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three weeks of gradually worsening pain over the dorsum of the right foot in the region of the third metatarsal, initially only during long runs and now present with walking and at rest, in a marathon runner who sharply increased her training mileage six weeks ago.
Analysis: This is a third metatarsal stress fracture occurring in the context of relative energy deficiency in sport, and the case additionally raises the female athlete triad. The strongest supporting facts for a stress fracture are the classic overuse mechanism (a significant increase in training mileage six weeks before presentation, with symptoms starting about three weeks later), the characteristic progression of activity-related bone pain that has advanced from occurring only with long runs to being present with walking and at rest, and the focal examination findings: point tenderness and mild localized soft-tissue swelling over the mid-shaft of the third metatarsal, a positive tuning fork test, and pain reproduced with axial loading of the third toe. Focal bony tenderness with pain on percussion and axial load is highly suggestive of a cortical stress injury rather than soft-tissue pathology. Crucially, normal plain radiographs obtained one week ago do not exclude the diagnosis: radiographs are insensitive in the early weeks of a stress fracture and may not show a periosteal reaction or fracture line until two to six weeks after symptom onset, so a normal film in the presence of this clinical picture is a false negative rather than reassurance. Her risk factor profile compounds the mechanical overload: irregular menstrual periods, a restrictive diet, and a BMI of 19 together suggest low energy availability with resulting menstrual dysfunction and probable impaired bone mineral density, the components of the female athlete triad or relative energy deficiency in sport, which markedly increase stress fracture risk and impair healing. Differential considerations include metatarsalgia and plantar plate injury (usually plantar rather than dorsal, without focal midshaft bony tenderness or a positive tuning fork test), Morton neuroma (interdigital, with radiating burning pain and a positive Mulder click, not focal shaft tenderness and swelling), extensor tendinopathy or dorsal soft-tissue inflammation (would not produce pain with axial loading of the toe or focal percussion tenderness over the shaft), Freiberg infraction (affects the metatarsal head, usually the second, and would generally be visible on radiographs), tarsometatarsal Lisfranc injury (requires an acute traumatic mechanism, absent here), and less likely bone tumor or osteomyelitis (no systemic symptoms, no trauma or wound described, and the mechanical history is classic for overuse). The third metatarsal is a common site of low-risk metatarsal stress fracture with generally good healing potential when loading is reduced, unlike the higher-risk fifth metatarsal base or the proximal second metatarsal.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the right foot is the preferred next investigation, as it is the most sensitive and specific modality for early stress fracture and will detect marrow edema and a cortical fracture line not yet visible on the normal radiographs from one week ago; a bone scan is an alternative if MRI is unavailable. Repeat plain radiographs of the right foot in two to four weeks may show callus or periosteal reaction if MRI is not obtainable. Evaluation for the underlying female athlete triad and relative energy deficiency: assessment of menstrual and dietary history, complete blood count, ferritin, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, serum calcium, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and a pregnancy test before further imaging or hormonal evaluation. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density scan given menstrual irregularity, restrictive dieting, and a stress fracture. Referral for formal nutritional and energy availability assessment by a sports dietitian.
Conclusion: A 26-year-old female marathon runner with a clinically evident stress fracture of the mid-shaft of the right third metatarsal following a rapid increase in training mileage, with normal early radiographs that do not exclude the diagnosis. The presentation is complicated by probable relative energy deficiency in sport or the female athlete triad, evidenced by menstrual irregularity, a restrictive diet, and low-normal BMI, which is both the likely predisposing cause and the main obstacle to healing and to preventing recurrence. Management requires activity modification and protected weight bearing, confirmatory MRI, and treatment of the underlying energy deficiency, not simply local rest.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Begin treatment now on clinical grounds without waiting for imaging confirmation. Stop running and all impact loading immediately. Because pain is now present with walking and at rest, protect the foot with a stiff-soled postoperative shoe or a walking boot and limit weight bearing to a pain-free level, using crutches if walking remains painful; the general rule is that any activity causing pain should be avoided. Use ice and paracetamol for analgesia; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be used sparingly given theoretical concerns about bone healing. Arrange MRI of the right foot to confirm the diagnosis and stage the injury, and refer to orthopedics or a sports medicine physician for follow-up; expect a typical healing period of six to eight weeks for a third metatarsal stress fracture before graduated return to running, guided by resolution of focal tenderness. Maintain fitness in the interim with non-impact cross-training such as swimming, deep-water running, or cycling, provided these are pain-free. Address the additional considerations explicitly and as a priority. The irregular menstrual periods, restrictive diet, and BMI of 19 must not be treated as incidental: these point to low energy availability, and a stress fracture in this context is a sentinel injury. Refer her to a sports dietitian to increase total energy and calcium intake and to correct the restrictive eating pattern, and screen for disordered eating with mental health referral if indicated. Investigate the menstrual irregularity with the laboratory workup above, including a pregnancy test, and refer to gynecology or endocrinology for evaluation of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and consideration of restoring menses primarily through improved energy availability rather than through hormonal therapy alone. Obtain a bone density scan and supplement calcium and vitamin D as guided by the 25-hydroxyvitamin D level. When returning to sport, rebuild mileage gradually with a structured plan of small weekly increments, appropriate running footwear, and adequate rest days, since an abrupt mileage increase caused this injury; the upcoming marathon should be deferred, and she should be counselled that competing on an unhealed stress fracture risks progression to a complete fracture and a much longer layoff.
Notes: Normal radiographs one week ago do not rule out a stress fracture and should not be used to reassure the patient or delay treatment. Failure to correct the underlying energy deficiency and menstrual dysfunction carries a high risk of recurrent or multiple stress fractures and of long-term reduction in bone mineral density. A pregnancy test should precede further imaging and any hormonal management.

Vignette:
A 6-month-old male infant is brought in by his mother due to small red bumps on his neck and chest noticed today. The family lives in a hot climate and the air conditioning has been broken for the past 3 days. The infant has been dressed in multiple layers. He is feeding well, has normal wet diapers, and has no fever. On examination, temperature is 37.1°C. There are numerous small erythematous papules and tiny vesicles clustered on the neck, upper chest, and skin folds. The infant is alert, active, and well-hydrated.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 6 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Small red bumps noticed today on the neck and chest of an infant, in the setting of a hot climate, broken air conditioning for 3 days, and dressing in multiple layers.
Analysis: This is miliaria, or heat rash, caused by obstruction of the eccrine sweat ducts with retention of sweat. The strongest supporting facts are the clear environmental exposure and the distribution. The family lives in a hot climate, the air conditioning has been broken for the past three days, and the infant has been overdressed in multiple layers, producing exactly the conditions of heat and occlusion that cause sweat duct obstruction. The eruption is located on the neck, upper chest, and skin folds, which are the classic occluded and friction-prone sites in an infant, and consists of numerous small erythematous papules and tiny vesicles, corresponding to miliaria rubra with an element of miliaria crystallina. Infants are particularly susceptible because their eccrine ducts are immature. Most importantly, the child is systemically well: he is afebrile with a temperature of 37.1 degrees Celsius, feeding well, producing normal wet diapers, and is alert, active, and well-hydrated, which excludes a systemic illness. Differential considerations include a viral exanthem (would generally be accompanied by fever and a more generalized distribution rather than one confined to occluded folds, and the child is afebrile and well), neonatal or infantile acne (typically facial, comedonal or pustular, not vesicular in the folds with this environmental trigger), candidal intertrigo (would show beefy-red confluent plaques with satellite pustules in the folds rather than discrete papulovesicles over the neck and chest), atopic dermatitis (usually more chronic with dry lichenified or excoriated eczematous plaques on the cheeks and extensor surfaces at this age, and there is no such history), contact dermatitis (would follow a contactant distribution), and folliculitis or bacterial infection (would show pustules with surrounding inflammation and often systemic signs; there is no fever or toxicity). Heat-related illness must also be considered given the environmental heat exposure, but the normal temperature, good feeding, normal urine output by wet diaper count, and alert well-hydrated appearance make dehydration or heat illness unlikely at present. The condition is benign and resolves within days once cooling is achieved.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: A well, afebrile, well-hydrated 6-month-old male infant with miliaria (heat rash) of the neck, upper chest, and skin folds, directly attributable to environmental overheating from a broken air conditioner in a hot climate compounded by overdressing in multiple layers. No investigations are required, and the rash is expected to resolve within a few days with cooling and reduction of clothing. The principal issue beyond the rash is preventing heat-related illness and dehydration while the air conditioning remains broken.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Treatment is environmental rather than pharmacological. Remove the extra layers and dress the infant in a single layer of loose, lightweight, breathable cotton clothing appropriate to the hot climate; as a rule, an infant needs about the same amount of clothing an adult would find comfortable, or at most one thin extra layer. Cool the environment: repair or replace the air conditioning as a priority, and in the meantime use fans for air circulation without blowing directly and continuously on the infant, keep the room shaded and ventilated, and move to a cooler room or a cooler location during the hottest part of the day. Give lukewarm or cool baths without soap once or twice daily and allow the skin to air dry rather than rubbing, and let the affected areas be exposed to air when practical. Keep skin folds on the neck and chest clean and dry. Avoid thick creams, ointments, oils, powders, and occlusive emollients on the affected areas, since these further block the sweat ducts and worsen miliaria; topical corticosteroids and antibiotics are not needed for uncomplicated heat rash. Continue normal feeding on demand, offering breast milk or formula more frequently in the heat to maintain hydration, and monitor wet diapers as an index of hydration. Expect the rash to fade within two to three days of effective cooling. Seek medical review if the rash does not improve within a few days or spreads, if the papules become pustular, painful, warm, or develop surrounding spreading redness or drainage suggesting secondary bacterial infection, if fever develops, or if the infant shows signs of heat illness or dehydration such as fewer wet diapers, a dry mouth, a sunken fontanelle, no tears, unusual drowsiness, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, or hot dry skin. Do not use aspirin, and do not attempt to cool the infant with ice or cold water immersion.
Notes: The diagnosis is clinical and depends on the child remaining systemically well; the environmental heat exposure that caused this rash is itself a risk for heat-related illness and dehydration in an infant, so caregivers should be counselled on both the rash and heat safety.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Vignette:
A 24-yr-old man comes to the emergency department (ED) because of sudden onset of
shortness of breath and back pain. Yesterday, the patient was completing a 2-mile run, which
he does 2 times/wk, when he suddenly experienced shortness of breath and sharp pain in his
spine and on the right side of his back. The pain is constant, mild, and nonradiating and does
not worsen during movement. His shortness of breath continued throughout the night and
caused difficulty sleeping. The shortness of breath is worse this morning, prompting him to
come to the ED.

Review of Systems:
General: Has been feeling well and doing his normal activities until symptoms began yesterday.
No fever, chills, or malaise.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: Reports frequent runny nose.

Pulmonary: Shortness of breath that is present at rest and worsens during exertion. No cough or
wheezing.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.

Gastrointestinal: Noncontributory

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal:Back pain as per his history of present illness.

Neurologic: No numbness or weakness of extremities.

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: None; sees a physician regularly for routine physicals. No history of similar
illness or symptoms.

Surgical history: None

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Both parents are alive; father has hypertension; mother is well. Maternal
grandfather may have died of lung cancer. No known coronary artery disease in family.

Social history: Lives with his parents and works full-time in a grocery store; does occasional light
lifting without difficulty. Smokes 7 to 10 cigarettes/day, which is decreased from 1 pack/day.
Drinks alcohol once/wk to once/mo. Used marijuana in his teens.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Well-appearing, normal body habitus, and in no distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.2° C
Pulse: 79 beats/min
Respirations: 18/min
BP: 122/72 mm Hg

Pulse oximetry: 94% on room air

Skin: No cyanosis, diaphoresis, rash, or other lesions.

HEENT: Anicteric sclerae, pupils equally round and reactive to light. Oropharynx clear.

Pulmonary: Normal respiratory effort. Decreased breath sounds on the right side.

Cardiovascular: Normal rate, regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Jugular venous
pressure is not elevated. Pulses normal and symmetric in upper and lower extremities.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen; normal bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Not assessed

Musculoskeletal: Chest, back, and spine nontender; no palpable crepitance. Extremities appear
normal; no leg swelling, erythema, or tenderness.

Neurologic: Upper and lower extremities have normal, symmetric strength, sensation, and deep
tendon reflexes in upper and lower extremities. Gait normal.

Mental status: Appropriate. Alert and oriented.

Age: 24 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of shortness of breath and sharp right-sided back and spinal pain beginning yesterday during a routine 2-mile run, with dyspnea persisting overnight, worsening this morning, present at rest and worse with exertion.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with a spontaneous pneumothorax on the right side. The strongest supporting facts are the abrupt onset of dyspnea with sharp ipsilateral pleuritic-type chest and back pain during exertion, the unilateral finding of decreased breath sounds on the right on pulmonary examination, and mild hypoxemia with pulse oximetry of 94 percent on room air in an otherwise healthy young man. His demographic and risk profile fit primary spontaneous pneumothorax closely: he is a tall, young, thin-habitus male smoker, smoking 7 to 10 cigarettes per day, and smoking is the single strongest modifiable risk factor for rupture of subpleural blebs. The pain is constant, nonradiating, and does not worsen with movement, and the chest, back, and spine are nontender on palpation with no crepitance, which argues against a musculoskeletal cause despite the exertional onset. Importantly, the patient is currently hemodynamically stable and well appearing, with a pulse of 79, blood pressure 122/72, respirations 18, no jugular venous distension, and no tracheal deviation described, so there is no evidence of a tension pneumothorax at this time; however, his dyspnea is progressive, having worsened overnight and again this morning, which mandates urgent evaluation because a simple pneumothorax can enlarge or tension. Differential considerations include pulmonary embolism, which must be considered in any young patient with sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain, but he has no leg swelling, erythema, or tenderness, no immobilization, surgery, malignancy, or other identified thrombotic risk factors, and unilateral decreased breath sounds are not typical; pneumonia or pleural effusion, which are unlikely given the abrupt exertional onset, absence of fever, chills, malaise, or cough, and a normal temperature of 36.2 degrees Celsius; musculoskeletal strain or rib injury from running, which would not explain progressive resting dyspnea, hypoxemia, or unilateral decreased breath sounds, and is further argued against by the nontender chest wall; aortic dissection, which is very unlikely at 24 years with normal symmetric pulses in all extremities, normal blood pressure, and no severe tearing pain; acute coronary syndrome, which is essentially excluded by age, absence of chest pain or palpitations, and the lack of risk factors; and asthma or bronchospasm, which would produce wheezing and bilateral findings rather than unilaterally decreased breath sounds. The combination of sudden exertional dyspnea, unilateral decreased breath sounds, hypoxemia, and a smoking history in a young man makes pneumothorax the leading diagnosis by a wide margin.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upright chest radiograph, posteroanterior and lateral, as the immediate first-line study to confirm pneumothorax and estimate its size. Bedside lung ultrasound if available for rapid confirmation. Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring with serial vital signs. Electrocardiogram to evaluate for cardiac causes and right heart strain. Chest computed tomography if the chest radiograph is nondiagnostic or if an alternative diagnosis such as pulmonary embolism or underlying bullous lung disease must be assessed; computed tomography pulmonary angiography specifically if pulmonary embolism remains a concern after initial imaging. Basic laboratory studies including complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, and arterial blood gas if hypoxemia worsens.
Conclusion: A previously healthy 24-year-old male smoker with sudden exertional onset of right-sided pleuritic back pain and progressively worsening dyspnea now present at rest, with decreased breath sounds on the right and oxygen saturation of 94 percent on room air. The clinical picture is highly suggestive of a right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax. He is currently hemodynamically stable without signs of tension physiology, but symptoms have progressed over 24 hours, so urgent chest imaging and emergency department management are required. Definitive treatment depends on the size of the pneumothorax and the degree of symptoms, ranging from supplemental oxygen with observation to needle aspiration or chest tube thoracostomy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Manage in the emergency department without delay. Place the patient on continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring, establish intravenous access, and administer high-flow supplemental oxygen, which both corrects hypoxemia and accelerates reabsorption of pleural air. Obtain an upright chest radiograph immediately to confirm the diagnosis and size the pneumothorax. If a small pneumothorax is confirmed in a stable patient, oxygen therapy with observation and a repeat radiograph after several hours is appropriate. If the pneumothorax is large or the patient remains symptomatic at rest, proceed to needle aspiration or small-bore chest tube thoracostomy with consultation of pulmonology or thoracic surgery. Watch closely for the development of tension pneumothorax, which is heralded by hemodynamic instability, hypotension, tachycardia, severe respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, or distended neck veins; if this occurs, perform immediate needle decompression before any further imaging. Provide analgesia for the pleuritic pain. If the chest radiograph is unexpectedly normal, reassess for pulmonary embolism with formal risk stratification and computed tomography pulmonary angiography, given the sudden onset of pleuritic pain and hypoxemia. Regarding the additional considerations raised by his history, smoking cessation is the most important intervention for preventing recurrence and should be addressed directly at this visit with counselling and offer of pharmacological support, noting that he has already reduced from one pack per day to 7 to 10 cigarettes daily; continued smoking substantially increases the risk of a further pneumothorax. Advise him to avoid air travel, scuba diving, and high-altitude exposure until the pneumothorax has fully resolved and he is cleared by his physician, and to avoid strenuous exertion during recovery. His frequent runny nose and family history are noncontributory to the acute problem and require no acute action. Arrange outpatient pulmonary follow-up with a repeat chest radiograph after discharge to confirm resolution, and counsel him to return immediately for worsening breathlessness, worsening chest pain, lightheadedness, or fainting, as recurrence is common after a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax and may warrant discussion of definitive pleurodesis or bleb resection.
Notes: The diagnosis is presumptive until confirmed by chest imaging; the physical finding of unilaterally decreased breath sounds combined with hypoxemia and sudden onset is the basis for urgent management. The current absence of hemodynamic compromise does not exclude progression, and worsening dyspnea over 24 hours indicates the process is not resolving spontaneously. Pulmonary embolism should remain on the differential until imaging clarifies the diagnosis.

Diagnosis10: Toxic effect: Organophosphate and carbamate insecticides
Vignette: A 45-year-old male farmer is brought in by coworkers after collapsing in the field approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment. Coworkers report he initially complained of blurred vision and a headache, then developed profuse sweating, drooling, and vomiting before becoming unresponsive. On examination, his clothes are damp with sweat and have a garlic-like odor. He is obtunded with labored breathing. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 48 (bradycardia), RR 12 (shallow, with audible secretions), BP 88/52, SpO2 84% on room air. Pupils are constricted bilaterally at 1 mm (miosis) and non-reactive. tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[4]
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old male farmer is brought in by coworkers after collapsing in the field approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment. Coworkers report he initially complained of blurred vision and a headache, then developed profuse sweating, drooling, and vomiting before becoming unresponsive. On examination, his clothes are damp with sweat and have a garlic-like odor. He is obtunded with labored breathing. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 48 (bradycardia), RR 12 (shallow, with audible secretions), BP 88/52, SpO2 84% on room air. Pupils are constricted bilaterally at 1 mm (miosis) and non-reactive. There are copious oral and bronchial secretions. Diffuse wheezing and crackles are auscultated. Fasciculations are visible in the extremities and face. He is incontinent of urine and stool. The patient is decontaminated, intubated for airway protection, and atropine 2 mg IV is administered with repeat dosing until secretions dry, followed by pralidoxime infusion.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 45 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Collapse and unresponsiveness approximately 30 minutes after spraying crops with an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment, preceded by blurred vision, headache, profuse sweating, drooling, and vomiting.
Analysis: This is acute organophosphate insecticide poisoning producing a life-threatening cholinergic crisis. The exposure history is definitive: a farmer sprayed an organophosphate insecticide without adequate protective equipment and collapsed within 30 minutes, and his clothing is damp with sweat and carries the garlic-like odor characteristic of organophosphate compounds, indicating ongoing dermal absorption from contaminated clothing and skin. Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and central nervous system receptors, and every finding maps onto this mechanism. The muscarinic effects are fully expressed: miosis with 1 mm non-reactive pupils, blurred vision, profuse sweating (diaphoresis), drooling (salivation), lacrimation implied by the cholinergic syndrome, vomiting, urinary and fecal incontinence, copious oral and bronchial secretions, bronchorrhea and bronchospasm with diffuse wheezing and crackles, and bradycardia at 48 beats per minute with hypotension at 88/52. The nicotinic effects are evident as visible fasciculations in the extremities and face, which progress to weakness and can cause respiratory muscle paralysis. The central effects are the headache and progression to obtundation and unresponsiveness. The critical physiological threat is respiratory failure from the combination of bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, central respiratory depression, and diaphragmatic weakness, and this is confirmed by shallow respirations at 12 per minute with audible secretions and severe hypoxemia with an oxygen saturation of 84 percent on room air. Differential considerations that the case effectively excludes include opioid overdose, which also produces miosis and respiratory depression but does not cause the muscarinic secretory storm of sweating, drooling, bronchorrhea, incontinence, and fasciculations, and lacks the exposure history and garlic odor; carbamate poisoning, which produces an essentially identical cholinergic syndrome but is reversible and generally shorter lived, and would be treated similarly with atropine, though pralidoxime is less often required; nerve agent exposure, which shares the mechanism but does not fit the agricultural spraying history; heat stroke, which is excluded by a normal temperature of 37.0 degrees Celsius and does not cause miosis or fasciculations; and a primary neurological event such as a pontine stroke, which can cause pinpoint pupils and coma but does not explain the secretions, fasciculations, incontinence, or the clear toxic exposure. The management already initiated is appropriate and correct: decontamination to halt ongoing absorption, intubation for airway protection given the depressed level of consciousness and secretion burden, atropine 2 mg intravenously with repeat dosing titrated until secretions dry, which is the correct therapeutic endpoint rather than heart rate or pupil size, and pralidoxime infusion to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before irreversible aging of the enzyme occurs.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, capnography, and frequent blood pressure measurement. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram with attention to QTc prolongation and bradyarrhythmias. Red blood cell acetylcholinesterase activity and plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) levels to confirm the diagnosis and to gauge severity and recovery, though treatment must not await results. Arterial blood gas to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status. Complete blood count, basic metabolic panel with electrolytes, renal and liver function, serum glucose, magnesium, and creatine kinase. Chest radiograph to assess for aspiration pneumonitis and to confirm endotracheal tube position. Ventilator monitoring with serial assessment of airway secretions and respiratory mechanics. Serial neurological examination and consideration of continuous monitoring for seizure activity. Poison control or medical toxicology consultation.
Conclusion: A 45-year-old farmer with severe acute organophosphate poisoning by dermal and inhalational route, presenting in cholinergic crisis with the complete muscarinic, nicotinic, and central toxidrome, complicated by respiratory failure with hypoxemia, bradycardia, and hypotension. He has been appropriately decontaminated, intubated for airway protection, and started on high-dose atropine titrated to drying of secretions with a pralidoxime infusion. This is a critical, immediately life-threatening poisoning requiring intensive care admission, continued aggressive antidotal therapy, and vigilance for the intermediate syndrome and delayed neuropathy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue and escalate the resuscitation already begun. Maintain mechanical ventilation with high-concentration oxygen; the airway is the priority, and frequent suctioning of copious oral and bronchial secretions is essential. Continue atropine with rapid dose escalation, doubling the dose every three to five minutes as needed, titrated to the endpoint of dry pulmonary secretions and clear lungs rather than to pupil size or heart rate, since miosis may persist long after adequate atropinization; very large cumulative doses are frequently required, and once control is achieved an atropine infusion should be started to maintain the endpoint, with the dose adjusted for signs of over-atropinization such as hyperthermia, agitation, delirium, absent bowel sounds, and urinary retention. Continue the pralidoxime infusion as a continuous infusion after the loading dose, given as early as possible to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before aging occurs, and maintain it for as long as clinically indicated by ongoing cholinergic signs; pralidoxime treats the nicotinic effects, including the fasciculations and muscle weakness, which atropine does not. Ensure decontamination is complete: all clothing must be removed and disposed of as hazardous material, and the skin, hair, and nails thoroughly washed, since the garlic-like odor and damp clothing indicate a persisting dermal reservoir. All staff must use appropriate personal protective equipment including nitrile gloves and gowns to prevent secondary contamination, and the exposure should be managed in a designated area with adequate ventilation. Support hemodynamics with intravenous crystalloid for the hypotension and treat bradycardia primarily with atropine; vasopressors may be added if hypotension persists despite adequate atropinization and volume resuscitation. Treat seizures with benzodiazepines, which are the agents of choice and may also be given prophylactically in severe poisoning; avoid succinylcholine for any further paralysis because its metabolism by plasma cholinesterase is inhibited and its effect will be markedly prolonged, and avoid other cholinesterase-inhibiting or bradycardia-inducing agents. Admit to the intensive care unit, consult medical toxicology or poison control, and identify the specific agent from the product label if possible, since lipophilic organophosphates can cause prolonged and relapsing toxicity. Monitor closely for aspiration pneumonitis given the vomiting and secretions. Anticipate and specifically watch for the intermediate syndrome, which typically develops 24 to 96 hours after the acute crisis and manifests as proximal muscle, neck flexor, cranial nerve, and respiratory muscle weakness that can precipitate respiratory failure after apparent recovery, so do not extubate prematurely and monitor respiratory strength serially. Also counsel about organophosphate-induced delayed polyneuropathy, which may appear one to three weeks later. Once the patient recovers, provide occupational health follow-up with education on pesticide handling, mandatory use of appropriate personal protective equipment including respirator, gloves, and coveralls, and consider baseline and periodic cholinesterase monitoring for agricultural workers; report the incident as an occupational poisoning and assess whether coworkers were similarly exposed.
Notes: Treatment must never be delayed pending cholinesterase assay results, as the diagnosis is clinical and based on the toxidrome and exposure history. Atropine dosing is titrated to drying of secretions, not to pupil size or heart rate, and doses far exceeding conventional limits are expected and appropriate. Persistent miosis after adequate atropinization is not a failure of therapy. Healthcare provider protection and complete decontamination are mandatory to prevent secondary contamination. Recovery may be prolonged, and both the intermediate syndrome and delayed neuropathy can occur after the acute crisis appears to have resolved.

A 70-yr-old man comes to his internal medicine physician with a complaint of waking to urinate.
This has been present for several years but has gradually increased in frequency from 2
times/night to 6 times/night. He is not urinating more during the day. He states that when he
does urinate, he has to strain to initiate a stream and that his stream is "not like it was when he
was 20 years old." He denies incontinence, dysuria, hematuria, flank pain, fevers, or any other
complaints. He is otherwise relatively healthy and has not seen a physician in several years.

General: Overall feels well, good appetite, no recent weight gain or loss, not drinking more fluids
than usual.

Skin: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Atrial fibrillation diagnosed 6 mo ago, not taking anticoagulation drugs after
informed discussion with cardiologist.

Surgical history: None

Medications: Avanafil 100 mg as needed; aspirin 325 mg daily.

Family history: His father died from prostate cancer at age 78.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

does urinate, he has to strain to initiate a stream and that his stream is "not like it was when he
