baseline_protocol:
Age: 70 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive nocturia over several years, increasing from 2 to 6 times per night, with straining to initiate the urinary stream and a weakened stream, without daytime frequency, incontinence, dysuria, hematuria, flank pain, or fever.
Analysis: The presentation is that of lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia with bladder outlet obstruction. The strongest supporting facts are the combination of voiding (obstructive) symptoms, namely straining to initiate the stream and a weak stream, together with the storage symptom of nocturia, in a 70-year-old man, and the digital rectal examination finding of an approximately 70-gram prostate that is smooth, non-tender, with no identifiable central sulcus and no nodules. Marked prostatic enlargement with obliteration of the median sulcus but a smooth, symmetric, non-nodular texture is characteristic of benign hyperplasia rather than malignancy. The very gradual progression over several years is also typical of benign prostatic hyperplasia. The workup already performed narrows the differential considerably. Urinalysis and urine culture are entirely negative for blood, glucose, ketones, bilirubin, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, protein, and bacteria, which excludes urinary tract infection and prostatitis as a cause of the symptoms, excludes hematuria that would prompt evaluation for bladder malignancy or stone disease, and importantly excludes glycosuria, so diabetes mellitus with osmotic diuresis is very unlikely; this is reinforced by the history that he is not drinking more fluids than usual, has no polydipsia or polyuria during the day, and has a normal BMI of 22.3 with no weight change. The serum PSA of 3.2 ng/mL is not markedly elevated and, in the context of a 70-gram gland, is broadly consistent with the volume of benign tissue, but it cannot be dismissed given his family history of a father who died of prostate cancer at 78, which raises his personal risk. Prostate cancer therefore remains a differential consideration that requires structured discussion and follow-up rather than outright exclusion, even though the gland is smooth and non-nodular without focal abnormality. Other differential considerations include nocturnal polyuria, which is common at this age and would be identified by a voiding diary showing a high proportion of 24-hour urine volume produced at night; congestive heart failure with nocturnal mobilization of peripheral edema, which is not supported here as he denies chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea, exercises daily, has no lower-extremity edema described, and has clear breath sounds; obstructive sleep apnea, which can drive nocturia; overactive bladder or detrusor overactivity, which usually produces urgency and daytime frequency, both absent here since he explicitly is not urinating more during the day; urethral stricture, which can cause a weak straining stream but is less likely without instrumentation or trauma history and in the presence of a clearly enlarged gland; and neurogenic bladder, unsupported by an unremarkable neurological examination. Two features of his history bear directly on treatment selection. First, he has atrial fibrillation, present on examination as an irregularly irregular heart rate, and is on aspirin 325 mg daily without anticoagulation after informed discussion with his cardiologist; the antiplatelet therapy is relevant to bleeding risk if prostate biopsy or surgery is contemplated, and his rate and rhythm control and stroke risk warrant ongoing cardiology review. Second, he takes avanafil as needed, a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, which is a clinically important interaction with alpha-blocker therapy because the combination can cause symptomatic hypotension. There is no evidence of complicated obstruction: he denies incontinence and there is no palpable bladder or suprapubic tenderness, no costovertebral angle tenderness, and no signs of retention or upper tract involvement.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: International Prostate Symptom Score questionnaire with a bother score to quantify symptom severity and guide treatment. A 24-hour frequency-volume voiding diary over at least three days to distinguish nocturnal polyuria from bladder outlet obstruction as the driver of the nocturia. Post-void residual urine measurement by bladder ultrasound to assess for incomplete emptying and retention. Serum creatinine and basic metabolic panel to assess renal function given long-standing outlet obstruction. Fasting glucose or HbA1c is reasonable as a screen given his age, although glycosuria is absent. Uroflowmetry to objectively document the reduced peak flow rate. Transrectal or abdominal prostate ultrasound to document prostate volume if surgical or size-dependent medical therapy is considered. Referral to urology for assessment of the 70-gram gland and shared decision-making about prostate cancer screening, with age-adjusted PSA interpretation, PSA density accounting for gland volume, and repeat PSA to establish velocity; multiparametric prostate MRI and prostate biopsy only if that assessment indicates concern. Electrocardiogram to document the atrial fibrillation and rate.
Conclusion: A 70-year-old man with several years of progressively worsening lower urinary tract symptoms, predominantly nocturia rising to 6 times per night with hesitancy, straining, and a weak stream, in the setting of a markedly enlarged 70-gram prostate that is smooth and non-nodular on digital rectal examination. The picture is that of benign prostatic hyperplasia with bladder outlet obstruction. Infection, hematuria, and diabetes are excluded by a normal urinalysis and culture, and the PSA of 3.2 ng/mL is not alarming for the gland size but requires follow-up given a paternal history of fatal prostate cancer. The condition is bothersome and quality-of-life limiting but not an emergency; management should proceed with outpatient quantification of symptoms, assessment of post-void residual and renal function, and stepwise medical therapy chosen with attention to his concurrent avanafil use and aspirin therapy.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Begin with objective quantification: have him complete an International Prostate Symptom Score and a three-day frequency-volume voiding diary, and obtain a post-void residual measurement, uroflowmetry, and serum creatinine. The voiding diary is especially important here because nocturia of 6 times per night without daytime frequency raises the possibility of nocturnal polyuria contributing alongside outlet obstruction, and the two require different treatments. Institute behavioural and lifestyle measures first: restrict fluid intake in the evening, in particular the daily glass of wine and any caffeine after the late afternoon; complete voiding by double voiding; time any diuretic-like intake earlier in the day; and elevate the legs in the late afternoon if any dependent fluid accumulation is present. For medical therapy, given a prostate estimated at 70 grams, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor such as finasteride or dutasteride is a rational choice because gland volume above about 30 to 40 grams predicts benefit, with the caveat that symptomatic improvement takes six months and that this class approximately halves the serum PSA, so his baseline PSA of 3.2 must be recorded now and subsequent values doubled for interpretation. If an alpha-blocker is added or used for faster symptom relief, counsel him explicitly about the interaction with avanafil: he must separate the doses and be warned about symptomatic hypotension, dizziness, and syncope, and a uroselective agent such as tamsulosin or silodosin is preferable; alternatively, tadalafil daily can treat both his lower urinary tract symptoms and erectile dysfunction, but it must not be combined with another phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, so avanafil would need to be stopped if this route is chosen. Advise him to avoid over-the-counter antihistamines and decongestants, which can precipitate acute urinary retention in a man with this degree of obstruction. Refer to urology for ongoing management and for shared decision-making on prostate cancer screening: his father died of prostate cancer at 78, which increases his risk and justifies a deliberate discussion of continued PSA surveillance with a repeat level to establish velocity and interpretation adjusted for his large gland volume, rather than either ignoring the value or proceeding directly to biopsy on a PSA of 3.2 with a benign-feeling gland. Should surgical management such as transurethral resection or a size-appropriate alternative eventually be indicated for a 70-gram gland, his aspirin 325 mg daily and atrial fibrillation must be factored into perioperative bleeding and cardiac risk planning in coordination with cardiology, and his decision, made with his cardiologist, to forgo anticoagulation should be revisited periodically as part of routine stroke risk assessment. Regarding his other history, he has not seen a physician in several years, so this visit is an appropriate opportunity to confirm blood pressure control, review the atrial fibrillation with an electrocardiogram and cardiology follow-up, and update age-appropriate preventive care; his recent sailing trip to the western Caribbean, daily wine, and stable weight are not contributory to the urinary complaint and require no specific action beyond routine counselling on alcohol intake. Advise him to seek urgent care if he becomes unable to pass urine at all, develops suprapubic pain with a distended bladder, fever, flank pain, visible blood in the urine, or new incontinence, as these would indicate acute retention or a complication requiring immediate attention.
Notes: The 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors approximately halve serum PSA, so the current baseline value must be documented and future results interpreted accordingly to avoid masking a rising PSA. Alpha-blockers combined with his avanafil carry a real risk of symptomatic hypotension and require explicit counselling. A PSA of 3.2 ng/mL in a man with a 70-gram gland does not by itself indicate malignancy, but his positive family history means prostate cancer cannot be dismissed and requires structured follow-up rather than reassurance alone. His decision not to take anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation was made with his cardiologist and is documented here for completeness; it is relevant to any future procedural planning.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 65 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Brought to the emergency department by neighbors for lethargy and confusion after an intentional overdose of several of his medications in a suicide attempt, with an empty oxycodone bottle found at the scene, followed by recurrent deterioration into profound bradycardia and hypotension.
Analysis: This is a mixed-agent intentional overdose in a suicidal patient, with two distinct toxicological processes unfolding in sequence. The first is opioid toxicity, established by the empty oxycodone pill bottle found beside him, pinpoint pupils noted by emergency medical services, depressed mental status, a documented history of chronic pain treated with oxycodone, a urine toxicology screen positive for opioids, and, most convincingly, the prompt improvement in mental status after naloxone 0.4 mg intravenously. That therapeutic response confirms opioid contribution. The second and now dominant process is a non-opioid cardiotoxic ingestion causing bradycardia and hypotension. This is the critical reasoning point: after initial improvement, the patient again became extremely lethargic and developed a heart rate of 30, blood pressure of 74/52, and respirations of 10, yet his pupils remained equal and reactive rather than reverting to pinpoint. Persistent normal reactive pupils argue strongly against pure recurrent opioid toxicity as the explanation for this deterioration and point instead to a second agent. His stated ingestion of "several of his medications" and his documented medication list make the culprit identifiable by exclusion: he takes three antihypertensive drugs, and beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker overdose is the classic cause of refractory bradycardia with hypotension in this setting. The bedside glucose of 68 mg/dL, which is low-normal to hypoglycemic, further supports beta-blocker toxicity, since beta-blockade impairs glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and characteristically produces hypoglycemia, whereas calcium channel blocker overdose more typically causes hyperglycemia. Even at the initial examination, before the acute deterioration, he was already bradycardic at 45 beats per minute with a borderline blood pressure of 99/72, indicating the cardiotoxic agent was active from the outset and progressing. Other differential considerations are systematically excluded by the test results: acetaminophen and salicylate levels are undetectable, so co-ingestion of these very common overdose agents is ruled out; the digoxin level is 0, excluding digoxin toxicity as a cause of bradycardia; TSH is 2.0 mcIU/mL, excluding myxedema as a cause of bradycardia and altered mental status; and electrolytes are entirely normal with sodium 138, potassium 4.0, chloride 100, and bicarbonate 24, excluding hyperkalemia and a significant metabolic acidosis or anion gap disturbance. Structural neurological catastrophe is unlikely given the fully intact neurological examination at presentation with intact cranial nerves 2 to 12, normal sensation, negative pronator drift, intact finger-to-nose, normal gait, normal speech and cognition, and no evidence of head trauma. His antidepressant is of unknown class and remains a concern, since tricyclic antidepressant overdose can cause cardiotoxicity, though it characteristically produces tachycardia with QRS widening rather than profound bradycardia; the rhythm strip obtained is essential to characterize the conduction abnormality and distinguish sinus bradycardia from high-grade atrioventricular block or a wide-complex rhythm. His unknown lipid-lowering drug is unlikely to contribute acutely. Alcohol is a relevant co-factor given 2 to 3 beers daily, and the urine screen was also positive for marijuana, which is not clinically significant here. Psychiatrically, this is a high-risk deliberate self-harm event: he explicitly states he wanted to die, has a flat affect, describes depressed mood and ongoing suicidal ideation, and carries multiple risk factors including male sex, age over 65, divorce, social isolation, disability from chronic pain, daily alcohol use, access to lethal means in the form of opioids and cardiac medications, and a diagnosis of depression. The lethality and planning of the act, combined with persisting suicidal ideation, make this a serious attempt requiring one-to-one observation and psychiatric admission after medical stabilization.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring and interpretation of the obtained rhythm strip, with a twelve-lead electrocardiogram to define rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, and QTc, which is critical for distinguishing beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker, and tricyclic antidepressant toxicity. Continuous pulse oximetry, capnography, and frequent or invasive blood pressure monitoring. Serial bedside glucose measurements, given the value of 68 mg/dL. Arterial or venous blood gas with lactate to assess perfusion and acid-base status. Complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, serum calcium, magnesium, and phosphate. Serum ethanol level. Serum acetaminophen and salicylate have already returned undetectable and need no repetition. Bedside echocardiography to assess cardiac contractility and guide inotropic and vasopressor therapy. Chest radiograph. Identification of the actual medications ingested by obtaining the patient's pharmacy records, medication list, and pill bottles from home, and a pill count if possible, since the specific antihypertensive and antidepressant agents are currently unknown and this is the single most important missing piece of information. Urgent consultation with medical toxicology or poison control. Formal psychiatric risk assessment once medically stabilized.
Conclusion: A 65-year-old man with an intentional polypharmacy overdose in a suicide attempt, comprising confirmed opioid toxicity from oxycodone that responded to naloxone, and a superimposed and now predominant cardiotoxic ingestion producing profound bradycardia at 30 beats per minute with hypotension at 74/52 and hypoglycemia at 68 mg/dL, most consistent with beta-blocker toxicity from one of his three antihypertensive medications, with calcium channel blocker overdose the principal alternative. Digoxin toxicity, hypothyroidism, electrolyte derangement, and acetaminophen and salicylate co-ingestion are excluded by laboratory results. He is hemodynamically unstable and requires immediate resuscitation, antidotal therapy, and intensive care admission, followed by inpatient psychiatric care for a high-lethality suicide attempt with ongoing suicidal ideation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Resuscitate immediately and treat the cardiotoxic ingestion as the priority. Secure the airway with a low threshold for intubation, since he is now only withdrawing to deep pain and his respiratory rate has fallen to 10; although he is currently protecting his airway, further deterioration is likely. Establish two large-bore intravenous lines, place him on continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator pads available, and give an intravenous crystalloid bolus for the hypotension with careful reassessment for pulmonary congestion. Treat the hypoglycemia of 68 mg/dL with intravenous dextrose and check glucose serially, since beta-blocker toxicity causes recurrent hypoglycemia. For the bradycardia and hypotension, give atropine as an initial measure recognizing it is often ineffective in beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker poisoning, then proceed rapidly to high-dose glucagon as the specific antidote for beta-blocker toxicity, followed by intravenous calcium salts and high-dose insulin euglycemic therapy with concurrent dextrose, which is the mainstay for both beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker cardiotoxicity; add vasopressors such as norepinephrine or epinephrine for refractory hypotension, and consider transcutaneous or transvenous pacing and intravenous lipid emulsion therapy for refractory cases, with extracorporeal life support as the final option. Consult medical toxicology or poison control urgently to guide this sequence. Continue to manage the opioid component with repeat naloxone as required, and because oxycodone has a longer duration of action than naloxone, start a naloxone infusion or give repeated doses, titrating to adequate respiration rather than full arousal to avoid precipitating withdrawal in a chronic opioid user; be aware that resedation is expected. If the electrocardiogram shows QRS widening, treat with intravenous sodium bicarbonate for possible tricyclic antidepressant toxicity given his unknown antidepressant. Do not administer activated charcoal to a patient with a depressed level of consciousness unless the airway is first secured. Address the additional considerations directly. First, the exact identity of the ingested medications is unknown and is essential: obtain the pharmacy record and medication list, contact family, and retrieve the pill bottles from the home to determine which antihypertensive and which antidepressant he takes, as this changes the antidotal strategy. Second, resedation and delayed toxicity must be anticipated; sustained-release cardiac medications can cause deterioration many hours after ingestion, so he requires prolonged intensive care monitoring rather than short-term observation, and the fact that he already deteriorated once after apparent improvement demonstrates this risk. Third, institute immediate suicide precautions: continuous one-to-one observation, removal of all personal belongings and potential means of self-harm, and a search of belongings; he has stated a wish to die and continues to express suicidal ideation with a flat affect. Arrange urgent psychiatric consultation with formal risk assessment and plan for involuntary psychiatric admission if he attempts to leave or refuses care, and assess his capacity accordingly. Fourth, once medically stable, coordinate longitudinal care: treatment of his depression with appropriate follow-up, restriction of access to lethal means with limited quantities dispensed and a safe medication storage plan, review of his chronic back pain management with reconsideration of high-risk opioid therapy and referral to a pain service for non-opioid alternatives, assessment and counselling for his daily alcohol use of 2 to 3 beers which increases both depression and overdose risk, and mobilization of social support given that he is divorced, lives alone, is on disability, and was found only because neighbors noticed his condition. Fifth, on medical follow-up, his three antihypertensive medications and hypercholesterolemia will need to be reviewed and safely restarted at an appropriate time, and his blood pressure was described as only moderately controlled.
Notes: The persistence of equal and reactive pupils during the second deterioration is the key finding indicating that recurrent bradycardia and hypotension are not due to opioid effect alone and mandate a search for a second cardiotoxic agent. The specific antihypertensive and antidepressant agents ingested are unknown, which limits definitive antidotal targeting and makes medication identification urgent. Atropine is frequently ineffective in beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker overdose and its failure should prompt immediate escalation rather than repeated dosing. Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than oxycodone, so resedation should be expected and monitored for. The rhythm strip referenced in the case was not available for interpretation in this protocol, and its findings should be incorporated into management as soon as reviewed. Psychiatric evaluation must not be deferred, but medical stabilization takes precedence and psychiatric disposition should follow it.

His antidepressant is of unknown class and remains a concern, since tricyclic antidepressant overdose can cause cardiotoxicity, though it characteristically produces tachycardia with QRS widening rather than profound bradycardia; the rhythm strip obtained is essential to characterize the conduction abnormality and distinguish sinus bradycardia from high-grade atrioventricular block or a wide-complex rhythm. His unknown lipid-lowering drug is unlikely to contribute acutely. Alcohol is a relevant co-factor given 2 to 3 beers daily, and the urine screen was also positive for marijuana, which is not clinically significant here. Psychiatrically, this is a high-risk deliberate self-harm event: he explicitly states he wanted to die, has a flat affect, describes depressed mood and ongoing suicidal ideation, and carries multiple risk factors including male sex, age over 65, divorce, social isolation, disability from chronic pain, daily alcohol use, access to lethal means in the form of opioids and cardiac medications, and a diagnosis of depression. Continuous pulse oximetry, capnography, and frequent or invasive blood pressure monitoring. Serial bedside glucose measurements, given the value of 68 mg/dL. Arterial or venous blood gas with lactate to assess perfusion and acid-base status. Complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, serum calcium, magnesium, and phosphate. Serum ethanol level. Serum acetaminophen and salicylate have already returned undetectable and need no repetition. Bedside echocardiography to assess cardiac contractility and guide inotropic and vasopressor therapy. Chest radiograph. Identification of the actual medications ingested by obtaining the patient's pharmacy records, medication list, and pill bottles from home, and a pill count if possible, since the specific antihypertensive and antidepressant agents are currently unknown and this is the single most important missing piece of information. Urgent consultation with medical toxicology or poison control. Formal psychiatric risk assessment once medically stabilized.

Digoxin toxicity, hypothyroidism, electrolyte derangement, and acetaminophen and salicylate co-ingestion are excluded by laboratory results. He is hemodynamically unstable and requires immediate resuscitation, antidotal therapy, and intensive care admission, followed by inpatient psychiatric care for a high-lethality suicide attempt with ongoing suicidal ideation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Resuscitate immediately and treat the cardiotoxic ingestion as the priority. Secure the airway with a low threshold for intubation, since he is now only withdrawing to deep pain and his respiratory rate has fallen to 10; although he is currently protecting his airway, further deterioration is likely. Establish two large-bore intravenous lines, place him on continuous cardiac monitoring with defibrillator pads available, and give an intravenous crystalloid bolus for the hypotension with careful reassessment for pulmonary congestion. Treat the hypoglycemia of 68 mg/dL with intravenous dextrose and check glucose serially, since beta-blocker toxicity causes recurrent hypoglycemia. For the bradycardia and hypotension, give atropine as an initial measure recognizing it is often ineffective in beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker poisoning, then proceed rapidly to high-dose glucagon as the specific antidote for beta-blocker toxicity, followed by intravenous calcium salts and high-dose insulin euglycemic therapy with concurrent dextrose, which is the mainstay for both beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker cardiotoxicity; add vasopressors such as norepinephrine or epinephrine for refractory hypotension, and consider transcutaneous or transvenous pacing and intravenous lipid emulsion therapy for refractory cases, with extracorporeal life support as the final option. Consult medical toxicology or poison control urgently to guide this sequence. Continue to manage the opioid component with repeat naloxone as required, and because oxycodone has a longer duration of action than naloxone, start a naloxone infusion or give repeated doses, titrating to adequate respiration rather than full arousal to avoid precipitating withdrawal in a chronic opioid user; be aware that resedation is expected. If the electrocardiogram shows QRS widening, treat with intravenous sodium bicarbonate for possible tricyclic antidepressant toxicity given his unknown antidepressant. Do not administer activated charcoal to a patient with a depressed level of consciousness unless the airway is first secured. Address the additional considerations directly. First, the exact identity of the ingested medications is unknown and is essential: obtain the pharmacy record and medication list, contact family, and retrieve the pill bottles from the home to determine which antihypertensive and which antidepressant he takes, as this changes the antidotal strategy. Second, resedation and delayed toxicity must be anticipated; sustained-release cardiac medications can cause deterioration many hours after ingestion, so he requires prolonged intensive care monitoring rather than short-term observation, and the fact that he already deteriorated once after apparent improvement demonstrates this risk. Third, institute immediate suicide precautions: continuous one-to-one observation, removal of all personal belongings and potential means of self-harm, and a search of belongings; he has stated a wish to die and continues to express suicidal ideation with a flat affect. Arrange urgent psychiatric consultation with formal risk assessment and plan for involuntary psychiatric admission if he attempts to leave or refuses care, and assess his capacity accordingly. Fourth, once medically stable, coordinate longitudinal care: treatment of his depression with appropriate follow-up, restriction of access to lethal means with limited quantities dispensed and a safe medication storage plan, review of his chronic back pain management with reconsideration of high-risk opioid therapy and referral to a pain service for non-opioid alternatives, assessment and counselling for his daily alcohol use of 2 to 3 beers which increases both depression and overdose risk, and mobilization of social support given that he is divorced, lives alone, is on disability, and was found only because neighbors noticed his condition. Fifth, on medical follow-up, his three antihypertensive medications and hypercholesterolemia will need to be reviewed and safely restarted at an appropriate time, and his blood pressure was described as only moderately controlled.
Notes: The persistence of equal and reactive pupils during the second deterioration is the key finding indicating that recurrent bradycardia and hypotension are not due to opioid effect alone and mandate a search for a second cardiotoxic agent. The specific antihypertensive and antidepressant agents ingested are unknown, which limits definitive antidotal targeting and makes medication identification urgent. Atropine is frequently ineffective in beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker overdose and its failure should prompt immediate escalation rather than repeated dosing. Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than oxycodone, so resedation should be expected and monitored for. The rhythm strip referenced in the case was not available for interpretation in this protocol, and its findings should be incorporated into management as soon as reviewed. Psychiatric evaluation must not be deferred, but medical stabilization takes precedence and psychiatric disposition should follow it.

The pain is constant, radiates to her right scapula, and is associated with nausea and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. She has had intermittent postprandial bloating and epigastric discomfort over the past year that she attributed to indigestion. She denies jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, heart rate 92, blood pressure 130/84. On examination, she is moderately uncomfortable. There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest during palpation of the RUQ). There is no rebound tenderness, rigidity, or palpable mass. baseline_protocol:
Age: 38 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of worsening constant right upper quadrant pain that began after eating fried chicken, radiating to the right scapula, with nausea and two episodes of nonbilious vomiting. Background of intermittent postprandial bloating and epigastric discomfort over the past year attributed to indigestion.
Analysis: The presentation is that of acute calculous cholecystitis. The strongest supporting facts are the fatty-meal-triggered onset, pain that is constant (rather than the self-limited colicky pain of biliary colic) and lasting more than 48 hours, radiation to the right scapula, nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever of 100.4 F with mild tachycardia at 92, and a positive clinical Murphy sign on right upper quadrant palpation. Ultrasound confirms the diagnosis: gallstones in a distended gallbladder, gallbladder wall thickening to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign. This constellation of imaging findings plus focal tenderness satisfies the criteria for acute cholecystitis with high confidence. The prior year of postprandial bloating and epigastric discomfort represents antecedent symptomatic cholelithiasis, indicating chronic disease that has now progressed to an acute inflammatory episode. Important differential considerations are addressed by the case data: choledocholithiasis and ascending cholangitis are unlikely because she denies jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools, and the common bile duct measures a normal 4 mm, arguing against biliary obstruction; there is no documented Charcot triad beyond low-grade fever with local rather than systemic features. Acute pancreatitis remains a consideration given gallstone disease, but the pain is right upper quadrant with scapular radiation rather than epigastric with band-like radiation to the back. Peptic ulcer disease and gastroesophageal reflux could explain the year of epigastric discomfort but do not explain the sonographic findings. Perforation or gangrenous cholecystitis is not supported: there is no rebound tenderness, no rigidity, and no palpable mass, and hemodynamics are stable at 130/84. Hepatitis and right lower lobe pneumonia are not supported by any finding in the case. The absence of peritoneal signs and of hemodynamic instability places this as uncomplicated acute cholecystitis, but it is nonetheless an acute surgical inflammatory process that will not resolve without intervention and carries risk of progression to empyema, gangrene, or perforation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count with differential to quantify leukocytosis; comprehensive metabolic panel including total and direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, ALT and AST to exclude occult biliary obstruction or hepatocellular injury; serum lipase or amylase to exclude concurrent gallstone pancreatitis; C-reactive protein as an inflammatory marker; coagulation studies, type and screen, and basic preoperative workup including electrocardiogram in view of planned cholecystectomy; blood cultures if fever escalates. Right upper quadrant ultrasound has already been performed and is diagnostic, so no further imaging is required at this point; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound would be indicated only if liver enzymes or bilirubin become abnormal or the common bile duct enlarges on repeat assessment.
Conclusion: Acute calculous cholecystitis in a 38-year-old obese woman with a one-year history of symptomatic cholelithiasis, confirmed by clinical and sonographic Murphy sign, gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening to 5 mm, and pericholecystic fluid, without clinical or sonographic evidence of common bile duct obstruction (CBD 4 mm, no jaundice) and without peritoneal signs or hemodynamic compromise. This is an acute surgical condition requiring prompt hospital admission and, in the absence of contraindications, early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Admit to hospital under surgical care. Keep the patient nil per os and begin intravenous crystalloid fluid resuscitation to correct losses from vomiting and reduced intake. Provide analgesia with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent or an opioid as needed, and antiemetics for the nausea and vomiting. Start empiric intravenous antibiotics covering enteric gram-negative organisms and anaerobes, given the fever of 100.4 F and pericholecystic fluid. Obtain the laboratory studies listed above, including liver chemistries and lipase, to confirm the absence of ductal obstruction and pancreatitis. Arrange urgent surgical consultation with the goal of early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission, which is preferred over delayed surgery given symptoms of only two days duration. Monitor vital signs, urine output, and abdominal examination serially for signs of progression such as rising fever, tachycardia, peritonitis, or a developing mass, which would indicate gangrenous or perforated cholecystitis. Explicitly addressing the additional considerations: because the common bile duct is 4 mm and there is no jaundice, dark urine, or pale stool, preoperative ERCP or MRCP is not indicated now, but liver chemistries should be checked and the duct reassessed intraoperatively or by cholangiography if enzymes rise; if the patient proves to be a poor operative candidate or fails to improve on medical therapy, percutaneous cholecystostomy drainage is the fallback option. Counsel the patient that her one-year history of postprandial symptoms reflected gallstone disease and that definitive cholecystectomy is required to prevent recurrence and further complications. Address obesity as a modifiable risk factor with structured weight management after recovery, advising gradual rather than rapid weight loss since rapid loss itself promotes gallstone formation. Provide a low-fat diet after resumption of oral intake. Give clear return precautions for fever, jaundice, worsening pain, or vomiting after discharge.
Notes: Fever is low grade at 100.4 F and hemodynamics are stable, so there is no evidence of sepsis or cholangitis in the data provided. White blood cell count, liver chemistries, and lipase values are not specified in the case and must be obtained before final risk stratification and operative planning. Pregnancy status, current medications, allergies, and comorbidities are not specified and should be established prior to surgery.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 32 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Painless vaginal bleeding at 36 weeks gestation (G3P1011), starting as brown discharge in the morning and progressing to dark red blood, without abdominal pain, cramping, fluid leakage, or trauma, with normal fetal movement. One hour after arrival she developed irregular cramping and contractions, passed approximately 50 cc of bright red blood, and her fetal tracing deteriorated.
Analysis: The initial presentation of painless third-trimester vaginal bleeding raises the classic differential of placenta previa, placental abruption, vasa previa, bloody show from early labor, and local cervical or vaginal sources. Placenta previa is excluded by ultrasonography showing a fundal placenta with margins clear of the cervical os, which is also what makes a subsequent internal examination safe. Vasa previa is not supported: the membranes are intact with no reported rupture, the amniotic fluid index is normal at 15.7 cm, and the initial fetal heart tracing was reactive at 150 beats per minute. Uterine rupture is very unlikely given no prior uterine surgery, a prior uncomplicated vaginal delivery, no surgical history, no trauma, and a nontender uterus of normal tone at presentation. A maternal bleeding disorder is excluded by a normal platelet count of 238,000, normal PT/PTT, fibrinogen of 402 mg/dL, no personal or family bleeding history, and no petechiae or ecchymoses. The negative Kleihauer-Betke test does not exclude abruption, as it has poor sensitivity for that diagnosis. The decisive change is the reassessment one hour later. Uterine irritability with contractions, a further 50 cc of bright red blood, and, most importantly, a fetal heart rate tracing with overall minimal variability, periods of absent variability, and recurrent late decelerations together indicate uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal compromise. Recurrent late decelerations with minimal to absent variability constitute a Category III or near-Category III tracing and signal fetal hypoxia and acidemia. In the setting of vaginal bleeding with a normally located fundal placenta, ongoing bleeding, uterine irritability, and this tracing, the working diagnosis is placental abruption. Concealed abruption is consistent with the modest amount of visible blood, since revealed bleeding underestimates true blood loss; the scanty visible bleeding from the cervix on internal examination despite an abnormal tracing supports concealment. Ultrasonography is insensitive for abruption and its failure to show a retroplacental clot does not exclude the diagnosis. Cigarette smoking, which she continues at 2 cigarettes per day, is an established risk factor for abruption. The hemoglobin of 10.9 g/dL and the mild tachycardia are consistent with early blood loss superimposed on physiologic dilution of pregnancy; blood pressure remains stable at 127/81 and there are no maternal signs of shock yet, but maternal compensation in pregnancy can mask substantial loss. Age: 35 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Five days of an expanding red rash on the right thigh, noticed after a weekend camping trip two weeks ago during which he removed an engorged tick from that thigh, now accompanied by fatigue, mild headache, arthralgias of the knees and wrists, and low-grade fever.
Analysis: This is early localized Lyme disease with early systemic features, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi. The strongest supporting facts are the highly characteristic skin finding and the exposure history. The lesion is a 12 cm annular erythematous plaque with central clearing on the right anterior thigh, which is erythema migrans; a diameter well above 5 cm with central clearing and progressive expansion over 5 days is the defining feature. The patient is an avid hiker in Connecticut, a state with among the highest incidence of Lyme disease in the United States, and he recalls removing an engorged tick from the same thigh two weeks earlier. An engorged tick implies prolonged attachment, generally required for Borrelia transmission, and the two-week interval fits the typical 3 to 30 day incubation period for erythema migrans. The accompanying fatigue, mild headache, arthralgias, and low-grade fever of 99.6 F represent the viral-like constitutional syndrome that commonly accompanies early Lyme disease. Importantly, the examination systematically excludes early disseminated and late manifestations: there is only a single lesion with no secondary skin lesions, arguing against multiple erythema migrans of early dissemination; there is no cervical rigidity and the neurological examination is nonfocal with no facial weakness, arguing against Lyme meningitis or cranial neuropathy; the heart rate is regular at 74 with no murmur, and he denies chest pain and palpitations, arguing against Lyme carditis with atrioventricular block; and the joints are nontender without effusion, so the arthralgias are myalgic and constitutional rather than the frank monoarticular or oligoarticular Lyme arthritis of later disease. The main differential considerations are addressed by the case. Cellulitis is unlikely because the lesion has central clearing rather than confluent erythema, is expanding slowly over days without marked warmth, pain, or purulence, and the patient has only a low-grade fever. A local tick-bite hypersensitivity reaction is excluded because such reactions appear within 24 to 48 hours, remain small, and regress rather than expanding to 12 cm over days. Tinea corporis can be annular with central clearing but does not develop after a tick bite with systemic symptoms and a two-week evolution to 12 cm. A nummular eczema or granuloma annulare would not produce fever or follow tick exposure. Southern tick-associated rash illness is geographically implausible in Connecticut. Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses produce a petechial or maculopapular eruption often involving palms and soles rather than a single expanding annular plaque, and no secondary lesions are present here. Human granulocytic anaplasmosis and babesiosis are transmitted by the same Ixodes scapularis vector in this region and can be co-transmitted, so they remain considerations for the fever and fatigue, though the case gives no cytopenias, hemolysis, or high fever to support them. baseline_protocol:
Age: 6 weeks
Sex: Male
Complaint: Parental concern about episodes of inconsolable crying occurring most evenings, lasting 2 to 3 hours, typically beginning around 6 PM and resolving by bedtime, during which the infant draws up his knees and appears distressed. He is calm and content between episodes.
Analysis: This is infantile colic, a benign and self-limited behavioral condition of early infancy, and the case provides an unusually complete set of reassuring features. The pattern fits the classic description precisely: onset at 6 weeks of age, which lies within the typical window of onset in the first weeks of life with a peak around 6 weeks; paroxysms occurring on most evenings; a stereotyped time of day, beginning around 6 PM and resolving by bedtime, corresponding to the well-described evening clustering of colic; duration of 2 to 3 hours per episode; and complete return to a calm, content baseline between episodes. Drawing up the knees during crying is a nonspecific expression of infant distress and is not evidence of abdominal pathology. The critical diagnostic work here is the exclusion of organic causes of excessive crying, and every relevant red flag is explicitly absent. There is no fever, which argues strongly against occult infection such as urinary tract infection, meningitis, or sepsis, all of which can present as irritability in this age group. There is no vomiting, and specifically no report of bilious emesis or projectile vomiting, which makes malrotation with volvulus and hypertrophic pyloric stenosis unlikely; pyloric stenosis would in any case be expected to produce poor weight gain rather than growth along the 50th percentile. There are no bloody stools, which argues against intussusception and against cow's milk protein allergy or allergic proctocolitis; intussusception is further unlikely because it typically presents somewhat later, with episodic pain accompanied by lethargy or pallor between spells rather than a calm content baseline, and here the abdomen is soft and non-distended with normal bowel sounds and no palpable mass. Growth along the 50th percentile with good feeding is powerful evidence against gastroesophageal reflux disease, cow's milk protein intolerance, and any chronic organic illness, since these typically impair weight gain. Flat fontanelles argue against raised intracranial pressure and against dehydration. The entirely normal physical examination, with a calm alert infant, also makes non-accidental injury, corneal abrasion, hair tourniquet, incarcerated hernia, and occult fracture unlikely, although those remain items to look for on careful examination of any excessively crying infant. He is exclusively breastfed and feeding well, so underfeeding and inadequate intake are not contributors. The absence of any abnormality on examination combined with normal growth and a discrete, predictable, time-locked crying pattern with a well baby between episodes establishes colic as a diagnosis of exclusion that is confidently reached here without laboratory or imaging investigation. The principal clinical risks in this situation are not to the infant's physical health but to the family: parental exhaustion, anxiety, guilt, feelings of inadequacy, disrupted breastfeeding, postpartum depression in the mother, and, most seriously, the recognized association between inconsolable infant crying and abusive head trauma from shaking. These must be addressed proactively.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The history is classic for infantile colic, growth is normal along the 50th percentile, and the physical examination is entirely normal, so no laboratory studies, urinalysis, abdominal ultrasonography, radiographs, or other investigations are indicated at this time. Ongoing serial measurement of weight, length, and head circumference plotted on growth charts at routine well-child visits is the appropriate monitoring, and testing should be pursued only if red flags emerge.
Conclusion: A thriving 6-week-old exclusively breastfed male infant with a classic pattern of evening paroxysmal inconsolable crying, a completely normal physical examination, normal growth at the 50th percentile, and no red flags of fever, vomiting, or bloody stools. The diagnosis is infantile colic, a benign, self-limited condition that typically peaks around 6 weeks of age and resolves spontaneously by 3 to 4 months. Management is reassurance, parental support, and safety counseling rather than investigation or medication.

A 27-year-old woman with a history of moderate persistent asthma presents to the emergency room with progressive worsening of shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough over 3 days. She reports prior exposure to a person who had a runny nose and a hacking cough. She did not receive significant relief from her rescue inhaler with worsening symptoms, despite increased use. She has been compliant with her maintenance asthma regimen, which consists of an inhaled corticosteroid and a leukotriene receptor antagonist for maintenance therapy and albuterol as rescue therapy. baseline_protocol:
Age: 27 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Three days of progressively worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough in a patient with known moderate persistent asthma, unrelieved by increasingly frequent use of her albuterol rescue inhaler, with nocturnal cough disrupting sleep and causing daytime somnolence that is impairing her job performance.
Analysis: This is an acute asthma exacerbation, most plausibly triggered by a viral upper respiratory tract infection, occurring in a patient with established moderate persistent asthma who has been adherent to her controller regimen. The strongest supporting facts are the triad of dyspnea, wheeze, and cough progressing over three days; the documented antecedent exposure to a contact with rhinorrhea and a hacking cough, which identifies a plausible viral trigger and makes respiratory viral infection the most likely precipitant, since viral infections are the commonest cause of asthma exacerbations; and, most importantly, the failure of the rescue inhaler to provide significant relief despite increased use with continued worsening. Loss of bronchodilator responsiveness is a key severity marker: it indicates that airway obstruction is no longer readily reversible with beta-agonist alone and that airway inflammation and mucus plugging have become the dominant mechanism, which is precisely the situation that requires systemic corticosteroid therapy rather than escalation of inhaled bronchodilator alone. The nocturnal cough disrupting sleep is a further marker of poor control and of exacerbation severity, and the resulting daytime somnolence affecting work performance documents the functional impact. Adherence to the inhaled corticosteroid and leukotriene receptor antagonist is stated, which is clinically important because it means this deterioration is not attributable to nonadherence and represents genuine breakthrough disease requiring stepped-up therapy rather than simply reinforcement of the existing regimen; it also raises the question of whether her maintenance regimen requires long-term escalation after recovery. The main differential and alternative considerations must be weighed. Community-acquired pneumonia can present with cough and dyspnea and can itself trigger bronchospasm, but the case describes wheezing as a dominant feature with a sick contact having a runny nose and hacking cough, a pattern more suggestive of a viral illness; fever, sputum purulence, and focal findings are not specified and would need to be assessed. Acute bronchitis in an asthmatic overlaps with this presentation and is effectively the same viral trigger. Pneumothorax is a recognized complication of severe asthma and must be excluded clinically if there is sudden worsening, unilateral findings, or chest pain, none of which are reported. Pulmonary embolism should be considered in any young woman with progressive dyspnea, particularly given that oral contraceptive use, immobility, and other risk factors are not specified in the case, but the presence of wheezing, cough, a viral contact, and a known asthma diagnosis with a three-day progressive course makes exacerbation far more likely. Vocal cord dysfunction can mimic refractory asthma but would not follow this pattern of gradual progression after a viral exposure. Anaphylaxis is excluded by the subacute three-day course without urticaria, angioedema, or hypotension. Cardiac causes of dyspnea are improbable at age 27 without cardiac history. Critically, the case does not specify vital signs, oxygen saturation, peak expiratory flow, ability to speak in full sentences, use of accessory muscles, or mental status, and these are exactly the parameters that determine severity classification and disposition. She has presented to the emergency room, and the combination of progressive symptoms over three days with failure to respond to escalating rescue therapy defines at minimum a moderate to severe exacerbation warranting immediate emergency assessment and treatment. A silent chest, inability to complete sentences, drowsiness, or a normalizing or rising carbon dioxide level would indicate impending respiratory failure. Her daytime somnolence is most plausibly explained by sleep disruption from nocturnal cough, but hypercapnia and impending respiratory failure must be actively excluded before accepting that benign explanation.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous pulse oximetry and full vital signs including respiratory rate, heart rate, and blood pressure. Objective measurement of airflow obstruction with peak expiratory flow rate or FEV1, recorded before and after bronchodilator therapy and repeated serially to gauge response. Focused physical examination for air entry, wheeze, accessory muscle use, ability to speak in full sentences, and mental status. Arterial or venous blood gas analysis if there is severe distress, oxygen saturation that remains low, poor response to initial treatment, or any suspicion of hypercapnia, given the reported somnolence. Chest radiography to exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, and atelectasis, indicated here because of the febrile or infectious exposure history, the poor response to bronchodilator, and the possibility of a complicating process. Complete blood count with differential if infection is suspected. Basic metabolic panel to monitor potassium, since repeated beta-agonist administration causes hypokalemia. Electrocardiogram if there is chest pain, tachyarrhythmia, or concern for an alternative cardiopulmonary cause. Respiratory viral testing including influenza and SARS-CoV-2 as locally indicated, given the sick contact, since a positive influenza result would permit specific antiviral therapy. Equipment required includes a nebulizer or metered-dose inhaler with spacer, supplemental oxygen delivery, and cardiac monitoring capability.
Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of moderate persistent asthma in a 27-year-old woman, most likely precipitated by a viral respiratory infection acquired from a symptomatic contact, characterized by three days of progressive dyspnea, wheeze, and cough that has become refractory to increased albuterol despite full adherence to inhaled corticosteroid and leukotriene receptor antagonist maintenance therapy, with nocturnal symptoms and functional impairment. Failure of rescue bronchodilator therapy marks this as at least a moderate to severe exacerbation requiring immediate emergency department treatment with systemic corticosteroids and intensified bronchodilator therapy, objective severity assessment, and observation for progression to respiratory failure.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology
Recommendations: Treat immediately in the emergency department without waiting for test results. Administer supplemental oxygen titrated to maintain oxygen saturation in the target range of 93 to 95 percent. Give repeated or continuous inhaled short-acting beta-agonist, albuterol, by nebulizer or by metered-dose inhaler with a spacer, and add inhaled ipratropium bromide to the initial bronchodilator treatments, since combined therapy improves bronchodilation and reduces hospitalization in moderate to severe exacerbations. Administer systemic corticosteroids early, orally if she can tolerate oral intake and intravenously if she cannot; this is the single most important intervention given her documented failure to respond to bronchodilator alone, and it should not be delayed. Reassess clinically and with repeat peak flow or FEV1 after each treatment cycle to determine response. Consider intravenous magnesium sulfate if the exacerbation proves severe or refractory to initial bronchodilator and corticosteroid therapy. baseline_protocol:
Age: 26 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of dysuria (painful urination), urinary urgency, and increased urinary frequency in a newly married young woman, without fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, back pain, vaginal discharge, or vaginal pruritus.
Analysis: This presentation is characteristic of acute uncomplicated cystitis, a lower urinary tract infection, in a healthy young non-pregnant woman. The strongest supporting facts are the classic symptom triad of dysuria, urgency, and frequency of short two-day duration, and the systematic absence of features that would point elsewhere. In a woman presenting with dysuria and frequency without vaginal discharge or irritation, the probability of acute cystitis is high enough that the diagnosis can be made largely on history. The mention that she is newly wed is clinically relevant because recent increased frequency of sexual intercourse is a well-established risk factor for cystitis in young women, the classic honeymoon cystitis pattern, reflecting mechanical introduction of periurethral uropathogens, most commonly Escherichia coli, into the short female urethra. The absence of fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and back or flank pain is the critical discriminator that excludes acute pyelonephritis, which is an upper tract infection requiring more aggressive and longer therapy and sometimes hospitalization; the infection here appears confined to the bladder. The absence of vaginal discharge and vaginal pruritus argues strongly against vulvovaginitis from candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis, or trichomoniasis, which are common alternative causes of dysuria in this age group and which typically produce external or introital dysuria accompanied by discharge or itching rather than internal dysuria with urgency and frequency. Sexually transmitted urethritis from Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae remains an important differential in a sexually active 26-year-old and can produce the urethral syndrome with dysuria and pyuria but sterile urine culture; it is less likely given the abrupt two-day onset and the absence of discharge, but sexual history, number and change of partners, and partner symptoms are not specified in the case and should be elicited, and testing should be considered if there is any risk factor or if initial treatment fails. Genital herpes can cause dysuria but is typically accompanied by painful vulvar lesions, which are not reported. Interstitial cystitis and painful bladder syndrome present with chronic rather than two-day symptoms. Nephrolithiasis would be expected to cause colicky flank pain, which she denies. The infection is classified as uncomplicated because she is a young, presumably healthy, non-pregnant woman with no reported structural urinary tract abnormality, no diabetes, no immunosuppression, no indwelling catheter, no recent instrumentation, and no recurrent infection history, although these details are not explicitly given. The condition is not an emergency and there is no evidence of systemic infection or sepsis, but it does require medical evaluation and prescription antimicrobial therapy, and it will not reliably resolve with self-care alone, so it warrants prompt but non-emergent outpatient care. Untreated, cystitis can ascend to cause pyelonephritis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urinalysis, ideally on a clean-catch midstream specimen, with dipstick for leukocyte esterase and nitrite and microscopy for pyuria, bacteriuria, and hematuria, to support the diagnosis. Urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing is not strictly required for a first episode of typical uncomplicated cystitis and may be omitted when the presentation is classic, but it should be obtained if there is diagnostic uncertainty, recurrent or recent infection, failure of empiric therapy, recent antibiotic use, or any suspicion of a resistant organism. Urine pregnancy test, which is important in a newly married woman of reproductive age because pregnancy would reclassify the infection as complicated and restricts antibiotic choice. Focused physical examination including vital signs and assessment for costovertebral angle tenderness to confirm the absence of upper tract involvement, and abdominal examination for suprapubic tenderness. Pelvic examination and nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae if the sexual history indicates risk, if there are any genital symptoms or findings, or if urine testing shows pyuria without bacteriuria or the patient fails to respond to therapy. No imaging is required in an uncomplicated first episode.
Conclusion: Acute uncomplicated bacterial cystitis in a healthy 26-year-old woman, likely related to recent increased sexual activity following marriage, presenting with two days of dysuria, urgency, and frequency, without any clinical features of pyelonephritis, systemic infection, or vaginitis. The condition is benign and highly responsive to a short course of appropriate oral antibiotic therapy, but requires outpatient medical assessment, confirmation of the diagnosis with urinalysis and a pregnancy test, and prescription treatment; it is not self-limiting to a degree that would make self-care alone appropriate, and it is not an emergency.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Arrange prompt outpatient evaluation, which can be same-day or next-day in a primary care, urgent care, or women's health setting rather than an emergency department. Obtain a clean-catch midstream urinalysis and a urine pregnancy test before prescribing, and check vital signs and assess for costovertebral angle tenderness to confirm this is confined to the lower tract. baseline_protocol:
Age: 2 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Parental concern about yellowish, greasy-appearing scales on the infant's scalp present for approximately 2 weeks, thick in some areas, in an otherwise well baby who is feeding well, gaining weight appropriately, and sleeping normally, with no rash elsewhere.
Analysis: This is infantile seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, commonly called cradle cap, and the case description is textbook. The strongest supporting facts are the morphology, the distribution, the age, and the complete absence of associated illness. The lesions are adherent yellowish-white greasy scales, which is the defining appearance of seborrheic dermatitis and differs sharply from the fine dry white scale of simple xerosis or the silvery scale of psoriasis. The distribution over the anterior fontanelle and vertex of the scalp is the classic site of predilection in infants. The age of 2 months with onset roughly two weeks prior falls squarely within the typical window: infantile seborrheic dermatitis characteristically begins in the first weeks to months of life, attributed to sebaceous gland stimulation by residual transplacental maternal androgens together with colonization by Malassezia species, and it resolves spontaneously as maternal hormone effect wanes, usually by 6 to 12 months of age. Three negative findings are diagnostically decisive. First, there is no underlying erythema, which argues against inflammatory or eczematous processes and confirms this is scale rather than active dermatitis. Second, there is no oozing, no weeping, no crusting of the honey-colored type, and no pustules, which excludes secondary bacterial infection such as impetigo and excludes acute eczematous inflammation. Third, there is no involvement of the face or diaper area and no rash elsewhere on the body, which is important because more extensive seborrheic dermatitis, or seborrheic-appearing dermatitis with intertriginous and diaper involvement, would raise consideration of more serious mimics. The main differential considerations are all effectively excluded by the case data. Atopic dermatitis is the principal alternative in an infant with scalp involvement, but atopic dermatitis is intensely pruritic, produces erythema and often oozing and excoriation, favors the cheeks and extensor surfaces at this age, and typically spares the diaper area; here the infant is content, sleeping normally, and has no erythema and no lesions elsewhere, which makes atopic dermatitis very unlikely. Tinea capitis is uncommon in a 2-month-old and characteristically produces scaly patches with hair loss, broken hairs, and sometimes boggy inflammation or lymphadenopathy, none of which are described. Psoriasis produces well-demarcated plaques with thick silvery scale and usually erythema, and is rare at this age. Scabies produces intensely pruritic burrows and papulopustules involving palms, soles, and axillae in infants, with a distressed and poorly sleeping baby, which is the opposite of this presentation. Langerhans cell histiocytosis is the critical serious mimic of refractory seborrheic-looking scalp dermatitis in infancy, but it typically presents with petechial or purpuric papules, erosive and hemorrhagic scale, involvement of the postauricular and diaper areas, and systemic features such as failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy; none of these are present, and the infant is explicitly thriving. Zinc deficiency and acrodermatitis enteropathica produce periorificial and acral erosive dermatitis with diarrhea and poor growth, which are absent here. The strongest global reassurance is that the infant is content and thriving with normal feeding, weight gain, and sleep, and the scalp finding is purely cosmetic without pruritus or systemic impact. This is therefore a benign, self-limited condition that requires no investigation and no prescription treatment, and it is appropriately managed by the parents at home with simple measures and reassurance.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. The diagnosis of infantile seborrheic dermatitis is clinical and is established by the characteristic greasy yellowish adherent scale at the vertex and anterior fontanelle in a thriving 2-month-old with no erythema, no oozing, and no extrascalp involvement. No fungal culture or potassium hydroxide preparation, bacterial culture, skin biopsy, blood tests, or imaging are indicated. Routine growth monitoring at scheduled well-child visits with plotting of weight, length, and head circumference is sufficient follow-up.
Conclusion: Infantile seborrheic dermatitis, cradle cap, of the scalp vertex and anterior fontanelle in a healthy, thriving 2-month-old male infant. The condition is benign, non-infectious, non-contagious, not painful, and not itchy, and it resolves spontaneously over weeks to months, typically by 6 to 12 months of age. No investigation or prescription therapy is required; management consists of parental reassurance and gentle conservative scalp care at home, with reassessment only if the appearance changes or red flags develop.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Reassure the parents clearly that this is a very common, harmless, self-limited skin condition of early infancy, that it is not caused by poor hygiene or by anything they have done, that it is not an infection and cannot be passed to others, that it does not hurt or itch the baby, and that it will resolve on its own, usually within the first year of life. Emphasize that their son is healthy and thriving, feeding well, gaining weight appropriately, and sleeping normally, and that the finding is cosmetic. For home care, advise gentle regular washing of the scalp with a mild non-medicated baby shampoo, followed by soft brushing with a soft-bristled brush or a fine-toothed comb to loosen and lift the scale. For the areas where the scale is thick and adherent, recommend applying a small amount of an emollient such as a plain mineral or vegetable oil or petroleum jelly to the scalp, leaving it in place for a period to soften the scale, and then shampooing it out and gently combing; caution that oil left in the hair without subsequent washing can worsen scale accumulation. Instruct the parents explicitly not to pick, scratch, or forcibly remove adherent scale, since this can traumatize the skin, cause bleeding, and introduce secondary bacterial infection, and to be especially gentle over the anterior fontanelle, which is a soft area, while reassuring them that gentle washing and brushing over the fontanelle is safe. The age of 2 months with onset roughly two weeks prior falls squarely within the typical window: infantile seborrheic dermatitis characteristically begins in the first weeks to months of life, attributed to sebaceous gland stimulation by residual transplacental maternal androgens together with colonization by Malassezia species, and it resolves spontaneously as maternal hormone effect wanes, usually by 6 to 12 months of age. baseline_protocol:
Age: 30 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Two days of high fever, body aches, headache, sore throat, and dry nonproductive cough, with mild rhinorrhea and fatigue, in a woman at 28 weeks of gestation who did not receive the influenza vaccine this season. Rapid influenza antigen test is positive for influenza A.
Analysis: This is laboratory-confirmed influenza A infection in a pregnant woman in the third trimester, which is a recognized high-risk group requiring prompt antiviral treatment despite the currently mild clinical picture. The diagnosis is secure: the presentation is the classic influenza syndrome with abrupt onset over two days of high fever at 101.8 F, myalgias, headache, sore throat, dry nonproductive cough, mild rhinorrhea, and fatigue, occurring in an unvaccinated individual, and it is confirmed by a positive rapid antigen test for influenza A. A positive rapid antigen test during influenza season has high specificity, so a positive result confirms infection and no further confirmatory testing is required to begin treatment. The severity assessment is reassuring at this moment. She is not in respiratory distress, her respiratory rate is normal at 18, her oxygen saturation is 97 percent on room air, her lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with no crackles or focal findings, her blood pressure is normal at 110/68, and her heart rate of 96 is mildly elevated but consistent with fever and with the physiologic tachycardia of pregnancy. She has no signs of dehydration. Obstetric assessment is also reassuring: fundal height is consistent with gestational age, indicating no growth abnormality, and fetal heart tones are reassuring at 145 beats per minute, within the normal range. There is therefore no current evidence of influenza pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia, respiratory failure, sepsis, or fetal compromise, so hospital admission is not required and she can be managed as an outpatient. However, the pregnancy fundamentally changes the risk calculus and the urgency of treatment. Pregnant women, and particularly those in the second and third trimesters, are at substantially increased risk of severe influenza, hospitalization, intensive care admission, and death compared with non-pregnant women of the same age. This is attributable to the physiologic changes of pregnancy: reduced functional residual capacity and diaphragmatic elevation limiting pulmonary reserve, increased oxygen consumption, increased cardiac output and heart rate reducing cardiopulmonary reserve, and the shift in maternal immune function that reduces the ability to clear viral respiratory infection. Deterioration in pregnant women with influenza can be rapid, so a well-appearing patient today may become critically ill within 24 to 48 hours. There are also fetal risks: maternal hyperthermia in pregnancy is associated with adverse fetal outcomes, and maternal influenza is associated with preterm labor, preterm birth, low birth weight, and fetal loss, largely mediated through fever and maternal hypoxemia. Her lack of influenza vaccination this season explains her susceptibility and identifies a preventable exposure that must be addressed after recovery. The main differential considerations are addressed by the case data. Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia is not supported by the clear lung fields, normal respiratory rate, normal oxygen saturation, and nonproductive cough, but it remains the most important complication to watch for, as secondary bacterial pneumonia typically develops after initial improvement. COVID-19 and other viral respiratory infections can produce an identical syndrome, but the positive influenza A antigen test establishes the diagnosis, though co-infection is possible. Streptococcal pharyngitis could explain sore throat and fever but not the myalgias, cough, rhinorrhea, and positive influenza test. Pyelonephritis, a common serious infection in pregnancy, is not supported since there is no flank pain, no urinary symptoms, and a coherent respiratory syndrome. Chorioamnionitis is not supported: there is no uterine tenderness, no rupture of membranes, and fetal heart tones are normal without fetal tachycardia. The critical management principle is that antiviral treatment must be started immediately on clinical suspicion, and here on confirmed diagnosis, without delay, because benefit is greatest when initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset, and she is exactly at the two-day mark; treatment is nevertheless recommended in pregnant women even beyond 48 hours.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: The influenza diagnosis is established, so no further confirmatory virologic testing for influenza is needed. Continued monitoring of maternal vital signs including temperature, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry, and a home thermometer for the patient to track fever. Fetal assessment with fetal heart rate auscultation or nonstress testing as clinically indicated, and continued monitoring of fetal movement by the patient. SARS-CoV-2 testing should be considered given the overlapping syndrome and the possibility of co-infection. Chest radiography with abdominal shielding if she develops dyspnea, hypoxemia, tachypnea, chest pain, focal lung findings, or clinical deterioration, since the radiation dose to the fetus is negligible and the risk of missing pneumonia is far greater. Complete blood count and basic metabolic panel if she becomes dehydrated, appears toxic, or deteriorates. Group A streptococcal testing only if pharyngeal findings are prominent and atypical for influenza. No other testing is required while she remains stable.
Conclusion: Uncomplicated laboratory-confirmed influenza A infection at 28 weeks of gestation in an unvaccinated 30-year-old woman, currently without respiratory distress, hypoxemia, dehydration, pneumonia, or fetal compromise, with reassuring maternal vital signs, clear lungs, appropriate fundal height, and a normal fetal heart rate of 145 beats per minute. baseline_protocol:
Age: 22 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A single painful sore inside the mouth for the past 2 days, arising during a period of final examinations with increased stress and poor sleep.
Analysis: This is a minor recurrent aphthous ulcer, commonly called a canker sore, and the case provides both a classic positive picture and a systematic exclusion of the important alternatives. The morphology is diagnostic: a single shallow oval ulcer approximately 5 mm in diameter with a white-yellowish fibrinous base surrounded by an erythematous halo. Size under 10 mm, shallow depth, oval shape, and the yellow-white base with a red halo define the minor aphthous type, which is by far the commonest form, heals spontaneously within 7 to 14 days, and does not scar. The location on the buccal mucosa of the left cheek is characteristic, since aphthous ulcers arise on non-keratinized mobile mucosa such as the buccal and labial mucosa, the floor of the mouth, and the ventral tongue, and specifically spare the keratinized hard palate and attached gingiva. The precipitating context strongly supports the diagnosis: psychological stress and sleep deprivation during final examinations are among the best-recognized triggers of aphthous ulceration in young adults, along with local trauma, certain foods, and hormonal factors. The negative findings do the essential work of excluding serious mimics. Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis and recurrent intraoral herpes simplex are the main infectious alternatives, but herpetic lesions present as clusters of small vesicles that coalesce into multiple ulcers, typically involve keratinized mucosa such as the hard palate and gingiva, are commonly accompanied by fever, malaise, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and in the primary form produce diffuse painful gingivitis; here there is a solitary ulcer on non-keratinized mucosa, no vesicles, no fever, and no lymphadenopathy, which effectively excludes herpes. Behcet disease is excluded by the explicit denial of genital sores and joint pain and by the absence of recurrent multiple oral ulcers, ocular symptoms, or skin lesions; oral aphthae are the cardinal feature of Behcet but require accompanying systemic criteria. Inflammatory bowel disease, particularly Crohn disease, can cause oral aphthous ulceration, but he has no history of inflammatory bowel disease and no gastrointestinal symptoms are reported. Hand, foot, and mouth disease and herpangina from enteroviruses produce multiple oral lesions with fever and often characteristic acral or palatal distribution, and are excluded by the single lesion and absence of fever. Primary syphilis produces a painless indurated chancre, and the ulcer here is painful and shallow, making syphilis very unlikely. Squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity is the critical malignant consideration for any oral ulcer, but it typically presents as a chronic, indurated, non-healing ulcer with rolled everted margins, often with a history of tobacco or alcohol use, in an older patient, and would not appear acutely over two days with a soft shallow base; the 2-day duration and typical aphthous morphology in a 22-year-old make malignancy essentially excluded, though duration beyond three weeks would change this reasoning entirely. Age: 68 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: A slowly growing lesion on the nose first noticed approximately 8 months ago, which has gradually enlarged and occasionally bleeds when he washes his face before healing over, in a farmer with decades of occupational sun exposure and multiple sunburns in youth.
Analysis: This is a nodular basal cell carcinoma of the left nasal ala, and the clinical, dermoscopic, and epidemiologic evidence converge on that diagnosis with very high confidence. The morphology is textbook: a 1.2 cm pearly, dome-shaped nodule with a rolled border and central depression, with multiple telangiectasias visible on the surface. Pearly translucency, a rolled or everted pearly rim, central ulceration or depression, and surface telangiectasias together constitute the classic description of nodular basal cell carcinoma. The natural history is also characteristic: slow growth over 8 months, with intermittent bleeding on minor trauma such as washing the face followed by apparent healing and then recurrence, a pattern often described as a sore that will not heal and one of the most reliable historical clues to a cutaneous malignancy. The dermoscopic findings are effectively confirmatory. Arborizing vessels, which are large-caliber branching telangiectatic vessels in sharp focus at the lesion surface, are the single most specific dermoscopic criterion for basal cell carcinoma, and blue-gray ovoid nests are a pigmented-basal-cell-carcinoma criterion; the presence of these criteria in the absence of a pigment network essentially establishes the diagnosis dermoscopically. The risk factor profile is entirely consistent: age 68, male sex, extensive cumulative and intermittent ultraviolet exposure from decades of outdoor farm work, and multiple sunburns in youth. The surrounding field shows significant solar damage with actinic keratoses on the forehead and ears, confirming chronic photodamage and indicating field cancerization, which carries a substantial risk of further keratinocyte carcinomas and of squamous cell carcinoma arising from the actinic keratoses.
